I've played this 2.5 years after the initial release. By this time all the famous bugs have been fixed and I haven't experienced any crashes. Instead, the game ran very smoothly on highest possible settings.
One issue I have experienced was that my graphics settings have changed mid-game on their own from a Borderless Window to Fullscreen mode. But it only happened once.
The controls seem improved from the previous games, but it still happened that Arno jumped somewhere I didn't want him to jump. But the "falling" mechanics have been improved - it is now more difficult to just fall down to your doom. Getting down from buildings is now more smooth, implementing the parkour mechanics.
I've completed the game two days ago and by today I already don't remember the music.
It was very generic, changing pace with the events on screen, but nothing that pops out.
This part of the series has slightly changed since the previous games. Some features were added, but some were taken away. One of the crucial bits that's now missing is getting the enemies attention. Previously you could whistle to lure nearby enemies. Not in this one. So cover kills only make sense on enemies that are walking directly next to your cover. I've actually had to leave cover, show myself to the enemy, wait until they started walking my way to investigate, then hide again and kill them. That takes the game-world immersion away.
A couple of times when I tried to do a ledge-kill, Arno jumped on to the ledge first to let everyone around see me, only then he grabbed the enemy and threw him over the ledge. But at that point I was out in the open.
Melting with the crowd to avoid detection is also done differently this time around, but that's not a good change in my opinion.
One thing that has improved is the option of moving down from various heights, you don't just jump down but parkour your way down.
I've also played the
that is now included as part of the main game.
I started playing this by accident - I wanted to fast-travel somewhere on the map, but instead of a standard fast-travel location I misclicked and got transported to this new location (Saint-Denis) and the DLC began. There was no way for me to come back until I've completed it. That itself has cause me some trouble.
First of all, the DLC was designed to play after the game, not mid-game. So I was weaker than expected, didn't have some skills unlocked yet. During the DLC you don't get skill points, so there was no way for me to unlock them there. But I still managed to beat it and while doing so I've earned some great, powerful weapons and also loads of money. So when I came back to the main game, I was strong and rich, which then made the second part of the main game too easy.
There was a silly bug in some of the cutscenes - my weapon of choice was a Guillotine Gun - a very powerful mortar with an axe attached to it. So I was fighting with that, killing anyone who came too close, and then a cutscene begins, showing me with my awesome weapon attached to my back, and some lame basic sabre in my hand.
Overall the DLC was ok, a lot of running around back and forth, but also some demanding puzzles and fights. And a Guillotine Gun, of course.
Was it better than Brotherhood? No.
Was it better than Black Flag? No.
Is it a good Assassin's Creed game? Yes, absolutely.

While not being a great game, it isn’t a complete waste, nor as bad as people make it out to be.
The bad:
-A completely boring, badly written story, that is completely throwaway, but thankfully doesn’t hinder you too often or too much.
-Some enemies can be annoying beyond belief, mostly the flying ones and enemies you need to shoot with a special power.
-A lot of throwaway attacks.
-Repetitive. Slashing and shooting enemies from start to finish.
-Below average boss fights that aren’t always explained well.
The good:
-Gameplay is decently fun, and it feels relatively good.
-Graphics aren’t overly high-fidelity, but they still have a nice cartoonish look for them and are appealing to the eyes.
-And yes, the main protagonist’s looks will probably carry this game for a lot of people.
So taking everything in account, the game is nowhere as bad as people often make it out to be. Is it repetitive? Yes, very. Does it have huge mechanical faults? Yes, and you will notice them immediately if you have played any better games of this type. But if you just want a mediocre hack-and-slash with little variety and can ignore some faults and the absence of a proper story, the gameplay and its protagonist (as well as her behind) might be enough to keep you invested and entertained. If you can’t overlook some of those bigger faults, and solid gameplay and aesthetics aren’t enough to convince you to spend money on it, you might want to give it a pass. Otherwise, this is a solid little time-sinker for fans of the genre which I recommend buying at any sale.

Starbound. It's a game where you build and travel through space. But that's not all that this game has to offer, oh no. not even close. I have put well over 200 hours into this game just in singleplayer alone, and the more you play, the better it gets at every turn.

The game starts you off in a defunct spaceship, stranded in orbit around a distant planet fleeing from persecution, hatred, genocide... it really differs for each race, and ultimately it's up to you to make the decision of what to do from the start. Do you stay on this planet and build a new home or travel the stars in a galaxy spanning adventure? Decisions like these make your journey memorable, and the feelings this game enduces while traversing the unknown is hard to produce from a pixel-based voxel building game. But it does. I can honestly say this game can really envelope you into its universe, through the deep lore and plot found through questing and exploring, to the creativity you can express through all the different building options. No matter what you decide, this game will have you begging for more, searching the web to uncover secrets and hidden lore you might have missed. 		Speaking of feelings, there is one particular feeling that hits the hardest while playing this game... Loneliness. The feeling of loneliness can almost be suffocating at times, and even through all the colorful worlds and exciting soundtrack you can never really escape it. you as the player, no matter what race you pick, are an outcast trying to make their way in the universe (Except for the hylotl, because they're just being all ambassador-like.) This especially goes for the humans. Where the other races spawn colonies and villages that are generally non-aggressive unless provoked, humanity has nothing. Earth's been shattered and broken, humanity has been spread, and there really is no place for us to call home. The worst part is, while other races can always meet a friendly face of their own kind, no matter where you go, human players only come across hostile npc's of prisoners or the USCM, which by the way, are the human military. Humanity is so broken that even the people who are supposed to protect and defend us will attack the player without so much as a second thought. Truly, the human race has it the hardest in this universe.

The feeling is a bit less prevalent in the more recent versions of the game, with the inclusion of the outpost, and quests given to you by citizens stationed there, but the feeling of loneliness is still there, mixed with confusion and mystery. You as the player do not have the information necessary to truly know what's going on in the starbound universe, and instead only get glimpses of it through codex entries or exploration. This coupled with the fact that most of the galaxy wants to kill you on sight, you truly feel at odds with the universe, and that pushes the feeling of independence and the strive to beat the odds and survive in this hectic universe. To put this whole video in perspective, Starbound is a game that you need to play to truly experience the majesty it has to offer, and the feeling of wonder and adventure presented to you right off the bat.
To end this review, I give this game a rating of 10 Florans out of 10. Now just hope you don't run into 10 florans at once. (TL; DR: The game is an amazing adventure in SPAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAACE, and you should buy it right now. Throw your money at the screen.)

Bastion is one of those games you just have to fall in love with 'cause it's incredibly intriguing from the very beginning.
The story takes place in the fictional city of Caelondia and its surroundings, now fractured because of a catastrophe called the Calamity. The Calamity broke the world apart and turned nearly all its inhabitants to ash. Now, the pieces of this world float in the sky, and the Kid (the protagonist of the game) awakens on one of these pieces. He sets out to reach the Bastion, a place said to be safe in times of trouble.
One of the many things I love about Bastion is how you build the world around you by exploring it. Your path forms in front of you as you fight your way through enemies and investigate the area. This, as well as the use of vivid colors, make the world feel very lively, despite the destruction the Calamity has brought upon Caelondia.
Also, the soundtrack is amazing. Seriously, buy it, it's gold.
Bastion is labeled as an action role-playing game, but I would specify that and call it a hack-and-slay game because of its focus on combat and variety of weapons (you're welcome to disagree with that point, but I think genres to be quite squishy anyway; Bastion just feels more like a hack-and-slay game to me). There we have another thing I love about this game: you can choose from plenty of weapons and combine them any way you want.
There are 11 unique items, either melee or ranged weapons, and you can carry two at once. By default, you equip one melee and one ranged weapon, but you can replace them anytime at the Armory. You want to carry two melee weapons, for example your trusty Cael Hammer AND the War Machete? No problem. Two ranged weapons, let's say, the Scrap Musket in combination with the Breaker's Bow? Why not?
The third equipment slot is reserved for Secret Skills you find, win, or buy later in the game.
There are many more possibilities to customize your character, for example Spirits providing passive bonuses; let's just say, you can choose equipment from a REALLY great range of thingies.
My favorite thing about Bastion, though, is the narrative style. The Kid himself is silent throughout the whole game, but there is a narrator whose voice accompanies the protagonist, providing the player with background information and reacting to what he or she chooses to do.
The voice is so incredibly great; really calm but rough at the same time. It feels like it belongs to an older, experienced man who grew a little tired of all the stuff happening around him after years of turmoil - and I think that is perfect. You get the feeling that you're hanging out in a pub, and you meet an aged man who tells you stories about his life as a young adventurer. This may be the greatest thing about Bastion - that you feel like you get to know the narrator, like he personally speaks to you and no one else.
All in all, I think Bastion might be one of the most beautiful games set in a post-apocalyptic world I've ever played. The art style and soundtrack go so well with the atmosphere, and the narrative style is breathtaking. The gameplay is really fun and allows for a lot of customization. I already recommend it to anyone who's into video games, and I don't think you would regret playing it.

I'd really really like to give this game a positive review.... but, well, I'll list the pros and cons and leave it up to you.
Pros
Some intresting new toys to play with
Some intresting new baddies to shoot
Stealth mechanic is kinda intresting if extremely simple and very flawed in parts
XCOM 1 was kinda good and its based on that
Mods do improve the game a lot
New LOS on move marker on enemies is really helpful
Cons
Feels like a XCOM 1 expansion rather than a new game. Very few new mechanics really, same game, a new senario.
Far too luck based
Explosives take out cover far too easily, game is so cover dependent its silly
Poorly balanced drops.... just give everyone repeaters for insta-kill chance
Too many missions are practically impossible due to timers or enemies literally starting on the defend objective and killing it on the 2nd turn.... before you can reach it at max move speed, even rushing everyone.
Contraditory rules, game forces you to rush, then punishes you for rushing. No chance to balance the two without suffering major casualties regardless of skill level.
Practically none of the major XCOM 1 flaws addressed at all.... its basically the same game. If you don't have XCOM 1, its worth buying... otherwise, not really.
Major plot missions actually easier than a lot of minor random missions due to really bad enemy placement that basically has them all rush you at the same time.
Would be nice if it would stop crashing....
Flaws from XCOM 1 not fixed:
Soldiers are the ultimate jar-heads. Absolutely zero reaction (other than overwatch/bladestorm) to anything that happens outside their own turn
Cover mechanics are at best poor.
For a game based so heavily on movement/cover/reaction fire, the movement/Action system is far far too oversimplified.

As a big fan of Fallout in general, I like Fallout 4. Generally, I dont post reviews of products because Im lazy, but I feel inclined to do so on this occasion.
As a whole, Fallout 4 is a very well made game, with amazing graphics, gameplay and mechanics. However, as with all games Bethesda makes, you will find some glitches (floating rocks, T-posing enemies, etc.), which is part of the charm of Bethesda games (in my opinion.).
However, when compared to Fallout 3 and Fallout NV, that's where things start to fall apart a bit.
1. Unlike the previous 2 games, FO4 has it's main character voiced. While this is a good aesthetic, it sacrifices the "make your character your own" feel for a more pre-defined character.
2. There are far less actions that rely solely on the amount of SPECIAL points you have or a specific rank of a perk to accomplish something (like repairing a fuse box only if you have 9+ Intelligence). These were quite common in FO3, and FONV. After playing FO4, I think Ive only found 3 or 4 instances of similar actions throughout the game.
3. Bethesda, in their infinite wisdom, started to fight the one aspect that gives their games such longevity; modding. While this isn't extremely terrible, they made it slightly more difficult to mod FO4, and a system that prevents you from gaining achievements if you have mods installed. (There are work arounds available online to fix the first problem, and a mod that allows you to get achievements just like in Skyrim.)
4. While the phrase "It just works!" does apply to the settlement system, it only works if you play by their rules and learn how to bend said rules. (Yes, mods can also fix this.)
5. Unless you get the Season Pass for this game, DO NOT buy the workshop DLCs. They are good, but they aren't worth paying money for. I do recommend Automatron and Far Harbor if you can only afford a few of the DLCs.
In regards to the Creation Club... That is also up to your own preference to use. Personally, I am not a fan, but that should not cloud people's judgement on a perfectly good game. There is nothing on the Creation Club that does not have an equal or better counterpart available for free from whatever modding resource you prefer. The main benefit for the CC I can see is just the much more simplified installation process for the mods. If you don't like the Creation Club, don't spend money on it.
Ultimately, I do recommend picking up FO4 (and FO3 and FONV). It is still a lot of fun, and is a very intricate game, regardless of its shortcomings if compared to its predecessors.

It doesn't seem quite fair to call 12 Labours of Hercules a bad game, because it is what it is, but it feels less fair to call it a good game. Because, well, let's just say that if your favorite part of Age of Empires, Rise of Nations, whatever, is manually telling your villagers what resources to collect over and over again, then this might be the game for you. Otherwise, it probably isn't.
Now, there's some enjoyment to be had from the first ten levels or so, when new features are still being added, but that's followed by thirty levels of creeping realization that that's all there is to it. While you gain a few new mythical helpers, they don't really change the gameplay - on most levels, most of your time is occupied by tediously gathering food sources and using them to clear eroded paths, before eventually getting to do the one unique thing in the level (which oftentimes isn't actually unique at all). There are a few levels that actually have unique concepts but even those are mostly just 'gather the right resources in an area where you're very low on some particular resource' and they're scattered between samey levels with slightly different coats of paint and terrible minigames (mostly 'click on the enemies slowly wandering towards you').
Since there are some redeeming features (the powerups are neat, the style is nice enough), this might all be fine if the core gameplay (what of that there is) were executed to perfection. It's not. If you try to queue an action that's only possible after your workers return with their current load of resources, it... sometimes works? The queue isn't very long, either, so a lot of time ends up being spent waiting for workers to do whatever they're doing and return so you can click on the next set of things and then wait another thirty seconds. The overall game isn't very refined either - when playing on Casual mode, you're told two different times for each level you complete (as one is 2/3 of the other, that probably means that rather than adjust goal times for each difficulty, your own time is simply adjusted, in an awkwardly visible way).
Again, it's not like it's a terrible game. It's just really, painfully mediocre.

Serena isn't a game as you might normally think of one, rather it's more of an interactive short story.
A man sits in his cabin in the woods, wondering where his wife is, and struggling to recall her face. Exploring the cabin uncovers emotional attachments and fragments of their story, gradually building a fuller picture of what happened. While playing you'll no doubt be guessing what the truth is - perhaps you'll be spot-on, perhaps miles off or perhaps, like me, correct, but with a twist. Whichever it is you're sure to enjoy finding out.
Serena is a short but affecting and emotive experience, and is very much worth the hour or so of your time it'll take to play it.
I look forward to any further projects from the creative team behind this.

Before I begin: Yes, the game is mostly fixed but sadly still has poor optimization.
Assassin's Creed Unity is, for the most part, a normal Assassin's Creed game with a Ubisoft Open World. However, the game offers more difficult and interesting combat, better parkour, gorgeous graphics and incredible customization alongisde a decent Shakespherean drama starring Flynn Rider from Disney's Tangled and Merideth from Brave. Not to mention Paris feels very, VERY alive. It's breathtaking honestly.
While the optimization might not be great, I can run the game at 4k 40fps on High settings (There's not much visual difference between High, Very High, and Ultra High to begin with, but they do require a lot more power to run smoothly). Additionally, I haven't experienced any stability issues. Certainly no crashes, and surprisingly, no bugs.
Overall it's probably the best Assassin's Creed game I've ever played. With everything it has to offer, it's a shame the game was plagued by a rocky launch and resulting poor reviews. I'd say that if your system is above the recommended settings (yes, above not just at), then you should be able to run the game fine and is definitely worth picking up while on sale.
NOTE: Performance based on GTX 1070, i7 6700k processor and 16GB RAM. Performance across different setups may vary, batteries not included.

Definitely one of the worst games in the series. Possible spoilers ahead! You have been warned.
The story is horrible and difficult to stay engaged in. The only reason I even beat this game is because I wanted to see what the end would contribute to the overall AC series story like some of the other entries in the series did. I ended up being quite disappointed, even with the low expectations I had prior to beating the game. There is little closure in the end and doesn't answer many questions. Where did Germain get the Sword of Eden? What happened to the other three Assassin Grand Masters after Arno was expelled? Why did this game not add anything to the AC universal story?! So many questions like this that really leave you with a bitter feeling after you beat it...
The characters are all very cookie cutter and predictable. Nothing ever seems to differentiate between separate targets. You kill one guy and he just leads you to the next head honcho, repeat this process 50 times, or so it feels like. Arno was an okay protagonist, but didn't really make you want to keep playing as him or get another game playing as Arno as most people did with Ezio after AC2.
There is so much extra crap to do, and I call it crap on purpose. It is distracting and pointless to do all the secondary missions and objectives. You can easily get through the game with mid-tier weapons and armor, so why waste your time trying to upgrade further? You get an OP set of armor and a sword to boot at the end anyway... All of it really just clutters your map and gets in the way.
As for the gameplay, the formula for playing the game is in stark contrast to the earlier games. AC Brotherhood really let you choose how you want to kill your targets. There were numerous ways to stealthfully assassinate a target. From a bench, from the roof, from the crowd, etc.  I really liked being able to figure out what path I could take in ACB when climbing, but lately all of the games seem to only have one path up a building or structure and it feels extremely forced. In Unity, you really don't get many choices and it ALWAYS ends up with you running away from a hoard of 25 guards at the end of the assassination. The series is so different because in the beginning, the goal was to try NOT to fight all the guards and to avoid have a pile of bodies, rather to take out your target quickly and quietly and then escape.
Speaking of bodies, why did Ubisoft remove so many functions from the previous games that were so nice to have?! You can no longer pick up bodies to hide or relocate them, you can't pick up their weapons, you can't use your fists, you aren't able to take human shields to block gunshots (which are way too common in Unity,) you can't use the dagger (which has been removed from use in the series for a while now..) It's like they're taking out all of the parts that made the game fun. It's more of a fighting/ combat game now where you're expected to fight and survive rather than sneak and stealthfully dispatch a single target without any extra combat involved.
I appreciate Ubisoft trying to change the game up a bit by adding choice of weapons and such, but I don't think it serviced the game all too well. With the combination of choosing your weapons and armor and leveling up skills with "experience points" made it feel like it was trying to be like an RPG, and that is far from what the AC games are. It didn't make the game any more fun.
One other thing about the gameplay that irks me is the idea of the factions or sides. I don't have a problem with there being a multifaceted "society" in the game, but what is the point of having factions that fight each other (i.e. the Gang members and the French guardsmen), but when you fight one of the factions and the other joins in to kill them as well, they attack you afterwards. The enemy of my enemy is my friend, unless you're playing AC Unity. Then everyone is out to get you at all times. Even if you simply run by a guard and do nothing else..
Let's not forget what this game was most famous for: THE BUGS AND GLITCHES! They're still here alright... I experienced countless glitches along the way of playing through this game. Random citizen NPCs in the windows three stories up, getting shot, stabbed, and executed through walls, getting stuck on top of a chair or bench while sqautting as if I were on top of a synch point, running up a wall and somehow falling down past where I jumped from and ending up dead, and lots more. One technical part that I REALLY wish Ubisoft would address is the clumbsy controls of the game. The movement is not tight at all which makes it so you have to rotate 90 degrees one way or the other to make a slight turn. It really is ridiculous, and this is not a problem limited to Unity, it's most of the games, but Unity seems to have it the worst.
In all honesty, the AC series is one of my favorites which is why I get so disappointed by them being lackluster like this. They can't all be gold like AC2 and ACB, but Ubisoft really dropped the ball on this one. The strategy in making sequels is usually to take what like likable and what worked from the previous games and apply it/ improve upon those concepts in future products, but Ubisoft seemed to do just the opposite. I am going to play Syndicate next because I would like to play all the games in the series; I don't want to give up on what I used to hold in such high esteem in the past! I will likely try out Origins too.
TL;DR
Characters - Bad and uninteresting
Story - Boring and adds nothing to the continuous story the other AC games are establishing
Gameplay - Polar opposite of the good AC games, meaning Unity's gameplay is the antithesis of an Assassin game. Ubisoft made the game only able to be played one way. WAY too much combat now.
Technical - Still quite buggy
I would not recommend this game because it is honestly a useless entry in the AC series. I sincerely hope that Ubisoft taking the year off from putting out a new AC game will pay off and give us a great entry into the series that everyone really wants to see again! I trust that with the extra year they had, there is much more room for picking up where they fell short in all the other entries.

So, first off a few things: This is not a re-skin of MOO2.  If you want that, this game will sorely disappoint you.  That said, I went into playing this game with that exact mentality.  I have had many systems over the years, and MOO2 was almost always among the first games to get installed on it.  I cannot even begin to imagine how many hours I've spent playing the game and inventing new ways to try and beat the game (Single Doomstar Antaran win, anyone?).  So, when I heard that a new MOO was out, I was excited to have my old MOO2 back with better graphics.
What I got was a game that is far different than that.  For starters, star lanes and non-turn based combat was a huge turnoff.  In fact, those two items alone almost made me uninstall initially.  But I decided to give it another shot, and what I ound was that, even though those elements were different, they were ultimately changes for the best.  Gone are the days where a Darlok fleet randomly drops a giant fleet in the furthest backwater area of your empire out of nowhere, and that's fine.  Do I miss that sort of random thing?  Maybe.  But does it make for a better strategic framework for a human vs AI game?  Absolutely.
In regards to combat, a few things need tweaked, but it is quite playable in its current iteration.  If you are thinking the real-time combat is like that unspeakable mess of MOO3, it isn't.  It likely is an issue where you are misunderstanding the controls (like I did initially), but a sticky on the official forums will bring you up to speed and bring you around on it.
Now, to the overwhelming good of the game.  The voice acting and research trees are great.  Are they great in the conventional sense?  Eh, it isn't Mass Effect or something, but as a huge sci-fi nerd, hearing familiar voices from my favorite actors is a fine bit of nostalgia.  Similarly, the tech tree creates many of the same feelings.  Researching jump gates, battle pods, and other techs from yesteryear are fun, and the more I play, some of the choices forced by the tech tree are genuinely meaningful.
Some areas of the game, still in early access, are up in the air for me.  Diplomacy seems pointless right now, the AI is a little too pacifistic, tech research a bit too fast and a passive afterthought (think autolab x100), and the spy process seems promising, but under-defined currently.  Also, MOO2 races need to come back, and even some of the races from MOO3 would be nice (races is one of the few things that game did right).
In summary, if you loved MOO1 or MOO2, buy this game and give it a chance.  If you can't stand early access titles, wait a bit and get it on release.  While it isn't a re-skin, it is a genuinely good title, and one that makes up for the abomination that was MOO3.

I have to agree with most of the reviews.  For me, there are several failings:
1)  Tech Tree.  It's basic.  There's no differentiation.  You plough through basically the same way regardless of race, and ultimately you don't really "feel" like any of it is making a difference.  You're simply clicking buttons to progress along the tree.  Sure, you're getting better ship firepower, but that's about it.
2)  Race differentialtion.  There isn't any.  Yes, there's some pluses/minuses at the beginning but there's no feel for one race versus another.  Ships look a bit different, but as far as technologies go; you all have the same stuff.  The devs could learn a lot from Sins of s Solar Empire on this one.
3)  Opponent AI.  It's terrible.  I managed to get everyone friendly and then ally with me.  Yes, all races.  You would think the game would be over since we're all in one big alliance.  No.  Then suddenly, one of them leaves the alliance and goes straight to hostile.  Not one other race keeps their word on the alliance.  They all leave, and all declare war on me the very next turn.  So don't bother with diplomacy.
4)  Specialization.  It would be nice to have the ability for planets to be more specialized.  But you can basically build all developments on all planets.  Since you can terraform and even convert gas giants to planets laster in the game, there's almost no point in aggessive expansion.  All your planets can be turned quite habitable.  So, grab enough planets so you have have a solid defensive fleet...and sit there.  Race through the tech tree on the econmic advancements and get enough money to buy the market and win the econmic victory.  Every other victory takes much longer, and there's frankly no point.  Wars happen because of resource shortages.  Since you're not fighting over resources, then what?  They need a complete rethink and take notes from Civ 5.  Not everyone gets iron, oil, or aluminum.  Either trade for it, of fight for it.  That creates politics.  Since no planet (except for Orion itself) has any unique value, then I could care less fighting over any of it.
5)  Pirates.  Outright atrocious.  They randomly spawn on any uninhabitable world and start creating ships.  Then they randomly attack anything they see, even if they are completely outmatched.  Again, Sins of a Solar Empire had a better pirate concept.  They were almost a faction of their own, and could be manipulated to attack your enemies.  I feel like they tried to go the Civ 5 route, but that doesn't make any sense in space.
This game is just way to dumbed down.  No one is going to play this game for 8 hours for a single playthrough for this dull of a game.

Another delightful Chucklefish game. Much like Starbound, there's so much to do it's almost overwhelming, and all of it's entertaining. You'll want to do it all! Initially I wasn't hooked on the hype of this game, but having delved into a farm of my own, I can see the appeal... and then some. Ironically, once I started making a farming colony in Starbound and had kinda reached its limit, I thought, "why am I not doing this in Stardew Valley, that farming game everyone raves about? Let's try it." I tried it. I'm in on the hype.
PROS:
* Bang for your buck, on multiple levels. Not only is this game cheap for the hours you could potentially spend, it's also one of the least taxing games on a machine. A potato could store and run this game, pun unashamedly intended.
* Highly cathartic. Probably the most cathartic game to have come out in recent years.
* Deceptively deep. At its surface it seems like a cheap knockoff of Harvest Moon and/or Animal Crossing, but it's unique in itself and just as deep as those titles (if not deeper, I haven't gotten far enough to attest either way).
* Leveling up! This might seem minor but it isn't stated off the bat that your skills level as you build them up, and you don't really know how much it will take, it just happens naturally and you level when you wake up the next morning. It's nice seeing your character progress, though.
* Somewhat interesting characters and stories. We're not exactly breaking the bank with plot here, but the beauty is, it doesn't have to--in fact, this is a story that calls for a very low-key, day-in-the-life style of storytelling, which it does beautifully.
* Inventory sort button! It's not perfect but it's better than nothing (looking at you, Starbound).
* Controller support! You might need or want to use your mouse for some UI functions but for the most part, you can play entirely with a controller. Yee boi.
NEUTRAL:
* I'm on the fence about the speed of the flow of time in a day. It feels a little rushed, but there's still a lot you can get done in that time. Still, it emulates that feeling of "not enough hours in the day" that happens when your schedule's cramped, for better or worse. Same with energy level. Watering your crops alone is tedious, and sprinklers aren't cheap, at least not early on. Rainy days are a godsend, freeing up your morning to fish or deforest or scour the mines for a while before going to town, if you need to.
* -Moderately- replayable. Yeah you can make a whole new farm with a whole new layout and pick different characters to befriend, a different marriage partner, maybe buy that Jojamart membership and play the cash-crop game, but I feel like once you've gone through one run you've probably seen it all. That doesn't stop it from being ultimately cathartic, however, and will always be a nice stress ball to keep in your Steam library.
* If you over-exert yourself (granted, the game *does* warn you, but accidents happen), you wake up the next day with half your energy gone. Neither eating to regain energy nor sleeping early remove the fatigue, but there is an item you can buy from the hospital for 1,000 that cures it. I've heard this echoed as a common complaint, and I think it's a little silly that you can't even take a mid-day nap to recharge or something, so just be really careful, and maybe keep one of those potions on deck when you have some extra dosh. Too bad the ol' farm wasn't in Spain.
CONS:
* Can't save (therefore can't exit without losing progress) without going to sleep, and the game doesn't warn you that progress will be lost upon exiting, so I assumed it would just drop me back in where I exited. Nope. Minor loss of progress, but something that should be at least warned of.
* Special events, should you choose to attend them, are a ripoff of an entire day. They say they last from, say, 9am-2pm, but when you attend and complete them you're spat out in front of your house at 10pm, effectively eating an entire day. So if you go to an event, make sure you at least water your crops or otherwise spend your energy.
* Similarly unannounced is the duration and rules of upgrades. When you go to get a tool upgraded, you literally turn in your un-upgraded tool for a couple of days to the blacksmith, and can't use it until it's completed. This is never stated or warned. To make matters worse, even though the blacksmith will still be in his shop while he's "working on your tool," his only dialogue is "um, I'm not finished yet" and you can't even shop from him or crack open geodes.
All in all though, like I said, great stress-ball of a game and hardly lacking for content. The hype ain't for nothin'. Looking forward to the official multiplayer that's in the works.

It is a little bit difficult to review a game like this, specially with popular opinion this game has already... either way, let me share my experience about it...
This time you step on the shoes(or boots) of Arno Dorian in Paris, France during the French Revolution. While the start is a little bit confusing as you start as a random assassin guy going through a random mission against some templars. Eventually you get to be on Arno's shoes and go through his whole Assassin training and then missions. While all of this is happening, in the real world you are just a normal guy using something called Helix, which is gaming device produced by Abstergo (the templar company) so, you can live or re-live different genetic memories from people in the past. While the story plot is not bad, is not really as memorable as you might think. That's all I would say about it as don't want to spoil it for everyone.
This game did a complete overhaul to the fighting system in the Assassin's Creed games giving the player an actual challenge and making you think twice before going all guns blazing on everyone you find. At least it becomes challenging until you find out you can just throw a smoke bomb and pretty much take 4 or 5 enemies down while they are confuse. If you are going into a sword only fight you will have to learn the timing to parry the enemies attacks as if you do them too early or too late and you will get hit. A thing to keep in mind when fighting a group of soldiers or rebels are the enemies shooting at you with rifles; but then again you are an Assassin and have a whole bunch of weapons to deal with your enemies, like mini arrows, pistols, smoke bombs and of course the hidden blade.
While go through the game you will level up Arno and suit it to your play style, by getting different pieces of cloth with different abilities, some are good for stealth while others are good to tank more hits. You really have the freedom to choose what play style suits you better.
In this game they introduced a "sneaking" mode which can help to take down enemies silently and without fighting an entire groups of enemies, but sneaking around is not your thing, you can always equip yourself with a battle axe and get everyone in your way. Another notable change was they completely change the parkour system and scaling and jumping from building to building is way easier and believe you will need it as 75% of the time you will be jumping around and doing Assassin stuff.
There is a lot, believe me... A LOT of side content to complete in this game. If you really want to complete the game to 100% like I did, it might take you a while. The side missions can go from collectibles, discovering the map, specific side missions, investigations, heists, etc. During some of the side missions for some rare glitch in the Abstergo system, Arno will be transported to modern times and you will see tanks, planes and stuff from World War 2; all of these is not related to the story at all but it is introduced to you as the player using the Abstergo gaming system.
While this game took out the multiplayer mode the previous game had, which are mostly if not all competitive, you looking and eliminating other players in this game they changed it out completely and made it so it was cooperative play only; of course the co-op mode only works for some specific missions, mostly heists and assassinations. The few times I tried to do the co-op missions have to say the connectivity it was not as good and not too many players are actually using it, so finding someone to do co-op is a chore. While is the co-op is not bad, is not as good either... in other words, is meh!.
This is where everyone pretty much bashed this game and have to say after the critical patches they did a way long time ago the game is pretty much playable, of course thinking you have a good graphics card and CPU as the performance is not really constant and being the type of game where you find a lot of NPCs on the streets constantly. Most of the times the game fluity will be affected mostly when you are outside, most of the indoors missions keeps the performance fluid, but you will be mostly outside running out in the street. Unfortunately, after this game was released in a really bad state and the performance not being as good as you might expect, the well known "Ubisoft Quality" that all Ubisoft games have nowadays where the performance in PC is not stellar and you most likely need to find a work around to be able to play.
If you like the Assassin's Creed game series and want something different from the previous 3 games, this game is definitely recommended for you, but having in mind you will need a good PC to be able to run it properly. The story is average and not really memorable, the gameplay it is good when you get used to it but at the same time it gets repetitive if you are going for 100% completion. Something worth mention it is compare to the launch date where you were required to have the app to be able to unlock some of the items in game, now it is not necessary to have the app now as everything you supposed to get from the app is now unlocked automatically. All in all, I'd recommend this game only if you PC supports it and if you have played the previous games, so of course, get it when it is on sale.

Assassin's Creed Unity is Ubisoft's first game in AC franchise designed as "next-gen". Set in Revolutionary Paris, France, it follows the story of young Arno. There are parallels with AC II in regards to "revenge" theme to the plot - both protagonists are primarily fuelled by executing justice on those who wronged them.
The city of Paris is the most detailed yet in the franchise, with new verticality and buildings with righ interior to be explored. The parkour system is vastly improved, flows well with the environment and is highly effective. Never before was traversing the obstacles so solid and enjoyable.
I got to experience this game almost 2 years after launch, so I can't really say much about bugs and glitches, though I believe the criticism and backlash was mostly valid. However, in its current state it's pretty much ironed out and fixed. Yes, there may be some issues with crowd-pop-ins, AI may do some of the dumbest actions from time to time, but hey - nothing gamebreaking. The graphics are simply gorgeous, the lighting is spot-on, facial animations one of the best in the industry, so is the voice acting.
Gameplay is improved, ability to "crouch" is finally added, aswell as better cover system. Take-downs are intuitive and fast, brutal. I'm not sure that I like the new combat system - it seems rather dull. I preferred the old one - based on counter-attacks. It made for much more fun and varied approach on how to deal with your adversaries.
Overall, I recommend AC Unity. It manages to do a lot of stuff right, sometimes taking one step back in regards to other things (like combat, unlocking basic abilities like "throwing money" - WTF?!). There is a LOT of quests to be done, most of them rather interesting, story is fine, voice-acting engaging and stealth is on a whole 'nother level.

Great engine, but still plenty of bugs. First of all, the replay feature is all but useless. You can't rewind or pause. All you can do is watch the match in real time. you can slow down and speed up a bit, but that's not that useful. Full control would be awesome; a pause button would make it a meaningful feature.
You can change player names, apparently. You have to do it before you buy the player, you can never change it again, and you have to go into the player's detail screen. As far as I know, there is absolutely no reason to look at this screen before you buy a player, except that it's the only way to change the name. It'd be nice to just click on the name of the player I'm about to buy to get an input cursor. You know, like every other windows application ever.
Dice are still broken. When it's one player vs. another, it's fair (if not well-randomized), but it seems that the die rolls in a single-player game take into account the difficulty level.
Custom lineups don't save properly. As long as I stay within the same game, the lineup I saved doesn't go anywhere. As soon as I start a new game, it's gone. so there's really no point in using the feature, since you still need to take time to set your line every single game.
This right-click/left-click♥♥♥♥♥♥has GOT to go. Just get rid of the right-click mechanism entirely. The game doesn't need to tell the difference between a "move here" click and a "select this player" click because you can only possibly mean one or the other, depending on where you actually click. I suppose this might make sense in a real-time game, but I've yet to encounter anyone who actual plays this game in realtime mode.
I think it's great that when a "new edition" is released, they very graciously offer a deep discount to anyone who already owns the game. But come on. You're essentially releasing DLC and re-packaging the entire game with each content pack. So when I bought Chaos Edition, I had to download the entire game again, instead of just having to download a patch and a content pack. Can't you just release DLC and regular patches like everybody else does?
A spectator mode would be great too. It would be nice to be able to watch a game as it happens and do commentary. There is officially a "spectator mode," but you're not watching the game live. When you enter "spectator mode," it just plays the game's replay from turn one.
There are just so many things that everybody else does properly and this game fails at miserably.
I love BloodBowl, and I love paying a one-time price to play it forever. I just wish we had some modern devs instead of these DOS-era non-conformists.

I'd love to be able to recommend this, but as it stands right now I just can't. I absolutely hate leaving negative reviews and this may actually in fact be the first that I have.
I love the idea and respect that they broke away from GMOD for the freedom to do what they wanted, but the performance of this game is just abysmal. Running a 4790K overclocked to 4.5GHz, GTX970 also overclocked a bit on core and memory, 8GB RAM, and running off an SSD, just trying to launch the game can sometimes take upward of 5 minutes to get past the splash screen to the main menu, then another 5 - 10 minutes load into any of the official lobbies where, regardless of graphics settings, I see 60fps no problem until I try to move, and then it can stay on a single frame for 5+ seconds, then it'll stutter, and if it doesn't go back to being stuck on a single frame, it'll jump back to 60fps for a quick moment and be a disaster again.
I'd love to tell you this is just a bad overclock that i'm running, but it was like this prior to the overclock and I am still able to play games like Ghost Recon Wildlands at 1920x1080 with some settings on high while others are on ultra and get a solid 60fps 90% of the time. 50fps if i'm livestreaming.
There is absolutely no excuse for a game of this scale to run as bad as it does on the platform that it is running on. I've slapped together solo projects in UE4 that have all run smoother. UE4 practically does most of the work for you.
I was mainly looking for another chill game to hang with friends and do random mindless stuff. I was mostly interested in having another Golf game, but even for that I cannot recommend this with how things currently are. If the person hosting the game is getting a low framerate, the physics are just broken. You click to take your shot and it's delayed by at least a full second. Automated moments on courses, that you have zero control over, land you out of bounds.
Dedicated servers let you host your own plazas, but since the plaza is basically directly connected to the in-game economy, you can't play in the casino and i'd assume the rest of the mini games directly in the plaza because they aren't sure of how to stop people from scamming it on their own servers so they just disabled it, thus making dedicated servers pretty useless. Not to mention the fact that no matter what I do, I can't see my own server unless I run it on a second computer in the house, even with all ports forwarded properly for the server and forcing the game to use alternate ports. They're all standard Steam ports. If you're set up for gmod, you should already be set up for this.
As I said before, I really want to like this game... I really do.. but this is still early access and only time will tell whether it is something that will get better with time.

Not too unlike Endless Space. It's interesting and fun for awhile.
But, sadly, it is caught in the 4x epidemic. Like all these games, this also suffers from the "4x Virus": mid-game it turns into a micromanagement department and becomes masterfully boring with no real difficulty, as you can already see what the outcome will be, and the rest of the game is just mopping up. The feeling of exploration and discovery, the unexpected events, the eagerness to advance your tech and build your empire fades away. The mid- to end-game really needs an overhaul if I'm going to waste any more time on these 4x games. Something more than an obsessive compulsive drive to finish what you started has to happen somewhere.
I usually quit at that point and start a new game. And repeat this until that also becomes boring. For this one it only took about fiver or six startups to get me bored.
If I was going to tolerate microtransactions I'd play Candy Crush, but at least then it would be a relatively bugless experience, and not when I've already paid a premium for the game.

This is probably one of my longest reviews, so if the review's too long, then skip to the bottom to see the Conclusion/TL:DR!
OVERVIEW:
As someone who played Harvest Moon (GBC), and loved the hell out of it; I figured I'd enjoy Stardew Valley, and I was correct. Stardew Valley's one of those games that sounds boring as all hell on paper; "It's just a farming simulator, right?" Wrong, but you're half-correct. Stardew Valley's primary focus is {player}'s Farm; However, you're not restricted to just farming. You're allowed to go on your own do whatever you'd like, such as; explore in the mines, fight mobs, build a family with the 12 NPCs eligible for marriage, although, there's 36 total NPCs to interact with, brew potions to create magic, become a fisherman, agriculture, etc. Stardew Valley has a small, but connected community, and you've just moved in, so you're allowed to "make your mark" upon the community. Anyways, that's enough about Stardew Valley; Let's get into the review!
VISUALS:
There's quite a few people who dislike pixel artstyles, and that's totally understandable, as I love the artstyle, but a lot of games don't make it work, and/or do it correctly, however, that doesn't mean there's not any "hidden gems" amongst the crowd. (Hyper Light Drifter, Stardew Valley, Owlboy, Terraria, VA-11 Hall A, etc.) Personally, I think Stardew Valley's done a stellar job with the overall artstyle. - 9/10.
AUDIO:
Stardew Valley has done audio so damn well, but mainly the OST/Ambience is what caught my attention almost instantly; From the second I booted up the game, to the final scenes of the game, there was always this "excitement", or "joy" whenever I'd listen to it; It was just calming, and I felt as if I were at peace. However, the music that stood out to me the most would be the Mines' music; specifically Floors 70 - 100; It was just really, really calming. I was definitely able to relax  whilst playing a casual game, and I believe that other games should follow Stardew Valley's audio as an example regarding "What good audio is", atleast, in my opinion. - 10/10.
GAMEPLAY:
From what I've seen and heard; People think that it'd get repetitive and boring, and to that; "You may be right, but personally; I haven't experienced that feeling with Stardew Valley." I just haven't felt a sense of boredom; I could play the hell out of it over and over, and still enjoy it to it's full extents. "I feel a sense of pride and accomplishment" for doing what I do in-game, especially with it's Skill System. (Yes, an EA joke; Sorry.) I just love indie games that have been executed such as Stardew Valley has; It's fun and replayable. - 9/10.
STORY:
Stardew Valley's about an ex-Joja employee who's been overworked, and eventually quit, who then took up his grandfather's farm, trying to find a new way of life, whilst trying to build a family. (This is just the main story, however, there's quite some amount of extra "story", but that includes spoilers!) - 9/10.
CONCLUSION:
Stardew Valley's almost perfect, and I love it to death. Eric Barone did a fantastic job with this, and I personally think that everyone should buy it and try it out; If I had the option, I'd totally buy it again. There's more I wanted to do with this review, but I may do that sometime in the future; 'Till then, Happy Farming.
OVERALL:
9.2/10. - "It's really, really good, and I think everyone should give it a chance."

Ebola virus disease (EVD; also Ebola hemorrhagic fever, or EHF), or simply Ebola, is a disease of humans and other primates caused by ebolaviruses. Signs and symptoms typically start between two days and three weeks after contracting the virus with a fever, sore throat, muscular pain, and headaches. Then, vomiting, diarrhea and rash usually follow, along with decreased function of the liver and kidneys. At this time some people begin to bleed both internally and externally. The disease has a high risk of death, killing between 25 and 90 percent of those infected with an average of about 50 percent. This is often due to low blood pressure from fluid loss, and typically follows six to sixteen days after symptoms appear.
The virus spreads by direct contact with body fluids, such as blood, of an infected human or other animals. This may also occur through contact with an item recently contaminated with bodily fluids.[1] Spread of the disease through the air between primates, including humans, has not been documented in either laboratory or natural conditions.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or breast milk of a person after recovery from EVD may still carry the virus for several weeks to months. Fruit bats are believed to be the normal carrier in nature, able to spread the virus without being affected by it. Other diseases such as malaria, cholera, typhoid fever, meningitis and other viral hemorrhagic fevers may resemble EVD. Blood samples are tested for viral RNA, viral antibodies or for the virus itself to confirm the diagnosis.
Control of outbreaks requires coordinated medical services, alongside a certain level of community engagement. The medical services include rapid detection of cases of disease, contact tracing of those who have come into contact with infected individuals, quick access to laboratory services, proper healthcare for those who are infected, and proper disposal of the dead through cremation or burial. Samples of body fluids and tissues from people with the disease should be handled with special caution. Prevention includes limiting the spread of disease from infected animals to humans. This may be done by handling potentially infected bush meat only while wearing protective clothing and by thoroughly cooking it before eating it. It also includes wearing proper protective clothing and washing hands when around a person with the disease.
No specific treatment or vaccine for the virus is available, although a number of potential treatments are being studied. Supportive efforts, however, improve outcomes. This includes either oral rehydration therapy (drinking slightly sweetened and salty water) or giving intravenous fluids as well as treating symptoms. The disease was first identified in 1976 in two simultaneous outbreaks, one in Nzara, and the other in Yambuku, a village near the Ebola River from which the disease takes its name. EVD outbreaks occur intermittently in tropical regions of sub-Saharan Africa. Between 1976 and 2013, the World Health Organization reports a total of 24 outbreaks involving 1,716 cases. The largest outbreak is the ongoing epidemic in West Africa centered in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. As of 11 April 2015, this outbreak has 25,626 reported cases resulting in 10,619 deaths.

So let me just put a few things out there. I have not played this game through steam, not that it should matter. I played hundreds of hours on their website. I was there for wild-shadow and the true ammy and I am still there for Kabam. With the transfer to Kabam came more monetization of the game. It is true that you can buy tops with actual cash. But that shouldn't discourage you. That does not make this game pay-to-win.
Starting the game off, you will be awful. Many players, such as myself, don't make it to level 20 consistently for a while. It's a build up of skill for a simple game. This bullethell game offers things like screen rotation that changes an entire gameplay style. Some people use it, some don't. Either way, you are destined to die. And seeing as it is a permadeath game, you will lose anything on your character, and yes you will probably cry for the next week. And then you will come back and start all over again.
Now back to the pay-to-win, "If anyone can buy the best gear, then how is it not pay-to-win?" Simple. It isn't the best gear. There are items that can only be received from boss loot drops and are only able to be picked up by one player. One thing that came with Kabam as well is the fact you can no longer trade these soulbound items. This means anyone you see with them, earned them.... probably. And even if someone walks around all hot with their top tier armor on, you can tell the difference between ptw and earned it. Put them in battle and see what happens. People who pay for their items 9/10 will be absolutely horrible and die promptly. The other 1/10 people are those who can't accept the death of their character and bought some items.
The economy is based mostly on the potions. Their are potions that increase your stats, they are dropped from random high level monsters and bosses. While you could buy top tier gear and sell it for these potions, it would be incredibly inefficient. So anyone with top tier armor and 0/8 maxed stats is likely to once again, be a noob. Someone who will die in no time. The gear doesn't make the player in this game. That is what is so special about it. You can't pay to win because you can't buy the skills to go balls-deep on Oryx-2. So don't be discouraged by the people who complain about paying to win. Chances are they are just upset they don't have the money to get the items and certainly don't have the skill to get it on their own.

I played the demo for Blades of Time, and I thought it was pretty good, so I bought it in a bundle and bought this with a 90% coupon I got for free.  To be honest, my expectations were low--X-Blades has a pretty poor reputation from what I've read, so it couldn't really go anywhere but up.  It took me nine hours to beat the game though I could've cut it down if I wasn't stuck in one portion.
X-Blades is the story of a young woman in a skimpy outfit destroying statues and vases while slaughtering scores of monsters and critters.  I guess I'd classify it as a beat-em-up of sorts, the kind where the game will seal off an exit and you have to deplete a health bar on the bottom of the screen with enough monster death to continue.  Or maybe you have to find these monster generators and destroy all of them AND kill all of the monsters in the area to continue.  Combat is fairly simple, as you attack with your gunblades with slashes or shooting at distant enemies.  There's a Rage meter that rises with damage dealt and taken, which falls with time or when casting spells, as it's kinda like an MP bar in a way.  You gain Souls from enemies you butcher and the things you destroy, which you spend on learning new spells or getting in a quick anytime heal or Rage boost.
Battles are largely repetitive barring the boss battles.  You usually have enemies spawn in over a series of waves and you destroy them, or do the same with the monster generators, and then you get a Level Complete and you're free to explore the stages for artifact pieces to power up your attacks or other goodies.  All while staring at your character's♥♥♥♥♥..I'm sorry, where was I?  There really aren't any puzzles to solve again barring some of the boss fights, and you typically get a bestiary update that tells you pretty much how to beat the foe.  This is the first game I've played where the bestiary updates BEFORE you kill something, but it's a handy hint system kinda thing.
For things the game did right...there's a pretty big variety of spells to spend your Souls on.  Granted there aren't many effects, but they are at least somewhat different.  Earthquake can't hit foes in the air, Ray of Light works best on darkness-aligned creatures, and Lightning Range is a kickass chain lightning spell.  There are only four quickslots for spells but you can call up the menu and cast a spell there if you have enough Rage, to make use of a few combos or to use something you don't have bound.  The music is a bit repetitive, being pretty heavy on the rock side during battles, but it kinda grew on me to be honest.  Even the title theme sounded bad...at first.  It's tolerable now, though I don't have to listen to it very much.  And the manual is written entirely in-character, which I realize is corny as hell but I kinda liked it.  There's also a results screen at the end of each stage so you can at least see if you missed any artifact pieces or are going for 100% completeness or something.  And you can go right back to the previous stage if you want, but no stage-select feature here, unfortunately.
As for what I didn't like, some of the controls kinda bothered me.  There was a section I was stuck on that required crossing a chasm or fall to my death, and more than a few times did I accidentally dodge-roll right off a ledge when I meant to jump.  Dying in this game means you start the stage all over.  Did you get a Level Complete and die?  Too bad, start all over!  And this happened to me a few times.  Thankfully that section was optional and this game has no platforming sections like that anywhere else...and you get to keep all of the Souls you had already, so that's some consolation.  Another thing was that the battles were rarely fun and felt like grinding more than anything.  Even when you knew how to kill something, some things just took forever to die, and I hate attrition wars like that.  I did kinda like the game, but at no point did I really tell myself, "boy, this game is fun!" I honestly bought it just to see how bad it was, and it was cheap, so no major loss to me.
So I'm not recommending this.  I try to be patient with games, even ones that are said to be outright bad.  This one...it's okay, I guess, but I wouldn't recommend this to anybody, or really most people.  It's a rough game, it's trying quite a bit, and while I haven't played the games this gets compared to, it's largely mediocre and probably "a poor man's" version of those games at best.  The game likely will be remembered more for the outfit the protagonist wears than the content of the game, but all in all, it's not a bad game.  Just not one I'd see myself coming back to anytime soon.

After having gotten and played this game for a while, I feel its time I give it a review.
The good news:
If you played enemy unknown, you will feel right at home in XCOM 2. The basic gameplay is the same, but the addition of several new features makes life much more enjoyable. The most noteworthy of these changes are that skill tree's feel much more distinct, skill choices feel harder to make, and the plot feels much better done. Another gameplay boost is a more varied set of missions, stealth mechanics, and more varied enemies. Another big upgrade is to the graphics, landscapes, and animations. Maps are now procedurally generated, graphics greatly improved, and the animations are all much smoother. Not to mention the character pool system. All of this and official mod support are great bonuses.
The bad news:
Some of the things people disliked about enemy unknown have carried over. Chief amongst these issues is that even when running pure vanilla, there exists a number of bugs that will impact gameplay. Another issue is the extensive use of mission timers. While it does add another challenge to missions, a few too many missions use them. Another problem is a lack of gameplay modifier settings, like those seen in enemy unknown. Its also important to note, that despite a better plot, it also packs a few plot holes.
Summary:
+Fewer bugs
+Same basic gameplay
+More varied enemies
+Random map generation
+Greater mission variety
+Just as tense as enemy unknown, if not more
+Mod support
+Character pool system is soldier dress up simulator (I spent almost my first hour just making characters)
-Still has game breaking bugs
-A few too many mission timers
-Some gameplay issues are only fixed with mods
-Occasional plot holes
Conclusions:
If you liked enemy unknown or enemy within, you will feel right at home with XCOM 2. The basic gameplay is retained, and the fact that the difficulty is higher is nice for veteran players. The mod support is also an excellent introduction, allowing greater creative freedom, and allowing players to make the game easier or harder then what is offered. That said, it still has numerous bugs, and the room for error is much smaller this time around.
Final score:
8/10 vanilla.
9/10 with mods.

As an original GMT player I have to say that playing this is quite a throwback. I really enjoy seeing the gmod servers that i used to play on in 2012-2013 as a reworked game now. I will list some of the pro's and con's that I have noticed while playing for a bit.
Pro's
- Miniolf and Ball Race are really good games to play with friends, they're small little arcade games that are challenging enough and mixes up gameplay on the different stages enough to stay fun for a little while.
- Condo customization is very cool. You can change everything you would ever need on the weather, time and even sun position. You can place objects around and you have to earn objects, giving you a bit of a satisfaction getting new furniture after playing.
- There's multiple condo's to choose from so there's plenty to choose from (even a flat world for complete customization)
- Player customization is a thing (although it needs some more options)
- Plaza is easy to navigate after walking through once and has plenty of minigames (many upcoming) and shops to look around in.
Con's
- The game feels a bit lacking in content, although with the frequent updates this might not be a problem soon!
- Player customization is a bit limited, there's only 4 characters to choose from and one of them is milk (?). There's no options to choose your own set of clothes, its all presets and you cannot change any facial features or hairstyles of your character. You can basically only choose 2 presets and then color them yourself.
- Condo customization feels a bit lacking at the moment, there's not really enough objects to really make a whole room that's really unique (for instance, only 1 type of fridge and only a couple styles of TVs), there should be a slightly bigger variety to choose from. The game also needs a bit of a better snap to grid more where it will instead of snapping globally snap on the object that you are placing on, so if you're putting items on a table at an angle they will be easily placed on top on the same relative position. A scale option would also be a welcome addition, this could be used to (for instance) decrease the size of trophies and have them as little chess piece sized pieces on a row or to make a cinema with a large screen.
- The load time (especially in big condo's) is horrifyingly long, it takes an absurd amount of time to render all the objects in if someone created a custom condo and the loading on the lobby isnt great either (not that bad with an SSD though) but could be improved upon.
- The lobby feels a bit cluttered at times and doesn't really have a "flow" to it. I liked the original version 1 of the lobby more where it felt a bit more like a mall than a city. This is mostly just personal preference though and isnt much of a negative thing.
All in all, great game with some potential in the future. Most of the con's are just lacking features which (I think) will be added soon judging by the fast and frequent updates. If you like messing around with strangers, finding weird sex dungeons in condo's and having fun with friends (i wouldnt recommend it if you really don't know anyone interested in the game, or you could meet new people, that'd work too).
This is a great game though and you should consider buying it!

A game that started PC gaming and my love for it. Released in November of 1998 (the year I was born), Half-Life was released. This game uses the well-known Goldsource engine, which was implemented in many other titles Value released like Counter Strike and Day of Defeat.
You are Gordon Freeman, a MIT graduate that arrives to work late at 8:47a.m. You are just going through another day, as most of your collegues like to express. You arrive at the Anomalous Materials Lab where you are told to put on your HEV suit for a special experiment. When you make it down towards the lower-labs, you are told that they will be analyzing a particular specimen and the Anti-Mass Spectrometer had been adjusted to specific parameters that weren't exactly "practical". When you arrive in the chamber, you start the Anti-Mass Spectrometer and put in the specimen. Little did Freeman know, the specimen GG-3883 was an unstable crystal but the most pure. Putting the specimen into the the beam caused a chain reaction known as a resonance cascade, resulting in the "Black Mesa Incident". This resulted in border worlds colliding and spawning in aliens, causing MASS destruction to the facility and its workers. Your job is to escape the mess you indubitably caused and reach the surface.
This game is one I 100% recommend to those of you who have not played the series. This game is what made me love first-person shooters.

I like the game. I give it a 8 out of 10.
Features
There's multiplayer, cosmetics to spend your winnings on, single player, friends versus mode, leader board, VOiP while playing the game, avatar character customization and more. There's Texas Hold'em. Chip stacks change in size when you lose or gain chips, making it visually possible to compare earnings.
Multiplayer
You can play other random people on the internet. You can play with friends but it's limited to versus mode with friends only. Winnings and earns are persistent. Finding a game is fast when using a 1000 chip buy in. Character names allow internet address which would be intersting to those who want to use Twitch or advertise a website. Direct player trading isn't allowed but play with your friend a private 1v1 game, go all in on a losing hand and you've just trade your friend chips. You can "gift" your friend clothes and items you've bought with chips.
Free-to-Play Section
There's no monthy subscription. No transcation fee anywhere in the game. There's a cosmetic cash shop. You can buy chips with real money but that doesn't guarantee you a win. Should you lose all your chips in all or nothing gamble, you can create another Steam account for more chips.
Conclusion
I like the game. A progression system, being able to compete with friends, leader boards, cosmetic shop and everything else will have me recommending this game. I can't wait to see what else is in store for this game.

It's really the only game of its kind in the FPS genre of naval combat, and I think that's what had had me exited about it for years. Many developers these days are too afraid to stray from the path of 'generic game that makes money' like a cut and paste MMO with microtransactions - or a survival game; the market is so saturated with them it's getting a little stupid.
The melee combat could use a little polish, but it serves its purpose.
All in all I'd give it an 8/10 in its current state. If they build upon it, it could be one of the best games of its kind.

I beat this one in every way I possibly could months back or I'd still be playing it today.    This game has a powerful mood, setting, and mechanics to back them up.  The narrator has a deep and powerful voice, and he's endlessly quotable.  Every level is memorable and has its own story you hear through the narrator as you play.  It's a bit on the short side, but it's perfect for what it is.  You really owe it to yourself to play this fantastic game.

*Author's note: Play it ALL the way to the end to understand what I felt. Also, viewer discretion is advised.*
A beautiful collaboration.
It may be an hour long. It may not look like a 2014 game. It might even feel restrictic at times.
But Serena combines a talented production team (fans and game developers), superb voice acting, haunting atmosphere, enveloping visuals, and an emotional range that most games can't tell with 10 hours. Its a throwback to games like Myst, Riven, Syberia, The Longest Journey, and Paradise. I'll go as far as comparing it to modern titles like Gone Home, To the Moon, The Stanley Parable, and The Dark Meadow.
Serena is worth playing. Adventure lovers of old will love the nostalgia. Story-lovers will love the story of two lives and their downfall. The voice actors will also ring some bells from their game repitoire or their Youtube history. There is a reason to appreciate this game. Plus its free. You shouldn't argue on that deal.
For anyone who loves games, if you can spend one hour, I emplore you to play this game. It may not be perfect, but its damn impressive.
I look forward to more collaborative wonders in the future.
So please play this game and make it ALL the way to the end before you decide on what really happened. Enjoy.
And to the developers, I thank you. Maybe I'll work on a project about this length. Won't be as good, but I'll try. Thanks for the inspiration. I respect you and your work that will be remembered for generations to come.
With the Sincerest of thoughts and Words,
~RB

Sure it could use more features and tools, but what is here works suprisingly well.  It claims to have more than 3300 templates, but in reality it's only 3292.  Where are the others?? Just kidding.  It's worth it just to have these templates to look through to give you an idea of what you want to do.  Pick a template and you can start tweaking it or use it as a base to build off of.
I haven't spent a long time in the program but I was shocked at how useful it seems to be, from the perspective of someone who exclusively uses Photoshop on a daily basis.  It won't replace it, but it's a neat little prototyping tool.

I know there are a lot of negative reviews lately because of the Creation Club. This review isn't about that. This review is about the base game only. No mods, no DLC. Just vanilla Fallout 4.
F4 is not a terrible game, but it feels so pointless, so much like just a timesink. And I love big open world RPGs, and I love Fallout. And I do appreciate that Bethesda is finally showing a little of their old ambition, and is once again trying to bring some genuinely new things to the genre. Maybe it's just because The Witcher 3 is such a brilliant game that after having played it Fallout 4 just can't compete. Or maybe this is just a disappointing installment. Whatever the case, after some 30 hours of F4, I'm too bored and frustrated to continue.
Pro
- Fallout!
- Base building is a cool idea.
- Fairly pretty. Some nice landscapes.
- Lots of crafting options.
Con
- Nearly all quests are "go there and kill some raiders/monsters". Hardly the only RPG to do so, but compared to New Vegas or Witcher 3, the quest design is really shallow.
- Nearly all locations are just places to kill enemies. There's rarely anything interesting going on, and there's rarely anyone you can talk to.
- Dialog options are super-simplified. You don't get to choose your exact words, only one of 4 general topics/tones. Intelligence and charisma don't matter very much.
- Mouse & keyboard controls are terrible. Press V to change the camera, but hold V to go to build mode. WTF?! Did we somehow run out of keys? Press TAB to go to Pip Boy, but also to cancel. Except sometimes it's ESC to cancel. Press I to go to the Pip Boy inventory menu, unless you are in another Pip Boy menu, then it won't work and you'll have to navigate there by clicking. The M&KB UI is a total mess. The game is designed for gamepad and gamepad only. I'm not an M&KB snob; I'll happily use my gamepad if that suits the gameplay. I played most of the Witcher 3 with one, even though the M&KB controls were fine. But F4 is half FPS, half base builder. Those are 2 things that a mouse is just a lot more convenient for than a gamepad. But in this game that means being stuck with a terrible UI.
- Base building has many limitations and annoyances. Without mods there aren't all that many components to choose from. You can't do obvious things like remove corpses. You can easily remove trees, but many bushes are indestructable. Component placement is imprecise, so it's hard to make things look nice. The way you need to assign settlers to tasks is ridiculously laborious. Plots to build on are usually pretty small. And as soon as you try to build something substantial (like a nice tower to use as a personal base), the game will inform you that you've reached the maximum number of components, so you'll have to stop building.
- The world is chock full of locations, but it doesn't feel like a real place. Everything is way too closely packed, and apart from the settlements and the people you send out, virtually everybody you encounter is hostile. You never wonder if you should risk approaching someone to talk to them. It's pointless; they're going to be hostile. I'm pretty sure there are at least 5 raiders for every settler. Best not wonder what they're raiding and from whom.
- Most objects you encounter can be recycled for crafting/building. This means that you have even more reason to try and take everything that you find lying about. But of course you can only take so much with you, so you'll be making frequent boring trips back to store or sell all that stuff from your inventory (which of course has a crappy UI). And while you can send provisioners to move stuff instantly between settlements, the game won't let you take one with you. Or even a pack brahmin, for that matter. For crying out loud, Daggerfall, the second Elder Scrolls game, was happy to let you take a horse and cart with you to carry loads of stuff. And Fallout 2 let you have a car. Both of those ancestors to F4 are from the '90!
Ugh. I'm getting ranty. Time to wrap this up.
TL;DR Fallout 4 is more of an action game than a roleplaying game, and should probably be played with loads of mods. If you want something similar to Fallout 3: this is the game for you. If you want something similar to New Vegas: best to skip this one.
