Thinking about whether this game deserves a positive review or not is pretty hard. Ultimately, it can be cheap, but also can be surprisingly fun enough at times that I believe it's worth a try if you enjoy time management games.
Like I stated, Twelve Labours of Hercules is a fairly simple time management game where you have to reach an objective, which can change between levels. There are enough different gameplay elements added in to keep you coming back, with different bonuses available for use and others. At the end of each 10 stages, you get to play a minigame, which I'll get back to later. The game lacks a clear storyline, making you wonder why you're trying reach some artifact or find Prometheus when your real goal is to save your wife. However, this game is also very easy, and it didn't take very long to fully complete the game, so don't expect a real challenge.
The main problem is that the production value can be very low at times. The drawn backgrounds look great, and the cutscenes aren't terrible either. The real failure here are the 3d graphics. They range from cheap to hilarious, and really bring down the game. Especially the minigames, which can look completely ridiculous. The sound effects for them are on the same level. Many different assets are reused frequently, and this is why the company's managed to make three more games in less than a year.
Anyways, if you want a casual, easy time management game, try this out, but expect some weirder moments. You can grab this for an absurdly cheap price on sale anyways, so why not?

This game is great, it really is. I love the artstyle, the music, the gameplay, the mechanics... I love almost every single aspect of this with every fiber of my soul.
So, why not recommend it?
Two words: Bad Optimization.
I can let "the every now and then bug that shows up" pass, that one thing that wasn't supposed to happen but it's acceptable to me, even as going as far as being okay when the game crashes during very rare (and random) intervals when doing stuff.
But even when I'm a fan as hard as I am and my love for the XCOM series is as disgusting as for me to let pass almost all that stuff that shouldn't be in a full release game, what makes me not recommend it is how it runs so poorly.
It feels like I'm running Crysis at max settings, my computer will hardly reach 30 FPS during gameplay, there are FPS spikes when it bumps to 1-5 during load screens / actions, the customization took me hours since the loading of the assets is quite slow and induces the system to drop FPS...
Keep in mind that I can run The Witcher 3, Titanfall 2, even MGSV at 60 FPS with minimal FPS drop, yet I hardly can prepare myself mentally and reassure that the game is fun every 3 missions despite the progress feeling like 5 times slower than it should be. This game runs worse than PC Ports like Nier: Automata or  Dragon's Dogma.
I'll always love you XCOM 2, but until I get a monster PC that can run you at medium settings without entering the next state of being and reaching temperatures hotter than the core of the planet, I can't forgive you for this.

(This is focused on being captain, which will only be a minor part of the game for most people).
Do you know the games where the description says something like: "Climb to ranks to become the greatest captain there ever was".
That usually just means that you go through some pre-determined single-player campaign, where completing some set line of missions means you are now the baddest captain of them all (looking at you Black Flag).
Blackwake is different, because everything involves actual people.
You can "climb the ranks" to become a respected captain, but doing so involves first being a good crew-member, then being a good captain, that is actually respected among the very real crew.
Being captain might seem easy, but it actually involves a suprising amount of skill. A good captain on a noob server (of which there are many this close after release), can easily turn the tides to his favor.
And as it says in the description; communication is key. If you do not intend to use a microphone (heavily), then your carrier as captain will be very short.

I'm sure, like many of you who own this game now (or purchased the key to the alpha (beta alpha? Grumpy Drop Bear edition?)), you're holding out a little bit of hope that the game will be like what we were told it would be like. In depth character customization options, armors that really mean something, different levels of loot aquisition, tons of fun little features, the full monty. Of course, I wasn't expecting this right from the getgo, but I had to confess, it was a little disappointing that what we were told wasn't entirely what we got. What it is, at its core, is a fair number of features short of a version of Random Number Generator Terraria in space.
A friend of mine asked me, "Dude, have you seriously been playing that game for four days straight after release?" To which I do not remember the reply, because I was exhausted from playing other games for four days straight, forgetting entirely that Starbound was still running in the background (which is my fault, really, but...)  unknown to me. Did I have fun playing what was there? Yes. Do I regret my purchase? No, because the team has finally unfrozen themselves from the London frost, and are actively working on the game. Not on features I would prefer them to work on, but then, I thought this would be a different game altogether. I'll hold off my opinion until they actually officially "release" the game as they had intended it to be, but at the moment, not really worth the purchase.
I hope some day it is, but until then, I'm gonna be a little grumpy about it.

I like the game so far.  I think it has captured some of the spirit of both MOO and MOO2.  Although it is early access, its playable and fun against the computer opponents, although they can be somewhat predictable.  Settle a colony near a computer opponent, when they ask you not too, and in my experience they almost always attack soon.
This is my opinion after playing a few EA2 games, and 2 EA3 games, one  I'm about 500 turns into.
Pros:
Voiceovers - well done and I appreciate the celebrity choices to do the voice overs.
Ship graphics - I like the ship graphics.  Each alien race has a unique style which I like.  Watching combat between the ships in tactical combat is fun, especially when you have a Titan launch a bunch of Plasma torpedos at a Star Base or hit a ship with 10 Graviton beams at once, or watch point defense phasors wipe out a group of missiles coming towards your Battleship.  :)
Colony cutscenes - Well done and fun to watch, and the cutscene includes the colony ship that matches the ship style of the Alien race you are playing.
Galaxy map and overview - I think its well done and I can usually follow what's going on and where everything is moving over a section of the galaxy.
Sounds and music - I like most of what has been done so far.
Colony view screen - shows most of the information I need to know and I like they way the build queue is setup.
Alien Diplomacy screen - I think this is well done and I like the different backgrounds and animations for each leader.
Tech Tree - A lot of tech to research and most of the weapons from MOO/MOO2 seem to be in the tree.  Takes a while to research up to Doom Stars, stellar converters, mauler, sub-space teleport, etc, so it seems like the game is reasonably well balanced in this regard.
Its addictive and fun - If I start a gaming session, its difficult to stop without playing at least a couple hours.
Cons:
Some Bugs - The game is still early access and has some bugs.  Its very playable, but it has crashed or locked up on me a few times.  The new ship designer in EA3 caused one crash, and I've had the game lock up going into tactical combat on 2 occasions.
Advisor Voiceover repetition - For the research the advisor animations and voiceovers are fun for a bit, but since they pick from a limited set of dialog, it does start to get old in a long game.  Although I will call out that each alien's advisors say a different set of dialog and they can be a bit humorous at times.
Combat - I have tried to take control of combat from the AI, but its not real intuitive how to control all the ships systems.  I did figure out there was a min-max range slider control and another control for ship speed.   That was EA2, I haven't figured out how to control combat in EA3.
Colony auto-build - the auto build doesn't always work that great.  It always seems to build a marine barracks first on a new planet, and then goes to missile base, starbase, etc.  It seems very defense/military biased even if you have the colony set on "balanced".  This can be a problem if the new planet needs food or production as a higher priority at the moment.
Bombing doesn't seem to work much better or differently after you upgrade to fusion bombs or anti-matter.  I was playing an EA3 game last night and had to bomb colonies 5 or more times with 2 cruisers and several destroyers and sometimes only a couple buildings or one population would get knocked out.
Antarans aren't around as far as I can tell, and there is only the guardian at Orion and some space monsters.  I hated the Antarans in MOO2, but they did make the game more interesting and it was fun once you had enough ships and tech to beat them.  It might be nice to have Antarans attack as an game "option".
Limited AI Opponents - I have played against up to 5 computer opponents, but the game won't support more than 5 as far as I can figure out.

WARNING: THIS GAME IS IN DEVELOPMENT! IF YOU ARE LOOKING FOR A FULL and FLAWLESS EXPERIENCE PLEASE KEEP THIS GAME ON YOUR WISH LIST AND CHECK BACK WHEN ITS DONE!
Now, I will be reviewing this with the question in mind being : ''Would I enjoy this games current and future content and should I support this games development?''
----------------GRAPHICS---------------------
For some people this is important for others it is not but because graphics are always a part of a game I hope I can give you a good indication from what you can expect and how good your pc might be able to handle it.
I play the game on high graphics settings and it runs smooth with very few amounts of frame drops. I have a medium ranged pc so I am pretty suprised I can actually do that however it varies for most people. Don't be worried though, you don't need the game on highest settings to make it look good. The textures are well done and sailing into storms can be a beautiful experience. You can get really easily immersed into the game and soon enough you will find yerself talking in a pirate accent.... or atleast thats what happend to me.
----------------OPTIONS---------------------
The game has a great amount of options for example the graphics options as can be seen here:
You can also rebind your keys may you so desire
----------------COMMUNICATION IS KEY---------------------
What is a good crew with a bad captain? Nothing! This game empathizes on teamwork this can really add to the immersion and fun to the game however this does not mean you are forced to do one job on the ship. You can repair the sails, holes, bow, douse fires, fire cannons, repair cannons, resupply, load the cannons, board ships and even mutiny your captain ;). If you hate it to climb the masts to repair the sails there will be always somebody else to do it also don't worry when there are few players on your ship since tasks will be made easier to do. If  you would like to you can even fire an whole broadside alone however I can't promise you you will hit anything or that your team mates won't become angry because you just fired their just loaded cannon.
This game also offers full mic support however don't worry if you don't got one, there are many voice commands in game. Even though a mic is adviced for a captain it is possible to do it without.
----------------PROGRESSION---------------------
This game uses cosmetics for level up rewards. Some may find this boring but this helps greatly to maintain the ballance in the game. When you join a crew all weapons and items in game will be available to you this will prevent an unfair fight. There are some guns/items definitly better than others so you will see them used more often but this is part of the ongoing ballancing since its still an in development game. But don't underestimate the cosmetic unlocks as you can truely make your character look epic and unique with probably more cosmetics added overtime.
----------------GAMEPLAY---------------------
The most important part about a game according to me. Now to be fair the gameplay in BlackWake is VERY basic. And can be mastered in the first match you play. The gameplay being basic does mean that is a very casual game and easy to get into that also makes it a great game to just jump in for a match and then jump out as there are no downsides for leaving since taksk will be made easier for the crew that just lost a crew member. The thing you will be doing the most in Blackwake as a crew member is loading the cannons and repairing holes, this sounds more boring than it is. When for example an enemy ship passes and you fired your cannon I bet you want to be the first that reloads the cannon and shoot the cannon again since its really statisfying. Also when you get a full broad side you will be under so much pressure that you just go repair holes and start pumping automatically without thinking to much about it. In the end you will become a kind of automated system that knows exactly what to do when something happens since there are not that many things that can happen yet.
If you can't handle pressure I wouldn't advice going as captain since you got a whole crew depending on you, Captaining is mainly sitting at the helm shouting commands at your crew. Fun for some, boring for others. Good then there is only need for 1 captain per crew. If you know how to take less damage from broadsides by turning and how to line up perfectly with the enemy ship to get a broadside off you are already on your way to become a great captain. Be wary though, this game does have a captain rating system but at this state I think it is kinda flawed and not many people pay attention on it. After a while there will be some people that are kind off always captain since they are blinking out and play the game often.
Boarding actions can be very fun but they are a bit weird at this moment or atleast that is my opinion. You will often see people jumping around decks slashing everything with there swords. There is a block mechanic but its really buggy for the most part. The most kills are made by guns however since you can fire both pistol and main weapon and you respawn both with them loaded again. Respawn times are really short unless you grapple the enemy ship and do a proper boarding action wich sadly doesn't really happen that often.
----------------ACTIVE DEVELOPERS---------------------
This game has 2 developers at its helm that are very responsive to feedback. They also have some notable members from the backing community as moderaters in the forums to answer most your questions.
----------------FURURE CONTENT---------------------
The developers haven't talked much about future content neither did they really confirm any thing however things we could expect are new modes, ships, weapons, cosmetics and things to do on ship. They had a fort mode in the test earlier and have said that they would like to add some type of fantasy game modes like fighting against monsters but again they didn't confirm or announce anything yet.
----------------ANSWER---------------------
Now for my answer to the question: ''Would I enjoy this games current and future content and should I support this games development?''
I would say that this is a project very likely to succeed and not to be abandoned. Also when you decide to buy the game don't forget the existence of the steam refund system as 1 hour is already enough to get a good taste of the game.
In the end it is offcourse your decision, I backed this game months ago and I am very happy with what it has achieved so far.

I'm a MOO2 player for years, so the following comments are based on my MOO2 preferences.
I've played about five MOO4 games so far and have enjoyed the experience, though there are some things that could be improved to make the game more interesting/ challenging.
1. The first thing I noticed was that any race can colonise any planet, regardless of it's type. In MOO2 you had to research the technology to allow colonisation of different planet types. The lack of this requirement in MOO4 makes it too easy. It also removes any advantage of choosing Silicoid as your race.
2. Star lanes are new but I don't mind this. Star lanes can be used for strategic effect so I'm happy with this change.
3. Technology progression is too fast in MOO4. It's too easy to get the technology you want and it doesn't feel like an achievement.
4. It's difficult to see the impact of new technology in MOO4 and some of the new technology seems to have been diluted in its value eg; Ground Batteries.
5. The duplication of the voice hints in the technology screens is annoying.
6. Diplomacy is still clunky in MOO4, It would be nice to be able to counter-offer proposals from other races rather than just accept/decline.
7. Space combat isn't very interesting. I just use auto-resolve to save the time it takes to load the graphics.
8. Space Pirates are just an annoyance really. It would be more interesting if  you could negotiate with them.
9. Minor civilisations are an interesting feature in MOO4, though they seemed to get wiped out before you can interact with them. It would be better if you could somehow offer them protection from other races.
10. The new GNN characters are funny. I'd like to see this further developed.
Anyway, those are my initial comments. I'm looking forward to seeing how the game further develops.

Wow. What an experience. Point-and-click isn't my kind of genre, but Serena was a home run in terms of what it set out to achieve. I was very, very impressed.
The narrative is incredible. A tense and upsetting mixture of atmosphere and voice acting that really got me horrified in a way not unlike Edgar Allen Poe...the kind of fate that sits and waits for us to realize slowly but surely that we cannot escape, that we are indeed doomed and there is nothing, no option left for us to choose.
The writing here was top-notch too, with the protagonist being a person that isn't hard to imagine--he's middle-aged, an author, and has high blood pressure--but the same cannot be said for the eponymous Serena, whose characterization fluctuates greatly as the game progresses. It makes for a riveting tale, that's for sure. Serious kudos to whomever did the voice acting (I didn't stick around to watch the credits...woops).
Graphics-wise, the game was pretty rough. Dim lighting masks some texture issues, and there's no options screen to adjust resolution, so you're stuck with what the game gives you. I did appreciate the floating bits of dust, however; a nice touch that made the cabin feel as old as our main character hints at during the whole game (which, incidentally, only took me about an hour and fifteen minutes; the game is short and sweet).
I would have enjoyed the addition of arms and hands in this game, as it would have put this game over the top for me, setting it apart from the conventional P&Cs out there. For a free game (I really wish I could give them some of my money!) though, I seriously cannot complain; Serena is a hell of a journey, and one I highly recommend you take--9.5/10.

This is an odd but very charming point and click from the makers of Machinarium. And like Machinarium, Botanicula takes place in an odd but very original feeling world. You play a group of little seeds and plant creatures who live in a tree under attack from some black spider creatures that are killing everything in the tree. Your group is trying to escape the tree with a seed from the tree itself. The game plays very similar to Machinarium where you move between various screens interacting with all the weird and unusual inhabitants of the tree ,trying to solve puzzles that allow you to advance.
The Good:
-This game has a lot of charm in the odd inabitants and the strange world they inhabit. Even better is how the game tells it's story without any character uttering a single world.
- The visual style is unique and beautiful in a strange way and really adds to the feel of the game.
-The puzzles are fun and at times challenging.
The Bad:
- The solutions to some of the puzzles aren't very intuitive and i found myself just clicking on everything to see what worked which takes away from the experience of trying to solve the puzzles.
-It's a short game which wasn't a major issue for me but might be for some people.
Overall this is a pretty enjoyable game and is worth checking out if you think an unusual point and click adventure might interest you. It's a 7/10 from me.

Thought that I might as well chip in my two cents, since I'm one vanilla campaign down and a third of a Long War 2 in.
Many Steam positive reviews tell you to discredit the negative reviews in some strange attempt at creating an in-group with you, the reader. That's not fair to the consumer, though, and I'd prefer to tell you to
to the negative reviews. If you aren't open to the idea of timed missions in a turn-based strategy, where you're looking at 8 turns to defuse a bomb, you may want to skip this title. Because there's a lot of that in vanilla. Long War 2 alleviates this a bit by extending timers to 10-24 turns most of the time, but then that is offset by other timers introduced by Long War 2, such as how long it'll take to infiltrate and exfiltrate a mission.
I'd also say the "recommended reading" for this game would be at least watching a playthrough of XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within if you're not interested in actually completing it on your own. Some of the elements may be more sci-fi B-movie than "Jesus Christ, that's a giant naked mole rat on twelve lines of cocaine", but the gameplay is very similar and knowing what each enemy can throw at you is second to none in keeping your guys alive. After all, Sun Tzu once said, "It is said that if you know your enemies and know yourself, you will not be imperiled in a hundred battles."
So now you're thinking, "Gee whiz, headache, you dashing individual, you. First you're saying I may outright not like the game if I don't like a certain mechanic, and now you're saying I need to play other games to fully understand it? What gives? Where's the good part?"
Here's the good part.
What you get with XCOM 2 is a highly modular, streamlined experience. Despite my eldritch-possessed laptop being easily half a decade old, I can tell through the 10-30 frames per second I'm getting that the controls are tight and the gameplay fluid. Classes have synergy in both vanilla and Long War 2, abilities feel potent, and our lord and savior Overwatch still has its use (though it's been relegated to more of a supportive role than an all-in role). Weapon modification feels purposeful and can be tailored to each individual role of your troops. Being able to pick the class your rookie gets gives you a sense of autonomy over what used to be a largely in-the-air affair.
Oh right, I said modular, too.
XCOM 2 has both Steam Workshop and Nexus support, meaning you can get a slew of mods for all your needs. Want a harder game? A Better Advent and Long War 2 are there for you. Want an easier game? There's stuff for that, too! Want to look like your soldiers walked straight out of Metal Gear Solid 5? Titanfall? Fallout: New Vegas? XCOM: Enemy Unknown? Gears of War? An unholy mixture of all five? You do you, Commander. There's also various tweaks and fixes available, such as the one that shows whether your move will put an enemy in range or flank them (Gotcha!). I'm running somethhing like ninety mods that range from giving me the sultry tones of Sergeant Johnson from Halo as a voice for my boots on the ground to entirely changing the strategic gameplay.
If I were to rate things with numbers, I'd probably take into consideration the situational entertainment value of XCOM 2 weighed against its capable content and player-driven narrative. But I'm not good at numbers, so all you get is that.
Now I'm halfway through that Long War 2 playthrough, and I realized a lot of these reviews (including mine) mention, but do not describe or review, Long War 2. Since it's strategically a different game, I'd say it's worth its own mini-review. If you're not interested in Long War 2, you can skip this last bit.
At six points in the base game, you are given a uniform upgrade to your most widely-used matériel. Either your weapons or your armor are upgraded, and while you can still choose to use previous tiers, there's no reason not to: you have an infinite amount of these new items at your disposal. Less-used items like grenades and specialty ammo still need to be produced randomly, but you often have the supplies necessary at your disposal.
Long War 2 removes these gamey stratifications and forces you to face the music of logistics. Each gun, each set of armor, and each utility need to be produced individually (with the exception of starter gear), and you will often not have the supplies to equip all your soldiers with your best items. This means you often have to weigh the difficulty of the mission against the skill of your troops to determine who gets the new guns and who gets the old model.
There’s also far more missions in Long War 2 – not just overall, but at a single time. This is managed by the infiltration system, which (flavor-wise) involves deploying your soldiers to a location where they observe enemy movements and wait for the ideal time to strike. This can take days on the strategic map (passed, as usual, by scanning) and is almost unavoidably necessary to avoid a complete squad wipe.
With each deployed squad requiring the equipment and infiltration time to accomplish their mission, you can begin to see the appeal (or lack thereof) for Long War 2. There’s a lot of changes, and not all of them are explained thoroughly. For example, I spend about as much time on the deployment menu as I do on the mission.  You’ll need trial, error, and time to really get the feel for it, and if you can’t spend the hours and stay cool when things go up in flames, it may not be for you. However, if you’re looking for something more akin to a reversed Total War (i.e.: turn-based battles and real-time overworld) about a global insurgency, this is your mod.

WARNING: THIS GAME IS IN DEVELOPMENT! IF YOU ARE LOOKING FOR A FULL and FLAWLESS EXPERIENCE PLEASE KEEP THIS GAME ON YOUR WISH LIST AND CHECK BACK WHEN ITS DONE!
Now, I will be reviewing this with the question in mind being : ''Would I enjoy this games current and future content and should I support this games development?''
----------------GRAPHICS---------------------
For some people this is important for others it is not but because graphics are always a part of a game I hope I can give you a good indication from what you can expect and how good your pc might be able to handle it.
I play the game on high graphics settings and it runs smooth with very few amounts of frame drops. I have a medium ranged pc so I am pretty suprised I can actually do that however it varies for most people. Don't be worried though, you don't need the game on highest settings to make it look good. The textures are well done and sailing into storms can be a beautiful experience. You can get really easily immersed into the game and soon enough you will find yerself talking in a pirate accent.... or atleast thats what happend to me.
----------------OPTIONS---------------------
The game has a great amount of options for example the graphics options as can be seen here:
You can also rebind your keys may you so desire
----------------COMMUNICATION IS KEY---------------------
What is a good crew with a bad captain? Nothing! This game empathizes on teamwork this can really add to the immersion and fun to the game however this does not mean you are forced to do one job on the ship. You can repair the sails, holes, bow, douse fires, fire cannons, repair cannons, resupply, load the cannons, board ships and even mutiny your captain ;). If you hate it to climb the masts to repair the sails there will be always somebody else to do it also don't worry when there are few players on your ship since tasks will be made easier to do. If  you would like to you can even fire an whole broadside alone however I can't promise you you will hit anything or that your team mates won't become angry because you just fired their just loaded cannon.
This game also offers full mic support however don't worry if you don't got one, there are many voice commands in game. Even though a mic is adviced for a captain it is possible to do it without.
----------------PROGRESSION---------------------
This game uses cosmetics for level up rewards. Some may find this boring but this helps greatly to maintain the ballance in the game. When you join a crew all weapons and items in game will be available to you this will prevent an unfair fight. There are some guns/items definitly better than others so you will see them used more often but this is part of the ongoing ballancing since its still an in development game. But don't underestimate the cosmetic unlocks as you can truely make your character look epic and unique with probably more cosmetics added overtime.
----------------GAMEPLAY---------------------
The most important part about a game according to me. Now to be fair the gameplay in BlackWake is VERY basic. And can be mastered in the first match you play. The gameplay being basic does mean that is a very casual game and easy to get into that also makes it a great game to just jump in for a match and then jump out as there are no downsides for leaving since taksk will be made easier for the crew that just lost a crew member. The thing you will be doing the most in Blackwake as a crew member is loading the cannons and repairing holes, this sounds more boring than it is. When for example an enemy ship passes and you fired your cannon I bet you want to be the first that reloads the cannon and shoot the cannon again since its really statisfying. Also when you get a full broad side you will be under so much pressure that you just go repair holes and start pumping automatically without thinking to much about it. In the end you will become a kind of automated system that knows exactly what to do when something happens since there are not that many things that can happen yet.
If you can't handle pressure I wouldn't advice going as captain since you got a whole crew depending on you, Captaining is mainly sitting at the helm shouting commands at your crew. Fun for some, boring for others. Good then there is only need for 1 captain per crew. If you know how to take less damage from broadsides by turning and how to line up perfectly with the enemy ship to get a broadside off you are already on your way to become a great captain. Be wary though, this game does have a captain rating system but at this state I think it is kinda flawed and not many people pay attention on it. After a while there will be some people that are kind off always captain since they are blinking out and play the game often.
Boarding actions can be very fun but they are a bit weird at this moment or atleast that is my opinion. You will often see people jumping around decks slashing everything with there swords. There is a block mechanic but its really buggy for the most part. The most kills are made by guns however since you can fire both pistol and main weapon and you respawn both with them loaded again. Respawn times are really short unless you grapple the enemy ship and do a proper boarding action wich sadly doesn't really happen that often.
----------------ACTIVE DEVELOPERS---------------------
This game has 2 developers at its helm that are very responsive to feedback. They also have some notable members from the backing community as moderaters in the forums to answer most your questions.
----------------FURURE CONTENT---------------------
The developers haven't talked much about future content neither did they really confirm any thing however things we could expect are new modes, ships, weapons, cosmetics and things to do on ship. They had a fort mode in the test earlier and have said that they would like to add some type of fantasy game modes like fighting against monsters but again they didn't confirm or announce anything yet.
----------------ANSWER---------------------
Now for my answer to the question: ''Would I enjoy this games current and future content and should I support this games development?''
I would say that this is a project very likely to succeed and not to be abandoned. Also when you decide to buy the game don't forget the existence of the steam refund system as 1 hour is already enough to get a good taste of the game.
In the end it is offcourse your decision, I backed this game months ago and I am very happy with what it has achieved so far.

Here's the TL;DR of my lengthy review as of the latest patch
:
Although it is in Early Access and most developers and fans will insist there's time for change, the game's core mechanics seem finalized, and it is those core mechanics that are deeply flawed, making for an
,
, and
experience. Unless you are a casual player, I do not recommend this game.
If you're still reading, you're probably curious to know why I feel this way. Let's start with what I
those core mechanics are, and what makes them deeply flawed. There are three, and you've seen them before in other, better games:
I don't believe diplomacy is a core mechanic, and I am fairly confident it will
become one, as spending just a few minutes in-game will show you how easy it is to abuse negotiations, and how illogical--and obnoxious--the AI is; in
match I've played (single/multiplayer) the AI demands credits from me, regardless of our relationship or my behavior, and if I fail to appease them, war is soon declared. If you've played even a handful of other 4x titles, this should sound quite familiar.
Planetary management consists of dragging and dropping colonists across three lines of resources: research, food, and production. The resources earned every turn depend on the planet type and the planet's modifiers (mostly positive, and a few negative), mid/late-game research, and specialized buildings, but consecutive colonists in a line provide diminished returns on resources. At a glance, it might seem worth it to distribute your colonists in a balanced fashion, but as a resource, food is overwhelmingly powerful, and as the research tree is terrible (technologies impact your empire in a lopsided manner) there's almost no reason to
assign colonists to research over food or production.
The turns needed to produce new colonists from food are on a relatively linear curve, meaning that the sooner you start massing food, the sooner you cap out your colonists. There is no "soft" cap on your colonists, only a maximum that the planet can support; you'd think that certain buildings would be required to steadily increase how many colonists you can sustain and provide for--especially on inhospitable planets--but the developers opted instead to determine that "hard" cap from a planet's size, not from it's structures, and reduce the available food on those inhospitable planets. This means that it is still desirable to colonize small worlds; in other games, small worlds are undesirable, as many turns/credits are needed to build/buyout structures which increase the population cap.
Terraforming a world can increase the maximum colonists that it can support, and a handful of late-game technologies can be researched that also increase this maximum (it is important to note that these technologies apply to
of your worlds), but the turns needed for these two things are substantial, and typically the game is decisive by the time they're available to you.
The only reason a player might be inclined to
mass food is the dimishing return, but this penalty is minor, and unless it is tuned to become quite severe, it will remain irrelevant. Immediately prioritizing food will make your worlds much, much stronger in far fewer turns than opponents who do not. Some of you might be saying that I am mistaken, that prioritizing food means you're sacrificing something critical elsewhere, like system defenses or ships, but considering the poor design choice of star lanes and scanners (structures that reveal incoming ships), you have potentially
of turns to adjust your production in response to threats. And since you will be earning more credits per turn than otherwise, you can afford more and earlier buyouts.
If structures were required to increase the cap on your colonists and/or they tuned the diminishing return on food, it could allow for more diverse gameplay. Unfortunately, that is unlikely to happen, as the bulk of gameplay is tied to what you research, and as I said earlier, the research tree is terrible.
The majority of it feels required, not optional, leaving little room for experimentation or alternate strategies. There's a clear meta. This problem is compounded by the incredible number of prerequisites required for each successive research.
You replace newly unlocked technologies--particularly for ships--with even newer ones before the effects of the former are even felt; it is possible to have your newest ships become nearly obsolete after only a handful of turns. Considering how long it can take ships to travel across your controlled systems, they're unlikely to even see combat before becoming obsolete. This happens constantly throughout all stages of the game, and keep in mind that I never prioritize research; I unlock technologies at a slower rate than was intended.
Few technologies feel satisfying. The developers had some technologies that were binary; you chose one or the other, and that was it. In the most recent patch, the developers changed a substantial number of technologies to binary. This would be an issue if not for the fact that you can get an upgraded version the technology you did
select in the
next research, making that previous choice completely pointless. This happens constantly throughout the research tree.
Outside of structures that modify your resources, the bulk of what you earn from the research tree feels
. This is constrasted by extremely overpowered technologies scattered in the tree, like the battle pods, or an empire-wide reduction in the production needed for structures and ships. Some technologies should require a minimum number of research-oriented structures before they can be unlocked--at least then I'd be penalized for not focusing on it, and players who do feel satisfied when they're given those overpowered technologies.
This is how a battle begins: each fleet deploys on the far side of a randomly generated field. There is often debris, like asteroids, in the field. When you un-pause (battles are paused by default), your ships immediately move towards the enemy fleet, regardless of their equipped weaponry, and they immediately fire any weapons that are in range. I have watched so many battles (spectating combat is only available in singleplayer) where a salvo of missiles fly right into an asteroid. Fire that gunner, please. If that doesn't happen, the salvo destroys an enemy ship. Because missiles have the longest range of any weapon, the first salvo effectively determines the battle. Fully armed, every generation of ships I produce equipped with missiles is guaranteed to destroy at least two enemy ships. There is no reason to equip any other kind of weaponry, especially when you unlock a "special" for your ship that gives missiles secondary targets.
Point defenses and weapon modifiers that take up more space within your ships are either unimplemented or a waste; and even if they were neither of those two things, the AI that brings your ships into what is basically melee range completely removes any advantages they might offer. Why do my missiles need more speed or armor when they're being fired point-blank? Why does my ship move into melee range in the first place?
I don't have enough characters to further explain the other lacking aspects of this game.

Assassin's Creed Unity is like the other games but with a twist.
You are able to customize your character way more than the other games could offer. This includes colors, hoods, belts, etc. While this may not be important to some, it sure can be immersive if one chooses to play that way.
One other cool feature is the outfits system. This allows you to unlock classic outfits from the previous games, as well as never before seen outfits. All in all, the customization is great.
One new feature is co-op. In this mode you play through a certain mission with another player, and you two must work together to complete it. This can give you the chance to show off your master assassin skills to other players. Not only that, but show off your cool assassin outfit that you customized. The co-op is very fun and very immersive.
Now to everything else... well unless you havent played any other games in the series, its the same deal. Aside from the story, everything feels the same in some sort of way. It feels kinda monotnous to the rest of the games. I cant really explain it, just trust me when I say its pulling a call of duty move. (COD move is where each game is basically the same with few minor adjustments)
I do reccomend Assassin's Creed Unity, it is very fun and the new features really bring out the creativity the player can utilize.

Originally, I was pretty hesitant on shoveling out $15 to buy a new version of GMod Tower. I was heavily mistaken.
I'm going to lump the introduction and the menus into one whole section. When I mean introduction, I am talking about the first few experiences a player might expect to have (coming from a person who has sunk hundreds of hours into both GMT Lobby 1 and 2).
I have played GMT for over 500+ hours, and both manage to capture the charm. Sure, there's no replacing GMT, but Tower Unite is slowly progressing into something that will transcend it.
Upon booting up the game for the first time, the game will bring up two consecutive menus: one that alerts you that you are currently playing an early access game, and one that informs you that if you have played enough hours in GMT prior to playing Tower Unite, you can transfer your credits into units, the game's form of currency. After going through the process, you are sent to the menus which are concise and allow you to enter one of Tower Unite's many game modes, the plaza (a form of lobby for players to interact and do different activities), and the condos, a place where you can use the units you've earned and put it into building a unique living space. The whole process of getting into the game is clean, but expect some longer loading times (1 minute to about 3, depending on your build).
The plaza is a main hub for a lot of activities within Tower Unite. Players spawn in the transit station, and upon walking up two flights of steps, you will see the plaza in all of its glory. People who are coming off of GMT will instantly recognize the map as Lobby 2, but there has been a lot of additions. As mentioned before, the plaza holds many activities. You could blow all of your money in the casino, hoping to reap the rewards of a jackpot. You might step into one of many shops that give you player upgrades. You might want to play a typing race against your friends, or bowl 10 frames with them. You could ride the ferris wheel and relax. You could watch a flick with a bunch of people. The decision to do what you want is up to you, and there is a lot of things that can be done. As stated on the
, the devs plan on adding ocean exploration, a large arcade, and more. Once again, this game is in early access, but there is a lot of content on offer here.
To gain coveted units to feed the desire for more money, you might want to step into one of many gameworlds. From the main menu, you can select all 5 available gameworlds on offer (which I suggest because trying to join a lobby through plaza doesn't guarantee lots of players). The only negative I can really think of is the fact that these games are P2P, meaning if the host is bad, you will feel latency. These modes include:
You've probably seen popular YouTubers enjoying the crap out of this mode. It's what you expect, but again, expect slight delay if the host is bad.
This mode is another fan favorite. Similar to Super Monkey Ball, you take control of a ball running through obstacle courses, collecting melons and racing people to the finish to gain credits. Again, pretty simple stuff.
Veterans to GMT will recognize this as Ultimate Chimera Hunt, but with all of the assets changed up to avoid infringing copyright. Knights attempt to slay a randomly dragon every round by pressing a button on its back through 15 rounds of play.
For those that have played Timesplitters, you will notice that it is basically the infection mode. Players are given about 15 seconds of peace to set up and prepare every round before someone is randomly selected to be infected. Survivors survive until time is up while the infected attempt to infect the survivors by touching them. Very fun and fast paced, but be wary of latency on this one.
Dogs and Cats battle it out in a small arena, attempting to gather up a larger number of balls by the end of the round. Players can carry 4 balls at a time and can shoot enemies to gain dominance. One of the goals the devs want to achieve is to make this gamemode more interesting, but until then, this mode is pretty much stagnant.
Condos are another feature that is given to players directly from the start. There are currently a handful of condos available: a condo from Lobby 1, a condo from Lobby 2, a house, an art studio, an underwater mansion, a highrise, and a large flatland to allow for creative structures. Players use units gained from play to buy different furniture and interactable features. The only real restriction of building is the boundaries of the condo. You could set up a night club, or a Drama Alert set with a Keemstar cutout. The possibilities are endless, as long as you play enough to buy the items.
The community for this game is suprisingly friendly for the most part. I remember seeing the casino having a singalong as the sounds of agony and slot machines droned in the background. I remember having a great time just talking while playing in minigolf. I can remember walking into a random condo and meeting the lead dev (S/O to MacDGuy, love you and all of the PixelTail crew). This all happened within 2 days. The only gripe I have is that this game doesn't quite have the population yet, but I hope that this changes in the future.
With the abundance of many terrible early access games put out on Steam, there are bound to be some gems, and I thourougly believe that Tower Unite is one of those games. Maybe I might be biased, but there is just something about the way GMT was that really hooked me. Granted, the population isn't as great as it should be, the devs are working nonstop to produce new content. If you walk into this game knowing that there are going to be new additions, then you will have a great time playing this game.

I was extremely disappointed with this game right from the start for the loss of the RP elements from the previous Fallout games, but I didn't ever feel the need to write a negative review because if this had been just some random new IP set in a similiar world to Fallout, it would have probably become my favourite FPS. Therein lies the problem though; I loved the previous games because they were amazing RPGs, whereas this game is an FPS/Action Game with a couple of extremely basic RP features thrown in.
I've seen a lot of replies to "It's a good game but a bad Fallout" reviews implying that we are just saying it because others have said it, but I feel that this means they are failing to understand the phrase.
If you had asked fans of the previous games why they were a fan, virtually all of them would have listed the elements that made it a good RPG; the countless number of playstyles, the variety of quests, the amount of choice you had in quests & dialogue, and perhaps most importantly, the degree to which those choices molded the game.
I honestly don't know anyone who loved it as an Action Game or as a Shooter, it was loved as an RPG.
Which is also why the second way I've seen people try to refute the argument (By saying that we obviously just wanted New Vegas DLC) also doesn't make a lot of sense. Expecting a sequel to atleast be the same 'type' of game as it's predecessors is just common sense.
More to the point, if our description of what made Fallout good was that it was a brilliant "RPG", it seems pretty obvious that we wouldn't consider a Fallout game that removed all the RPG elements a "Good Fallout", so I'd say that "Good game, bad Fallout" is about the most fair assessment you could possibly give as an existing fan of the series, considering it takes a balanced view to refer to a game that fundementally disappointed you as "A good game" in any regard.
However, a review that starts with "It's a good game" isn't truly negative, just like a review that ends "BUT a bad Fallout" isn't truly positive, which is why (If nothing had changed) you wouldn't have seen a positive OR negative review from me.
When the Creation Club was released, it didn't in any way change my opinion because I was of the mindset that I just wouldn't use it, however I've finally been pushed from feeling 'neutral' about the game to viewing it negatively after discovering that CC screws us over even if we don't actually buy anything, here's why;
Whether you purchase the content or not, the assets are downloaded with steam's auto-updates and stored ON YOUR HARD DRIVE, so they're actually taking up your hard drive space (Not to mention the bandwidth used to download it, which might matter to some people out there) with content that they then charge you to use. [Edit: This is no longer the case for PC, but unfortunately will remain true for console players, with Bethesda saying that it is required for the 'service' to work on those platforms]
However, the above is trivial compared to the worst thing about CC; the updates almost always break F4ScriptExtender (For those who don't know, Script Extenders allow modders to do more than they usually could, which is why anyone familiar with modding Bethesda games will know that most of the best mods for their other titles use a Script Extender), so the CC is actually damaging the free-modding community, since people are now having to avoid making/using mods that require a Script Extender as it'll require an update to work almost every time the CC is updated, and then on top of this most mods will then require an update to work with the updated Script Extender.

I've been a  long time fan of Moo2 and 4x  games in general. I really think they hit the nail on the head with this one.
Using star lanes  means you can actually set up a defensive perimeter around your area.  Ship design and  combat is good and the way it works has done away with the late game combat tedium that I used to dread.
Tech tree is pretty good  and it does hearken back to MOO2 where you sometimes have to choose between techs. (there's no creative trait). The only doenside of the tech tree is that it is too finely granulated. I think they should combine some and just make cost more tech.
The AI can use some work but it's still early release. I suspect they'll work on that. As it is I'm playing on the higest difficulty witht the largest galaxy with al the races  and, while it took me some time I've  managed to outpace every civilization pretty easily. I'm playing with a custom race so that might have something to do with it.
Races are fairly well balanced and I can see all of them being useful (still waiting on spying mechaism and some of the missing races) and they , sort of , off set the custom race advantage by giving pre-built race a 10-20 point bonus. Still custom races are very powerful (This game I'm using +50% production, +25% research and -20% ship cost and an disadvantage of -25% ground combat. Last game I swapped production and research).
The ship design is decent, you can't add or modify every flap or wing but you choose the load out (although there's no reason to not go for the best "systems" other than production time). Right now beams are at a high disadvantage, it's go missiles or go home (which also means that races with beam advantage aren't as  strong right now). Even at the later stages of the game there's a reason to build small frigates (I load them down with a couple of torpedoes and some engine mods  and they can basically take out strong opponents while keeping out of range). Best is to keep a mix of sizes...Also, you can only have one doomstar
Combat is Real-Time-with-Pause (and speedup) which works beautifully. I know M002 purists will hate this but it really does work better. the turn base design of M002 worked for that game but was mostly a constraint of the systems it rain on. There's no more multiple hour slog through combat (literally the thing I remember most about moo2)
There's a couple of galaxy offerings: Ring which is just a collection of stars with connections to nearby stars and spiral. Spiral is interesting in tha tyou start in the arms of the galaxy with mostly awful planets (That play through I went through with the klackons which start out with a poor planet- mistake)) You have to research enough tech to get into the center of the galaxy where nearly every planet is awesome. This makes tech more important because if you can get in there and colonize before your neighbors they can never catch up.
It's still early release and it needs some polish and balancing. Also I'd like some abilities to set up some stuff automatically (e.g.when you reach max population build a civil transport and go do either pre-designated planet or the planet with the biggest need for population).

Tower Unite - All minigames in one game
Tower Unite is a casual game, made for players who like minigames and just having fun with other players around the globe. It has serveral games you can play, some are taking longer, other are just a matter of luck and so on; I will get this later on detail.
Besides the minigames, you can also customize your home and yourself. Your own home is a big house with some rooms to fill with furniture from shops that you can buy in the city of Tower Unite. There are of course other homes to buy and also more furniture that will be added by updates and time.
And there is this city that I already mentioned. The city of Tower Unite is the centre of the game, because from there you can go anywhere what the game offers you. To the casino with lots of gambling machines, to shops that sell the furniture, to the minigames which you can play. And besides other attractions that will be added by time, there is the Tower of Tower Unite.. u know? Basically from there you can go to your home/apartment or just party on the roof with some other players.
Now let's get to the minigames, but as a whole: There are a lot of games, kinda. Not only games where you have to do lobbys and stuff, but simple quizzes, bowling or gambling and the big ones (lol) take more time and are more sophisticated than the smaller ones (2x lol). The big games are minigolf, zombie chase and dragon quest and some more that also be added by more updates. By every game you play you gain coins which allow you to buy stuff like furniture, special things for your character and tools you can use.
Maybe you noticed that I often said ''...by time/updates.''. That's because the game is not finished yet. For me the game has a really early alpha phase where a lot of things are missing and not enough things to do. But I don't blame the developers for this, because they really putting a lot of time and effort into this game and you can clearly see that by looking at their development diary and the updates that come out (nearly) regularly.
By that I personally like this game and I'm looking forward to see even more of Tower Unite.

Thought that I might as well chip in my two cents, since I'm one vanilla campaign down and a third of a Long War 2 in.
Many Steam positive reviews tell you to discredit the negative reviews in some strange attempt at creating an in-group with you, the reader. That's not fair to the consumer, though, and I'd prefer to tell you to
to the negative reviews. If you aren't open to the idea of timed missions in a turn-based strategy, where you're looking at 8 turns to defuse a bomb, you may want to skip this title. Because there's a lot of that in vanilla. Long War 2 alleviates this a bit by extending timers to 10-24 turns most of the time, but then that is offset by other timers introduced by Long War 2, such as how long it'll take to infiltrate and exfiltrate a mission.
I'd also say the "recommended reading" for this game would be at least watching a playthrough of XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within if you're not interested in actually completing it on your own. Some of the elements may be more sci-fi B-movie than "Jesus Christ, that's a giant naked mole rat on twelve lines of cocaine", but the gameplay is very similar and knowing what each enemy can throw at you is second to none in keeping your guys alive. After all, Sun Tzu once said, "It is said that if you know your enemies and know yourself, you will not be imperiled in a hundred battles."
So now you're thinking, "Gee whiz, headache, you dashing individual, you. First you're saying I may outright not like the game if I don't like a certain mechanic, and now you're saying I need to play other games to fully understand it? What gives? Where's the good part?"
Here's the good part.
What you get with XCOM 2 is a highly modular, streamlined experience. Despite my eldritch-possessed laptop being easily half a decade old, I can tell through the 10-30 frames per second I'm getting that the controls are tight and the gameplay fluid. Classes have synergy in both vanilla and Long War 2, abilities feel potent, and our lord and savior Overwatch still has its use (though it's been relegated to more of a supportive role than an all-in role). Weapon modification feels purposeful and can be tailored to each individual role of your troops. Being able to pick the class your rookie gets gives you a sense of autonomy over what used to be a largely in-the-air affair.
Oh right, I said modular, too.
XCOM 2 has both Steam Workshop and Nexus support, meaning you can get a slew of mods for all your needs. Want a harder game? A Better Advent and Long War 2 are there for you. Want an easier game? There's stuff for that, too! Want to look like your soldiers walked straight out of Metal Gear Solid 5? Titanfall? Fallout: New Vegas? XCOM: Enemy Unknown? Gears of War? An unholy mixture of all five? You do you, Commander. There's also various tweaks and fixes available, such as the one that shows whether your move will put an enemy in range or flank them (Gotcha!). I'm running somethhing like ninety mods that range from giving me the sultry tones of Sergeant Johnson from Halo as a voice for my boots on the ground to entirely changing the strategic gameplay.
If I were to rate things with numbers, I'd probably take into consideration the situational entertainment value of XCOM 2 weighed against its capable content and player-driven narrative. But I'm not good at numbers, so all you get is that.
Now I'm halfway through that Long War 2 playthrough, and I realized a lot of these reviews (including mine) mention, but do not describe or review, Long War 2. Since it's strategically a different game, I'd say it's worth its own mini-review. If you're not interested in Long War 2, you can skip this last bit.
At six points in the base game, you are given a uniform upgrade to your most widely-used matériel. Either your weapons or your armor are upgraded, and while you can still choose to use previous tiers, there's no reason not to: you have an infinite amount of these new items at your disposal. Less-used items like grenades and specialty ammo still need to be produced randomly, but you often have the supplies necessary at your disposal.
Long War 2 removes these gamey stratifications and forces you to face the music of logistics. Each gun, each set of armor, and each utility need to be produced individually (with the exception of starter gear), and you will often not have the supplies to equip all your soldiers with your best items. This means you often have to weigh the difficulty of the mission against the skill of your troops to determine who gets the new guns and who gets the old model.
There’s also far more missions in Long War 2 – not just overall, but at a single time. This is managed by the infiltration system, which (flavor-wise) involves deploying your soldiers to a location where they observe enemy movements and wait for the ideal time to strike. This can take days on the strategic map (passed, as usual, by scanning) and is almost unavoidably necessary to avoid a complete squad wipe.
With each deployed squad requiring the equipment and infiltration time to accomplish their mission, you can begin to see the appeal (or lack thereof) for Long War 2. There’s a lot of changes, and not all of them are explained thoroughly. For example, I spend about as much time on the deployment menu as I do on the mission.  You’ll need trial, error, and time to really get the feel for it, and if you can’t spend the hours and stay cool when things go up in flames, it may not be for you. However, if you’re looking for something more akin to a reversed Total War (i.e.: turn-based battles and real-time overworld) about a global insurgency, this is your mod.

An amazing and heartwarming adventure.
There's something special about Botanicula. It's a warm and welcoming game that lets its puzzles grow organically, developing them as it builds its brightly coloured world.
But it's not just that over arching atmosphere it gets right, it's the little touches as well.
From the glee-filled sound effects when you successfully complete a task, to the grumpy grumble of an inadvertently tapped bug, the game is awash with charm.
And on top of that charm there's an overt feeling of wonder in each screen. A child-like glee that pulses through the scuttling footfalls of the five main characters, and finds a hold in every corner of the experience.
and some of the puzzles might require a bit too much prodding around at the scenery in hope, but Botanicula is such an enjoyable place to visit that it's unlikely you're going to mind.
There's a living, breathing world to explore here, full of mysteries and secrets that are a joy to discover.
There aren't many developers brave enough to tell a story without words, but Amanita Design pulls it off magnificently in Botanicula.

Let me be clear. This game is a cinematic point and click adventure game. But not as in the sense of old school Lucas Arts Point & click games ála Days of the Tentacle.
Let's say this games forte is in the storytelling and creating illusions of you making valuable choices and putting them right in your own hands. The preset is good and episode one sucks you right into the world, directly from the getgo you care and want to be involved in the main characters adventure and see what the story is about and how it all plays out.
The best part of this game, outside of the story is the pacing. Very rarely do you get frustrated by getting stuck somewhere in the game becuase you are unsure of what to do next, which usually is the case in such games. It only happened to me once in this game where I had to go and youtube it and to see how to get to further ahead in the story (The keys in pharmacy shop).
That's what's so great about this game and maybe also not so great. Since the choices are so clear and given, it leaves you, the player, with little to no alternatives to do what YOU want. Say that perhaps in an heated arguement I would like to get out of there, or perhaps in an outbreak I want to stand and shoot more zombies and play hero, or I would like to escape with everyones valuables in the middle of the night and leave them stranded and so on. Of course these actions would not jell well with the main storyline, which I do get, but in a game like this, if there is anything I could wish for, it would enabling more choices for the player to make and truly effect the goodness or badness or the meh-ness of the character and the fates of those whom the character encounters.
However, wIth the given choices also comes the responsibilities with the chosen actions, and this is why I think the pacing of the story is so good. With fever options a clearer story emerges and you are hooked in it all the way from the beginning until the end, at around 2,5-3 hours of gameplay, with some replay value if you care, I personally don't.
The Walking Dead is simply a fresh take on the Point and click genre and makes me want to play some more.

I've been playing since about Alpha 4, and the developers have been consistent in their development cycles to improve the game, often focusing on one aspect at a time. This game has a 2 person dev team, so often does not launch massive features all at one time, but instead opts for a more incrimental approach.
NOTE THAT BELOW IS AT THE TIME OF REVIEW, AS PRODUCT GOES ON, THIS MAY BE UPDATED MORE OFTEN
Pros:
- If you like guns of icarus, you'll probably like this
- Very stable and very playable pre-release build
- Can be incredibly fun in fleet mode battles
- BOARDING OTHER SHIPS AND SLAUGHTERING UNSUSPECTING VICTIMS
- Become a stowaway and time your attacks against the enemy with your team's broadside to maximize damage
- MUTINY YOUR AWFUL CAPTAIN
- No awful class system
- All weapons have significant pros and cons to distinguish them from each other in different situations
- Multiple cannon types and shot types increase strategy involved
- Leveraging your crewmembers unique strengths against your enemies weakenesses makes for a wide variety of whacky turn around situations
- THE WHOLE SHIP IS ON FIRE
- THE WHOLE SHIP IS UNDER WATER
- Dedicated server based, which means generally consistent ping
- Low pop mode makes 2 players v 2 players on one ship each possible
- Developers are committed to the project and are wholey committed on seeing all their goals achieved and producing content even after official release
Cons:
- If you hate guns of icarus, you may not like this
- Only two factions currently (Currently no factions planned to be added at this time, but potentially in the future)
- Only two ships currently (although at least a 3rd is planned)
- Gamemodes only consist of DeathMatch currently (although more modes are planned after initial pre-release)
- Noticable skill gap in both crew members and captains, and either can easily cause issues on a ship, or a whole team if one ship in 3v3 is less skilled then the rest
- Captains with voice will often be able to learn and command a crew much faster then those without (although a good player can get by without voice)
- Client side code may cause hacking to be an issue initially
- Skill balancing non-existant for sides, so skilled players can accidentally stack sides
- If one side is losing really bad, a server will empty almost garunteed
- Low pop mode makes distributing your team-mates evenly amoung ships a no brainer to maximize effectiveness and win against a single ship with too many players
- Minor strange bugs tend to crop up that often do not seem easy to reproduce, or do not affect the game in a significant way (launching 100 feet in the air, UI glitches)
Reasons you should buy this game:
- Liked guns of icarus
- Giddy about the idea of pvp navel warfare in the ~1500's
- Enjoy unique takes on the FPS genre
- Excited about mutlifaceted skillsets and strategy between cannons, captaining, and traditional FPS elements
- Did I mention extremely competitive PVP players
Reasons you should not buy this game:
- Want to be a pirate
- Want to get drunk and play (you will have a really hard time keeping up, personal experience here)
- Want a casual pve carebear friendly exploration game
- Expect massive updates on a weekly basis (most likely close to a monthly basis if all goes well)
My final buying question for any steam game at this point is "How many hours am I going to put into this" and if I know off the bat i'm going to play more then 1$/ hour I'll buy the game and put the time in. Otherwise, I say "Maybe I'll wait" and add it to my wishlist and wait for more content to be added or steam sale.

For a new 4x space strategy, their is nothing innovative or unique about this game that has not already been done in prior 4x space strategy games over the last two decades.  At best, this game is a MOO2 remake with some simplistic GalCiv2 elements.  MOO suffers from some severe gameplay imbalances:  1) random events can wreck your entire empire within a few turns, leaving you open and exposed to attack by AI; 2) Space Pirates can respawn on the same planet that you just nuked, one turn later; 3) AI will ask for/demand peace, then instantly attack the very next turn.  Lastly, like MOO2, the AI is predictable and a tech rush will always win the long game.
With the upcoming release of Stellaris at a $40US price tag, MOO is in deep deep trouble since it can not even compete with Paradox's newest 4x *grand* space strategy due out May 9.  This game is not worth the $50US for early access, and even when complete, will be little more than a modern remake of MOO2.  Sadly, I can't help but feel as if this game is nothing more than a franchise name money grab.

I'm never having as much fun with the XCOM series as it feels like I should be having. And I got to thinking about why.
XCOM is a game about odds. You minimize your chances of losses, you capitalize on your chances of success, and you set yourself up to beat the mission in every way possible. But sometimes your soldier misses that 86% chance to hit. Sometimes that alien lands a crit at max range on a guy behind full cover, and he dies.
I'd figured XCOM would feel like a new spin on Fire Emblem, but it doesn't, and for a while that struck me as strange. But it's the difference between commanding 4-6 people and 4-20 people. If Eliwood misses a 96% chance to hit, you have an entire cadre of solutions to fix the situation. You can pick him up, shove him aside, kill nearby units with others, shield for him with knights, use a dancer to grant him another turn, cast a... you get the idea.
XCOM is a game where if you make every decision perfectly you can still fail. And that's just not what I'm looking for in a game.

Fallout 4 is a very enjoyable game although it has it's short comings. The game lacks depth that is seen in previous Bethesda Game Studio games and has lost its identity as a RPG first and foremost. I am someone who was attracted to Fallout 4 because I love to play a game the way I want by making tough choices and making deliberate actions to get the results that I see as suitable for my type of character. In Fallout New Vegas (Obsidian Entertainment's game not BGS's but a proper Fallout RPG) I had much fun playing many different types of characters and this ability to shape my playstyle on a whim is what made me enjoy New Vegas. In Fallout 4 you make choices but very few of these choices actually affect the game in any meaningful way. I find myself desiring mods to improve Fallout 4 as I did with FNV, Fallout 3, Skyrim, etc. but at a greater extent than before. I am someone who uses a great amount of mods but I can still enjoy these games with a limited selection of key mods that greatly compliment the game's base experience and make it what it could have been if BGS/Obsidian were given more time to fulfill the vison that these games were likely planned with in mind. With that said I find myself finding the vanilla experience of Fallout 4 to be even more disappointing than their previous installments. Fallout 4 is an action/adventure game at heart that has a wonderful world to explore and things to discover but past that there seems to be nothing left to offer. The main quest is worth experiencing but not very tantilizing. I have not even actually played the main quest all the way through (I watched a lets play to see what happened) because it simply does not interest me. When I played Skyrim I only ever played the main quest once all the way through and never completed it afterward. The difference with Skyrim is I found the factions to be fairly interesting and much more enjoyable and worth replaying with different characters. What makes Fallout 4 seem pathetic to me is that no matter what you say, what you do, it does not really matter. Skyrim has this issue also but not quite to the same extent as Fallout 4. I personally am a fan of the combat in Skyrim and with a few mods it becomes an excellent RPG with a great element of action and adventure. With that said it brings me to my next point, the problem with Fallout 4 to me personally is that it has departed from what I enjoy in a Bethesda title. I want my decisions and the way I interact with the world to be the most important feature in these games. You can have a beautifully designed world that is worth just exploring for the sake of exploration but once you see everything there is no motivation to continue. Every play through easily becomes repetitive in the vanilla game and mods become a must. Many will argue that Bethesda games have always needed mods to be objectively good and as I definitely understand that I find my joy comes from the characters in the game, the way you interact, and the amount of choices and deliberation that is allowed with the vanilla content to be what keeps me coming back to these Bethesda titles but it simply is no longer present. I am desperately awaiting a mod that will allow F:NV inside the Fallout 4 engine because the technology in Fallout 4 is great but the human element is lacking greatly and leaves me disappointed and just sad honestly. Do I believe Fallout 4 is worth playing? No, not unless you get it for $20 or less in my opinion. I pre-ordered the game and felt I wasted $60 as I found myself having no desire to boot up the game after a couple weeks and I only got back into the game after the Creation Kit was released, which leads me to the next topic of discussion:
THE CREATION CLUB
Oh boy. What a mess. Do not pay for mods unless you specifically want to support mod authors and if that is your goal you are better off donating to them individually and downloading their content from a free website such as NexusMods. The Creation Club is little more than Bethesda Softworks wanting to get payed for the content that the customers who ALREADY PAYED FOR THE GAME (except pirates who likely never planned to pay for the game anyway) created in order to increase their profits in just the same way as other games that require you to purchase the game then have the nerve to charge you more for content that becomes necessary to enjoy the game you already payed for. Now many will argue the "cosmetic argument." I believe some games do microtransactions properly such as CS:GO or H1Z1 since the items they charge for are not needed to enjoy the experience that the game aims for. The issue with Fallout 4 is I find mods NECESSARY to enjoy the game the way it was intended to be.
Side note: I love Todd Howard and the guys at BGS but the truth is that greed is outshining creativity in the video game industry. You cannot blame the actual developers building the games in many instances. Developers work ridiculous hours to create a game they will be proud of but at the end of the day they still have their bosses who will intervene in the creative process in order to have a game that increases profits rather than the enjoyment of the customer. In short, do not pre-order. Do not buy dlc if you do not support microtransactions that are needed to play the game the way it should have been in the first place. Buy content that compliments and adds to the game in a way that will not leave you disappointed in the end with an empty wallet. As consumers and the target audience of these games do not stand for spending unjustifiable amounts of money just to get the enjoyment you expected. I do however support spending money on games and developers who actually add new experiences and content that genuinely makes the games better to you. My review is a reflection of what Bethesda Softworks has given us as this is their product. I do not blame the developers and only have good wishes for them to continue to make the games they desire to make because these guys are not incompetent in the slightest, I just yern for a day where AAA game development returns to providing a complete game for a fixed price that is adequate compensation for the developers and an enjoyable experience for the customer. Serena is without a doubt the worst game I've ever played. Basically, it is the videogame equivalent of every superhero movie made after the Dark Knight trilogy. You know how after that trilogy, every single superhero movie tried to be dark and introspective? Well, this is a fragile attempt at making a game like Dear Esther or Gone Home. It places the player in a location in the point of view of a protagonist who laments and narrates about life...but the voice acting and the writing in this game is so awful that I couldn't help but laugh throughout the entire hour I wasted on it. The story it is trying to tell is one with no justification, with no character development past charicature models, with no real reason for the twist (singular) that it takes.
