Not kidding, this is the best naval action game published so far.
I have discovered this game on Kickstarter a long time ago.
All backers were invited to play the alpha, which I joined since the first day.
I followed the game through it's development.
Of course the alpha versions of the game were a bit buggy but the testers have pretty much gotten rid of every bug in the game.
Currently running it smooth at high FPS on max graphics (GTX 970).
This is not a realistic game, the development was focussed on gameplay.
When joining a server you can choose a team (if not unbalanced).
Within that team you can choose a crew to be part of.
Every crew votes a captain.
The captain takes the wheel and controls the ship and sails.
The rest of the crew has to do tasks like:
Repairing the ship, using the hammer, fixing the holes in the ship.
Hoaling supplies, going to the back of the ship to get a crate, bringing it towards the ammo boxes near the cannons.
Reloading a cannon, put gunpowder in the cannon, put a round shot in there, ram it with the rod.
Firing cannons, using the ignition stick, wait for the ship to line up and light the fuse.
Repairing the sails, climbing the nets on the side, using the hammer to patch the holes in the sails.
Shooting anti sail cannons, slowing down the enemy ship by aiming at it's sails.
Shooting swivel guns, a gun with low penetration and a little difficult to aim but it makes one shot kills.
Boarding, prepare your muskets, pistols and swords, as soon as the enemy ship is nearby or within swimming distance, board the ship and kill everyone repairing the ship.
Currently the game offers 2 ships:
The hoy, which is a smaller ship for about 7-9 players with 4 cannons on each side, the hoy turns quickly and sails fast.
The galleon is the bigger ship that requires at least 7 players to have an advantage on a hoy, the ship has 8 cannons on each side (16 both sides), 2 bow chasers and 2 stern cannons. Being a little slower than the hoy, it can deal a lot of damage.
The game has a few game modes:
Hoy vs Hoy: 8 players fight 8 players on a hoy, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink the ship to win.
Galleon vs Galleon: A 15 players fight 15 players on a galleon, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink the ship to win.
2 Hoy vs 2 Hoy: 2 hoys with 8 players on each team, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
2 Galleon vs 2 Galleon: 2 galleons with 13 players on each team, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
Fleet: One galleon and two hoys vs one galleon and two hoys, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
PROs
- Completely debugged in closed alpha
- Most stable early access release I've seen so far
- Fun community
- Skill based, no level advantages, only cosmetics
- Game being updated regularly
- Developers are actively responding to feedback from the community
- Hilarious moments (example: see H2ODelirious on Youtube, Venalis_21 on Twitch)
CONs
- Not fun without headset
- People might rage on the losing team
- Not many ship models, these will be added in the future
- No progression, only cosmetics have to be unlocked.

I purchased this game the moment I was able to toward the end of the Alpha. It is not expensive, and for what you pay you get a very refreshing experience.
BEGIN WALL OF TEXT (TL;DR AT BOTTOM):
As stated by the main developer, the game is based off the ideas behind the old Garry's Mod gamemode known as Pirate Ship Wars, as well as a few other notable titles in the pirate genre. Speaking of the main developer, he is very, very involved in the community for Blackwake and constantly answers questions in the official Discord for Blackwake. The dev team primarily consists of two people. The game is excellent and issues are quick to be quelled, which is a pleasant surprise. The dev team may be small, but make no mistake, there has been immense work and dedication that has gone into Blackwake.
Don't let the fact that it is an Early Access game fool you, the core gameplay systems are all in place and with the exception of further optimization, even more maps, possibly new weapons, and of course more cosmetic items, the game feels pretty complete.
Now, onto the details of the game itself. Blackwake consists of two teams (Navy and Pirates) duking it out on a variety of maps. While the maps usually don't feature very much other than a few islands and, of course, water, there are a variety of different atmospheres to the maps. It could be night, day, storming, snowing, etc. This really adds to the experience, and I can tell you from experience that there is nothing more epic than two galleons unleashing fury upon each other in the middle of a storm at night.
There are a few different gamemodes available that cater to different numbers of players. There are small engagements with just 1 ship on each side, be it a Hoy (a small ship crewed by a max of 8 people) or larger battles that feature over 50 players with 3 ships on each side.
At the beginning of each match, both sides have a limited number of "tickets" which are used up when one of your side's ships sinks, or when people respawn. Whichever side loses all of their tickets will lose the match.
The game requires a fair amount of coordination and listening skills really help too. Players can choose to vote for their captain from a list of players who have opted to be captain. People who are in the running to be captain have their overall captain score shown by their name to give an idea of who is a decent captain and who is not. This is good, because a captain of a ship who knows what he is doing can often turn the tide of a match, BUT, only if his crew knows to listen. Many matches have been lost due to a crew failing to coordinate well despite an experienced captain, however this can mostly be attributed to players being new at the game instead of intentionally not following their captain's orders.
There are a limited amount of supplies available on ships. There is a central supply storage on each ship, and then smaller boxes of supplies next to cannons. When the small crates next to cannons are out of supplies, it falls upon someone to grab another crate of supplies and bring them to the gun crews so they may continue firing.
The combat itself feels very satisfactory yet brutal. You may be below decks, manning a cannon when the man next to you is turned into mincemeat from an enemy cannonball. As ships take fire, they begin to accumulate holes and take on water. The more holes, the faster the ship begins to sink. These holes can be patched up, and at the same time there are pumps on each ship that can be used to slow the sinking of the ship while the rest of the crew fixes damage.
END WALL OF TEXT
TL;DR: All in all, the game is incredibly fun and it is very clearly a well-made labor of love. For such a small dev team, the graphics more than do their job, the sounds are not bad, and the gameplay is simply addicting.
I highly reccommend Blackwake, not only because it is insanely fun, but also to support the developers so they can further fine-tune the game and give us improvements that might not be possible without such support.
You know what to do boys. Nominate this game for The "TEST OF TIME" Award.

One recommendation: buy the deluxe edition, little bit higher price but if it's on sale not too different. what does this version add you might think? well you get all the dlc's which add so much new stuff to the game so definetly do it this way because i tried to upgrade my version to the deluxe edition and it generally isn't possible. Only way is to ask for a refund and buy the deluxe version only way when i made this review.
Now the game overall i wont go into the pro's or cons because well i think it's a well made game and every well made game will have flaws. I haven't encountered any flaws that i can think of atm. the game can be brutal if you make a mistake:  being to aggresive and  just dashed to the best cover you see and oh no there are a few packs of aliens. the game is trial and error but you'll learn pretty fast especially if you've played XCOM and any other strategy game in this type of field.
Were the game shines the most is that you can create your own soldiers, good friends, family or just really funny looking soldiers. You'll gain a bond with them and if they die well you'll be quite sad that you just lost one of  your best soldier or soldiers. You'll create your own story because everything you do is your choice. The world at the core of Unity is much denser than anything we’ve seen before in the series. There’s no loose overworld connecting disparate cities or the high seas to sail your boat on, the entirety of AC Unity is heavily urban. Paris itself is a sight to behold, and Ubisoft has really pushed the boat out in creating a believable cityscape, comfortably outdoing anything in the series before. The increase NPC count is the most noticeable addition and it adds a real air of business and chaos to proceedings, with streets actually appearing chock full of people jostling for position amid the hubbub.
Overall world detail is fantastic and Unity is easily one of the better looking games out there, particularly in respect to the vastness of its open-world. While there’s obvious repetition at times Ubisoft has done a good job of keeping the environments varied, and there’s enough focal points and landmarks to distract from the copycat houses jutting into the streets.
In AC Unity there’s the usual treasure chests to track down, this time with some gated off behind advanced lock picking techniques or insanely accurate rhythm skills. Then there’s the Cockades, which act as a marginally more interesting alternative to Animus fragments, and collecting them all does actually do something this time around.
The rest of the map is littered with activities, which range from murder mysteries to Nostradamus riddles, co-operative heists, Paris Stories, rifts, and more. There’s an overabundance of things to do and you’ll doubtful be left wanting for content, helped in part by the co-op missions which are repeatable for additional loot.
The heists are a little neater, and have a renewed on stealth, the only problem being that being spotted and an alarm bell going can desynchronize the event for everyone and force a restart. Ultimately stealth games rely on patience, so once you have four people playing together online, patience invariably goes out the window, so you’re going to need quite a tight knit group of mates to get the most out of this experience. Playing each mission nets you one of three bits of loot though, encouraging multiple replays to get all the kit available.Ah, the loot. Equipment plays a far bigger role in Assassin’s Creed this time around. As a player you are ranked on a 5 point scale in regards to the quality of the gear you are equipped with. Everything from weapons to bracers, belts and chest plates comes with its own unique stats, providing boosts to the likes of stealth, hitpoints, damage, and more. Each subset has dozens upon dozens of equippable items, ranging from just a few hundred of the in-game currency to upwards of 250,000. Both gear and money are more important than ever before in the series, and you’ll finally be actually thankful for the cash you’re grabbing from chests. Using new gear on your character can make a noticeable different, extending the segments of your health bar or ensuring you can take down some of the weaker enemies in just a single sword swipe.Ranged enemies in particular can wipe you out in just a couple of shots, lending a renewed focus to stealth and the use of cover. It means you have to pick your fights carefully and make use of all the tools at your disposal, whether they be Phantom Blade’s, Cherry Bombs, or a good old fashioned mace to the face.
The stealth overhaul feels like a real step back to the roots of what an assassin should be, forcing you to think through each counter and opening up the opportunity for some slick maneuvers. This is reinforced by the return of the dynamic assassination missions. One early mission has you taking down a target inside Notre Dame, the opening segment informing you there’s 11 different entry points, one signature kill method and a bunch of side missions to help you if you see fit. Pickpocketing a guard in a pub outside can give you the keys to just waltz on in, while clambering onto the roof can see you sneak in through a handily placed window. In here you can drop down on your target from the rafters, or you could kill off the priest and take his place in the confession booth, stabbing your target through the head before calmly leaving as his personal guard watch on, blissfully unaware.
Now, performance is a  real sticking point. Assassin’s Creed Unity is undeniably gorgeous game, with the hustle and bustle of street life every bit as jaw dropping as the stunning vistas atop sync points. Texture pop-in is also an issue, particularly in the crowds. Up close the citizens of Paris looking wonderful, but stray more than 15 feet or set and the detail begins to drop dramatically, and you all too quickly realise they’ve resorted to a stock set of a handful of character models, simply differentiated by the colour of their clothing.

Not sure if you want to get DayZ Standalone or looking for something with more features?  Then look no further!  The Arma 2 DayZ Mod is great, and has so many different features already implemented.  Base building, vehicles, zombies, zombies, and more zombies!  I will say it is a bit of work to get it going, because as far as I know you actually cannot find any servers by loading up the DayZ Mod.  Here is what you will need to play this mod:
-Arma 2 (paid)
-Arma 2 Operation Arrowhead (paid)
-DayZ Mod (free)
-DayZ Commander (free, outside program from steam)
You install all those items and then just run arma 2, arma 2 OA, and DayZ Mod once so it can do the first time setup.  Then you will never touch those programs again in steam, you will use DayZ Commander to update and launch the game.
You feel up to all that?  If you do, you like zombie survival, with big servers full of friendly players (or not friendly) then give this a go!

A really good plant-themed point and click adventure game.  A lot of your attention might be drawn to the wacky characters, but I think what I really liked about this game is the pace.  It plays out kind of like a good kids movie.  When you succeed in a puzzle, your cast of four plant buddies give out a 'yoohoo!' and charge onward with an upbeat riff of music.  There are funny scenes that will definately make you laugh, some impressive sights and vistas that give a sense of awe, and dark scary environments for the 'villains' of the game.  Again, it feels like a well done kid's movie.  I'm not usually a fan of wacky / weird themes like this, especially since I didnt like it in other games like Psychonauts, but I feel like it worked really well here.  The pacing and sound design, which uses a lot of human vocal noise and mixed sound, really helps a lot I think.
The game runs well, has a good set of options, and a very clean save / load / inventory system.  Since it is a point of note for P+C games, it should be mentioned that it is not possible to game over either.  A good game, but comes in a little short since its no more than 3 or 4 hours long.  I'd still reccommend it.

If you dont want spoilers then stop reading and play the game.  Its a FREE download and is about 30 long (give-er take)
Serena and you are happily married, or so you (the husband) say you are.  One day the husband wakes up and Serena is nowhere to be seen.  There is a photo of you and her on the table, but her face, is smudged out.  You do what you would do in ANY adventure game and CLICK ON EVERYTHING!!  You must desperately search for something, Anything, that will remind you of what she looked like.  When you finally remember her face you look back at the picture, but, she doesn't look happy.  She's kinda frowning.  Clicking on more objects prompts the husband to to remember the, slightly less, good times.  After that you take another good look at the photo you see that her frowning intensified.  Going around the room another time make the Husband remember the bad times and going so far as to curse out his wife saying that she was horrible and its all her fault that there were problems with there relationship.
After that.  The Creepy side of the game starts to reveal itself.
You walk over to your closet and look inside.  You find a Corpse.  Decaying.  It looks like its been there for months.  The husband suddenly starts to think "did I, kill Serena?" "Was I so mad at her for some reason that it drove me to kill her?"  As you click around the cabin some more the Husband starts to contemplate his actions and what he could do with the body.  As he stumbles around his home he hears people talking.  He thinks its the police but when he walks up to the Curtain drawn windows he sees shadows of 2 people talking about what they should do with the "evidence".  This results in them burning down your cabin with you trapped inside.  THE END!!
It took me a while to figure it out but YOU are the Corpse in the Closet and the 2 people outside are Serena and her New Lover.  Serena killed you and hid your body in the closet and burned down the house to hide the murder.  You are simply your "spirit" ,or whatever you want to call it, Observing the horror from beyond.
But that's JUST my thoughts on it.  There may be more to this story than I thought...

Let me be clear. This game is a cinematic point and click adventure game. But not as in the sense of old school Lucas Arts Point & click games ála Days of the Tentacle.
Let's say this games forte is in the storytelling and creating illusions of you making valuable choices and putting them right in your own hands. The preset is good and episode one sucks you right into the world, directly from the getgo you care and want to be involved in the main characters adventure and see what the story is about and how it all plays out.
The best part of this game, outside of the story is the pacing. Very rarely do you get frustrated by getting stuck somewhere in the game becuase you are unsure of what to do next, which usually is the case in such games. It only happened to me once in this game where I had to go and youtube it and to see how to get to further ahead in the story (The keys in pharmacy shop).
That's what's so great about this game and maybe also not so great. Since the choices are so clear and given, it leaves you, the player, with little to no alternatives to do what YOU want. Say that perhaps in an heated arguement I would like to get out of there, or perhaps in an outbreak I want to stand and shoot more zombies and play hero, or I would like to escape with everyones valuables in the middle of the night and leave them stranded and so on. Of course these actions would not jell well with the main storyline, which I do get, but in a game like this, if there is anything I could wish for, it would enabling more choices for the player to make and truly effect the goodness or badness or the meh-ness of the character and the fates of those whom the character encounters.
However, wIth the given choices also comes the responsibilities with the chosen actions, and this is why I think the pacing of the story is so good. With fever options a clearer story emerges and you are hooked in it all the way from the beginning until the end, at around 2,5-3 hours of gameplay, with some replay value if you care, I personally don't.
The Walking Dead is simply a fresh take on the Point and click genre and makes me want to play some more.
But for 10$-20$ I am not so sure if I can say it's worth all your money.
But if you can get it on a sale somewhere, around 3-4 dollars/Euros, it absolutley is worth both your time and your money. The game will get you invested and interested, which is all that really matters in the end.
I can't wait to get started with episode two.

This is one of those times your prayers come true. A prayer that somone would come along and remake one of those classic 90's games you loved so much, without changing anything. (Almost) If you played Masters of Orion or Masters of Orion 2: Battle at Antares just buy the game, don't think, you'll thank me. If you've never played a game in the series before think of this as Civilization 2 or 3 in Space, or a more fun Galactic Civilizations (sorrynotsorry). The civilizations you can choose to play are all the classic sci-fi alien archetypes: Cat people, lizard people, greys, robots, and so on.
Overall this game at the moment is an 8.5 out of 10, taking into account it is unfinished. I have spent probably hundreds of hours playing Masters of Orion 2: Battle at Antares, and this game replicates that experience almost perfectly.
PROS: The races are all solid and familiar, but their abilities differ somewhat from previous versions of the game. This is more interesting than problematic, and it should be clear to the new player what race reflects their play style.
The tech tree is pulled right from Battle at Antares, as well as ship classes, weapons and upgrades.
The new voice acting and art for both the racial models and ships is much more immersive and brings the races to life.
The biggest change to the game from Battle at Antares is the way you can move between stars. One can no longer travel to any nearby star within range of your ships, but rather, follow pre-determined hyperspace lanes that only connect to certian other stars. At first this was a con to me but I've come around. Although this map setup can lead to the awkward situation where the nearest star to your homeworld can only be reached by passing through several other star systems. It creates a lot of interesting strategies to control star systems with a lot of cross traffic in order to control large sections of the map. Because you are able to build military outposts on each node that leads out of a system you control, you can "seal up" whole portions of the map from races you aren't allied with.
CONS: These are all minor and non game breaking, but cons nonetheless. I also know some of these complaints are because this is based off MoO1 not 2
Missing Races: Elerians, Trilarians, Gnolam

Not kidding, this is the best naval action game published so far.
I have discovered this game on Kickstarter a long time ago.
All backers were invited to play the alpha, which I joined since the first day.
I followed the game through it's development.
Of course the alpha versions of the game were a bit buggy but the testers have pretty much gotten rid of every bug in the game.
Currently running it smooth at high FPS on max graphics (GTX 970).
This is not a realistic game, the development was focussed on gameplay.
When joining a server you can choose a team (if not unbalanced).
Within that team you can choose a crew to be part of.
Every crew votes a captain.
The captain takes the wheel and controls the ship and sails.
The rest of the crew has to do tasks like:
Repairing the ship, using the hammer, fixing the holes in the ship.
Hoaling supplies, going to the back of the ship to get a crate, bringing it towards the ammo boxes near the cannons.
Reloading a cannon, put gunpowder in the cannon, put a round shot in there, ram it with the rod.
Firing cannons, using the ignition stick, wait for the ship to line up and light the fuse.
Repairing the sails, climbing the nets on the side, using the hammer to patch the holes in the sails.
Shooting anti sail cannons, slowing down the enemy ship by aiming at it's sails.
Shooting swivel guns, a gun with low penetration and a little difficult to aim but it makes one shot kills.
Boarding, prepare your muskets, pistols and swords, as soon as the enemy ship is nearby or within swimming distance, board the ship and kill everyone repairing the ship.
Currently the game offers 2 ships:
The hoy, which is a smaller ship for about 7-9 players with 4 cannons on each side, the hoy turns quickly and sails fast.
The galleon is the bigger ship that requires at least 7 players to have an advantage on a hoy, the ship has 8 cannons on each side (16 both sides), 2 bow chasers and 2 stern cannons. Being a little slower than the hoy, it can deal a lot of damage.
The game has a few game modes:
Hoy vs Hoy: 8 players fight 8 players on a hoy, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink the ship to win.
Galleon vs Galleon: A 15 players fight 15 players on a galleon, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink the ship to win.
2 Hoy vs 2 Hoy: 2 hoys with 8 players on each team, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
2 Galleon vs 2 Galleon: 2 galleons with 13 players on each team, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
Fleet: One galleon and two hoys vs one galleon and two hoys, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
PROs
- Completely debugged in closed alpha
- Most stable early access release I've seen so far
- Fun community
- Skill based, no level advantages, only cosmetics
- Game being updated regularly
- Developers are actively responding to feedback from the community
- Hilarious moments (example: see H2ODelirious on Youtube, Venalis_21 on Twitch)
CONs
- Not fun without headset
- People might rage on the losing team
- Not many ship models, these will be added in the future
- No progression, only cosmetics have to be unlocked.

It is clearly far form the best games created, but it is also far from the worst either - at least in current latest version.
Story:
Guy meets girl. Guy's father is killed, girl's father is killed. They take revenge.
Positives:
- Very nice graphics and animations, well optimized
- Good art direction
- Good voices, sound effects
- Very good music
- Likeable characters (which I found to be no the strength of the series)
- Co-op is fun
Negatives:
- The story is acceptable, there is an OK idea, but it is not that good, overall it felt forced (in the way that I almost felt they had the count of the missions, and needed to come up with something supporting that)
- Ending felt as a let down - no interesting thing revealed
- Stealth gaming without quicksave/quickload and a more forgiving visibility system is not very useful, many times it is just way more efficient to just kill anyone between you and your objective
- Way to much killing, way to much enemies - it would be much better if it would have fewer strong enemies, Arno (the protagonist) is a killing machine, I am quite sure that the body count is many thousands,
- Game design by the numbers - many things to spend time on, but mostly repetitive
- Many mission types are implemented very primitively (no mocap, or properly animated faces for dialogs, useless rewards)
What could make it better?
- Making it an RPG - really, if they would add RPG elements, e.g. weapon and armor stats, crafting, inventory, that would make the repetitive feeling greatly reduced, as there would be always change for great look
- Or making it a shorter, more fucused action-adventure
- Or by making it proper steath game - with much less killing, and much more hiding from enemies etc.
- Dialog trees, instead of fixed dialog, characters to talk to (even if does not affect the story, just to make it feel more detailed and interactive)
- Add more detail to the word, more interactions
- Even if cannot mocap all dialogs, at least do a character closeup while talking
- More dialogs - especially for side quests
How to play the game for most fun?
- Do main missions, co-op / heists, and side missions which pay well
- Can skip all collectibles, lowly paying single player missions (they are not that interesting)
- The murder misteries are OK, but if you do them from long, they start to feel boring and lifeless
- Upgrade the café quickly as it manufactures money for you

Botanicula manages to be massively cute without feeling saccharine. Its art is amazing and the sounds - mostly people mouthing sound effects in silly voices - are equally good. Its world feels like a picture-book for kids and the story is sweet and sincere. You play a little guy called Mr. Lantern, who vaguely resembles a hazelnut. He has a vision of evil spiders that are sucking the life out of trees. He gathers up some friends (for the record: Mr. Twig, Mr. Poppy Head, Mr. Feather and Mrs. Mushroom), and sets out to stop them.
As your little group moves about, you will run into obstacles that require you to collect one or more items to pass to the next area. This, in turn, requires you to explore your surroundings and click on anything that looks clickable to see what will happen. Even if what happens doesn't really help, it will likely charm you and make you smile. You'll encounter lots of imaginative, strange bugs and plants which are then helpfully catalogued in a little folder for you to browse.
I can imagine that this is a game you'd want to play together with your kid, assuming he or she is patient and won't be traumatized by evil spiders. Things do get a bit dark and weird later on, but Good - of course - prevails. I would advise doing a first run-through on your own, though, as finding your way around gets a little tricky later in the game - despite an in-game map - and some of the puzzles are obtuse. If you missed out on clicking on something vital at some point, you may need to backtrack but be unclear on where to backtrack to, requiring a look at a walkthrough.
If you want to relive that feeling of running wild in the forest during summer as a kid, gathering chestnuts and being in awe of the greenness all around, Botanicula is the game for you.

Pulstar, with its intriguing choice of colors and the promise of a fast paced shoot em up, has so much wasted potential. The game is basic, almost barebone, which is fine for me and many others. However, it suffers from two major issues: horrible contrast and jerky movement controls. The game starts out easy but soon becomes overwhelming with continuous waves of enemies. Pulstar's replayability stems from the single and multiplayer world ranking that it offers. In the advanced wave stages, it becomes unnecessarily difficult to identify enemy elements due to the overdone graphics saturation. Additionally, you won't be able to adjust the jerky movements which makes advancing in this game more of a matter of luck than skill. Finally, the multiplayer option is limited to local co-op with no online functionality. The developers have decided to keep the game as is which is truly a shame.

If you're contemplaiting grabbing the games needed to play this, I will tell you two things:
1) Get ready for a bit of frustration (though it is worth it in the end)
2) Keep an eye out for them to be on sale (They constantly drop to like 5 bucks for the whole package)
DayZ Mod is one of my all-time favorite games with the caveat that its the Epoch Mod for the Mod (modception) that I love the most. Vanilla DayZmod is decent, but nothing beats the base crafting and additional features of Epoch.
If you do end up grabbing the game, go and get DayZ Launcher. Some will say to grab DayZ commander, which is fine...I've just had much better experiences with Launcher over the two. You'll need to verify all the files, and both of these programs do that. After that, you can install mods, I'd highly recommend Epoch.
When you get into the game, spend some time getting used to the controls. You will eventually make use of nearly every listed control from corner leaning to get a shot in, to the helicopter controls, to the button to toggle your lights on and off. My advice for the first bit of the game is to find a nice, easy PVE server and just♥♥♥♥♥♥around until you get the hang of it.
Epoch Survival is then, unoffically, in tiers:
Tier 1: Newspawn; you've got what little invetory you have and you need to find food and water to survive. You'll be going house to house looking for weapons and what not. Even if you start with a gun, you don't want to fire it. Sneak around and keep a low profile. Avoid Zeds at all costs until you find a melee weapon.
Tier 2: You've got your melee weapon, now find a car or something you can sell to get a car. Make your way north and look for one of the trader towns and sell your loot for enough gold to get a el cheapo car. You'll then use the car to go out looking for better loot -AND- the car can be locked for a kind of mobile base that is safe to store things in when logging off.
Tier 3: Save your Gold and get an MTVR. This military truck will hold a TON of items, it can take a hail of bullets, and handels really well off road. It will be your mobile base for a while, and you'll probably hold onto it even after you get 'better' cars and a base. With it, head up to one of the military bases and raid the barracks for weapons. Sell the weapons  you don't upgrade with and start saving for a plot-post (on servers that require them, which is default).
Tier 4: When you get a plot post, you'll need to make sure you have pretty much all the toolbelt items (Crowbar, E-tool, hatchet/axe, etc). Find a nice spot and stake your claim by dropping your plot post. Then its time for Lumberjack Simulator 2015. Get out in the woods and start chopping down some trees and collecting wood to start building your base defenses. You don't really need a safe as long as you have a lockable truck, but its up to you.
Tier 5: Sticking with the MTVR runs to the military bases, keep farming gold until you get enough to buy a helicopter. Leave your truck at your base locked up and make the run, bike, or whatever to the airbase and buy a Mozzie. Why this uselss♥♥♥♥♥heli? Because you're probably going to crash it. Everyone I have played this game with has crashed their first helicopter, regardless of how many hours they've spent in Arma's helicopter training or Bohemia's helicopter game. Get the mozzie, take it slow and easy staying low to the ground, then when you've got it down, sell it and get your real chopper. Go for the civillian chopper, since its basically an airborn MTVR.
Tier 6: Keep hitting military bases, which should now go by even faster. If you think you're up to it, you can try and smash some bandit missions (Depending on the server) for some fast cash and good mats. Keep builing up your base and consider getting a fuel truck. From this point on, you're done 'surviving' Epoch, you're now 'thriving'.
Play the game with friends and have even more of a blast.

(April 10th 2016 - review based on playing EARLY ACCESS, SECOND STAGE release)
The developers of the new game are promoting it as "a worthy successor" to the original Master of Orion, and that's why I purchased it. Based on the current release, it is
. In fact, it seems to have far more in common with Master of Orion 2 than the original.
I'm old enough to say that I played all the original Master of Orion games when they were new. I played MOO1 when I was in university and spent an obscene number of hours on it, sometimes missing classes after playing all night. I purchased MOO2 back when games came in a box with CD-ROMs and a printed manual. I did the same when MOO3 was released.
MOO3 was pure crap, so I won't even discuss it. MOO2 was fun, but lost much of the 'epic' feel of the original. The UI in MOO2 was clearly worlds beyond what was in MOO1. The atmospheric background music in MOO2 was excellent. MOO1 is still my favourite though. It was released in the early 90's, and a PC from that era had less horsepower than a cheap smartphone of today, so the graphics, sounds and UI look horrible now. Despite that, MOO1 really captured the feeling of starting small in a big galaxy, expanding in all directions to stake your claim for more, and eventually fighting for it. One of the best things about MOO1 was how the tech 'tree' was different in each game. Each race was only able to research a random subset of all the available techs. The rest could only be obtained via trading, espionage, or conquest. That was brilliant. It made the game very replayable and unpredictable, and forced you to adapt if your preferred early-game techs were not open to be researched.
MOO2 dumbed-down some core mechanics from MOO1. In MOO2, you were limited to a number of ships less than the overall 'Command Points' for your empire. The tiniest ship size cost 1 CP per ship, and the biggest cost 6 CP per ship. The number of CPs in the late game was often small, like low 100's. Late game MOO2 fleets were not very epic.
The new game closely resembles MOO2 in several ways. Most notable is the boring always-the-same tech tree (even tech names). They also kept the Command Points.
I really hate the way they implemented the galaxy map.
The new game has stuck with the terrible MOO2-style tech tree, even keeping many of the technology names. The tech path in MOO1 was possibly the best thing about that game. Each play-through gave you a different set of techs you were allowed to research, and there were more of them than in MOO2. If you've played and enjoyed MOO1, you'll know what I'm talking about. The new game should have kept this.
The new game does have some aspects that I like.

Absolutely incredible indie game! With fast-paced, in-your-face action, Altitude keeps you on the edge of your seat. Reminiscent of an old-school DOS game I used to play on my 386, Altitude brings back memories. The keyboard controls are as simple as in the good ol' days, but you can also control your plane entirely with the mouse. Games don't need much realism; they need the simple elegance that Altitude has, with it's solid gameplay and balanced variety.

Botanicula manages to be massively cute without feeling saccharine. Its art is amazing and the sounds - mostly people mouthing sound effects in silly voices - are equally good. Its world feels like a picture-book for kids and the story is sweet and sincere. You play a little guy called Mr. Lantern, who vaguely resembles a hazelnut. He has a vision of evil spiders that are sucking the life out of trees. He gathers up some friends (for the record: Mr. Twig, Mr. Poppy Head, Mr. Feather and Mrs. Mushroom), and sets out to stop them.
As your little group moves about, you will run into obstacles that require you to collect one or more items to pass to the next area. This, in turn, requires you to explore your surroundings and click on anything that looks clickable to see what will happen. Even if what happens doesn't really help, it will likely charm you and make you smile. You'll encounter lots of imaginative, strange bugs and plants which are then helpfully catalogued in a little folder for you to browse.
I can imagine that this is a game you'd want to play together with your kid, assuming he or she is patient and won't be traumatized by evil spiders. Things do get a bit dark and weird later on, but Good - of course - prevails. I would advise doing a first run-through on your own, though, as finding your way around gets a little tricky later in the game - despite an in-game map - and some of the puzzles are obtuse. If you missed out on clicking on something vital at some point, you may need to backtrack but be unclear on where to backtrack to, requiring a look at a walkthrough.
If you want to relive that feeling of running wild in the forest during summer as a kid, gathering chestnuts and being in awe of the greenness all around, Botanicula is the game for you.

People are really overreacting to the microtransactions. They're not forced on you, so if you don't want to pay $4 for a suit of armour (which is far too much for what you get) then don't buy the suit of armour. Same goes with the rest of the stuff on there. Don't like it, don't buy it.
Bethesda are a business, businesses want to make money. They realise that they have something special when it comes to modding and they want to see if they can monetise it. I don't believe they should, but it's their decision. They're going to fail several times, as they did with the Skyrim paid modding fiasco. If something works, they'll keep it. If they can't find anything that works, they'll give up.
Aside from the Creation Club, the game is rather average. The story is extremely disappointing, not only because it's bad, but because it could have been great. I feel that the plot for this game needed to be done in a linear fashion where the urgency that the story needs could be added. The mass of side missions, especially those for the different factions in the game (looking at you, Preston) quickly throw you off from the main story. The side quests are often quite enjoyable, whether that's for factions or the odd 1 quest story kind of thing. The Minutemen are the exception to the rule there, with repetitive quests to aid some settlement and only 3 proper quests, not really leaving much space for a storyline there.
Gameplay is average for this style of game. The only thing which really stands out to me is the settlement building. This is one of the more enjoyable aspects of the game for me as it lets me get a bit creative and the scarcity of some resources really forces you to go out exploring. This is especially true if you like to arm and dress your settlers, in which case you'll need a lot of adhesive, something that's not all too easy to find. The vanilla options for settlement building doesn't leave much room for decorating though. The placement options can be a bit clunky at times and the collision can be weird for some items. Add on the fact that settlements have a "budget" for how many items they can have and you'll find yourself stretched for what you can really do with the system. This is where mods come in.
For settlement building, mods can offer a myriad of different items to customise your settlements with, make placing items a lot easier and more pinpoint, and allow you to place as many items as you want and not having to worry about hitting any budget caps (though lower end PCs may want to be careful of having too much in a small space, it can cause issues). Sim Settlements also adds a new, more hands-off way of building settlements which can be used to complement your own building. I personally like to use Sim Settlement jobs and build my own housing for settlers. I could go on for ages about this mod so instead I'll just refer you to Kinggath's YouTube channel if you want to know more about that since he's the guy making the mod.
As well as the mass of settlement mods, there are plenty of other mods which will help you change pretty much every aspect of the game. Once you find the right mods for you, this can become quite the enjoyable game. I've got over 700 hours playing this game. Without mods, I doubt I'd have even hit 70. As with Skyrim, mods are what make this game.
All in all, if you find the right mods and the right playstyle, you'll enjoy this game. You don't need to worry about the Creation Club aside from the fact that you're paying to unlock the content, rather than download it. If the CC grows to a point where there's a wide range of content to choose from, maybe keep an eye on how much space it's taking up on your drive.
It's a hard game to recommend because it's been hit so badly by poor decisions but if you like shooter/RPG games and you can find some mods you like then it might be worth getting.

Pulstar is a colorful top down shoot'em'up. I found myself enjoying this game for it's interesting design and immense challenge. Containing only 3 types of enemies, I thought this game was easy, that was before I made it past the 3 minute mark. Playing for the high score and my spot on the leaderboard, I got all the way to 119th before getting burnt out due to the game's difficulty and RNG mechanics.
~Mechanics~
The games mechanics goes everywhere from RNG enemy spawning, RNG powerup spawning, RNG score multiplier spawing to acceleration in movement. When you first open up the game it reminds you of a normal top down shoot'em'up. The first thing you find odd is the movement, that is because there is acceleration on the player model itself, making it nearly impossible to stop when you let go of the keys. But the acceleration is a constant and is very easy to learn after about 15-20 minutes of practicing. The points system works by adding 1 point per kill to your unit destroyed reward counter that adds to your total every kill you achieve. It's a bit difficult to explain in text, but essentially the first kill you get +1 to your total points, the second kill you get +2 points, so on and so forth. The points increment also resets when you get hit and lose a life, so if you got a kill worth 45 points and got hit, your next kill would be worth 1 point to your total. Every now and then an enemy will drop a +10 kill worth token which increases the points per kill by 10. Much rarer is the life saving CLEAR SCREEN token, which when you pick up, kills everything on screen, visible and offscreen, this process adds to your total per enemy killed, so if you get 50 kills you will get the kill worth value up 50 and get the amount of points relative to the kills as if you got them one at a time. The one power up you get to control when to use is the time slow device, this device has saved my life multiple times and has allowed me to bob and weave through enemies to get the screen clearing token. The one thing I found the game was missing is a crosshair, I kept losing track of my tiny mouse pointer that blended with the background at times.
~Gameplay~
Playing this game for points, different strategies in movement and shooting produce different results providing a mixture of gameplay routes. I found sitting in the center and shooting in circles to work exceptionally well. After that I found moving and doing that worked better than remaining to sit in the center. The fact that every game ever played has lasted under 12 minutes (highscore) shows the pure difficulty of this game. My longest game was about 6 minutes long. The difficulty of this game is highly welcoming for high score seekers and fans of the Genre alike.
~Story~
When entering the game for the first time you are introduced to the shortest stories for a game I have seen so far. What is there in the story is basic background to why you are playing this game lore wise as well as the funniest opeining line ever by referencing starwars in a family guy style manner. I wish there was a story mode, but I am content with what there is.
~Replay Value~
I found myself wanting to come back to this game for the prospect of being #1 on the leaderboards. Other than that, I would most likely not come back to play this game. This game does not have replay value for non competitive people. If you don't want to try and be the very best, like no one ever was, this game is not for you.
~~~SCORING~~~
Mechanics - 9/10
Gameplay - 7/10
Story - 4/10
Replay Value - 5/10
Price to Playtime Ratio: 5/10 (3 hours / $5)
~~~~~OVERALL SCORE~~~~~
~~60/100~~

Excellent Game, very well thought out with a stunning UI and great gameplay. If you've ever played Endless Space, you will love the latest installment of Master of Orion. Very similar 4X gameplay, but with more options in terms of ship designs, scales, weaponry and special modules, also more terraforming options. Unlike other 4X games like Endless Space and Civ V, when you start a battle, you go opt into a very quick real time combat, sort of like real time combat in total war games but so much shorter, battles that last maybe two or three minutes maximum. It makes for a more interseting time, as sometimes you can push through better in real time, not often, but I have noticed that units that have a lot of missiles and not much else don't tend to have a very high auto resolve rating, but can crush in real time. In terms of bugs, I have encountered one game ending bug, but that has only happened once and is to be expected when it comes to an early access game, but the auto save feature saves every turn, so I reset the game and pressed continue and I was maybe 30 seconds behind where it crashed, and it didn't occur again. Also the cool little landing cinematic that happens when you first colonise a planet are such a small touch, but it honestly makes the game that much more stunning, I just wish that they would have varying intros rather than just the same angle and landing intro every time you land on a barren planet. I would also love to see a cinemativ when you land troops on a planet and successfully conquer it, that would be cool. Overall I would say this game is definitely worth a buy, even in early access, although I would warn about the addictiveness that comes with games like this, definitely a great way to bring back a franchise.
Tl;dr: Beautiful, fun to play, even in early access.

2) Landing scenes part 2: No ship sounds...just music. I hope this gets changed. I have tried turning down the music, but the ships just float down without sound. Also, when the ships get ready to land...no landing struts? The scene just cuts out (and some of the designs don't look like the will land too well...with parts that will be buried deep into the ground and cause the ship to crash!)
3) The Psilon AI (helper) voice is the MOST annoying voice in the game. No way to shut off the AI helper yet. Please get rid of the Psilon AI voice or change it's tone. Too shrill (IMO).
4) Sol, the home system of the Humans usually only starts with 1 planet? I'm pretty sure our Solar System has more than one. Also, along that same note, I have yet to play a game where your starting system has more than one planet that you can use. Sure, late game tech lets you change gas giants and asteroid belts into planets, but that doesn't help you to start off.
5) There needs to be more options under advanced options: Such as: Minimum planets per system and Max per system. I have had several games where I found yellow stars (which should generally hold the best planets) without any planets. Also, needed: 1) Distance between star systems, 2) A "Huge" galazy size, 3) Difficulty setting for each AI (some species are more aggressive than others). 4) The abiity to customize your ship types (the models shown. I love playing the Psilons, but hate their ship shapes). 5) The ability to choose your empire color and flag.
6) Combat right now is a major sore point for many players. Some absolutely hate real time and want the turn based of the original MOO. Others are on the other side of the fence. I like both ways personally. However, The orders for the ships need to be fleshed out a great deal more. I don't want my long range missle armed ships to closed to point blank range. There also should be a chance to get some tech points or something from wreckage I think (maybe have to have a salvage drone on your ships?).
7) Asteroid belts need to have a chance to have some kind of bonus (have rare metals (bonus production/research if a base is built) or artifacts or something. Right now, they can be explored...but I have yet to find anything special about them.
8) Ship designer needs to have an option to edit your military bases and star bases. Right now the computer chooses what tech to place on your bases and it will upgrade it, but if you have choosen a missle heavy approach and beam weak...the beams on your station won't due you a whole lot of good will they?).
9) Ship designer needs to have more stats about the weapons. When I am building my ship, I want to see the range of the weapon I am placing on the ship. I would also like to be able to test my ship (either against another design of mine or against known ships that are out there), before I start building a fleet of them.
10) The tech tree is a bit limited. There are no race specific techs and some of the explanation for the techs are wrong. Example: Cloning centers should increase your growth by a certain percent. Yet for months they are listed (and any other structure that is supposed to give a bonus to growth as well) as -x%, not +x%.
11) The game in general feels very watered down. No artifacts that you can discover on planets that give bonus tech, ships or credits (though there are some things floating around in space that you can pick up, rare though).
12) The game stutters some (like all WG platforms I think). I have a 2.67Ghz i7, 24GB Ram, Geforce GTX-980 (not the crappy version).
Okay, the pros:
1) If you are a fan of 4x, you will like this game. Is it 100% ready? No. I would say it is about 70-80% there (I hope they are going to flesh it out a bit more).
2) The graphics (when they get them right) are good.
3) The special effects of battle are good (when you can zoom in and see them).
4) The replay value is good, however, it can get boring since parts are still missing.
Overall, I would rate this game a 6.5/10. It has the potential to be a 9. If future patches change my opinion, I will update the review. However, I am personally waiting for Stellaris to come out on May 9th. That game seems to be just fricking awesome. Disappointed on how WG seems to have dropped the ball on this game.

TL;DR at the bottom.
Oh boy, Fallout 4. There are a lot of things to cover with this game, so I'm gonna do my best here.
The first thing I ask that you notice is that ^^^ 460+ hours of gameplay, and that's where I'm gonna begin this; I really like this game. It's fun. It makes you want to continue playing the game, and if you're looking for something that you can spend a lot of time on and be consistenly entertained, there's 235 individual location cells in here for you to take a gander at. It's a big world with good gameplay, pretty well-balanced diffuclty settings, and that doesn't mandate TOO much processing power. I definitely reccomend it. I wouldn't have that many hours if I didn't like it (inb4 those are rookie numbers, gotta pump those numbers up).
But now, let's talk about what's not so great. The first thing you'll hear a lot about this game is that it didn't live up to the player freedom in previous fallout games, and that's true. Objectively. Compared to New Vegas, the player doesn't have a fraction of the kind of control over the plot and key events. Not only that, there are less factions in Fallout 4, all of which are much less interesting. Compare the nine major factions and countless minor factions in New Vegas to the four major factions and ~10 minor factions in Fallout 4. It is in this way that many veteran fans of the series feel that Fallout 4 was a letdown, and there's merit to that, but I really feel as if that's an issue exclusively for veteran members of the series. If the hundreds of potential endings in Fallout: New Vegas are a priority to you, then you might be a little bummed by the 5 or so in Fallout 4. But if you haven't played any of the older fallout games, and you don't want to play a game that released the sunny side of a decade ago (which I sincerely doubt you do), then start here. Yes, the dog could use a bit of Nvidia magic, but at least the people don't look like bad wax models, the physics engine isn't just a bad port of that from Skyrim, and it's actually possible to go into a gunfight without using VATS for pretty much everything.
Now, for the other thing that especially recently has become a sizable point of criticism; mods. Ever since TES: Skyrim, Betheda games have been defined by their innate ability to be modded, and the incredible things that community members will do to completely transform even the most core game mechanics with no compensation whatsoever. If you don't know what I mean, go look up Fallout: The Frontier. But then, at E3 2017, Bethesda announced a new "feature" to their games; the Bethesda Creation Club, and as much as they would deny the title "paid mods," everybody knew what it was; just another way for a AAA Game company to sap more microtransaction money out of their fanbase. It was a joke. A scam. Players hated it. Betheda's PR was trash. Modders were happy because now they could actually get paid for making their content, but that hardly justified this new, terrible addition to Bethesda's software.
Now, you may be thinking, "Free community mods still work right? So what's the big deal? Just keep using those." The problem comes in the fact that every time Bethesda adds new items to their creation club (which is proving itself to be rather frequently) the game is updated to a new version, and many mods and mod tools (including the all-important Fallout 4 Script Editor) become extremely unstable or completely unable to function. And to twist the knife, there's no way to stop steam from automatically updating the game without always playing in offline mode. Needless to say, it's a bit of a mess. Why do you think the recent reviews for this game are "overwhelmingly negative?"
It's at this point that you might be wondering, "Bruh, if everything is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥, then why are you giving it a thumbs up?" Because it's still a good game. Regardless of whatever stupid decisions Bethesda has made in the past month, or stupid decisions they made two and a half years ago, I still like the game. It's fun. I sit at my computer, I play the game, and I enjoy it. It's a big game, there are lots of things to enjoy. The gameplay is smooth, the fights are tough, the crafting and survival elements keep it interesting, and the mods make all of that even better, even if they aren't what they were before creation club.
TL;DR: It's a good game, just not a very good fallout game. If you're new to the franchise, you should start here. Bethesda has made some stupid decisions, yes, but that doesn't change the fact that if you buy this game and play it, you will more likely than not enjoy said experience. I know I did.

TL:DR
Unity feels like the dev wanted to evolve the series to new heights, but fell short on time to polish all of it. For every part where unity feels awesome, something broken will remind you that this game could have been incredible, given 6 more months of development.
It's a playable and sometimes enjoyable game, but definitely a disappointment.
Personally i love the game because of its setting, but the flaws are constantly reminding me why i'm not "enjoying it".
Pros :
- extremely pretty at high+ detail. the shaders and lightning works are incredible.
- streets look busy and full of life
- revolutionary paris is a very interesting setting
- improved combat mechanics
- a memorable eiffel tower mission
- free form of assassination missions
- a strong coop mode ... when you can find other players
Cons :
- the AI is still embarassingly stupid
- the plot started well, but looses it midway trough the game. by the end, you won't care about it.
- static state of paris : even tho the game takes place over several years, nothing actually change in the gameworld
- broken parkour : the character will stick to anything in the environment without some sort of smart discrimination, making the parkour mostly annoying and sometimes unpredictable. the controls will make you thow the controller away after landing in the middle of guards while trying to be sneaky.
- stealth is a two-faced story : on one hand, it actually forces you to totally avoid sight-detection without "gamey" things like magical bushes. on the other hand, it doesn't give you the gaming tools to make this endeavor satisfying (you can't draw the attention of guards), and results in many moments of frustration, and "waiting" for guards' paths to align in your favor. it's supposed tyo be "difficult", but in the end, it's boring.
- absolutely terrible collectible designs. it's mindnumbingly boring and overwhelming. a simple fix to that would have been to remove the chests icons from appearing on the map, and make them unnecessary for 100% synchronization. but they didn't...

Pros: Still unique in its field of gameplay. Has a base build addiction with cool ability to customize soldiers. Cons:
The missions aren't scaled correctly with the skill of your team. You'll be in seriously difficult scenarios by the 3rd mission where it's not necessarily skill based - boss mobs will have multiple turn moves to their advantage pummeling team members regardless of where you place them. The probability rolls for actions are significantly cast against the player. I have had multiple snipers on teams that couldn't hit an enemy 10 feet from them with over 70% hit chance.
Additionally, it's choatic in the way the enemies gain actions and can ambush, even whent hey are the ones getting ambushed. You'll engage from concealed mode, hit one target, and the others will get to cover and flank WHILE IT'S STILL YOUR TURN. It's simply not as crisp as the original.

This is a twin-stick shooter where you blast intergalactic parasites and-Oh why do I even bother? Let's skip ahead to why I gave this game a thumbs-down.
Typically in an arcade game you can be awarded a 1up for passing certain scores. Let's say the first 1up is for 50,000 points, the second is at 200,000, and the rest are every 500,000 thereafter.
This doesn't apply to Pulstar. I got my first 1up at 2,137 points, the second at 13,854, and didn't receive anymore even after crossing 1,418,255 points.
In my next game, I got my first 1up at 22,478 points, the second at 24,890, and 1-2 every few seconds from about 4:01 to 4:30.
The following game? I got my first 1up at 486,977 points, and..didn't receive anymore lives for the rest of that attempt.
But guess what? It doesn't really matter. Getting a high-score in this game practically requires that you don't die, so all those extra lives are just trolling. Congrats! You bought yourself an extra second of survival. When you die you lose your kill-streak, and that's a massive multiplier that simply disappears into the ether. Screen-clearing bombs are several times more useful, but they rarely make an appearance. Power-ups stay on-screen indefinitely, so it's in your best interest to save those bombs for when they're really necessary (after the 4 minute mark).
Visually, this game is a mess. It's easy to lose track of things in most twin-stick shooters, let alone one with shifting brightness levels. There's a slowdown ability for when things get too hectic, but it messes with the screen really badly.  Surrounding the playfield is a mess of clouds, they hide where enemies appear from. This is information I probably could use to avoid getting blind-sided for the 177th time.
Pulstar is supposed to appeal to the hardcore with its singular focus and extremely difficult achievements, but there's not enough there to justify giving it any serious time. Getting the best run feels more like something that will happen when the planets align, not when my skill reaches a certain level. On average I spend the first four minutes of every game preparing for everything going to hell at 4:01. Afterwards I stumble semi-blindly into a series of brick walls for a minute or two. This isn't fun, this is just me trying to prove that I'm actually putting in effort. I don't want to be that guy who doesn't like a game because he "doesn't get it". But man, this isn't worth the headache.

Not really an adventure as such, more of a point and click story. There are no puzzles to solve, you just move about clicking on objects listening to the narrative, which tells the story.
Initially, the game is very non-intuitive, you're not really sure what you're supposed to do after you have clicked on everything once or twice. You can't go anywhere, there are no objects to pick up and use with the environment, or each other. This is nothing like the "true" adventure games such as Monkey Island, Manaic Mansion, etc. What I didn't realise is once you've visitied each item, you then go back round the items to to see if anything new happens. There are trigger points that activated by clicking on items, and and this seems to be what progresses the game onwards. All in all, this approach makes the game somewhat tedious, as you don't know which object is likely to trigger the next stage, so round and round you go clicking on everything. In some ways this detracts from what is a nice short story, as you stop paying full attention to the narrative, in your quest for "hunt the trigger point".
Another fruastration is the limited range of dialog. It won't be long before you've heard the same phrase repeated over and over again. This is largely borne by the fact you have to click on everything numerous times in your "hunt for the trigger point" quest. This is another reason why you stop paying attention to the story.
The game only takes 30 minutes or so to play through. This is not a bad thing, as there appears to be no save feature.
On the plus side, the story is intriguing, and has a nice twist to it, although it's a little clichéd thanks to the movie industry. The visuals are nice and atmospheric, and draw you in. The audio is fitting and adds to the atmosphere, although spoiled by the constant repetition.

I have been playing farming simulator games since I was 11 years old (cough cough harvest moon) So take that how you may!
I love this game, but there is absolutely no way I can talk about it without talking about harvest moon, and anyone who says that harvest moon didn't have a significant influence on this game would be straight lying. So buckle in! I'll break it down for you.
Farming mechanics- Simple farming mechanics, crops and animals, nothing too fancy, you can also do things like honey and fruit trees. I like that you have the ability to plan how your farm is arranged and to rearrange the buildings if you want to. Mostly basic animals, cows, goats, chickens, ducks, and sheep, but also with the addition of pigs and rabbits which is fun! There is a horse but I haven't gotten him because he seems entirely useless and isn't free. I appreciate the collection of hay to feed your animals that you can grow on your land or let the animals graze, that is a nice mechanic.
Relationships- You can be gay in this game! That makes me so happy. And something that has never truly happened in Harvest Moon. It's mentioned, but treated normally. I no longer have to choose between being a girl or marrying a girl.  Relationships build at a reasonable pace, it isn't impossibly hard to build relationships but it isn't too easy either. You can easily build and maintain relationships as long as you talk to people around town frequently and no one is too difficult to give gifts too. The dialogue changes are sweet when you start to build a relationship with a character, either romantically or platonically. There are also interesting, unique, and realistic family dynamics, from half siblings, to sisters living together, to out of town characters. I really wish we could have rival marriages though!
Storyline- The JoJoMart storyline intertwines well with the small town farmer character you have. The challenges at the community center are fantastic. They're very connected to the game play, and allow you to progress in the story without blocking you until you reach a certain goal. I also appreciate the two different approaches to the game, for replayability. There is also a little bit of additional story line after you complete the main storyline.
Hobbies- The mines are straightforward, although the monsters can be irritating when you're just trying to get ore. I like that time passes within the mines so that you don't have to go to bed at noon because you spent all day in the mines using up energy when time didn't pass. Cooking is always irritating to me but it is there, and not as irritating as it could be. I always suck at fishing but I like the little fishing mini game, and the thought they put into having different fish in different places at different times.
Other- The character customization is simple, but very cute.
Overall this game reminded me very much of Harvest Moon DS cute, my favorite Harvest Moon game, without the slow pace that made it less great, and some of the better features from newer games. Despite it being the same niche genre, I wouldn't say this game is a copy of Harvest Moon at all and I really enjoy playing it!

Botanicula is the strangest game I have ever played. I say that with pretty full confidence in my gaming memory. Don’t get me wrong, strange does not by any stretch mean bad. In fact, Botanicula is one of the best games, if not the best, that I have played all year. I love nearly everything about it, down to the absolute simplicity of the story. It’s a tale that’s been done many times before, but never quite like this.
A fantastic tree is the home for many wonderful creatures. Magical life seeds grow from every limb… seeds that allow beings on the tree to live in peace and harmony. One day, a dark entity, one greatly resembling a dark spider, comes and begins to ingest all of the seeds, drawing away all of the life and happiness that the tree houses. It is up to a small group of nuts, seeds, and feathers (yes, you heard me right) to save their home from this evil that has fallen upon them.
It’s an odd take on a classic story. Botanicula takes a step in a direction most games won’t take. They’ve assigned the main roles of their tale to a bunch on inanimate, absolutely regular objects that live in a world of what I can only describe as magic. When was the last time you saw a game that had a feather diving in and out of holes to solve puzzles? It’s a daring move… or just weird, depending on how you view it. It’s a pleasure to play something that’s different, even from most indie games.
Botanicula is a point-and-click adventure game. This is a genre in which I am not very well versed. I’m ashamed to admit that I haven’t played some of the classics, like King’s Quest. Botanicula is more streamlined than traditional point-and-clicks, but that isn’t a bad thing. There was only one or two points in which I truly couldn’t figure out what to do, but sitting there for an hour stuck on one puzzle never got overly frustrating. I never felt like the game was calling me out for being an idiot. If I couldn’t figure out a puzzle and I needed to sit there and solve it without moving, the game wouldn’t do any unnecessary movements or sounds reminding me that I need to move on. I appreciated that more than I thought I would.
Botanicula’s puzzles are a mixture of movement-based solving games, exploration, and fetch quests. Yeah, I know, a game having good fetch quests? Well, but that’s what the genre of point-and-clicks are partially about. I mean, a lot of what they’re about are trying to solve what piece of which goes where. And, if you go back even farther, they are also “how the hell do I pick up this god-forsaken crowbar?” Botanicula doesn’t do that. It doesn’t hold your hand or give you hints, but it gives you as much time as you need to solve a puzzle. You can’t die, you can only be knocked part of the way back. It’s a nice touch.
Exploration is one of the best things about Botanicula. Some areas are completely pointless to the actual puzzle or storyline, but they’re added just so you can experience the beauty that this game truly has to offer. As you look around the tree, you’ll find different creatures and beings that you can interact with. Some of these creatures will give you cards or a pretty display of some kind. Adding the collectable cards into the game gives meandering a purpose, beyond just being a wonderful and rather relaxing pleasure.
I usually save the art design and music for last when I’m in a review, but I simply can’t avoid talking about it any longer. Everything about this game is flooring. Everything. From the silly little sound effects down to the horror that the environment gives you in the later levels. With the exception of Bastion and Badland, I’ve yet to see a game with this quality of art this year.
The music is just indescribable. Really, it’s quite difficult to do. Everything about it gives off a mystic sense, but none of it seems to fit in any one genre. It all sounds like it comes from the same source, which is excellently implemented, as the tree is the centerpiece for the entire game. The music will make you feel what you need to. If you need to feel accomplished in this scene, you will. If you need to feel terrified, you will. If you need to have a feeling of foreboding, believe me, you will. It’s one of the best soundtracks in any game I’ve ever played. Ever.
The game doesn’t have any real talking in it, and I’m 100% okay with that. Dialogue would add absolutely nothing to the game. The story will make you feel for the characters without the use of speech. Sure, there is some humming, or quiet gibberish, or squeals and gasps, but they’re varied and far between. They only happen when they need to. There is no fat in this game. All of it is cut out. You only get what you need; what you deserve.
The sound effects are just as appropriate as the music, clearly. The group you play as has their own sounds that they make, generally as a group. The other characters in the game all make different noises as well, and each one seems to fit the situation perfectly. Some of the sound effects are annoying, but that’s not a bad thing. Except for when you’re stuck on a puzzle in which you have to hear an annoying sound over and over and over.
Visual art is arguably the best part of the game. It’s beautiful. It’s also quite psychedelic. Those two seem to go hand in hand when it comes to good games. Every area on the tree is fitting to the characters in it, and everything feels… right. It’s hard to explain, really. I suppose it’s one of those things that you just need to experience for yourself.
The group with which you play all have different abilities that you can use at certain points, but it’s very rare you do so. This is one of my few complaints with this game. You’re playing as a group of five, but you only use each character’s special properties once or twice. At the end of the game (spoilers) you have to rescue four of the five characters from the dark spider. I would care a lot more about saving them if I felt like each of them had their own personality, and I didn’t really feel that.
Speaking of the giant spiders, they are the perfect antagonist for a game like this. They’re scary, but not scary in the same sense that we humans would find terrifying. Instead they make the characters (and, by proxy, you) feel nervous and uneasy about what they are and why they’re doing what they are. They are silent as well. It’s never explained why the spiders are trying to engulf the tree with darkness, but I think that’s one of the beauties of this game.
In case I haven’t made it clear already, Botanicula doesn’t make much sense. It doesn’t have a pulling backstory like Bastion or a continuous reactionary setting like Badland, but it makes a perfect balance with these games. Badland makes a perfect quick and easy yet puzzling reaction game. Bastion makes you cry and seriously feel for the characters within it, as you help them fight their way back home. Botanicula fills the gap as it sets you on an adventure that you can solve at your own pace, a way to save your home from an evil that’s never truly explained.
I love the fact that Botanicula doesn’t explain everything. It makes the experience so much more innocent. Everything about it makes you want to keep playing, makes you want to explore the homes of hundreds of creatures, makes you want to save your home from a masked villain. Botanicula proves that you don’t need a huge budget to make a game that is truly fantastic. Trying to choose the game of the year this year is going to be damned near impossible, because Botanicula gets a

Pulstar is similar to twin-stick shooters like Geometry Wars, Ultratron, Waves and others.  While it does not revolutionize twin-stick shooters, it is a very good entry into the genre.  If you enjoy twin-stick shooters, you will probably enjoy this one as well.
Up Front:
Pros:
* Nice, fluid graphics
* Short rounds that you can pick up and put down
* Good controls (at least with a controller)
Cons:
* Sound (specifically background music) could be a bit more varied.
Nice to Haves:
* More enemy types
* Online Multiplayer
--- Full Review ---
You might notice that at the time I am writing this review, I do not have many hours into the game.  That is because a single round of the game lasts only a few minutes.  There are not multiple levels, various environments, or a ton of depth.  What the game lacks in length, it makes up for in no nonsense twin-stick shooter gameplay.
Graphics: Visuals are very fluid, and the game has a nice ambience.  The visuals are not over complicated, and that is a good thing for a shooter like this.  Between trying to dodge various enemies and scoring as many points as possible, there is not a huge need for overdone graphics.  In addition, the HUD is simple and does not distract.  In Geometry Wars, the point value of an enemy appeared above the enemy after you killed it.  That is not the case with this game.  Your running score is kept at the top right, out of the way.
A note that might matter to some.  The game seems to be locked at a 16:9 aspect ratio.  Available resolutions are 1280 x 720, 1536 x 864, and 1920 x 1080 in both windowed and full screen modes.
Gameplay: With no long story or epic battles, the gameplay comes from the challenge.  This game challenges you to improve your skills and pits you against other Pulstar players via leaderboards.  This is evident in the achievements.  Almost half the achievements are gained by doing better than others or the developers (either in single player or multiplayer).  A controller definitely makes the experience better.  The controls are simple: the left stick moves, and the right stick shoots.  If you need to use a special item, the trigger button is there for you.
There are three basic enemies.  It would have been nice to have a few more enemy types, but the enemy types the game does have are different enough that this is not such a huge deal.
The time dilation mechanic is an interesting one, and is similar to the one in Waves.  You hit the button, and time slows down so you can more easily maneuver around enemies and take them out.
Sound: The soundtrack is simple and is not something to write home about, but it gets the job done.  The background music is very strong, but the sound effects are very light and almost fragile sounding.
Multiplayer: I did not try the multiplayer, but something that might make it more appealing is online multiplayer.  This is not a dealbreaker though.
