First off, to those who can't log in:
- Change the folder name in steamapps/common/ so that it doesn't contain Chinese symbols
- Start the launch.exe with Locale Emulator (on Win10) or AppLocale (on Win7) with language set to Chinese (simplified)
If you're stuck in the main menu:
- Your name must consist of 2-7 Chinese symbols
The game itself is very similar to Vindictus. You have towns which act as hubs for the players, instanced dungeons that culminate in boss fights and a combat system that relies on perfect dodging. The game looks good and runs very smooth. I had an average ping of around 360 and it seems that at least the perfect dodges are client-side making it easy to dodge once you got the timing figured out. I have played 4 characters and reached level 20 with the katana wielding emo weeb.
Pros:
- Vindictus style combat, if you can dodge perfectly you can beat anything in the game regardless of gear (every perfect dodge drastically increases your damage)
- Abilities don't require mana
- Instanced PvE dungeons with speedrun leaderboards
- Raids and group content
- Duels and 3v3 PvP (possibly more PvP modes)
- So far no P2W mechanics
Cons:
- Very limited arsenal when it comes to abilities (just 5 abilities per hero)
- Chinese servers means 300-600 ping
- Except for the main menu there are no pictures to guide international players
Other:
- Boobs jiggle
- Cosmetics are ridiculously overpriced
- Default graphics settings are set to medium
tl;dr: If you liked Vindictus you will like this game if it ever gets an English language patch and international servers.

This game is not finished by a long shot. However, it looks done and that has convinced the higher-ups to stop bleeding money and release an unfinished project. I don't recommend purchasing the game unless it's on sale or after the first one or two patches are released.
Overall, it's a shiny tablet version of MoO, dumbed down but full of tedious micromangement.
Pros-
Excellent audio and visuals.
Real Time combat & Squads provide a fix for the old combat failures (but bring their own issues to light).
Game feels like the old ones, but is very different at the same time. In a good way.
Ship design is confusing but once you figure it out it works nicely.
Cons-
Combat still has things to work out, most important is a lack of information and the lack of difference between beam weapons.
AI is pathetically weak or extremely aggressive. Mixed reports. AI has come a long way since EA1. Almost there.
Diplomacy *still* feels useless.
Random events are lacking.
Antarens? Plot? Orion system discovery?
Custom races are weak and held back by the developers intentionally.
Spying...*everything*
*Edit*  The lead dev has a vision that doesn't coexist with the majority of long time MoO fans. In my opinion, he is the reason this game feels like a tablet version with shiny graphics and voices.
Audio
-I love the audio except in combat.
- Combat - I think I heard some lasers. Can we have different audio files for different weapons please? That would significantly add to customizeability and replayability. It gets old hearing the same weapon audio a few thousand times. Engines and specials could have their own audio too.
Visuals
- Everything looks fancy.
- Then you see the same buildings on the same planets and all of a sudden you've got 30+ gaia planets with the same exact layout.  This is not important, but would be nice.
- Ships - PLEASE add many many many more ship designs. I love Psilons but why do I have flying saucers with purple paint or crop circles? That's ridiculous and is an immense turn-off. If I'm going to get 3D real
time battles, I sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥want more than two ship designs to look at. Especially if I have a long range ship and a short range ship that look the same.
- Battlefields are terrible. Some nebulae gas clouds and some asteroids on a blank canvas. Cinematic view or bust.
UI
- If you've played MoO2 and other 4x space-strategy games, you're familiar with this UI.
- Combat UI - Come a long way since EA1 but would still like actual tooltips or detailed information. Works well enough however and once you figure it out it's nice.
- Ship Upgrade UI - *almost* there. Again, come leaps and bounds since the beginning. A few minor kinks to work out but for the most part works very nice.
Combat
- The AI thinks "run in and shoot" is intelligent. As such, creating specialized roles or a diverse fleet is useless if you don't manually fight every battle. A cruiser with nothing but missiles and torpedoes should not be rushing off to the front lines. Battleships with displacement devices should actually use them instead of lumbering along while everyone else dies in agony in the midst of the fray.
- Pew pew, shoot the asteroids! Ohnoes, they shot the asteroid I ran into three times! Pathing AI could be more intelligent.
- Ships refuse to keep their minimum engagement distance, so you end up with a cluster♥♥♥♥.
- Invading is rather pointless
Research
- Tech tree is great....but feels like Civ V
Diplomacy
- I'm not sure the devs will figure out how to make a properly working diplomacy AI before release. Maybe after.
Random Events
- Few and far between. Please add more, and add a failsafe so that I don't get three or four negatives in a row while no one else gets anything.
- Sometimes really cool. Sometimes your planets get ♥♥♥♥ed over. I like it.
Specials/Monsters
- Oh look, a monster. Well, they're probably not even guarding anything worthwhile anyway. Let's just ignore them till mid-game when I can slaughter them.
- Why the F did you nerf Orions Guardian? Such a terrible idea, especially in EA7.
- Planet specials are...almost useless.
- Anomalies are cool and a nice addition, but add more of them.
Antarens
- ...wait, there aren't any?
Orion
- I love getting all four techs, this is a wonderful change. BUT YOU NERFED THE CRAP OUT OF IT SO WHO CARES. Not even worth the effort for one decent planet in the entire system.
AI
- Where's the backstabbing? The aggressive expansion? Underhanded cheap tricks (otherwise known as common
sense to the AI)?  *There it is, finally showed up* Now fix it so we don't get mercilessly slaughtered immediately upon discovering a species.
- The AI is capable of doing well on it's own, but makes few decisions in terms of other players. As it is now, the AI won't attack me while my forces are on the other side of my empire just because...well I don't know why.
- AI needs to be significantly more aggressive in each races' respective ideology. I.E. expansionists need to expand instead of twiddle their thumbs because they were blocked in on one side. Humans should be diplomatic monstrosities and making treaties/friends/etc.

TLDR: Game is very good, but needs a lot of AI improvements and a rework (or removal) of the star lane system. Some balance issues.
+ Real time combat, though it needs a lot of refinement. Ship scale needs to be increased so we can see what's going on.
+ Variation of planets and biomes is pretty good. Perhaps it needs the equivalent of Precursor worlds from GalCiv 3 however. Uber planets are decent but they're just beefed up versions of regular planets with no unique bonuses.
+ Voice acting is outstanding. Hearing "Q" from Star Trek: TNG voice the Human Republic leader is awesome. There isn't enough variation in the lines though; this needs to be expanded.
+ Visual effects are good, and the interface design is excellent - minimalistic but very much functional.
+ The potential of this game is immediately apparent- maybe not quite a plus point but in some early access games you know it's not going to become much better than it currently is. Not the case here. It could become THE definitive 4x game if some features are expanded and the game systems are refined further.
- AI is quite poor. This is the make or break point for the game. If the AI is vastly improved for release, the game could be very successful. I don't claim to understand the game dev process in the slightest but if their current AI team can't do a good job I'd hire more experts. This game needs the equivalent of Sorian AI from Supreme Commander. Devs: If you need to hire more people to get this sorted then please do it. Giving the AI large bonuses on Hard/Very Hard is all well and good but if it doesn't have a clue about how to play effectively then it's wasted.
- STAR LANES (think phase lanes from SoaSE): these need to be optional. We need a ship range system similar to GalCiv3 instead- star lanes are just a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I've read the devs are considering making them optional; I sure hope they do. It'd make a hell of a difference.
- Not enough ship templates.
- Game balance is a bit messed up: missiles are way OP compared to torpedos for example. Some beam weapons are weaker than they should be.
- UI could do a much better job of explaining ship weapon stats and characteristics.
- Research is too fast. Early/mid game war is a pain due to this; ships become obsolete very quickly,
- Related to the real time combat system: we need small/medium/large variations for ship weapons. Larger ships fire massive volleys of beam weapons (because we can fit so many onto the ships) which looks terrible.
Even with these negative points, I'd say the game is still worth the money. The AI is the main problem in the game, along with the star lane system. Give it a go at least; it's no risk with Steam's refund system.

TL;DNR = you can now play this game without having to connect to the internet first - but don't count on that remaining the case.  Steam changes their minds about this stuff at will and you have no recourse because they already have your money.  In the meantime - thank heaven for GOG.
I have recently discovered that you can now start and play this game not only in offline mode (Steam is NEVER really offline anymore and hasn't been for years) but even when there is no internet connection at all (which is the only way to force "offline" mode in Steam to actually be offline.  It is SO super annoying to start Steam in offline mode only to have it take 20 or 30 minutes to "update" the steam client - which is what happens on slow internet connections).
So my objection to and disappointment with the game is assuaged, at least for as long as this remains true.
Sadly my son has recently discovered that he can no longer play the steam version of Civ IV in single player mode without an internet connection at startup, which has greatly reduced my interest in acquiring THAT game.
C'mon Steam, stop being such a jerk.  There are a whole lot of us who don't have reliable (or sometimes ANY) internet access.  Say, guys on oil rigs.  People who live where there isn't cable.  POOR people.  People with crappy ISPs that go down all the time.  We should be able to play our games even without going to the library to use the free wi-fi.
I am updating this review while weeding out my wishlist - mostly by removing all the games I can buy on GOG - because of nonsense like not being able to play when the internet is down or otherwise unavailable.
Original review follows:
This is a pretty typical time management game - except I recently discovered that it requires an internet connection.  It will not start at all if you have Steam in Offline mode.  If you bring Steam up in online mode and then turn off your connection, then you can start it, but it warns you that you will lose all your "progress" - eg they are storing scores in the cloud.
Since I could care less about "progress" per se, that's not really much of an issue for me.  But not being able to play it in offline mode from the start IS a problem.  I am frequently without internet and in need of a time killer.  This is clearly not suitable unto the cause.
Now that I know, I looked for some hint of this in the game description and did not find it.  I really object to being sold a game, any game, no matter how cheap, only to find out that there are restrictions on it that prevent me from playing it offline.  This is why my GOG collection is so much larger (and older) than anything I have had on Steam to date.  I expect it will likely continue to be the case.

Since this is an Early Access game, its a subject of change, so I tried to focus more for the recent reviews, than the older ones, yet, I was a bit worried. Then a fellow forum mate told me that its a pretty fine MoO game... I LOVE the second game, so I wanted a good MoO game soo much. So I bought it...
This review is based on my first 10-12 hours of gameplay:
Man this game is fun even in this stage. The graphics is beautiful, the races and the characters (leaders, advisors) are great, and the voiceover... They nailed it. The pollution has now an actual effect (I always ignored this in MoO2, i could win without dealing with it), you can build on gas giants, asteroids, etc. Its much more limited (but more logical) how you can pass people from one planet to another, the time when you could jumpstart a new colony with near-full population in a couple of rounds are over. The ship upgrades are more convenient, the tech matrix need some re-learning, but its ok... The space battles are quite spectacular (especially when you arrive), but a bit chaotic for me, at least now.
Ofc there is plenty of space for improvement. I would like to see more ship design per race (I like the Meklar race, but I dont like their ships), it would be great if you could choose your color, and ofc more custom race skills and talents... I can't decide about the AI yet, since I played just an easy and a normal game for checking my possibilities.
Nonetheless, I recommend this game for the 4X fans.
Edit #1: With the EA3, we got 2 new races and spying. You can finally turn off the advisor talk and popup, so its definately an upgrade over EA2... And most importantly... It keeps sucking me back into game. I play a "round", after 10+ hours I'm done and I had enough from this game... But after 2-3 weeks, I just want to play again. And that is good.
Edit: possibly more comments will come later on.

I played Gmod Tower for almost two years. I was so impressed with what the developers of this game were able to do with the Source Engine and create Gmod Tower. I put in a little over 200 hours into Gmod Tower, and was excited to see that they were planning to make a stand alone version of Gmod Tower, with little to no engine restrictions for what they wanted to create.
When the Kickstarter failed, they instead made a Indigogo with a more reasonable price goal, and they exceded it by $20k. I'm happy to be one of the supporters for the game financially. I am very, VERY happy with how the game is coming along. The graphics are great, with the most recent update (2.0.0) they've reduced the very long loading times to something more reasonable, the currently implemented games are very fun to play, and even more to come in the future.
Not only are there games, but you can use the money you collect from games and activitys to furnish and customize your own condo, you can sit down and watch youtube videos with others. Overall, this is a very casual expirence, and it's amazing. They plan to do so much with this game, and what they have delivered already makes me feel my $200 investment was well worth it. I cannot recommend this game enough, and encourage people to buy it, even in it's early stages. The game is still amazing to play.

Awesome game.  I was a bit turned off by the 2D graphics at first but gameplay is everything.  This game is huge.  You can spend hours on hours on the starting planet, then... you can go explore unlimited numbers of other different planets. Pros:
Great gameplay.  Large universe and unlimited playing potential.  TONS of crafting recipes and a variety of different places to visit.  Lots of different items, weapons and armor to make and find.  If you like the prodedurally-generated, sandbox, survival crafting games in this genre you will enjoy this game.
Cons:
Still in beta, so it has some development to go.  A bit crashy, but  I imagine that will be fixed.  UI is a little bit clunky, windows get in the way sometimes when you try and drag things our of your inventory.  Not too many complaints overall.
Overall, great game.  If you liked Terraria or Minecraft, buy it.

The Walking Dead Season 1 Review:
Controls: full controller support is mentioned in the game description. but personally i feel shooting and selecting during quick time events is difficult compared to mouse.i used the windows x box 360 controller.(pc masterrace)
Story: the plot is episodic , non linear and quite immersive. Your past choices affect the next arcs in some way , from minor to major way. There are quite difficult choices(mostly you have to choose between two options) and quite emotional ones. May cause you to book an appointment with a shrink.
Characters: good character development throughout the game for the major recurring characters. You can build the protagonist a true hero, be honest ,liar or an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's all up to you.
Gameplay: very simple point and click. you have to sit through lot of cut scenes depending upon your in game choices. puzzles don't take much of your time.surprise quick time events are challenging enough. auto save is ♥♥♥♥♥ but you can rewind and re write/play the in game -history .
Overall a solid game with good ratio for replayability per $ (You can play Episodes with different choices.).
Edit:DLC 400 days buy it on sale.

Fun third person platform.  Mostly simple without too many difficult areas to get past.  This game took me many years to get back to so that I could finish.  But now that I'm done, I enjoyed it. You play as an alien who has a "pet", the Maw.  Your pet can help you destroy obstacles, eat creatures in the world and also change into different types of attributes.  One type is the ability to electrocute.  Another type is to be a rhino and another type is to allow you to jump really high and float as if your pet was a balloon.  Finally, you will also have the opportunity to turn your Maw into a fire breathing monster.  All of these are used in a sort of puzzle like manner to get through the levels which are short, but good.
Overall, it's a cute, fun adventure as your character and the maw plow through each level.

A nice little game, easy enough to 100% (took me 5.5 hours and it can definitely be done faster than that) plus you can make a few cents of money by buying it on discount and selling the cards. But let's talk about the game itself.
The art style is alright, it has this cheery cartoonish style typical of casual games and/or mobile ports. A new level can often look really overwhelming because there's stuff EVERYWHERE so it can take a while to even realise where the objectives are and how you should reach them. The timer doesn't start until you click for the first time though so you can plan things out if you like.
The music is catchy, if a bit repetitive. But seeing as you can finish the whole thing in 5 hours or so, that's not a huge deal. The voice acting in the cutscenes made my brain hurt though, the guy was trying WAY too hard to sound intense.
As for the gameplay, it's really easy (possibly because I played on the lower difficulty setting) most of the time - what you need to do is just click everything that's clickable at the moment and you're likely to get gold time even without thinking about anything. Some levels do require some strategy (i.e. deciding what to spend your resources on first) and you can even lose a few of them (by 'lose' I mean 'reach a state in which they can't be finished'), but the difficulty remains quite forgiving until the very end. Just keep clicking. Which is exactly as repetitive as it sounds.
The minigames are a joke, by far the easiest part of the game.
So yeah, if you feel like you have just a few too many hours of time on your hands and want a casual game that won't require you to use your brain too much, this could be the thing for you.

This is a review as of April 3rd where the game remains in Early Access.
Master of Orion is a game that deliveres on most, though not all, of the promises that the title makes. No one needs to hear about the 4x mechanics and there are few surprises in the MOO reboot.
But a 4x game can be implemented in many different ways, so I'll try to explain what directions the game designers have gone on a couple of key-points
I go on and on about this things, so here's a summery with scores on a scale of 1-10, 10 being the highest :)
Complexity: 4 (Fairly simple)
Graphics: 8 (beautiful and functional)
Sound: 7 (Quietly immersive)
Originality: 2 (Not nuch in the way of innovation)
Conclusion: if you're a fan of the 4x genre, and you like games to be simple enough that you don't have to read a 2000 page wiki before playing, then this might well be a game for you. If you're a fan of the MOO franchise and you can get past the fact that there's no turn-based combat, then you won't be dissapointed.
If you used to play MOO2 in hotseat mode with a friend and you're looking to relive those times you will however be disapointed. Hotseat not implemented :(
If you wanna check out some videos, I've recorded my first playthough here.
And then the wall of text...
Master of Orion is (at least in the Early Access version) a fairly simple 4x game. This is not neccesarily an inherently good or bad characteristic, as it depends on what kind on game experience you're after.
When I say 'complex' I'm thinking about the number of mechanics, or choices that the player has to consider at game start, or thoughout the game. A complex 4x game offer lots of choices at game start, normally in terms of which side to play and certain start conditions, as well as numerous dicisions throughout the game than often are irreversible.
Other factors include 'mini-game' mechanics such as tactical combat.
MOO has plenty of mechanics, but they aren't particularly deep. For example, you can choose your race or create a custom race using a pointsystem, but the amount of diversity is fairly small and I found that I'm able to play the game in pretty much the same way regardless of my pick. I'd compare the race selection to that of Civ5, where your civilization give you a small advantage in a given field. An example of a complex 4x game would be Age of Wonders 3, where the choices of class, race and speciallities are much more important to the kind of game you can subsequently play.
It also has tactical combat (not turn based to the lament of many die-hard MOO fans), but the choices you make do not have a huge impact on the eventual outcome. To be fair, I think tactical combat is something that will receive a lot of attention as the game developes - I'll update this review, when that happens). The game DOES have tactical combat, and it is posible to enhance the outcomes of battles if only slightly, so this aspect is certainly more advanced than civ5 to make that comparision again, where combat is pseudo-strategic but it's nowhere near as important as it is in games that focus more heavily on the strategic aspects, like the HOMM series for example. On the other hand units in MOO who fight, do not gain XP (as they do in Civ5 and most other modern 4x games). This makes losses from combat a matter of economy only - not emotional to any great extent.
The Tech tree in MOO is very, very standard, and something we've seen a thousand times. A linear progression of techs from left to right with pre-requisite techs being needed to start research. The thing that made and makes MOO a little different is, that some techs are muturally exclusive, meaing you get to choose between two techs. This is great, but since you can obtain the 'other' tech later through diplomacy, the choice becomes a little irrellevant. I'd have preferred more choices that was FINAL... The tech-tree complexity is only present if you've never played 4x games before :)
Planet and millitary buildup is a function of the tech tree, and it is equally simple. Planet structures are unlocked by tech and usually improve either, resources, research, food, or currency either directly or inderectly. Other buildings improve morale  or planetary defences but there aren't THAT many structures in total, and although each building incur an upkeep cost, you'll want to build most builings in every colony. This makes the developement of colonies a somewhat trivial decision process, that you end up automating, either my muscle memory of allowing the AI to handle it. More complex games add dimensions to colony/city/castle developement by putting a cap on how many improvements of a given type you can maintain in your empire or implement some sort of diminishing return. in the 'central star system with multiple planetary colonies' structure that MOO uses, it would be nice to have some structures that improved a given thing (like research in the whole system).
The part of the game that offers the highest level of (potential) complexity is ship design. You can create your own version of a given ship-class (frigate, destroyer, cruiser etc.) up to some pretty ridiculous ship sizes. All very cool! This offers the promise of a mechanic, where a clever player might exploit weaknesses in an opposing player's ship design (too heavy on the missiles maybe?) to exploit and defeat. As of right not the ship design feature still feels a little incomplete and you can't review the designs of your oppsing players, even though you've met them in combat. That, in combination with the unfinished tacticat combat makes this a mechanic of great potential complexity. but not quite there just yet.
Moving away from the gameplay I'll briefly say a little about the 'wrappings'. A little unfair maybe, for the game is drop dead gorgeous and the music and sound effecs have yet to annoy me.
All colonizing is preceeded by a cutscene showing your colonyship landing on the pristine planet, while all space combat shows the opposin fleets warping in. Very cool stuff, in you're into that kind of thing. I don't spend a lot of time reveiwing  this sort of thing in a 4x game as I usually end up skipping them quite quickly, but there's no denying that the game looks beautiful, and not just in the cutscenes.
There's a pretty good VO on your various tech advisors and good sound effects on the weaponsystems etc. No complaints there!
Finally in terms of originality, I have to say that MOO bring very little to the party that we haven't seen before. This is a reboot of the MOO series and it seems like the developement of the game has been focused on NOT to repeat the mistakes of MOO3 (which I didn't play so I can't tell you if they succeeded). But it means that you're not gonna find a whole new take on the 4x genre here - you're gonna find a game that you can by, install, start and be playing in no time at all, with a very flat learning curve.

MOOX is basically a reskinned - and simplified - version of MOO2. Note that MOO2 was not at all a complex game to begin with. The AI is much more forgiving than in MOO2: it is less aggressive, less intelligent, and also gets a much smaller production handicap.
The diplomacy is an awkward mix of the rather outdated and opaque systems from MOO2 and Civ3: you can create deals a la carte, but it is difficult to predict whether the AI will accept them (and there is *always* a rep penalty for a failed proposal, even if your offer is only marginally less than what the AI would accept).
The game fails hardest at the strategic level. The basic problem with the game is lack of player choice, combined with pig-headed AI that sends out fleets to destroy everything in their path until they are ground down by attrition by the player. In sum, the AI has the level of intelligence and sophistication one would expect from a game written 25 years ago.
The game has a very low skillcap and basically plays like a piece of freeware or one of those no-name 4X games you can find in the bargain bin at Staples. These days, one could literally get a better game for free. This is not a game worth the same retail price as Starcraft II or Fallout 4.
MOOX has the makings of a good game, but I think the dev team is overly cautious and uninspired - I get the feeling the devs are from B-game companies and the dev team leadership is really tepid and just copies features from other games, rather than innovating and doing internal testing - and the end result will fall far short of its potential, which is a shame because MOOX does, like I said, have a lot of unrealized potential. Maybe modders will play with it later. Frankly, I think the goal at the corporate level was just to make a low-budget, B-team $50 cash cow players would plop down money on for sheer nostalgia. From a financial standpoint, I have no doubt they succeeeded.
Anyway, bottom line - in terms of game experience, this game just isn't worth it. Don't waste your money.
Game elements in MOO2 gone from MMOX include:
- Almost all tech implementation picks (a handful of techs have them on an individual basis)
- Intra-system colony pods
- Boarding parties and self-destruct
- Freighters
- Spies (apparently not yet implemented, although the overall structure of the game suggests this functionality will be very limited)
Compared with MOO3:
- Spacelanes, a really bad design element, are in evidence
- System (sublight) ships, which were actually a cool idea, are not in evidence
- Moon development does feature in the game but is very, very limited, offering only a few bonus points for a couple touch-and-go improvements
Suggestions for devs:
- Remove spacelanes
- Buff AI intelligence and strength
- Add more options overall
- Make the game pacing more variable; differentiate short/long-game choices
- Add system ships, the ship design system from MOO3 was basically good but poorly implemented
- Reintroduce features from MOO3 without making them overwhelming or inconsequential
- More terraforming / economic customization
- More races
- Less cliche in race design (hurr durr big tough guy / indigenous nation mystics)

As a MoO2-Vet, I was rather sceptical about this reboot. But in the end, it seems to turn out pretty good. Even in its current state, I could smoothly play through my first match, without any crashes (minor bugs and glitches are still present, of course), and I have to say: This is fun! The interface is a lot more comfortable than in MoO2 (made possible by borrowing heavily from CiV). Starlanes change the progression of warfare alot, compared to the original, but I like the "move around inside the systems" aspect going along with them, and they have their own advantages gameplay-wise. Tactical combat is a lot more fun to watch (naturally) and a lot less tedious than in MoO2 (many combat options back then were pretty unnecessary in SP and bogged a somewhat slow combat routine only down more). Of course, combat AI needs some improvement.
The only thing I really don't like is ship editing and upgrading. The slot-system (compared to MoO2's free distribution of space) is okay and feasible, but the numbers during blueprint editing do not seem to add up correctly all the time. Often I also miss a little bit more information about how (or rather: how much) a certain weapon or subsystem effects the actual combat.
And upgrading ships like in CiV does not really seem to work in a MoO. Sure, in MoO2 it could be tedious to upgrade all ships in a large fleet through production, but maybe you could add an "upgrade all"-button?).
It's a bit buggy and takes some getting use to, but all'n'all a good game.

Double the number of races, double the number of techs, work out the vario bugs in visual style and in combat, and get the combat rules to work (which of course, MOO3 never really did) and you have a game that would be one of the best of its type. Wow, I can't believe I have never done a review on Fallout 4 before! I believe I will do one now, in an attempt to reduce the damage done by the recent review bombing, which while I understand if the changes made to a game at a certain point directly affect the game's functioning in a major way, it does not do so for this game, and thus does not warrant this very harsh review bombing.
The Creation Club is an interesting concept. Say what you will about paid mods, they are a way for a maker of a game to extend the game's moneymaking capabilities, and thus viable for them (in this case, Bethesda). Like I've said, in my experience this move does not negatively affect the game in any way that I can detect. Please do not think less of this game or the company who made it simply because "paid mods, how evil!"
For those who been living under a rock for the past almost 2 years, this would be the latest installment in the storied Fallout franchise. You play as a fully voiced character for the first time in the series, either male or female, and for that, the level of customization and characterization is somewhat limited compared to, say, my favorite in the franchise, Fallout: New Vegas. However, it does a great job with what it has, despite the limitation of only four given responses for each dialogue tree branch.
Anyway, again for the first time in the franchise, you see what life is like before the Great War which reduced the world to a nuclear wasteland. You play either a war veteran (if you choose to be a male character), or lawyer (if you choose a female character). They are husband and wife, and they have a child, who will actually play a great role in the story to come, no spoilers here :-)
You or your spouse are cryogenically frozen as part of the insidious experiments taken on by the vaults of the Vault Tec Corporation. And you wake up about 200 years later, after the world has already been blasted by nuclear devastation. You are a resident of Sanctuary Hills in Massachusetts, a suburb of Boston, the sole survivor of Vault 111.
One of the first tasks in your quest has very little to do with exploring the large wasteland, but improving and fortifying your own hometown which has been as ruined as the rest of the Commonwealth, the area around Boston. The settlement building mode is new to Fallout 4, and you can lose yourself for many hours building up the perfect home for yourself and other settlers in about 30 locations throughout the map.
If the game simply were a sum of how it was released, I definitely would not have over 500 hours of playtime racked up! No, like Skyrim, mod support greatly expands the potential of the game. I would most definitely recommend picking up Sim Settlements on the Nexus, which more or less automates the running of any and all settlements that you choose to build up with these new functions. It is far and away the best mod for the game that I have seen.
[REDACTED: everything is fine now.]
In closing, I urge you all to please stop the review bombing. It does not get anyone anywhere. It doesn't seem that Bethesda is going to take off the Creation Club as it seems to be, as I said, a big moneymaking arm of the game now, and as I said does not break the game in any major way. It does break my heart to see the review scores here on steam now, "Overwhelmingly Negative" recent reviews, and now the overall reviews are at "Mixed." That is NOT what this game deserves! Please, see this and change your reviews if possible. Thank you. I love you all; please take care!

'Serena' is a point and click, interactive story, developed by numerous people that could only be listed in full in the credits.
The controls are limited to mouse only, but with no option of mouse sensitivity (worthy of note that I found the default sensitivity to be uncomfortable for the first few minutes) it begins showing shortfalls. To put it in a larger frame, there are no options-- at all. Escape is binded to closing the application, the game starts in fullscreen mode and no screen is available to list any of this information or how to change it, rather a "press everything, find out what it does, hope for the best" style of instruction for settings, oddly quite apt giving that the game is a point and click.
And here comes the crux of the problem with 'Serena': It's not a game.
Much like 'Dear Esther' and 'Gone Home', it sells itself as an interactive story whilst also posing as a game, however there is no failure state to this, no objective even, and since it features no puzzle to solve in the story it cannot even rely on it being an adventure. To put it in a blunt form, 'Serena' is as pretentious as it is rail-roaded; it would show elements of adventure and puzzle, however it would much rather critically analyse itself and admonish the player whenever they made any notion towards initiative by cockily noting "No, you can't open that trunk/armoire/door yet. Stop ruining my story."
The plot has brief glimmers of interest, particularly the Irish folklore poem to commentate on the characters, however it is painfully overshadowed by the dozens of lines of narration and "muh intellectualism" attitude. This is one point that got me the most aggravated, though entirely subjective, that the story features heavily towards anti-rationalism, treating knowledge and intelligence and secondary to life experience and Human emotion. Again, a subjective area that is one of the few features the game can be used for debate on.
Much of the singular scene is used to contrast each character: Serena the deific woman, detailed in the poem as a fey creature, and the player as the mortal man, also in the poem as a warrior-poet. This does provide the single red-herring of the piece, where the main character is a warrior and Serena is a weaker fey, coined with his disregard of the Bible and religion, does present an idea that he would challenge magical or immortal things in a violent fashion-- ergo, he may have killed her.
Written and acted in a homodiegetic style, 'Serena' would have you feel as the main character, placing you in the shoes of him to experience his ethereal experience of post-death. What it fails to do is placing you directly in these shoes, detracting from the experience by giving voice to the character's narration and allowing him control over how the player (I use player for the purpose of this review, not as a meaningful statement of it being akin to a game) interacts with the scene. I found two such occurrences where the armoire and trunk where unable to be opened until the character had entered the correct "mood", something only obtained by progressing through the story by the skip-able narration.
However, if the player ignores the self-contained literary analysis, mutes the sound, and focuses on the visual aspects and their own interpretation, 'Serena' can be a very enjoyable and thought provoking experience. The paintings and poem are, by very far, the gleaming aspects of this interaction, where foreshadowing and contrast are heavy in these giving much room for speculation and realisation, but it is quite obvious that the paintings were not given the same attention as the rest, due to them not being required to be viewed to progress the story nor do they contain any dialogue or interaction. If the developer team cut out the rest and just left those items in the story, it would easily show just how weak the rest of the plot devices are in comparison; an unfortunate situation that the best of an experience is the most undeveloped part.
I would not recommend this, on the basis of the complete lack of settings, instruction and poor narrative choices. If, however, a prospective player took their time out to research the key bindings, muted their sound and entered the story with an interest to explore and not have their hand-held, this is most certainly recommended. But, due to the common shortfalls, I'm listing this as a general "Do not recommend". Maybe this could be used as an example of how to improve, especially in terms of literary analysis, now that gaming has entered an era of being treated as an art form that it has so sorely deserved.

Wow. What a game! I feel like I’ve been put through the wringer. This is certainly the most emotional game in recent memory that I’ve played. Telltale has created an amazing thing here.
If you’re into Walking Dead, I don’t think there’s much need for a background. However, it doesn’t follow the TV show and just takes small pieces from the show, like a name or character likeness. Otherwise, it’s a completely new story that starts from a Day 1 outbreak. I really don’t want to give any part of the story out. It’s a much better experience playing it blind with no previous knowledge.
The main mechanic is the dynamic story. You will be faced with many dialog options to many scenarios. What you choose
affect the entire rest of your game with how it plays out and who may be in it. The other characters will reflect back on your past choices and will react accordingly. It’s extremely immersive and well done.
You will be second guessing yourself a lot and kicking yourself for making a dumb split second decision. But that’s what makes it great. You’re forced to make some awful decisions and sometimes very quickly.
The graphics are highly stylized and display nicely a majority of the time. Some low-res textures are present but that’s not the main focus of the game. The story is front and center.
The voice acting is worth noting. It’s spectacular. Each character expresses true emotion when speaking. Great voice acting is needed as to spark an emotion within you too, as you make decisions along the way.
I also like how the devs didn't make any specific achievements. You just play the game and they unlock. You don’t need to worry about unlocking something by making a certain decision. It lets you experience the game how you want and still not miss out on anything.
+Fantastic story
+Immersive
+60fps
+Stylized graphics
+Great voice acting
+A few dialog choices gave me too little time to read all the options (maybe on purpose?)
This is a fantastic game that elicits a ton of emotions from beginning to end. I highly recommend this to anyone and is easily worth the full asking price.

Adolf Hitler (German: [ˈadɔlf ˈhɪtlɐ] ( listen); 20 April 1889 – 30 April 1945) was a German politician who was the leader of the Nazi Party (Nationalsozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei; NSDAP), Chancellor of Germany from 1933 to 1945, and Führer ("leader") of Nazi Germany from 1934 to 1945. As dictator of Nazi Germany, he initiated World War II in Europe with the invasion of Poland in September 1939 and was a central figure of the Holocaust.
Hitler was born in Austria, then part of Austria-Hungary, and raised near Linz. He moved to Germany in 1913 and was decorated during his service in the German Army in World War I. He joined the German Workers' Party, the precursor of the NSDAP, in 1919 and became leader of the NSDAP in 1921. In 1923, he attempted a coup in Munich to seize power. The failed coup resulted in Hitler's imprisonment, during which time he dictated the first volume of his autobiography and political manifesto Mein Kampf ("My Struggle"). After his release in 1924, Hitler gained popular support by attacking the Treaty of Versailles and promoting Pan-Germanism, anti-Semitism, and anti-communism with charismatic oratory and Nazi propaganda. Hitler frequently denounced international capitalism and communism as being part of a Jewish conspiracy.
By 1933, the Nazi Party was the largest elected party in the German Reichstag, which led to Hitler's appointment as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Following fresh elections won by his coalition, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, which began the process of transforming the Weimar Republic into Nazi Germany, a one-party dictatorship based on the totalitarian and autocratic ideology of National Socialism. Hitler aimed to eliminate Jews from Germany and establish a New Order to counter what he saw as the injustice of the post-World War I international order dominated by Britain and France. His first six years in power resulted in rapid economic recovery from the Great Depression, the effective abandonment of restrictions imposed on Germany after World War I, and the annexation of territories that were home to millions of ethnic Germans—actions which gave him significant popular support.
Hitler sought Lebensraum ("living space") for the German people. His aggressive foreign policy is considered to be the primary cause of the outbreak of World War II in Europe. He directed large-scale rearmament and on 1 September 1939 invaded Poland, resulting in British and French declarations of war on Germany. In June 1941, Hitler ordered an invasion of the Soviet Union. By the end of 1941 German forces and the European Axis powers occupied most of Europe and North Africa. Failure to defeat the Soviets and the entry of the United States into the war forced Germany onto the defensive and it suffered a series of escalating defeats. In the final days of the war, during the Battle of Berlin in 1945, Hitler married his long-time lover, Eva Braun. On 30 April 1945, less than two days later, the two killed themselves to avoid capture by the Red Army, and their corpses were burned.

Obviously "inspired" by Katamari Damacy and Ico, the Maw is quite disappointing.
1) TOO SCRIPTED.
Everything you do has nice funny animations, but is too scripted. Quite often the funny interactions are very passive - you're being dragged, something happens without your intervention in a cut-scene, etc. It feels like a movie, not like a game.
2) LAME SCALE.
The game doesn't scale well. The maw grows gradually to the size of a giraffe - it took me 5 hours of tedious eating to get to that size in a linear fashion. And then... at the end of the level he suddenly grows from the size of a giraffe to the size of a planet eating blob. They didn't do the intermediate part - which games like Pudding Monsters, Katamari Damacy, Heat Signrature or even Beyond Good and Evil (at its very end) do.
3) UGLY.
Even though the game is done by people who understand expressive animation very well, it's very ugly in an environmental sense (this also applies to their next creation, Explosion Man). I usually don't care about graphics, so something has to be very ugly to make me say this.
4) BAD PORT.
The game is so badly ported on the PC, that the mouse doesn't move the camera. Fortunately, I had a gamepad, and the camera controls worked that way.

Since the game is still in development, there are still small bugs and many blocked/not-yet-implemented features.  With that caveat out of the way, the game so far is great.
As someone who played a great deal of both MoO and MoO2, I had great expectations for this game, and so far it does not disappoint.  Obviously there's still a lot to go--spying, for instance, doesn't exist yet, and at least six more races are in development--but it's fairly faithful to the original games.  It is 'closer' to the MoO2 gameplay, which is no tragedy; while I did greatly enjoy the simplified colony management of the original game and the massive fleets of stacked ships, the gameplay in MoO2 is more 'interesting' being more hands-on and everything.
Interestingly, and quite pleasing to me, the character models were more based on the original MoO races rather than the (sometimes greatly changed) MoO2 races.  The Psilons are like greys with 4 arms, the Mrrrshan is a cat-lady, and the Alkari are birds, not pterydactyls.  Nice shout-out to the original.
The voice-acting, particularly for your chosen advisor, can get repetitive, but it's a nice touch.  The narrator (Michael Dorn, Mister Work himself) rarely gets old, although the GNN is my least favorite VA collective (they can still be amusing, tho)
All-in-all, it's hard to recommend an unfinished game for $50, but if you are a die-hard MoO fan it might be worth it to leap into it now.  Otherwise, if you're interested, you might want to wait for the finished project or at least for it to be further along before picking it up; but in the latter case, you should keep an eye on it, because it is already looking to be as successful a go-back title as XCOM.

This review is based on my limited experience in the CBT for Twilight Spirits (龙魂时刻)--I did NOT reach end-game. TL;DR at the bottom. Added an update after playing to level 25 in OBT.
So currently this game is only available in Chinese. If you're not familiar with the language and have not played games in foreign languages, you may find yourself having some trouble going through the game. I use Google Translate's camera on my phone if I ever find myself stuck, or need clarification on skills/combos. Just FYI, you'll need to enable Chinese input on Windows, because your (account-wide) name must be in Chinese, and I was unable to copy-paste characters from Google.
The combat and dungeon system in this game is similar to Vindictus/Kritika, with character/class aesthetics a bit similar to Revelation Online (both RO and TS by NetEase, I believe). It's an instance-based, third-person action combat MMORPG, with gender-locked classes. I mainly played the emo guy with the sword. I found the graphics very appealing (I'm a sucker for good character models, clothes with physics, and flashy skills), and many of the environments are gorgeous. There's a sort of witch-time effect (everything except your character is in slow-mo) that's great for dishing out some awesome damage, and it plays out well in groups.
The dungeons are rather linear. I'm not a fan of PvP in general, so I can't really say if the gamemode is any fun (3v3), but I did play a match against a group of 3 healer lolis and wanted to off myself (whether from boredom or frustration I don't remember). There's no character customization beyond picking a class, and armor changes are limited to fashion cosmetics (from what I believe is mainly/only from the cash shop); items you get from dungeons will not change the clothing your character wears. The only thing that changes appearance with dungeon drops is your weapon.
The game seems to actively support up to 144Hz. As an MMO (though instance-based), you'll likely need both a decent GPU and CPU to run that at max graphics. I stuck with the wimpy medium graphics at 60Hz.
Overall, I love the combat, and definitely recommend this game to fans of the genre, and specifically those who are familiar with playing Chinese MMOs. My ping sometimes gets so bad my skills don't initiate for at least a full second, which is frustrating to say the least, but when it's stable, it's fun. I'm not sure how repetitive the game gets beyond the early levels. The content I've went through has been pretty limited so far, but I'm likely missing things that require actually knowing what I'm doing.
TL;DR try it out if you're familiar with foreign asian games and enjoy the vindictus-style genre. customization and ping sucks but ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
UPDATE: Alright, so I've played around with a few of the classes; my highest level character (emo sword boy) is still only 25, but I just want to clear some things up. My average ping is about 300ms in town (I'm in west coast NA); it's a pain to play with, but it's just enough to get the witch time off a decent amount of the time, depending on the speed of the boss' attacks. The game advertises their UU ping booster through private messages; it dropped mine to about 200ms after I started the VIP 3-day trial. Without the trial, no matter which server I chose, it would raise my ping at least 100ms. Anyway, it may just be because of the big delay I have to deal with, but witch time feels very rewarding to initiate, especially if you activate it multiple times in a row (there's a combo counter that pops up the first time you do witch time).
Queues for PvP are long, but I'm usually playing when most Chinese players are probably asleep or at work or school. To bounce off what another reviewer said, the environments/missions DO get repetitive. It's not too bad at the start, but quests will often have u repeat the same mission 2-3 times. Taking and turning in quests becomes a chore, as you'll have a questgiver in one zone and the actual mission in another. Compared to CBT, they made the town hubs a lot larger, which certainly looks nice, but it's a pain having to run from NPC to mission portal and vice versa. Basically, the combat is what carries this game. If you don't like it, there's pretty much no reason to play. Oh also, the fashion items in the cash shop are time limited, with a maximum of 180 days.
Ultimately the game feels very limited. It feels like it was built specifically to look good in trailers. The size of the dungeons make them seem like they're for basic tech/engine demos. This game has a lot of potential, but with how sparse and spread out the content feels, it isn't totally satisfying. But the fact that it's a free game makes this an easy recommend. If you don't like it, you'll probably know within the first hour.

Full disclosure: I never played any of the original MOOs. I came into this one blind wrt to its lineage, just looking for a decent space 4x and for me, it ticks all the boxes. The asthetics and sound are superb, really catches that old style soft-SF theme without seeming out-of-date. The game play is simple but solid. If you're into micromanagement this might not be the game for you, it doesn't take much effort to manage an empire with twenty or so planets, although there is enough micro to make you have to think about how you're going to develop and use those planets.
I've read some crticism and debate over the star lane FTL system: you can't travel anywhere but can only jump to nearby systems making the map a network. I find the system quite refreshing. It creates some good tactical scenarios like grabbing systems, even if they have bad planets, because they are choke points for travel. It can make it difficult to send ships out in the later game without open border treaties but overall I think it works.
The game is still in Early Access but it seems nearly finished. Could do with a little polish on the bugs side (mostly graphical) and there's still some fleshing out that needs to be done but even in its current state its a lot of fun. Fingers crossed it will continue to improve.

This is a fantastic addition to the MOO franchise!  If you are a gamer of the 80s and 90s and experienced the death of your social life due to MOO 1 or MOO 2 then you must pick this game up.  All of the pieces that make MOO 2 such a fantastic game of "...just one more turn." are in this game.  I've seen a lot of negative reviews on this game and I admit there is much to still be accomplished, but that's why it says it's an early access game.  That said, I played Master of Orion in the beginning of March 2016 and now at the end of March since the latest patch was released and the improvements are impressive!  The new races are a fantastic add.  The balance issues I saw before with the Psilons massively dominating with no negatives to those big brains of theirs have now been put in place.  Combat is much improved with the ability to set how fast your individual ship classes will rush into battle, and at what distance they will attempt to keep the enemy at bay.
At this time I will not create a pro/con list because it's just silly.  This game is not complete.  Spying, space combat, ground combat, diplomacy, and several other features are still being worked on.
The bottom line is this.  If you were one of the unfortunate few like myself who purchased and played MOO 3 and then cursed the sky for the game being so terrible look no further than this latest installment to restore your faith in the franchise.
That's it for now.  Time to return to Master of Orion and keep my social life at bay.

Short review here, but this game got a lot of flack, and I didn't understand why. Apparently, it used to be riddled with game-breaking bugs. I'm about 68 hours in, and so far, the bugs had been very few and minor, not dissimilar to AC: Syndicate (the only other AC game I've played so far).
In fact, as enjoyable as AC: Syndicate was, the side missions feel more varied and interesting in this one. Syndicate had basically 3 kinds of side-quests repeated over and over. The main drive to complete them was just to conquer more of the city.
Also, if the recorded hours are anything to go by, Unity will have given me more bang for my buck. 68 hours in, and while I seem to have completed 2/3 of the side-quests, combined with the story missions, it says I'm something like 30% finished the game. I know from Syndicate that you can complete the games well under 100%, so it must be charting collectables as well, but still, I feel like it has more content than Syndicate.
Solid game. I wish I could rank it among all the AC games, but with only one other under my belt, I have much more to go.

H.E.V.: "Welcome to the H.E.V. mark IV protective system for use in

Atmospheric contaminant sensors activated. Automatic medical systems
engaged. Defensive weapon selection system activated. Munition level
monitoring activated. Communications interface online. Have a very safe
day."
The guard now allows Freeman through and uses the retinal scanner to
open the door to the test lab.
Guard: "Go right on through sir. Looks like you're in the barrel
today."
Gordon proceeds through the test lab and comes upon a group of three
scientists.

the test chamber. "

gamble, but we need the extra resolution."

length to get it."

What an amazing interactive story. I really loved this. Although I could easily anticipate most of the story premise right away it doesn't matter because the writing is superb and that is what is important. Both main characters are so finely sculpted through all those inner monologues you can actually believe they are the real persons (which is sadly quite scarce in games). And the way how story progresses and the overall tone is gradually changing into more depressing and sinister. I have to say that the writers are very talented and people could easily relate with most of the story...a great parallel to many real relationships. The sounds and especially the music helps to build the atmosphere even more. And the voice acting. Voice of the protagonist is done so well most of the other games could envy this performance. All those emotions in his voce yet the believable civility really amazed me. Voice of the Serene was a bit worse, if I can say it like that, she was a little bland. Yet still the actress made an above average performance, especially for a free project. Graphics are nice too even though I believe that a real 3D engine would be better for this type of a game instead of prerendered scenes. But the most important thing, the feeling is there, nonetheless. If I should point to just one thing I think that could be done better it is the very ending. Don't take me wrong it is strong and emotional but I lack there something...a small hint of redemption for the main character. Something that would give a bit of a light into that depressive tone. But maybe, maybe I didn't looked well enough maybe there is more then I could have seen in my first play. In my final words, I highly recommend this great piece of storytelling art to everyone who can appreciate a good writing and a really mature story about relationships.

The best way I can describe it is a mix of A Turn Based Sins of a Solar Empire and Endless Space. You start in a sector of the galaxy which itself is made up of a combination of planets, asteroids, and gas giants. Leading out of that in what I think are called warp points, they take you out of that sector and into a connecting sector. And so on and so forth. The game is beautiful and nicely detailed, the races are well animated and have great voice acting. I esp like the Terran Kahnate, I guess they are like the Klingons of the game but in human form. I was making the game harder than it had to be by just clicking through the turns waiting for this or that, but it's important to manage every planet, every turn, to maximize population effectiveness.
My only real complaint is the A.I. are very bold jerks and I don't like that you can't try to compromise on a deal they want you can only agree or disagree. They also seem to work in unison againest you, know where your ships are, and will come together if you are doing slightly better than everyone else, no matter how much they hate each other. I have been a faithful ally to the Humans in one game, went to war againest a common enemy with them, and they just decide to abandon me when someone declared war againest me. Then declared I was taking too many sectors for my own good. Oddly enough, I asked for an alligance again the next turn and we were buddy buddies again. Except I was in two wars and they were in one.
Game features custom race option like MOO2 and I really enjoy it. I didn't like that the game didn't feature different government options but thats not a dealbreaker for me. But you can build a Doomstar and blow up planets so that's a relief, though I still haven't gotten that far in the game yet. Looking foward to how spying will be handled in this game, probably my least favorite part of MOO2, though I do love the Darloks.
Ships can be customized to suit any loadout you want, but I think you can only have 5 Custom loadouts at a time? Kind of a Bummer. Make that 8-10 slots and I think that issue wouldn't be a problem anymore. The other issue, though I guess it's not a plus or minus is the command point limit. I had twice as many planets as another empire and I still felt like I didn't have enough fleet strength to close off key sectors to keep them from expanding, and for every point over the limit, you lose about 10 or 20 BC a turn. It can add up quickly but it is managable as long as your constantly working on improving your command point limit by building more star bases.
All and all a very enjoyable experience, I'm glad they took the time to reboot a much loved series but I think most people are either going to really love this one or really hate it. But I'm looking forward to many more game time with this one.

12 labours of Hercules is done by these people
and the game ofcourse is very loosely based on the Greek Myth of Hercules the greatest of heroes who after becoming mad and murdering his wife and sons goes off to find some sort of penance for his actions by performing 12 incredible labours. The Maw is a pretty fun little action/adventure game in which you are a cute little alien that is imprisoned on a space ship next to a giant mouth with an eyeball. The ship crashes on a planet and you proceed to throw every living creature into that giant mouth.
While the Maw seems pretty light-hearted and not all that-challenging, the game has a darker side behind its cute and seemingly innocent exterior. The first adorable little creature that you see (and hug) is eaten by the Maw, and your character is noticeably shocked by this, but those feelings of sadness and disbelief at the Maw eating that cute little marshmallowy alien baby are quickly forgotten as you try to fill the Maw's insatiable craving for adorable little creatures. This game, in short, is about addiction. Possibly also genocide. Why am I throwing cute babies into a bottomless pit filled with teeth? I don't really know why, and I don't care about their feelings anymore, I just need to throw more alien babies in the pit. I could stop any time I want. Really.
The control scheme is pretty good - I can't speak for the keyboard functions, but the game handles very well with an xbox 360 controller, providing button prompts in the game where needed.
I was pretty disappointed by the DLC for this game; it's simply just some extra levels that should have been included in the game anyway given how short it is. Having said that though, if you are going to buy the Maw, I would recommend getting the Mawesome pack because without the DLC there just isn't enough game here and it doesn't cost a whole lot more than the game by itself.
The final verdict? The Maw is short, but sweet. The game is fairly easy, but it's somewhat cathartic to throw helpless creatures into your own pet monster.
7 out of 10, would throw more cute alien babies into a bottomless pit.

Story:
Maybe it is myself growing old but this world didn't wow me like 3 or NV. Plot wise it makes sense that the world isn't as dark and scary as 3, as this game takes place later and in a different area. There were different groups that led to difference quests for the player, and so there was some decent replayability (hence hundreds of hours of gameplay for me).
Gameplay:
I've recently played through on survival difficulty which puts several restraints on the player as far as needs: eat, sleep, drink, carry weights, etc. This makes the game fun to play because it is challenging. Even on the higher end of the difficulty the game felt too easy, but I'm experienced with shooters so that makes sense. And there i said it, shooters. Because without survival mode, F4 is mostly just an openworld shooter. A very large openworld mind you, but large enough to get lost in all there is to explore.
In closing: F4 was a worthwhile purchase for me because I upped the difficulty over time as things got easy, and there is enough variation in the story and things to explore that I can replay a few times. The ability to make this an RPG is up the player, as you are able to tailor your skillpoints to a particular build, but the game was far too easy if you don't care about RPGs and just want to play it as a shooter.

Still the best singleplayer FPS campaign I've ever played. As long as the dated graphics don't bother you, the level design, pacing and sense of style and immersion are all superb, and the campaign being decently long means you have plenty of time to enjoy it all. The selections of weapons and enemies may not be terribly large by modern standards, but both are very diverse, and the variety of different level layouts in the game mean you never really feel like you're doing the same thing twice. And if you do get bored of the campaign, there are dozens of high-quality singleplayer mods that have been developed over the years to let you wring out even more playing time.
The multiplayer aspect is also decent, if you can actually find any active servers. The movement system and selection of weapons both make for a very high skill cap, which may be a good or bad thing depending on your tastes.
Besides the dated graphics and the dearth of active multiplayer servers, the main caveat I found with Half-Life is that its engine is very bad at supporting large, wide-open outdoor maps. As a result, almost all maps (in both singleplayer and multiplayer) are fairly small indoor areas, while the largest maps tend to be very blocky and low-detail in order for the engine to handle them. The sort of big, beautiful landscapes that you see in something like Halo or Far Cry are just not possible here. With that in mind, I still absolutely recommend the game.

Flight Control HD is one of these games that I'm willing to try because it seems easy and fun. It's not my type of game but being older made me more open towards new genres. The first time I've reviewed it on Steam with a few words were in 2010. I'm not surprised that I had the game since that time: I was probably influenced by the cheerful screenshots.
Your goal is to land aircrafts on the right path, avoiding also collisions between them. The more you advance, the more aircrafts you'll have on your screen, and the more difficult it will be to manage everything. Also, you'll unlock new airfields: island, jungle, snow (as part of an old Christmas stuff), circus (where you have to go through portals), etc..
It's very fun and makes you very aware of what is happening on your screen: some aircrafts are faster than others and it may be a problem at one moment (if their paths are crossing each other). Also, they're coming from every part and they're also different: choppers, big aircrafts, biplanes, military jets, etc.. You can easily spot them because of their shapes but also of their different bright colors (that's also how you can spot the right lane to land). It's a true challenge to manage every one of them once your screen is full of them.
Don't worry though for a collision, you're warned about them: the aircrafts are circled with red and you have, if I remember correctly, a little alarm going off. Also, you're warned from which side they're coming.
With a perfect landing, you'll be rewarded by a text in different languages, congratulating you. Everything is done to make you proud and also to encourage you to keep the good work.
The graphics are very colorful and simple and it's perfect for that type of game. Besides, the soundtrack is very cheerful.
Flight Control HD is really a little good game on PC, even if I can see the potential of it on any tablet or mobile device. However, while the game is for everyone, I can also understand that some players will be frustrated by the collisions and the repetitive gameplay: you're landing aircrafts by making them follow a path, praying that no other will cross them unless you decide that it's worth a shot given the speed of each vehicle.
I've played the game a lot for the achievements. I remember mainly one not unlocking despite being sure to have met the requirements but I suppose that it wasn't clear enough for me, or it was my English, or it was just the wrong use of words.
As I've said, the game was released in 2010. The game is still fun to play today, however, after a little search, the PC version is the less updated: the Android/iOS applications have more content or were at least updated until 2015. The Mac version has an exclusive map too.
I had fun with that game and I never regretted that purchase.

Fantasy Mosaics is a series of nonograms (also known as griddlers) games released for iOS and Android before being ported on PC and Mac. I know that because I've added the whole series on Neoseeker. That's why when I saw it on Greenlight, I voted yes, despite the fact that it's just puzzles after puzzles.
The thing is that the 15th opus isn't so much different from the 14th. The only difference is that I wasn't bored at firt, as I've grown fond of the series. Also, the number of hours passed in Ancient Land has decreased by half, as I've acquired some thinking patterns, allowing me to go faster and with less errors.
But the question is: what's a griddler or a nonogram? You must reveal a drawing by "blackening" a certain number of tiles in the row or in the line. However, each number represent tiles being next to each other: if you see 3, you know that you have three tiles without any space. The difficulty can vary: between full lines or columns or only tiles possibles at the end, you have to think when you have a line or a column of 1-1-1-2-1-3. But like I've said, some tricks can help: when there is a space between two tiles, you know that this space can't be used at all.
The plot isn't really important: a family of penguins travelling around, discovering more colors or unlocking new items for the "garden". What's really keeping me is to make no errors to have three stars or a golden cup (no hint, no mistake). Like in the 14th, the drawings aren't really interesting for me.
And if it's the challenge which is keeping me in the game, it means that you need to be interested to challenge your brain and more if you want to play without the numbers being crossed (which I'm not even doing as I find the casual difficulty hard enough).
The real negative point is a price I find a little too high for what's provided, however, with a discount, it may be interesting to buy. However, the 14th and the 15th games are really similar, it could be only one game if the PC/Mac version wasn't following how they were released on iOS and Android - because, yeah, it's a port of a mobile game.
The 16th game, just released on Steam, is providing more change as the palette of colors is now extended to six, just for your information. But I'm still curious about the earlier works and how the series evolved.

(This is For DayZ: Epoch, because lets be real, who the f**k still plays normal Mod)
It may look a little dated and be a bit buggy, but DayZ Epoch is better than Standalone in every single possible way, except maybe Arma 2s appaling inventory system.
Set a little while after the Apocalypse, Epoch sees society slowly being rebuilt, so there is more of a focus in faction forming and base building and the like rather than surviving, trader cities are on the map where you can go to sell weapons/equipment/food for small chunks of Copper, silver and gold, each with increasing value respectivley.
The player can actually purchase ammo/weapons/food/Helicopters/cars/equipment from NPC's without having to find it which in my oppinion is alot better. However, as mentioned above, you need currrency to buy these things. So in order to do that, you need to either scavenge or go do bandit missions.
Scvenging is almost completley redundant but is ALOT safer than bandit missions, bandit missions are small waypoints on the map where the player and his m8s can kill NPC bandits and take their supplies to sell, this is VERY dangerous because the bandits usually number from 10-25. HOWEVER it is worth it as you can get a lifetime supply of guns/ammo and maybe even a car, that is unless another player doesnt get there first, or shoots you while you scavenge the NPC bodies. Keep in mind, one stray STANNAG round (most common type) can cripple you if not kill you, so be careful, bandit missions are best done with friends.
Unlike Standalone, Epoch has a humanity system which increases as you heal and help other players, and decreases rapidly upon injuring or killing another, once 5000 or negative 5000 humanity is reached, the player becomes a hero (positive) or a bandit (negative) once one of the two, the player can travel to hero/bandit traders that sell increadibly more powerful gear (Kevlar vests, Armoured cars, Armed Helicopters, and even on some servers, tanks) This is why people on Epoch are generally more friendly because having postive humanity can get them to Hero status and thus better gear.
It takes a while, but you can build massive bases from scratch to house all your items, these can be as simple as small, well fortified bunkers, to massive sprawling fortresses complete with three helipads and a airoplane runway.
Overall, Epoch can be tedious, but with friends it is a blast. Bandit missions are one of the highlightes of the game, and returning from a succesful one with your car loaded with guns to your very own base is an amazing feeling. Any fans of the Walking dead series or any other zombie production ever will love this game. A must buy.
P.S Be prepared, The distant rumble of a armoured car engine, or the growl of an armed blackhawk will never sound scarier, especially when its headed towards your location.

Having played countless hours of MOO2  and being extremely dissapointed by MOO3 I had very high hopes for this game.
It did not let me down.
Every negative review I have read for this game is based  on the content not yet implamented or minor game balancing issues due to the fact this game is still in early access.
Having finished my first playthrough I have to say that the UI is the best I have seen in any 4x game. It is very streamlined and intuitive. All the strategy and empire management elements from MOO2 are still in place. The tech tree has many familiar technologies that function essentially the same, but the order in which techs unlock is different. You still have to prioritize carefully and try to balance Infrastructure and military technologies.
The main fundamental gameplay difference is on the galaxy map with the addition of starlanes. This is a point of contention for some.
I didnt like the idea at first but it is not too much of a travel hindrance as most systems have 3 or 4 warp points. It helps with empire planning.
It enables you to shelter your research and economic inner systems by having systems with heavy military instillations on  your  outer borders.
Though there are still some minor balance issues but the game devs have been active reading feedback and responding. Rest assured even in its current early access state this is the best 4x space game available.

This early release is overall very promising, though has a few major issues it needs to iron out in order to be a truly great game. Hopefully the developers are bold enough to make those changes, so far it seems they are. Although it's a tad pricey it does give you the original three games, two of which have been rigged to run on new computers, some bonus features, an extra playable race and it allows you to troubleshoot bugs and make recommendations for alterations to gameplay or new features. So far the developers have kept their word and have tried, mostly successfully, to make changes the players desire. They even went so far as to make an overnight patch so that some players experiencing bugs on certain systems could play the game properly, which shows great promise and dedication. While they were at it they applied a few player-recommended patches and encouraged us to give both positive and negative feedback.
As it is about thirty per cent of the game's features are disabled and about half of what is present seriously needs work. Nevertheless in the first update alone there were significant strides in this area, and it was all to a high standard of quality. Sometimes in updates they'll put in slightly whacky or unbalanced features, but it seems to be a deliberate move to guage how players respond and to find out what the majority of gamers strongly desire, as well as to find out what gamers -do not- desire.
If you are passionate about the Master of Orion series and want to see Master of Orion 4 be a success, you should seriously consider buying this early release and helping to fund the polishing of this potentially great game, and be able to give feedback that will shape it into something awesome that will be played eagerly for years to come.

Okay guys,
As you can tell I've sunk my teeth into this game over the last 8 months or so. I was a patient gamer and waited for the game to get patched, which in this case was a GREAT idea. Playing on a GTX 960 2GB I must've fiddled a good dozen hours to play between the recommended 30fps and ratcheted down the graphics to get about 60fps, so I got a flavour of both. This game is by far the most complete, gorgeous open sandbox I've ever played. The progression of the AC series saw it's best with the next gen Anvil engine, which was also used for AC: syndicate but I have not played yet. Is is as significant a bump in scope and quality from its predecessor as AC II was from the first. Bravo Ubisoft!
Now about the meat and bones of the game, Anvil being the remarkable bones. This game attemps to be an action game, a sleuthing game, a cooperative game and finally and maybe its most weakest aspect with respect to the others, a puzzle game. My biggest gripe is always the AI, though quicker there were a few overlaps in windows which seemed unplanned, but could be turned off if you wish so. Gameplay-wise, the fluidity with which Arno climbs over and under obstacles is the most fluid I've seen. Combat, though slightly confusing at first, is medium difficulty and medium fun.
The thing about this game is the scope and the way Ubisoft meshes its own alt-history (I Know, I know) with the epoch in which you play. I heard they won't lean as much on the historic aspects for Empire, which would disappoint me greatly. Chances are though I won't be around.
Enjoy this game! Thank Ubisoft for always extending their scope and giving us quality games like we've never seen before. Rock the casbah!!! Just not my casbah motherf***ers!!
