Still the best singleplayer FPS campaign I've ever played. As long as the dated graphics don't bother you, the level design, pacing and sense of style and immersion are all superb, and the campaign being decently long means you have plenty of time to enjoy it all. The selections of weapons and enemies may not be terribly large by modern standards, but both are very diverse, and the variety of different level layouts in the game mean you never really feel like you're doing the same thing twice. And if you do get bored of the campaign, there are dozens of high-quality singleplayer mods that have been developed over the years to let you wring out even more playing time.
The multiplayer aspect is also decent, if you can actually find any active servers. The movement system and selection of weapons both make for a very high skill cap, which may be a good or bad thing depending on your tastes.
Besides the dated graphics and the dearth of active multiplayer servers, the main caveat I found with Half-Life is that its engine is very bad at supporting large, wide-open outdoor maps. As a result, almost all maps (in both singleplayer and multiplayer) are fairly small indoor areas, while the largest maps tend to be very blocky and low-detail in order for the engine to handle them. The sort of big, beautiful landscapes that you see in something like Halo or Far Cry are just not possible here. With that in mind, I still absolutely recommend the game.

Ubisoft's black sheep. Unity ♥♥♥♥ed up big time and unlike most other companies, Ubisoft fixed their mistakes and made up for it. The game's not perfect, no. There are still some bugs, most of them pretty humorous or easily fixed by fast travelling, but overall it's a smooth experience. Here are some pretty notes on gameplay:
- There's actually stealth in this game. I had to harken back to my Metal Gear Solid days to get through many sequences. It's obviously not as in depth as Metal Gear but damn, they're really trying.
- If you're coming from Black Flag or before which is highly likely, you WILL die if you treat it like just another Assassin's Creed. Dodging bullets is nearly impossible now and your items pool is limited based on your equipment. Enemies will surround you on all sides and easily slaughter you without proper planning or quick thinking, even with high tier gear.
- Oh yeah, there's a tier system for gear and enemies now. It's...pretty lackluster to be completely honest. You won't use over half the many, many items in the game and there's literally no benefit to going back once you've got something worth using, especially when you'll be fighting enemies who are also higher tier.
- For a game built around the concept of co-op, the amount of things you can do while with your friends feels a bit limited. The many Paris story missions or club objectives should've been multiplayer as well, but at least the heists and actual coop missions are fun.
- I don't think I'd play this game just for the story, but it's nice to run around gay Paree as Arno, your neighborhood friendly Assassin whom all the Parisians seem to know.
Overall Unity creates a beautiful and ugly picture of Paris during one of its most turbulent times. The immersion is absolutely amazing, with citizens rioting in the streets, carrying bodies, burning furniture and books, handing out cockades or just stumbling around drunk in a brothel, among numerous other events. Seeing Assassin's Creed like this makes me wish Ubisoft could go back and remake Constantinople or Damascus in this light. If you've read this far, then I highly recommend setting the language to French with subtitles. It really helps the whole thing along.

This game might not appeal to fans of a more 'open world' experience style of game.  It is a visual novel with occasional direct character control, so don't go in expecting an open world 'roam/loot/survive' style game.  If you want to be the star of a 5 episode Walking Dead series, then this is a game for you.
Cons: Not open world, much of the game you don't have to use the keyboard/mouse.  This shows when it comes to the bits where you DO have to walk the character around, in that the wasd controls weren't always intuitive in where they would carry you.  The game is always 'in engine' as far as I can tell, in terms of how it renders you when you are and aren't in control.  I noticed some glitching on character models w/extra lines around the shoulders in various bits.  Not enough to personally put me off.
Pros: Choices feel very 'real' and there are many places where you do have to make a choice as to which character of several to help.  I'm sure to some extent certain scenes/locations will be in every playthrough of the story, but it seems like you could explore scenes with a totally different set of companions depending on who you pick.  Each episode of the 5 took me around 2 hours, each one did manage to kill me at least once.  Death isn't *too* scary in that they have an autosave system that seems pretty frequent, as I only remember one death making me think "I have to do ALL this again?"  I got this game on sale for $6.24, not sure I'd be quite the same level of pleased with it if I had paid the usual asking price.  I will say this: I just finished it and am already tossing around ideas of replaying it with a different 'style'.  Most choices had the same 'set' of options in that it was often 'really calming', 'neutral', '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥', etc.  I more or less tried to play the protagonist like I would have reacted in their setup.  Between possibly saving different people to 'behaving' differently during encounters I think I would feel pleased with a replay.  I'm also tempted to just try and 'do better' at the way I did this time, to see if I can get an ending that isn't so .... well, no spoilers, let's just say I got this dust in one of my eyes at one point.  :-P

There was a time after Black Flag where I simply got bored of the Assassin's Creed and no longer cared to play any new release during that time. However, after having had the chance to play Unity I can't help but call my past self a fool.
Yeah, the game has its fair share of bugs and the AI is questionable at times but they pale in comparison to the improvements that this game implemented.
Freerunning is smoother than ever before (you'll still get stuck quite often however), letting you climb up and down with ease, you can actually go inside buildings now, whether as an escape route, for a mission, or merely in your search for one of the many chests available for looting. And to top it off, they're usually populated in one way or another. Speaking of the chests, there are 4 different ones in this, the standard white ones, the patriot red ones, blue uPlay chests and finally the yellow ancestor chests, some of these containing iconic outfits from the previous games in the series.
Combat has been vastly improved, gone are the days of merely spamming X to chain kill people, now you actually have to fight and if you can't master parrying then you can and will die... a lot. Customisation is also a thing in this and there is plenty of it, allowing you to mix and match armour sets, decide which of the many melee and ranged weapons are best for you, the colour of your attire etc.
The city of Paris itself feels alive in this game, with Red Redemption-like side stories happening at random that you can partake in for extra gear, a myriad of co-op missions to do (if you can still find anyone online these days), and the sheer amount of npcs walking around.
Overall, Unity is a solid game and fits in well within the AC universe.

Now lets say you spend 15 dollars on a currency pack, that 15 dollars goes to Bethesda whether you have picked any mods or not, which automatically goes into their wallets.  From here you are allowed to pick mods that range in prices of currency and when you purchase said mod a portion goes to the modder, the rest into Bethesdas pocket.  Because of this Bethesda is literally making extra money of modders hard work before you even get to pay the modders themselves, terrible business practice.
Fix: Do away with currency and let us buy directly from the modder if its worth what we want to pay.
Next:  Everytime they add stuff to the Creation Club it will require an update to make the game bigger as it downloads the items but wont unlock them until you purchase said paid mod.  This is causing issues with big free mods like F4SE that needs to be updated literally every time the Creation Club has a new item for sale.  Bethesda said they didnt want to stop free mods but they are trying to hardest to make it so people dont want to have to update their mods every week on a game that has been out for 2 years already.
Fix: Only have us download a paid mod if we actually pay for it, forgoing updates every 2 days.
Finally I'd like to say fallout 4 is a good game that is worth the 30 dollars, but with the new turn of events I definitely have issues with the developers try to bleed their community dry, I mean I have paid 110 dollars for fallout 4 and all of the DLC and yet they want more and more money from me which is really a big turn off.  Bethesda please dont ruin your future games with the current Creation Club and stop stealing money from hard working modders.

You play as a French assassin during the French Revolution through an Internet cloud-based animus simulation through a VR headset.
Overall I though the game was acceptable despite all the bad press and ubisoft bashers railing against all the bugs and glitches found during the release. Since I didn't buy it at the release, when I look back in hindsight the game was in a deplorable state (just youtube unity glitches) and should have been delayed to fix the issues. Although now in 2017, patches have fixed around 90%-95% of the glitches so you shouldn't encounter any. I for one have found a few on the odd occaision but nothing too major.
The story is much shorter than it's predecessors and is lacking in content when compared to much richer games like AC Black Flag. In terms of content, there is not much aside from Helix Data Harvesting, Chest Hunting, Assassination Contracts, Paris Riddles, Side Quests, Co-op missions and collectible gathering.
Gameplay from previous games have changed drastically especially the parkour and the combat. The parkour is much more refined and stylish but can be very fidgetty when in certain spots. Combat is more difficult only because counterkills have been removed and you can easily be mobbed and taken down quickly. In this way, the game discourages you from outright melee unless you grab melee armor+ and melee damage+ from gear menu.
Graphics are reall really pretty, you'll need a pretty good system to run this game. Just make sure you set appropriate graphics options in the menu and you may possibly need to tweak your .ini settings to have a runnable game. My primary specs are an Intel i7 6700K and a Radeon R9 390X and have been able to achieve around 60-80 fps on ultra settings with SSAO, so if you can't achieve similar or better results then there is something very seriously wrong with your computer setup.
What bugged me about this game was the enemy AI behavior, the AI is either really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or really overpowered. Sometimes I get aggroed by enemies in the most ridiculous situations. Either aggroed at a 90 degree angle on top of a building, phantom/berserk blade from cover, sighted from 3 building lengths away.
It is also really hard to double air assasinate when eagle vision removes the "outlines" on the enemy that allow for a successful double assassination.
Sometimes cherry bombs don't work as well as you think and stun grenades aren't as useful when you finally get smoke bombs, same with money pouch, it's kind of useless.
Here some changes that you might notice from previous games:
- No human shield to block bullets
- No counter-kill
- No grass cover (AC3 or AC4)
- No grabbing
- No combat disarm
- No whistling
- No rope-darts
- No tranquilizers
- Lockpicking is back
- Timelimit on eagle vision
- Smoke bomb duration is reduced
- Dedicated stealth "crouch" mode
- Can now freerun downward
- Can enter buildings now
- Wide array of weapons and equipment
PSA: Don't waste your UPlay points on the reward equipment, stats on late-game equipment are superior.
PSA: Throw cherry bombs about 1-2 meters further to get enemies to actually go to where you want them.
PSA: The merchant in the assassin's den sells supplies to you for a cheaper price (anecdotal)
To be honest I would really like to give this a neutral review, although this game is one of the most visually stunning Assassin's creed game I have played so far, the gameplay is unpolished and the story lacks the depth that the Ezio saga contained. Despite the shortcomings I did have fun with the game so I would give this a recommend if only my fellow assassins can catch this game at a sale price.

I would highly recommend buying the current bundle for both civilization 6 and XCOM 2 right now. Both are good games and they are fairly cheap for the moment, unless you want to wait 20 years for them both to be worth pennies. THAT BEING SAID, XCOM 2.
The game is absolutely fantastic. If you're a beginner to XCOM in general, I highly recommend getting this as your first. I also was new to the game, and it was not too difficult to get into. I have only played the game through one time but I am starting a second, harder game now that I understand it. Basically, when you begin, you can choose between 4 difficulties which change the number of enemies and their strengths, and you can choose Ironman/...Bronzeman? Anyway, if you are new to XCOM, not choosing Ironman means you can rewind to fix the countless mistakes you are bound to make, and in a game like this, the mistakes would mean the end of the run. Without this feature, I would say simply don't get the game unless you have a TON of patience. But because of savegame loading, you can see the mistake you made, learn from it, and then play on so you can not make it again. I played on "Rookie" difficulty, but once you get the hang of it you can work up the difficulty.
In terms of mods, I haven't delved too deep, but I know there are thousands of mods to fix bugs or add customization etc, and that will probably keep you going for a while after you get bored of vanilla. The DLC's also add substantial content, but they are not on sale so buy at your own risk I suppose.
I personally love customization in games, and the more I can do the better. This game offers a fairly wide range of customization, but there is not a ton without modding the game, so your soldiers may feel a bit repetative after a few playthroughs, since I already am kind of limited on unique designs for some of my soldiers after my one playthrough.
In any case, get the Strategy Game of the Year Bundle, get this game, enjoy. It's amazing.

The UX design is a pain point of this game. The buttons/options/widgets are just not very responsive. You may very easily misclick or select on wrong option. Then the whole battle is ruined, and you have to reload or suck it. For first few play through, you just don’t know how some researches/items work, unless you search online. You pay extra time to figure out something that they suppose to tell you in the game.
3. Ridiculous battle system
Seriously, the designer must really hate people. The battle system is not just hard, but makes no sense.
The whole RNG design is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. For Civilization 4, the battle RNG is okay. Because you can product a large enough army, so one bad luck consequence is minimized. Rr you can avoid war to avoid rolling the dice. But in this game, the battle scale is so small, one bad luck may determine whether you win the battle, or fail the mission and your whole elites get wiped out. A game can be hard, but it has to be hard for a reason. You can punish players for their bad choices but not their bad luck.
Many settings are just anti common sense. Like enemies get a cover bonus, even if the cover is not even in the way. At the moment you release it, you find out you stand on front of enemy, can’t cancel,  hit, miss and get killed in next turn. Then again, you have to search online to see what exact the cover condition is and try to memorize it.
The way enemies engaging the battle is also ridiculous. After lose your concealment, There is no way you can predict the when to engage the enemies and yet it is the most important part in the battle. It is very likely you get engage battle with two group of enemies at same time for no reason and just lose your best soldiers. Again, luck plays an important role here, which makes the game experience even worse.
A game can be hard, but shouldn’t be hard like this way. A game can have RNG, but shouldn’t punishing players hard for their bad lucks.

I had no idea this game even existed, or what it was, until Steam had it on sale.
I read some of the reviews, and downloaded the demo to give it a try, still not really knowing what this game was.
Turns out, it's kind of a puzzle game. I say "kind of" because the puzzles aren't particularily puzzling. It's just various ways that the Maw can eat things.
You play as sort of an escaped alien convict, and the Maw is like your pet. You feed him, he gets bigger. You feed him special creatures, he gets special powers. Use the special powers to get to things to eat, so he can get bigger, get big enough and he can finish the level. It's not overly complicated, but it's fun. It reminds me a little of Katamari, only with eating, instead of rolling around.
The good:
-Adorible graphics that aren't really out-dated, even though the game is old
-Simple game design/game play if you're looking for a very casual game
-Eat various creatures and see how large the Maw can get
The bad:
-Clunky controls. Half the time it feels like you're trying to wade through molasis. And the other half you're wondering why the mouse is so sensitive.
-Too much hand-holding AND not enough. Sometimes it'll tell you the stupidest things (like press "space" to dodge) and keep throwing it in your face. Other times you'll have no idea what to do (like press "space" to use Maw's ability) and you'll be struggling to figure out what to do, not because the puzzle is hard, but because you didn't know what key to press. When in doubt, press space.
-Camera angles..... the camera angles are just SOOOO frustrating sometimes. When you turn, the camera decides to turn in random directions, and you can move the mouse to turn the camera, but it only moves about a centimeter at a time, more often than not it'll take you more time to turn the camera than it will to complete the puzzle.
All-in-all it's not a bad game. But it's certainly not worth it at full price. I  got it on sale for $2.39 (including the DLCs) and that's around what this game is worth. It's fun, but it's not very engaging. And if the controls were less infuriating I would probably be feeling differently about it, but as it stands, I would not recommend this game at full price. Buy it on sale, and it'll be worth your few dollars.

I'm going to be honest, I bought this game on sale for 14 cents so I could profit from the trading cards. I had no idea what to expect from it and I gotta say I was more than pleasantly surprised.
12 Labours of Hercules is a simple casual strategy and time management game, mouse-only, with a very simple but very good soundtrack.
There are two difficulty settings, Casual and Expert, with no achievements directly related to them (i.e., beat the game on expert is not an achievement in itself, although it interferes on the amount of time you have to get gold score in every level). I only say this because I don't really like games that include difficulty specific achievements and in case you are like me and like to get 100% achievements.
The game itself is not too dificult if you play on Casual and if you plan a little bit before starting each level, but even so I had to restart a few levels to get gold score, which means there are more strategy elements than meets the eye. That said, if you really want a run for your money, I suggest playing it on Expert from the start.
And if you really enjoyed the game after playing it, there are 2 other sequels available, with another one greenlit by the community and hopefully on its way to the store very soon (at the time of writing this review).
I am not a big fan of these types of games and I do not usually write reviews, so this might not be the best review out there, but I just have to recommend this game to everyone, because it is worth the time and money. And even though I bought it at a lower price, I would gladly give 3€ for it.

Meh.  Not giving this a thumbs down or anything, but it's a little too cutesy kid like for me.  Probably pretty entertaining for a 10 year old if they want to drag around a strange purple gellatenous carnivore alien while it eats everything in sight.  Not for me though.  All I care about is Dark Souls!  Have you heard about Dark Souls?  Let me tell you about Dark Souls!
It's hard to describe why Dark Souls is so, so good.
Yet, it's so incredibly easy.
Why? We just need to look at the core attitude of Dark Souls, from a design-to-player perspective.
Dark Souls is challenging. Yes, that much is clear. But it's not to laugh at you or to discourage you.
It's hard because it knows what you're capable of, and it believes in you. It does't want you to give up.
Despite killing you all the time, it respects your intelligence and holds you of the highest regard. Dark Souls wants you to succeed, and this gives it the framework to do so many things right.
In that regard, Dark Souls does absolutely no hand holding in almost every aspect. The story and lore of the world will completely pass you by if you don't take the time to read item descriptions, examine the world, and talk to every NPC you meet. You will be torn apart if you don't take the time to familiarize yourself with your weapon and shield. Most of all, if you don't take your time, you will be seeing YOU DIED a lot as well. The game grounds itself in patient manner when it comes to enemies and bosses: it wants you to slow down, weigh all of your options, experiment, and most importantly do whatever it takes to survive.
Combat is slow, but weighty; everything about the fighting is spot on. Small weapons swing fast like they should. Large weapons swing slow, and when they hit the ground they emit satisfying "clunk" sounds. Every swing depletes a certain amount of stamina. It's a simple mechanic but it puts so much choice and consequence on the player. You can try to attack like a madman to burn your enemies down as fast as you can, but you won't be able to hold a block with your shield if you run low on stamina. All of this goes double for the intense boss fights - most of the bosses won't hold anything back and they will be a true test of applying everything you've learned thus far. You will die, a lot, but finally defeating one of these bosses grants you such an immense feeling of accomplishment, because YOU DID IT ALL WITH YOUR OWN SKILL!
The world of Dark Souls is completely open. There are very few loading screens, there are no transitional airlocks between areas; everything is seamlessly connected to each other. At times, the geography will seem strange but once you take a look around and realize that you can actually see areas from other places, suddenly everything feels natural. Dark Souls' atmosphere is done with careful and precise attention. At times you'll be exploring dark, moody caverns, other times you'll be wading through a dense, moonlit forest with nothing but the ambience to accompany you. Sometimes you'll even find yourself deep in the middle of a trap filled fortress. Make sure you always have your wits about you and you're actively paying attention. The world is just flat out beautiful and knowing that the game is one big connected overworld makes it feel so real and alive, and it really drives home the sense that this world is huge and it brings back that "adventure" experience I've come to miss so bad. The world is yours, and you're free to go wherever you please. At times, you might feel like you're a bit lost, and I do admit the game is sometimes a little obscure with the regard of pointing you towards the right direction, but there are subtle clues and hints. Are the enemies too hard in a certain area? Is there a locked door? There's probably another way you haven't explored yet.
The world is also home to many NPCs. I mentioned before that if you don't take the time to talk to the NPCs you meet and try to piece together who they are, what they're doing, and how they got where they are, you're going to miss out of a lot of Dark Souls' story. This is where I feel Dark Souls' thematic focus comes full strength. The entire game is about overcoming, and fighting through your own struggles. In that same sense, all of the characters you meet along the way are also fighting for something. Something they thought was important, or something they hold dear. Really, take the time to get to know these people and pay attention as well. You won't know where they go next if you don't listen! With that said, if you make the effort to witness each of these stories, you'll watch them struggle along with you, fighting their own battles. Yes, Dark Souls is rich with lore and backstory, but I think the real beauty is watching these characters fight for what they believe in, while you yourself are fighting your own battles too.
Dark Souls also has a very unusual multiplayer system. At all times, your character will be in either one of two forms: hollowed, or human. You spend a somewhat uncommon item called "Humanity" to turn from hollow to human. This enables you to partake in jolly co-operation! If you're in an area where you haven't beaten the boss yet, you can summon fellow players to your world who are also in the same area, as long as they're relatively near your soul level. Sounds good right? Just like the combat, there's another consequence you might have to face when you turn human. Dark Souls allows players to "invade" the worlds of other human players. They will appear as red phantoms, and they will hunt you down and kill you on sight, essentially marking this game's version of PvP.
Now, this is where I feel Dark Souls' biggest community strength comes from. You see, once a player invades you, all bets are off. They might be insanely twinked out. They might be a fair fight. They might want to honor duel you. You might even have a couple friends already summoned to help you out. Some players have taken it upon themselves to create a sort of "honor" code when it comes to PvP. They like to designate certain areas of the game for official dueling, with no help from other players or no healing, stuff like that. Some players agree with doing this. Some players prefer the chaotic nature of invading in random places, not knowing what either party will be up against. Some players are firmly rooted in the idea that PvE and PvP should not intertwine. They'll even go as far as to never turn human. What "honor" or "etiquette" should be included in Dark Souls' PvP, if any, is still being debated today. I feel like there will never be one solid answer but I think that's okay. It allows for more discussion and I think there's something inherently beautiful about a community being on two complete opposite sides of how an in-game mechanic should work. Bottom line: try, at least a couple times, to play through the game in human form. The invasion mechanic is a part of the game, and even though sometimes you'll get ganked, it's an experience quite like no other.
Dark Souls is challenging, but not unfair. To be honest, the difficulty this game is notorious for isn't as bad as a lot of people make it out to be. Don't get me wrong though, there is still a lot of obstacles you'll have to overcome and at times it'll feel like you're stuck. But don't give up. Never give up.
In today's world of modern game development, it's very pleasant to play a game that actually holds you with a high regard and respects your ability to think, perceive, and act. Dark Souls is a hallmark of intelligent and masterful gameplay design, and it stands as one of my all time favorite games. Highly recommended. The premise of this game is nuts. Celebrities turned butlers to learn how to treat women right? Yeah. Spoiler alert: they don't treat MC-chan right.
While sprites and CGs are gorgeous, the backgrounds are blurry and pixelated (some have been fixed in an update, but many are still pretty wonky lookingg). The music playing in the background is okay, few forgettable tracks that don't get in the way. I like that.
Now, about the guys.
I brute forced Yonekura's achievements by skipping, since the very first scene of his route made me kinkshame his foot fetish pretty hard and then I couldn't take him seriously anymore. I can't say much about him, despite the fact that I kind of thought he was cool in the other two routes.
Kira was a pleasant surprise. I often whine that in these games, the S-type characters throw terms like 'punishment', 'naughty girl' and other 50 Shades-lite stuff. His route was like that, but with the added bonus of him being actually pretty clumsily in love and his conflict being explored quite well. He was surprisingly cute with MC-chan in the second half of the route.
Kamisaki... I feel like his description isn't actually telling anythin about his personality. I thought he would be the cute fluffy romance option, but he's a super annoying tsundere going for yandere. I thought his route was actually pretty creepy, given that everybody around MC-chan was warning her that he wasn't behaving in a healthy way, but the choices to reach the happy ending were those in which MC-chan was oblivious and forgiving of his toxicity. Eventually in the end he realizes he crossed the line and apologized, but man...
Despite the name 'My Butler', the only real butlers are the two guys in the background (me wants a Kagurazaka route!). Also, the focus is literally on the budding relationship, as MC does nothing for 3 months (which means she has no goals, little motivation, no friends... super generic, overly pure & clumsy & oblivious MC).
I did enjoy to a degree the two routes that I read, but I would have preferred getting Kira's route on mobile instead of the bundle. On the positive side, the bundle has all routes, sequels and date scenarios, so if all the guys sound appealing to you, it's a better deal.

As a fellow butler connoisseur, let me explain to you why I find butlers so appealing:  Butlers are gentlemen, emphasis on gentle. A true butler is respectful, kind, and puts the comfort and well being of others above his own. His duty is to serve, and he takes said duty very seriously. He is also well dressed; a suit and tie is the staple of his wardrobe. Although he may wear a more ornate uniform, his attire is ALWAYS impeccable.  Now, you may ask, how can a butler romance possibly be appealing? And this is where I tell you, it's the "forbidden romance" aspect that makes him so attractive. You know, the exact title of this otome series? A real butler struggles against his romantic feelings because it conflicts with his duties. This inner conflict manifests in romantic tension between him and the object of his desire. He fights these emotions, although hints of them may surface from time to time leaving his lady confused and conflicted about her own. Ultimately, the butler will be unable to hold back his hidden desires and gives in to temptation. However, he will NEVER stop treating her gently or with respect. He has taken care of her for so long that he cannot think of acting otherwise, even in love.  Now tell me, how can a game about romancing butlers get it SO wrong?!?

I have no delusions that Dogenzaka's games are anything more than cheap smut.  I get it.  There's obviously an audience for this stuff, and it sells.  Even so, I had a glimmer of hope that perhaps I'd get at least one decent butler story out of this thing, even if it was filled with lusty situations, a little bit of butler-filled romantic tension would have sated my fetishy hunger.  But the game doesn't even give us that much.  When butler-like characters in other VNs do a better job of being butlers than actual butlers in a game with "butler" in the title, you know there's a problem.
Unfortunately, there was little chance for My Butler to succeed in the first place as the premise stifles any potential it had. On break from her university studies, the protagonist's aunt whisks her away to a mansion where her job is to be cared for by one of 3 butlers for three months.  Truthfully, that's not the part that bothers me.  Let's be honest, getting a character into a situation in which she's cared for by a real butler is going to be contrived and stupid, but I can totally suspend disbelief as long as the situation is fun and entertaining.  My issue is that these butlers are actually famous celebrities who work for the MC's aunt, and who are forced to take breaks from their busy careers to learn how to treat ladies properly.  Yeah, her aunt thought it was a good idea to leave her niece alone with lusty celebs for three months, men she couldn't trust enough with their own fans let alone her sister's daughter.
We weren't even out of the first chapter when Mr. Actor strips naked and forces the MC to bathe with him.  That happened.  Mr. Model wasn’t much better with his incessant teasing which often brought the protagonist to tears, but its okay because he thinks she’s adorably cute that way.  Mr. Idol was probably the most idiotic with his totally obvious childhood-crush-turned-stalker-obsession.  None of their personality quirks made them interesting or endearing, just annoying.  If you want me to care about the characters, give them likeable characteristics.  I need a LOT more to go on than a pretty face and the idea he’s a celebrity.
Even viewing this as a “celeb fantasy,” which is essentially what it is, it fails.  The appeal of those types of stories is in experiencing the allure and thrill of a glamorous world through dating famous suitors.  We get none of that here with the characters locked away in a secluded manor for months.  How do we even know these guys are celebrities other than being told so?  Sure, the protagonist may have heard of him before, but we as readers barely glimpse that side of him.  The fact that he chose her over every other girl in the world means nothing when we don’t even get to see that world.
Look, I’m not expecting realism, but these characters and situations are so stupidly implausible, they completely murder what little suspension of disbelief I had.   There’s absolutely nothing of merit here.  Even the smut is tame compared to Dogenzaka’s other offerings, which given these characters, is quite surprising.  Sure, there’s plenty of teases and innuendo (and quite a bit of stripping), but when it comes to the actual sex scenes, they fade to black before getting much further than a few passionate kisses.  Now, I don’t read VNs for the smut, but if that’s what you’re here for, you’ll probably walk away disappointed with what feels like a whole lot of build up with very little payoff.

Ultimately, I don’t know who this VN is aimed at.  Butler fans will be livid at the lack of real butlers, celeb fans frustrated at getting none of the escapism those stories offer, and the folks looking for a bit of cheap titillation are likely to leave unsatisfied.  It boggles my mind how this game has so many positive reviews.  Outside of some fairly nice character sprites and CGs, there’s little value here.  Just do yourself a favor and turn the other way.  There are much better games out there, MUCH better, even within Dogenzaka’s own catalog, and that’s pretty sad.
Bottom Line: NOT recommended

If you play AC games for the parkour, the combat, the pretty world, the level design, then this game is for you.
-The combat is definitely a tiddly bit better than the rest of the games (with enemies attacking more aggressively), and they even have flashy two-person finisher moves for when you get teamed up on.
-The freerunning system with up/down buttons might turn you off at first, but you get used to it. It's smooth, it's fast, and it's flashy. Not once did Arno get stuck, run up a wall, or make a jump I didn't want him to.
-Paris is a ♥♥♥♥ing big and dense city, with nice rooftop construction that makes scurrying around a blast.
-The outfit customization gives me a woody. I don't like stat-based costumes, but the ability to customize yourself to THAT level makes it feel like you're really investing in Arno.
If you play AC games for the story, however...
-The story is a laughable revenge plot that gets convoluted and straight-up lazy at worst, mediocre at best. Love interest feels forced, and Arno isn't even two-dimensional, he's one. Always felt like a slog of going from one mission to the next.

XCOM 2 is a game that, in my personal opinion, is a must-have for any PC or console gamer regardless of whether or not you're a returning XCOM player, or new to the series. A few things people should know about the game is that it most certainly FEELS more challenging than the last. I've played through the original XCOM multiple times and, at least on Normal difficulty, have rarely ever lost a soldier. For those who dont know, XCOM has a feature where if/when a soldier die on a mission they are removed from play for the rest of the game. This means all XP, weapons, items, and so on are lost forever. I think this is a great feature that has gone on to be included in games such as Darkest Dungeon, and really makes you care about your soldiers and think a lot more about what move you're going to make and who you want to send in to those especially challenging missions.
The game is also beautiful, with varying and randomized (as far as I can tell) maps and encounters. Runnign this game at full graphics output may not be possible for some players, but it does not hamper the gameplay in any way. The destructable environments also add a new level of gameplay since some characters and weapons can actually rip either your soldiers or your enemies cover away, leaving them exposed for a counterattack.
The story is somewhat generic in my eyes. Essentially, afte the events of XCOM 1 the aliens somehow managed to take over the planet and successfully integrate into our global society. You, as the commander from the last game, are tasked with leading the resistance and foiling the new alien plot of the Advent Project.
The game also introduces a plethora of new customization options for weapons, soldiers, and your new base. These include visual appearances, weapon add-ons, and psychic powers for certain soldiers later on in the game.
The turn based gameplay is easy to pick up, but hard to master, and with game modes that can ensure that you have no chance to take back a move or retry a botched operation, it can be a very intense and stressful game.
All in all, I would highly recommend XCOM 2 to any gamer who enjoys RTS, RPG, or strategy games in general. Picking it up now while its on sale (something like 60% off) is just the icing on the cake.

The usual suspects of an action game are present: you can roll, block and use a handful of weapons and customization to destroy enemies. Though that might sound like slim pickings compared to other action RPGs (specifically Diablo clones). The hammer does more damage if you aren't moving, the sword can be thrown and is speed based, etc. and there are upgrades that make so that all of the customization options can be felt.
Personality is the key to this game's design. In a way, this game plays how you want it to. There is a high degree of difficulty customization (eventually, by way of "idols" in game), a few very important story decisions and combat customization. Alcohol acts as equipment in the game, and they can drastically alter how you play, on top of this you have special skills you can use and switch  out freely (unfortunately some of these skills are similar). If all of this sounds like an old hat, I can't stress enough how much you can change your gameplay experience: you can have enemies explode on death while you use two melee weapons for some nice reflex based challenge, or you can make your shields counter hits heal and do critical damage as you turtle along.
The highlight of the game features is without a doubt the narrator. There are certain portions of the game where what you do or don't do is spoken by the narrator in that golden voice of his. I even caught myself smiling as the narrator called me out on having fallen off the ledge so many times. When you change up your weapons he will remark how that reminds him of something, or some of the items history. What is great about the narrator is that he adds more to the narrative and lore, bit by bit, and adds more personality to the game. The story is solid, it is not experimental, but is great and delivered extremely well.
This game is worth your time. It is not a grand epic like any of the Elder Scrolls or a loot fest like Diablo. What you have here is an earnest gem of a game that isn't trying to be anything more than a solid action RPG.

The Maw is a delightful action platformer released in 2009 by Twisted Pixel Games, who has gone on to release a slew of really tight, inventive downloadable games. The game centers around space adventurer Frank who comes upon a cute little one-eyed pink monster (heh) while being held captive on an Imperial ship. After making their escape, Frank becomes tethered to the Maw by an electrofied gauntlet, allowing him to guide the creature around like a guard dog. It becomes clear pretty quickly why the Maw was imprisoned, for he has an insatiable appetite for anything and everything, with each new meal causing the Maw to grow in size.
This game was an absolute delight, combining all of the elements that I love from the action platformer genre popularized by Nintendo, Rare, and Sony’s third party studios. The gameplay is really fun, introducing new enemy types and abilities at a pretty frequent clip, such as Frank learning to use his arm tether to sling enemies, hijack ships, and grappling-hook his way around the beautiful alien landscapes. Who doesn’t love a grappling hook, am I right? The Maw also sees quite a bit of progression, not only by growing in size, but also by absorbing the powers from defeated enemies during boss fights.
This game is really charming, and has a refreshingly colorful and bouncy animation style. The characters are undeniably cute, and have funny interactions during cutscenes. The game is not an incredibly long experience, as it can be completed in under 10 hours — including all three DLC expansions. Despite its short running time, the game is full of content, and keeps the game progression moving along at a comfortable, natural pace. It’s not often that we see new platformer franchises being released these days (with the exception of the mildly well-recieved Knack on the PS4), and although The Maw is by no means a spring chicken, it is still as fun and refreshing as the day it was released.
Highly recommended.

The rumors of multiplayer could make or break this, so we'll have to see what happens in the future. Your character walks agonizingly slowly for a video game--especially when you can waste whole in-game days trying to track down a neighbor to give a daffodil to on their birthday. It's sort of like The Sims in that respect.
On the downside, the characters don't really pop like the casts of Rune Factory or Animal Crossing. They're really only memorable for their over-the-counter melodramatic backstories. Really, they could've called this game "Harvest Moon: Edge of Despair: Gay Marriage Edition". Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons is a little...quaint, by comparison, naively lacking the same sex option as of yet. Stardew Valley meets its criteria for providing a rewarding and satisfying gameplay experience while providing the option for the player to enjoy the game with a friend. I spent many an hour now discovering the game's secrets playing alongside someone, and it's been a stellar way to get through the game.
The game comes to its epic conclusion when, strapping your farm implements to your back, you borrow Sebastian's bike to catch up with a runaway Joja Mart train, sent by its secret Dwarven AI overlord to obliterate Pelican Town for not succumbing to its nefarious plot to control the population and drain its resources for the formation of an escape vessel for the Dwarven race to return home. The producers force-fed the developers more than they could chew, but decided that choking on their pride was preferable to discretely spitting their mouthful of half-chewed product into a napkin.
You'd think that Ubisoft had learned from the Watch_Dogs debacle not to let the marketing department promise more than they could deliver. Unfortunately, the execs learned the wrong lesson. Rather than tempering expectations to more reasonable levels, they have demanded that every feature announced must be delivered regardless of whether it's technically feasible to do so.
As a consumer, I had done my due diligence and waited for this title to go on deep discount before even considering it. I was fully aware of the game-breaking issues experienced by many during launch. I expected little, yet still got even less.
The biggest selling point of the new graphics engine when Unity was announced was the size and density of NPC crowds that the game could display. I was about to say "...that the game could handle" but that is clearly not the case. Any time there is a large crowd on screen, the game engine buckles under its own overambition.
Other people have been remarking about framerate drops due to the large crowds. I couldn't honestly say if I noticed this myself, because I was more more concerned with an issue that had a far larger impact on my enjoyment of the gameplay. In certain areas of the game with large mobs and busy architecture (the street along the north side of Notre Dame being the most consistent location for me) the game engine seems to put a far higher priority on rendering these visual elements than on reacting to player input.
The end result is that while running through a crowd, the camera may start drifting on its own accord as though it were locking onto a point of interest. Nudging the camera stick briefly to correct this drift will be met with
.
Character movement is similarly impacted. Attempting to run around hostiles ends up with the character either faceplanting into a wall or, more commonly, veering directly into the enemy to trigger combat. All the while, the game engine itself is not displaying any signs of graphical slowdown. So I end up watching my character being pummeled to death at 60fps because because he walked down the wrong street and had an aneurysm.
Unless your game's primary gimmick is all about intentionally janky controls (Surgeon Simulator, Octodad, etc.), this blatant disregard for the basic principle of usability is completely unacceptable.
Again, the poor performance happens around large crowds and busy architecture. Guess where a majority of the story missions take place? The end result is tailing missions where Arno heedlessly beelines to the person he's tracking, chases where Arno decides he'd much rather make love to a wall instead of run down an alley, and combat where the only solution is to drop a smoke bomb (after being told seven times) because the engine might not be paying any attention to your time-sensitive parry command.
In previous games, learning the streets and staying on the ground was often a faster and safer means of traversal through a city. Rooftops took ages to climb to and there were snipers everywhere yelling at you to get down. In Unity, the roofs are far preferable to the quicksand at street level.

GTX 1080 (8 GB VRAM)
These are far more than the recommended specs and significantly better than the minimum, so it should run at least adequately, right?
There's a difference between slow code and bad code. Slow code can eventually be overcome with more powerful equipment. But if it's been coded to run like♥♥♥♥♥♥ faster gear just means it'll be fast♥♥♥♥♥♥
Like most Assassin's Creed games, 80% of the game's content is based around collectibles and optional side-missions. Unlike most Assassin's Creed games I've played, I've actually opted out of 100% completion because it's so incredibly pointless.
In the early game, you're introduced to your home base. Investing a bit of money to buy improvements and running a handful of missions guarantees that you'll be making roughly 10,000 in cash every 20 minutes. By the late game, you finally get the ability to open the highest difficulty of locked chests. Those chests typically return 250-1000 units of currency. A mere pittance compared to the fortune you've amassed by then.
Actual assassination missions start off with a fly-through of the zone featuring points of entry and side-objectives like freeing prisoners to create distractions. Most of the time you can just ignore all that, climb over a wall, run up to the target, stab them in the face, drop a smoke bomb, and run away.
Combat is -- I wouldn't exactly say "dumbed down" compared to its predecessors, but it is significantly less enjoyable than AC IV: Black Flag or the AC II trilogy. Parries are still in, but one-hit kill counter attacks are gone. So, too, are chain kills.
The combat camera stays at the same distance as the navigation camera instead of pulling back. So in a 6-man fight, the camera is so close to Arno that two or three enemies will be attacking you from offscreen (usually with firearms.)
You end up wasting time fishing for parries and clumsily flailing in retaliation. Defeating one enemy produces zero momentum to turn the tide of battle. The end result is that combat feels more like an annoying chore than an enjoyable distraction.
If you've been following the series you know it's about the Assassins and the Templars getting involved in historical events and influencing politics from behind the scenes. This is tied together with a series-spanning B-story about the modern-age organizations digging up magical relics of unspeakable power.
The French Revolution makes for a nice backdrop, but it is often little more than a backdrop. Arno has next to no direct impact on the events of the French Revolution. Napoleon doesn't show up until near the end of the main game, has you do one or two errands for him, and then promptly disappears (only to make a cutscene cameo in the DLC.)
The main plot boils down to Arno's quest for personal revenge and some intra-office politics on the side. Seems there's a traitor in the midst of the Assassins, when you find out who it is and confront them it pretty much plays out like it did in Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory -- a game published by Ubisoft nearly 10 years earlier. Then Arno goes rogue
just like in Splinter Cell: Double Agent released the following year.
And as far as the MacGuffin that the modern Assassins want to find? You find out where it ends up, then everyone just shrugs and goes "eh, it's not worth going after," thus invalidating the 16-20 hours it takes to plow through the game.
At least AC: Rogue was okay. Good job, B team.

Fractured Space is an interesting yet simple concept. 5v5 capital ship combat with 2 lanes and a special center lane you can capture for a team buff.
Pros:
-Wide variety of ships to suit many different playstyles
-Looks fantastic, ships are very detailed down to the tiny mining ships and fighters zipping around the map
-PvE is a decent time killer and you can still earn rewards while playing against bots
Cons:
-The learning curve will kick your♥♥♥♥♥br>-The grind for unlocking new ships is tedious at best and a major annoyance at worst
-Crew pods, special crew aka the Pirates and Dark crew give seemingly insignificant stat boosts which actually add up very quickly, this can be both good and bad for you
-Microtransactions and premium currency. While it's not Battlefront 2 by a longshot, the devs are pretty keen on making premium ship skins and bundles instead of actual new content
-The playerbase. What playerbase? I wish I was kidding when I say I've been in queue for over 10 minutes for a single PvE match, the people you do find are usually pretty nice, probably because they're happy they finally found a game.
Overall it's a fun concept executed well but it's still rough around the edges, maybe with time it'll get better, I certainely hope it does as this is one of my favorite f2p games on Steam

I got XCOM2 on the day one and have invested a little bit of time in it since then, so today I wanted to share my thoughts with you about how this game ultimately turned out.
While at the beginning it looked like a rushed, buggy and poorly-optimized mess, it had the most important feature going for it - full support of Steam Workshop mods. Not long after the release we saw a steady flow of mods improving different aspects of the game, while Firaxis also worked on the patches that have finally eliminated most of the problems that's been plaguing the game from the get go.
As of now XCOM2 offers a challenging gameplay that differs greatly from its predecessor, nice story with beautiful cinematics, cutting edge graphics, and of course an astonishing variety of high-quality mods,--adding new maps, classes, enemies, cosmetic items, and even introducing completely new game-changing mechanics--I'm talking about Long War II of course.
With the new big expansion "War of the Chosen" coming up August 29, and promising three new factions, enemy heroes, new cinematics and even new game mechanics, XCOM2 is looking as a very good deal, offering a lot of value for your money. Especially now when it's on sale with a huge discount!
______________________________________________________________
Я купил XCOM2 в первый же день и с тех пор успел немного поиграть, так что я хотел бы поделиться мыслями о том, какой игра получилась в результате.
Хотя её выпустили явно в спешке, она была забагована и плохо оптимизирована, но у неё была главный плюс - полная поддержка модов Steam Workshop. Почти сразу после релиза начался постоянный поток модов, улучшающих различные аспекты игры, в то время как Firaxis трудились над патчами, которые исправили почти все проблемы игры.
На данный момент XCOM2 предлагает вам сложный и интересный игровой процесс, сильно отличающийся от игр-предшественников; неплохую историю с красивыми видеороликами, ультрасовременную графику и, конечно же, безумное разнообразие высококачественных модов, добавляющих новые карты, классы, врагов, косметические предметы и даже  совершенно меняющих механику игры, - я конечно имею ввиду Long War II.
А совсем скоро выходит огромное расширение «War of the Chosen», обещающее три новые фракции, вражеских героев, новые видеоролики и совершенно новые игровые механики. Таким образом XCOM2 представляет отличное приобретение, особенно сейчас, когда игра продается с огромной скидкой!

First off...Don't let my hours decieve you.
Go back 1 year, and I would highly recommend it to all people. Ever since the expansion pack and all this new "playable" content, Trove has taken a massive downfall.
Trove itself is probably one of the biggest GRIND games out there, I understand its an MMO, and MMO's are suppose to be repetitive and grindy, but Trove takes it to a WHOLE NEW level.

Server Lag:
Its been here since the start up of Trove. Also, in game you can be teleported randomly back or down, which can highly screw up gameplay, it can cause you to die and miss your chance on killing some Boss. F2P/P2W/P2P:

You cant get the best set of gear in the game for a single character without commiting at least 200 hours for that single character for gear (AT LEAST).
The Devs can't stick to an idea long enough to make it a reality, all alpha/beta testers know this for a fact. Trove has been ruined, the first year of gameplay of Trove (First year of Trove) was the best gameplay you could have.
New Features/Content:

After playing through the whole game, I've got to say. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ This is fantastic.
Although it's nothing innovative, the gameplay is what games should be: fun. The combat is really enjoyable, and a diverse set of weapons makes it interesting. Usage of various upgrades, like a simple weapon crafting system to the various Tonics in the game, keep the game varied, all the way to its final minutes. Special modifiers (similar to Skulls in Halo) give the choice of Risk vs Reward. Do you want to power up your enemies, to get more loot and XP? Or keep them easy so you won't die? The gameplay keeps thing fresh, adding new and cooler elements as you progress. (+) (+)
The writing is fantastic. This game IS going to be remembered by the fantastic Narrator (played by Logan Cunningham). His voice spans your adventure, and you will love hearing it. (+)
The game also offers New Game + after the main adventure closes and a score attack mode. Both adding very nice replay value to a game that'd only be around six hours without it. With it, it bumps it up to 13-14 hours. (+)
The game can vary from Kind of Easy to Damn Hard, depending on the modifiers mentioned earlier. I do suggest putting some of said modifiers on, because the game is very easy on it's own. (-)
Soundtrack? Gorgeous. I hummed "Build that Wall" throughout my adventures countless times. It's a fantastic sound track with very good sound design. (+) However, I can't help but notice some default Sony Vegas noises weaving themselves in. (-)
The game also looks friggn' beautiful. The art style Supergiant Games decided on looks fantastic. The cartoony esque look gives every creature in this world a distinct look. (+)
Through the ENTIRE game, I only encountered a single technical issue. The game runs great, with barely a bug to see. Very polished. (+)
Supergiant Games really impressed me with Bastion. It tells a very awesome and engaging story, with fun gameplay to boot. Nothing to sneeze at for their FIRST EVER GAME. There is a reason why it's earning 100+ awards, from Best Indie game, to best soundtrack, even game of the year in some cases. And how much is it? $15.00!? WHY ARE YOU NOT PICKING THIS GAME UP?

Mindless fun-- appeals to the collector in me. It's a serious grind, and aggressively monetized. Unless you want to play for six months just to reach current "endgame", you'll have to drop a decent amount of cash.
Trove started off as a game where you essentially didn't have to pay a dime, and the devs were upfront about the fact that this initial business model made it very difficult for them to make money. So around February 2016, they started to monetize the game hardcore. The cheapest packs were $20-- and that was in addition to a $15 a month subscription. With the introduction of the Mantle of Power expansion, they added such an extreme element of RNG to the game via the gem system that it seemed impossible to advance without either crazy luck, or ridiculous amounts of cash. The outcry from the playerbase was severe, and over the past couple of months, Trion has dialed back the RNG and monetization. There's still plenty of it, don't get me wrong-- but a lot of concerns have been addressed, and now they've started to offer $5 packs. And with the upcoming push to consoles, I think the game is going to get a second wind of content.
All in all, this game was rough for a while, but it's slowly getting back to a satisfying place. For those of us who love simple action combat, collecting, building, and mindless grinding, Trove is magic. But if you want progression in any reasonable amount of time, prepare to drop AT LEAST the $15 a month for a sub. Anything less and you'll be playing until the end of time without ever catching up. The packs aren't completely crucial, but being willing to buy one or two a month will definitely put you in a better place. If you don't want to spend a dime, ever, then this is not the game for you. But if you try it and love it enough to want to invest in it, the way you would a hobby, then Trove will be an immensely fulfilling experience.

12 Labours of Hercules is a casual time management game developed by Jetdogs Studios and Zoom Out Games in 2015. 12 Labours of Hercules is the first installment in the series. The game takes you back to Ancient Greek as you aid Hercules to rescue his kidnapped wife Megara from the evil Hades. There are 40 levels in this game, including 4 mini games. There are two modes you can choose when you start a new game, relaxed and expert mode.
Basically, in every level, you'll start off with a map and a few objectives. There is a starting point in every level. From there you must command your servants to build, collect resources, remove obstacles, etc. Later in the game, there will be more characters you can command. You must remove obstacles and enemies to complete the objectives using various resources like food, supplies, and gold. You use them to clear obstacles, destroy enemies, and collect other resources. To complete the level, you must complete all of the objectives. In each level, there is a timer. The longer you do, the less score you'll get in the end of the round. You won't lose the level if you run out of time. There is also a star system. If you finish a certain level before a specific time, you'll get three stars in the end of the level.
The game is very addicting. For a 2D game, 12 Labours of Hercules has a very good graphic. The soundtrack is also fantastic. I really like the narrator's voice acting. The game mechanic is pretty solid as well, and the artwork is superb. I really like how this game is integrated with Steam Cloud and Steam Leaderboards. Making progress in this game worth it. It also has Steam Trading Cards.

Colin McRae Rally might bring up memories of better times. For me, the Colin McRae series was what got me into racing games. I remember playing the first one back when I was a child on my own personal computer. (2000-2001)
Now I must start off by mentioning that is in no way, shape or form, a remaster of the original Colin McRae Rally. Rather this is actually a port of a mobile game. With that being said, it does slightly affect the way I would assess this game.
Colin McRae Rally just feels like a "lite" version of Colin McRae Rally 2.0 (2000). To be fair, it is just based around 2.0, there's just less content. 15 cars in the original, only FOUR in Rally. I find that to be very disappointing, because of the great selection of vehicles the CMR series always had to offer before. Rally just seems so empty, lacking what you'd expect from a Codemaster's racing game. I had gone into this blind, expecting a good old-fashioned Colin McRae racing experience, only to be let down by one of the things that made Colin McRae and DiRT so great; content.
Physics are what you would expect from a game originally from 2000. There's simple deformation when you crash, but you hardly notice changes in driving dynamics unless your Steering/Suspension is badly damaged.
Simply put, If you're an old-school CMR fan and you're looking for your fix on Steam, you might as well hop right into DiRT.
So the question, would I recommend this game?
Full-Price: No.
On Sale: Yes, but if it's CHEAP. It's only $7, but I personally wouldn't pay that for a mobile port.
It's sad this is just a mobile game and not a remake of a classic. It's probably only worth a couple bucks, but it's fun for what it is.

Tower Unite, as many know, is the spiritual successor to the popular Gmod Tower. Now, I personally have never played Gmod Tower, so I went into this game without any real prior knowledge about what the previous game was like. The game is still in Early Access, and from what I can tell there's still a LOT of content that the developers are wanting to add to the game. But let's go over what the game has right now...
The biggest a most-fun part of the game is definitely the Mini-Golf. With several unique courses in multiple different settings, the Mini-Golf definitely had the most thought put into it. It's easy to get into and learn the controls, and when I got the hang of it I feel that this is the most fun Mini-Golf I can find on Steam. Even playing alone you can enjoy yourself simply by getting used to the different holes in a particular course and try to beat your best score. People can drop in and out of any game no matter how far along it is if they so wish, and balls can be customized with hats that you can buy for your in-game avatar with the in-game currency.
The big point to the game, I suppose, is to play games to collect in-game currency to purchase furnishings for your condo, where you can invite friends over to to hang out. As far as I can see, there isn't REALLY a lot to do around the condos with other people other than to show off your stuff and watch videos, though. Maybe that'll change in the future.
Other activities include a few other mini-games (such as a shooter game or a Monkey Ball-type game) and some different, smaller activities in the main lobbies such as a casino, some game-show trivia and a bowling alley, with stuff ike bumper cars, an arcade and laser tag being planned for in the future (judging by the so-far under-construction buildings in the lobbies). Once everything gets finished and put out, there will be no shortage of things to do.
Now comes the biggest drawback to the game. The game can lag quite a bit in the lobbies. I run the game on Windows 10, and on a computer that I largely purchased to play games, and the game can still lag for me. I find that the game lags more on high-populated servers, so because of this I don't even bother trying to get onto a server that's more than half full. Hopefully the lag will decrease when the game leaves Early Access, but for now it's a bit of an annoyance on an otherwise very-enjoyable game.
Do I recommend it? Absolutely. I have a lot of fun with the game and I look forward to seeing where it goes in the future. The lag is a bit of a problem at times and something I hope they're able to fix in the future, but otherwise I think this is a solid game with a lot of content, and more to come along the way.

I didnt want to have to do this.  I love fallout 4 and it has always been a good game, even better when modded.  But as of recent Bethesda has tried to force "paid mods" onto the community.  I dont have an issue with modders getting paid and getting to work with the game creators to make mods but what is going on behind the scenes is what makes me upset.  Bethesda will charge you to buy currency to pay for these mods.  Now lets say you spend 15 dollars on a currency pack, that 15 dollars goes to Bethesda whether you have picked any mods or not, which automatically goes into their wallets.  From here you are allowed to pick mods that range in prices of currency and when you purchase said mod a portion goes to the modder, the rest into Bethesdas pocket.  Because of this Bethesda is literally making extra money of modders hard work before you even get to pay the modders themselves, terrible business practice.
Fix: Do away with currency and let us buy directly from the modder if its worth what we want to pay.
Next:  Everytime they add stuff to the Creation Club it will require an update to make the game bigger as it downloads the items but wont unlock them until you purchase said paid mod.  This is causing issues with big free mods like F4SE that needs to be updated literally every time the Creation Club has a new item for sale.  Bethesda said they didnt want to stop free mods but they are trying to hardest to make it so people dont want to have to update their mods every week on a game that has been out for 2 years already.
Fix: Only have us download a paid mod if we actually pay for it, forgoing updates every 2 days.
Finally I'd like to say fallout 4 is a good game that is worth the 30 dollars, but with the new turn of events I definitely have issues with the developers try to bleed their community dry, I mean I have paid 110 dollars for fallout 4 and all of the DLC and yet they want more and more money from me which is really a big turn off.  Bethesda please dont ruin your future games with the current Creation Club and stop stealing money from hard working modders.

Even in the early-access stage, the game has managed to capture the spirit of the earlier Master of Orion games, while streamlining colony/empire management and tactical combat. The tech tree is still my favorite in the 4X genre. Ship design is exactly the same as in Master of Orion 2, with firing arcs, targeting computers, shields and utility modules.
As to the new additions, I'm surprised how well the real-time combat works. Pause the game, issue orders, resume. It's much faster than moving each unit individually, and it doesn't sacrifice any tactical depth.
I also liked building up the new military outposts. They restrict enemy ship movement, allowing for the creation of a militarized border zone on the outskirts of the empire.
The only thing I'm not sold on is the unlimited travel range for all ships. Discovering other races is much faster now, but somehow feels a bit out-of-character for Master of Orion. Still, this minor gripe hardly affects my overall enjoyment of an excellent game. Highly recommended!

I got XCOM2 on the day one and have invested a little bit of time in it since then, so today I wanted to share my thoughts with you about how this game ultimately turned out.
While at the beginning it looked like a rushed, buggy and poorly-optimized mess, it had the most important feature going for it - full support of Steam Workshop mods. Not long after the release we saw a steady flow of mods improving different aspects of the game, while Firaxis also worked on the patches that have finally eliminated most of the problems that's been plaguing the game from the get go.
As of now XCOM2 offers a challenging gameplay that differs greatly from its predecessor, nice story with beautiful cinematics, cutting edge graphics, and of course an astonishing variety of high-quality mods,--adding new maps, classes, enemies, cosmetic items, and even introducing completely new game-changing mechanics--I'm talking about Long War II of course.
With the new big expansion "War of the Chosen" coming up August 29, and promising three new factions, enemy heroes, new cinematics and even new game mechanics, XCOM2 is looking as a very good deal, offering a lot of value for your money. Especially now when it's on sale with a huge discount!

This game and the others like it in the series are real gems for wargamers both computer wargamers and those that used to play board game style wargames from Avalon Hill, SPI, GDW, and other classic wargaming companies. The amount of detail and historical data the game encompasses is thrilling. As an exampe, you don't just have a an armored unit. You get an armored unit that is broken down by the type of equipment it has, its morale, training supplies and so much more. You have can interact with high command to get more supplies, trucks, new artillery pieces, even additional command staff. If your prestige and polical points (consider it in game gold for purchasing replacements) is high enough, you may be able to convince high command to abandon some set objectives and to go after another objective. Individual generals have a large effect on battles via their stats and can play differnt cards which represnt differnt command functions. For example, one card may allow your infanty to attack better, while another card may help out a division's sagging moral or help with recon. The games in the series are a little pricy but worth it, particularily if you catch them on sale.

Trove is a fun, repetative but addicting game. I enjoy this game with the fun mix of fighting, collecting, and upgrading in a blocky world. There's just a couple things that are horrible about this game:
1: The launcher. When you launch Trove from Steam, you exspect to launch the game, but insted you get another launcher called Glyph. Glyph has to be the most glichy launched I have ever seen. I have had countless problems with Glyph and customer support sucks so much that I had to spend more time attemping to launch Trove than actually play Trove.
2: The bug fixes. There are multiple problems with the updates/bug fixes. First of all, the updates always crash the Glyph launcher and make me have to restart the launcher multiple times before I can even play the game. Not to mention the fact that the updates, although very small, take forever to download and be applied. The bug fixes and an even bigger problem. Every single bug fix that is released comes with a package of new bugs that need to be fixed. That means that bug fixes and constantly coming out and are barely even improving that game, if not making it worse.
3: The Trove servers. Most of the time when I play Trove, things don't run all that smoothly. Constant lag spikes occur that can effect gameplay drasically, and sometimes happen so often that you can't even play the game and enjoy it. This could be result of my own internet connection, but I doubt it because my internet connection works perfectly with other online games. I believe that the servers Trove runs on are simply not the best and need improvment.
Conclusion: I do not recommend this game. Although it is fun, all the trouble that one might have to go through to play the game is simply not worth it. If the creators of Trove get rid of Glyph, hone in their bug fixing skills and technology, and get better-performing servers, then I would return to this game. I would still recommend attempting to download and play the game yourself but you might end up experiencing the same problems that I have experienced.

This wargame has an interesting focus on Your army management, that I really like. Each turn You get some amount of equipment of different types (different models of guns, armor, trucks, infantry, speciality units, etc.). Unused equipment is automatically stockpiled in Your main HQ unit and then it is distributed to the frontlines, where it is needed. You can even force Your units to redistribute some equipment back to the HQ resource pool and then back to other units that needs that equipment more. You can designate a new type for Your division and it will automatically get a new equipment to fulfill that role. You will need to keep supply routes open for that and need a bit of patience because it will not happen automatically. This is really nice feature to play around and see how Your force evolves.
