I'm going to start off by saying that this game is much better than I thought it would be.
I played Soccer Manager 2015 and 2016 and I wasn't entirely impressed by them. I felt they were lacking and had a few problems that seem to have been worked out. *Note - This isn't anything close to how Football Manager is, so don't go in expecting that.
I'm currently playing the game as a placeholder I suppose for the lack of a better name until Football Manager 2017 comes out. You can start off with any team you want. Player ratings are done a bit weird, but it isn't a big deal. For the most part, transfer budgets are fairly small (about 20ish million). That budget is the norm for all big teams as far as I know. You can purchase 'Cash Injections' but you really don't need too, it is very easy to make money (Raise youth players and sell them, bring in players on free transfers and sell them, sell fringe players, etc. If you're losing money every month then that means you have a player who has a very large wage and you don't have enough cash so becareful of that.)
The game does 1 thing that I've seen never before in Football Manager: Players arrive late for training and don't perform well. I thought that was a cool and interesting feature, and funny when it was Nicklas Bendtner that did it.
Games go by very quick, not much to them. Pick one of the few formations available, set few tactics, and you can assign player roles. All games are done on a 2D match engine. I'd love to see a 3D match engine.
Transfer tips: Sign Christian Pulisic and take a look at the free transfers, you can get Martin Caceres and Alex on a free in the first season and some other decent mid to high 80 players.
I'd love to see the microtransactions disappear. I wouldn't mind spending 10 - 15 bucks on this game to have no microtransactions and a 3D match engine.
One last thing, I'd also love to see a redesigned UI and more information on players and clubs, in similar fashion to Football Manager.

My competition owned the public house across from mine, but I owned the only croft in town. I saw they had a pastry setup as well. Their public house was more upgraded than mine, thus they had all the townsfolk flooding their establishment. I noticed that they were saturating the market with their stock they were producing, driving down the prices of porridge/wheat beer/weak beer.
This led me to suffering great losses each turn due to me paying wages without making sales. But alas, I owned the only croft in town. I locked my doors, refused to sell them the precious wheat and beets needed to craft their mind numbing nectars. I watched as the remaining stock prices in the market for wheat/beets went through the roof. The Klippingens were paying top dollar for the last pidly remaining scraps of wheat they could get their hands on.
Four years passed without me once opening my stock to them. After they sold their remaining product for mere pennies, they had no choice but to close their doors and put their establishments up for sale. I was just a lowly pub owner myself though, barely supporting my wife, daughter, and employees. How was I to afford acquiring their business's?
After nearly being forced to sell my own home to feed my family, it dawned on me, "we have a guild house that gives out loans". I immediately ran over to the guild house, and borrowed whatever money they were willing to lend me. Sadly, although they knew me as an honest man, I hadn't yet proven myself as an intelligent business man. They only loaned me enough money to buy the other public house (sealing the fate of my competitor forever), with enough change left over to take my family out to dinner that evening.
This wouldn't work for me however. I had failed my family too many times, I refused to take them on "one night of fun" in exchange for a mediocre life. I instead bought that public house, and left my wife and daughter sleeping that night. I wandered the streets for hours, watching my shadow chase me from dark alley to dark alley, looming over me like a curtain of failure. It was on my walk home that I crossed paths with an out of work rogue from the next town over.
His name was Corwin Fielding, he was but 23 years of age. Agile, strong, confident - if somewhat arrogant. He offered me absolution that fateful night, he offered me the pride I had been searching for all these years. I didn't ask questions, I just gave him the remaining money left from the loan and the purchase of the Prancing Pony (public house).
When I woke in the morning it had all felt like a dream. As my wife prepared my porridge before I left for work there was screaming through the streets. I went outside and stopped a man carrying a bucket of water, I asked him what all the commotion was. He explained to me that the pastry shop at the edge of town had burned down last night. It happened so late that no one was around to put out the fire or seek help, he explained.
The owner all but abandoned the building and I was able to take title of the pastry shop. I ended up hiring Corwin on fulltime as my personal escort. It made me feel more important in town, and it felt like the right thing to do after all he had just done for me. My competitor lost all of his business's in one single day...I was victorious.
Things were quiet from then on. My wife raised our daughter well, my business's flourished. I was the life blood of the town, my farms provided the resources needed by my tavern and bakery to make the goods needed by the towns people. Life was good.
Sometime after my daughter finished her apprenticeship at my tavern, I offered her- her own way in life, my croft. She gladly stepped up and accepted the gift from me, she wanted to breed cattle as she heard the capital city was thriving with this new meal called "roast beef". I was proud of her ambitions and supported her venture.
My daughter was 20 years of age the night she decided to stay and work the corral after she sent her staff home. She wanted to put in a few more hours to get the last load ready for transport to my tavern. It was on this night that the Klippingen family decided they wanted their retribution. They sent a group of "thugs" to my daughters corral "The Flying Unicorn". After they beat her mercilessly, the father, Peter Klippingen stood over my daughter, drew his dagger, and cut her throat in that very corral she worked so hard in.
My wife fell ill four years later, and she passed on a cold winter night. They say it was the plague, but I believe it was her broken heart that finally did her in. She was always attached to our little Marie, from birth she did her best to raise her well, and be as loving as possible. Although she never spoke it aloud, I feel she never forgave me for what happened to our Marie.
Life has to continue, for our family, for our dynasty. I had to go back to work, hire someone to take Marie's place on the farm, keep things ... normal. I eventually remarried, to a learned woman, a scholar of all things. She too had suffered loss in her life, it almost seemed meant to be. We eventually bore a son, she let me name him Junior. Our dynasty was yet again flourishing.
My new wife never made me hide my past from Junior, he was raised with a firm understanding of the transgressions we suffered early in this town. Junior decided to attend an apprenticeship at a different guild, the guild of rogues. His reasoning was that he wanted to run tolls to help keep bandit activity away from our town. I reluctantly agreed.
In my wifes later years, with Junior out of the house, she decided to enter politics, something she seemed born to do. She excelled in the local town meetings, moving up from one position to the next. I was happy for her, as I knew it was something she was very passionate and gifted at. My business's were booming at the time, so I had no quarrels with funding her political aspirations. Before we knew it, she had been elected Village Reeve, a position right below that of Mayor itself.
Around this time Junior had completed his apprenticeship and returned to us a man. He requested that I relieve Corwin of his escort duties, explaining he deserved better than that. Corwin seemed eager to join Junior, so I didn't hesitate, an old brute like that didn't deserve to be following me around all these years later.
My wife approached me one night and asked for my support in her running for Mayor. This was a sensitive subject because it was Peter Klippingen whom was our current Mayor. She promised me it would be okay, that she would be safe. She explained to me how she had made some good friends in town, and things were more sophisticated than when I first arrived and had my falling out with the Klippingen family. Everything was political now, she said reassuringly.
The night before the elections we all gathered at my house for a massive feast, I spared no expense. That night, after all the guests had left, Junior came in and asked me about his sister. We sat up till well after 11pm talking about my baby Marie, he was intrigued to learn about her, and obviously saddened by her passing. Him and Corwin left to run errands I'll never forget the morning of the elections, on the doorstep to the Assembly House lay Peter Klippingen. His throat slit ear to ear, blood as thick as the porridge I serve at the Inn. The townsfolk almost seemed relieved by this sight. People running up and down the streets...as if they were celebrating. It was voted, and agreed that the elections would still be held, life had to continue after all.
My wife won the election for Mayor, due to the recent passing of Peter, and she was the only eligible candidate. Our town soon became a city under her watch, things again were going great.

Arguably the weakest aspect of Theatre of Doom. The game itself is far from ugly, but it has the graphical appeal of Path of Exile in its early days. There is much left to be desired, especially after being inundated with well optimized UE4/Unity titles these past couple of years.
There's a lot of repetition in monster variety in Theatre of doom, but the levels themselves are somewhat varied and help keep the campaign from feeling too stagnant.  Your character also remains visually consistent throughout the entire game, and the only time you will see a switch up is during versus/couch co-op modes(each player is a unique color[red,blue,teal,etc]).

Apart from the gameplay, the sound is my favorite part of Theatre of Doom. The main soundtrack seems to have been created/produced by an artist known as
. It's an excellent throwback to the 80s synth horror genre, and reminded me a bit of the soundtrack to 2014's "It Follows." The difference between the soundtrack of "It Follow's" and the soundtrack of "Theatre of Doom" is intensity and speed, with the latter being more supersonic.
Gameplay will be hit or miss for a lot of folks. For me, the gameplay was largely a huge
.
There are times when you'll be frustrated at the controls: target lock-on might not lock-on, even though you swear up and down that you and your target indicater were facing your target while mashing your lock-on bind furiously. There's also moments of aggrivation because the depth perception in the game is somewhat poor; given that one of the central movement mechanics is the ability to use a jetpack to ascend/descend, the isometric camera can make for difficult depth perception which will lead to many failed strikes and shots.
But failure and practice are key elements to success. You'll be able to better orient your character after a few hours of zipping around with your jetpack in combat, but your depth perception will never be flawless in this game's environment.

So you've decided that you're tired of being made fun of for having buttery man paws and you wanna get dirty for once in your life. Well hoist up those britches boyo, we're going in. Say goodbye to your days of drinking soylent through a bendy straw.
Stardew valley is one of those games that produces output of how much effort you shove in. Want to really press youself to meet as many goals early on and keep a tight schedule? Go for it. Want to be a lazy chump and rifle through your neighbors garbage to sell their yesterdays lunch for gold because you can't be bothered to actually farm like I do? Heck yeah!
This game will be familiar to anyone who has played this genre of game, especially the most well known series being Harvest Moon, or as I like to call it, Reap Planetoid.  You clear out your plot of land of debris, collect wood and fiber, destroy local wildlife. Y'know, the whole shebang. Grow crops, go mining in the cave at the back of town, hit on purple haired girls who shop at hot topic and drink your sorrows away at the Dewdrop Saloon while crying about how you will never drink another Triple Venti, Half Sweet, Non-Fat, Caramel Macchiato.
The ebb and flow of the gameplay is pretty simple, you balance time to harvest crops and resources to make you money to upgrade farm structures and get livestock, to make more money to keep on upgrading your house, tools and-WAIT. I forgot to give Haley this Daffodil! AHH. Decide what you want to do early, because the first year is probably the toughest while you're still trying to amass gold to ugrade your farm and wooing the ladies with your meaty biceps. Down the road you can even marry potential candidates, and live on the farm together!
If you plan on trying to win everyone over, participate in every festival, do the daily side mission for some extra gold thats posted at the seed store, worry about a potential relationships with girls around town, gather resources for upgrades, deposit your crap you found on the beach that nets you money (Why can't I shove my trash into my mailbox for free money? :c) and make sure everything is set for the next in-game day, then you'll have your hands full right from the start. But it's very satisfying busy work, one of the reasons Reap Planetoid is so popular.
Stardew Valley isn't all too original, most of these concepts have existed before. BUT. It is a very solid rendition of the genre of farm-sim games with it's own basket of charm and whimsy. Just don't try to give cute girls junk you found in the trash can outside their house, they tend to not like that.
I give Stardew Valley 3.5 dumpster fish dinners out of five.

Hallelujiah, the Apocalypse has arrived. (TL:DR at bottom)
I bought into DayZ StandAlone last year. For a year I've been trying to participate in and enjoy, that game, and rarely have I walked away pleased. The glitches, hackers and terrible zoombie mechanics left me disappointed too many times to recommend StandAlone.
When I saw Arma 2 Complete go on sale for less than $9 I had serious reservations about giving Bohemia any more of my money, but I really wanted a DayZ experience the devs have promised me dang rabbit!
So, I pulled the trigger and purchased Arma 2 Complete and immediately kissed the rest of the games in my library goodbye!
Set-up wasn't easy, I was plauged by the error messages seen everywhere in the forums by recent puchasers of the same set, but with some patience, determination and a LOT of reading I was able to overcome the BattleEye bugs and, again, with some little annoyances I also got DayZ Commander set up and the Epoch & Overwatch mods installed..now, what about this DayZ mod?
My time is recorded through Arma 2 OA so since purchasing Thursday so I'm closer to 15 hours in and it's been absolutely AMAZING. DayZ Mod was the experience I was hoping SA would bring me and never did. I've had more intense, blood curdling, panic-inducing moments in DayZ Mod than any other game on my steam list.
The Zombie AI, imo, is the best on Steam. Coming from a pretty hefty zombie/survival/open-world gaming list, DZM provides more thrills than 7DTD, The Forest, The Dead Linger etc. The pathfinding is superb, the animations are great, the sounds are excellent. They provide a real atmosphere of tense-horror at just the right time.
The one big issue in SA (out of many, believe me) is the zombies are still broken. The have x-ray vision which stretches miles, can run through a lot of obstacles and are very hard to "lose", imo. The zoms in DZM act exactly like I would expect zombies to act. I can't explain to you the joy I felt when I was crouched in the ditch of a road, night settling over me, with two lumbering Zeds slowly shambling my way having yet still notice me. Staying extremely still, not breathing IRL, I remained crouched as these two denizens of the undead proceeded to ramble past me, mere INCHES from my face, without knwoing I was there. One wrong move or sound from me and I was Zombie Dinner! I've been waiting for that experience for a long time, through a lot of games, and it was a joy to finally see it realized.
Installing DayZ commander and getting at least Epoch and Overwatch working (out of a lot of other intense mods) are almost tantamount to give you the DayZ experience you are looking for. They add so much flavour to the game including trading posts, custom building and crafting (up to massive bases), wandering AI, including Bandits, which add SO much flair to the game, roaming bandits, Aircraft Bandits...truckloads driving from village to village looking for hapless victims to strip them off their gear and sell them at the nearest vendor. The different MODS through Commander add new maps, missions within the game (find an Alpha zombie, kill a scientist for a cure, find a downed plane for it's supplies); plus many servers have their own lore and stories built within the game. Basically you can tailor you Apocalypse scenario any way you want...creating the experience you want.
Graphically I find the MOD looks almost exactly like the SA, and plays very smooth. I have a mid-grade pc and on the server I have picked as my favorite so far I have been getting FPS in the 50's, which is great for my machine (I'm used to 30 FPS for a lot of games), so technically it isn't as demanding as I thought it might be.
If you are turned off by a lot of buttons then DayZ may not be for you. It is very demanding in it's use of the keyboard, utilizing a lot of keystrokes for the experience. If you're new to this structure then allow for extra time in-game to really get a feel of the flow, but once you're used to it there is no denying how satisfying it is being able to use 4 buttons at once to scope out around corners, or scan far off to the North while feverishly running South.
The Gear screen is a little confusing to me still, as I'm still fiddling with how different items work together, and I haven't even begun to touch crafting or building. But running around a few servers with player made creations shows that the system is deep and immersive. There are a lot of clans out there that have spent hundreds of hours building, scavenging for parts and building a community within the game. The nice thing is, especially through DayZ Commander, you can find as casul or hardcore an experience as you wish.
I haven't come across any bugs or glitches in my almost 15 hours of play or so, not that I'm saying it's perfect, but coming from SA to the Mod I was expecting it to be a horrid, buggy mess, so I have been very pleasantly surprised with the fluidity of the game and it's contents.
I have tested in many types of servers, full PVP and PVE, and have been lucky to have picked really incredible community servers, so griefing and KOS'ing (so far) have been a non-issue for me, but I do a lot of research on servers before hopping in. What I did find nice was with the addition of Bandit AI, even in  a server that's PVE with no one but me on it, the threat from man is JUST as palpable as the threat from zombies. It's quite a thrill to run into a village looking for supplies and taking out a zombie population with a silenced pistol, freely exploring buildings, and at any moment hearing the sounds of a truck coming around a corner, running to hide in a a building JUST before the headlights light you up, and watch as  5 bandits jump from a truck, fully armed, going from building to building, shooting anything they see. It's exhilarating and challenging, but in no way breaks immersion or the feeling of Apocalyptic Doom.
If you can get this package on sale it's a HUGE bonus. But, to be honest, now that I'm in DayZ Mod and experiencing the thrill of DayZ as I was hoping I would have had over a year ago, the retail asking price of the package is completely worth it. For now, I am am uninstalling my DayZ Standalone, saying a silent prayer for all the games on my list that I won't touch for many months to come, and immersing myself in the Zombie Apocalypse game I have always wanted and now have found. :)
TL:DR; An immersive experience that blows away it's struggling little brother DayZ Standalone. Worth the price (especially on sale), and the finest example of a Zombie Apocalypse game on Steam yet. If you can get past the installation issues and have the patience to get DayZ Coammander up and running, then this game is unparallelled.

The RNG is bipolar as all hell and sometimes it feels like the percentages dont mean a thing. That being said, it still offers the same grid based control that hooked me on Xcom and it manages to do that mostly well, besides some lousy elevation selections when you want to move some one. (Too many times I have had soldiers run to the base of a staircase and end their turns rather than go up it like I tried to originally do before the cursor glitched away suddenly)
All in all, I would say it is worth it for the sales price, and hopefully some patches roll out to solve the angry AI controlling the RNG. If that happens, then I'd even say full price is worth it.

While fans of the MoO series will easily be able to adapt, there are a number of changes that have been implemented (such as star lanes) that impact the gameplay by making it more similar to some modern space 4X games. Whether or not this is a Good Thing (TM) probably depends upon how old you are.
In its still unfinished state, most major features are implemented. Some features need some TLC: customizing star ship designs isn't as fun or friendly as it could be, switching between screens make an annoying sound, finding and selecting what to build in the selection menu is something of a chore, and pollution isn't the threat that it should be. I haven't experienced and thus don't review all races or spying in this review.
I'd like to see pollution scale in severity to the planet type. Gaia worlds should be very sensitive to high levels of pollution and should provide a more clear benefit. There is little clarity as to what the planet "specials" do (Dark Quartz = ?) or why you want them and you don't get new tech for exploring or colonizing Artifacts planets. Tech research times are also much too rapid, you will find it difficult to keep your fleet up with your pace of technological development. Several of the techs have poor descriptions. I expect much of this to be cleaned up as the game moves towards production.
Tactical combat is no longer turn based and is now real time (also similar to other modern space 4X games). You can now control the speed ships move at and control the rate of time. I would personally prefer to see a return (or option for) turn based tactical combat. Battles also don't last very long, taking some of the fun out of them. The planet screen needs some more work; I don't like the rather "cartoonish" icons for workers/researchers/farmers.
Good: Return to classic gameplay, modernized interface. Nothing like the soul crushing nightmare that was MoO 3. Less micromanagement and more fun overall.
Bad: Combat isn't as fun as it used to be, some adoptions of "modern" 4X games add questionable value to the game. Turn-based tactical combat was fun.
Ugly: The end game on large maps gets laggy and crashes more often. A "failed to create new game" bug causes the game to crash every 50 or so turns for me.

By and large, most choice-driven games have followed the same formula, inviting you to make your mark in the world by deciding if you want to be “good” or “bad,” and accepting the binary nature of existence. But in the post-apocalyptic world of The Walking Dead, where the dead walk the decaying earth, the notion of good and bad is somewhat dated. There’s no “right” when right can mean shooting an innocent child before it can turn into a flesh-eating beast, and there’s no “wrong” when wrong can mean stealing the supplies you need to survive from those just as needy as you. The Walking Dead is the story of the choices you can’t live with, and the choices you can, coming together to create an experience as depressing and pessimistic as it is remarkable and memorable. This game will linger like a good book.
In stark contrast to the rest of gaming, The Walking Dead is more focused on what you do than how you do it. There aren’t many traditional puzzles as much as there are tasks that you’re asked to perform to move the story forward. Menial activities like finding batteries for a radio or starting up a train aren’t all that engaging by themselves, but they serve a very necessary pacing purpose, as well as give you a chance to explore the world a bit and get to know the characters better. If you’re looking to rampage around Georgia blasting the heads off of undead monsters, you’re better getting one of the many other zombie games on the market. L4D comes to mind.

Quick Summary: An interactive movie with some quick time events and light puzzle solving. The only Telltale game I played before Walking Dead was Game of Thrones, so in comparison I’d say Walking Dead has slightly more “thinking” involved (because of puzzles), and slightly fewer quick reaction events. I haven’t read any of the Walking Dead comics, only having watched the television series. While a couple of characters from the TV show appear in the game, they play small roles and quickly disappear. You do not need to have watched the show or read the comics to understand what’s going on in the story.
In this game you play the role of Lee Everett, a convict on the way to prison for murder. Not too much detail is given for his past, but Lee doesn’t seem like a bad guy. His incarceration will need to be postponed though, because the dead are coming back to life with a hunger for human flesh. Suddenly they’re just all over the place and pretty much all of them look like they’ve been rotting for weeks. The story follows Lee and Clementine, a little girl he finds early on, as they make their way through Georgia looking for Clementine’s parents and doing whatever it takes to survive without becoming monsters. You have the opportunity to ally yourself with people you meet along the way, but group conflict is unavoidable. Some people will hate you no matter how nice you are, and some people will stick with you no matter how much of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you choose to be.
The game is broken up into 5 episodes, each one taking a little over 2 hours to finish, and roughly every minute or so you get to choose your dialogue options and/or plans for proceeding. It’s kind of like Mass Effect or Dragon Age where most of the time you get 2-3 dialogue options of varying politeness, and you pick what you want to say. While the game reminds you at the beginning of each episode that your decisions shape the story, I’m pretty sure that 90% of the outcome is pre-ordained, so for the most part don’t worry about making “wrong decisions.” People that are going to die are doomed with or without your input. There are only a handful of pivotal moments that really affect outcomes, and at the end of each episode these will be listed for you, along with the choices made by other Walking Dead players. For example: You and 75% of all players chose to kick this guy out of the group. The only way to “lose” the game is to fail a quick time event and get shot/chomped on.
Pros:
+The game is played for the story, so with few exceptions gameplay is very easy. Quick reflexes might be necessary in a few places but overall you can relax and enjoy the show. If you accidently have your hands off the controls and die, the game usually resets to only a few seconds before you died.
+The story is thought provoking and compelling, where you don’t really know what’s going to happen next. As it goes on you’ll care about what happens to some of the characters (even if it’s just wanting them to die).
+Game hardware requirements are not demanding since the graphics are cel shaded (like Borderlands).
Cons:
-The game auto-saves, and not as often as I’d like. If you’re forced to quit for whatever reason, there’s a decent chance you’ll need to replay 5 minutes or so, and you can’t fast forward / skip cutscenes or dialogue. This was only a problem for me in the DLC when I was trying to win a luck-based mini-game.
-As I mentioned before, most of your decisions don’t really impact the plot that much. You might make someone mad with a dialogue choice but it’s not like you have a friendship/romance meter to fill for additional options. I don’t think you can make someone so mad that they never talk to you again. The game just displays something like “He will remember that” and oftentimes it never comes up again. Because of this, there isn’t that much appeal for re-playing the game. Once you’ve finished the game, you know what’s going to happen (regardless of most of your choices) and never play again.
Overall, I’d recommend The Walking Dead if you enjoy plot driven games and don’t mind a relative lack of “action.” The puzzle elements are simple for the most part, and even though you need to scrounge for items a bunch of times, you’ll never think to yourself “I should have picked up that screwdriver from the previous area.” The game will not let you progress without picking up what you need.  The story is very linear and there’s only one place I can think of where you might get “stuck” (fixing the train). If you have the DLC for the game, 400 Days, you will have access to a 6th episode, in which you play multiple characters in short stories that will impact the next game in the series, Walking Dead Season Two.
It is still a classic game and I love it.

I recommend 12 Labours of Hercules provided you agree with the following considerations:
-You enjoy playing casual/mobile market games.
-You are looking for a game that is light on strategy and more relaxing to play.
-You want some easy achievements/badges/cards.
-You are looking for a not-hard, feel-good game
-You are looking for something that is very child-friendly, which is presumably the intended audience for this game
12 Labours of Hercules is a simple, (relatively) fun stage-based strategy game and I've concluded makes a good casual game for children. There is some loose story based on ancient Greek mythos but I found the "Old" style of writing to detract more from the plot and often skipped through cutscenes personally. The rough objective of the game is to get from A to B, usually by clearing a number of objects and hindrances from a map board to reach the ending and unlock the next point on the world map. Similar to many games currently on the mobile market, you can earn a rating of 1-3 stars for completing a level. Earning stars is completely based on completing the level quickly, though most missions can be accomplished with a gold rating without any real strategy or planning (this isn't a very hard game)
There is almost no challenge to the game. There is really no fighting or reflex based gameplay in the entire game, with the small exception of some very short, easy boss fights, which are kind of interesting since they all employ completely different gameplay mechanics from the actual game. (Each boss is basically a small minigame.) So far I've played the game for two 1 hour spurts, both which ended with me getting severely bored with the fairly repetitious gameplay and in this time I've completed about 60% of the game, with every level 3 starred without that much real effort.
If you are looking for something for your kid to play that you can just leave him alone with for a few hours, this is a good title to consider. Or if you like to give yourself pat on the back without really exerting any actual effort. They get stuff to click and achievements, cards and what not to give them sense of accomplishment.
7/10 if I'm thinking of the children
3/10 adults (only buy for yourself if you are looking for a casual clickfest where you can put your brain to sleep)

Hallelujiah, the Apocalypse has arrived. (TL:DR at bottom)
I bought into DayZ StandAlone last year. For a year I've been trying to participate in and enjoy, that game, and rarely have I walked away pleased. The glitches, hackers and terrible zoombie mechanics left me disappointed too many times to recommend StandAlone.
When I saw Arma 2 Complete go on sale for less than $9 I had serious reservations about giving Bohemia any more of my money, but I really wanted a DayZ experience the devs have promised me dang rabbit!
So, I pulled the trigger and purchased Arma 2 Complete and immediately kissed the rest of the games in my library goodbye!
Set-up wasn't easy, I was plauged by the error messages seen everywhere in the forums by recent puchasers of the same set, but with some patience, determination and a LOT of reading I was able to overcome the BattleEye bugs and, again, with some little annoyances I also got DayZ Commander set up and the Epoch & Overwatch mods installed..now, what about this DayZ mod?
My time is recorded through Arma 2 OA so since purchasing Thursday so I'm closer to 15 hours in and it's been absolutely AMAZING. DayZ Mod was the experience I was hoping SA would bring me and never did. I've had more intense, blood curdling, panic-inducing moments in DayZ Mod than any other game on my steam list.
The Zombie AI, imo, is the best on Steam. Coming from a pretty hefty zombie/survival/open-world gaming list, DZM provides more thrills than 7DTD, The Forest, The Dead Linger etc. The pathfinding is superb, the animations are great, the sounds are excellent. They provide a real atmosphere of tense-horror at just the right time.
The one big issue in SA (out of many, believe me) is the zombies are still broken. The have x-ray vision which stretches miles, can run through a lot of obstacles and are very hard to "lose", imo. The zoms in DZM act exactly like I would expect zombies to act. I can't explain to you the joy I felt when I was crouched in the ditch of a road, night settling over me, with two lumbering Zeds slowly shambling my way having yet still notice me. Staying extremely still, not breathing IRL, I remained crouched as these two denizens of the undead proceeded to ramble past me, mere INCHES from my face, without knwoing I was there. One wrong move or sound from me and I was Zombie Dinner! I've been waiting for that experience for a long time, through a lot of games, and it was a joy to finally see it realized.
Installing DayZ commander and getting at least Epoch and Overwatch working (out of a lot of other intense mods) are almost tantamount to give you the DayZ experience you are looking for. They add so much flavour to the game including trading posts, custom building and crafting (up to massive bases), wandering AI, including Bandits, which add SO much flair to the game, roaming bandits, Aircraft Bandits...truckloads driving from village to village looking for hapless victims to strip them off their gear and sell them at the nearest vendor. The different MODS through Commander add new maps, missions within the game (find an Alpha zombie, kill a scientist for a cure, find a downed plane for it's supplies); plus many servers have their own lore and stories built within the game. Basically you can tailor you Apocalypse scenario any way you want...creating the experience you want.
Graphically I find the MOD looks almost exactly like the SA, and plays very smooth. I have a mid-grade pc and on the server I have picked as my favorite so far I have been getting FPS in the 50's, which is great for my machine (I'm used to 30 FPS for a lot of games), so technically it isn't as demanding as I thought it might be.
If you are turned off by a lot of buttons then DayZ may not be for you. It is very demanding in it's use of the keyboard, utilizing a lot of keystrokes for the experience. If you're new to this structure then allow for extra time in-game to really get a feel of the flow, but once you're used to it there is no denying how satisfying it is being able to use 4 buttons at once to scope out around corners, or scan far off to the North while feverishly running South.
The Gear screen is a little confusing to me still, as I'm still fiddling with how different items work together, and I haven't even begun to touch crafting or building. But running around a few servers with player made creations shows that the system is deep and immersive. There are a lot of clans out there that have spent hundreds of hours building, scavenging for parts and building a community within the game. The nice thing is, especially through DayZ Commander, you can find as casul or hardcore an experience as you wish.
I haven't come across any bugs or glitches in my almost 15 hours of play or so, not that I'm saying it's perfect, but coming from SA to the Mod I was expecting it to be a horrid, buggy mess, so I have been very pleasantly surprised with the fluidity of the game and it's contents.
I have tested in many types of servers, full PVP and PVE, and have been lucky to have picked really incredible community servers, so griefing and KOS'ing (so far) have been a non-issue for me, but I do a lot of research on servers before hopping in. What I did find nice was with the addition of Bandit AI, even in  a server that's PVE with no one but me on it, the threat from man is JUST as palpable as the threat from zombies. It's quite a thrill to run into a village looking for supplies and taking out a zombie population with a silenced pistol, freely exploring buildings, and at any moment hearing the sounds of a truck coming around a corner, running to hide in a a building JUST before the headlights light you up, and watch as  5 bandits jump from a truck, fully armed, going from building to building, shooting anything they see. It's exhilarating and challenging, but in no way breaks immersion or the feeling of Apocalyptic Doom.
If you can get this package on sale it's a HUGE bonus. But, to be honest, now that I'm in DayZ Mod and experiencing the thrill of DayZ as I was hoping I would have had over a year ago, the retail asking price of the package is completely worth it. For now, I am am uninstalling my DayZ Standalone, saying a silent prayer for all the games on my list that I won't touch for many months to come, and immersing myself in the Zombie Apocalypse game I have always wanted and now have found. :)
TL:DR; An immersive experience that blows away it's struggling little brother DayZ Standalone. Worth the price (especially on sale), and the finest example of a Zombie Apocalypse game on Steam yet. If you can get past the installation issues and have the patience to get DayZ Coammander up and running, then this game is unparallelled.

The past 2 weeks made the game pretty unstable for a majority of the community and with the fix(es) they did, it did not correct 100% of any of the problems done so far. And yesterday, they added a new gem mechanic that looks way more horrible because it requires the daily currency (cubits) instead of the main game currency (flux), you would originally swap gems at the cost of flux, which was pretty easy to test out some "builds" with the stats you wanted on your class(es). Now, it requires a shop item, at the cost of 500 cubits, which is what a non-patron (person who did not pay for a patron boost in various stats) receives daily, unless it's an empowered gem, which requires double the amount (meaning a normal player would have to wait 2 days, while a patron user would only have to grind it in 1 day, since he receives triple the amounts of it (1,5k)).
Reason of this change : prevent people from abusing snipe/camping the top tiers leaderboard, which most of them, are patron users that already have possibly tons of cubits and can whatever still snipe the leaderboard.
Problems of this : Now it locks beginners from testing with gems on which and what they like or not, mid-game players that wants either that or just simply switch the gems to another class to not waste the gem and give a boost to them, unless they have about 60-120 days of stacked cubits unused, which is never the case because you essentially use them on various important items. Plus the fact that they changed most leaderboard rewards for less anti-cracking gem boosters, and more empowered gem boxes, it makes it even more game-locking (or blocked) because either you take the risk of having a gem levelled to be cracked, or do nothing to not break them, which blocks you from going further.
Tl;dr I'll quote this guy on their forums that said "If you have a flat tire, you don't change car", and this is what they did, they had problems with leaderboards, so they changed gem mechanics.
If you don't care about many changes, paying or whatever, this game has potential, except that you'll need to grind countless hours to max a class, level up mastery, get good basically.
But overall, this game doesn't look like a game, it still looks like straight out of beta;
1 patch = Multiple new bugs,
1 fix = not really,
1 announcement = Did not ask their community before for it.
Unless they make the game more stable, proper to multiplayer gameplay without any global changes that creates unfair inequalities between people who pays and not, I do not recommend this game for the time being as the last 2 weeks patches shown me enough of it.

Stardew valley is more than just a clone reminescent of the old Harvest Moon games.  Rather, it is a labor of love as an homage to games LIKE Harvest Moon tha borrow upon task and purpose. That said, this game is a testament to what can be accomplished by willpower and create a modern day success story for the developer, as far as I know it was primarily one person.  Whether you buy Stardew Valley with the intent of enjoying a throwback to a game that I think captures evey essence of a simple yet enjoyable game that favors organizing, planning and strategy over twitch response times then this may be your game.  This game is also proof that modern day success stories in the gaming industry are still possible when back by dedication and passion and the developer is deserving of the financial success they will recieve for their work on this piece of art.

Codemasters’ Colin McRae Rally launched on Steam earlier this week for $6.99, but it’s probably not the game you’re hoping for.
Though the game’s description on Steam says it’s based on content from the 90 percent Metacritic rated Colin McRae Rally 2.0 originally released on the first PlayStation, it’s actually a port of the mobile version of the game released in 2013 (which has a Metacritic score of 69 percent).
The game’s trailer also says that it’s been “remastered for HD,” and that it includes “original cars and locations.” Add to that the fact that it only mentions the mobile version once in the "About the Game" section, and one could easily come to the wrong conclusion that he or she is buying an HD remake of the classic PlayStation game.
Besides offering a fewer number of cars to drive, the game’s controls and interface were clearly originally designed for smartphones, and so it doesn’t play like the game you remember.
The Colin McRae racing game series is still around today in the form of the DiRT series, which are quite good, and are also available to purchase on Steam.

Couple of things off the top. I love the AC universe, I have played almost all of them and several of them to 100% completion on Xbox. This was an okay game.
TL:DR - Decent game, stream lined weapon management, they attempted to improve free running. I highly suggest playing it in french with english subtitles. All the characters of British accents otherwise it seems.
Story:
It was okay. It doesn't advanced the Assassin vs Abstergo story at all and I don't know where it fits in the over all AC story but it was fun to run around revolutionary Paris for 30-40 hours. If you are a history buff and like this time period you will enjoy the game. I recommend playing this in french with subtitles to get the best effect. Unlike in Ezio's stories where they had the proper accents to the english all the characters sound like they are from London, England which was very distracting until I made the change.
On Co-op:
I've heard people complaining about the co-op missions getting in the way or breaking the game but I disgree with that assessment so I want to address it first. I did do it once but it now suffers from a very small player base which means for some of the co-op missions that you need 4 members for you simply won't find a match which is fustratin.
Skill tree and upgrading equipd:
These are back/in this game, you can have different types of melee weapons such as heavy, one-handed, etc. Fustratingly the assassin blade is no longer a "weapon" but rather something you can ONLY use when not detected unless you knock someone to the ground and spec into using it. You now need to unlock talents through points and there are many options for gear all era specific. They stream lined this but most combat styles end up functioning the same.
Free running:
They tried to improve it and did in someways but broke it in others. The ability to run through buildings and explore buildings necessarily meant they had to change it but the effect was the free running didn't always work great and was fustrating compared to other AC games.
Overall: Decent game that has been patched and I had none of the issues that plagued this game at the start. I would buy on sale, however, the DLC is nothing to write home about as perusual with AC games and you don't need to buy it if you don't want to.

In this story game you'll play in a world full of dead walking people. You play as Lee, a guy who stumbles upon a little girl called Celementine. Together, you have to survive in this dangerous world full of zombies, but also other dangerous people like bandits for example. Mostly these are just some big details, since the headline of the story will be the same for everyone, but it will really make a difference. Of course, I will keep this review as spoiler free as possible, so I won't tell much more about that. But you have to be careful about the decisions you make.
The story and the voiceacting is really great, and the story will get more interesting over time. I kinda enjoyed episode 1, but after episode 2 it got way more interesting for me. You'll form a band with Clementine and some other people, so you want to do anything to protect them. This story will also have it's sad moments, overall it's just a wonderful experience.
I really recommend this game, especially if you like story games where you have to make decisions. The 400 Days DLC wasn't that interesting to me, since it's a small side story about new different characters. If you want a real sequel, then there's The Walking Dead Season 2, wich will continue the story (including the decisions you made) of this game.

Xcom 2 is a pretty fun sequel to a much better Xcom Enemy Within. Starting off, the graphics are improved greatly and the enemy models are interesting and unique from the first. That being said, the soldier customization feels lacking of more actual armor. Most of the choices seem nothing short of a tank top or vest.
The gameplay is where I waver. I have a sniper that has killed two aliens, those aliens being the only two shots she has ever landed. The RNG is bipolar as all hell and sometimes it feels like the percentages dont mean a thing. That being said, it still offers the same grid based control that hooked me on Xcom and it manages to do that mostly well, besides some lousy elevation selections when you want to move some one. (Too many times I have had soldiers run to the base of a staircase and end their turns rather than go up it like I tried to originally do before the cursor glitched away suddenly)
All in all, I would say it is worth it for the sales price, and hopefully some patches roll out to solve the angry AI controlling the RNG. If that happens, then I'd even say full price is worth it.

Being a huge fan of the 4X genre and having played an endless list of 4X games, like Master of Orion 2+3, GalCiv 1-3, Sword of the Stars 1+2, Endless Space, Distant Worlds, StarDrive 1+2 and many more and even supporting upcoming games like Predestination, I really wanted to like this.
Unfortunately it is a huge disappointment, serving a dumbed down 4X experience totally out of touch with why people still enjoy turn based games, for instance considering the recent huge success of XCOM. Sure, they got it to look almost as pretty as XCOM, but all the research and a lot of the ship systems you could add in MoO2 are not to be found, because they went for simple RTS combat implementation. Combat is ridiculously simple and vastly inferior to great RTS space games like SotS, Homeworld or Battlefleet Gothic: Armada. Combat, ship technologies and ship design in this game feels more like an insult to fans of the genre and few games makes ship design as meaningless and combat as dumb as it is in this game. This mass selecting clickfest where kiting the AI is basically the only "advanced" technique at your disposal is just not appealing to guys used to much more juicy space combat offerings both currently and in the past.
I recommend that you save your money for one of the other more recent 4X space games (Stellaris, Galactic Civilizations III, Predestination, and many more worthy of your cash), which offers a much more satisfying strategy game experience either turn based or RTS.
I will revisit this review an edit if if they update the game to be more fun. If they add turn based tactical combat with ship initiative in some future DLC, this game would finally be a worthy successor of MoO2 and I would probably be able to recommend it.

I will preface this review with this; this game is not for everone, if you enjoy constant action, verbal schematics and a gutteral experience, you will most likely not enjoy this game.
Botanicula is a point-and-click game developed by Amanita design who are most famous for Machinarium (which I also highly suggest.) The game, in terms of mechanics, is very similar to Machinarium but is more adventure centric, with most puzzles revolving around walking around the environment and finding what looks out of place. But the atmosphere is definitely this game's strong suit. You play as a bunch of seed-like creatures who have formed an alliance to save the tree that they live on. The story is very vague, all that is shown is a viral, black creature that begins to dismantle the tree. There is no dialogue in this game, this does not hinder the game though, the game has a way of telling you everything that you need to know without actually telling you anything, and you find yourself growing attached to the seemingly one-dimensional seed people and their goals and aspirations.

Early Access Review:
I played MOO and MOO 2 A LOT up till very recently. MOO 3 was a train wreck that had good intensions but just was a horrible implementation. Seems this version is slowly going down the MOO 3 path with a glossy version of MOO 2 graphics slapped on top.   Graphics are good for a 4x game, sounds ok I guess but I do not play these games for a good soundtrack. In fact I play with them muted as it is about tactics and what you are going to do next turn not how nice the alien leader sounds. They spent way too much time and money worrying about that when the gameplay is lackluster.
To start star lanes really make it so easy and unplayable. Basically defend 2 planets and you are good to go. There are definite choke points which make those systems critical.
Combat, ah combat. Pre beta people that are younger wanted real time combat. True MOO fans that are older and enjoy the tactical nature of turn based obviously didn't. Well they went real time, but not really. You just build a fleet, and click fight. Trying to do any sort of maneuvers or tactical layout really doesn't matter. You can try as I did, but you will find out that in the end is useless. The combat system is a glorified combat viewer of the simulation. Once you realize that just skip combat. But wait, you want to control your ships, this system and game doesn't really allow for it to make a difference or change the outcome much at all. So sad, they could have done a really nice turn based or even a put in your moves and both sides move and fire same time type of setup and would have worked well for this game. As it stands this game "combat" just doesn't stand out from anything else in the 4x world of games and thus they missed their chance.
The races seem to be missing their big differences that existed in MOO and MOO2. I have played most and they all seem the same. You research the same, build the same, build same type of fleets, etc.  I would have preferred if each race really did well on one type of planet type, or you could take pros and cons like in MOO 2 where you can customize each race. I cannot nail it down but they all seem very generic with a different skin.
The ship builder looks nice and works well but again is really useless as the whole combat system really doesn't work. Since real time combat just isn't meant for this type of game the upgrades to weapons with fire arcs and such just won’t see the light of day when you can just cram on more weapons in same space without having to worry about such mundane details which made MOO 2 much better.
They need more areas of the map that affect game play like nebula, super large asteroid fields, etc that affect areas of the map differently. Adding those would add a lot of depth to the map and gameplay.
As mentioned on the discussion board AI is just awful. As much as I hear people say, "just play multiplayer and your problem is solved", have you tried to play and FINISH a 4x multiplayer game?  I have maybe finished 5 in my lifetime. Most games with 4 people, 1 will drop early, 1 will get run over for various reasons and drop out, thus leaving 2 people who then you hope have the time to play out the game over the next few days/weeks. But invariably 1 of the 2 will drop out making the game you vs. the AI in the end. So the single player game has to be somewhat resilient to keep me engaged between multiplayer matches. This game doesn't even come close, period. As AI programming is a bit of a hobby for me, this game makes me want to cry how someone is paid to create an AI and this is what they came up with.
If the game wasn't ready for beta, then delay, and delay again. Any sort of alpha test would have found or shown most of these issues.  AND IF the development team would listen to the outside alpha testers the game could be fixed. My guess is another development studio thought they knew best and missed the boat on this one. The best games I have played in the past many years are games that change and adapt to its core player base. Because if they are somewhat happy, they spread the word, others come and like the game and lo and behold you have a hit. This game seems to rest on the past IP glory and hope to make millions on people like me that paid and hoped for more but got a lot less.
I would at this time NOT recommend this game unless combat, star lanes and AI are fixed which may take a more in depth rewrite than this publisher has time/money.
I will change/update review after some major patches/final release comes out and things have changed, hopefully. :)

I tried Stardew Valley at the end of 2016 on the Xbox One and just couldn't get it into and eventually left it alone for a while. Nearly a year on, I got this on sale on PC and pushed myself to play it again and I am so glad that I did.
The charming graphics and endearing soundtrack will pull you in at once and not let go.
Stardew Valley presents a slight learning curve that comes hand in hand with the overwhelming amount to do in the game. This can make your first playthrough very daunting but once you get the hang of everything and learn how best to manage your time in the game, you won't want to stop playing. You soon begin planning ahead and working out your days in advance and reaping the rewards of this.
The story of how this game came into fruition is as charming as the graphics and soundtrack and definitely shows in every aspect of the game, from the deep unwinding story to the lovable characters and events you can participate in.
The only slight downside of this game for me is the lack of multiplayer, which was supposed to arrive by the end of 2017 but this has however been pushed back into 2018. However it is understandable why they have had issues bringing multiplayer to Stardew Valley.
Despite being a small indie game, with a price tag that reflects that; Stardew Valley is worth so much more than most triple A titles these days and offers a hell of a lot more playability.
If you're even the slightest bit intrigued by Stardew Valley, you should definitely buy it and at least give it a chance, especially for the price.

The Starship Asss Simulator
The loading screens, the video at the end of a game and the camera show us the wonderful bums of our beloved ships.
This is also a part to take care of, because the enemies will often shoot at it! So watch your butt.
More seriously now.
It is basically a MOBA but with less tactical elements and less important deaths. The emphasis is put on cooperation, as what serves as exp is shared between the team. Every few minutes, an event is triggered in a special area; to the team capturing the objective is granted a strong bonus for 3 minutes.
There are 5 “sectors”: two bases (one to defend, one to capture), two “lanes” with three mines each (which give exp) and two “forward stations” (to capture to be able to jump to the enemy base) and the special area.
You control one ship of the usual archetypes (tank, DPS, support, stealth) with 5 abilities (counting the main attack). Every 3 level (up to level 9), you may upgrade your damage, health or support. You jump from a sector to an other, fight the enemies for the control of the mines, forward stations, enemy base and special area.
I won’t go into more details now, but there are special features (you take more damage when you prepare to jump, the forward stations, if captured, enable to regen health, the ships have armour, you can create a crew…).
A few questions and their answers:
Is the game interesting? Yes, fun, a bit tactical too.
Is it pay-to-win? I’d say no, but if you pay, you may have an small advantage, but it’s still possible not to pay.
Is it too grindy? Yes and no. If you only play against AI and don’t make any missions, buying the ships may take you a long time. But the game is surprisingly generous and gives a lot of premium currency (I bought expensive ships with it, without paying).
To conclude, I will only say it is a nice game, a bit repetitive, with a small community and rather active devs.
Being free, if you want to try it, well do it ^^

This review is sectioned off into segments for returning GMod Tower players and newbies who couldn't tell a Hatsune Miku from a good admin.
As someone who has played over 100 hours of GMod Tower on and off, I can say that Tower Unite, at least in the last week that I have been playing it, easily surpasses the Source "powered" mod. Despite the change to the Unreal Engine, much of the "feel" of the old Tower is present, from not just aesthetic and sound, but also movement, interaction with the world, and minigames -  and also some familiar issues, such as load times and crashes. For better or worse, it's surprising how much of that Source feeling they were able to get out of Unreal. It certainly helps that, to my knowledge, the key players of the GMod Tower team are working on Tower Unite.
If you're looking for a point to jump in, now's a pretty decent time, considering that Tower Unite at this point slightly edges over GMod Tower in terms of content and polish, with much more to come over the next few years. Considering 15 bucks was the minimum VIP donation amount back in the day (and you bet I paid it), and also considering that past players and donators also get some neat bonuses, it's a pretty reasonable deal in my humble opinion.
Tower Unite is a spiritual(?) successor to GMod Tower, a GMod gamemode in which, to put in as simple terms as possible, players are able to chill out with friends, watch videos, deck out their own condo, and play minigames. A really casual comparison amongst my friends is Second Life, but with less clunky building tools, decade old menu design, and lonely S&M-loving geriatrics.  I'm sure there's some online-chatroom-avatar garbage that's more in line, but I wasn't dragged into those by my degenerate friends so I can't really compare them. Where was I? Oh yeah, GMod Tower was all about having fun with friends and relaxing.
Then something brilliant happened. The guys behind GMod Tower (who now go by Pixeltail Games) realized that GMod, and extension Source, were buggy, clunky pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥who's updates often broke literally everything and, to make matters worse, weren't the best to develop for what they wanted to produce. Seriously, GMod Tower sometimes felt like it was held together by nothing but copper-wire and the hopes and dreams of disgruntled server owners. So what were these bright-eyed idealists to do? Shut GMod Tower down of course,
But not without reason - they saw big potential in making a standalone version of the Tower, one on the more supported, recent Unreal Engine, and that could support massive updates and new content. Enter Tower Unite, a brand-new, copyright-free, paid replacement for the now-dead GMod Tower.
In the past year Tower Unite has very quickly begun to eclipse its predecessor in terms of content and scale, and still promises much more to come in the next few years. Seeing how dedicated Pixeltail is to achieving something they've been working on for nearly 7 years, I wouldn't worry about them abandoning it anytime soon. With a growing community and tons of stuff to do, Tower Unite is the very definition of a go-to-game.

The gameplay is okay. I thoroughly believe that this game (along with Syndicate) have some of the best parkour elements with how seemless it is compared to the earlier games. The animations just flow together, making it feel more natural. However, I believe that the combat is meh. Sometimes, the sword and heavy weapon play feel very sluggish at times. While you get some satisfaction out brutally murdering your enemies, it feels like a chore. It doesn't really feel based on skill, rather about making your character as OP as possible to beat them easily. That's another thing about this game. It's either too easy because you're too OP or it's too hard because the AI beats you based on level not skill. The worst part is when then they try to push these co-op missions. I don't know about everyone else, but when I try to play alone, it says I can't. I really wish the game would have catered those missions to both single player and multiplayer, but that just nitpicking at this point.
The graphics are top notch and I love the detail that went into this open world. The beauty of France in this game is top notch and I was blown away by the beautiful skyline, the realistic weather effects, and the realistic details that went into each building and street. However, good graphics don't make a good game. The performance I got with this game is 50/50. I played on 1440p, high settings, V sync off on a 980 Ti. On most of the game, I got a consistent 60 fps. It never went above which makes me wonder if Ubisoft capped the game due to its terrible performance at launch. However, in other scenes, it would would sometimes dip to the 40's, mid 30's. But credit to Ubisoft, due to the frame pacing, it was a smooth experience. But it's still disappointing that this game didn't run at a smooth 60, at least.
One thing Assassin's Creed always had was a crap ton of missions to do throughout all of its open worlds. However, most of them aren't all that great. Most missions just have you doing the same things over and over. Kill this guy, kill that guy, destroy this, destroy that. I wish that instead of having multiple missions doing the same thing, we got less missions with more substance. I'd rather play a mission that is memorable rather than the average "Oh, take out this Templar base" or "Kill this guy for no reason other than we couldn't come up with a better way to implement this. It's just fodder for completionists.
You may have noticed I haven't talked about the story and there's good reason for that. It sucks. You play as Arno Victor Dorian, Templar kills off family member, Assassin gets revenge, yada, yada, yada. Rather than playing to bring justice, you're playing for a vendetta. And it's not even the reason you become an assassin. Arno becomes an assassin because his girlfriend is a Templar, kicks him out because he didn't deliver a message to her father, warning him about his death simply because he was too busy flirting with Elise. He proceeds to join the brotherhood, break every rule in said brotherhood, and become a master assassin, somehow. Elise and Arno make up, take down the new Templar order and kill the bad guy. Honestly, Arno is the worst assassin i've ever played as. He breaks every rule in the brotherhood, he never consults said brotherhood about any of his actions, and he whines. A LOT.  He makes Altair look better in comparison. This story is just bad and only done to imitate French love stories.
Overall, this game is a 6/10. I only recommend playing if you care about the gameplay more than the story. However, if you want a good story, you're better off getting Assassin's Creed 2. I prefer gameplay which is the only reason I recommend this game.

First of all, I'll say that I didn't really enjoy this game. But I can appreciate the effort that was put into it, and I must say that the final product couldn't be much better than it is, I'd say. But it's not my kind of game.
If your familiar with Amanita's games, you'll know this already, but the highly stylized world and characters is their main focus. Like its predecessors, it's a point n' click game, and it has the same problems I have with nearly every game in the genre: you simply click everything on the screen until something happens. And that's not fun for me. It doesn't matter how pretty the world is, that alone simply isn't enough to captivate me.
On the other hand, if you enjoy these kinds of games, you'll most likely be amazed with this! The amount of detail put into the "bugs/creatures" and the environments is mesmerizing, and I have to give them credit for that. Amanita Design strikes again!
It's a shame that they always do point n' click games. I'm always impressed with their world design and charming way of memorably presenting simple stories... But the gameplay really lacks, with the amount of downtime there is between traversing from a screen to another.
Also, level design was a bit too labyrinthic in levels 2 and 3, having huge areas for the player to go back and forth to get different objects to progress. That's something that wouldn't be as bad if there was something to the gameplay other than clicking an edge of the screen and waiting for the little guys to walk there.
Aside from the traditional gameplay, there are some animated scenes, which are really great, one even representing how the "Amanita Universe" was created, with the Big Bang and both Samorost and Machinarium worlds forming. I feel like I would have enjoyed "seeing" a let's play of this game, rather than playing. They've scored everything in this, except for the gameplay.
The soundtrack fits the game's aesthetic very well, so I simply can't have any complaints about its presentation, it's amazing.
So, if you like point n' click games, go ahead, you'll have a blast! Otherwise, don't expect this to change your mind.

Upon first downloading it, Serena seemed to be a horror game.  It soon proved itself to be something greater than a game based on sole fear, and as the game progressed it seemed that the main character was experiencing the stages of grief after losing a loved one.  The way the game leads the player through the emotions and inner conflict of the main character is very realistic.  The plot twist near the end will catch every player off guard.  The ending, (don't worry, no spoilers here,) for me was extremely confusing and strange, and to me seemed extremely inconclusive.  I was not fond of the ending at all.  Even if it had taken the time to explain things at least a little bit more, it would have been a lot better.
The game itself ran relatively smoothly, though if I were to suggest features to add to the game, it would be a menu, with a save feature, so that when you close the game it doesn't make you start over when you return to it.  A pause function would also be very handy, especially since switching windows was very glitchy without first pushing Shift + Tab to go to the Steam chat.  Near one end of the cabin (near the armoir and the nightstand) there was also a minor glitch which caused the motion of the main character to pause and then jerk to the next scene, unlike the rest of the cabin which transitioned smoothly.
Overall, if you're interested in the kind of emotional journey this game has to offer, I would highly suggest it.  If you don't like confusing endings, Serena would not be at the top of my recommendation list.

I still put in a yearly playthrough of this title. Half-Life is often thrown around as one of the best games ever, and to truly appreciate why you need to understand how influential and groundbreaking this game was. Half-Life introduced all sort of tropes and mechanics that we very much take for granted today.
Half Life was the first game to let you play through the intro rather than watching a cutscene. Half Life was the first to generate new sounds depending whether you were in a big echoy chamber or a tight tunnel. I have now finished a play through and feel I can leave a review which will be meaningful. I won't get into what features are missing, or suggestions for updates, that will be on the discussion boards. This is for those of you looking at this game and wondering, is it really MOO?
The answer is a resounding Yes.
I have been playing MOO games since I got my hands on 1 back in 1993. A friend and I were just getting our of highschool and we played it on his old 386. It was glorious.
I got my hands on MOO2 a few years later, and didn't play it much until 1999. Initially I was thrown off, the interface was more like Master of Magic, than the MOO I had come to be used to. In time I realized that MOO2 was a worthy successor to the title.
I bought MOO3 when it came out. I really can't state my disappointment with that title.
This game, this game feels like MOO. The mechanics are balanced, much of the tech and the strategy of MOO2 is available here. I think they may even have lifted sections of the text from MOO2.
The original races are here, or soon will be.
The beauty of MOO was that it had enough micro management, without being too much. You have control, but you also don't need to babysit every planet constantly. The build queue is not as long as it was in MOO2 and some technologies with the same name now have different purposes. Biospheres is very different.
The combat is realtime, but the speed can be increased or decreased and ships can be controlled, there is also a cinematic camera for when you know you will win and want to savor some up close and personal views.
There are some changes I hope to see, but if you loved the origionals than you should enjoy this game. This is what MOO3 should have been, but is actually better. I never cared to take a screen shot in any of the previous games, my profile is getting filled with them here. The game is beautiful and amazingly fun.

Assassin's Creed: Unity, now, is a pretty good game. I recall when it first came out the number of issues it had. After five patches and a free DLC, I think Ubisoft was satisfied considering the debacle. When it first came out, it was "unplayable", as in the frame rates were incredibly low and there were bugs everywhere. Now, the frame rates are fine. The game is playable, that's for certain. However, there are still issues. The first issue you'll likely notice is the atrocious LOD (Level of Detail) for distant buildings. Basically, the textures and details on distant buildings are incredibly flat. There's also the matter of random NPC's having their outfits change sporadically at times. I tried to not let that deter me as I did enjoy the story and the abundance of side missions available in the game. But it's noticable enough that you have that instinct feeling that Ubisoft gave up on this game after it came out. The executives clearly didn't care enough about delaying the game as 3D programmers could have worked another six months to work on it and polish these issues. But, you know, they gotta get that money$$$.
On the other hand, Unity has a great story. I mean, I'm basically a sucker for the Assassin's Creed games and stories as I really enjoy the historical aspects and exploration of historical cities. Paris is absolutly beautiful, and when you're up close to some of these buildings, you have to respect the attention to detail. Notre Dame is massive as are the other notable landmarks.
The story involves Arno Dorian in a sort of pseudo revenge story. In the beginning of the game, spoilers, his father is assinated by a Templar. But it's not him you're avenging, as you don't really know much about who assassinated him. It's your adoptive father you avenge. Francois De La Serre. Francois took Arno in after the assassination of Arno's father, and you also grow up and fall in love with Elise, Francois' daughter. She knows all about the Templars and Assassins as Francois is a Templar himself. Basically, there's turmoil within the Templar Order, and after breaking out of prison, Arno was blamed for Francois' death, Arno ultimately works with the Assassins to figure out what's going on. You ultimately allign with Elise as, deep down, she knows you didn't kill her father.
It's a great story that did get some comparisons to AC: II, but I felt that it was unique on its own. The DLC, Dead Kings, was okay, but some of the ghost stuff felt a bit off. I just wish the bugs and random issues were resolved.
8.0/10

This is the first game in the series that gives me the actual feeling the creators tried to fix some of the game's biggest flaws. The addition of a pretty decent skilltree and equipment system allows for tons of customisation and lets you adjust your assassin to your own playstyle. Random events, side-missions and storyline missions have a much better design than the game's predecessors, never feeling repetitive or lineair, but instead granting you an incredible degree of freedom to achieve your goal the way you see fit: Which is pretty much what we all wanted missions to look like since the first Assassins Creed. Difficulty has been upped (it's not quite there, but it's heading in the right direction) by making enemies stronger and more aggressive and by having missions require more thinking and planning. Powerful skills, such as bombs, disguise or double assassination, need to be unlocked first, which is actually a pretty nice touch.
Honestly, I don't think ACU gets all the credit it deserves because its technical issues overshadow the gameplay changes.

I don't normally bother with reviews, but with the recent review bombing I figured I'd join in.
First, some stuff that is actually about the game:
Fallout 4 lacks any and all depth. You need to mod it to know what your character is actually going to respond when you choose their response. Your impact on the world is superficial. Stats/perks/abilities are very simplistic compared to many games. If you're looking for a competent RPG, this isn't it.
If you buy into the idea that any large gaming company is evil and that whenever they try to make money they are evil and should be chastised, this isn't the game for you.
If you're fine with those things though, it is a great big park that you can stroll around in, killing raiders and wildlife along the way. Rummaging through abandoned houses, picking up junk to build a neat little settlement and mod your equipment, doing simple side quests here and there. Leveling up your character and picking perk combinations to make something you want to play. And that's enjoyable. For lots of people that's hundreds of hours worth of enjoyable. The cause for the recent upset in the review section hasn't changed that in any way at all. As a new buyer, you can still get all those hours out of it as well.
As for why people are review bombing - The Creator's Club, a new system where people can get paid a one-time fee for a mod which Bethesda then sells and make profit off of. People are going mental over this. Apparently, this is the most diabolical testament to greed that has ever been. What people seem to forget is:
* Old mods are still available. This isn't Skyrim Special Edition where they tried to kill off support for old mods. That was a horrible move, but not present here. Free mods will still be created for you to use.
* Content creators don't need to sell their stuff to Bethesda if they don't want to. If they feel Bethesda is cheating them because Bethesda will keep making profit with every sale while they just got profit once, they don't have to sell their product. Problem solved.
* Consumers don't need to buy anything from Creator's Club. I won't.
* When I create something for the company I work at, I don't retain ownership of it and I won't get royalties from it if I leave the company. I get paid for performing the job. This is common practice, people. In some lines of business royalties are more common, but that's not the business model set up here. Again, if creators don't like it, they can simply choose not to sell their product. They are not being forced into anything and are thus not being scammed or deprived of anything either.
So yes, I recommend this game. Creator's Club didn't stop it from being fun. Creator's Club didn't kill modding, it didn't scam people out of their money, it's just a system where you won't get your money's worth because everything there is overpriced. Just don't buy anything from it and you'll be fine.

Half-Life is often thrown around as one of the best games ever, and to truly appreciate why you need to understand how influential and groundbreaking this game was. Half-Life introduced all sort of tropes and mechanics that we very much take for granted today.
Half Life was the first game to let you play through the intro rather than watching a cutscene. Half Life was the first to generate new sounds depending whether you were in a big echoy chamber or a tight tunnel. Half Life was the first to have enemies covered in different textures, so a shot on flesh or armor would generate different particles.
A full list would be too long to share here, but what it boils down to is that Half-Life is a cornerstone of gaming history, and the game that turned Valve into the giant it is today. Absolutely worth checking out, even this long after release.
