I'm not really sure why roughly half the people have implied that this review is UNhelpful by taking the time to discredit it. Helpfulness is my primary concern, and while I continue to stand by everything I have said to this point with sincerity, my primary concern implies that I also hope to avoid having anyone feeling mislead by my typical glowing reviews, noting that I normally only care to write reviews for games I especially favor.
In an effort to better advise those who are easily turned off by certain "types" of sandbox games, I therefore provide general acknowledgements to what I feel are among the primary concerns of potential customers.

Yes, block/sprite-based resource collection and crafting is a fundamental aspect of the game, but, like most of the game's activities, can be easily tweaked and custom-balanced to the player's liking. There is a wide field of natural resources for utilization, including mining (you can also suck up liquids like water, dump it in a pit and use it for aquaculture to farm plant-fibre-rich kelp, which are like the underwater version of land-based trees, or play with magma taken from volcanoes and planet cores), woodcutting, hunting (on land or UNDER it, as well as in water and underwater "fish-hunting," plus bird hunting), crop farming, and perhaps others that have slipped my mind for the moment. Hunting (land, sea, and air) is basically combat with the intention of harvesting the prey's meat. Combat is sprite-based, and when hunting (with weapons like bows, guns, swords, spears, knives, and more, as well as shields for one-handed defense), slain creatures typically bounce out a chunk of raw meat that can be cooked into various edibles. Felled trees fall to one side and turn into unrefined wood, for crafting purposes, on ground impact. Most crops, I have seen, are interactive and are immediately harvested by pressing an action button when near the plant.
These resources can be used to create basic survival tools at any place, but anything more complicated than bandages and torch-making (only a couple of examples) require crafting stations, starting with basic campfires and wooden clothing, cooking, and general wooden crafting stations, which you can easily craft by cutting a few trees (which also produces plantable saplings to sustain the tree-life) and hand building. I've built several permanent resupply stations at key points so I don't run into trouble as I descend to one planet's core. Very useful. Meat, fish, metal, and other resources are used in a similar manner, which, once again, can be modded for those whom may find this tedious and would better enjoy the game if a certain resource were bypassed. I do this all the time.

Earlier, I mentioned my love for the game's "character development" or "creation," "starship customization," and general "support [for] a user's imagination." Modding possibilities are still "vast," but in case some have been mislead by my highlighting of these gameplay features, I will attempt to portray the level of customization in the vanilla game (at the time of this writing) and its significance.
is basically the same as planetside construction/development. However, the hull shape is unchanging (except through ship upgrades as you progress in the game, bringing your ship from a tiny boat to a gigantic megaship), and exterior blocks cannot be manipulated like on most types of planets. I am a big fan of 4x games and strategy games, and loved the original two Master of Orion games.  This new iteration of Master of Orion feels like a shallow example of a 4x game, with weak attempts at being a rts. To me it feels like a disaster of an addition to the Master of Orion series.
Many of the core elements that made the originals great have been stripped away completely or deluded so much that they are almost unrecognizable. This is to the point where several aspects of the game that have been brought over from the previous iterations just don't seem to function as they should anymore. Several of the playable races seem ineffective and pointless in comparison to others. Weaponry and technologies have little logical uses and are therefore trumped by a handful of superior options. Combat has been reduced to what equates to tactless skirmishes with extremely limited control. The game has ship customization, however it seems like a mute point when all elements of strategy and tactics have been removed from combat.
The game is pretty to look at, but only to an extent. It seems as though there are a very limited number of well crafted objects in the game, but the small amount of them get redundant very quickly. The same ships fly past the same planets, while your advisor rambles off the same line of text he has said dozens and dozens of times before.
The game as a whole seems extremely skeletal in many ways without any real substance.
A Very Fun And Strategic Game At The Same Time, I Would Highly Recommend It.

MoO is really a love or hate type of game. Do you want a full graphical & UI update for MoO2? Then leave it. Better yet: pretend it does not exist. Here are the main reasons:
It lacks turn-based combat, the arena is very small, the AI of your ships is horrible in the realtime one, the AI OFF button is bugged, and you can't always select single units, only "fleets" of ships.
Now you have fixed slots (e.g.: 4 weapons, 1 propulsion, 1 computer, 1 shield, 6 special...) you can fill up to the capacity of the ship. Again, this lessens the combinations you can come up with.
Instead of completely separate research branches, MoO has a Civ-like tree. You can leave a few techs out, but not much. You can't specialize in one branch and then trade or steal the remainder. There are some techs that present you with a choice of a technology duo, but those are nowhere near the choices you could burden yourself with in MoO2 using the uncreative perk.
They all appear utterly insane so far, with absolutely zero sense of reality. I've seen better sense of it from Civilization enemies at launch date.
Completely missing functionality.
Space lanes and infinite fuel instead of fixed max distance before needing a refuel. I don't dislike this most of the time, but some might. It does make cutting off a segment of space harder and easier at the same time.
...I could go on with smaller nuances.
The main problem is, the devs stated they will not be adding turn-based combat or rewamp the research. They will add custom races, espionage, but not much else that is missing now. They created a "more accessible" game, not a successor. One without much of a character.
There are positive changes as well, for instance, I love that at the end of the game, you can reload the game from any given turn. There are voiced characters, although your advisors get annoying really, really fast. And the UI responds to the now-standardized way, although there are many, many shortcuts that are missing for a power gamer. And there is a catgirl with cleavage, if you're into that.
So if you are a fan of old Master of Orion and want at least that complexity, go to
, buy MoO2 again, and forget this ever existed. It's way cheaper and way better.
If you are new to the world of 4X space strategy games, this might be a good watered-down tutorial. Kinda like how American beers compare to European ones.

To the developers I would recommend two things:  Please implement the governors and fleet captains from MoO2!  And don't overbalance the single player game too much, just implement a scoring system and "balance" that (giving bonuses to score for harder racial picks)
I think the game was a little pricey at $50 (because it's not finished), but the $30 final price tag is definitely on target!  Pick it up early if you're a fan of the classic games and to have that MoO2 itch scratched right away :)

The thing that immediately stood out to me about Botanicula was how charming it is. This is due in large part to the excellent audio, both from the folktronica soundtrack and the sound effects, which incorporate a wide variety of unintelligible vocal sounds that make the game feel really lighthearted and playful. Another contributor to the charm is the animations, which are very exaggerated, like a cartoon. They are key to communicating the story and objectives since the game doesn't use text or spoken word at all. Also, the game looks pretty great; I was impressed by the large variety of creatively-designed creatures you encounter throughout the game.
On the gameplay front, it's pretty much what you would expect from a point-and-click adventure game. You are primarily clicking (or clicking and dragging) on objects in the environment in order to solve puzzles and advance through the game. In general, the puzzles are reasonably difficult; while a fair number of them were not all that challenging, a few had me stumped for quite a while. For one puzzle, I came up with a solution that I didn't think the game would acknowledge, but lo and behold, it totally worked, which was a great feeling.
A lot of adventure games become tedious when you have to cycle through your large inventory of items, trying to use them somewhere in the environment. Botanicula takes great care in reducing the need for this because you only ever have a small number of items at any one time, there are no item combinations, and for any given scene it's easy to check if an item can be used or not. I really appreciated this about Botanicula.
My gripes with the game are pretty minor. When I first started playing, differentiating between interactable objects that were just for show and ones that would help me solve a puzzle was a bit difficult. Also, the first area, where you are walking on tree branches, was too visually similar from scene to scene, which made navigating the area a bit difficult. The future areas, fortunately, greatly improve upon this.
In short, Bontanicula is a pretty great game. It never stops exuding its charm and does away with what has frustrated me about adventure games in the past.

So, like a lot of you, I never played MoO2 when it was crowned the golden 4x game of a generation.  In 96' I was focused on school and well, being a seven year old.  I came in with little knowledge of the game that has inspired so many.  After two near-complete games (and several restarts) in MoO: CTS, I had to boot up MoO2.  Then Endless Space, then buy Starbase Orion for moblie, then go against my own better judgement and pick up StarDrive 2 with its new DLC.
Sadly, Master of Orion has been recreated by two other studios, in my opinion, than what the holders of a beloved IP have created.  While I understand the game is Early Access, it is missing several features found in games like I've mentioned above, with a much heftier buy in price.  With the release of Stellaris announced for May, and Endless Space 2 on the horizon, I just don't see this game being released with the amount of depth I want from a 4x strategy game.
While starlanes are not a terrible way to go, Endless Space just does it better, especially with things like arp technology.  Compared to a free movement games like SD2 or Orion (MoO2 as well), it is a stark difference.  Never figured out why I couldn't get past a few hours with most space 4x games until playing the games I have mentioned.  I much prefer the Civ styled movement of anywhere you want to go you can go (with technology) and enjoy it a lot more in space 4x games.
Combat currently is a glorified, pretty, cinematic viewer.  Currently your ship designs don't matter much as a lot of weapon systems are non-fuctioning, and A.I. fleet loadouts are rather unbalanced (scout and cruiser spam).  As per their feedback page, this is something they are hoping to expand upon.
For a reinvisioning of the MoO2 technological system, other games do it much better.  The choices of which technology to use are few and far between, and further are pigeon-holed into pretty obvious decisions.  Compared to Civ styled research systems, games like Endless Space, Endless Legend, or Civ 5 do it far better.  Their are more choices to be made while filling out the tech tree (Masonry vs Calendar etc), providing a more rewarding progression system, even if they don't follow the system provided by MoO2 and SD2 (locking out techs to be stolen/trade for/conquered).
There is currently no leader system or unit leveling.  While many might consider this as so what?  It really kills replaybility.  In Civ 5 having one of your main military units through the ages is a huge boon.  They have several upgrades that drastically change the unit, and create a connection to the game.  You will do what you can to use, and save, your beloved high level units.  There is no attatchment here.  Unlike MoO2, SD2, Endless Space, or Endless Legend (also having unit leveling), there is no leader system.  Nor is there an abstracted one like Civ 5 (great persons).
Colonial depth is pretty barebones for a game like this.  There are no luxury resources or strategic resources currently in the game, and I feel that is something that will not be added.  In Civ 5 you have all sorts of different resources that affect your empire (just as SD2, Endless Space, and Endless Legend have) and can also drastically change gameplay.  In ES, if I don't have say anti-matter, I can't even build certain powerful ship systems.  It will require trading or war to advance my ideas.  In Civ 5, it is basically the same.  I want to build nukes but hold no uranium.  Either I'm trading or conquering my way to them.  It creates a believeable universe, for me, as it akins back to real world geo-politics.  Wars are fought over resources.
To expand Galaxy (and colonial) depth, it is missing several events found in games like Gal Civ 3, SD2, and ES.  While some are there, they are miniscule and few compared to the games above.  Further, their only resource(s) called Artifacts don't add much to the game.  Each one is a flat bonus to science, industry, food, or credit generation.  Take for example the relic system provided by Endless Space which leaves a plethora of 'wonders' that enhance planets left behind by the Forgotten (Masters in MoO).  Or SD2 which had things like habitats pre-built, or angry beings already on the planet that will require wiping out or dealing with the negative consequences.  In MoO: CTS, it is really hard to care about system X or colony Y.
Races are aesthetically different but don't add much variation to the game.  Endless Space, and especially MoO2 and Endless Legend have very different races that can alter a gameplay in several small ways or in a few drastic ways.  For example, not being able to research but instead using currency to move up the tech tree, or not being allowed to grow at all beyond your initial city.
Presentation is where the game shines, and for at least me, it doesn't equate to an amazing game.  The voice-over work is pretty good, but can also become annoying after a while.  The GNN is a good example of this, it has several cringe worthy moments not helped by lackluster voice editing.  The graphics are decent for a 4x game, nothing amazing but good.  Better in some ways and worse than others.  Some GUI things need to be cleaned up, current planet management is pretty ridiculous when trying to demolish an old building no longer needed.  Currently, buildings are randomly plopped on a globe and you get to wade through them one by one.  A list of what is built on the planet would help a lot.
I won't say much about the A.I. as it is a known problem, but it really can't be said enough: it can barely play the game and won't challenge even a newcomer.  Hopefully this can be ramped up drastically in the coming months.
All in all, I don't think I would have bothered with this if it wasn't for its IP.  I can't suggest this game to a newcomer to the space 4x genre as currently, I think Endless Space is far more appoachable.  Teaching a lot of intricate systems in an easy to use GUI, allowing you to expand in the genre if you want more complexity and depth without hitting another huge brick wall of a learning curve.  For veterans of the genre that date back to Civ 4 and 5, or even further with games like MoO2, Distand World Universe, and Gal Civ 2:  the first playthrough will be enjoyable but the 'itch' to play a 4x game will be inflamed as you scour through suggested games to scratch it.

Soccer Manager 2017 has been released and I am writing this review on 9/16/2016
The current team I'm managing with this simulator is Borussia Dortmund.
This manager game for the sport of Soccer/Football includes many leagues with real team logos and real player names and portraits, no mods needed.
This game allows you to select a team from your desired league and manage the players and the club to try to win games and cups.
You start with the real life list of players and can sell/buy new players.
The simulation seems fine, with tactical changes affecting the game.
PROS AND CONS:
Pros -
FREE Football Manager
Good UI
Runs smoothly
Easy to learn
Real players and clubs
Real icons with no need for mods
Good simulation
Cons -
You can inject cash and buy players with "coins"
Cash is hard to come by - You lose more than you make without spending real money
Games are pre-determined. I tested this out by saving and then re-loading the game, the fixtures will always come out the same no matter what.
It seems like fouls come too easy in this game, even on softer tackling.
Once again, pre-determined games ruin the immersion.
OVERALL -
Good Soccer/Football manager for someone who can't spend any money
If you have the money to buy a football manager, it is 10x better than this game at the moment.
I will give this game a positive rating since it works as intended and I believe for the person who doesn't want to spend money, this game will be satisfactory.
TL;DR - Good game, good simulation. Pre-determined matches and coin buying ruins it for me, but may not be a problem for other people. Pick it up and try it out for yourself.

Won this in a Twitter giveaway; I gotta say, even though I have fond memories of doing very badly at Colin McRae Rally 2.0 growing up, I still got a good deal of enjoyment from this. If you treat it as its own thing (albeit one that rampantly reuses assets from plenty of previous games), it's a pretty enjoyable arcade-style rally racer, one that's not as punishing as the original series (for better or for worse). A lot of the sponsors are rather anachronistic, there's only two kinds of surfaces, and the six championships are just shuffled around to make for "more" events.
Events are simple time-based affairs. There's no actual in-race opponents; a bar at the top tracks your position compared to your best-performing opponent (pretty much always Colin McRae himself), and the race against the clock tends to be rather satisfying once you've gotten the rhythm down. Like I said, it's a lot less punishing; I don't know if I've actually gotten extremely better over the years since or if it's significantly easier, but considering I was able to recover from some rather galling cuts and significant wrecks without issue, it seems to be the latter.
Maintaining vehicle damage is simplified to the point that it's easy to keep track of, but still tricky to balance. You can only repair so much before heading back out onto the track, and even a perfect run will cause some routine wear. Different vehicles do feel properly distinct, making the small pool of choices a bit more understandable, and when I went for a certain outdated classic, I found that it realistically got smashed to bits far, far easier than its more modern counterparts. You'll learn to recognize - and loathe - the sound and effect of each particular point of failure. Especially suspension.
The original store listing definitely deserves the infamy it got. This isn't the original Colin McRae Rally at all (nor is it the sequel that it pulls all of its content from). It's a small sampling of cars and courses from that game given a semi-new coat of paint. As is said of many titles on Steam, it's one of those "worst version of a great game" kind of things. In the end, though, I found myself really, really enjoying it. It was kind of hilariously disappointing when the end screen told me to look forward to new cars and tracks in upcoming updates; with the reception this has gotten, that's never happening. This'll remain a grim reminder to be clear with your advertising, and a fun little diversion for those looking for a small spot of classic point-to-point rally.

This review may sound a bit random because I just write down thoughts I had while playing the game.
TL:DR: The worst AC of them all so far BUT it's still a good game.
Release Problems:
Most bugs were fixed and the game is playable now.
The companion app stuff was removed, which is good because I don't want to use my phone while playing a game.
Story:
The story is not good at all compared to earlier titles. Feels like the writers were a bit lazy but like always they did a good job including historical figures in the game. To understand everything you need to have at least some knowledge of the french revolution.
The side stories are really interesting or funny though. Finding the secret lab of Nicolas Flamel, helping Napoleon to find the right woman to marry or meeting the Marquis de Sade (my BDSM friends know why that's interesting ;) ).
Controls:
I actually like the new free run controls even though Arno likes to randomly jump on flower pots.
You now hold E for a decending free run and space bar for a climbing free run. It makes the climbing less complicated.
Combat:
It's much more challanging than before. I love it. You can't just fight 20 soldiers at once like before. Regardless how good your weapons are, fighting is always a challenge in Unity. Enemies have different skill levels now and don't attack one after another. Also: Every enemy has a gun.
Try fighting a group of 5 soldiers while 2 snipers shoot at you from the roofs. I never used so many smoke bombs before.
New Stuff:
Murder mysteries are fun!
Lockpicking gets annoying after the first 10 chests.
Nostradamus riddles are interesting.
Rift missions are a nice diversion from the usual game play because you get to visit different times eras including occupied Paris during WW2.
Minor annoyances:
The map is so full of stuff that you can hardly find what you're looking for sometimes.
Some popups lay over each other so you have to wait until they vanish to read what you're supposed to do or what some clues say (murder mysteries).
I recommend this title for: AC fans obviously and people who thought the older titles were way too easy

Quick review:
It’s a good game with simple floaty controls that plays like a MOBA but controls like a World of Tanks style shooter. The game runs well on most gaming PC's but good luck trying to play it on a potato from 4 years back. It’s not a game that you can just pick up and play within the 1st few hours of the game since its unique playing and control schemes gives it a steep learning curve. Its more tactical than a twitch shooter so don’t expect super speedy frag runs like CS: GO or Overwatch but the game does play faster than World of Warship for example.
Detailed Review:
The Bad:
The game has a typical 3D control layout (WASD with SHIFT and CTRL for up and down) but the controls are slow to respond and after you start moving you build momentum which means you slide around a lot making precision movements hard (just imaging playing on ice levels if you don’t understand what I mean).
The game really makes you play hundreds or thousands (cheap ships are not the point of this argument, I mean the ships that cost 1.75 million to unlock kind of problem) of games just to buy ships which I find completely overkill. The skins do nothing unless you get the legendary variant’s which give credit boost so it’s not a pay to win aspect.
The crew skill however is a pay to win aspect, since you have to play hundreds of games just to get enough credits to buy loot boxes that randomly drop skills that you might not even use EVER and more often than not you get the same skills so it gets wasted as free crew EXP which at that point you won’t need since you played hundreds of games so your crew is probably fully trained by that point (I say this pay to win because you can just buy crew pods with real money so if you spend money you can get a lot of good skills whereas a F2P player probably doesn’t even have all the skills of the same set). This is not the same with unlocking crew since you can browse through the list of crew that you can pick and hire the ones you want.
Other problems are that this game is still very buggy even after release with the same bugs not being patched after many patches (which are also months in between). This game is also graphically demanding which means unless you have a Good Gaming PC your chances of the loading into a game and possibly crashing upon starting just increase significantly. Also, good luck trying to play on a non-gaming laptop.
Also, the player base for this game is highest in EU servers only and with all other servers being pretty much dead for players (I play on SG server and I have never been able to get into a PVP game even Quickplay players are sparse so I don’t bother playing after midnight since I can never get a game at that hour) but if you play on EU server well then you won’t have a problem the player base there is still active.
The Good:
This game is overwhelmingly generous with its loot boxes with daily mission boxes that can be gained just by playing a single game and with the weekly boxes being not that harder to gain either so at the start the grind won’t be as painful but late game when you’re trying to get specific skins or skills it’s a real pain because of the loot box system.
Gameplay wise it’s a great game, I love the MOBA like skill system but using big heavy capital ships size destroyers and cruiser. Which makes it an interesting mix of World of Tanks plus DOTA 2 type game and it keeps the same tactical team focus gameplay from both games. This game pretty much follows the conventional Heavy, Healer, DPS, Support system that most games use which makes for interesting combination especially with some of the mix type ships that can be both Heavy DPS, Healer DPS, Heavy Support and with the stealth ships also making gameplay interesting.
I also love the graphics of just massive ships colliding and with the Point defence system firing at fighter aircraft makes it feel like a great space battle is taking place (Though if you zoom out the illusion of a massive space battle kind of disappears as you see only your ship making it feel small).
So, if you want to know if this game is for you just try it for 50 games and see if you like it because this is one of those games that have a specific niche for this kind of gameplay. Honestly for me personally, I love playing this game and will keep playing it just to get that feeling of a grand space battle but also, I’ll keep playing because of the players that have I met in this game that are a fun bunch of people to play with.

In 2008, I picked up a copy of Fallout 3 for the first time, and I don't regret it one bit; nearly a decade has passed me by, and yet I still play Fallout on a pretty regular basis.
You should have seen my face when Bethesda semi-stealthily announced that this game was coming out, as soon as I heard about the mysterious countdown, I was there. I waited for what felt like an eternity, until finally, the clock hit zero. My heart was racing, my hands were sweating, my knees were spaghetti, I couldn't contain my excitement.
I remember seeing that the Special Edition was going to drop right after the E3 confrence, and in seconds I had it ordered.
"No regrets," I thought, "this is definitely going to be a good game."
How wrong I turned out to be.
I expected a linear plot from Bethesda, and upon discovering that the main quest was going to involve me tracking down my son, I shrugged it off.
I thought to myself:
"I'm sure there will be more for me to do in the game, I've spent hundreds of hours in Skyrim without doing much of the main quest, this will be fine."
I expected changes to the character building process, and upon discovering that the perk system was all that remained, I shrugged it off.
I thought to myself:
"Well I bet there's going to be some incentive for me to make a specific build instead of maxing out the same skills every playthough."
I expected deep, dynamic characters, at least a fun DJ like in Fallout 3, and upon finding out that most of the characters were intolerable at best, including the radio DJ, I shrugged it off.
I thought to myself:
"Surely there's more to them that I can find out as I progress through the game, doing quests for them and stuff, I mean there are only so many settlements in the commonwealth, how many actually need my help, this has to be building up to something."
I expected colorful and memorable locations, booming with life in a lifeless wasteland, and when I found out that all the locations were nothing more than simple shooting galleries, I shrugged it off.
I thought to myself:
"There definitely has to be some really interesting stuff around here, I'm sure Bethesda just did a really good job with hiding it all this time."
I expected the settlement creation to add a new level of dynamism to the wasteland. I envisioned grand cities and lavish houses, and when I realized that I was limited to just a few snappable shack modules and some ruined furniture.
I thought to myself:
"Oh, I bet I can get around this by exploiting the game a little bit and using some creativity."
And when I realized the game didn't meet my expectations (and believe me, they weren't that high compared to what most people had for the game), I shurgged it off.
I thought to myself:
"Mods can definitely fix all this, by the time I'm done with my vanilla playthrough, the GECK should be out, and I'll have some amazing new mods to spruce up the game with."
When the mods came around, even before the creation kit, I happily installed literally hundreds of improvements, and for a while I was content, for a little under two years, I was perfectly happy.
Then came the update.
Immediately I hated it because I couldn't launch f4se, and without f4se, I couldn't have Fallout 4. At least half of my mods relied on f4se to work, and boom, it was unplayable for a few days. Those were rough days, too, my girlfriend left me for college while I remained a lonely manchild at his computer desk. I hated myself, I needed Fallout.
Sure, I could play New Vegas, but I had a laundry list of things I wanted to do in Fallout 4, and starting a new character in New Vegas just didn't seem as appetizing.
When the f4se team came through, I was happy again, I could have my game, and I was sure that me and Creation Club could live like a divorced couple in the same house; casually ignoring eachother, but aware of eachother's presence. I simply thought that was the last of it, Bethesda would continue adding mods how they're added in Bethesda's built-in mod workshop, but apparently I was wrong to expect that of Bethesda as well.
I hate paid mods as much as everyone else, I think they're pointless, but I stayed quiet and shrugged it off for my favorite franchise. I've given this game so many chances that I have lost count, I was wrong to do that. It's just like being in an abusive relationship at this point, you give that person every opportunity to improve, hoping that they become better, not wanting to leave them because you think you need them in your life. It sucks, it ♥♥♥♥ing sucks.
I was so wrong to ever love this game as much as I did, I miss having a game that didn't require updates every three minutes. I just want to have my old Fallout experience back.

Overall a very promising sim, can tell it's still early days though, I would very much like to see a multi-player version be realised, I think that will attract more players, as well as a tutorial for really green beginners to iron out the steep jaggared learning curve. Hopefully the devs will listen to the feedback in ways they can improve it to make a good game that can compete with the DRL sim.

I'm not really sure why roughly half the people have implied that this review is UNhelpful by taking the time to discredit it. Helpfulness is my primary concern, and while I continue to stand by everything I have said to this point with sincerity, my primary concern implies that I also hope to avoid having anyone feeling mislead by my typical glowing reviews, noting that I normally only care to write reviews for games I especially favor.
In an effort to better advise those who are easily turned off by certain "types" of sandbox games, I therefore provide general acknowledgements to what I feel are among the primary concerns of potential customers.

Yes, block/sprite-based resource collection and crafting is a fundamental aspect of the game, but, like most of the game's activities, can be easily tweaked and custom-balanced to the player's liking. There is a wide field of natural resources for utilization, including mining (you can also suck up liquids like water, dump it in a pit and use it for aquaculture to farm plant-fibre-rich kelp, which are like the underwater version of land-based trees, or play with magma taken from volcanoes and planet cores), woodcutting, hunting (on land or UNDER it, as well as in water and underwater "fish-hunting," plus bird hunting), crop farming, and perhaps others that have slipped my mind for the moment. Hunting (land, sea, and air) is basically combat with the intention of harvesting the prey's meat. Combat is sprite-based, and when hunting (with weapons like bows, guns, swords, spears, knives, and more, as well as shields for one-handed defense), slain creatures typically bounce out a chunk of raw meat that can be cooked into various edibles. Felled trees fall to one side and turn into unrefined wood, for crafting purposes, on ground impact. Most crops, I have seen, are interactive and are immediately harvested by pressing an action button when near the plant.
These resources can be used to create basic survival tools at any place, but anything more complicated than bandages and torch-making (only a couple of examples) require crafting stations, starting with basic campfires and wooden clothing, cooking, and general wooden crafting stations, which you can easily craft by cutting a few trees (which also produces plantable saplings to sustain the tree-life) and hand building. I've built several permanent resupply stations at key points so I don't run into trouble as I descend to one planet's core. Very useful. Meat, fish, metal, and other resources are used in a similar manner, which, once again, can be modded for those whom may find this tedious and would better enjoy the game if a certain resource were bypassed. I do this all the time.

Earlier, I mentioned my love for the game's "character development" or "creation," "starship customization," and general "support [for] a user's imagination." Modding possibilities are still "vast," but in case some have been mislead by my highlighting of these gameplay features, I will attempt to portray the level of customization in the vanilla game (at the time of this writing) and its significance.
is basically the same as planetside construction/development. However, the hull shape is unchanging (except through ship upgrades as you progress in the game, bringing your ship from a tiny boat to a gigantic megaship), and exterior blocks cannot be manipulated like on most types of planets. The interiors can be furnished all the same, though.
is currently basic. Most has no effect on gameplay. There are several vanilla races, and the appearance of your ship and story depend on your selection. You can name your character and choose difficulty level (essentially how severe the penalty is for death, from a *moddable* percent-money-loss to perma-death) and adjust your appearance (like gender, and race-dependent appearance options for things like skin/fur/feather/leaf color and hair/feather/etc. style, and colors and style for initial clothing, which can be mixed, matched, and replaced with armor and colors, or just plain removed).

I've seen several complaints that are merely insults to the developers by people who feel that the the game should have been completed by now, prefer more frequent updates rather than the large, stable improvements made by the developers, and/or simply need to calm down before they publish their judgment. These negative reviews contain little or no thought or effort to provide information, based on the firsthand experience from a current player, the author, to help a potential
player more accurately predict their own experience if they play the game, and decide if that experience is worth the price of the game. It was for me.

I hope many find this review helpful, and I strongly encourage people to purchase this game. :D

Casual and rewarding time-management game
With this, the first installment in the 12 Labours of Hercules series, Zoom Out Games hit bull's eye upon release in March 2015. The mere fact that only half a year later the fourth game in the series has already been greenlit, speaks tons about the game's success.
12 Labours of Hercules is being advertised as a casual strategy game, but in reality it's a time-management game with very limited strategical options or choices. The story, although rooted in Greek mythology, is shallow and serves merely as a framework for the 40-odd levels. These levels are almost all based upon the same principle: control your workers (and now and then a very lazy Hercules or some other mythological figure) in order to clear the path towards the objective. In order to do so, you'll need three resources: food, materials & gold. These can be found or collected in several different ways, such as constructing and upgrading appropriate buildings.
Since each level is timed, it's quite important to take a look at the map before rushing off, noticing the places where buildings can be put or gold can be found. Playing on "casual" difficulty let me progress through the game without much of a hassle, collecting "gold score" on almost every level at the first try (and I am a complete noob at this type of game). But the higher difficulty setting was an entirely different story: all of sudden every second counted, and one wrong action early on in a level could ruin it. An extra difficulty level in between these two extremes would have been nice, but that's a very minor criticism.
During the course of a level, the player can activate one or more "powers" which boost some aspect of the gathering & building process. This provides a neat extra layer of gameplay, something the game needed more and more while progressing since the levels are nearly all built upon the same principle. Happily, the levels are never too long: most of them last somewhere between 5 and 10 minutes, which makes the game perfectly suited to be consumed as a gaming snack.
12 Labours of Hercules comes with full Steam integration such as trading cards, leaderboards and a varied bunch of achievements. These are not very difficult but still entertaining, and the game can be completed to 100% really easily or without any tiresome grinding.
Highly recommended to everyone with an even remote interest in time-management games. Or to all of you looking for a quick but very tasteful snack.

A solid entry in the series, it doesn't really do anything particularly innovative or exciting but also largely avoids doing anything terrible as well.  Ultimately pretty forgettable, the plot (both future and past) feels like an afterthought with a lot of hanging threads left behind.  What it has going for it is a return to the giant buildings of the earlier games, and it's a treat to rush around the rooftops of Paris (and along its clogged streets).  The backdrop of the French Revolution is fascinating if a little underutilized, and they couldn't resist filling every single encyclopedia entry with "witty" comments by the endlessly annoying future tech-guy.  The game looks gorgeous though the hair looks dated already, and there is far too much in the way of equipment/abilities locked away behind utterly irrelevant "social" settings/multiplayer aspects that you can safely ignore entirely.
Overall it's a perfectly reasonable game to play but nothing you should go out of your way to bother with.  If you can get it cheap or as part of a package deal, sure go ahead and get it.  But if you just wanna skip to AC: Syndicate you're missing absolutely nothing either gameplay or plotwise.  It's a pretty skippable if inoffensive game.

Be wary of the bad reviews, they are invariably by people who simply didn't read the
clear description that describes
what this game is:  "Colin McRae Rally features the car and track list from last year’s top selling mobile title and features THIRTY amazing rally stages in three environments taken from the PlayStation classic Colin McRae 2.0. for this PC and Mac edition."  So, it's derived from the mobile game which was inspired by the original PS classic CMR.
It's great.  It really took me back to the feel and fun and challenge of the old PS game but with modern look and sound.   It is not a simulator, it is a great game! Game as in fun.  Game as in play for 10 minutes or play for an hour.  You don't have to wait an age for it to load, or endure the latest in bad, loud synthetic music, or consult a manual and a physicist on car set up.  You just play!
Some people criticise the physics of the cars.  I have never driven a 4WD but I have driven plenty of 2WDs on very bad surfaces and when I unlocked the Lancia Stratos I finally was driving a car that behaved how I remember cars behaving, including the sudden total and catastrophic loss of all control when you mess up!
I bought this on a nostalgia trip when it was offered on Humble Bundle and it's now the game I've played the most hours on Steam.
If you're looking for a sim or some kind of pseudo reality and hours of tinkering and stats and so on then look elsewhere.

This is a great game for anyone who can read a short product description and wants to race for fun.

At launch, this game was a mess, just like everyone states, but after playing for some time - the game became extremely fun. The graphics are amazingly well done, all the way down to the small things in the streets to the fabric and clothes. Although getting a new PC did not allow me to fully play at ultra settings (seems to be a fault in-game, showing 300fps in the Uplay fps counter, whereas it's actually 30...), I was still amazed by the graphics in game. Rarely I run into an instance of odd cloth physics or an out of place animation on character interactions, but other than that - the city is beautiful.
The gameplay is amazing and not a button mash-fest like some in the series, meaning your attacks actually have 'weight' and an 'umph' when doing actions, this of course makes you take your time and sort of plan what to do depending on your enemy and the class that they are. In all fairness, the thing I enjoyed the most was the fact that you really have to plan out how to complete the mission. For example, Sequence 12 - Memory 3: The fight with Germain in his Temple wasn't that difficult, but getting into the actual temple and bypassing the guards took a lot of time. Not saying it's a bad thing, but I feel its more engaging this way and makes the game a lot more enjoyable and fun.
The sounds and effects of the city are actually really well done when you stop and pay attention to every little thing going on around you. The sound of footsteps changing depending on the terrain, the chattering of the locals, the fabric creating noises depending on if your wearing leather, cloth, or chainmail...its very impressive when you think about everything that is happening.
All of the  things above make this an awesome addition to the franchise - althouh I have not played the full sequence of all AC games, I can say I really enjoyed playing the game - even with minor texture bugs where NPCs walked upside down or appeared from walls a few times... The only thing I would improve is the co-operative mode, but of course, not a lot of people play the game anymore, so maybe that's the issue. I tried to find a partner for one of the multiplayer missions, and after waiting 23 minutes, I gave up.
Overall, with a rating of 8/10, I strongly recommend the game to anyone who loves climbing around on roofs and a long storyline. (:

It has much promise, but it has issues (gameplay and aesthetic) that I hope the devs are aware of:
-When a new tech is earned, and ship blueprints update, the player has to go back in and re-customize the weapon and option layouts that weren't even effected by the new tech. This is unnecessary, time-consuming, and potentially damaging to the game experience if the player isn't diligent and doesn't correct the issue before more units are built.
-On the bombing screen, the only bomb name shown is "nuclear" even if the ships contain "fusion" bombs. Is that aesthetic or a bug?
-Diplomacy has (so far) been non-existent from the AI. The only time they contacted me was to threaten. MoO2 wasn't really any better, but I would presume game AI processing has improved significantly since then.
-Tactical space combat isn't. I like the idea of more real-time combat, but the tactical combat is more like trying to guide balls of varying size and speed while they are rolling downhill. I can select ships, right-click to set priority targets, (sort of) set a formation, and alter course...but ultimately the ships just turn right back toward the enemy and go full-frontal attack.
And speaking of full-frontal attack, the enemy ships just sit there until your ships get close...then they just head toward your ships without the slightest deviation. The obstacles are no more useful than as eye candy, which is really unfortunate.
If the devs can make the space combat into an actual real-time, flowing, tactical experience, this game would be amazing. It could garner YouTube videos galore.
-Not sure why only so many slots are allocated for production or food, while research appears to have unlimited slots. In MoO2 I liked how one could specialize ultra-rich planets to crank out the ships by putting everything in production.
Also, the technology, separate building, and separate (mandatory) ongoing order to share resources intra-planatarily makes little sense. Think how the fictional conversation would go in the game:
Planet 1: Hey, do you have extra food sitting around?
Planet 2: Yup.
Planet 1: Think you could send that to us?
Planet 2: Yeah...let me just put *everything* we're building *on hold* and have *all* our production workers fly that extra food of ours over to you.
I could accept the tech requirement, and the building (that requires 5BC maintenance), but a production-halting order is unnecessary and just plain dumb.
-Not sure why the game has an arbitrary cutoff at 500 turns. Building a decked out titan-class ship can easily take 30 or more of those turns on some of the better planets thanks to the aformentioned limited slots for production.
I'll leave it at that, for now.
Thank you for reading.

This is a review for anyone thinking about purchasing MOOcts early access.
I have completed two play throughs of the game with the humans. Although there are some good points I can not recommened the game and its 50 dollar price tag in its current state.
Things I liked
-Looks nice (ships, planets, races)
-Voice acting is well done
-Music and SFX are good
-UI is easy to navigate
Things I don't like
-Combat is too fast and boring. You can try slowing it down by using the pause option but really it's pointless. You can win almost every battle simply with numbers and let it auto play while you watch. Faster to just simulate battles than go through the cinematic tactical fighting.
-Customizing ships is pointless you can easily win with the default set ups the AI chooses for you
-AI currently isn't implemented so diplomacy plays no part in a game (other than extorting money from the weak)
-Tech tree choices don't feel like they mean anything. I can easily get through a game just randomly picking.
Conclusion
Don't buy this game in early access. If it goes on sale maybe. I don't think it's worth more than $25 in its current state and that's only because it comes with MOO 1 and 2. It has potential I hope that the developers use the player's feed back to improve the battles and AI.
***EA5 UPDATE***
So I tried the EA% update and can still not recommend this game. First I'll have to say that the developers made some great changes that fixed many early version problems. For example
Improved AI both in diplomacy and overall strategy
Ship designer finally in a good place (was pretty bad until around EA3 or 4)
Custom race designer and galaxy generation paramaters greatly improved
They put spies in EA 3 or 4 (can't remember exactly) and improved their functionality some what in EA5
RTS battle UI improved and it's a bit easier to  control ships now
These are some of the things that I thought were well done by the dev team. Having said that the following issues are simply holding this game back and will continue to do so in my opinion.
Absolutely horrible UI camera during empire management. I can't stress enough how annoying it is when the camera moves and zoomes from one side of the galaxy to another to make sure you aware of some mundane event (congrats you just found a planet...ugh) and now you have to zoom back out, find where the camera was focused just so you can continue playing normally. This happens ALL THE TIME and is incredibly annoying.
Planet management is absolutely boring. It's so boring in fact that they are planning on adding preset building queues to the game as a feature. Now some might say 'yay preset building queues!' but to me it's the same thing as admitting that there is a boring part of the game no one likes to do so we are finding a way to automate it. Now this happens with a lot of 4x games but it's especially bad in MOOcts. Some 4x games try and get around this by using a grid system for building placement and assigning values to each box in the grid so that there is at least a level of randomness and value in building on one box over the other. In MOOcts however its the old boring build queue that might as well be the same for every planet (again why they are making preset build queues). For sure this was a flaw of the original moo2 and should have been identified as an area where they could innovate.
And the big one BATTLES. Lets face it 4x games are about big space battles. Everyone wants to  see their super badass fleet mass up against another empire's super badass fleet and PEWPEW till there is a clear winner. And although there can be big space battles in MOOcts they just aren't fun. You would think an RTS style battle system would guarantee awesome big fleet battles but nope. Most of the time you just end up sitting watching it happen like a little movie. Sure there are tactics to use and ways to move ships around but it's nothing like the strategy someone would use in a game like starcraft for example. The system lacks the feeling of speed and split second decision making that will make or break the battle found in traditional RTS and at the same time has managed to simulate the boring sit back and watch as things happen found in turn based combat.  I can't stress enough how boring battles are in this game. It's a killer failure imo.
Again I very much appreciate the work put into this game. The graphics are nice, sound is excellent, atmosphere is very MOO style but the game is just dull to play. Why pay 50+ dollars to play a mediocre 4x game when there are so many out there that are doing everything this game offers but better and for less money.

imagine you're in a town centre full of sideshows and attractions you can just walk up to and play with other people bowling, trivia competitions, typing speed contests, a casino with poker tables and various slot machines.

TL;DR - The final score for this game, a 6 out of 10.
Fallout 4 is a direct sequel to Fallout 3. The game sets in a futuristic apocalyptic Commonwealth or Boston, Massachusetts, riddled with dangers. It's running with Creation Engine, so it's a recycle engine from Skyrim. Without further ado, I am going to discuss in depth of this game's strengths and weaknesses.
The game starts on Pre-War setting or before fallout apocalypse. You play as a
(what a shocker for hardcore fans but nonetheless I don't mind voiced customised character) and enlisted as a vault dweller for Vault 111. After you wake up from cryogenic sleep, you noticed that your only child has been taken away by an unknown assailant and killed your wife/husband (depending on what gender you're playing as). After you got out of Vault 111, the game gives you an amazing impression, where everything is... just chaotically beautiful. It is up to you how you find your child by unravelling the clues. There are multiple endings to choose from.
The gunplay in Fallout 4 is simple. It feels like I am playing some sort of generic first person shooter game. The leveling system has perks and basic stats (also known as S.P.E.C.I.A.L.). It has RPG elements to it, such as apparel clothing, aids or temporary buffs, legendary loot system and crafting system. The game includes settlements, so let's make it in depth. Settlements are your base building, you need to maintain their happiness by building electricity, water, food, defenses and shelter. It can be frustrating at times where Preston Garvey bothers you to defend each settlements all the time, but I will save that discussion for later. You might come across with side quests and exploration during playthrough, it is your choice how you play. Power Armor will no longer needed the Power Armor training perk, so you can wear it in the beginning of your playthrough. Companion system is intact, now you can take whoever you want.
I like the new V.A.T.S. system, it changes the pace of the gameplay. Instead of being stopped and pick any limbs, it's more of a bullet time. The crafting system is way better than its predecessors in my opinion. Weapons now have attachments. The loot system is a mixed reaction to me, like when killing countless of legendary enemies, I get the same loot unless I have to turn the difficulty up to increase the chance of getting better items. Companion system seems to be the same from Fallout New Vegas as I remember, it can be customised (wearing armor, equipping guns, carrying junk for you). You will earn a perk from companions by increasing the affection level of the companion. There are new factions added, but I'd rather not to spoil it.
There are technical issues on this game. The graphics looked outdated for a 2015 triple A title until they release the HD texture download which is over 50GBs of texture files if you have DLCs implemented (holy ♥♥♥♥, that's insane amount of storage). I'd suggest not to download the HD Texture Pack for now. The modding community are still angry about adding the paid mods called Creation Club, yes you heard me. I am sure you can get away with it by downloading mods from NexusMods (even though I am not into modding). This game is poorly optimized for the latest hardware. The AI in this game is horrendously dumb. Especially companion gets in your way but can't get out of the doorway (Dogmeat found something, dies by a trap). The game gets difficult when underlevel, so it is the best way to level up by doing side quest and exploration. The gunplay feels lackluster.

I feel like this is the most repetitive and fetch fest game I have ever played, period. Like take an example of The Witcher 3, where the side quests are so fascinating and much freedom of how you get the reward. Can I talk about the settlements? Because that♥♥♥♥♥♥is irritating as hell. "Our settlement needs our help", yes Preston Garvey I get it you piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ The quest design are poorly done, it's about fetch quests and dungeon clearing. Seriously, that is purely lazy as ♥♥♥♥. The main story is somewhat forgettable in first 10 hours since you have to figure out what to do. The story is kind of weak to me because there is nothing to change significantly and do some end game content, that's it.
So, what is the verdict or my final score for this game? Well, the official critics nowadays are ♥♥♥♥ing suck, giving any game 90 out of 100 which is impossible to review the product in a day while they're in a middle of their playthrough. Do not listen to the critics. I bought this game around 30 Australian Dollars during sale and I don't think it is worth buying at full price. Besides, the GOTY edition is coming out soon. 2. I would like to be able to bypass warp points and cross pure space with large penalties later in the game
3. Large planet or system wide construction projects that would require the resources of at least a half dozen planets for the small projects (halos, specialized planetoids), and even perhaps half a huge galaxy for the big ones (ring worlds, Dyson spheres) Production could easily be rerouted to such projects from an Interplanetary Administration.

I would like to be able to negotiate exceptions to treaties to prevent conflict and make it easier to maintain relations by allowing you to do things they might not like, but needing to pay a large cost to mitigate their displeasure. It's a shame that this is the only real option for NBA basketball.
Every aspect of this game seems pay to win. Even certain aspects of single player, like story mode, is a farce. I don't agree with having to buy a game and then spend additional money in the game to make it fun. That's bad game design.
Your "pro" is rated at the start of MyPlayer like a YMCA pickup game has-been.
Want to try MyTeam? Any AI opponent you face has glaring advantages. Near perfect freethrow percentages. No turnovers; you can't generate steals. Your 85 speed rated SG can get chased down from behind by Robin Lopez in the open court. Your 80 rated 3 point shooters miss wide open shots. Controller stick pass directions miss their targets. Teams that rank worst in the league fail to have the weaknesses that rank them worst in the league, so you can't strategize around them.
Finely balanced pay-to-win games make it so if you're willing to grind and you play the game well you will be rewarded over time. This game utterly ignores that idea. And pay-to-win games are usually free to play. This is a triple-A title with pay-to-win elements with absurd imbalances that make grinding unrewarding. That's shameful.
Never spend full price for a game like this. Don't support pay-to-win titles that disrespect the fans who are willing to grind. You should never feel pressured to spend more of your money because the game you're currently playing makes you angry with its blatant disregard for your enjoyment. Games designed like that are supposed to fail. They're called "bad games."

Assassin's Creed Unity manages to turn a solid action game with a satisfying combat experience in to a horrid crossbreed of a dated stealth game and an RPG. It seems that Ubisoft's goal with this game was to create a more focused assassin experience, à la Hitman, but they failed. Horribly. I honestly wanted to like this game, even managed to at times, but never before have I felt so conflicted about an Assassin's Creed game.
They improved upon the freerunning system, which they honestly don't deserve too much credit because everyone was expecting that one. Nevertheless, the new system works pretty well and the ability to freerun down from atop buildings and into the streets makes moving around more fluid and natural. If only the character didn't feel so floaty and weightless.
They messed up the combat system for reasons beyond my comprehension, deciding to bring back the good ol' combat of the very first Assassin's Creed. That's right, no more chain-kills or fluid termination of opponents. Instead, fighting is now a slogfest, where you are battling against the controls just as much as you are battling your foes. This makes it difficult, that much is true, but not fun. Not in any sense of the word. The animations are slow and during this time any of the soldiers you are fighting can shoot you. Not only that, if you choose to run from them, they can snipe you from any distance as long as they see you and their bullets go through crowds, buildings, walls etc. Have fun trying to survive!
Ubisoft also thought that "hey, since people like RPG's so much, let's turn our flagship action game into an RPG instead!" and that turned out... awful, you guessed it. It could've maybe worked if they had actually sunk some time and effort into creating a cool leveling system to actually specialize your assassin, but it's all smoke and mirrors. In truth you are only spending skill points into skills and abilities that were granted right from the start to us in most of the recent titles (double-assassination, blending etc.) and all this system managed to do is disappoint you. The only positive thing is the outfit customization system, where you can choose each piece of armor individually. But guess what? They have stats. Like that hood you have right now? Forget it, it's gonna be obsolete sooner or later. This is somewhat, crudely, remedied by the ability to wear a "skin" with no stats ontop of your mix-and-match armor, like Ezio's robes for example.
I have completed approx. 50% of the game's single player missions and I am considering of deleting the intallation and just going straight for Syndicate. I'm a fan of the story (can you believe that?) and have never ever even considered of skipping a major title in the series. With Unity, I have nothing but regrets.
I am going to add a short list of pros and cons below that I can think of at the spot.
Pros:
- Freerunning system has been improved with the ability to "freerun" down from atop buildings and obstacles
- Missions, especially the bigger assassinations, seem very open-ended
- Sidemissions are numerous and I enjoyed the majority of them so far. Never did this many sidemissions in any previous game in the series
Cons:
- Arno feels like a rip-off of Ezio. A very poor one.
- Character movement has no weight to it like in previous titles
- Horrible amount of grinding required just to advance the story
- They brought back the combat system from the very first Assassin's Creed without counterattacks
- Removal of hidden blade combat
- Fewer combat animations, gets repetitive really quick
- No fast walking, dumbed down movement controls when not climbing
- RPG elements (Seriously, you have us level for basic abilities, like double-assassination?)
- Foe's have supernatural detection abilities, new stealth mechanics (=sneaking) do not make up for this
- A variety of different bugs and glitches, never encountered similar in prevous titles
All in all, I can only recommend this to die-hard fans of the series like myself. Everyone else should either watch a let's play or just pass this one. I managed to like it only because the freerunning system feels almost fantastic now and some of the missions are very fun, but all in all it's a half-arsed attempt to turn AC into a hybrid of Hitman and The Elder Scroll's and it simply doesn't work here, not with this level of work and commitment anyway. How Ubisoft failed to foresee this and launch the game regardless is anyone's guess. I hope the guy(s) responsible for the design choices got fired. He/they deserved it.

I guess I'm a bit of a softie or something, but the Walking Dead devastated me and left me choking up as it finished. The game starts off simple enough, with you trying to survive a zombie apocalypse, but as more people join in on your adventure and you end up taking care of a little girl, Clementine, tutoring her so she can, perhaps, survive the dangers of this new world by herself, the character conflicts and oppressing story elements start to mount to such a degre that I had a hard time actually playing the game!
From an audiovisual point of view, the Walking Dead is a bit crude. Textures and models aren't exactly top notch, but they get their job done. The animations, on the other hand, seem far too stiff sometimes, and as such take a little bit away from the immersion, but not too much. The voice acting and sound design is impeccable and while I was afraid that the game would be ruined by annoying child characters, the Walking Dead proved me dead wrong in that regard, by having Clementine grow up into a full-fledged and interesting character.
Truth be told, I finished this game a while ago and have been trying to build up courage to play the second season, but due to how bad I felt after the first, I haven't been able to. Again, that's probably just me being a big ol' softy for this kind of stuff, so make of that what you will.

So much potential gone to absolute waste. It is actually so saddening that I have to write this negative review as I love the AC franchise. I ignored all prior negative reviews on this game and went into it with a positive mindset. "How bad can it be? It's Assassin's Creed, you can't balls it up that bad!" Oh how naive I was. This game is cleary rushed and I'll be going through how bad they messed this game up.
1. Free-running: They've changed the controls for free running, although this may be slightly annoying it isn't a deal breaker. However, it feels clunky as you can't manouver the way you could in prior games. For example, wall jumping to an opposite wall is just impossible, literally, you can't do it. The free running just feels "scripted", in the sense that it isn't free, it just doesn't feel like Assassin's Creed free running. Remember when you could take on multiple opponents in previous games and actually feel like a master assassin? Yeah well forget that too as if you get into combat with multiple people, not only will you have suffer with the flimsy and rushed combat system, but you'll also probably die because of the same rushed flimsy combat system.
2. Combat: They had to touch a great combat system and just balls it up didn't they? ACBF combat was great, so was AC2, AC3, ACB and ACR. There is no longer blocking, you have to either parry (which is essentially a counter-move) or dodge. There is no variation at all and it just feels slow and clunky once again. Remember how you could take human shields when you are about to get shot? Yeah, well forget about it as you can't do that anymore so there isn't a counter for it. Unless you run up to the shoot and hit him, you are going to get a bullet to the face no matter how amazingly you zig zag away. Combat is ruined.
3. Gameplay and Missions: The missions are quite standard but are frustrating when the simple game mechanics that AC was known for have been ruined. Making missions more tedious and annoying. This game feels like a chore and it shouldn't. You have to run a marathon each time you complete a mission just to get to another mission. Obviously done to increase longetivity in the game. Furthermore, once in a while you'll get these BS "get to point B from point A cos Abstergo have found you" type missions which add literally nothing to the game, story wise. It's just a filler mission aimed to increase longetivity of the game, completely useless and annoying.
However, the stealth in this game is quite interesting, nothing revolutionary (pun intended) but still quite fun. The game looks great visually. Voice acting is on point but the story seems rushed. I won't spoil anything but you'll see what I mean if you choose to buy this game.
If this is going to be your first AC game then don't buy it. Get Brotherhood or Black Flag. Basically, any AC game that isn't this one. If this isn't your first AC game, buy it with caution. It doesn't play like the other games and can get frustrating.
All in all I'm really dissapointed with this game. It is clearly rushed and just feels like a chore. If you're going to purchase this then wait until a sale.
Final verdict: 3/10 - and thats me being nice.

First off I want to say I am a classic moo player from way back that never stoped playing. Ive even gone way out of my way to get it to work multiplayer even after that aspect of the game went down. That being said, I have seen a lot of negative feedback about this new verson of MOO and I just wanted to address some of the unfavorable responses I have seen.  I understand there gripes, It is not a MOO clone exactly.  But to be honest, i didnt want a moo clone or i would just boot up moo 2.  Yes the trade lanes add a different feel to the game. But IMO they can be used to add a stragety element to the game.  I can colonize a planet in strategic places to block off entire sections of the galaxy to myself.  Some people claim that you can have every tech in the game. Well, when i first played i was given this impression myself.  but on closer inspection there are some techs that are one or the other.  An example would be I can choose to have either Fusion Beam or Fusion drive.  On the tech tree it appears as Fusion Beam | Fusion Drive.   I can CHOOSE to be faster in space faster, or have better beam weapons right now, if i choose one, it will be a while before i have something better in the other field i didnt choose.  This is not the only example on the tech tree.   Now for the battle system.   All together I think this game is a great addition to the moo franchise. It is AMAZINGLY better than MOO 3 at any rate and the best addition I have seen to the game in decades. We should be thanking NGD studios and WG Labs for taking a chance on a game that took a lot of hard work for a fan base that doesent seem to appreciate a gift.  If this game does well, they may attempt yet another version down the road.  And maby they will incorporate the things you dont like about this game.  As it is now, it is a well polished game, with a few bugs for them to work out. Its in early access, give it a break while it is a work in progress.

is a casual time-puzzle game. Hades has kidnapped Megara, and it is up to Hercules, and especially his servant, to travel ancient Greece to save her.
: While Hercules is taking a nap, you order his servant around in single-screen puzzles, where you must reach your objectives within a set time limit. The point is to optimize the order in which you pick the resources and accomplish tasks that consumes those same resources, tasks such as fixing the path or upgrading buildings that generate resources or supply additional servants. As you progress, you will get access to a few bonus powers, and gather allies such as the Medusa, the Pegasus, the Cyclops and the Cerberus, each of which can defeat enemies blocking your path or accomplish special tasks. The colorful map is overlayed with symbols of the game achievements you accomplished, and landmarks that gets build as you get gold rating at each levels.
: The game is extremely easy, you'll rarely ever need to restart a level to get gold rating. Due to lack of randomization, it's unlikely you'll ever replay any levels except for the slightly less easy-to-get achievements. The story really is an excuse to give the world a setting.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
This game is basic, even for a casual game, and might be a bit more challenging for a much younger audience. But keeping in mind its price, I'd recommend it for children and achievement hunters, but anyone seeking any form of challenge in a puzzle should stay clear.

BLOCKADE 3D is an free-to-play online first person shooter that is currently in Early Access that has been both developed and published by Shumkov Dmitriy. As you can see from the screenshots, it takes its visual style from Minecraft, but also throws in placing and destroying blocks as well, which allows you to edit the maps that you play on as you go. The game modes this game has are:
4-way king of the hill. Capture and hold the centre of the map to earn points. Not sure how many points you need to win. It doesn't say.
A PvP zombie mode. Surivors v Zombies. One player is chosen to be a zombie and the Suvivors have 15 seconds to prepare. When a Zombie hits a Survivor once, they turn into a Zombie. Zombies have one life. Zombies win by killing all the Survivors and the Survivors win by surviving for 4 minutes and 45 seconds.
This game mode is rather poorly executed. In the 15 seconds that the Survivors have to prepare, groups of about 3-5 will run into the nearest building and will create an impenetrable fort by finding the nearest empty room and filling it with blocks in such a way so that they can see you from all the way at the back of the room. but you can't get to them, as the room is filled with blocks which allows them to gun you down if you attempt to get anywhere near them. Combining the fact that Zombies only have one life and the fact that Suriviors can place blocks at their free will tips the scales so far in favour of the Survivors that its just plain rediculous. Now, if the Zombies had more than one life, then I could see this being a better game mode overall but it gets boring very quickly, regardless of what side you are on.
See the following pictures for example:
Not capture the flag. This is an 4-way area control gamemode. The map is split up into 16 squares and capturing a square will passively give points to your team. Capture a square by eliminating any other players that are on different teams that are in that square. Get 5000 points to win.
Team Deathmatch. Teams Red and Blue fight to the death to be the first team to reach 500 points. Simple.
Melee only Team Deathmatch. Same as above, except melee only.
PvE Zombie survival. Work together with up to 31 other players to survive waves of zombies.
Team Deathmatch again. But with tanks.
Now, onto the important question.

It has space ships. It has explosions. It requires you to work together as a team. It's got lasers, too!
But the question on your mind is probably: Is this pay-to-win?
The answer to that would be: No. It is definitely NOT pay-to-win. It is free-to-play and you'll be able to get a few ships of your own within the first day of playing. An average match nets you about 10 to 15k credits and you require about 100k to 900k to purchase any of the ships. However, you will get a lot of boosters which means you'll end up with around 20 - 30k per round. You get no benefit whatsoever for purchasing items with real money (converted to 'platinum' with the only possible exception of gaining 20% more credits if you fly an 'ultimate' skin (note: not a spaceship!). These give no in-game advantages whatsoever, though. They just change the look of the ship.
So now that's off your mind, what can you expect?
Five-versus-five games where everyone picks their favourite space ship, customizes its loadout (load-outs can be unlocked by spending credits.) and then heads off to battle, capturing the enemy mines and every so often, gamma, the big station in the middle that gives you a temporary boost. At gamma 3, you jump toward the enemy base and attempt to capture it. Trying to unlock every ship there is for free is quite possibly going to take a long while. I've played about 40 hours so far and earnt roughly 5 million credits. I haven't spet the mayority of that because I'm still having fun with the ships I unlocked way at the start!
You can also spend your credits in the store. Most items can be bought with both credits and platinum (the in-game money).
In the mean time, you'll battle the enemy by hiding behind asteroids, using your abilities or even ramming them if need be. You can also attack the enemy base by capturing their forward station. You will be using WASD to do so so there's definitely skill involved when it comes to movement. There is no aiming prediction and although some weapons feature auto-aim, a lot of them have to be manually aimed. FPS-players will find themselves right at home!
Teamwork is highly essential in this game and I really appreciate the community. Most people are friendly and communicative. There's a reporting system in place that can also be used to praise people, which I find quite refreshing.
Outside of the game you'll be optimizing your ships by leveling up your crew and assigning them implants (or replacing crew members altogether). They add passive bonuses to your ships during gameplay and although these may look unimportant at first, they can really make a ship handle differently once you start collecting enough of the useful implants.
I played League of Legends for a few hours and thought it was the most boring grind ever. I played Fractured Space and became instantly hooked. I love the aesthetics, the way the game feels, the community and the very honest free-to-play model the developers have got going. I have witnessed no cheating but it's hard to tell, I suppose.
Also important: there seem to be enough players to guarantee continuous gaming and fresh faces. I usually have to wait around 1 - 2 minutes for a game but never longer than 5 minutes. A game usually lasts around 20 minutes. Some end early at around 15 and sometimes they drag out for 30. The latter is rather rare but it happens.
Don't want to play against real people? Stick to Quick Play! It matches you with 5 players against 5 bots. Great way to test out new ships or just get ready for the real deal.

Double Fine has graciously allowed 2 Player Productions to invade their personal space for the duration of the development of Broken Age, and gamers should thank them greatly; because what we got in the end was not just a game, but also the greatest video game documentary of all time. 2 Player Productions, for the first time ever, have documented the entire game development process from start to finish in an unfiltered, candid look at the great highs and crushing lows that come with making a game.
I urge you, regardless of your views on Double Fine, to pick up the documentary.
If you have never worked in game development, your perspective will widen, and you will finally get to understand the process not just from a consumer perspective, but from the perspective of a hardworking, devoted team of passionate game makers.
I sincerely believe that this documentary will change your perspective on video games, it certainly has for me.
