One of the best, if not THE best, documetaries on game development in existence. A lot of what game development entails is pretty boring to watch (insert person sitting at computer staring at lines of code for six straight hours here), but fortunately you don't have to endure that kind of boredom in this doc. It was filmed and edited by the brilliant team at 2 Player Productions (also famous for the Minecraft documentary and the first season of Penny Arcade The Series). They skim over all of the boring, monotonous parts of game dev and present something that is very viewer friendly. You get to see interviews with the individual team members, be a fly on the wall during team meetings, and watch each person on the team perform and describe their role. One of my favorite parts of the entire documentary is watching all of the game's concept artists have an art jam, admiring each other's work, swapping information on the utensils they are using, etc. Who doesn't love watching nerds feed off of each other's enthusiasm?
It pretty much also goes without saying that you'll get a lot of one-on-one with some legendary game industry figures including Peter Chan, Peter McConnel, Ron Gilbert, and (of course) Tim Schafer. You'll also get to see a variety of other famous faces along the way, including some behind the scenes with Jack Black, Elijiah Wood, and Jennifer Hale. Also some famous people who you never saw before until this documentary, such as Richard Horvitz (Raz in Psychonauts, Zim in Invader Zim, Dagget in Angry Beavers, etc)!
The documentary is truly a great game dev documentary because you really do get to see the good as well as the bad. On one hand, the company manages to develop and ship a successful game, so you get to see that. But you also get to see the company react to both the positive reactions and negative reactions to the game. There is also the interesting problem in the middle of development where a lot of rumors and misinformation about the project start going around and then mainstream gaming news sites start repeating it, which naturally creates a lot of distress. And even though this particular game ships as a successful project, another unannounced project gets cancelled at the very end of the doc, which results in a handful of layoffs. It is a very sad turn of events not only because layoffs are sad, but also because it is the first time the company has ever had to layoff any employees. And since you just spent the entire documentary getting to know each of the developers and even growing fond of particular ones, it is really hard to have to witness that Sophie's choice the company has to make at the end. It's interesting, if sad, to see what all of that looks like from the inside.
TLDR: Think MTV's The Real World, but with game development! And famous people!
FULL DISCLOSURE: I have been a fan of Double Fine since their first game and have been a member of their community for many years. I was a happy backer of the Double Fine Adventure kickstarter. I therefore had already watched the complete documentary before acquiring it on steam. I received my steam key as a prize in a Double Fine community contest.

Assassin's Creed: Unity is a third-person open world game developed and published by Ubisoft. The game was released in November 2014. You play as Arno Dorian, a servant-turned Assassin who participates in the fight against the Templar Order during the French Revolution in the late 1700s.

Unity features a good campaign. It mashes a main storyline with the open-world formula that includes various side-missions and feature various districts, or suburbs. The main story has very good storytelling, marking for a very strong narrative. I will provide a quick background, Arno is the son of Charles Dorian, an Assassin who was assassinated by Shay Cormac in Assassin's Creed Rogue. François de la Serre, the grand-master of a division within the Templar Order, adopts Arno and raises him in Versailles. The campaign begins with an forgettable and uninformative introduction, which very briefly explains to an 'Initiate' they will be playing as Arno in the new Animus. Unity lacks any modern storyline as in the previous games other than you're in the Abstergo headquarters.

Regarding the actual main missions, I believe they are a step-up from prior AC games. Unity excels in allowing freedom of approach to these missions, as for example, in prior AC games if you were tailing a character and get spotted, you would fail the mission, whereas in Unity, it alters the nature of the mission without you failing it. Each mission has opportunities that assist you in completing your mission. For example, one mission has an opportunity where you need to steal poisoned wine that has been delivered to the palace, allowing you to sneak up and poison the enemy character's wine. So, these new approaches and opportunities freshen up the gameplay and enjoyment of the missions.

As written, the campaign is good and there is a very good story, however similar to the most helpful review for this game at present, there is too much online content. There is two different types of coop side-missions that have interesting objectives, but unfortunately I couldn't play them, which will be a theme for new owners. Otherwise, there is a nice variety of side-missions that are both entertaining and different. Among some of the side missions, there is Paris Stories, featuring mini-storylines within Paris. There is Murder Mysteries, where Arno plays detective and investigates murders and finds the culprit. Lastly, there is Helix Rift missions, which tasks Arno to rescue Assassins stuck in simulations. Compared to previous AC games, Unity's side-missions are diverse and add some enjoyment into the game. However, one type of side mission incorporates the Companion App, which was patched out of the game. These missions were a gimmick and are useless because it granted you rewards for the App, therefore, Ubisoft kept the missions in but patched out the rewards for the Companion App.

I want to quickly discuss renovation and upgrades. In the AC series, I like building and equipment renovations. For instance, I loved the renovation system in AC: Rogue because you had the ability to upgrade and renovate your base and ships and there were visual differences and rewards for what you upgraded. It's a small thing that I immensely love. In Unity, you can upgrade your weapons and purchase skills, purchase Social Clubs, which were abandoned taverns, and renovate your Café Theatre. I like that there were more benefits for upgrading your weapons in this compared to previous games. And, I like the idea of purchasing social clubs and renovating your Café. But, as I love renovation and visual difference, I feel Ubisoft missed an opportunity to create a proper renovation system similar to Rogue because upgrading your Café does not provide any major visual difference, it only just opens rooms that were previous non-accessible. So, I personally would have liked Unity to have an upgrade system that actually improves the quality and alters the design of buildings.

Another little feature that I love in the AC Series is the database. Unity's database includes information about characters, locations, landmarks, and newspapers. The content in the newspapers changes as the game progresses. As usual, Unity does the database really well and I enjoyed reading the information. My only negative was the little and unnecessary statements that would randomly appear on the database's information, which usually has a * next to the statement.

Lastly I will very briefly discuss gameplay. Unity features different animations, new gameplay mechanics, and a new movement system. In Unity, you must unlock new skills for you to use instead of having access to all at the beginning. For instance, you have to unlock double assassinations or have to unlock environment blending. I believe this small change has big effect on the game, as you need to decide how to play the game because you do not have everything unlocked at your disposal. Otherwise, I liked the new movement system. Movement overall feels more fluid than previous games, as it feels like less of a hiccup to navigate through the areas. I credit the new parkour system to this because it feels smoother to pass objects or pass large crowds. On the contrast, I don't like the climbing system, as (de)climbing buildings is clunky and it just is a pain to do.

Unity utilises three cities of Paris, Versailles and Franciade. The city of Versailles showcases the beginning of the campaign and also where Arno grew up. Franciade is where you play the Dead Kings DLC. It is one district bigger than Versailles and incorporates diverse landscapes, notably the church and cemetery in one district and a big farm and quarry in another district. Furthermore, it has much more of a focus on underground exploration in tunnels and quarries. Paris is the main location in the game. It features six districts that have sub-districts within it. The city excels in its design because each sub-district is different in its buildings, behaviour of individuals, and socio-economic status. For instance, the districts in Le Louvre has a variety of middle and rich class individuals who dress elegantly and showcase different behavioural attitudes, such as movement, compared to the sub-district of Les Invalides that has more of a military focus with many revolutionaries and French troops in bases. With military AI, the only difference was the difficulty of those enemies in each sub-district, so there was nothing special in regards to military in each area.
All cities in Unity look beautiful and the game’s graphics are remarkable. I loved the attention to detail on the landscape and in the variety of characters. I have the specs on my profile, so I managed to play Unity at max graphical settings at mostly 60FPS, I never dipped lower than 55FPS and when I dropped below 60FPS, it was very quick.

Unity had a lot of controversy regarding bugs at launch. Unfortunately, I still noticed a ton of bugs. Specifically, I encountered a variety of gameplay bugs, particularly movement bugs. I noticed a decent amount of graphical issues, but not as bad as it was near launch. Overall, the encountered bugs were annoying, but it would not keep me from purchasing this game.

AC Unity is an overall enjoyable game. It features a fun story. All cities are all beautiful and have unique traits that separates the cities and districts’ look and feel. There are a variety of issues, but it is in a good and playable state. I recommend this on sale or at any price under USD$30.

- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

The single most compelling reason to continue playing Fallout 4 is having a virtual Lego set to play with (aka Settlement Building).  The main storyline is uninspired, the combat is repetitive, and Power Armor is way too common to really inspire more than a few play throughs.  However, building fortresses, cities, villages, farms, zoos, or even secret lairs with the Lego set was fun.
But to play with the Lego set beyond a basic level, the game requires mods like "Place Everywhere", which depend on the Script Extender.  And of course every new patch to the Fallout 4 version requires the dedicated modders to update their mods accordingly (kudos to those guys, they have done an excellent job).  But after many patches, Fallout 4 had finally achieved the most desirable state in any software system:  stability.  It still had bugs, but they were known and could generally be avoided.
And now along comes the Creation Club.  Apparently every new addition to the Creation Club is going to require a new Fallout 4 version, which leaves the heroic modders referenced above scrambling to keep up.  And it leaves those of us wishing to play with the Fallout 4 Lego set afraid to ever go online with Steam because Fallout 4 will auto-update (and yes, I've looked at the enable auto-update settings -- they appear to be Yes, Yes, and Yes).
Since Bethesda has decided to sacrifice stability for micro-transactions, I cannot recommend this product.

Best way to describe the new Master of Orion? Imagine if Sins of a Solar Empire was turn-based. That pretty much nails it.
Look, I've never played MOO before this, but I have played a ton of CIV, and various Space-faring games over the years, and here's my take, as a simple guy looking for a simple Space strategy game.
This game has held my interest like no other. EVERY SINGLE OTHER Space game I tried either bored me, the mechanics were too difficult to grasp properly and I gave up after 5 hours, or I just didn't like the way the game worked. Other than SoaSE, but that was real-time strategy, not so much Turn-based 4x.
This game is simple to grasp, fun to play, looks amazing and runs brilliantly, and is just a joy to breeze through. That being said, I have gotten to points where I just got bored and ended up clicking the "Next Turn" button repeatedly because I had pretty much done everything that there was to do at the time, and I then had ages to wait for the next big thing to happen, but I do get that this game is still EA and not all content is there yet. I mean, I'm hoping I'll see "more" things added to each race (I doubt it at this point though) and I am still looking forward to seeing the remaining races being added... However, managing planets is so far very basic, and trying to set up colonies on "bad" planets is an absolute nightmare.
But yeah, so far I've really enjoyed this game, and I'll reserve judgement until release. I do think it might get boring the longer a session goes on, but we'll see, I suppose it also depends on difficulty and number of races playing (last thing you want is to be overwhelmed and hate the game) and I will admit I was playing rather "light" games in systems mostly blocked off with unstable wormholes.
My score so far for EA: 7.0 / 10
Edit: A few niggles I just noticed. One: In real-time space battles, your ships just charge the enemy, and while they are being pummeled by gunfire, they start CIRCLING AROUND the enemy and STOP SHOOTING while they do this!!! So I'm left with half my fleet flying around in circles doing nothing for up to 30 seconds at a time while they get hammered. WTH?? They will try to shoot through asteroids instead of waiting until they get clear line of sight (asteroids block shots) and it's impossible to position them tactically because they just beeline straight for the enemy every time. This is a big no-no.

Grading system is super flawed, I do not like being penalized for stuff I do not do, or penalized in general or taken out of the gameplay to watch AI flub about because the dumb AI coach won't give me a chance.
Vintage teams of course not filled out all the way which is a huge pain for people who care about the vintage teams and then getting half the players being named Johnson or Smith and all have 50-60 ratings (I miss the days of legend pools and true full on vintage teams back in the live days in the early 2000s).

I love some parts of this game, but I also hate when I am yelling at the screen for the game saying it's going to deliver on one thing and then completely fail and glitch out the next. Whether that be a missed shot that should have gone in, or a an AI zapping in and out of place or lollygagging in the lane like a dumb fool. Or like right now where I have been playing a full on season every game full games getting to the finals and then game 1 crashes after I post a solid game and it's like nothing happened? What?!? THE ACTUAL... gahhhhhhhhh. So all the progress is kinda for nought? And apparently according to forums I have to play the game 3/4 the way and then sim the rest to get it to save? Is it this hard to fix this type of thing?
They addressed and fixed a few of these things in the next iteration but large issues still weren't completely fixed in 2k17 and won't be in 2k18, and so on and so forth because the only thing the devs seem to care about is VC.
So overall, Good (when and only when you are playing the most stripped down non sugar coated parts of the game), terrible when it tries to do anything else because largely that extra layer they claim is going to make something really great falls flat or bugs out or there's no community for or just in some other way fails, and shame on devs and marketing people still charging 59.99 for this and still having VC in these games but not really adding anything in actual value.
In my opinion if the company acknowledged it's players (of the game it makes) more and talked less about what the next flashy thing 2k(insert number here) is going to have in it people might be happier and the games might actually get better instead of being so stagnant as they seem to be, relying only on the real life NBAs glitz and grandeur that comes around every year with new talent emerging in the league.

Anyways apologies for the long windedness....2k16 is a decent game just not worth 60 bucks nearly 2 years later. While I would play again XCOM: Enemy Unknown again anytime, this sequel surely makes up for a poor experience in comparison. It feels like the developers had a lot of nice ideas to complement the first game's mechanics, but had no time or no interest in actually fleshing them all out.
What we're left is with a game that's unimpressive from the technical standpoint (rather poor graphics for how much of a resource hog it is and a lot of animation bugs and weird camera angles) and not really deep from a tactical perspective (most of the missions will rush you trough a timer and be heavily dependant on luck aka RNG). Save scumming (the act of reloading a savegame a thousand times to try and find the best outcome in a given situation) is almost a requirement in the higher difficulties, while every single time you get punished (and you do get punished a lot) you will feel that it was due to a random event (like a patrol happen to stride by while you pass your squad's turn) or a scripted storyline event that floods the map with a lot of missions on a timer, not only blowing up your plans while making you choose what you can live without.
Pretty much the only good thing is the storytelling/ambience, which is a really sad destiny for a series with such notoriety as XCOM. For die hard fan of the series or people extremely resilent to tactical frustration there may be some fun under there, but don't expect anything as close to the polish of the first one.

OpenCanvas is a wonderful piece of software, it really is.  The development staff was helpful when I requested help, also.  It is good software.  A new gif export was added, which works in most browsers, but may not load in OpenCanvas.  The event files still open and you can still make event files.  The layers can be outputted as sequential for animation.  The big standards of png, jpg, and psd are supported filetypes on input and output.
However...
As of the end of July this year(2016), the most unique feature of OpenCanvas, the education gained from playing event files within OpenCanvas that were were found in the PG community is now gone.  This is because the PG Community has been taken down, so if you know where some of your files are, don't delete them.  Prior to this wonderful PG Community feature, the original OpenCanvas had multi-user files, so a few people could be on computers at a distance and draw on the same file.  This prior feature is still requested today.  So, OpenCanvas has a tendency to take their most unique team-like features and drop them at some point.  This last one can be blamed on DeviantArt's newer web painting app, but this dropping teamwork benefitting tools pattern with OpenCanvas could be repetitive.
Say hello to Muro on DeviantArt...and rest in peace PG.

Very similar to Master of Orion 2 (this review requires some knowledge of Moo2).  I sat down and couldn't stop playing it.  A few differences that could be seen as detractors to some.  This is going to sound like a giant bash of the game, but I'm just putting the difference out there, I'm not going to stop playing it anytime soon.
Tactical combat is real time - however you can pause during it, so not sure why so many people don't like it.  There is less to do in combat, you can make your large ships go first, eat some shots and make your small ships move in to do more damage.  You can also position your ships behind asteroids and missles hit them (a really cool addition to the original).  I like the combat myself, but right now you can't disable weapons and select specific ones like you could in Moo2 (say to stop your missles shooting an asteroid).
Ship building is also fairly difficult because you cannot chose to refit specific ships in a specific manner, this ability to micro might be added later, but for now you have to change your base design, then either refit or build a battleship, if you go to upgrade it later because you got better armor or shield tech, you have to redo the schematic.  To refit or upgrade a ship there isn't a production option, the only way is to spend credits on it at a starbase or starlanebase.
It feels like food and population growth is too easy, you are able to farm "barren" planets, and with soil enrichment technologies, they provide alot.  I haven't yet settled on "toxic" or "volcanic" planets... so maybe barren just got an upgrade.
The Diplomatic victory is a misnomer - right now it's all about your current popluation (other races don't have to like you, you can be at war with them all).   If you can grow your empire enough, you win the game if you have over 66% of the galactic population.  That does seem like alot, but I've won 5 games by just expanding and maxing food growth - all vs the standard AI.  It seems like with the current setup you'd never win by pure combat - the vote would probably finish when you conqured 2/3 the galaxy.  Also, if you start to conqure the more numerous faction you are likely to win faster.  Obviously the AI is weak, and technology victory isn't in the game.  Actually I think I would have won all 5 games with tech victory faster then dipolmatic, so I guess it's a moot point, still strange there is no diplomacy involved.
Heavy/Low gravity needs balance - Low gravity isn't a negitive at the moment, you can still settle on "normal planets" - actually Low grav is a bonus, I'm pretty sure if you have lowG you can settle low and normal with no penalty and HighG with -50%.  If you are normal low and highG get you -50%.   Moo2 was HighG = no penalty (maybe -25% on lowG it cost points to pick up), LowG -25% on normal and -50% on highG (it gave you points to spend).   Normal was -25% on Low and High
One of the biggest changes is there is no "creative" - you get all the techs, except a few where every race has to pick between two or three choices.  Some are really tough, you have to pick heavy armor OR reinforced hull, you can never have both.  This is a good balance option and hopefully the AI choses different things so you can either trade or steal it from them (spying not in game as of yet).
Oh another big change is "Starlanes".  I actually really like the stratical implication of this and is one of the best things.  Every star system has only a few ways to access it, and from only specific other systems.  This creates chokepoints, and makes it much easier to decide where to go. I have settled on farther planets with less physical value (poor/small etc), just because it protects 1 or 2 other systems that I want full control over later.  One game I settled pretty far out and close to an AI, and he got completly boxed in by myself and another AI and only had access to 3 systems...  It does make actually finding your way to Orion much harder though, there is an "open borders" option in diplomacy, so I guess you can spend a few credits or whatnot to get through someones terrian.
In Moo2, you kinda had to have your fleet centralized near important planets, then once you saw someone moving there, you'd have to respond.  I never really played multiplayer, but I think it would be impossible to defend anything, because once you got tech to tell your ships to change direction, you could tell them to go to somewhere nearby, and just instantly stop at a closer planet... there was a tech to help prevent that and increase movement to it, but seems kinda silly.
One thing I'd love to see in the game is ship and colony heroes, but they have some touching up and retweaking ship design and refits before a custom ship hero is going to do too much.  At first I was thinking of putting off my purchase until they got added, but after reading everyone elses review and the forums I decided that heroes are just kinda a garnish add-on that make the game fun to player longer.
I have no idea how long this is, and I've probably skipped some changes (well there are no antarians... no ship to ship combat or boarding - one of the best things ever in moo2 was capturing an antarian ship and scrapping or using it with its really good tech)
TLDR;
A few changes - Still Moo IMO - I love the game.

It is always changing, and always getting better. They always make new design choices, and whether they go in the right or wrong direction, it can change again at any time.
Starbound, as a game, is a story about doing better than it's predecessors, and a journey into game development. I've been with this game since Offended Koala, which was one of the codenames for it's betas back 3 to 4 years ago. It had been more of a survival game then, with a heat and hunger system, and all of the mods supplemented the content with more biomes and things to do.
When the Giraffe updates came around, they steered away from this design and worked more on giving it more story and a better reason to explore, and while it was great, it recieved a bit of smack from people (Myself included) for steering away from or losing some of it's appeal and being more like the game before it, Terraria.
Now though, the game sits at a comfortable and amazing position not quite like what it was before, or what it was inspired by. The game itself is fun and amazing to explore, the story is (optional) great, and the modding community is an active and amazing one. This game also sits at a comfortable and semi-frequent update schedule, so you can expect both modders and the dev team to make more and improve content.
Development aside, the game itself has a lot of charm, as the aesthetics and music compliment each other and the gameplay mechanics, especially in the story sequences with dungeons and boss fights. When you're out exploring worlds, all the things you find don't feel out of place for wherever you're at. Dungeons, ruins, and villages all feel natural, and worlds feel different and unique, even to other worlds with similar biomes. NPC's react naturally (
).
This game can appeal to a ton of different audiences. Whether you want to explore and fight monsters, build and farm, roleplay, barely survive, or make mods, this game features a lot of stuff to do on it's own, but becomes even more open-ended with mods. I'd totally suggest this if you like Minecraft, Terraria, or Don't Starve. I'd also suggest playing it with a friend, as it's great to share with friends too.

While I would play again XCOM: Enemy Unknown again anytime, this sequel surely makes up for a poor experience in comparison. It feels like the developers had a lot of nice ideas to complement the first game's mechanics, but had no time or no interest in actually fleshing them all out.
What we're left is with a game that's unimpressive from the technical standpoint (rather poor graphics for how much of a resource hog it is and a lot of animation bugs and weird camera angles) and not really deep from a tactical perspective (most of the missions will rush you trough a timer and be heavily dependant on luck aka RNG). Save scumming (the act of reloading a savegame a thousand times to try and find the best outcome in a given situation) is almost a requirement in the higher difficulties, while every single time you get punished (and you do get punished a lot) you will feel that it was due to a random event (like a patrol happen to stride by while you pass your squad's turn) or a scripted storyline event that floods the map with a lot of missions on a timer, not only blowing up your plans while making you choose what you can live without.
Pretty much the only good thing is the storytelling/ambience, which is a really sad destiny for a series with such notoriety as XCOM. For die hard fan of the series or people extremely resilent to tactical frustration there may be some fun under there, but don't expect anything as close to the polish of the first one.

( This review is to present the good things about XCOM 2. If you had criticism about my last list, I understand. And, on the 'two-missions-and-a-boss' thing, I was exaggerating. Deal with it. )
XCOM 2 is the followup to XCOM: Enemy Within, a game where aliens are invading Earth, albeit slowly, and you, as the commander for XCOM, have to keep members of a council of nations on your side, command a squad in battle against these extraterrestrial beings, and manage the base you operate from.
However, in XCOM 2, you'll find things went to sh!t after the last game.
The aliens have succeeded in invading Earth, and within 15 years, have the whole populace under control.
Except for a special few.
Those who resist ADVENT generally end up with the Resistance, a rag-tag group of former members of the XCOM project, people who don't enjoy ADVENT's rule, or just plain don't know anything else.
Your first mission isn't even playing as you: you take command over a small strike team that takes heavy losses about halfway through, and you are recovered via Skyranger dropship.
And you dive right in to managing the Avenger, a captured alien freighter for transporting supplies across the planet. Building facilities, items, researching things, etc. And setting up your first Guerilla Ops is a piece of cake; I beat that in about 7 turns.
All in all, you have to find out the rest yourself. If you want to learn this earlier, incoming spoilers. You have beem warned.
AAAAND this is about where I got to. I haven't gotten any farther.
XCOM's few problems are listed in my other list, along with this one, right here:
It just doesn't feel new. Sure, the graphics are great, and the story's been updated, things have changed. But it's the same old game, just with a new coat of paint.
I still reccomend this, in spite of my previous review, so that you can play this game for yourself.

TL;DR
Don't Buy. If you can get the game for under $15 then consider it, but only if you really like AC games and only after you have played every other assasins creed game, because this is the lowpoint of the series in almost every aspect.
The Bad:
1. Movment - The new movment system looks good it really does, but it does NOT play well. AC games are well known for having a movment system that gets a bit infuriating, and this is the worst of the series. The new system CAN work better, as seen in the successor game AC: Syndicate, however in this game its♥♥♥♥♥♥ pretty looking♥♥♥♥♥♥but still♥♥♥♥♥♥
2. Combat - Combat is much like the movment, the new system makes it look smooth and more realistic at the expense of gameplay. Combat feels slow, and is still filled with bugs, your character may freeze up for a seccond or two at random,  and (although slightly less important) combat sounds may cut out every now and then. It IS more challenging, which would be a good thing if every other aspect of the game weren't so bad, having challenging combat mixed with♥♥♥♥♥♥controls/movement with a nice layer of bugs on top is not a recipe for a good game.
3. Story - Havent finished it, but about half way through it is very standard AC stuff. Tease complex plot and then just make the templars the Big Bad Evil Guys and the Assasins the freedom loving heros. Just now with x2 the characters that "betray" their order, except but nothing really comes of it. If I dont edit this, then the rest of the story is the same.
4. Level/Mission design - Most is standard fair for an AC game (not great), linear paths that look open. Unfortunate but at least easy to navigate. However, some missions are very subpar for the series. You will come accross a few missions, even in the main story, that are so baffling in their design that you either are left feel like you wasted an unreasonable amount of time or you looked it up just to get it over with.
5. Microtransactions - Not needed, really you can go through the whole game and never know they were there. Still, it exists in a full priced AAA game, that's a paddlin.
The Good:
1. Customization - The only thing AC: Unity does well it also does better than any other AC game. This is the most you have ever been able to customize your weapons and apearence in the main game, and given how AC: Syndicate walked all that progress back it may remain that way. If you do pick it up, take a moment to enjoy it.
Not my area:
1. Co-op - didn't use it, but for those interested the co-op missions are very specific, not main story.
2. Multiplayer - Why do you care about this? it is dead, the majority of multiplayer players are playing other AC games, not this one.
The storytelling, the voice acting, the choices, everything about this game is exemplary. Highly recommended.

The free agent system is completely broken, and that is one of the most important elements of a team management simulation.  To sign a free agent, you engage in blind auctions, meaning you make a contract offer, and then every other team gets to make a contract offer, and then a player just signs with a team at some point.  There are no negotiation updates, ie, Dallas offered me 3 million over 3 years, will you offer me more?  The player just signs with a team based on initial offers - at least to a degree.
I did some save as and reload testing to try to get a better idea of how this blind auction works, and the results were very disappointing.  I offered a player a max bonus and max salary for 5 years, ie 73 million dollar bonus, and 43 million dollars a year salary for 5 years, and for some unexplained reason he signed with another team that offered him 1.5 million bonus and about 1.5 million a year for 3 years.  I can't imagine a reason for this kind of game design.  With this kind of Free Agent system there is not any team building element to the game, and balancing payroll and salary cap are an illusion.  There is certainly no strategy to any of it.  You are just hitting continue buttons and hoping for the best.

openCanvas is a rather simple/advanced program to utilize.
That "simple/advanced" means everything here. If you seek to do simple art, you don't have to dredge through settings to get something simple out. No vectors, no strict, out of the ordinary brush types, no real issues with any tablets.
As for the advanced user, making brushes is quite an easy task, on top of having access to
the layers and the respective settings you can expect out of them.
With a maximum canvas resolution of 10000x10000, you have plenty of room to do whatever you need to (But to be fair, if you're doing high detail 10k 1:1, expect images larger than 200 MB).
I suppose the only downside to this program is that it is strictly a static output. If you seek to animate frame by frame or layer by layer, your only option is to output image by image to a program like Gimp.
While the program is distinctly used for anime/manga style art, it is quite feasible to establish whatever style you wish. Don't be afraid to branch out and explore. Pour your mind onto the canvas as you wish.
Take into consideration: What works for one may not work for another. While a tool may not feel right in your hands, it may take some polish or a different perspective to make itself useful.

Open Canvas 6, what a nice program we have here, is light (only 17mb), fast, doesn't crash very often (at least for me), and all you can do in Sai or Photoshop can be done here (only in illustration of course, Open Canvas is not a photo edition software), the tablet coordination is really nice even when you don't have a wacom (like me, i have an ugly Genius); Doing line art is a pleasure, the stabilization levels are really good and you don't need a really powerful computer in order to work with the program... unless you have PS, AI, ID opened at the same time... don't do that lol.
The "Event" function is amazing and let you understand which errors you had in your process and let you correct them immediately.
Pros:
-Light
-Fast
-Compatible with Photoshop (to edit and to save files)
-The Event Function
-Really nice coordination with every tablet (even when they're generic)
-Don't need a lot of resources
-Customizable interface and brushes
-You can use the Adobe Photoshop palettes
-Receives updates and improves very often
-Has vectorial tool, is not as good as Illustrator but is good enough.
Cons:
-Only Use HSV/HSL color (which is similar to RGB), would be nice if we can have pure RGB and CMYK, so we can directly edit files that will be printed... the reading of CMYK files is quite awful xD
-If you're used to photoshop is quite hard to understand at the start (that's not a big problem)
-The "Smudge Tool" is awful BUT this is not a really big problem since the over use of this tool is not good (at least in my opinion).. makes you lazy and you picture will look quite dead
- The community is quite small compared with the Photoshop and Sai ones, that makes some tutorials really hard to find or even understand (remember, this software is mainly japanese)... then you rage, and after that you realize that the same tricks that works in photoshop and sai works here... except for for smudge.

10/10
Update:
Now with the 6.1 Release we got some interesting features like converting the event file into a GIF or even creating a gif without having to use photoshop or CSP Pro/EX and also we got the pure RGB palette that make this software more viable in the "profesional" field and more compatible with the softwares said above.
8/10

+ Time management strategy game
- Cliche'd story, generic music, technical issues (on Nvidia hardware)
12 Labours of Hercules is a game about the ancient Greek hero Hercules, who has lost his wife Megana, who was abducted by Hades and taken to the underworld. You follow Hercules in his quest to get his wife back. The game contains 4 chapters, each containing an opening cutscene, 9 normal levels and a boss minigame level. In each level you need to complete a few objectives, usually related to clearing the path to the exit. For this, you have a few minions available that you can use to concurrently clean up obstacles. At the same time, cleaning up obstacles takes precious resources, so in order to complete the objective the fastest, you need to allocate your resources properly: Should I upgrade my farm first, providing me with the resources I need to clear the obstacles or should I push on towards the exit, so I can finish this level more quickly. Optimizing this process is the main challenge of 12 Labours of Hercules.
The storyline borrows a lot from the ancient mythology of Hercules, but overall I'd say that the storyline isn't very interesting to follow. It is very cliche'd and badly voice acted. The music also didn't grab my attention: I've listened to it for a while, but I quickly grew bored of it. In contrast to the gameplay, which is pretty well executed, the storyline and music feel pretty generic.
Initially, I had some technical difficulties running this game on Linux: It turns out this game is incompatible with at least the proprietary Nvidia drivers and crashes on startup. I have not tried Nouveau, but the open source Intel drivers work fine. If you really want to play the game and you only have a Nvidia card, you could try using Wine, the game runs fine on Nvidia cards in this way, though running games in Wine is never desireable. I'd recommend that when you buy this game, you should quickly try if this game is compatible with your machine, so you can refund it otherwise. I do not own any AMD hardware, so I cannot test on these configurations. I have emailed the developer about the issues a few months ago, but as of yet the game is not fixed and probably will never be. The other games in the series suffer from the same issues.
Conclusion: You should buy this game if you like time-management games, but be wary of hardware incompatibilities: There are issues, mostly with Nvidia cards, causing the game not to refund. Test the game immediately so you can refund it, if it isn't working for you.

It's also true, that some features are still missing and the game is far from being finished and polished. But any point of complain I read so far is allready addressed by the Devs, that they are going to work on it eventually. And I believe them. This isn't an unknown independed Developer working on this project in his free time, it's an established company whos reputation might be depending on this game.
But what the Devs allready have achieved is a great atmosphere, something most other MoO-like games are missing. The game felt like good old MoO2 from the first minute and soon after I felt into this "Just one more turn..." state of mind, that will cause you to loose some precious hours of sleep. That's impressive in this early state the game is in.
Even though I belong to those people who would have prefered a turn based combat system, I can tell that the system the Devs have chosen isn't dumb. You can loose a battle against a weaker enemy because you have been careless or you can win against a much stronger enemy if you use the right technology and tactics (and maybe a bit of luck). If they continue to work on the combat as they promised allready it might be pretty decent.
The only complain I have are the star lanes. I'm still not a fan of it, allthough I have seen games where star lanes have been implemented worse.
Again, the atmosphere of the game is great, it's allready a incredible fun and you can allready see where additional features are planed. I think this game looks very promising and I don't regret buying it. Instead I am excited for every comming patch.
This game is a lot of fun! I can't wait until it's finished but each update has me coming back for more.

First of all, calm down, it's Early Access.
Don't expect it to be exactly like Gmod tower because it's not. Not only because they can't use copyrighted assets, but because they're adding cool new content.
So the developers are still the same, they didn't sellout or anything like that.
It's the same Towers, but not on Gmod. This is how a good game does it by itself, but they need time, money and support.
The good stuff!
+ All old minigames are back (Virus, Ballrace and Minigolf, so far).
+ New minigames out and coming soon.
+ New items, new currency.
+ Very nice graphics. (though read the not-so-good section as well)
+ Developers are always there to answer any question.
The not-so-good stuff...
- If you have a low-mid end PC, you won't be able to run it very well, specially when you're in a server with many people.
- Virus doesn't feel the same (it feels much more fast paced, but maybe that's just me).
- Character customization is very limited. I hope this changes in the future, because all people have the same body types atm.
- Servers. This is what I don't like at all. 2 reasons:
1. People won't be joining your condo because it's going to be another server, and that's just a waste of time.
2. Too many servers that aren't official, even though they're dedicated. (so you'll see random people's dedicated servers filling up the list).
- If you play a minigame in any server, if the host leaves, the minigame is over.
- It doesn't feel like a community anymore, people just straight join into a minigame, or their condo. I don't know if there's any reason to join the plaza anymore. I miss the waiting queue for the minigames, but maybe this is more practical (I really wish everything would be in the same server though).
- Some annoying bugs to fix, but you know, it's Early access.
If this game never grew and stayed the same as it is now, I'd actually rate this bad, but since the developers are so hard-working and dedicated, I have no problem giving this a good review, because I know it will get better.
I was in the Private Alpha and content came out frequently and this doesn't seem to change. So give it a try, even if you don't play it now, you'll play it later for sure.
UPDATE:
Due to the hard work from the develpers adding new content from time to time, I'd recommend it to anyone, because it's getting really fun. I only wish there was more people around. Come play! :)

Ever since I was on Playstation Home, and after it's final shut down, I was curious if anyone would try to find a way to recreate the whole experience, or at least a similar experience. I missed being able to buy my own home, decorating it how I wanted, playing minigames to earn points to help me buy stuff, etc.
Now I see this and I am amazed. It brought back the Playstation Home, only on PC. Now you can come here and have that same experience. The plus side is that there's no micro-transactions to have to pay for all your furniture or home. Now you just play minigames to earn "credits" which you can then in-turn, use to buy stuff. Furniture, appliances, outfits, you can buy it all.
Mind you this is only the early access I am playing at the moment, but it all looks good so far. Minigames play great, credits/transations work very well, and so far some neat stuff you can put in your home. A few of the interactive items work so far. (Flatscreens play youtube videos, canvas items allow you to post pictures, etc.) From what I seen so far, it looks like it will also include tons of other interactive items, such as radio control toys, pets, even jet packs that let you fly in the air when you are in the Lobby or your home. They also seem to play to make so you can get all kinds of homes and more interactive items you can use in your home. So far only a small handfull of items work properly, the ones that seem interactive have a "Not active" notice, so only time will tell if they will get these to work later.
Overall it's a very neat experience and I can't wait for them to add more updates to this. It's about time someone brought Playstation Home, only a PC version with a lot more things to do. Can't wait to see what they update next. ^_^

The Walking Dead is an episodic adventure game developed and published by Telltale Games, the same people behind other such great adventure games as The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones. The game is based on Robert Kirkman's comic book series of the same name
Although the game does not follow the same exact storyline as the comic book series, it follows the same universe as the comic book follows only seeing it in a different point of view. The story follows Lee Everett, a convicted murderer who as the game starts is being taken away to prison
However, something on the highway causes Lee to crash and find out that the world is going through a walker (zombie) apocalypse. He then meets a young girl called Clementine and through their story of survival, we see how their lives and the other lives around them change for better or for worse
The game is split up into five episodes with an additional episode called The Walking Dead: 400 Days which is only offered as DLC. The game works as a normal television series. Each length of an episode is roughly two to three hours or more long with the DLC's length being roughly between one to two hours long
The gameplay is very simple, you move around, selecting stuff and talking to people and using button prompts when told to. The main bulk of gameplay is through the dialogue options. What you say and what you do will effect the game in the long run. Choosing who survives and who dies, choosing who stays and who leaves is all effected by your choices
The game's graphics are nice for the most part however there are some ugly texture work here and there. The sound and music options also vary in quality. Sometimes the sound quality is really good and sometimes the sound quality is bad. I have encountered numerous amounts of glitches which seems as if Telltale Games never got round to fixing them, too many to mention in this review
The Walking Dead shines in its character creation, each character is superb when it comes to their own personality and backstory and especially the final moments of the game will surely make a few people upset. The game also deals with heavy amounts of gory bloody violence which although fine with me can be a bit disturbing for some people
Telltale's The Walking Dead is a superb Telltale Game and the continuation of the story through it's DLC; The Walking Dead: 400 Days, The Walking Dead: Season Two, The Walking Dead: Michonne and the recently announced (2016) The Walking Dead: Season Three make for a stellar Telltale series

is a basketball game. And it seems to have.. all the things. It's got regular play, career mode, franchise mode and a rather in depth online (that's completely absent as far as I can tell) using MyPark, a sort of open world giant basketball land with multiple courts that you can roam and “call next” on.
I use to be heavy into sports games playing deep into franchise mode selecting every draft pick, setting beer prices... granted this was back in 2006 and thus since then I have completely lost touch with modern players. However, this brings me to my most enthusiastic point. There are so many options in this game, there is almost too many. Coach substitutions, intentional fouls, play calling can all be set to let the AI take over as little or as much as you'd like. There are also a number of graphical settings, more than you'd expect, such as turning the crowd completely off or simply lowering the quality represented by them) to be adjusted for lets call them less than modern machines (like mine) to run the game at a nice smooth 60fps.
Now, I mentioned I haven't really been playing sports games since 2006, back when the hit stick and QB vision cone was being introduced in Madden: Back when.. well, back when NBA Live wasn't a name that was laughed at. Hell, back when 2K was published by Sega. I say this because this style of gameplay took me some getting used to, there was no user release for shot timing in EA games. But once you do get used to it can feel quite tactical. Albeit, perhaps a bit overly animated in exchange for lack of responsiveness.
The Career is mode interesting, following the progression of a user made character from high school to the NBA draft and beyond. However, the cut-scenes are all very strange: Directed by Spike Lee, it takes on this very stilted and forced perspective that I certainly could have done without.
There is also an in-game currency that must be used to upgrade the characters skills and acquire any custom animations you might enjoy. These can be earned slowly through simply playing however they can also be purchased with real money. An idea I can't really endorse. But, I understand why the method is employed. As far as a business model.
Too many "finish this in 6 moves"-type scenarios. Lame and annoying. Way less fun than the older XCOMs.

I've played all AC games available for PC except for Origins. I've been a fan of the franchise ever since, not the best in the series but not also the worst one. It has its flaws but I say you should still give it a go and try getting it on sale :D
GRAPHICS
+ Still legit look cool even on low settings
+ The lighting, ambiance, color scheme, and structural design are impresively well-made (easily one of the most beautifully made games in the franchise)
+ The visual aesthetic it provided along with Paris is just 11/10
+ Best-looking AC game IMO. (Yes, better than Syndicate and Origins, for me, at least.)
(No flaw on the graphics, really. Carry on.)
GAMEPLAY
+ Class system (Health, Melee, Stealth, Ranged, or mix-and-match, really your choice)
+ This is where sneak mechanics are introduced, now you'll feel more of a shneaky ashashin
+ Parkour and kill animations are boss (and BRUTAL *cue black metal sound*)
- Harder combat (con for me since it kinda made the battles a bit more slow-paced)
- Parkour can be a bit frustrating since Arno's grip is sometimes unpredictable
CUSTOMIZATION
+ dressupyourassassin.jpeg
+ Provides you tons of cosmetic choices for Arno to wear in-game.
+ Unique combinations with matching stat effects to personalize your own build.
- Not enough color palette for your dressupyourassassin.jpeg
- Some equipments are a bit "flashy". A massive feather on your hood? Not so stealthy to me.
STORY
+ Interesting play throughout the history of the French Revolution
+ Iconic characters like Napoleon Bonaparte
- Story's a bit sub-par compared to Rogue, considering that both are connected.
WORLD
+ Variety of missions, and tons of stuff to do and collect
+ I had 80+ hrs worth on single-player alone :'D
+ Map is massive, plus the underground caves, and more buildings are actually enterable. Sweet.
+ You have Paris and Versailles as main locations.
- The voice acting accent is just *cough* not French enough *cough* (It's so weird that everyone sounds British, really.)
- If you're a completionist you're gonna have to grind a lot
- Some optimization issues. FPS drop here and there.They might have fixed some of it but not all of it.
- Minor glitches (NPC stuck in a tree, NPC climbing poles and buildings, Arno getting stuck mid-air, Arno's weird hand glitch when picking locks lol)

First thing's first, I played this game when it originally came out for the PS4 and it was an absolutely abysmal experience. The game started to drop frames whenever there were large masses of NPCs, there were game-crashing bugs all over the place, and it didn't feel like a brand new Assassin's Creed game overall.
Coming back to this game now after waiting for Ubisoft to fix all of the previous problems of this game was a great idea. I have been having a blast with this game. The graphics are phenomenal, the new system for moving and climbing is very intuitive and feels more realistic and responsive, and for the first time in the series you can actually have a good chance of dying in combat, which makes you plan more strategically when you're about to enter combat. Another good addition to this game, in my opinion, is letting you plan out your path for assassinating targets. It feels a lot more personalized and is more rewarding overall once the assassination is completed. Revolutionary France is an amazing setting as well and really makes you want to explore every inch of it.
The story is great right up until the very ending, in my opinion, but overall this is a very solid entry in the Assassin's Creed franchise, even though it had a very rocky release.
My personal score: 8.75/10. I would highly recommend getting this game.

This game has a steep learning curve -- hard to get at first, but once you do, its nearly impossible to set aside.  "One more turn" turns into "one more season" in no time at all.
Obviously this isn't the game for those who like graphics -- but this IS the game for those who want the details that are lacking in Madden.  Restricted versus unrestricted free agents?  First draft picks flopping and 7th round picks leading your franchise?  Players holding out over contract disputes?  Having to make tough calls about injuries because you don't really know 100% when the player will be available again and bringing him back too soon could injure him even worse?   Relocating to nearly any city or town you can think of?  Choosing your entire coaching staff?  Even former players becoming coaches -- I watched as Ben Roethlisberger ended up joining the coaching staff of the Falcons before rising up to become their head coach.
I have some minor criticisms -- mostly that player ratings are randomized (there's an option to only "slightly" randomize it but even that is too much, as half the time, even "slight" randomization causes Joe Flacco to not be the starting QB of the Ravens in 2016, for example.)  I'd like an option to completely remove randomization all together,   Also, I think coach ratings are ENTIRELY randomized...half the time, Mike Tomlin gets fired from the Steelers after the 2016 season and no other team wants him.  That's ridiculous.
But once you get past that first 1-3 years of willing suspension of disbelief, the game becomes INCREDIBLE.  Absolutely fantastic.  You can play for 100 years and look back at every detail.  Amazing.
Highly recommended!

After playing 138 hours I've decided to uninstall.
It's really not worth the timesink and grinding to get to end-game where the gameplay has already been super repetitive and boring for a long time. The game has a lot of carefully planned daily and weekly bonuses (cubits or shadow tower rewards) that kept me wasting hours to make progress when I already lost enjoyment playing the game. New classes cost real money or 95k+ flux on the market for a tradeable class coin. It took me most of my gameplay so far to earn enough flux to unlock another class, which some veteran players had already unlocked all classes back when they could be unlocked using cubits. Making another account to play other classes isn't helpful since that requires grinding all over again to acquire end-game gems for the new account, also not fun. And grinding to get 95k flux just to throw it away on a class that many veterans already have, it leaves a big sense of regret wasting that much time to get something so basic when there's things like gear that the flux would be better off spent on. Leveling new classes adds to Mastery Rank, so to hit Mastery 300 and get the dragon it requires a lot of time wasted on flux farming (perhaps 1000 hours or months of Shadow Towers). Even if some people could acquire enough class coins to unlock them all at a faster rate than that, it wouldn't be fun by then.
This might have been good as a standard purchased game without the blatant vampiric microtransaction system and the intentionally addictive daily and weekly events. It's not worth the addiction and eventual realization "I'm playing this everyday and I've really grown to hate it." There's just nothing fun about it anymore. It revolves around doing the same dungeons millions of times, mining the same ores millions of times, doing the same events and bosses. Higher end gameplay is simply enemies with higher damage and health. End-game bosses are the same as lower teir bosses but with higher damage and health, that means a 10-15 minute fight instead of 5 minutes. End-game equipment is where your weapons and helmet get rather shoddy graphical effects like flame or electricity or shadows. Fly for Fun did it better and players could get those weapon effects easily.
Anyway my review is simply that this game could have been a lot better but it became used for a money making system that is based a lot on gambling and wasting money for things that lots of other games give you for playing (for example Chaos Chests giving out items you can't acquire during normal gameplay). Also there's an optional monthly Patron thing but you're better off buying other games on Steam or eating good food with that money.
The easiest part of my decision to quit and also give this game a bad review is when I realized I played over 60 hours this week, didn't enjoy it, and wanted that time back.

Open Canvas 6 comes with all the essential and a few unique features for a digital art program!
- You can tweak your Brush settings, which gets the job done for sketches and line art, but when it comes to coloring/shading, the options included with the watercolor and air brush is fairly limited.

- The workspace can be freely arranged
- Just like Photoshop, Open Canvas comes with a selection of filters and layer options.
- Pressure settings can be edited to your preference.
- The Pen nibs and Tone Editor are a pretty nice addition.
- The bucket tool detection sometimes has trouble detecting vertices in very fine line arts.
- 24 levels of stabilization for all the types of lines you’ll need!
Open Canvas is essentially Photoshop but suited more towards free form designs with a graphics tablet, if you already have Photoshop and any other digital art program, there is no need for Open Canvas.

As of now, I still mainly use Paint Tool Sai + Photoshop, but anything that requires perspective or if I’m lazy and can’t be bothered exporting from Sai to Photoshop, Open Canvas is used.

You'll realise how lazy Hercules actually is as his servants repair broken roads, haul stones and wood, cheese, and coins, back to Hercules' base. While it does not offer a true-to-text overview on Hercules, it provides a decent enough story.
+  Achievements easily obtainable
+  Pegasus; what more could you ask for?
+  Tight gameplay: very responsive to your commands
+  All important information is laid out in a neat UI format
+  Offers enough at its small asking price (more on this later)
+  Very generous graphics: for a cheap game, the quality is simply amazing
+  Requires strategy while also remembering the casual nature of the game
+  Levels are doable; you can choose the gameplay difficulty (casual all the way to hard I believe)
+  You can get it at a dirt cheap price: in my case, I bought it at around .99$, but I've seen the price as low as .29$
±  This was my first time management game, so I didn't know what to expect. I couldn't play it all at once and sometimes it felt like it dragged (repetitive nature of the genre)
-  Little to offer in terms of music: quite repetitive but doesn't detract from the game quality itself
With a lot of companies now copying

Tower Unite has been on my watchlist for quite a bit of time and I was checking the updates regularly. After a while, I made a decision to finally purchase the game and I have no regrets. Here is a full review of the game.
You have something to do literally at all times. Doesn't matter whether you want to relax while decorating your condo or test your skills (and nerves) at various reflex/skill based games, TU has it all. I find it hard to turn the game off, as there's always something for me to do.
Graphics is very polished and overall nice to look at, doesn't lag even on older PCs and with the weather settings some sceneries look insanely amazing.
If you love to decorate as much as I do, this game is going to be paradise for you. You can choose out of various housing options, such as huge condo with a beach and piece of the sea, suite which is smaller and cozier option with small garden, house with spacious garden and lots of places to decorate or you could buy just empty lot for you to built it up from the ground and use your imagination. The possibilities are endless. Lots of furniture and even custom items (you can use pictures from the Internet and make items from it).
In this game you're rarely alone. Doesn't matter if you're in plaza, condo or just playing some activities, people will always come and talk. What I really like is the ability to voice chat everywhere, it makes it a bit more personal and fun, ignoring the weird individuals of course.
First in-game casino that's actually not trying to ruin you financially and emotionally. Well except for the wheel of despair, you're hardly ever losing money in the casino. I have found blackjack and grand quest most profitable so far, but it's lazy way of making money, minigames are much more fun.
It's really wonderful how hard the devs work on this game, which is apparent from the amount and frequency of updates, also they let you know what are they working on and what are the plans for certain time periods.
I was surprised on how this game doesn't try to suck your life out just to purchase a few items, everything is pretty much affordable and you don't need to grind on anything in order to earn units for whatever you might need them for.
Walking around plaza you're going to see bunch of unfinished and missing buildings, few of items are having the unfinished tag as well, but you can expect that from early access, yet some people can see it negatively.
Seen too many people to lose themselves to this wheel in particular :( don't fall into this trap, save yourself and your units.
Overall, I think this game is so worth its price, doesn't matter if you play it alone or with friends, it's super fun and social. It's constantly being updated and you won't be able to put it down.

Starbound is a great sandbox/exploration game all about exploring a vast (infinite) procedurally generated universe and finishing missions. Through finishing these missions you discover new things which lead to you progressing in the game and eventually beating it. You can play as six different alien races, or a human as the seventh. You have an upgradeable spaceship custom to your race. You can use said spaceship to navigate to different solar systems, asteroid fields/belts, planets, planet systems, moons, moon systems, a mix of unlandleble gas giant planets and landable solid planets....... and the "Mysterious Gate"....... leading to much of the games plot. One thing about Starbound is that the world definitely does not feel "lonely", as many space games do. There are many sentient intelligent beings all throughhout everywhere you go, some friendly, some not. As a side note, there are also many fun refrences throughout the game. This game is still in mid-ish beta and is not yet released. There is a constanly updated "nightly" build of the game which is a bit glitchy but brings in lots of new content for you to see a window of what Starbound's developer's are doing. On
, there is a frequently updated dev blog. Starbound is a bit expensive at fifteen dollars right now, but is definitley worth it in the end, as it is a very fun game with and it's great to see the game develop over time.

I was gifted this game by a friend, and I had been waiting a while to play it, and finally took the plunge. I don't think I was really aware what was in store for me.
This game, is like many of Telltales other games, whichs plays like a choose your own adventure book on steriods. You are mostly watching a movie, making choices that determine the direction of the narrative, and sometimes clicking or doing a quicktime event. No big surprises there, that part of the game I fully expected. That type of gameplay would turn many people off, and I understand it is not for everyone. I was fine with it, it's a good type of game to set and relax, and watch what could almost be an interactive movie.
That COULD be what it is like, The Walking Dead is not very relaxing though. If you allow yourself to get into the narrative, some of the choices are downright nail-biting. Despite it not being an action horror game, I found myself feeling a deep dread as some of the choices were presented. If you like the tone and subject matter of the comics or tv series, I don't think you'll be disappointed.
I tried to play the game commited to each choice I made, never going back. I'm sad to say I ended up breaking that promise to myself because when I saw the way Clementine reacted to me after one I my choices, I immediately restarted the game and remade the choice. I got so into the story, that I couldn't take her reacting in horror to something I'd decided to do.
There was plenty about this game that drew me in. The art style is heavily inspired by the comics. Normally cell-shading isn't my thing, but it lends itself to this story well. I loved the voice acting, most of the actors made the story that much more griping. The story itself was phenomenal. While I was able to guess some of the twists and turns, I really didn't care. I was still enthrall.
Be advised it is a shorter game. I finished it in less than 14 hours, and that was not a hurried pace. There are plenty of achievements for all you cheevo hunters as well. None of them are skill based, you get one for each chapter of each episode. I don't see much replay value either, unless you were to wait a while and want to experience the story again.
The best way to sum up the game overall was what I told my friend who gifted it to me after I had finished the first episode. "Thank you, and ♥♥♥♥ you all at the same time."

It's another Assassin's Creed game, so you generally know what to expect.  The graphics on this one are great but are very taxing, even for high powered systems.  Expect performance issues unless you are close to top of the line with your graphics card or are willing to turn settings and resolution down.  In terms of gameplay, I'm enjoying it but not as much as AC IV or Rogue.  I miss the sea battles.  They made some improvements to the parkour system but there's also a lot of extra stuff they added to this game that makes it hard for those who play mainly solo.  Fortunately they've removed the need to use the companion app to unlock things.  Overall, this game is a lot more tedious to get all items on, and not quite as fun as some of the entries in the past.  This will probably be the first game since they implemented the sync system that I haven't gone for 100% sync.

Story
You, Dr. Freeman are a theoretical physicist who one day screws up at work and opens a rift to another dimension. Next thing you know you have to crowbar yourself through a facility to find a way to escape or stop the invasion. Yes, this is the plot. Sadly there is not so much lore that you actually get told. Though the plot is very deep, especially towards the ending, you do not know exactly what is going on all the time and just follow your path clueless.
Gameplay
Since Half-life runs on the source engine, you might be familiar with its controls and gameplay. The game is a nice mix between shooting stuff and solving puzzles and trying desperately to find out how to get further. Sometimes this can be extremely frustrating and I once stopped playing it for about 6 months before picking it up again. On the other hand you feel really smart when you do not get stuck for an hour. One small uncomfortable thing is switching weapons, because in order to do that you must klick to confirm your weapon switch.
Graphics
As you already saw in the screenshots above, the game is older and thus does by far not come up with modern graphics, models, animations or other. It will not bother you, but if you are used to modern games with high end graphics you might miss many details.
Bugs
One time a gate did not open, even though it should have. It took me a while until I realised that, but the best way to solve this problem is to simply use the console command noclip and fly through it.
The game is a classic and I recommend you playing it, since his sequels are even better and when half-life 3 comes out one day and you want to play it, why not play the other ones too. Maybe do not buy it for 10€, rather think of buying it in a bundle when it is on sale.

One of my favourite games and possibly the most enjoyable in the point and click adventure genre. Everything has been designed so beautifully (in ways words cannot describe). Its visually stunning, the characters are funny, memorable and loveable and the soundtrack is amazing. The levels/ environments are fluid, organic and interesting (you'll be clicking on everything). You are rewarded with animated collectable character & creature cards for exploring the world and interacting with stuff... and you won't get bored of seeing the same things over and over, as the surroundings change at nearly every screen. The diversity is truly astounding. The pace of the game is good too, meaning you are not stuck at the same screen trying to solve a puzzle for ages, but not moving so quick as to miss the hidden gems and soak in the scenery.
To contrast the beautiful lively 'spring-like' levels, there are also darker and more isolated spaces, which relate to the story. The story is simple yet brilliant, and it is told in an interesting way without even uttering a word. It's one of those games that's fairly challenging at times but without being too frustrating. The puzzles are enjoyable and make me laugh, rather than them feeling like a chore to complete. It certainly makes me smile... and at many points its just so beautiful and amazing, it might just make you all teary eyed with sheer joy.  :)

TL;DR: It's not a game and it's pretty average, but it's free, so why the hell not?
Well, first of all this isn't a game, it's an interactive story. Just like Gone Home and all those other pretentious titles. Except this one doesn't sound like a fanfic written by a 15 years old and isn't trying to make you feel buyer's remorse.
You control a man in a cabin in the middle of a forest who's trying to remember his past. To do so you need to interact with some objects in said cabin. Each time you interact with one of the many objects the protagonist will share his thoughts and memories (all the dialogue is dubbed), refreshing his memory and letting you know more about his past and personality.
Both the narrative and the POV in the story are in first person. You walk around and interact with objects by clicking on them, making it feels a little like a point & click game.
The graphics and sound effects are good enough to hold your attention and let you immerse yourself into the story.
And by the way, the atmosphere slowly changes as you listen to the plot. At first it feels like a sad romance tale and it slowly goes towards a more gloomy atmosphere.
There's a plot twist and stuff, but nothing worth mentioning.
I'd give it a negative rating, since it's so short (about 45 minutes) and it's an interactive story being sold as a game.
But it's free! So... yeah. Even though it's so average, go for it.
