I've been trying to decide how to best review this game for newcomers.  I've finally decided with the following.
FOF8 is my first version of this franchise.  I'm a long time gamer, programmer, sports simulation enthusiast, etc.
The Good:
FOF8 is a pretty darn good game.  It gives you some flexibility in building a team, and managing it.  There's some opportunity to call plays, as well, which can add a layer of depth to the game for some.  The bulk of the game, though, is dealing with your roster and improving your team.
Overall, it's what most people want from a sports sim that does not have a graphical component--it's a number-crunching engine, and produces reasonable statistics, for the most part.  The hardest part is managing your salary cap.  The second hardest is managing your injuries.  I found the injuries to be a little to frequent with the default setting, and dialed them back each year until I got to something I thought was about normal.
The Bad:
Many of these are tiny issues.  There's very little "flash" or "pop" to the presentation of the game.  It's very similar to looking at a bunch of spreadsheets.  Some of the "cool factors" that are added (Green Sheet, Grey Sheet, Scouting Report, etc.) don't feel like they add as much flavor as they could.  Some features aren't properly documented, and some things that feel like they should be no brainers aren't in there
Perhaps my biggest beef with the game comes when I'm calling plays.  First, I don't sense much effect with regards to calling plays.  I can call for a deep route on 3rd and 20, or on 2nd and 1, and it feels like defenses cover it the same.
Also, it feels as though virtually every 3rd down play is successful.  I had a spell of 8 games where my (undefeated) team only stopped opponents on 8% of their 3rd down attempts.  It didn't matter if it was 3rd and 4, or 3rd and 25, the opponent almost always got 4 yards more than they needed.  Even after drastically improving my defense, this continued (although, the opponents success rate did fall toward, but not into, more normal ranges).  In short, I have the league leading defense in yards per play, yards per run, and yards per pass, but I can't stop a 3rd down, almost ever.
I gave up play-calling for that reason.  I strictly manage the team and the rosters now.
One other little thing--12 year veteran lineman will try to get you to sign them to 4 year multi-million dollar deals pretty regularly.  I don't know how realistic that is.
Finally, if you are in playcalling mode, there's no way to change your personnel packages.  You can't sit your awesome QB in the 4th quarter of a late season game to keep him healthy for the playoffs.  Packages are set from game to game, and I have yet to see a backup get playing time, outside of pre-season.  That makes it pretty hard to nurture your up-and-coming first round QB pick.
Otherwise:
The game is fun, if not perfect.  There does seem to be tendencies for players to resign with you when they have high loyalty, for example.  Most players want unservicable salaries after a couple of years, and you end up with decisions to make.  Every once in a while you'll find a veteran that's willing to renegotiate to lower your current cap problems, so you can bring in someone new.  Even superstars are hard to trade if they have a big contract.
The game doesn't really tell you what you're doing wrong.  It will tell you what positions you need help at, but it's not specific at all.  I had a situation where I had what I thought were good D-linemen, but I was getting killed in the running game.  It would be nice if the assistant coach might say, "we need some run-stopper linebackers," or something to help me figure out, "oh, I'm getting owned in the gaps."
I hope this was helpful, and I hope you enjoy the game!

This is by far the most immersive American Football simulator on any market.  You can take over an existing team, start with a fantasy draft, start with fictional players, or even simulate up to 50 seasons to create a history.  The all-new play designing system allows to you to be as in-depth or as hands-off as you'd like to be.  Whether you decide to call plays in a game, just simulate them, or just watch the plays unfold, FOF8 brings gridiron football through text properly.  There are many good things about this game, and just enough changed from FOF7 to the new version to make it worth an immediate purchase.
However, this game lacks any type of in-game editing, so if you are looking for a sandbox experience, this is not the product that offers it.  Always 32 teams, always 2 conferences with 4 divisions, always 6 playoff teams from each conference, and no in-game player editor to be found.  You can edit players previous to starting the game by editing files, but there is no quick and easy way to do so.
That being said, this game will provide many, many hours of true football fun to anyone who wants it, and is definitely worth its price tag at sub 30 dollars.

Other reviews have gone over what's good with the game and I concur with those reviews.
Here's why I ultimately can't recommend it.  Let's talk rosters. Each player is graded on a scale from 1 to 9, with 1 being a scrub, and 9 being a rare Superstar.  So the game ranks all the players, but their individual attributes are NOT ranked, only their overall skill.  Example: If Todd Gurley has a grade of 7 the game will randomly determine his individual attributes based on that 7.  We know that Gurley is a bruiser with average speed.  When you start your league, however, the game may look at that 7 and determine that Gurley's actually got 9 out of 9 speed and 4 out of 9 tackle breaking ability. It's completely random every time you start a new league.
You can manually override this randomisation and assign the attributes you desire (at least in single player mode), but there's no in-game option to do so, you first have to export a player.csv file and then edit a spreadsheet using Excel and then import your newly edited file into the game. To make matters worse, the spread sheet is highly abbreviated forcing you to consult a legend frequently to make edits.
Additionally, many of the game's overall grades for players seemed way off.  Example: Aaron Rodgers was a 5 out of 9 while Brady was an 8 out of 9.  Vic Beasley, who just led the league in sacks, was a 2 out of 9.  I tried a fantasy draft and it had Carlos Dunlap as the best overall player in the league while some of the elite players like JJ Watt were average at best.  And this is all due to the randomization.
The rookie draft was also odd.  There's not a way to scout players manually.  Instead, your coaching staff's "Scouting Ability" attribute determines the accuracy of the grades that the potential draftees get.  There's no other way to ensure you're drafting good players that I could see.
The UI is another negative.   It's drab and unintuitive.  Small font and abbreviations for nearly everything make it a chore to navigate.  I also never found an easy solution to organizing the depth chart or making substitutions.  I'm sure the feature exists somewhere, but I was nearing the 2 hour mark of the game I didn't want to go over my time limit so that I could ensure the refund.
Hate giving this a thumbs down, as there's nothing else like it out there, but it needs massive changes to it's logic with rosters and UI to be enjoyable.

I really guess it wasn't an easy decission for wargaming, but by targeting multiplayer for final challenge, there simply wasn't any other choice. Just think about a single battle lasting 20min while 4-6 other players just sit and watch empty screen...then you'd more likely accept RT battle system. Well, if they deliver a turn-based system exclusively for singleplayer later, it would be perfect.
Game is well made, no greater bugs or broken mechanics so far. It is still Early Access, which means, game and content will certainly undertake massive changes till release. As for my personal rating, it is ok. It is fun to play and explore the game, while I rate 45€ for an EA quite ambitious. ^^
If you could get it on sale or could grab you a key from other store price should be more balanced. Something near half the current price I'd give it a go.
Only thing I recognized to be a bit disturbing so far is steady ship-design upgrade after researching new tech. Quite nice automation, but that might switch your personal designs deeply, so be prepared to re-visit ship designer every now and then for control.
Still not found all tech, but looking forward to get lot of fun till I reach my goal.
**EA2 patch**
New update brought 2+1 new empires. Klackons, Mekklars and another human (Terran) for early access buyers. Also you could design your very own custom version of given empires.
Research is a bit delayed now, which is great as it was too easy to get through the whole research plan on the run. Single technical steps do get more weight and enhances gameplay.
Some slight changes in options allows more customization...like starting battles on pause and else. AI seems to be enhanced...not yet tried on hard mode...looking forward.
Best thing is plenty of written localizations, so everybody could play game in his favorite language. Advisors speaking still in english or russion of course.
All in all stable and fun. Still early access, but all things point in promising direction.

Definitely one of the best Strategy games ever made, and a true sucessor to the original X-Com. Aside from a few stability issues, there's nothing that's not fantastic about this game. Meaningful decision making, nail-biting combat, a polished tactical system both robust and approachable, the recover-research-build technology that defines XCOM, all these come together to give the game a well deserved thumbs up from this long time fan.
And that's just the base game. The workshop content from XCOM 2 is nothing short of delightful: Everything from cosmetics, to gameplay tweaks, even new classes are availible. Want to play with Commander Shepard or Doomguy on your team? There's a mod for that. Don't like how the mission timers hurry you along in the missions? Mod for that. Need more classes to expand your tactical choices? Mod. Want new maps? You get the idea.
Long War 2 (a total hardcore conversion mod) takes the cake however, allowing a familiar game to feel like a whole new experience with new mechanics, new classes, a much longer campaign, new research, everything a hardcore fan would enjoy. It was The Long War mod from XCOM: Enemy Within that convinced the designers of XCOM 2 to put in the workshop, and it payed off.
Like I said, a few stability and optimization issues with the game, but with Steam's return policy, you can safely return the game if your compy doesn't like it. Knowing that, I don't see any reason not to give this game a try. Prior experience with the series or the gerne not required.
So what are you waiting for Commander? Humanity needs you!

Having played most of the Assassin's Creed products I have to say this was quite a let down.  If you loved AC2 and AC:BF then this game will be a complete disappointment to you.
Liked:
-Didn’t have odd flash forwards to present, instead incorporated more of a link to how you were tactically using hacked servers
-Money seemed much thinner and felt like you had to be very resource cautious when leveling
Disliked:
-Skill Unlock system seemed un-needed. I would have rather had an attribute system that made up for the health/damage buff to allow you to specialize your character more for combat/stealth
-Some mission checkpoints required skills you might not have unlocked
Hated:
-Combat system revamp, probobaly one of the most frustrating things about this AC compared to the almost perfect(perhaps a bit easy) combat system of the others. I understand the need to make it slightly more difficult, however I think they made to strong of an adjustment.
-Enemies can be off screen(and often are) and can charge and execute fully powered attacks
-Enemies often use pistols in combat(which adds realism for sure), but the seem to not have friendly fire. They can and    will often shoot through crowds, comrades without issue to hit you.
-There is no story based explanation to how to dodge bullets or unparry-able attacks.
-You seem woefully underpowered with the lack of abilities to break parries(AKA Sand attack)
-Story was utterly boring. Period. I mean how can you be in the most crazy, brilliant, excellent era for an AC game and it ended being utterly disappointed.  Our character seemed to basically float alongside the events rather than be a part of them, having no utter impact on the world/timeline around him.
Overall, its seems like a very bland AC game...like a box of cereral thats "Cereal" Brand and "Cereal" flavor.
Get it on sale if you want to play it.

You've spent years assembling a competitive football franchise, and you've finally seen the success you have anticipated. It's the Superbowl, and you're down 35-28 with two minutes left. Your franchise QB (dare I say future Hall of Famer?) leads a decisive two minute drill to tie the game at 35-35, and for the first time ever the Superbowl goes into overtime. You receive the kick and once again drive down the field, but you are stopped near the opponent's 40 yard line. It's fourth down and 1 yard to go, and it's too far to kick a reliable field goal. You could punt the ball away, but your defense has been exposed today, and you doubt that they can hold. You could go for the first down, but if you fail you'll give your opponent's high-flying offense the ball back with a chance to win the game in excellent field position. Weighing your options, you finally decide to try and go for the first down. You line up in a power run formation, with your opponent in a goal line formation, and you run the ball straight up the gut of the defense. Your RB takes the handoff -- and is stuffed by the opponent's defense.
You turn the ball over on downs and the opponents march down the field and score the game-ending field goal.
Only then do you realize the sheer effort required to create a championship franchise, and only then do you realize you could lose it all in overtime of the biggest game of the year. There are no medals for valor, and no trophies for second place.
But hey -- at least your franchise left tackle is signed to a team-friendly deal for the next five years. Surely if we've made the Superbowl once we can make it again?

This game is VERY close to being a 'thumbs up', but once you discover what I discovered you'll never want to play the game again which will take you about 18 hours of gameplay to realize.  A complete waste of money.  I played about 10 seasons until I concluded that the stats and results don't matchup with the player and team attributes.  Basically, the engine that simulates game results is severely flawed.  Poorly rated teams and poorly rated players are generating positive results far higher than they should be.  For example, my pathetic team with a rookie QB with a skill rating of 12 (100 being the max) gave my team the best record in the NFL with 11wins/5 losses while the same team with a better QB (35 of 100) just 1 season earlier put me at 5wins/11 losses.  I saw pathetically rated LBs racking up loads of sacks, it just wasn't realistic.  It can simulate an entire season for all teams in less than a minute which means it's NOT using a very complex and detailed algorithm to generate the results.  This is why I'm giving it a thumbs down.  Oh, and the default playbook loves to run the ball on 2nd and longs (ridiculous and a sign of developer incompetence).  You can change the game plan and playbook based on the situation (although quite complex to do), but the broken simulation engine is what ruins the entire thing.

TLDR first - in 12 Labours of Hercules, there's a very thin line between a very challenging and interesting game and utter boredom and aimlessness. This line is choosing your difficulty and challenges wisely.
12LoH is a time management game, where you collect a few types of resources (basically food, wood and gold), and with this, construct structures, enlist the help of mythical creatures and solve specific objectives. Presentation is flawless, as it looks pleasing to the eye, the sound and music are decent, and the controls are simple and intuitive. Level design is either superb or totally irrelevant - see difficulty again.
So why the duality? In a game like this, challenges can come from two sources: figuring out how to solve the levels, and solving the levels within a limited amount of time. 12LoH simply omits the first - most levels can be solved by arbitrary clicking on the screen, it's not easy to create a situation where you can't go on. As there's no challenge, walking through the game easily loses its appeal after 3 or 4 levels. So it's up to the time constraints to make the game interesting - however, you automatically get bronze for walking through. For silver, you need to finish within the par time. This is also very easy - even on expert difficulty, you'll either do it on first try, or, if you walk into a couple of traps, you'll avoid them on the second playthrough and easily get the silver medal. No challenge here, either.
What about gold? Every level has a gold time constraint, and if you're going for that, the game suddenly comes alive! All of a sudden, you need to appraise the level's paths, judge resource requirements for the final outcome, and continuously forecast a few steps ahead to make sure your people keep moving. If they don't, then bye-bye gold medal. With the gold constraint, the levels are very good and often quite wicked. With the gold constraint, the game offers a lot of challenge. With the gold constraint, it's very much recommended, as it's tremendous fun.

Front Office Football has been on my desktop since the very first version. But, I am not a fan boy. Nothing of it's kind has ever come across my path to supplant it. Those that give it the investment of time, will surely find a rich environment that gives a complete experience of NFL team management.
While others can go into specifics and mechanics, and they are both in depth, and challenging, I will just relay that the experience takes you from the micro enjoyment of getting that player in the draft you wanted, or nabbing that under valued free agent who is your missing piece to greatness, to the macro of matching your stats against the greats and seeing years roll by as you create a dynasty, or fall by the wayside.
Push button fanatics, will not like this game, and those without the patience to learn it's rhythm really shortchange themselves. But those in the middle, won't be let down. The game allows quick simming most areas, and the seasons can be as short or as long as you wish. Find that sweet spot you enjoy, and it will be there waiting.
For instance, I wanted to learn the salary cap, and how to really apply it to real world examples. This game has been the best instructor than any college could provide.
Even after 17 plus years of playing this, I still get surprises and enjoyment. It has never left my desktop, and I can say that about no other game.

Not sure why I waited so long to review this game, but as I'm nearing 1000 hours I knew it was time.
I barley hit 50 hours on most games so that in itself should tell you how much I like this game.
Top notch visuals and fun action sit on top of great mechanics and deep strategy.  Bit of a learning curve getting into it but its so rewarding and loads of fun if you stick with it for awhile. A few matchmaker issues due to low-ish playerbase are probably it's only negative.
Its true F2P, everything is earnable with in-game credits and you have plenty of opportunity to earn them (or you can buy outright if you're impatient/want to support game). With all the ship unlocks and RNG drop pod rewards the game appears to be a F2P P2W but it really isn't - the ships are all really well balanced and fit different roles so no ship is "better" than another.
I think the most appealing aspect is probably the potential you can see in this game - it's so fun and well polished that I can see lots of fun down the line if the devs experiment with more game modes and ships.

The game is definitely a good looking remake of Master of Orion 2. The graphics and sound are excellent. The details are very nice. The game is already very polished at the moment.
The issues of the current version as I see them are
1. Star lanes
Systems are connected by star lanes and you must travel through them between systems (unless you have built jump gates). In my first game I got coined in by AI blocking exactly 2 spots in the universe with a starbase. I could not go further unless I attacked him or sorted it out diplomacally accepting his ridiculous price. Well... it's supposed to be the 3D space modeled as 2D space...and it has been made a 1D space in fact. Why? The defense strategy is just to defend a few frontier points which does not require much of strategy really...
2. System travel points
In a system, besides the travel points that are one end of a star lane, the ships can stay at each planet... when travelling from a system, they need to go to the travel points on the "edge" of the system...and then continue by the connected star lane...So basically in a system, they do not travel at full
That is one more feature of the freeness of space movement that is somehow diminished in the game...
3. Battles
You can simulate a battle, that's fine. You can enter a 3D battle and ...well, watch it. There are some controls but you cannot really influence the battle much, or, have a feeling that you actually do something. I need to compare this to MoO2 now since there you saw how your ship designs perform. You could control every aspect of the battle and thus took care when designing ships. At this moment, the battle in Master of Orion (4) is just as bad as in MoO3...
4. Minor issues
There are some minor issues that will hopefully get fixed. For instance, the UI of the ship design part needs a bit of work: once you have many components, the large icons are not very clear. There is a feature of MoO2 that has been copied: all troop transports get eaten when you invade a planet: I should be able to choose how many marines I want to invade the planet and after the battle how many of them should stay boarded to ships. (The ships of dead or garissoned marines will still be eaten .... )
Once more, I know the game is in early access and might change. And hopefully it will change and be the best MoO2 successor.

Downside, like any Random Number Generation(RNG) based hit system, the severe lack of true randomness, makes the player suffer absurd statistical anomalies...far too frequently.
For example:

Easy way around that in games like this is just save and retry until you succeed, since there is no F$%#ing way I am missing 95% shots.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of my favorite games of all time. It was difficult but amazing.
XCOM 2 is something else entirely. I'll just lay out a couple of the cons:
-It starts with Timers. Everything is timed, so your success is based on the luck of your team. Did they just miss a guy a couple tiles away who had no cover (because I blew it up) and over a 90% hit chance? Yes. Does this happen regularly? Yes.
-You are not rewarded for sneaking up on the enemy. When you spot them, they almost always notice despite you being behind cover, and every enemy gets a free move. Suddenly, you don't have the drop on them anymore.
These are the main two reasons I can't recommend this game. A mod will fix Timers, but unless someone has one that removes the free turn from an enemy when you spot them, this game isn't worth it.

This game is fun, polished and challenging, but I find it impossible to shake the feeling of being rushed through the campaign by the avatar project and for that reason I cannot recommend it. As a strategy game with many facets and mechanics to explore, you'd think there would be time to play around and experiment while still enjoying a challenge; but on the higher difficulties, unless you're doing everything flawlessly right off the hop, you are punished by cumulative enemy buffs and the game over timer (which can only be slowed, not stopped). There are likely many veteran commanders out there who enjoy the the thrill of trying to stay a step ahead of the aliens, but as someone who likes to build a narrative over the course of a campaign, and enjoys seeing long terms effects of my decisions, I'm frustrated with how rushed everything feels.
TLDR: you will like this game if you like trying to meet quickly approaching deadlines with success heavily dependant on RNG.

AC Unity is an embarrassment - even after all this time. And it could have been so good! That's what really hurts... the fact that - under all this steaming CRAP - you get the sense of a feeling that you SHOULD be enjoying this. But all you'll have (usually starting about halfway through) is this overwhelming sensation of WHEN THE ♥♥♥♥ WILL THIS BE OVER?!?!?!
Let's start with the story - it's your usual Batman story with a French twist. The only real difference being that instead of YOUR character being obsessed with vengeance... it's this mouthy French tart who you CONSTANTLY have to save - much to her objection because she doesn't NEED to be saved. She's a Goddamn Templar, ♥♥♥♥♥! Your character's sole defining trait is that he WANTS to get in her pants because his carelessness cost her someone she loved. That's it. Apart from one very cute scene involving a mongolfiere; there is NEVER any REAL reciprication of this love because the Goddamn Templar ♥♥♥♥♥ is too busy seeking vengeance. Enter the supporting cast - the Templars and Assassins in this story have NO RIGHT to call themselves Templars and Assassins. What should have been a FASCINATING premise (the french revolution has led to the two factions calling for a cease-fire) is chucked out the window the minute the Templar leadership goes into a shakeup. Further, not only are the rest of the Assassin's upset (shall we say) at the current enforcement of the status quo; but they then proceed to have their own 'shakeup' when one of the Assassin leaders goes rogue and almost wipes everyone out! Best of all - when your character STOPS Mr. Crazy-Assassin from slaughtering everyone; he's PUNISHED! Turns out that the rest of the leaders who survived Crazy-Assassin don't LIKE your character - further; this isn't even RESOLVED in the story! I'm serious! By the end of the story we're just left to ASSUME our character get's back together with his true love (re: the crazy-as-♥♥♥♥ top secret murder cult) because... he's... supposed to. And if that isn't enough for you - in the DLC story - one little weird dream and a few trips underground with a mouthy♥♥♥♥♥brat and your character decides he's not only going to go on being an assassin - oh no! He's going to be the Hero France needs! The whole arc is INSANELY cringe-worthy -  and leaves you finishing the game just to say you finished it.
Then we come to the combat - yeah; it's still AC combat. But it's been given a... fun? Twist... EVERYONE has a gun. No, I'm not kidding, EVERYONE has a gun. The guy in the street has a gun. The guy you've been sent to kill has a gun. That woman with thirty petticoats has a gun. That guy who just got his head chopped off - YES! Even HE has a gun. So what's the obvious solution? Smoke bombs... so many smoke bombs. I want to get my hands on the guy who thought that making smoke bombs practically required would 'shake up' traditional AC combat. Further, we have new weapons - you want to slowly swing an axe and realize that you can be countered by everyone with a sword? You can do that. You want to stab with a spear and find out your smoke bombs are nearly useless because you then have to close the gap between you and your target? You can do that too! Best of all, thanks to the FreeLC Dead Kings - you get a mortar axe! A huge♥♥♥♥♥gun... with an axe-head on it. AC Rogue introduced a neat psuedo-historical weapon called the Air Rifle that could be fitted with a tank that would launch grenades. ACU gives us a gun with an axe-head on it that is not only NOT psuedo-historical; it's also stupid looking and ranges from near-useless to death-wish to overpowered-if-used-in-the-right-situation.
Want to talk about crafting? There is no crafting. Everything is done through skills and leveling up. As if the grind-fest that ACU is known for wasn't already bad enough - they make it EXTRA FUN by adding in MORE grinding. Grinding that can be side-stepped for only a few dollars... or a♥♥♥♥♥♥TON of hours for the same price.
Want to talk about ship combat? There is no ship-combat. There are no ships. For old-school AC fans this is no big loss - for the rest of us there's the earlier games to play for ship combat. Their lack of presence, however, should be filled with something equally enjoyable. AC Rogue, and a few other AC games, had bases you could clear out which would net you regenerating profits. ACU tries to follow that premise in the form of 'clubs'. Of couse, you'd automatically assume, that you clear these clubs out from evil people and then take them over. No. You buy the land they're sitting on and you own them. You're fighting against the Templars and the instutitions they stand for... by making your own institution. Then, once you've done your taxes (AC taxes just doesn't sound as cool as AC pirates, sorry) you get these clubs. You know what you do in them or with them then? Nothing. You can hang out with the npcs on the ground floor - but they don't migrate to the upper floors. So your left with these three-quarter empty buildings that serve no purpose but to generate a TINY profit for you. I think that ♥♥♥♥ing butler is skimming my books, personally. Best of all, the main club-hub, your club-hub (and basically the French version of Wayne Manor) has MORE stuff you can unlock. MORE nearly worthless quests you can unlock... by paying MORE money. Not through combat or through the story or through crafting or any OTHER method to unlock... but through money. Are you starting to notice a theme here?
As I mentioned before, with the removal of sea combat, there should be something to fill the gap. Further, there should be a REASON this game is called Unity (France is tearing itself apart. The Templars are tearing themselves apart. The Assassins are tearing themselves apart. French Batman and the Goddamn Templar ♥♥♥♥♥ are tearing themselves apart - Unity? Where?!) Ubisoft(in the head) decided that the way to fill that gap was through clubs AND (wait for it kids) inworld multiplayer. Great. Combining the MMO playerbase and the AC playerbase - two of the MOST vitriolic and ♥♥♥♥♥y fanbases in the whole of the gaming community (I reckon the only way they could have made a WORSE choice would have been trying to find a way to throw the FPS fans in there) and you've lumped them together in one game through content that unlocks some of the best armor. Some of the best weapons. Some of the best costumes - and guess what! If you want to get all that stuff WITHOUT playing the same mission over and over? You HAVE to group!!! Unless you want to play the same mission three or four times - you HAVE to group. Because, if you don't, the missions are set up to fail your♥♥♥♥♥in some way or another that keeps you from getting the maximum rewards. So, instead of playing with three or four players, you're playing FOR three or four players.
This brings me to the BIGGEST problem with this game. Do you like to be about half-way done with a mission and then start over? Do you like to fall through the worldspace? Do you like a mission objective simply not starting? Do you like NPC's not spawning? Do you like getting stuck at the loading-saving-loading-saving-loading-saving screen? Do you like being forced to group with people only to have the mission glitch out or your partner(s) getting kicked for no reason? If so - this is the game for you. I think Honest Trailers said it best when they dubbed this game 'Assassin's Creed: We'll Fix it Later' because (even after TWO YEARS) there are STILL game-breaking bugs in this game. And a special mention should go to the Dead Kings FLC for the most 'drop-to-desktop' crashes. Stuff that should have been fixed pre-launch (if not post-launch) and is STILL a problem is STILL present in something that was sold as a triple-A title. Seriously, for your mental health, unless your are a sadist or a die-hard fan avoid this game. Go play AC3 - it's a rough gem... but at least it can shine. This 'thing' is a turd. Pure and simple.

The purpose of this review is to go over the free to play model that the game Fractured Space uses. As for the game itself, Fractured Space is a well balanced team based multiplayer game with the main attraction being the variety of large space ships that you can pilot.
Fractured Space uses a free to play model which lets you play the game starting with access only to a few starter ships. To unlock more ships, you need to earn in game credits or pay money for a special currency called platinum. Credits can be earned upon completing matches and from completing missions. On average, completing a match will get you ~10,000 credits or more. Missions are side objectives listed in the hangar such as "get 24 takedowns" or "capture 15 mines". Completing missions will typically get you a drop pod, which can contain extra credits, platinum, and other useful items.
Ship costs vary from about a half million credits to about one and a half million credits. If you want to unlock ships without paing for anthing, you will need to play quite a few matches. Since the average match time is about 30 minutes, that translates into a lot of playtime.
Personally I would recommend buying the "Fleet Pack". It is normally priced at 50.00 USD, and usually go on sale for 25.00 during major Steam sales. The Fleet Pack gives you access to a staggering 34 different ships to try out. This means you can spend more time playing as ships with playstyles you like instead of feeling like you got stuck with something terrible that you need to use for another 40 matches before you can test out another ship. And while you try out new ships, you will be able to spend your credits on different weapon types and crew members to personalize your ships.
There is only one thing that I have seen in Fractured Space that you cannot get by using credits: ship skins. Otherwise, you can use credits to purchase what you want.
Fractured Space is not pay to win. Fractured Space is pay to avoid grinding, and I would recommend avoiding grinding.

Ok, so I am now in 90'ish hours, having now played all races through to victory in all available victory conditions, so here are some initial thoughts - in generalised rather than specific form.
Yes, I recommend the game; that doesn't mean I don't think the game is currently without its issues, but it is early access and I expect that there will be continuing support by the devs for what is a high profile franchise (I note they have already patched in some content to reflect early player feedback).
So it's MOO. For those who have played the MOO franchise (let's ignore MOO3), yes they have managed to imbue the game with some of the same kitschiness that its predecessors had.
The races offered with the initial release are humorous enough and offer some amusing gameplay via quality voice acting, and more races are to come.
The UI is largely functional, operable, logical and without much in the way of glitches. That might not sound like a ringing endorsement, but the fact it enables you to get on and play the game without really noticing its there, is a positive for me - it means nothing is wrong (the same can't be said for all 4x games).
The battle intro cutscenes are some of the best I've seen in any game, and seriously I want to get into battles just to see and hear my ships warp into the combat zone. These are some of the only cutscenes in any game that I don't want to Esc through after the first few times. Similarly, most of the graphical/audio content in the game is polished and of a high level. The ships are decently rendered and you have a choice between two models/designs for each race-based ship (as well as three basic ship artwork choices), which is a nice bonus.
The game hasn't paused, slowed, glitched, locked-up or crashed on me once. When you're in late-game, turn cycle calcs take the game a few seconds longer, but that's about it.
It's enjoyable to play, and has a lot of promise.
I am still enjoying the game and will wait to see how things develop.
Cheers

Good and simple mechanics, balanced yet challenging difficulty, decent length… this is what anyone would want from an indie title. It is a bit interesting to see no plot from something based on mythology, but ‘12 Labours of Hercules’ is still a good game for its genre.
12 Labours of Hercules is the first instalment in a fairly successful line of time management games that are supposed to be based on the mythical jobs of Heracles, the famous Hellenic hero. I say “supposed to”, because none of the games have actual stories, the myth is used as a visual theme only.
The mechanics are fairly simple: you gather three types of resources with your servants in order to remove a set of obstacles. When the road clears, you gather more resources, ad infinitum, until you finally reach the end of the path. For some added variety, sometimes you need the help of Hercules himself or one of his mythological buddies.
As for most time management games, the difficulty balances on a very narrow ledge. It is rather easy to pass a level within the basic time limit, but reaching the more constrained goal can be– pardon the pun– a Herculean task. Be ready to constantly retry several levels until you learn the only working sequence. On the plus side, this easily boosts an average play time of 2-3 hours into well over 6-8 hours.

12 Labours of Hercules is a nice, not quite short sort of puzzle game. It has good cartoony graphics and comes with two difficulty levels, Relaxed and Expert, each adequately describing the associated game experience.
In theory the player is supposed to min-max their actions, resource use and resource acquisition, in each level to beat the simple time limit or even beat the level within gold time.
As far as I can see, the two difficulties differ in exactly only how fast the timer runs out. While Relaxed is pretty forgiving and gold time is in reach even after a massively bad decision, Expert requires the player to know what they are doing, otherwise they usually won't make gold time.
+ Ok music
+ Good cartoony graphics
+ Clear design
0 Relatively short
0 Easy "puzzles"
0 All achievements can be gained in Relaxed mode.
- Levels have to be learned
Basically you enter each level and the game waits for your first click before it starts the timer. So the player is supposed to plan out the level without pressure, then execute the plan. Although some information is available at that point, e.g. resource consumption and production at interaction points, some necessary information is missing. Interaction points are on a path or to its side, and correspondingly an obstacle or not. Just by looking at the level layout I cannot always tell which is which. Once you click something that is not directly available the game indicates the first obstacle on the presumably shortest path to whatever you clicked. I'd rather know the last obstacle on each path to the object. Also, as I mentioned, this kind of information is only available once you click an interaction point/object thus starting the timer. Finally, a few interaction points can be upgraded. For those you simply have to learn cost development. Altogether that means, you can not really plan out a level.
Despite that incomplete strategy mechanism 12 Labours of Hercules provides a few hours of okay entertainment.

Like so many others, I still regard Master of Orion II the epitome of galactic 4X games.  I was surprised to see this update materialize unheralded, and intrigued enough to purchase an Early Access game for the first time.  Watching the videos, one has to commend the studio on its selection of actors who give life to the various faction leaders.  "Worf" (Mr. Dorn) is back!  The animated characterizations of the leaders are a treat to behold, a huge step up from the caricatures of the original.  There is a subtle humour in the exchanges, as well as with the GNN commentators and news stream.  Granted, the variety is limited, but if the game continues to be developed, I hope dialogue and events will be increased.  This IS an early release, and the development team focused, sensibly, on getting the main mechanics right.  This game plays true to the original, except as already noted in other reviews, with warp lanes/points.  The technology tree has been streamlined, ship building is refreshingly easy and enjoyable.  Colony development will be familiar but with a few new twists.  Effort was made to make the star map attractive.  While not 3D, it is perfectly fine and gives the illusion of depth.  Ship models are distinct and detailed.  Battle animations are well done, basically a video to watch, but one cannot help admire the fighters, missiles and torpedoes streaking towards their target from your battleships and Titans.  Does it, as some have mentioned, get a bit repetitive?  Yes, but then so did the original.  This just looks far better.  For an early release game, I am impressed (and surprised) that it plays so well.  It is better than several supposedly "finished" games we could all name.  After two playthroughs, I had no crashes, glitches or lockups.  My hope is that the developer will continue to refine, expand and add to this game.  There are four more races that are suggested.  As well, at this time, there are only two map selections.  Steam offered a package which included the new update along with all three of the old series.  I already had them.  I don't regret the purchase. All in all, I appreciate the love that went into this update/remake of a cherished classic.  Kudos!!!

Following the very grounded release of Machinarium, Botanicula seems much closer to Amantia Design's beginnings. Machinarium was a much more somber view of a machine's wasteland, it also used more traditional means of gameply (solve everything to continue, whether through traditiona puzzles or point and click cleverness). Botanicula is a much more vibrant world and takes a different approach to its gameplay. Though there are plenty of puzzles that can be solved without too much headscratching, there are also little secrets and optional creatures to encounter.
Botanicula is both a beautiful and strange world. Though some objects and settings are recognizable (such as a tree, seed, insects) everything is so alive and full of wonder. One of the more polished turn based shooters(more so than it's predecessor). Fun, great graphics, great gameplay.
Downside, like any Random Number Generation(RNG) based hit system, the severe lack of true randomness, makes the player suffer absurd statistical anomalies...far too frequently.
For example:
You line up a shot with an insanely high hit chance (anything over 85%) and you miss. twice, three times...0.34% chance of that happening, and it happens a lot. Unfortunatly it is a symptom of all luck/RNG based games, no programmer has figured out a reasonable system that doesn't use terrible RNG like drand48()
Easy way around that in games like this is just save and retry until you succeed, since there is no F$%#ing way I am missing 95% shots.
Still full of bugs onfortunatly. Soldier getting stuck. Camera getting locked, or bugging out. Too much lag when there is lots of clutter/fires/debris/corpses, I should be getting 0 lag with my system(32Gb RAM, and 8Gb GPU, i7 4.00GHz x8...etc) and in the last level it was bad.
Buy on sale, and you will get a solid game.

What can I say about starbound. Lets start with what I like to call PC, or Penguin Content. The icon is a penguin, the loading screen features a waddling penguin, so I figured, this is a game filled with penguins. But out of the multiple races you can choose from, each with their own pros and cons, there are no penguins. So I figure, they've gotta be coming later right? I progress through the amazingly biomed worlds, everything from dense forests to deep, dark tar pits collecting everything I can get my grubby little hands on (and almost running out of my copious inventory space more than once) and yet.... still no penguins.

One.
ONE.
This game is severely lacking in a fundamental component of gameplay.
Who cares that there are multiple worlds to discover, each different than the one before it in terms of graphics. Who cares that you can farm and craft more things than I've been able to find so far. As someone who loves penguins, this game was a real bait and switch man.

Terraria and minecraft come close, though neither involves such intricate yet simplistic lands, crafting and ease of controls. Those two games are also severely lacking in penguins as well.
I reccomend giving this game a shot. Who knows, maybe more penguins are forthcoming?

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of my favorite games of all time. It was difficult but amazing.
XCOM 2 is something else entirely. I'll just lay out a couple of the cons:
-It starts with Timers. Everything is timed, so your success is based on the luck of your team. Did they just miss a guy a couple tiles away who had no cover (because I blew it up) and over a 90% hit chance? Yes. Does this happen regularly? Yes.
-You are not rewarded for sneaking up on the enemy. When you spot them, they almost always notice despite you being behind cover, and every enemy gets a free move. Suddenly, you don't have the drop on them anymore.
These are the main two reasons I can't recommend this game. A mod will fix Timers, but unless someone has one that removes the free turn from an enemy when you spot them, this game isn't worth it.

Apparently the dev is working toward multiplayer, and I can't wait!  The plan seems to be for one player to own the farm and a handful of others to be able to work as farmhands, including being able to woo and marry their own picks from the town folk.
The game itself is a labor of love, one man's quest to capture the spirit of the Harvest Moon franchise with simple, delightful graphics, a quaint and calming atmosphere, and an incredible variety of activities you can choose from as you improve your farm and get to know the people in town.  Whether you plan to grow crops, raise livestock, go fishing, gather wild plants, or descend into the mine to pick up minerals while tackling monsters, you can enjoy the game your way.  About the only thing I can think of that isn't currently in the game is being able to work directly for someone in town (I always did like the grapes-picking days in Harvest Moon: Back to Nature).
Where Harvest Moon had the little sprites, Stardew Valley has its own sense of mysticism: tiny forest spirits who slowly warm up to your presence and give you gifts.  There's also a wizard, and I've heard about a witch but haven't played far enough into the game to encounter her.  Unlike the first Harvest Moon and Back to Nature, there isn't a church, but some of the villagers meet in the general store owner's main room for a gym class, which is kinda neat.
None of the characters that I've interacted with have been simple or predictable; I think they're quite well written.  And there's a wide variety of marriage candidates, of both genders.  Unlike the original Harvest Moon, the married characters still have some individuality and will still actually do things; I never did like the "marriage ends your life" vibe of either the original HM or Back to Nature's female counterpart (where it literally ended the game).
I've recommended this game to friends and family, and if you like the idea of a fairly open-ended farming role-play / simulation experience, then I'd definitely suggest giving Stardew Valley a try.

Revolutionary Paris is very much my dream setting for an AC game, however with the state this was launched in, I'd given up on Unity, and basically the series. However I managed to get it dirt cheap lately, and from the reviews it seemed like the issue had been fixed. And it turns out, they are for the most part. It didn't crash on me a single time and though I did have some graphical glitches (including some hilarious ones), I didn't encounter any game breaking bug.
For a time it was a pleasure to run around Revolutionary Paris, which is beautifully rendered and feels geniuinely alive. However this is an AC game, which means the gameplay got stale a while ago. They do try to improve things but, as has been the case in the past, namely for controls and stealth mechanics, they take a step forward then they take a step back. They added some things that could potentially be good to stealth, but removed others that were working (like hiding in bushes) and the controls have been improved for some things, but are the most frustrating in the series to date for other things.
The map is probably the biggest in the history of the franchise but as all Ubisoft games for the past 5 years, it's filled to the brim with pointless collectibles and boring side activities. While you don't have to do them, it does make finding the worthwhile ones hard.
The story is okay at best, the final mission is easily the worst in the franchise's history, and you can see the ''plot twist'' coming from a mile away. You do however, as is the norm with the series, get to meet many historical figures, which is always nice.
All in all, I recommend this to history buffs, especially if you love the history of France, and the most dedicated AC fans when it's on sale.

This game is fun, polished and challenging, but I find it impossible to shake the feeling of being rushed through the campaign by the avatar project and for that reason I cannot recommend it. As a strategy game with many facets and mechanics to explore, you'd think there would be time to play around and experiment while still enjoying a challenge; but on the higher difficulties, unless you're doing everything flawlessly right off the hop, you are punished by cumulative enemy buffs and the game over timer (which can only be slowed, not stopped). There are likely many veteran commanders out there who enjoy the the thrill of trying to stay a step ahead of the aliens, but as someone who likes to build a narrative over the course of a campaign, and enjoys seeing long terms effects of my decisions, I'm frustrated with how rushed everything feels.
TLDR: you will like this game if you like trying to meet quickly approaching deadlines with success heavily dependant on RNG.

This is one of the greatest tools ever if you want to learn how to draw digitally!

There are brushes like Pencils, calligraphy pens, air brush, and pastels. Also there are pen nibs for almost everything. You can, for example, change the brush size, Opacity and spacing.
However, if you don't have any experience in digital painting, you can download event files from
and replay them. In that way you can learn from other people's drawing methods.
The first time drawing with a tablet might be difficult for most people who are used to traditional pens. But if you spend a decent amount of time, you will get better. Even if your first drawings are not very good, it's fun when your skills start to improve.

Warning! This is a Review of a hobby artist. I have no clue about professional programs.
The programs I used before are: GIMP, Photoshop CS6, Photoshop Elements, Paint Tool SAI
After playing around with the program for a couple of hours I have to say... It's simple. But really, the best program, I have ever used to draw.
It helps a lot, if you want to draw outlines. Especially with a graphics tablet. With the built in function to smoothen the lines, you will draw perfect lines around the second or the first time trying. In Photoshop, you have to make first a reaaally big picture and draw like this, so you can make it smaller afterwards to hide eventual wobbly lines.
Or in SAI, you may be confronted with vector based lines, which are perfect, if you want perfect quality outlines. In openCanvas however, all you need is a stroke with your pen or mouse, and it already looks great.
All the brushes are perfectly adjustable and easy to work with. I was really impressed by the kalligraphy pen, where it took less than a minute to adjust it to my needs, while in Photoshop, it took quite a while and didn't look good after all. Or maybe it was just my imagination. In fact, I was really impressed, how easy this little program works.
I wasn't very sure, what to expect with the filters, when I saw them advertised on the shop page. But they have some really nice little filters, which can twirl the image, make waves, pixelize(mosaic), diffuse in a very smooth way etc. etc.
The user interface is adjustable to the maximum. While it has similarities to how GIMP handles the many windows, it feels a lot more stable in handling and using.
Now one thing, I wasn't really sure if needed. But it came in handy when using. Perspectives. You can practically adjust for very impressive static structures and visual effects. It is for sure damn good to use when you are a beginner and don't draw in perfect perspectives from the beginning of your picture. But I could imagine it to be also really handy for professional artists too.
(I think, I will have much fun with it!)
Rotating the picture as you need while drawing makes hard to draw lines easier and you don't have to turn your tablet upside down. Really nice to have this implemented. It is a far nicer rotation tool than GIMP, Photoshop or SAI. Also it is more handy.
The last two things (And I am sorry to put the least good things in the end)
You can add text. Well, every other tool I know has this feature. I don't know, why it is worth mentioning. But okay.
And.. this is ACTUALLY really neat, if you think about it. The program itself takes up only 18MB. It makes it the smallest, but best program to draw, I own.
Sure, I feel really hyped about this and I will update the review in a few weeks with a speed art and a much more settled opinion. But I hope you liked this review and it helped you considering to buy it. It is worth every dollar/euro/septim/gold coin or whatever you like to buy stuff with.
Here are the prices of the porgrams compared:
GIMP - free
Photoshop CS6 Standard - 699$
Photoshop CS6 Extended - 999$
Paint Tool SAI - 5400 Yen (Around 50$ And no, it is NOT freeware)
openCanvas - 49,99$
If you have questions or want to correct me, just comment and I will try to answer it, correct it or add it to the review if important.
Edit #1:
As I am not sure, why my "play time" is so low, I was quite busy with it.
There are actually some bugs, you should be aware of.
- Your stylus may not be recognized after using the arrows to scroll on your drawing. This isn't really a big problem, but can be really annoying after a few hours. You can also solve it by either Alt+Tab out and in again, or by drawing a line with your normal mouse.
- Sometimes, you are not able to load up a .psd file. If you want to keep working on a picture, you have to copy every layer, save it as a separate picture and import it to OpenCanvas. This happened to me only once after switching very often between Photoshop and O.C.
Rather use .oci
If you find yourself having the same issues, consider reporting the bug.
End of Edit #1

is an absolutely beautiful game with amazing narrative and atmosphere. The plot is enigmatic, but engaging, told by the dark-voiced stranger as the protagonist rebuilds the Bastion. With each level, new objects and background information are revealed, providing a growing perspective of the "Calamity" that destroyed the world.
The story is only delivered in bits and pieces and never told outright, so it does like the game is being intentionally vague. However, the little snippets that you do get really show how expansive this world really is. Every creature, weapon, faction, god, and alcoholic beverage has a little story. Pay attention to the lore. It's so worth it.
Shoot enemies. Kill enemies. Don't die. There are a variety of different weapons and passive effects that you can pick and choose from depending on how you want to play. Experimenting with different combinatiions is what makes this game a lot of fun.
If the game is getting too easy, there are also idols to the gods of the
world that you can activate to ramp up the difficulty. Each idol adds an additional effect you have to account for as you fight through the world. For example, the idol of Hense makes enemies hit a lot harder, while the idol of Acobi will cause enemies to explode on death. Combining all the idols at once makes this game so much harder, but so much more rewarding to beat.
Story and progression is linear, but you won't really mind because you are constantly unlocking new things to play around with. Side areas and skill trials are a lot of fun. Later, you also unlock "dreams" which are basically survival arenas where you must fight wave after wave of enemy. They're a lot of fun!

I'm not going to give some groundbreaking review so i'm just going to give my short opinion which is what drove me to purchase the game. If you've ever played any turn based game (like civilization) this game is very close to that, with a substantial amount more of relating details (such as what cover your troops are using and what equipment they brought with them into the field.) to affect the end result of the battle. The damage and combat are very realistic (for a sci-fi era game). The story is good and you feel involved the longer the game goes on. This game is (from what i've been told) is much harder than xcom1 and has a substantial learning curve attached to it. But once you understand the games mechanics, you can easily pull 75-100 hours out of this game.
Now for the cons, there are only two:
1) The fact that the developers took co-op mods out of this game destroyed any chance this series had for any type of true longevity play. It's now a single-player experience and the "multiplayer" is buggy and seems pretty dead.
2) The game (despite having a great story line) doesn't change after your first play through. So unlike Civ where you can win games in multiple ways, this has a linear story path. So take your time on your first play through and enjoy it, because once you've played the game all the way through to the end, you've seen all it has to offer. After that happens the game starts to become mundane with repetition in combat. Well, it did for me at least. I've also seen reviews on here with 500 hours played, so to each his own I guess.
TLDR; It's a fantastic game with a fantastic combat system and story line. However after you've beaten it once, I don't really see a lot of replay value with this game.

The thing about Stardew Valley is, it's not a farming sim.
It's an RPG, with farming elements.
And as an RPG, it's refresing to get away from the "you are minor soldier/common villager destinied to rise to greatness as you are thrust into a great war of global proportions" kinda thing that most more popular RPGs do, and makes it something more...relatable. It's still fantasy, it's still engrossing, it still has emotional stakes, but the loci are more familar. There's the allusions to the ennui of office work, the toil clearing the old farm, the satisfaction of growing your first crop. You develop relationships with the people of the town, and if you're like me, you'll actually dream of them when you turn off the comuputer and crawl into bed for the night.
And when you're at work, typing away at a keyboard in a cubicle or stacking cans on a shelf, you might look up at the fluorescent lights above you, and try to remember the last time you tried to help a friend develop her passion into a profession, or if you've every really had homemade parsnip soup.

The darkness of the forest leaves you restless as you wait just in the treeline a few hundred meters away from the airfield. Pulling out your rifle, you switch on your nightvision, and aim down the southern side of the runway to the helicopter for the third time. Satisfied that no players have boarded the chopper, you put away your rifle and finally head down to the hangers about a hundred meters from the bird. Stopping just behind the fifth hanger from the north, you check the area once more for hostiles, only this time a bullet barely misses your head and slams harmlessly into a tree twenty away. Instinctively you back away behind the hanger and flank around to the other side, making sure no players threaten you from behind. Peeking from the front of the hanger, you identify the shooter, pull out your rifle, and take the shot. As you pull the trigger, three things happen; firstly, you killed the hostile player that shot at you moments ago, secondly, you've just alerted the player hiding inside the hanger to your presence, and lastly, you've alerted the mass of zombies patroling the airfield looking for fresh meat. Flanking back around to the back of the hanger, you then sprint for the chopper you've worked so hard to repair, only to get shot by the player inside the hanger you used as cover.
Experiences like these are hard to come by. And ArmA 2 does it right.

When reviewing a game, it is sometimes important to know what is already in the market. This game is effectively inferior to Beat Hazard, a game with a much higher production and better gameplay than this one. Why waste your time playing this game when that one exists?
Before going into this game you must understand what sort of music this game adheres to. Music games in general all have a specific preference. Some generate more varied gameplay for more genres and styles of music than others. Audioship is pretty accepting of its music vs others, however those who listen to music that might leave a certain aspect of music out (like no bass) or have very few instruments will still be frustrated.
Pros (any pro that this game has will be one that Beat Hazard doesn't):
- Up to 4 people can play.
- 2 people can play on one keyboard.
- Navigating music menu is easy.
- "Test Your Luck" mode is excellent for parties.
- No game soundeffects that take away or cover your music.
Cons:
- Accepts very few music file types. Only mp3, wav and ogg.
- .wav music type apparently doesn't actually play, it just cuts straight to the end.
- Music menu does not remember position. Annoying if you have large libraries.
- Cannot change specific volume settings. The menu sound effects are loud and irritating as ♥♥♥♥ because of this.
- Cannot map the keys. Irritating if you are playing solo and it would be much better for wasd to be on arrow keys etc.
- Cannot back out of the "controller settings" if you selected more players than you have responding controllers for.
- Enemies are uncreative and boring. They are just coloured "shapes".
- Enemies do not follow the music very well. They may spawn in time with the music, but we are not fighting them in time with the music. A break or solo in the song results in a screen covered with enemies that we are not equipped to fighting.
- There is no apparent musical pattern to how the enemies appear.
- Your control responsiveness changes depending on which button you press to ready up. Both R and P give you slow and accelerating commands (which are not desireable in what is effectively a bullet hell) whereas enter does not. However enter does not let you change colour nor rotate.
- Bug: In multiplayer, after activating your rainbow "be able to shoot everything" power, player 2 will have its colour forcibly changed.

Straightforward time manager with in a Greek mythological antiquity setting.  You have workers for mundane tasks like collecting food, chopping woods, clearing paths, and have Hercules for bigger tasks like tossing boulders or buidling temples.  Each task either yields food, wood. etc., requires a certain amount of those resources, or is some combination, e.g., requiring food and wood to mine gold, which is another main resource.   The workers have to run back and forth to their little house which takes time, so the order in which you do the tasks matters.  Not only is distance the workers have to run a factor, but how quickly you can upgrade your house to get another worker, or build a farm to generate food periodically, can also have a big impact.
All in all a solid time manager that is reasonably priced at $3.  It is also available on iOS, but it is not clear whether this was a port to or from iOS since the release date (according to Metacritic) was Oct. 30, 2013 for PC, but April 23, 2014 for the iOS version.  Regardless, this game stands on its on as a PC game, while it certainly would make a good touch-based game, since you are mainly just clicking the next task for workers/Hercules to perform, the game has enough depth and variation to retain one's interest.

See I'm going to recommend this game with a caveat.  This game is not easy to pick up and learn, and the game does itself few favors in that regard.  The developer approaches the Interface in the same utilitarian way that ToadyOne, of DwarfFortress fame, approaches their UI: The UI is a means to display as much information as is possible, not necessarily as efficiently or as beautifully as possible.  But if you can look past the UI issues, you'll find probably the best Gridiron Management game out there.
FOF8 has built upon FOF7's solid Owner/GM experience while fleshing out the playcalling and gameplanning for those of us who want to try their hand at coaching.  Now you have the ability to build an offensive playbook each year, filled with up to 200 different plays.  These plays can be made yourself or you can generate a given amount automatically, and each play has it's given style that can synergize with your Off. Coordinator's preferences.
Once plays have been generated in your playbook, you'll need to actually build up a gameplan.  This too can be automated, a feature that you will probably avail yourself of if you're anything like me.  You see, on both sides of the ball you'll need to plug in plays for each possible situation.  1st and 10, 3rd and long, 3rd and One.  Ect.  However the current setup requires you to adjust 1 play at a time.  This adds up to a
of clicks.  This is by far my biggest gripe in an otherwise fantastic new feature.    Additionally, there are existing limitations to the # of unique plays in the playbook.  On defense it is 12, and on offense it is 50-60, depending on your Offensive Coordinator.  This system makes perfect since and is a fantastic way to add depth to your coaching choices.  However, in addition you are limited to around 80 plays in the gameplan in total.
especially on the defensive side of the ball.  Why the hell wouldn't the defense be able to remember the same 12 plays as often as they need to?
Unfortunately because I play as a coach first, and a GM second, these issues have entirely ruined my experience.  Forcing myself to run with either a generated playbook that I have no investment in, or a hamstrung playbook that doesn't have the depth I need just makes me want to walk way from the computer.  As such, I've uninstalled the game until the developer can address these issues in the gameplanning system.
This game has a lot of progress to go before it's what most would consider 'polished', however it is already the absolute best Gridiron Management game on the market.  If you you are looking for a GM experience, and are ok leaving coaching to the game's AI, I am confident you will find yourself hooked.  However the new features in the coaching realm have hamstrung those of us who prefer to focus as much as possible on the day-to-day running of the team.  That said, the developer's history of releases also all but assures us that he will continue to support his product and address these flaws.

I've played the FOF games for years and they've always been great in every way except one -- presentation.  If you have to have nice graphics, or really any graphics, then this is not the game for you.  But if what you want is a deep and accurate simulation of NFL football, then this is the only game in town.
Among the new features, my favorite by far is the updated log.  It now spells out everything about the play, who was in at what position, and even gives a grade for each player.  It's a magnificent addition that allows you to evaluate how your players are playing throughout the game.  It is almost certaily possible for someone to make a graphical viewer using the information given in the log that would dsiplay at the very least what the formations looked like and highlight who did well and who didn't.  If such a thing were added to Solevision it would finally make that feature useful for me.
A feature I'm not quite as keen on, at least not yet, is gameplanning.  I usually want to play as GM anyway, but if I were to want to try my hand at coaching, making a plan is too laborious a process as it stands right now.  It needs some streamlining before it's user friendly enough for anyone who approaches it casually.  Fortunately, the game makes fine gameplans on its own.
And this is reminding me of another of my favorite new features.  It's such a small thing, but it makes a big difference.  Coaches now have styles.  It's no longer so easy as hiring the best young coach you can -- he also needs to fit your team.  Or, if he's too good to pass up, you'll need to make changes in your team to accomodate his style.
And of course the best part of the game is its ability to generate decades of NFL-realistic stats as you play.  I have never seen a more accurate NFL sim than the FOF series, and I think this one is probably the best one yet.
I'm stoked about the new release and look forward to many years of enjoyment.  And oh yeah -- one thing that's easy to overlook about this game is how well supported it is by its developer.  It was only just released last week and we've already had the first patch, which fixed all the issues that I had any trouble with.  The developer also likes to surprise us with updates (for free!) whenever he has something new.  This can be something as simple as a roster update, to even including major new features.  I'm not promising unannounced new features will happen but I can tell you that they have happened before.  Other developers would make you pay for your yearly updates.  Solecismic won't promise them -- or even really let you know they are likely to come.  But when they do you'll just wake upone day and have them.
So I recommed this game and its developer wholeheartedly.  If you like sports text sims that are accurate and realistic, you can't do better than this one.

is an absolutely beautiful game with amazing narrative and atmosphere. The plot is enigmatic, but engaging, told by the dark-voiced stranger as the protagonist rebuilds the Bastion. With each level, new objects and background information are revealed, providing a growing perspective of the "Calamity" that destroyed the world.
The story is only delivered in bits and pieces and never told outright, so it does like the game is being intentionally vague. However, the little snippets that you do get really show how expansive this world really is. Every creature, weapon, faction, god, and alcoholic beverage has a little story. Pay attention to the lore. It's so worth it.
Shoot enemies. Kill enemies. Don't die. There are a variety of different weapons and passive effects that you can pick and choose from depending on how you want to play. Experimenting with different combinatiions is what makes this game a lot of fun.
If the game is getting too easy, there are also idols to the gods of the
world that you can activate to ramp up the difficulty. Each idol adds an additional effect you have to account for as you fight through the world. For example, the idol of Hense makes enemies hit a lot harder, while the idol of Acobi will cause enemies to explode on death. Combining all the idols at once makes this game so much harder, but so much more rewarding to beat.
Story and progression is linear, but you won't really mind because you are constantly unlocking new things to play around with. Side areas and skill trials are a lot of fun. Later, you also unlock "dreams" which are basically survival arenas where you must fight wave after wave of enemy. They're a lot of fun!

Your best outside linebacker is holding out.
Sam has been good for your team in his three seasons, since you drafted him out of Florida State in the second round of the rookie draft. You thought he'd develop into a solid pass rusher -- and that came true. 6 sacks last season was third best on the team. But as training camp approaches, and your roster is starting to gel -- he thinks he's worth a raise. You look over his performance -- pass rush great, but he's only been so-so in coverage. You've got another guy who could play in the role, but Sam is better -- and he's better than anyone who you could find in free agency. But you have some gameplan ideas that might help use him effectively and limit his liabilities. He wants to be making $3 million a year -- and if you give him that money (with guaranteed bonuses) it might squeeze out your cap space to re-sign your game-changing tight end next year. You make the call... it might hurt to pay him this much, but he'll be angry if you don't pony up.
Interested yet?
THIS is the essence of Front Office Football. This isn't a button-mashing game. This isn't about absurd stats and silly power-ups. And this isn't a game which will test your graphics card. It's going to test your brains, your balls, and your gut instincts. This is a game where you... "put yourself in the front office."
Your tools are scouting reports, rookie combine data, on-field statistics, and personality traits. Your decisions include salary cap management, roster-building, young player development, depth chart decisions, gameplan architecture, and finding value where others might miss it. Take on as much control as you want, turn over details to your hand-picked staff if you prefer. You can run the whole show, be just the GM, just the coach/gameplanner, or you can call the plays yourself in-game from a vast menu of options.
Play a whole career, build your team in your own image, and tune your skills for a great challenge across a robust universe of multi-player leagues, with options to suit nearly anyone's tastes.
If anything I'm describing above is what you're looking for in a football game... you owe it to yourself it play this one. FOF 8 takes a long tradition to a new level, and is a must-buy for the under-the-hood types who love the gridiron.

That being said, there is such a wonderful quality to the game. I find myself constantly smiling at the sounds and sights of the world of Botanicula.

A wonderful game with stellar art, awesome music, and a charm that can't be denied.
Give it a go, and have some smiles.

If you are a fan of point-and-click adventures, you will love this. Serena is a "love letter to the adventure game community", as stated by developer Senscape. I cannot begin to describe how emotionally charged this game is. It will intrigue you, mystify you, and shock you to the point of shaking. At least, that was my experience.
Serena puts you in a wood cabin in the middle of a forest. Your wife, Serena, is not there with you. Why? Hopefully something in the cabin will make you remember...
As with most point-and-clicks, the game is entirely played with the mouse. You click on objects, and the main character will give a short comment. I highly recommend exhausting all the dialogue, as the voice acting is terrific.
Be prepared for a short session however, as completion time will take about 20 minutes to an hour, depending on your level of immersion. It is worthwhile though. Short, but sweet, as some would say. The best part is that it's completely free, so I urge you to try it out.

At its core, Serena is a point-and-click story game, with the player interacting with objects in order to hear the protagonist deliver his thoughts relating to that item. In this way, the game tells a story through the character's monologue, as he recalls the events that occurred within the cabin the game is based in. Yes, this entire game takes place within a single cabin, and while this may seem limiting, I feel that it's what makes the way the story is delivered so impressive.
The game opens up into the first-person perspective of a man sitting in a cabin. There is no menu and there are no options to adjust; the game begins immediately upon launch. I don't feel that this detracted from the accessibility or usability of the game too much (if at all), since the game doesn't really need much customization, though at times, I felt the lighting within the cabin was a bit dark or obscure, and could have appreciated an option to adjust in-game brightness.
Serena competently demonstrates that there are many ways to view the same thing. An item is just that; it has no meaning until we give it one, and this is subject to change depending on our experiences.
Voice acting is delivered with appreciable and believable emotion, which really helped me to connect with the mental state of the characters. An equally well-done soundtrack only serves to complement the atmosphere and emotion of the game.
Had it not been for the surprisingly engrossing story, Serena would just be another point-and-click problem-solving game, requiring the player to find objects and interact with them in a specific manner or order. The moving story, well-delivered audio, and competent writing that has gone into this short game make it one of the better point-and-click games around. I found myself actually wanting to hear what the character had to say about all the items in the cabin as the story progressed, rather than just trying to find the next trigger to proceed further.
As a free, short, story-telling game, Serena is at least worth a look, if not the hour or two you may spend finishing it.

The universe should be a vast place full of profound variety and diversity.... not walking, talking bears, birds, cats and lizards.

Unless you're looking for a very simple 4X experience, one designed for kids, look elsewhere; the $49.99 price point is certainly not justified.
