A real big shock!!!!
I went into this game thinking it was gonna be another remake i would hate. This game had me hooked from the word go. The fancy intro, to the talking help the game really does grab you quickly and game play quick to pick up.
So where to begin
First thoughts did not seem promising from the download. Even though this game is in BETA it was still a really small download which did raise initial concerns. These however were quashed quite quickly from starting the game. Graphics are good but nothing fantastic and the intro is relatively short. Not complaining myself as i like to get stuck in, but anyone wanting a background story there isn't much to go on. (however this is still a beta and could change).
The initial character selection is as would be expected with the description of races and perk. However i find the perks to be a bit lacking of a decription and so far don't make a noticeable amount of difference. Once you have selected a race you jump straight into the game, which has helpful advice on how to play.
The game play had me hook. Once i started i had to finish, this game really does draw you in and has a sins of a solar empire sorta feel. The AI is quite poor though but as the BETA stands you cannot change the difficulty. Fingers crossed the hard AI will have some kick when the game is finally released. The battles look amazing but have limited ammount of input from the player. Anyone who has played the previous games might find issue with this. However i do feel that the battles will benefit the multiplayer aspect of the game, hopefully cutting game times down from a full day  to complete a small galaxy.
Diplomacy on this game is still as bad as the predecessors, the AI is unreasonable and trying to set up any advance treaty will take so much time and effort. The diplomatic victory is also easy to achieve if you expand quickly. This does have to be my biggest bug bear with the game. If 4X would make the AI vote tactically i would be so much happier with this already awesome game.
Planetary interaction has been improved slightly so has the monetary and tax systems. With this game you will find you are paying alot more attention to tax rates, pollution, construction etc. Also there is a new addition which is warp point structures. I really do hope they develope these just alittle bit more as the idea is great but as they dont provide much protection unless you camp them.
The game runs very smooth, sounds great and has relatively low load tiimes. The sound is pure excellence and have found no real bugs with the game so far.
Pro's and Con's
Up Side
1. Looks great
2. Gameplay is simple
3. Alot more thought to multiplayer
4. People who are new to Master of Orion can jump straight in
5. Planetary interface has been improved
6. It is the much needed update for Master of Orion
7. Not many bugs for a BETA

Downsides :(
Most of my downsides are going to stick out more to Master of Orion enthusiasts

1. Battles are really lacking user input
2. Diplomacy still sucks
3. Warp lines. gone are the days of direct travel
4. Ship range mechanic has been removed
5. Pirates are terrible
6. AI are not very tactical
7. It feels more like Sins of a solar empire than Master of Orion

12 Labours of Hercules is the first installment of its' series developed by JetDogs Studios and Zoomout Games. There are other installments from this series: The Cretan Bull, Girl Power and Mother Nature. 'Girl Power' is already out on other casual gaming sites and 'Mother Nature' is currently being worked on.
Note: There is a storyline for the game but it isn't much to it nor its' rememberable.
This is a time management game, where careful planning is required, limited amount of resources that are available throughout the game; henced the word management.
This game has the total of four episodes with ten levels each; totaling out to 40 levels altogether. There twenty-two different achievements but each of them come with a requirement.
There are two modes, relaxed and expert, two difference between them is the timer speed and scoring. In relaxed mode, the timer drains at a slower rate and the scoring is low. In expert mode, the timer drain quicker and the scoring is much higher.
The stars that are earned from completing the level depends upon on how much time is left on the timer.
Three Gold star is when the time has not gone pass the arrow. Two Silver star is when the time has gone pass the arrow. One Bronze star is when the timer is completely empty.
Replaying any of the levels will improve the game score and the amount star.
There are few special bonuses: Freeze Time, Worker Movement/Work Speed, Additional Worker and Increases Resources. All of these special bonuses has a certain time limit but they can be used again once the bar fills-up. These special bonuses are very useful when the game is being played on expert mode.
I don't think that this game much of replay value to it. If you're into time management games then you might find this game somewhat enjoyable to certain extent.

This is the best version of the best pro football simulation on the market.  Version 8 has revamped a lot of the playcalling aspects, almost all for the better.  The game goes into offensive and defensive philosphy to allow you to really feel like you have control over the team you are building.  If you see a player in the draft with great potential, you still have to decide if he fits the team that you are trying to build.  It isn't just about plugging in good players without a plan in mind.
The game also allows you to set pretty much every aspect of your team to AI control.  This lets you focus on what interests you.  If you want to simply build the team as an owner/GM and not worry about the day to day aspects of the team, you can do that.  If you want to build every single play in your playbook and call every single play of every game, you can do that, too.
Version 8 has also added fast simming to allow your league to build up a history (all teams on AI control) with one click.  That is a nice little feature to add.

This is the 8th edition of the Front Office Football franchise. It's a franchise that has come a long way and continues to impress more and more people. Much like the other mainstream text-based sports games, such as Football Manager and Out of the Park Baseball, it feels and plays much more intimately than a Madden Franchise mode. With that said, let's get into the review!
‣
: The real names of players are included, and they are on their real teams.
‣
: You can customize their name, number, and even attempt to change their position.
‣
: One of my personal favorite features is that there are a TON of cities that you are able to move your team to, but it isn't easy; you need to get a new stadium approved, which is hard to do in small cities. Other things are involved as well, such as the cities' other entertainment options and their desire for a team/closeness with other teams.
‣
: The cities, along with what was mentioned above,
For example, the South could experience rapid growth, sparking a huge growth rate for the city of Orlando. In turn, this could lead the owners of the Jacksonville Jaguars to move to Orlando. The options are nearly endless.
‣
: After Week 5 of the regular season, the game allows you to simulate the odds that the teams left in contention make the playoffs. This is a new feature from FOF7, and just adds even more value to this game.
‣
: The game is deeper than the Mariana Trench. In all seriousness, it has more realism than anything I've ever seen. You can design your own plays, set up your depth charts, and much, much more. You also have the option to leave all that to the AI and just focus on signing and managing the players. This deepness is a result of the hard work that the developer puts into each and every aspect of the game.
‣
: The amount of depth of this game could and should leave you a little lost, but the help menu provided in game is incredible at explaining what everything is and how they all work. Give it a read.
‣
: The teams do not have their real NFL names or logos. However, this is an easy fix due to an incredible community and the in-game team name changer.
‣
: If you play this game long enough, you will occasionally run into crashes. Not a big problem, just remember to click that save button!

Oooh man, it's been a while since a simple little 2D game has captivated me like this...
The general style is very similar to Downwell, in which after succeeding in levels, you're awarded with progressively more abilities to choose from. The levels alternate between the winding, procedurally generated labyrinths of enemies that you have to eat to unlock an elevator, and boss levels, each with their own unique theme and style. Despite the baseline difficulty being tough, the difficulty curve feels really good, and it's incredibly rewarding to get past that one boss that's been wrecking you.
After your first handful of runs, once you have a wider selections of abilities to choose from, it becomes incredibly strategic trying to decide what monster / ability combinations you think can get you the farthest. The game also features a really incredible high score table, which organizes based on the main game and the weekly challenge. Trying to slap your name up on the table for all to see is a really great incentive to keep coming back for more.
On the technical side of things, after about 3 hours, I have yet to encounter a single glitch or bug. Even with a really crappy laptop, the game ran great, and I never had any stuttering or framerate issues, even with massive swarms of soldiers and robots trying to gun me down. You can tell the devs took their QA very seriously, and their passion for the game shows.
For less that 10$, I feel like I got my money's worth for a solid game with an incredibly addictive experience. For those that love tough, arcade-y goodness, this is definitely the game for you.

Here's the deal. This isn't a new game. It's the 8th iteration, modification, and improvement of the best American Football Franchise simulator around. A true indy, one man written and developed, you won't find fancy graphics or big budget presentation, but you will find statisical accuracy, the challenge of the draft, who to resign when your team runs up to the cap and all the frustration of running the Cleveland Browns franchise into the ground, year after year.
New and rewritten for FOF 8  are playbooks for teams, along with thousands of playcalling combinations, personnel packages. You'll be able to import entire playbooks for your team, design your own plays, or let the AI handle all of that for you. You'll have to deal with contracts, inactive players, injuries,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off rookies who think they are really something special. You'll have to deal with career ending injuries, cap management, the challenge of trading players, draft picks, or all of the above for that shot at Ricky Williams (GO YOU!!!!)
Players will boom and bust like in real life. You'll get to track their progress through training camps, and they'll need playing time if you want to get the develop quickly. The draft can be where you decide on who to fill out your roster with. There'll be players with skill but terrible combines, players with terrible skills who are amazing atheletes, and you'll eventually get a shot at players with the total package. How you manage all of that, who you draft, sign, trade will be totally up to you.
The game will track the stats for all players, all teams, for the life of the game. You'll create a world all your own. The game is very deep. There isn't a pro football franchise simlulator with the kind of under the hood mechanincs that this one has. There are numerous ways to personalize the game through settings, like alternate player files, importing custom graphics, fog of war settings, and getting fired for sucking♥♥♥♥♥ Start the game with stock teams, a full draft, or a preference draft where you put emphasis on player groups and the scout does the drafting for you.
If you didn't think that this was overwhelming enough, all this can be played against human managers in the many multiplayer leagues, some that have been going on for years and years, or new ones that are bound to start. There's no challenge like matching wits with human GM's in FOF. You're guaranteed to be humbled.
Even though the help file and manual is robust, you can find answers to questions on the game, strategy, modifications and find a multi player league to join at Front Office Football Central, the unofficial home for all things FOF.

For a free game that you can complete in under an hour, I enjoyed Serena. It's an adventure game that really plays out like a visual novel. There are no puzzles, just lots and lots of story that you have to uncover in a fairly linear order to reach the end. You'll be clicking on the same objects over and over to hear new observations and revelations from the first-person narrator.
The story itself is interesting, though not completely original or surprising. If you're like me you'll guess how the game is going to play out within the first few minutes and be pretty much correct. That said, the story is presented in such a way that the journey is still enjoyable. The voice acting is pretty well done which is good, because otherwise the game would not have been effective. The sound design and music also help to build some creepy tension in the right places.
I recommend spending a dark and depressing hour with Serena.

First off, let me say that I'm a huge fan of procedural generation and more specifically, roguelikes, in which randomized content is an absolute must in order to provide a fresh experience during every playthrough. While you can play Starbound with permadeath (Hardcore mode), I tried it and found it to be quite unpleasant after dying 2 times from falling damage on the first boss, so I started playing on Casual since I don't enjoy losing my ores every time I die and it's an annoyance having to stash them away every time you go out of the safety of your settlement/spaceship.
Anyway, this last week I finally sat down and played a lot of Starbound after a very long time of having the game but having only played it when I first got it for a couple of hours, and I have to admit, I had a lot of fun with it, at least up until the mid game. The reason I tried it again now is the winter update, of course. Anyway, onto the pros and cons:
I believe that the game's strong point is Sandbox building rather than the current weak storyline and that the tier-based progression is rather stale and feels like there's some major power creep involved whichs makes advancing to the late-game equipment more of a job than an adventure.
PROS
+ LOTS of different materials you can use to build your fantasy world with and lots of decor to mess around with
+ Gathering resources is rather fast and efficient with the right tools (feels a bit too easy near the end, tbh)
+ Wiring objects together to create cool contraptions is nice
+ Very customizable character during character creation screen with each race having a different ship that advances differently in shape every time you upgrade it
+ Nice graphics if you're the type that enjoys such graphics
+ Nice music (not very sci-fi but it's good)
+ No two planets ever look or even feel the same
+ An infinite universe to explore and conquer
+ 360 degrees melee combat
+ No need to always craft/keep ammunition on you
CONS
- Seems to be poorly optimized atm, but that's to be expected at the game's current unfinished state
- As stated above, progression feels incredibly mind-numbing, at least after your start making durasteel. Basically, it goes exactly like this: build crafting table of the next available tier, then build the associated furnace, then the associated anvil to that tier of crafting so you can make the best mining tool to find the next higher tier of materials until you can craft the next crafting table and the circle begins anew...
- Even though it's a sandbox game, in order to unlock all materials and recipes you HAVE to proceed in the main quest line, which seems counter-intuitive for a game of this kind.
- The same vaults appear again and again while you're mining underground, there needs to be MUCH more variety in those if we're to feel like every new vault is a surprise and not just the same two crates at the exact same spot every time.
Today, after beating the 4th boss on my second attempt (unspoiled), I made an Impervium armour set + weapon after gathering 600+ solarium ore from a "dead planet" and I think I'm done with the game *for now*. I don't feel like building anything in my world in single player atm, so I'm pretty much done until further updates rekindle my interest.
So, to give you my opinion on whether you should buy it or not, you need to understand that there's a problem with recommending games of this genre; If you're the creative type, or you like to play with friends often, you can sink hundreds upon hundreds of hours building stuff and hanging out with your friends in the fantasy world you've created, making the game's price irrelevant since you more than enough got your money's worth in play time. However, if, on the other hand you're most likely to be playing this alone all the time and are hoping for a relatively complex platformer rpg, I can't honestly recommend it, at least at full price, since the enemies' AI is laughable, until you get to bosses which are pretty well done, imo.
Even though I did like the game for a while (until tier progression started getting repetitive and unnatural), imho I can't recommend it to anyone at full price, except for the very fanatic sandbox enthusiasts. It still has a lot of growing to do to be worth the full price tag. I do realize that it's a massive undertaking for an indie studio, and I respect the hundreds upon hundreds of hours each developer has put into shaping the game, but if we're going to be honest, it's still got ways to go in terms of meaningful progress. Adding more decorations and costumes is fine and dandy but it doesn't make for interesting combat, for example, which imo is one of the game's most unrewarding parts, as of this review.

Over-all Rating: 8/10 - While I don't think Xcom 2 provides a particularly significant gameplay overhaul from Xcom: Enemy Unknown, it does add some interesting story elements, and I really like the general setup, and the "if it isn't broken, don't fix it" saying does come to mind here, as Xcom: Enemey Unknown was a very good game to begin with, and naturally there are SOME improvements. Unfortunately, there were also a few setbacks.
Economy: 3/10 - The game is heinously expensive. Despite being a dated title by now, it still sells for 60 bucks on steam. The DLC for the game is also overpriced and I would say, if you already own Xcom: Enemy Unknown and could stand to play it some more, I'd do that and wait for the price of Xcom 2 to come down, as it is pretty much the same game.
If you haven't played Xcom: Enemy Uknown, however, I'd start there, as that game is much more affordable and the stories of the two games are tied together anyway.
Replayability/Impact: 10/10 - Xcom 2 is one of those games you pick back up many many times. If you like the genre, you're certainly not going to regret buying it.
Closing Comments:
Xcom 2 improves on quite a few things from Xcom: Enemy Unknown, but it also takes away some of the elements that were very nice from Xcom: Enemy Unknown, such as the slightly more diverse classes.
I feel like the classes in Xcom 2 are dumbed down too much.
Fortunately, there's a mod for that.
If you're going to be playing either Xcom: Enemy Unknown or Xcom 2, I recommend checking out the Long War mods for those respective games.
Again, if you haven't already played Xcom: Enemey Unknown, do that first, because Xcom 2 is really, when it all comes down to it, just extra levels of the same great game. There are some mechanical and gamplay changes, but it really is extremely similar and the predecessor is so much cheaper and not at all bad to look at or ancient by comparison.

This is actually a pretty good game relative to other 4X games currently out there. This is largly because it takes some of its content from a genuinely great 4X game, MOO2, that was so good that it is still excellent (in spite of some flaws) after 20+ years.
The research categories are taken from MOO2, but they are broken up into smaller pieces that are incremental. Where, for example, in MOO2 an Automated Factory would give +5 production and an additional +1 production per person, in this game the Automated factory merely gives +2 Production, making it an incremental change rather than a major strategical achievement.
The designers, in their words about design admitted openly (see Steam discussions)  that building an almost chess-like 4X game like MOO2 was beyond their programming capacity. In MOO2 the one who went first in major battles would depend upon something called initiative, based on speed and maneuvering capability. This worked very well and typically with two relatively equal human players in a large battle the best ship or two of each side would go first and then the other ships. It worked extremely well, while the developers of this game called it "unwarranted complexity" and claimed they just couldn't do it.
Please read some of the positive reviews for discussion of this new games virtues. There are all some and sadly it is better than many 4X attempts there because they did take a lot from MOO2... but not nearly enough. That is the reason this is very sad.
Hopefully, someday, a genuine reboot or sequel to MOO2 will be made. The tragic part is that the existance of this game might give potential backers the false impression that such a reboot/sequel has already been done, which it has not.
I did pay my $50 and play this game to give it a shot. I could give a balanced look at the positive qualities, but instead, in this review I merely wish to share my deep feelings of heartbroken disappointment. It is frustrating when designers just cannot understand what is great about a game they are trying to reboot or give a sequel to.
For comparison there is a great colony building game called Outpost that was turn-based and genuinely great but rushed too quickly into production without completing it. When Outpost II came out it had been made by some clueless executive at Sierra into an action game. As an avid Outpost enthusiast waiting for a sequel/completion of the original, I was offered a free copy of Outpost II which I refused. I don't care about the $40 then or the $50 I paid now. I care because a great game like MOO2 has never been rebooted or done with current graphics, refinement of the random event/initiative systems, a better AI, etc. This game took from MOO2, but changed way too much of what made it great.

I've recently got really into the NBA during the NFL off-season so thought I'd give this game a try. I got it for £9.50 (about $12) and I'm loving it so far. I've mainly played the MyCareer part of the game along with the MyGM. I also managed to get the NBA2K16 Companion App which works very well with this game, the extra VC from using it is very useful.
I first started playing through the MyCareer using mouse and keyboard and really didn't like it so the next day I went and bought an Xbox360 wired controller (The afterglow one) and it made the game so much better. Special moves and tricks are much easier to perform with it and it just generally makes navigating menus so much easier.
The graphics are nice. The players look great and gameplay is mostly smooth (only lags sometimes during the loading of the game during the pre-game show that plays before every match to keep you entertained while the game loads).
The customisation of the player and the MyCourt is good. My only gripe is that during the MyCareer, you get to connect with NBA stars who give you rewards when you spend off days with them. Some of these rewards state you get a special jersey/shoe, which I (and many others by the looks of it) presumed you could wear, this is not the case. Some of them you can wear, but most are put on display in your MyCourt which, although looks nice, I think I would have liked the option to wear them.
The actual story of MyCareer is... meh. It's very generic and some of it dosen't make for an authentic experience (yes, I'm talking about the fact that even if you are paper white, your parents and sister are still black) which feels odd. Also, I'm not too keen on the voice of your MyPlayer. I would have much preffered them to have a customisable voice which better represents you or what you want your MyPlayer to sound like.

Fallout 4 is a disappointment. Bethesda reached high in some areas, at the expense of other, perhaps more critical elements of the game.  It's a severely flawed, ambitious attempt, hindered by attempts to broaden its appeal or monetize beloved aspects that have grown up around the Fallout series since it fell into Bethesda's lap.
Perhaps the weakest element of the game is the story. The characters feel heavily restricted in what paths you can take, what options you have available. At various points, you lack the ability to talk down or overcome conflicts through dialogue, and while the setting is intriguing, it more or less fails to live up to the potential it had. Even more so, I had more difficulty finding an emotional attachment to the character due to the voice acting, which made me feel removed from the scenario my various playthroughs have always inevitably led to. It's not my voice that is reading the dialogue, not my way of speaking, and so I feel like I'm watching a character in a movie, rather than being drawn into the setting and scenario that game puts forth. It discards interesting character development in lieu of a trite revenge story that feels tacked on to the rest of the game. Bethesda should strongly reconsider its approach to writing mainline story elements and take a hard look at what players really want. But this is a theme that is repeated throughout other parts of the game.
Some of the gameplay, especially shooting and weapon manipulation is significantly superior to its predecessors, but it has weakened the skill system a fair bit and makes progress through the game feel gimmicky and less natural. While I applaud the changes to power-armor and how nice it is to not use VATS for combat, I feel that the dialogue progression trees were severely hampered by the interface choices made, and the overly simplistic, unimaginative character lines you deliver break immersion.  Faction building, something I looked forward to is largely a bland slog of "go-here-and-do-this" type quests that feel like they have no real impact on the Commonwealth or improve the actual status and standing of the Factions you may be working with. Furthermore, you have no options to really be a 'bad guy's and join one of the mercenary or raider groups in the game, during vanilla, non-DLC choices and quests.  While settlement building is fun, it feels tacked on and doesn't really make you feel like your settlers are anything more than generic figures who have no real impact on the actual story line. I cannot, for instance, convince a settlement to become an outpost for the Brotherhood of Steel or set a building project up and watch settlers complete it. Instead, immersion is broken by giving me near god-like powers of creation, without other options being available.  Furthermore, enemy factions do not seem to build their own settlements and you cannot have larger scale faction conflicts, an element of gameplay that would have made the game and its setting feel significantly more alive and interesting.
Graphics were acceptable, verging on good at times, but it's not the most technically beautiful game, without mods,you can play.
The Creation Club is the single worst choice Bethesda has made regarding this game and the desires and interests of the thriving community that surrounds its games. It is a tone-deaf, blatant money-grab with a hamfisted and undesirable set of features that do not let people opt out of downloading the content it 'offers'. It is not just a naked display of greed, it was done in spite of what players wanted out of the game and demonstrates an ever growing arrogance and disregard in Bethesda towards the fans of its RPG series. While I get that they would like to monetize the game further, this was entirely the wrong way to go about it, and players are savvy enough on a whole to see it for what it is.

Developed by Wolfire Games, Lugaru: The Rabbit’s Foot is a cross-platform third-person action video game heavily inspired by the martial arts sub-genre of 1970’s cinema.
Designed and developed independently by David Rosen and released in 2005 for Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X and Linux platforms, Lugaru (pronounced Loo-GAH-roo) follows Turner, an anthropomorphic rabbit, who embarks on a quest for revenge after finding his family and closest friends slaughtered by raiders.
As the highly political plot of Lugaru evolves, Turner uncovers an underlying conspiracy that threatens the entire rabbit kingdom of the island of Lugaru. It is up to you to utilise Turner’s impressive combat skills as he is forced to fight in hand-to-hand combat against raiders, the corrupt leaders of the rabbit republic and the bloodthirsty wolves.
This is where Lugaru’s strength ultimately lies; in it’s unique combat psychics which in many cases can also incorporate knives, swords and bo staves, usually through the disarmament of an opponent. Utilising only three context-sensitive commands that allow for evasive manoeuvring, attacks and counter-attacks, timing becomes a key element within each fight and strategy is tantamount to survival. It is this sense of realism and freedom that makes every decision in Lugaru feel tense and satisfying in it’s execution.
Since Lurgaru’s release in 2005 the video game has developed a significant online modding community which has led to several new campaigns and graphical upgrades. Tim Soret’s HD texture pack, for example, was so well received that it is now included in Lugaru by default which led to the re-release in 2010 entitled Lugaru HD.
Although the central campaign in Lugaru can be completed in just under a few hours the additional difficulty settings, challenge levels and it’s addictive “pick up and play” gameplay really add to the replay value. Easy to learn, but difficult to master Lugaru HD is unique in it’s execution and highly recommended.

Bastion.
It's simply down an amazing game, it looks great, has a good story (I did not use the word great for reason; it has room for improvement), good gameplay, and an amazing soundtrack.
Gameplay:
The game itself starts off slowly paced, which might be discouraging. In the later stages of the game, however, once you unlock more weapons and get more stuff to play around with. It becomes so much more better. In fact, the further you go, the more "enjoyable" the weapons become. I'll not spoil anything, lets just say they become bigger, better, and heavier.
A level lasts about 5 to 10 minutes and can be replayed to recover things you might not have found during your first time.
Story:
Additionally, the story - It is just a good story, the narrative idea of the game is very appealing and the voice actor leaves down a stunning performance.
The bad part is though, it's not very long. While I should not ignore the fact there are plenty of minigames, optional things to do and layouts for replayablility*, three hours of gameplay is roughly in it to complete the game doing a mixture of main & optional tasks.
Exploration:
Bastion has a good mixture of exploration in my opinion, you can side-track a little bit off the main areas and find some goodies. They are not crucial to beat the game, but definitely help out a lot.
Soundtrack:
Honestly, I can't lie, the soundtrack is just down right amazing. It adds to the environment, sounds pleasant and fits right in. If I was not a Spotify user; I would have considered laying down the extra 2 euros and purchasing it from Steam.
Rating, conclusion:
This sums about my experience of Bastion, based off of four hours of gametime in the game, completing the story once. Having a balanced playthrough of exploring, completing optional tasks, and doing main quests.
So without further ado, here is my opinion, laid down in scores:
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Story: 8.8/10
Price: 9.5/10**
Soundtrack: 10/10
Replayability: 7.6/10*
All in all, I'll rate the game a solid 9 out of 10.
-----
* I have not tried new game + or any of the other new games yet. So my opinion based towards this might be factually incorrect
** Although the original game is 14 euros at date. I picked it up for 3 during the summer sales. The price however, is judged from full price.  14 euros is not a bad pickup. Although we can all agree to it that 3 euros is a better grab.

This is my review of Tower Unite as of December 31st 2016. As of writing I have around 140 hours in the game.
As someone who was supporting the game from the minute the original Kickstarter went live I can say that around 9 months into Early Access Tower Unite not only shows a lot of promise for the future but is incredibely fun right now.
----PLAYER CUSTOMISATION AND CONDO----
Right now the game's customization system is a lot of fun. Unlike a lot of other Virtual World games Tower Unite doesn't restrict how you customise yourself to realism. In this game you can be a man in a business suit, A dancing milk carton wearing a cowboy hat and even a purple skeleton with a computer monitor on its head. With lots of accesesories and four playermodels as of now Unite's customisation is incredibely fun and lets users express themselves in lots of ways.
The Condo system is also incredibely strong and surprisingly flexible. While upon first glance the Condo system may appear to be a simple drag and drop furniture system its actually so much more exstensive than that. With grid snapping and lots of construction items you can build your own unique structures not only that but the items on sale have lots of range from crummy old Victorian furniture, luxarious items like hottubs and even laser projectors and dance floors. There are a lot of oppurtunities to show off your creative juicies in the condo and I've seen some absolutely crazy creations in other people's condos.
----PLAZA GAMES AND CASINO----
The Casino is one of this game's most popular features and its easy to see why. The machines are not only varied but fun with machines like Grand Quest where you play a JRPG Battle game where you slay a dragon to win your Jackpot, Spin To Win where you spin a wheel in hopes of getting cool prizes, theres also traditional games like Texas Hold Em' and Video Blackjack. So all in all the Casino is a bunch of fun and is a great way of earning money.
The Plaza is also a fun place to be as it hosts a variety of games currently being Typing Derby, Bowling and Trivia. Trivia is hooked into an API meaning that it boasts over 1,500 questions. Trivia is extremely addicting and lots of fun to play with friends. The rivalries me and my pals have had in Trivia have been intense.
Typing Derby is simple but fun, its not really addicting like the other games but is still a nice little bit of fun here and there.
Bowling is really great fun for four or so friends. Its quite a relaxing experience and pays out very generously. You can even spend units on buying fancy bowling balls, right now I'm hosting a nice fireball bowling ball with a cool explosion effect when you throw it,
----GAMEMODES----
Out of the four gamemodes right now Minigolf is by far in the best condition. It has the most maps and all of them (except for Waterhole) are fantastic. The physics are supersmooth and the maps are excellent. They feature really nice gimmicks such as bouncing off bongos, shooting out of canons and even teleporters. Mini Golf pays out very generously and is always a blast. I also really like how your hats show up on the golf ball, thats a nice touch.
Ball Race is also lots of fub with levels featuring speed boosts, jumps and bumpers galore you're going to be having a fair bit of fun on this mode. However the mode suffers from a poor map selection. While some maps like GLXY, Summit and Paradise are lots of fun those are probably the only maps you're going to be playing as Memories, Midori and Nimbus simply aren't fun. The ones listed later suffer from blocky and unfun level design which can sometimes but downright unfair.
Virus is still in Beta and it shows. This mode can be a bit of fun but just isn't really worth playing. The large problem with this gamemode is the poor shooting mechanics which according to the Devolepment Team are getting fixed very soon. Also if you have less players this mode is extremely pro-survivor. The map selection isn't too bad with Hospital and Overtime being fairly solid maps. Overall Virus has a lot of potentional but is ruined by awful shooting and questionable balance choices. If these can get fixed I can see myself potentional playing Virus a lot.
Planet Panic, where to begin with Planet Panic? This mode is in Alpha and much like Virus that can be seen. I love the asthetic of this mode, Cats and Dogs in UFOs is such a pleasently bizzare thing to see flying around on my computer screen. Also the Vaporwave music is super good thanks Will. However, there is zero fun factor in uncontrollable and slidey UFO physics combined with sloppy and floaty shooting. This mode is still in Alpha so I think I can let in slide but god damn there is no reason to play this mode.
Overall Tower Unite is an extremely fun and charming game, that coupled with the extremely transparent devolepment team and you have a game that has a bright and promising future on its hands.

Brigador: Up-Armored Edition
Is a game that isn't hard to learn, not too hard to master, but keeps you interested for a pretty long time.
The game is basically a mix between Syndicate & Mechwarrior 3050.
The graphics and atmosphere are very Syndicate like when it comes down to this Blade Runner like feeling and the music does a good job to support this setting also.
The Mechwarrior part is where it comes down to what combat vehicle and weaponry to choose for the next mission.
Although the missions are basically all the same, (Kill and or destroy X units of type Y) it doesn't get boring.
As a matter of fact, it's just a lot of fun to test your configurations, tactics, doing combat and exploring the various maps, reading the lore, etc.
It's a game that packs a lot of universe behind the scene and it shows in the small details; which is a great thing.
Is there something I would like to see in the game?
Hmm, maybe a sort of endless battlefield mode. (Random map, endless waves of enemies and see how long you can last. Just for the fun of it.)
But, something tells me that this wouldn't really fit in this particular game universe/setting. Although it could be lots of fun, I think.
The DLC is also worth every penny. If not just for the cool audiobook that comes with it. (If you like such things)
Fun games don't have to be triple A studio productions.
Brigador is proof of that.

I've recently got really into the NBA during the NFL off-season so thought I'd give this game a try. I got it for £9.50 (about $12) and I'm loving it so far. I've mainly played the MyCareer part of the game along with the MyGM. I also managed to get the NBA2K16 Companion App which works very well with this game, the extra VC from using it is very useful.
I first started playing through the MyCareer using mouse and keyboard and really didn't like it so the next day I went and bought an Xbox360 wired controller (The afterglow one) and it made the game so much better. Special moves and tricks are much easier to perform with it and it just generally makes navigating menus so much easier.
The graphics are nice. The players look great and gameplay is mostly smooth (only lags sometimes during the loading of the game during the pre-game show that plays before every match to keep you entertained while the game loads).
The customisation of the player and the MyCourt is good. My only gripe is that during the MyCareer, you get to connect with NBA stars who give you rewards when you spend off days with them. Some of these rewards state you get a special jersey/shoe, which I (and many others by the looks of it) presumed you could wear, this is not the case. Some of them you can wear, but most are put on display in your MyCourt which, although looks nice, I think I would have liked the option to wear them.
The actual story of MyCareer is... meh. It's very generic and some of it dosen't make for an authentic experience (yes, I'm talking about the fact that even if you are paper white, your parents and sister are still black) which feels odd. Also, I'm not too keen on the voice of your MyPlayer. I would have much preffered them to have a customisable voice which better represents you or what you want your MyPlayer to sound like.
I heard quite bad things about the soundtrack for this game and, when I listened to it myself, it's not too bad, but, the thing that lets it down is that, as quite a large amount of the songs are censored, you often end up with lots of 'breaks' during each track as it is just muted out. Some songs have tonnes of censored words in which makes it even more annoying. The soundtrack is redeemed for me as it has some good songs on it such as 'Cult of Personality' which I was quite surprised by.
In conclusion, you would definatly benifit from having a controller with this game. The customisation of assests within the game is great, and once you get past the cutscene parts of MyCareer and start playing full seasons, it's really good (the 'story' part should only take about a few hours to complete so it's not bad). The NBA 2K16 Companion app is very much reccomended and it's fun to play when you're not at your PC.
I would reccomend this game to anyone :)

I've played  all the major AC (I, II, Brotherhood, Revelation, III, IV, etc.) before this one and this is hands down the one with the worst controls and interactions. Trying to control Arno feels like pressing the button and hoping for the best. Yes it has impressive animations and graphics but I don't think they compensate the frustation that this game can cause.
PROS:
- The recreation of the 18th century France is damn impressive
- The graphics are pretty cool. The facial expressions and illumination are a major leap in the franchise.
- Nice parkour animations, very fluid between movements.
CONS:
- Awkward controls. The "magnetic" grips from past games are even worse in this one. The way in what the character chooses which grip should he stick to looks so random. A lot of times Arno will jump to an unexpected location because he thought that the grip that was 2m away in a random direction was better than the one you had half a meter in front of you. The cover system is awful as most of the times I cannot predict where will Arno stick if I switch between covers .
- Combat system is still not good enough. Ubi has artificially raised the difficult by increasing the enemies damage and making the counter chances harder to see. A poor man's Batman Arkham combat system.
- Bad AI. It wasn't that great in previous installments of the franchise but in this one is plain terrible. In the past games at  least enemies were somewhat efficient when in the pathfinding but in this game I've found many situations where a group of enemies were stuck against a wall or an obstacle trying to cross it just because they have vision of me through a crack.
- The story is pretty plain and the main characters not likeable enough. This is a very personal one. Arno is like Ubi has tried to create a new Ezio but without his charisma. The story is again, just the typical vengeance stereotype.
- Technical issues. Typical in the franchise. NPCs that jump, falls or walk against a wall with no reason etc.
- Horrible framerate and stuttering. With an i7-6700k, GTX 1070 and 32 GB of RAM the game sometimes suffers random framedrops that render it almost unplayable. Not even choosing the lowest setting seems to fix it. WTF Ubi, WTF.

Fallout has been one of my favorite game franchises for a long time. Ever since I first booted up Fallout 3 and created my first character, stumbling around the wasteland trying to figure out what I was doing, I've enjoyed countless hours of these games. I've technically bought 3 copies of Fallout 3 and New Vegas over the course of my life. (Vanilla versions and GOTY versions for X-Box from Gamestop because a used GOTY copy was cheaper than buying the DLCs individually, and a copy of each for PC.) I've enjoyed this series so much, and that coupled with all the fun I had in Skyrim made me start to become a fan of Bethesda. I looked forward to Fallout 4 with so much anticipation that when the game launched, I woke up at 2 in the morning due to sheer excitement keeping me from sleeping. Then I couldn't play the game because it crashed on launch. But a year later I tried again and it worked fine. I went into the Commonwealth later than I anticipated, but I stepped out of that Vault with wide eyes, full of joy. I pretty much completed the game, including the Nuka-World and Far Harbor DLCs. (Not the Automatron DLC because I couldn't afford it at the time and preferred to not bring a companion, which seems to be the biggest drawing point of Automatron.)
After having nearly burnt myself out with Overwatch, I decided to play a single player game. I chose Fallout 4. I came back, and a new option appeared on the main menu that I didn't see when I last played. Creation Club.
What a ♥♥♥♥ing mess. Remember when Valve and Bethesda last teamed up for paid mods for Skyrim and there was thievery between mod creators stealing each other's content for profit? And people were outraged to the point where Valve shut it down nearly instantly, and were forgiven because ♥♥♥♥ it it's Valve?
Bethesda's back at it again with paid mods. I thought I could ignore it and go on with my life but then I learned that Creation Club content is already installed onto my hard drive, and that when I buy and "install" it, I'm just installing some key that unlocks the files for use. So I just chose to turn off auto-updates to not run out of disc space for this awful business idea. But that didn't last long because now there's an update to Fallout 4. And instead of the update being the removal of Creation Club, it's the addition of more content to it.
Fallout 4 was a fun game to play while the fun lasted. It wasn't the best RPG, but it was a fun game regardless. I genuinely enjoyed Fallout 4, if I didn't I wouldn't have put so many hours into it. But now Bethesda is pulling their nonsense again.
At the end of the day, Fallout 4 is a fun game. It's built up a community of people with a big enthusiasm for the game franchise, and we've all had a lot of fun sharing stories of our adventures in the Commonwealth and such. But until Creation Club goes away, and Bethesda learns that paid mods, which is what this is, regardless of what they excuse it as, I'm afraid that I'm going to have to stay out of the Commonwealth.
It was a really fun ride while it lasted, and I'm glad to have shared it all with you guys.
That being said, if and when Creation Club is removed, I'll leave a review on my actual thoughts on the game. But until then, should you play Fallout 4?
No. Unless you have it on console where it's free from Creation Club's vicegrip, just turn off auto-updates, leave a review criticizing this horrible business direction, and hope that we get our game back.

You control Hercules' servants as the gather wood, food and gold and clear obstacles with these resources to move on to the next level with the ultimate goal of saving Herculeses' wife Megara who was kidnapped by Hades. Hercules himself chills in his hammock as his servants run about and wakes up only a few times per level to show off his strongman skills. During the game he gets help from his BBFs Medusa, Pegasus and Cerberus, each with their unique ability. Slightly mythologically incorrect, but their mechanics work well with the game.
Very charming game, cute art, fun music (though it does get repeatative after a while). Simple and intuitive mechanics. A sort of 'my first time & resource management game' that is still fun for more experienced players. All achievements are easiliy obtainable and do not require parts to be played expert mode.
The 'poems' explaining the story are so bad they're good and I didn't care much for the narrator. For some reason this game does a Disney and calls Hercules by his Roman name and keeps the Greek names for everything else.
The full price is perhaps a bit much, but on sale this is definitely worth the money.

What can i say about Retool that.... It's a game? it has idea's? I'm sure the developers have had the best of intentions with this title, but from top to bottom this title is a mix of bad mechanic to worse execution.
Full review:
Text:
As always, watch the video for the best possible impression of a title.
Retool markets itself as a hacking puzzle game, where you would assume that would be it's two main focuspoints. Hacking mechanics and puzzles.
Sadly, starting from the top, the hacking is ... weak. you use a console and suddenly to can reconfigure some lines on the map, sometimes you need TWO consoles, but the base is really that. The UI is annoying with different buttons for actions that have no reason to be separate actions, with MANY of the "hacks" serving no purpose, boiling it down to "lets move to the lines so the doors open, and remove all the other lines so I don't get shot by a turret".
The AI doesn't react to any of that, fellow AI will gleefully ignore a corpse and keep moving on their linear path. Also, the AI doesn't use sound, movement, hacks, triggers or audio warnings of any kind to be alerted.. merely it's VERY tight (and exploitable) view cone (that you can always see and cant turn off).
Oh, and all the puzzles are exploitable. Yay.
On the graphics department... you play in SPACE... on floating platforms. I wish i was making it up, If this was a prototype it would be bad, but this is a full release. Also, both character animations and the VERY repetitive graphics just makes the entire thing feel.. ugh.
Lastly, the sounds are poor as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Everything from movement to guns doesn't sound close to good.... so honestly, from top to bottom this game has taken very good idea's and ♥♥♥♥ed them up top to bottom.

Oh Starbound. My love. We have had a rocky relationship, haven't we?
I liked starbound back before the major winter update and I still like it. I think it is a great game with great gameplay, art direction, etc. It is honestly one of my favorite games.
And I really don't why some people have issues against it. The game has a lot to offer and is extremely fun, especially with friends. Many people like to think of it as terrario 2.0 in space but I believe there is more to this game.
Some of the best aspects of this game include:
-The Races (+ their ships, armors, weapons, etc)
-The scale of the universe
-The random encounters on planets with settlements, prison camps, labs, etc
-The combat
And much more.
But no game is without its flaws.
One of the biggest issues, in my opinion, is the fact that a lot of the planets are uninteresting. They all have some form of a random encounter as you explore but more often than not, you will be seeing the same ones over again. Something that would really help this is making some special planets that are more interesting like the various race's homeworlds for example.
Also the ship upgrades are really hard to get and aren't that interesting seeing as the races have the same quests. The all are pretty much fetch quests (some of which are extremely specific things that are hard to come by naturally so most of the time you'll have google ready) with the occasional dungeon map with a boss at the end. If they could find a way to have more variety in the quests based off what you do and which race you are, it would make the experience that much more enjoyable and give players reason to try the different races.
And, for me at least, the worst part is the fact that they changed needing to eat to it being a buff. This completely negates a huge chunk of content, being farming and cooking. Sometimes it was annoying to need to find food to survive but that was part of the fun. In these games you start with nothing and build yourself up to have everything. What's next? Being able to spawn in finished buildings and to have a button to give you everything? I want them to bring this back so badly because I really miss having a reason to farm [Insert saddest face you can imagine here].
Now you might be saying "Razu, why do you go over the good stuff so quickly and talk so much about the bad?"
Its because what they did great is already great and the devs only have to focus on what needs improvement to make Starbound the best it could possibly be. And I honestly believe Starbound can be great and I really want to see it too.

Stardew Valley is a beautiful, relaxing and thoughtfully made farming sim - but it has so much for players beyond this niche interest.  While it is chiefly concerned with repairing and building up a farm from the ground up, the extra features of interacting with townspeople, exploration and simplistic dungeon-crawling make this an extremely accessible and enjoyable experience on many levels.  For the traditional harvest moon, animal crossing type player - there is plenty to get stuck into, but there is a world beyond this that is far more involved and engrossing.
My only detractions are that for any player not enamoured with the farming mechanics-access to and exploration takes real game time - some dependent on your advances with your farm/character level, others on season and time elapsing during play.  Also, the finite time and energy  that you are afforded to make progress with each day keeps you backtracking - a lot.  Repetition in farming I can take, but with the RPG elements, more freedom would be nice.
These two issues are not inconsiderable, but part of the charm of this game is the real sense of progression you feel as you make your farm viable, then diversify and are rewarded by these ancillary options and tasks.  The game is intentionally lengthened by the day/night and energy mechanic limiting your progress, and by the expense attached to upgrades-but this makes advancment all the sweeter as a result.  It has the "one-more-turn"appeal of a quality strategy game, and yet the feel of a freemium game without the paywall.
With the inherent charm, relaxed pace and retro atmosphere, this is one game that I can happily recommend.

This game is coming along really nicely from the time I first got it. A few major updates have come out, and have really stemmed the tide of complaints people had that the game was some sort of abandonware title.
First off, the introduction of the outpost and merging of systems into a cohesive universe is incredibly refreshing. The progression, while unbalanced due to lack of necessary story elements, is logical. You can definitely see where it is going and how things are going to work.
In preparation for the combat and story updates, the crafting progression has been nerfed, which is disappointing. In the long run, this may make more sense (though I hope they add a bit more complexity) as the story is really what they are preparing for.
The rewrite of the engine that allows for missions has now been utilized to create challenge portals, which are super cool to find, and a fun distraction. The amount of new items in general adds a lot to the exploration aspect of the game. With hundreds of new structures to find, I'm excited to explore again.
The plethora of new items and item sets also plays into the new colony aspect of the game. While before, in earlier versions, exploration was the main point of the game, the new colony feature has shifted that focus to building and maintaining your colony. Different item sets and combinations allow for different types of citizens --guards, civillians, and merchants-- that act differently depending upon the nature of their contents. Make a house full of sword furniture, and you'll probably get a guard. Fill a house with treasure chests and jewels, and you might get a guy that resembles the monopoly man. The possibilities are endless, and make great usee of the objects found all over space that were so fun to collect, yet hard to find use for.
All in all, a solid product, with two more solid updates planned for the future. 10/10 for an early access game.

This love letter to the 80's not only has a bombastic synthwave soundtrack, it lives and breathes it: dark humor sci-fi that laughs at the absolute carnage that a mechanized war machine can wreak upon densely populated urban areas. Story is lacking, but this game makes up for it in style and gameplay.
While the campaign at first shoehorns you into only one loadout per mission, it branches out about 40% of the way through to allow you 3-4 different loadouts per level, each one changing the way you play drastically, from taking and dishing out massive ordnances, to hit-and-run tactics.
The game is best in the former as you're likely to get swarmed by large numbers of enemies. It never gets tiring firing a 140mm cannon into a large group of enemies. The visual feedback in this game is phenomenal.
As to what I didn't enjoy, the isometric angle also makes it difficult to tell exactly where your shot will land, leading to plenty of missed shots.
The limited ammo system can be hit-or-miss. It adds a lot of tension as you often have to pick your shots instead of simply spraying everywhere, which is a plus. However, if there are no enemy ammo drops to be had, your only recourse is to reload at ammo dumps.
This is no fun at all given that it has to be the RIGHT type of ammo dump, often ALL the way on the other side of the map AND it is easily blown up AND it has limited ammo. Even less fun if you have a slow, lumbering vehicle and there are a million obstacles in the way. Running out of ammo happened more often that I would have liked, and I feel I was already playing conservatively when possible.
Thankfully, there is a built-in infinite ammo cheat easily accessible through the developer console via F1. So these negatives are moot depending on how you want to play this game (namely if you just want to blow stuff up). Even then, these negatives largely don't get in the way of the mountain of fun to be had.

I took my chances and bought this game knowing its never ending story of bugs and plain gameplay.
First of all, I'd like to say that I'm in fact a fan of the series. I've played every single Assassin's Creed except for Syndicate. I like the games, so this might influence my point of view regarding this review.
Performance: I don't have an awesome computer. I played Black Flag upon release and the game did not run smoothly at all.  Suprisingly enough, Ubisoft has made some big improvements to this game in particular. I had a solid framerate on high settings, practically no game breaking bugs that could hinder my experience and hardly no crashes, only a few upon launching the game and only once did I have to restart the game because I had gotten stuck. However, thanks to the checkpoints, I didn't lose anything. Great job Ubisoft, you managed to partially fix a game which everyone said was unplayable.
Game mechanics: If you are coming from any previous AC, you'll gave no surprises when it comes to climbing mechanics. Furthermore, combat has been greatly improved. We finally have difficult combat in which you can and certainly will die if you don't play your cards well. Avoiding being detected is almost never a requirement anymore, but you'll try to meet that requirement anyway, since facing 5-7 guards it's quite the task. Still, the game was not thaaat hard, but I like how they've improved combat.
Missions: Not that many tail missions (Yay!) and a lot of assassination ones, which I LOVED. You can have practically any approach to them; you can be offensive and get into big fights, taking guards one by one without being detected or maybe just climb your way to a secret entrance and kill only your main target. I found this missions really enjoyable, and there are quite lot of them. Great job Ubisoft!
Story: Big part of this game. I liked it. I wanted to keep on playing every time I finished a mission and that tells a lot, specially after games such as AC3. France atmosphere, the revolution, Assassins and Templars, romance. Well, it's got a nice set of resources to tell a good story. I think it delivers. Is it too linear? Maybe, but I still enjoyed it. I only focused on the main missions and took me 16 hours, which is a decent amount of time. I still have plenty of other content to go through. If I had to compare this to others Assassin's Creeds, I'd say it's at the level of AC4 or Revelations.
Map and lore: Paris is beautiful. It's been done perfectly with the people and their clothing, the famous buildings, the events on history, riots, revolutionaries against loyals to the crown, rich and poor areas, etc. If you want immersion, I'd definitely recommend you read the biographies and pieces of information that they give you of every place, it'll be worth your time.
Conclusion: I bought it for 10 USD and it's a nice deal. Full price, nah, but what game is worth its full price nowadays? If you are thinking on buying it but you are afraid of performance issues, don't worry. Pay attention to the next sale and buy it.

I have played Realm of the Mad God for many years, and it has gone through a lot of changes.
For a year or so, Kabam bought WildShadow Studios and fused ROTMG into a Pay-for-Advantage game and everyone hated it. A lot of the community left after that.
But if you give it another shot, you'll see that everything can be obtained thru just playing the game.
Skins, cloth, and bonus weapons can be obtained from a new addition called the Tinkerer. Complete all 4 of his quests, (they reset each day,) and you will get an alchemy orb. Use an alchemy orb for a chance to get one of the featured items. Weapons can be obtainable by Oryx, event bosses, and dungeon bosses. So can armor, eggs, and pots. (potions that increase your max stat by 1)
I encourage you to give this game another shot if you haven't already. It's not filled with nearly as much third-party websites, although there still are a couple. There's over 500 enemies to fight and they're all unique. And the loot is so very satisfying to get. The PAIN in your chest when you die is still there (I'm not joking it LEGITIMATELY HURTS YOUR SOUL WHEN YOUR CHARACTER DIES) so why shouldn't you give this another go?
TL;DR, I give this game an 8/10 for what it is right now. It's still not rid of all of the P4A, but it's damn near close.

Okay, I just played the game for an hour and fourteen minutes (I timed it) and honestly, it wasn't too bad. For all the bad reports this game has gotten I haven't encountered any issues with banning. (Maybe I'm just lucky) However, I would not recommend this game. It has many flaws in it and you can easily play Roblox instead. This game suffers from issues such as...
-Spawn Killing
-Bad Tank Movement
-Lack of reason to build things
-Poor weapon balancing
And the list goes on and on. I wasn't expecting much out of this game, but it wasn't the worst game I've played, no sir. Its up there but its not the worst.
I'll elaborate further.
Spawn Killing
This game doesn't protect your spawn in any real way. Your base can be destroyed, other players can build on top of your base and since you can't see the bullets fly, its incredibly difficult to catch campers. Trust me, I did this, and it was extremely difficult to get rid of me. The spawn should be changed so no bullets can go in, or out. The good news is, they can't trap you forever. The blocks are easy to break but that doesn't help much when Sniper McGee is waiting outside.
Bad Tank Movement
The tanks are absolutely garbage. They're fine in terms of damage and don't feel overpowered. However, they move so awfully. On flat terrain they're fine, just a bit stiff while on a "hill" they're atrocious. They go so slowly... like... as slow as Russian internet. (Sorry Russia, you made the game, you're getting hit with the mean jokes) Even downhill, you'll go extremely slowly. Just run to the enemy base and hijack one of their tanks and spawn kill!
Lack of Reason to Build Things
When I first played, I was the only one building anything. I soon realized why. There's no point. Your blocks will inevitably dissapear from gunfire or maybe they just despawn, I dunno. In addition, you have a limited ammount of blocks, thus limiting how much you can create in one given life. You can't make a base. A decent one anyway. All you can do is make stairs to get to the top of the enemy base and spawnkill them.
Poor Weapon Balancing
Snipers are king. They're so easy to shoot, headshots are insta-kills, and all the other weapons suck in comparison. Use your default M14 and you'll be golden. The shotgun naturally is useless and somehow unintuitive, and the MP5 just doesn't kill as quickly as the M14. End of story.
I know this game has a lot of flaws, but in the end, its not the worst game I've ever played. Just don't spend any money on it. If you get banned, uninstall... in fact just don't install it in the first place. There's way better games to choose from, like Dirty Bomb for instance and TF2 to name a few. Its just mediocre and thus, it gets a 4/10.

After playing 4x games for.....decades at this point, I still list MoO2 among one of the best I have ever played. After playing the remake, I can't help but feel extremely disappointed. Looking down the discussions list, I really do question what people VALUE out of this genre.
I do have a big problem with the lack of tactical combat. I think it's a damn shame. However, I will avoid talking about the lack of turn based combat, you can find about a thousand topics about that fairly easilly. But what about everything else that seems to be so poorly thought out and designed, or just plain doesn't follow what established Master of Orion as a great 4x IP?
To start: Star Lanes.
Why? There was already a very logical method to travel in MoO. Do you have X amount of fuel? Great, you can move Y amount of parsecs. If you can't get to a system you want to get to, you either make a priority out of fuel research, or build an outpost, which is also good for your ship count. This made exploration a much more active affair, forcing you to change your build order/priorities based on the system that was generated. Star Lanes are boring for exploration. Just mindlessly click the next thing on the path you've taken. Fuel also brings me to the next thing:
Research.
Simplified into (or copy/pasted from) Civilization. I like civ, but not as a 4x space game, which should take research very seriously. Research was half of what made MoO interesting. You COULD NOT know everything, unless you were creative, which was an ungodly expensive race trait (which got even more expensive after a patch). To know as much as you could, you had to trade. Or steal. Or invade. The "branched" techs in this remake are shallow, and boil down to extremely superficial choices of numbers (get more industry, or more research. Woohoo). In MoO 1 and 2, the choice was very difficult. Like mentioned above, you needed fuel. New fuel was often one of three researches, and the others in the same pool could be very useful, but if you wanted to fly farther, you had to make sacrifices. I don't feel like any of the remake's branched techs make you sacrifice much of anything. However, one in particular caught my eye, and that brings me to my next point:
Diplomacy
Why, oh why, is the ability to make a trade or research treaty stuck behind a tech choice? The other race, upon viewing my ship, called me up on my space phone and told me that they wanted to lay their eggs in my stomach. Could I not figure out how to say the word "trade" in their language? The method by which you do diplomacy also seems to be lifted directly from Civ, from the interface to the presentation of the alien race, lounging in their background of choice and talking at you as you decide how best to screw them over. What about the audience screen from MoO2? Or the holoconference from MoO3 (one of the few decent things from MoO3...)?
Cosmetics
Gone are the days of HR Giger inspired artwork. I understand why, it's hard to have art that detailed in a full 3D environment, but much of the game looks to be constructed of clay and coated in KBToys brand plastics. I won't say much on how the game looks, as that is as deep into opinion as I care to go, but I will say that for a PC exclusive game, I expect it to look much better.
All in all, I really think MoOremake is still in desperate need of work. Of course, we all know the game is easy access, and much will probably be changed. However, I doubt any of the changes will be drasticly different from what we see before us now.

The Good
Fractured Space aims to do space battles the way you'd expect them to be in real life. Large hulking ships (even the small ones). They don't move like fighters, the move like beasts.
No one ships is meant to be "better" than another. Rather, they are meant to be tools under the command of a skilled admiral.
This gives playability a fresh vitality as you learn to master each ship, and figure how the different abilities work.
Likewise you can customise your bridge officers, and their abilities to enhance the ship; especially if you want to focus a specific ability.
Thus, Fractured Space pursues a tactical depth while simultaneously also rendering an actionpacked play that can at times be heart-pounding.
The Bad
That's not to say it's all good though. The game suffers from issues common to other games such as ongoing balance problems, getting the best out of your crew or choosing the right ships in a match can be complex. Teams are not always evening matched, and if your team lacks experienced captains or fails to cooperate the end is always the same: you lose.
Though I'm bound to say that both winning and losing are fun, naturally you want to win. So, bad matchup after bad matchup gets frustrating. With a small playerbase, this can sometimes exacerbate the problem, and occasionally the wait times in queue (fortunately you can minimize the queue and look at stuff while you wait).
All in all, it's a good game with a fair amount of depth. I hope the game catches on with more folks, and that the unique ships, playstyles and focus on unique mechanics while still be the focus.
Considering it's free to try out, and dirt cheap to get into it's definitely worth your time to try out.
tl;dr; Unique space battles with big ships. Interesting tactical depth. Try it out yourself.

12 Labours of Hercules is the best Time Management game I've ever played.  The extremely tight tuning, flexibility of play and excellent presentation makes the game incredibly fun and rewarding, especially for those who aim for perfection.
As with other titles in the genre, you're tasked with completing a set of goals in order to proceed to the next level.  While the goals vary, the general concept is the same; collect resources and construct buildings to beat the timer.  Efficiently managing your workers is at the heart of the gameplay, although it's by no means necessary if you want to play more casually, but doing so adds strategic depth to what is in essence a very simple game.  Ultimately, the more effort you put into challenging yourself, the more reward you'll get out of it.
There are multiple ways to complete each level, but to earn gold, especially on Expert, not only are your multi-tasking skills put to the test but strategic planning as well.  Figuring out which routes need to be cleared first, the order buildings are to be constructed (and whether to level them fully or at all), and which of the multiple power-ups are most beneficial to reaching your goal is what makes the game so  fulfilling.  You can tear your hair out spending dozens of tries on a single level, but when you make that one small change that brings your +5 second run to a -5, the feeling of accomplishment is like nothing else.
A handful of mini-boss levels breaks up the standard gameplay with Hercules fighting off mythical beasts and smashing through barriers on his quest to save Megara.  These are enjoyable little interludes that add variety and humor to an already fun game.
Presentation is great as well.  I generally don't expect much graphically from these games, but the artwork is cute and the animations fun.  Musically, the soundtrack is a joy featuring plenty of classically inspired themes that are quite impressive for a casual title.  Topping it off is full Steam integration with achievements, cards, cloud saves, and even leader boards, something ALL casual games benefit from on the platform.
It's not often that I walk away from a game with not a single complaint, but 12 Labours of Hercules has managed that feat.  My only worry is that I will now hold all future Time Management games to the excellent standard of this gem, and that's a high precedent to reach. But excellence always comes at a price. Unless you absolutely abhor the genre, there's no excuse not owning this gem, especially considering the very generous sales it often receives.
Bottom Line: A must have gem that belongs in every gamer's library.

I have been playing Fractured Space on and off for just over a year now and in that time, it has remained my absolute favorite game.  It isn't perfect, but I just cant stop myself from loving it.  A warning though, for those of you who want an in depth space sim, you are looking in the wrong place.  Though the offspring of the space sim and MOBA genres, Fractured Space definitely gets a lot of its DNA from its MOBA side.  The flight controls are very simple and movement is limited to a submarine style navigation through space rather than full three-dimensional movement.  This is not a problem for me, but I can understand why some people might take issue with it.
Positives:
1. There is an incredible attention to detail given to the ships.  Each manufacturer has a signature design language, but each of their ships looks and feels incredibly unique.
2. Gameplay stays relatively fresh and the wide variety of ships available means that there are many strategies that can lead to victory.  Having played the similar Dreadnought, I can say without a doubt that the combat in Fractured Space is much more dynamic and engaging.
3. I think that Greybox is one of the few studios that has executed free-to-play very well.  Unlike other titles, spending money in this game is purely optional and buying a premium item will not give you any sort of combat advantage over other players.
Negatives:
1. There is very little in the way of progression, you can buy any ship at all so long as you have the credits.  While this prevents you from simply being outgunned by a higher level player, it does decrease my motivation to purchase new ships.
2. Matchmaking can be very lopsided at times, but I think that is a function of the relatively small player base.
3. Though the whole point of the game is space combat between capital ships, the sense of scale the developers were going for just isn't there at times.  There is simply too little variation between the sizes of the ships and objects in the environment to make the player feel like they are truly piloting some massive space ship.

However the middle lane is a buff that comes online and therefore you mostly only play in 2 lanes. There are no turrets only at the enimies homebase. You capture mines which help you level your in game level and upgrade your ship. The minons are the enimes mine carts.
Secondly, there is no shop. When you level up your given three options Attack, Defense, or Utility upgrade. Each of which is self explanatory. The game does counter this with a loadout for your ship. Example I can buy a turret or cannon that does more damage then the base turret, however it will have less range and maybe a high cooldown, you get the point.
Thirdly, ship control. Ship control is very smooth and balanced. Theres no roll, but that makes sense. I have never found my self stressing about the controls its super smooth!

Name: 12 Labours of Hercules
Release Date: 31 October 2013
Developer: ZoomOut Games/JetDogs Studios
Sets in Ancient Greek, help Hercules break the way to rescue his wife from the evil Hades! This is the first time that JetDogs has developed a Time Management game, to be honest, they have done well.
If you are a hardcore Resource/Time Management player, you would feel like you have played this kind of game so many times. 12 Labours of Hercules is nothing out of the ordinary, with simple gameplay, simple quests and similar story. The visual design is very flat and the colors could have been much more colorful. Despite that, the graphics are very sharp and quite calm to look at.
12 Labours of Hercules is not a challenging game, most of the levels are pretty easy even when the difficulty keeps increasing. It is a great game fro beginners as all the objectives are clear, the controls are nice and you also do not need to wait for your workers to come back before assign them with new tasks.
The game does have all the features required for a good game of this kind though. It has voice-overs, relaxed mode you can choose to play as well as pretty exciting Boss Battles every 10 levels. We also like the Achievements this game featured, it has some standard ones as well as some unique ones that require some work to achieve.
12 Labours of Hercules is based on a simple gameplay and plain designs with a couple of innovative aspects. Although it does not offer any challenges, it is a good, fun, relaxing game for those who are new to the genre.
