From my review posted here
"This point-and-click adventure is just as captivating for the details it omits as well as the ones it includes.
Serena was released today on Steam for PC, Mac and Linux. A collaborative effort between fans of older adventure titles and indie developers, it tells the story of a man reminiscing time spent with his wife and of how it all went wrong.
The gameplay consists exploring an old dusty cabin for memories of your wife and clues for what might have happened. Objects you click on trigger thoughts in the narrator's head, or dialogue from the wife. And that's pretty much all the action you'll find in this game.
You progress through the game by clicking through every single nook and cranny of the cabin, multiple times. Each time you've exhausted every clickable possibility, a new small space in the cabin becomes available for exploration. Pictures, a clock, and a poem all change subtly as the narrator passes through different states of emotion: bliss, confusion, anger, realization, fear, and morbidity. Funny the game should progress in this way. Hint: You don't get a happy ending.
I must admit, I found the writing to be extremely sappy and overwrought in the first stage of the game. But as I progressed, I realized that kind of tone may have been an intentional construction. It contrasts well with the later horrific pace and gives insight into the narrator's own peculiar mind.
Exposition in this game is top-notch. You'd be surprised how much backstory the game's 40 collaborating developers could pack into clickable scenery. I suppose this kind of imaginative detail must fill in the empty space left by the utter lack of video game action, and to the credit of Serena, this approach totally works for the game.
The music and the graphics add a nice touch to game's feel. The narration complements the writing. Although the game is boring for the first third of its length, if you stick with it to the end, you will be left with a sense of grotesque intrigue into what other things we may never know about the narrator's character. It's a game that stays on your mind long after you finish it. So if you have the time, go play Serena- it's free on Steam."

I'm about two or three hours into the game now so I can safely recommend it. It's ridculously fun, a little challenging (once you start to get to the missions where it gives you a lot of playstyle choice) and very very cool. You select from a series of hella cool mechs in order to complete various general tasks in big open maps that can (and most assuredly will) be reduced to rubble. The firefights here are intense and frantic, with shells, bullets and explosives flying back and forth with satisfying whooshes and thumps. Many isometric or top down shooting games can feel a little flat or limited, but thanks to the destruction and carnage this manages to feel meaty and deep enough to warrant a few replays. Whereas with one tank you might just run in and blow everything away with twin cannons, another might require you to make small rabbit holes in the terrain in order to smash and run on large groups of enemies and defensive positions. Sometimes the missions feel a little unfair for a chosen character, one springs to mind where you must avoid numerous suicide bombers with no ammo until you reach the depot beyond - with the slow moving tank it's nigh on impossible to even get out of the first area.
This aside, the challenge is there if you want it. I haven't dived in to the freelancer mode yet, but it appears that you can fully customise your mech loadout for maximum badass.

As with all my reviews, this is a lenghty one. In short, don't commit to this one - play 'Enemy Unknown/Within' because that game's brilliance has not been recreated here.
Oh boy, where to begin? So after the first one, the guys at Firaxis asked themselves: 'How do we top perfection?' Well, add more of everything, of course. Standart sequel procedure, I'll take that. However, in a motion that lets you question, wether or not the designers actually comprehend their own creation, the team also meddled with core concepts and mechanics of the game. Much to its detriment, I must say.
XCOM 2 puts you into the perspective of having lost the first game. Kind of a nut-punch, sure. But arguably, the story was never the drive of these games anyway, so let's just go with it. The organisation of old is now the resistance movement, objecting to alien rule on earth and your old 2IC needs you to lead again. Many of the game's limitations, like being only ever able to conduct one operation at a time or fighting a worldwide war with only a handful of people, actually make more sense in the context of fighting the status quo than representing it, like you did in the first game.
Now, to ram the alien Illuminati of their figurative seat of power, the game starts to put you through a wider variety of mission types than its predecessor and more often than not, killing everything that doesn't pass the 'human-or-not-human' test, is no longer of paramount importance. Oftentimes, you run in, steal some research, trash some radios, rescue a prisoner or assassinate a collaborateur. And then you hustle out of there, like noone's business. While you're at it, the game makes an effort to come across more difficult than XCOM 1, based in new enemy types, which you prepare to get frustrated with again.
Frustration is the keyword, however: The percentage system, for instance, does not seem to matter anymore. Wether you succeed or not, is always precalculated at the beginning of the turn. Same is true for the first game of course, but that one came tangibly close to the numbers it flashed at you. Here, you'll be making 30% and missing 80% in the same turn, because it's the former soldier's time to gain experience over the latter. Reviewing 'Enemy Unkown', I spoke on the topic of fairness. It was in no need of unfair moments. This game, on the other hand, will throw 'em at you a dime a dozen. Enemies pop up to flank you and by doing so, get a critical, which is to say lethal, damage bonus, resulting in more one-shot kills than are believable ... or bearable. On the topic of frustration, the mission timers need to be addressed, as well. I've played through the game once, with them in place, before seeking redemption in the mod workshop. I completely understand Firaxis' criticism stating that there was no urgency in the first game. That you could just wait and overwatch your way through a level. However, forcing the player to run the shortest, most unsecured path to his objectives, oftentimes at the expense of tactic or foresight, is not, I repeat, not the answer to this problem. Personally, I felt the timers to be deliberately too short, rushing me in my decisions.
Furthermore, this game ails from the same predicament that the first one suffered, which is its difficulty curve. After roughly half of the game you steamroll the competition without much of a strategy or use of the arguably pretty awesome abilities your soldiers can amass. Also, I still experience performance issues, specifically when buildings collapse into debris, each piece in need of a computed flight path. Although, again, this might be me only, for I'm running it on a toaster driven by a potato-battery.
Would I recommend it? Not in the state that they shipped it in. The only redeeming quality is the mod workshop. Everything I listed can be fixed here. The problem of balance still remains, though. Without some tweaking from the community, the game is too frustrating. With mods, its almost too easy, if a bit more enjoyable .... Buy it on sale. Do buy the first one, though. That was a damn good game!

When I discovered this had been released, I was very excited.  I saw "Mostly Positive" and read the reviews, because I felt burned by Master of Orion III and I didn't want to waste $50.  It scared the hell out of me that all the reviews were negative.  It gave me the impression that I shouldn't buy it, and I carried a bitter taste in my mouth for a couple hours.  Then I decided to do it.  I played MOO1 when it was a new release, and I keep the disks on my desktop.  (the only floppies I have that are not in the attic)  I'm a game developer, and this game has always been a personal inspiration.
So this review is coming from someone who knows and loves MOO.  I think this game is every step in the right direction.  I had so many concerns, and now I have none.  It looks to me like the designers went back to MOO1 and updated it.  I notice this isn't MOO4, it's MOO:CTS, right?  You could call it MOO4, if you wanted, but that sort of validates MOO2 and MOO3.  Now, I got MOO2 on release day, and I played the hell out of it and enjoyed myself very much.  I don't keep the CD on my desk, though.  I'll probably never play it again.  So I'm now happy to forget MOO2 and MOO3 existed, because these wonderful people have remastered a classic.
Each part of the game stays true to the original, yet is reimagined using modern game development techniques.  Systems are fun to fly around, look great, and make good strategic choke points.  Ship Design and Tech Trees have familiar technologies.  Planetary economies are simple to manage.  Realtime combat is great.  I am very happy with the decisions that the designers have made.  It is a beautiful game, and lots of fun.
When I reread the negative reviews now, they look like a bunch of people who don't understand the concept of Early Access, and that upset me enough to come on here and share.  I am a fan of the original MOO.  I enjoyed MOO2.  I thought MOO3 was horrible.  This game is MOO 2016, and it does justice to the original.

I wanted to hold off until I got a couple game completions under my belt before writing a review. I do recommend it, however I would suggest waiting for the actual release. There are several positive and negative aspects of the game, which I will try and go through in as much detail as possible.
+ Graphics and Music: The ship design and battles look and sound impressive. The score is reminiscent of Master of Orion, which is definitely a boon.
+ UI: The user interface is clean, easy to navigate, and provides a decent amount of information.
+ Races: The races are true to form for the original Master of Orion, though the racial bonuses are significantly weaker than they once were.
+ Next Turn Addictiveness: I found myself trapped in a civilizationesque pattern of hammering next turn to see what would happen. This is a good thing as it shows the game is immersive.
+ Ship Design: Mostly positive, I wish we could remove some systems entirely so I could build swarms of shield less missile frigates.
+ Excellence Mode: Allowing a turn cap is useful but unneeded really. I would mostly leave this off.
- Battles: The battles in this game, while visually impressive, are extremely shallow. There is no retreat button, there are no formations, there is no weapon selection. In every fight I wanted to watch, I simply let the AI command the ships because giving orders in this game is quite cumbersome and unneeded.
- Diplomacy: At one point during my playthrough the Alkari were on the verge of collapse. They sent forth their most diplomatic of ambassadors and... demanded a planet from me to stop? I bombed their capital into the ground a few turns later out of annoyance. It seems that no matter how good your diplomatic skills are, once you start expanding over a certain number of planets or systems, everyone hates you and will declare war on you if you don't supply them with credits frequently. This is not a good diplomatic system.
- Auto Build: Why does auto build always build Military structures first? Surely the population of my radiated planet would prefer hydroponic or fungal farms first instead of marines?
- Difficulty: Average difficulty is incredibly easy.
- GNN: Love the information, liked the droids for a brief period, now hate the droids.

I've played Skyrim, Magicka and Shadow of Mordor. I've read Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings and His Dark Materials. And yet this game remains the most magical experience I have ever had with anything ever. Only in this game are the rules of reality bent to a point where cars will roll over of their own accord, without you even telling them to (that's one step better than dogs!!1!). Only in this does 4 cars constitute a game (yep you read that right 4 whole cars omg wow ikr), and only in this game do textures like this constitute and I quote from the game description "beautiful challenging environments". I live in Australia and I can confirm that while we have roads as wide as the ones included in this game in Australia, they also happen to be OUR HIGHWAYS. This game was released on PC on 31st July 2014. THERE ARE WALLS TEXTURED WITH TREES AS THE EDGES OF THE LEVEL. THE TREES ARE 2D SPRITES. IN 2014. Another little happy magical addition to this overwhelmingly lovely experience of a videogame is the so called "handling model" which I'm fairly sure is based loosely off a shopping trolley they found in the Codemasters parking lot because the cars handle with all the predictability and elegance of a wet lettuce. For example let me talk a bit about jumps. When a car goes over a hill in a road, if it is going fast enough and the hill is steep enough, that car may leave the ground for a period of time in what we refer to as a "jump". Under no circumstances (other than the ones in this game obviously) do the laws of physics stop applying and we switch to moon gravity just because the co-driver decided to call that there was a jump, Such that you can be doing 60mph and COMPLETELY BARREL ROLL THE CAR OFF A FLAT JUMP. If you are looking for a realistic, enjoyable remake of the original Colin McRae Rally (which was a masterpiece), I suggest you go and watch paint dry. It'll probably be more exhilarating, and at least it won't crash between levels.

Let me start this by saying that if you are thinking of buying this game because you think it will be worth you're time, you're 100% right. Darkest Dungeon is a very unique, high risk dungeon crawler that is brimming with sadistic entities that exist only to stop you from continuing your progress and finishing your mission. If you're a strategist that loves a challenge, and you also would love a refreshing perspective on modern gaming, this is a game for you.
I've seen a good many reviews for this game become negative simply by the fact that it seems unbalanced and the odds are heavily stacked against you. And that's true; you can expect this game to really test your patience, as it is all about stacked odds, damaging situations with little room for recovery, and, as the game states every time you play, "Darkest Dungeon is about making the most of a bad situation."
For the sake of argument, the game will often stress its player and, in fact, discourage the player from even finishing the mission. A few "unlucky hits" on your enemies or "lucky hits" from the latter become a wound on your party. The implementation of the "stress" status effect in the game adds a whole secondary battle that the game forces you to play, and for a player that is used to diving into dungeon after dungeon without consequences other than physical health, this will be new territory.
The key to this game is to empathize with your party. Put yourself in their situation; weekly adventures into forsaken, dark, Lovecraftian- horror- filled- dungeons will do a number on your mental state. The same circumstance with the only light source you have snuffing out during your mission, which has to be finished regardless of the level of light. Again with the choice of abandoning the wealth of the mission to save the life of a party member, who may or may not have been useful to you, or having to venture into a dungeon with four party members, and leave with three.
The first few hours I had played this game became a very humbling game experience. The choices were brutal, characters were flawed to the point of aggravating, and every outcome was either bad, or both good and bad.
However, this isn't your typical gaming experience. It had undone much that I knew about turn- based combat and advancing in levels, and gave it a realistic spin, as if to say "this is what you knew about strategy games, and this is what a normal strategy game ignores."

If John Carpenter had ever made a film about mechs on an off-world colony, this would be the accompanying video game for that film.
Extremely detailed visuals that don't waste any of the pixels on your screen. The accompanying soundtrack fits perfectly and is good enough to stand on its own as well. For those few times when you
turn down the music, you'll be able to hear the whine of servos, hum of a particle beam, and the jarring crackle of high caliber munitions.
The story won't be fed to you during your missions, but if you're interested there is a 'lore' section accessible in the main menu (if those reams of text aren't enough to flesh out the world, there's also an audiobook/e-book available that gives more hints about the nature of Novo Solo and the city of Solo Nobre).
Controls on the game are challenging, but ultimately grant a very high level of control over each vehicle. This may feel like a twinstick at first, but do not let yourself be misguided by the top-down view. While some encounters can be won by brute force and reflex, most will require a level of tact to survive.
Brigador is brutal, deep, and unflinching. However, it can also feel clunky and unfair too. Trying to master the game in spite of those challenges has provided an extremely rewarding video game experience though.

This game may seem like a Terraria rip-off at first... but start playing it and you'll see how much more this game has to offer. There are bosses that have actual missions and quests.
The randomly generated dungeons have a very particular feeling to them, with each racial dungeon giving you a 'silent story' that you know is there even though you've not read it.
Villages of NPCs from different races, where different races will react differently to your presence (an Apex village will not try killing you as long as you sheathe your weapons, but a Glitch castle will hunt you like you're a Muslim and their Christians in the Crusades).
You can place ANY armor in your vanity slots, so that even if you have a favorite armor but it's kinda crappy stat-wise, you can still look the part with the stats of a top-tier armor.
You can pick from 5 different races, but the amount of customization you can give your character makes your character unique no matter what race he is. Chairs where you can actually sit on, mechs that you can build, a plethora of cooking recipes and much, much more.
Get this game if you like sandbox games. It is well worth it. Moreso than Terraria. Keep in mind: it's still in Beta. You won't want to wait to see the finished product.

Ok, so where do I start?
Having played XCOM:EU and XCOM:EW (the latter being more to my liking) and finding it good, but with a slightly too high reliance on randomness, I gave this game with the Reinforment Pack a try.
The graphics have been improved, the different setting (having lost the war) is intriguing and the gameplay options are exciting, basically allowing for many different skill- and itembuilds and therefore lots of experimenting.
The story is probably the most cheesy thing I've experienced in the past, but the cutscenes are nice and the story builds some kind of arc over the game, even though it wouldn't win a smile had it been a child's essay.
The game however, so many years after release, is an utter mess.
I had a couple of missions, where the boss gets to move after every action any member of my squad does, which is massively unfair in the first place, but the game bugged out and would block all actions except for movement the boss himself would fail to select an action. Ofc I had to restart the mission. Had this been on iron man, I would have been very♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
The navigation in the mobile command post is atrocious, with ever single action triggering 1s of an animation, that blocks all user input.
The performance is utterly abysmal, maxing out a GTX 1070 at 60 fps and some turns (especially in the last mission with a lot of enemies) thouroughly taking a minute to complete, without maxing either bus, gpu or cpu.
A part of the game is to move the command post over the world and reacting to events, for example supply drops.
Some of which taking 7 DAYS to get, rarely not interrupted by some important mission. 7 days for a huge crew to find a supply drop is extremely slow as well, for all those arguing with "realism".
The worst thing of all are the mechanics, that weren't really polished coming from XCOM1.
So the first game led people to creep and overwatch every turn until they found enemies. Firaxis said "No, that's bad". So they added a timer to about 60% of the missions, which is set extremely short (average turns left is 2.70 worldwide), forcing you to rush into the enemy, which you couldn't see before. Remember the XCOM1, where enemies would get a free move when they were detected. Here, they get it as well, unless you are concealed. So when you rush in, not only do you lack the AP to move back, but also the enemy can get closer FOR FREE. This should have been removed in exchange for the rushing and the time limits.
Also, don't you hate when you can determine before the move how probable it is to hit an enemy? Here, your troops like to miss enemies standing 2 meters away with a shotgun. Snipers on a roof, behind cover, can miss a straight line shot downwards on an enemy without cover, and the response fire can crit and kill the sniper.
Units like to fire through the floor, the roof, walls and trees.
To mitigate that you can get modules for your guns (which in itself is great) that allow you to deal up to 3 damage when you miss (which is absolutely braindead). Why not just add a mode where you don't hit all bullets, but some, dealing damage based on the amount of hitting bullets?
This makes the game extremely frustrating, and in conjuction with the RNG that's likely to let you miss  3 70% shots in a row forces save scumming.
But is it balanced at least?
Well, there are 2 spikes in difficulty: The start (first few missions) and the period of the 3 bosses. The rest is quite easy in comparison.
But why is it like this?
In the earlygame, the enemy has way more hp than your units, deals more damage, and has a mindcontrolling 6 hp guy right away. Remember the sectoids in XC1? The went to the gym and are on steriods now.
The boss era also is only difficult because the enemy boss gets extremely many moves, not because he'd require a special tactic or something.
Snipers and rangers are massively overpowered, both being able to crit for 20 damage in a single attack and allowing for successive attacks if a target dies, rendering the 3 other classes largely useless in comparison.
It's pretty sad, XCOM2 is not a bad game, not by a long shot. But compared to XCOM1, what did we get? Optimization is worse, balancing is worse, content is a bit bigger, but not too much compared to the long war mod, the gameplay on the worldmap is irritatingly erractic and the menus are even worse.
So in the end, it's a question of price.
60$ are way too much for this, as it lacks any Triple-A qualities.
I got it for around 30$ and I'm don't think it's a terrible price, but considering how old and still buggy this thing is, probably getting it for 15 bucks should be about right.
Ah, mainly I'm just disappointed by how many chances the good concept took to just be bad. I can only recommend this to very frustration tolerant people.

In short Brigador is a fantastic game that's niche enough that it isn't for everyone.  If you're interested in driving stompy robots buy Bragador.  If you like isometric shooters buy Bragador. If you like challenging yourself buy Bragador.   If none of those things are true or you want something casual to spend your time on there are better choices.
Now for the long version.  Brigador is an isometric vehicle shooter with both a campaign and freelance mode.  Either pays out money on successful mission completion which you use to unlock vehicles, weapons, special abilities, freelance missions, and lore.  The learning curve is relatively steep but managable, the tutorial missions at the start of the campaign are decent enough to learn the ropes.  The game can be quite difficult but that difficulty is always fair.
Campaign mode have fixed enemy spawns and a selection of 4 loadouts to bring to that mission.  Difficulty of campaign missions mostly ramps up with earlier missions being much easier and later missions being harder.  There is one curveball mission in the middle which probably rage inducing for some. The loadouts for each campaign mission tend to have a mix of reasonable and challenge loadouts.
Freelance mode is the meat of the game.  In it you choose a pilot which replaces the difficulty slider found in most games.  From there you select a vehicle, 2 weapons, special ability, and mission.  Freelance missions range from 2 maps to 30+ maps.  Individual maps have fixed layouts and psuedorandom enemy spawns.  Depending on the pilot, vehicle, and mission choices difficulty can range from cakewalk to 'I'm a skeleton in a golf cart, today the enemies will probably be exploding me for a change.'
Weapons range from a lowly peashooter machine gun to city block leveling artillery with a huge range of weapons in between.  Almost every weapon has a niche that needs to be considered when choosing your loadout.
Vehicles range from heavily armed nigh invincible supertanks to fast and agile but fragile agravs.   And a golf cart.
All of the choices available for for freelance give a ton of replayability.  Different vehicles give a ton of variety, a Lowmill plays nothing like a Hoker.  Even within a vehicle different loadouts can play very differently, a Raider with Kraken, Pinch, and smoke, plays very differently from a Raider with Harvester, Donkey, and camo.
Lorewise the game is set on a dystopian colony world far distant from earth.  The lore entries, pilot descriptions, and weapon descriptions are all written from the perspective of characters in the universe.  Each has their biases and knowledge gaps.  Personally I've found the writing to be uniformly excellent.  It's one of the better crafted worlds I've come across in a game, to the extent that when a new patch comes out the first thing I check is to see if there are new lore entries to unlock.
If the above sounds interesting buy Brigador it will be worth every penny once you have an idea what you're doing.

Brigador feels like a game that I missed in... 1995. A game where deaths feel like a collection of mistakes I can remember, not a game mechanic working against me. The music is great. The aestetic and graphics are great. The gameplay is great.
Brigador is a game that has been lovingly crafted, and I do mean that. Looking at the game while it's running (in a high resolution anyway) may not key you in on how it's doing what it does, but the game is entirely 2D. Even with the massive amount of rendering space on screen at once on my 1920x1200 monitor, the game still runs over 200FPS, and never drops. It's not an unoptimized mess, and it still manages to have a lot of pretty features for those who want the most to look at out of their game (The aiming path is rendered to make the 2D look 3D, and there is a lot of dynamic lighting to do the same).
With Brigador's Campaign mode you'll have most of the game's learning curve explained to get you on to a plain where you may start to use any of the vehicles, weapons and defences you purchase effectively. The first 12 missions aid you in controlling a Mech, a Tank and an Agrav (Anti-Gravity, or
, if you will). Controls are currently available to split between Agravs between Mechs and Tanks, and while some people want a unique control preset between Mechs and Tanks, if you aren't bothered by the same control scheme on both, you won't need to change it every time you want to use one or the other. Controls are available between forward being
north on the map (North being selectable as top left or top right),
north on the screen (always up, you control 45 degrees against the map's grid), and
forward is forward to the vehicle's heading (allowing you to hold W and D to walk in circles). Agrav controls are mostly the same except for
, where W will move the vehicle towards the cursor. Pressing A and D will still strafe relative to the vehicle's heading. This occurs mainly because a mech has heading of the legs, and the turret. The legs move, the turret does not. A tank has the heading of the treads and the turret. The treads move, the turret does not. An Agrav has the heading of a turret. The turret moves. If you've played Hotline Miami or are used to the way it handles movement, an Agrav might not feel too far off when played in
mode. There are a few options for control toggles: mech crouching, orientation lock, and Agrav low-fly height. Players may also change gamespeed (the default is 80, and the slider goes up to 100, or down to 50); the ingame loadingscreen hints recommend changing it down "if you use a controller or like seeing stuff explode in slow motion." I personally have left it at 80, but allowing people to change it is definitely a plus. Too bad you can't set it to 150% and play
.
The music is quite enjoyable, and I'd recommend the Deluxe edition from the start to save you a dollar (or two, depending on your currency) to get it's soundtrack (The Deluxe edition comes with an audio book and the soundtrack in MP3.) So far, my only complaint with the entire game is that the soundtrack isn't administered in FLAC. That's pretty impressive when you consider that I have no other problems.
Do I think Brigador is worth your time? Absolutely. Brigador's gameplay allows you to jump in at just about any time after you've made some bank to choose what pilot, vehicle, weapons and defences you want and then a set of zones to just play whenever. Pilots dictate the game's difficulty and additional victory cash rewards, with some pilots ranging from easier difficulties, to a pilot who's difficulty is at max on the first map you will load on (each pilot has a Bio, and visible stats for difficulty and payout bonuses, regardless of wether you've bought them using ingame currency. There are no loot boxes, and no way to use real world money to get anything in this game).
Brigador, post Up-Armored relaunch, is quite possibly the second best game of 2016 to me, second only to Titanfall 2. It is well worth your time and money.

Since I'm about to uninstall this one I figure I owe it a little review.
First, it should be noted that I've never played any of the other Assassin's Creed games and I downloaded this one long after its infamous bugs had been patched. I also bought it specifically as an 18th century Paris parkour simulator and historical tour first, with its murder 'n' mayhem gameplay a secondary consideration. As a result, I'm coming at this with very little baggage.
I enjoyed my time in Unity a great deal. Wandering its surprisingly accurate, slightly scaled-down recreation of the city was eye-opening and informative, like stepping out of a time machine. Killing awful people was a nice bonus. I played it with the French voice-over, and I was impressed by its quality and gravity. The story was servicable enough to follow all the way through, but it's the set pieces that leave an impression rather than the characters.
Tracking down the glowing Nostradamus riddle symbols was a fun sub-quest at first, but it's quite long and unfortunately the reward for completing it was only aesthetic, so I'd suggest skipping it.
Although the game makes a big deal about its multiplayer function, it ultimately wasn't important to the experience, so I mostly skipped it, did my own thing, and never felt anything was missing.
Overall I feel it was money well spent. I'd keep it on my hard drive as a museum, but it ties up too much memory.

TL;DR - Game is great, well worth the money.  Highly recommended.
-Pasted from a comment I made somewhere-
Awesome graphics, if you're a fan of the sprite style.  Everything is so detailed, all the buildings, mechs, enemies, piles of rubble you leave behind and even the little civvies running around.  The lighting is great too.  The flash from the various guns and lasers, all the neon lighting around, and the frantic little flashlights that kick in when you scare the civilians.  It also interacts with the environment really well, the shadows from your vehicles lights look awesome on the rubble and grass and stuff.
Sound and music are great.  Guns, vehicles and explosions sound very powerful and punchy, the audio helps everything feel like it has weight to it.
Everything is destructible.  For me this is more about seeing♥♥♥♥♥♥blow up in a battle than necessarily pathing through structures, which is slow and loud (but still fun)
The vehicles have 3 types, mechs, tanks, and anti-grav vehicles.  Within those three categories, there are a variety of sizes, with differing stats, weapon mount types and difficulty multipliers (more on that in a bit)
There are 3 factions that each have vehicles in those three styles.
Each faction has visual differences and, if I remember right, faction specific stat tweaks.  Nothing game-changing, but one faction may favor shields over hull strength for instance.
Each vehicle has a certain amount of hull strength, shields, and overcharge shield capacity.  Hull strength is just your hitpoints, can't remember if there's any way to replenish it (I don't think so).  Shields can be replenished, though they won't do it passively over time, but from pickups from destroyed enemies.  And overcharge is bonus shield capacity that deteriorates over time.
Each vehicle has two weapon mounts, from types like auxiliary, main, heavy, small (and a few others I think), that determines what guns you get to pick from for your loadout.
For weapons there are ballistic weapons, lasers and mortars/artillery.  Ballistic and lasers have a few variations like cannon, chaingun, machine gun, shotgun etc., and artillery has varying sizes/ranges.
Individual weapons have different stats for things like shield damage, hull damage, fire rate, reload speed, structure damage, penetration, magazine size and total ammo pool.  Penetration is pretty neat, some of the big cannons can fire right through multiple structures.  Nothing like rear-shotting an enemy tank through a city block.
You also get to pick one of four or five special abilites, like smoke screen, cloaking, emp charge.  They have a cooldown, but unlimited use.
I Haven't really played campaign at all, below mission info is about freelance/sandbox mode.
You start by picking an operation from the list.  Any op will always have the same maps and the same number of them.  So "Operation Whatever" will always take place on the drainage map, the slums and the canal for example, but the placement of objectives and enemies will be randomized.
Aside from taking place on different maps, each mission plays out the same.  You unlock the exit by doing at least one of the main objectives - kill a % of all enemies, kill all the commanders, or blow up all of the big artillery structures.  There are also a few side missions that are the same each time.  The more you do, the more money you earn for unlocking stuff.

A bit of background information. I've played every big AC title since we first ran around Jerusalem with Altair and the franchise and since come thus far that I feel it's fair to start comparing the games amongst each other. I did not enjoy Assassin's Creed Unity as much as I did the other games.

I've been playing Stardew Valley since about a week after its original release. As a former Harvest Moon junkie with a love for games that help me unwind, Stardew Valley has been a peaceful and fulfilling farm sim experience, coupled with a genuinely dedicated developer in ConcernedApe, who has invested himself fully into making his game as perfect as possible. It is truly rare to find a game with so much heart, and it is inspiring to see how the game continues to grow and evolve.
Feel free to play this game in whatever way makes you happy, and know that you cannot lose.

Before anything else in Unity, do yourself a favour and set the spoken language to French. I guarantee you, there is
more annoying than sitting through a conversation between French aristocrats at Versailles, performed in cockney English – it is just intolerable. Even if you don’t speak a word of French, set the language to French and enable subtitles. The game is
twice as immersive in French as it is in English.
Besides that, Unity is the game that could. It
have been the best in the series. It
have been a smooth experience. The technology is there. The visuals are there. The gameplay is there. The difficulty is, for the first time in this series, there. Unity takes place in an absolutely stunning rendition of revolutionary Paris. There are crowds shouting in the streets, burning furniture and books, there are people going about with heads on pikes after beheadings.  Guards are smarter and more lethal and for the first time in the series you may
from combat with enemies. You can also move better, more precisely and actually go and land where you want to.
The Nostradamus enigmas are absolutely enjoyable and give a high feeling of reward once you solve them – if you resist the stupidity of looking them up on the internet. The same applies to the murder mysteries – absolutely enjoyable if you play them straight. The main storyline is solid and has a good pace, though it can’t compete with the likes of AC II or Black Flag.
So why isn’t this the best AC ever? Basically, there is too much extra content and too much online focus. Too many weapons. Too many outfits. Too many co-op missions that need to be grinded again and again to unlock the aforementioned too many items. There are too many pickpockets on the streets of Paris and you get too many prompts to chase them down. Mind you that I played version 1.5 where these things are milder than the original release. However, the fact that even after 5 patches there are still some npc’s floating in the air above their market stalls is simply unacceptable.
The Dead Kings add-on is ok but really – it adds nothing to your experience other than a grenade launcher and some more hours of mercilessly assassinating thugs.
All in all though – you simply have to play Unity – because for all it’s little annoyances it is still an absolutely visually stunning game, with great gameplay, interesting characters and set in an interesting setting. Just as long as you do it in French….

Short, easy, but fun!  This game is a casual resource management strategy game.  You start each level with one or two workers who travel on set pathways and gather resources.  But they also use resources to clear debris and to build bulidings like a farm.  In later levels you have to carefully choose from multiple pathways to start out otherwise you run out of resources.  When there's a heavy boulder in your way you can call upon Hercules to get his lazy♥♥♥♥♥out of his hammock and heft the boulder out of the pathway.  Some levels have other characters that help you out like Medusa (yes, she's an ally in this game, not an enemy!), Cerberus, Cyclops, and Pegasus.
The levels are timed but it only matters if you want to get all the achievements and get the gold rating on all levels.  I found them very easy to complete in plenty of time for the gold rating.  I only had to go back to redo a few levels to get gold.
There are some "boss" levels which consist of Hercules alternating shooting arrows at enemies and using his strength to move boulders out of the way or break chains.  There is one really cool boss level where instead of fighting you have to gather specific ingredients to make a healing potion.  There are fruits and colorful potions scattered about and it tells you which specific one you need each time.
The levels do not take much time to complete, a few minutes, so it scratches that itch for quick build management strategy when I don't want to take the time to play a long involved game.
Can't wait for the sequel!

12 Labours of Hercules:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
After all these centuries, we have the truth behind this great hero of the Greek mythology. . . Ladies and Gents, Hercules always enjoy a snooze lying on his favourite red hammock! But we were never told of his faithful servants who helped him to achieve greatness.
“12 labours of Hercules” is an enjoyable casual / strategy game which offers you 50 levels to complete in a specific amount of time to get a “Golden Time”.
At the start of each level, you will usually start with one servant at your disposition.  You will be able to have more servants to follow your orders as soon as you upgrade your house. Sometimes you may come to their help and free them from captivity. You will use them for collecting foods, supplies, cutting trees, repairing roads, building farms, workshops and removing other obstacles.
Make sure you get a clear access to the regeneration spot (that is what I called them). Each of these spot has an item on it. It could be food, supplies or coins.  It will take 1:30 minutes to regenerate the item after you took it. Every order given to your servants needs foods, supplies and coins to be executed.
Further into the game, you will be able to use bonus powers that will make your servants run, build, regenerate supplies faster or even stop the clock for a while.

In regards to our extraordinary energetic Hercules, he will remove boulders, open gates, build temples, etc.  And yes, you will encounter minotaur’s, ghosts and other villains!!
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Easy to master
-	Great casual game
-	Achievements

Negatives:
~~~~~~~~

A great time passer.

Played this game long before it was on steam and loved it a lot. It has a very fast paced fighting mechanic that is very flexible. An enemy is jumping over you? Grab him and slam him into the ground. There are many hidden techniques to discover and master. The game is full of physical details that you may not expect.
The health system is very interesting because it is a mix of heal over time and permanent damage mechanics. A series of blows can weaken you a bit but you can recover from it if you get out of there. Being cut by a sword though will permanently hurt you and you can eventually bleed out.
Weapons can give you an edge but there is still a lot of detail in their use. You can throw knives but your enemy can catch them if they notice. A sword can end a fight quickly but the AI is pretty good at countering it and even stealing it right out of your grasp.
The levels are a series of missions that involve killing all the enemies. You are offered many choices in how to approach a level. Whether you stealthily take them on one by one, or jump into the middle of a group and mostly likely get wrecked. The story is a revenge story which is simple but presented very well.
Enemies vary in strength with wolves being the most powerful and can kick you across the map if they hit you right. Mostly you will be fighting other bunnies.
Graphically this is an old game and looks a bit like Morrowind but it does have some cool graphical tricks. Blood splatter is one that will attract your attention. Characters bleed realistically when cut or have their faces smashed. Models are great and the animation is pretty fantastic.
The sounds of the game consist of lot's of natural animal sounds with good impact sounds. Fight music is really memorable and gets your blood pumping.
Overall this is a very fun 3rd person brawler and the next game Overgrowth is a great successor to the game.

Every time I try to write a review of this game it starts turning into a book, not sure if that's on me or if it says something about the game. There is a suprising amount of depth to the game, and once you start going into one part of the game mechanics you end up having to cover all of it in detail and it just grows from there. Anyway, if you like gritty old-school cyberpunk with great worldbuilding and moral ambiguity, if you like the idea of an isometric shooter with a hefty graft of simulation and highly tactical gameplay, give Brigador a go.
It does have a fairly steep learning curve (probably not so bad since the Up-Armoured Edition added new tutorials and lower default speed, I started on the original release) but it's really worth it, and there's lots of replayability with the variety of loadouts and difficulty levels. Everything from huge mechs and tanks with heavy artillery which can level a whole block with one shot to tiny powersuits with gamma lasers which can cook the enemy through walls and nippy agravs which can flit through enemy fire and circle around to attack their weaker rear armour, you can find a build for pretty much any playstyle you want. At higher difficulties with the smaller, more vulnerable units you really need to think ahead and take full advantage of your environment and equipment to survive.
The devs have done a fantastic job of supporting and extending the game despite it sadly not being a huge financial success for them, adding new levels and units and improving the graphics, with more to come in future updates. Linux and OSX are both fully supported, I spend most of my time on Linux so I appreciate that.

As with all my reviews, this is a lenghty one. In short, don't commit to this one - play 'Enemy Unknown/Within' because that game's brilliance has not been recreated here.
Oh boy, where to begin? So after the first one, the guys at Firaxis asked themselves: 'How do we top perfection?' Well, add more of everything, of course. Standart sequel procedure, I'll take that. However, in a motion that lets you question, wether or not the designers actually comprehend their own creation, the team also meddled with core concepts and mechanics of the game. Much to its detriment, I must say.
XCOM 2 puts you into the perspective of having lost the first game. Kind of a nut-punch, sure. But arguably, the story was never the drive of these games anyway, so let's just go with it. The organisation of old is now the resistance movement, objecting to alien rule on earth and your old 2IC needs you to lead again. Many of the game's limitations, like being only ever able to conduct one operation at a time or fighting a worldwide war with only a handful of people, actually make more sense in the context of fighting the status quo than representing it, like you did in the first game.
Now, to ram the alien Illuminati of their figurative seat of power, the game starts to put you through a wider variety of mission types than its predecessor and more often than not, killing everything that doesn't pass the 'human-or-not-human' test, is no longer of paramount importance. Oftentimes, you run in, steal some research, trash some radios, rescue a prisoner or assassinate a collaborateur. And then you hustle out of there, like noone's business. While you're at it, the game makes an effort to come across more difficult than XCOM 1, based in new enemy types, which you prepare to get frustrated with again.
Frustration is the keyword, however: The percentage system, for instance, does not seem to matter anymore. Wether you succeed or not, is always precalculated at the beginning of the turn. Same is true for the first game of course, but that one came tangibly close to the numbers it flashed at you. Here, you'll be making 30% and missing 80% in the same turn, because it's the former soldier's time to gain experience over the latter. Reviewing 'Enemy Unkown', I spoke on the topic of fairness. It was in no need of unfair moments. This game, on the other hand, will throw 'em at you a dime a dozen. Enemies pop up to flank you and by doing so, get a critical, which is to say lethal, damage bonus, resulting in more one-shot kills than are believable ... or bearable. On the topic of frustration, the mission timers need to be addressed, as well. I've played through the game once, with them in place, before seeking redemption in the mod workshop. I completely understand Firaxis' criticism stating that there was no urgency in the first game. That you could just wait and overwatch your way through a level. However, forcing the player to run the shortest, most unsecured path to his objectives, oftentimes at the expense of tactic or foresight, is not, I repeat, not the answer to this problem. Personally, I felt the timers to be deliberately too short, rushing me in my decisions.
Furthermore, this game ails from the same predicament that the first one suffered, which is its difficulty curve. After roughly half of the game you steamroll the competition without much of a strategy or use of the arguably pretty awesome abilities your soldiers can amass. Also, I still experience performance issues, specifically when buildings collapse into debris, each piece in need of a computed flight path. Although, again, this might be me only, for I'm running it on a toaster driven by a potato-battery.
Would I recommend it? Not in the state that they shipped it in. The only redeeming quality is the mod workshop. Everything I listed can be fixed here. The problem of balance still remains, though. Without some tweaking from the community, the game is too frustrating. With mods, its almost too easy, if a bit more enjoyable .... Buy it on sale. Do buy the first one, though. In 2007 DLC was mostly restricted to map packs on consoles. Mr. Howard, our ever truthful dovahkin of a project leader decided in 2008 that Oblivion should have paid DLC that wasn't in the normative form of an expansion pack. To test the waters, the concept of the microtransaction was for something completely cosmetic: horse armor.
Now why would the audience be upset about something cosmetic costing $4 more than you've already spent on the game?
Well, why should any content be kept out of the game? Why should we have to pay extra for something that is useful? And if it isn't useful, then why bother?
If this paid scheme supplied us with games that we actually wanted to play: A new Obsidian spinoff, a Morrowind successor, or a "Fallout: Van Buren" remake then maybe the community could understand.
BUT, there's a huge problem here. We aren't getting the games that we want. We got ESO: Morrowind. We got an empty Fallout 4, and now insted of getting a new engine for the next generation, we are going to have a GoT game.
So what does this all add up to? In the last 10 years since Oblivion, nearly every single game on the market has DLC, is in early access, or has cosmetic microtransactions. TF2 literally broke underneath the weight of all their hats.
The takeaway in my opinion is that this incentivizes developers to release EVEN LESS content, knowing that they can outsource every missing feature to the community. Why bother programming a "vault" command, or a "climb" command when you can sell it as a "paid mod", and give the modder a small percentage of profit to appease them.
So i won't be buying any of your paid mods. And i probably won't be playing any new Bethesda games in the future, because i don't feel as though the player matters. We're just little cash cows that can be milked in as many different ways as possible, simultaneously.
All of this? It just doesn't work.

Starbound does for me what Minecraft couldn't.  Instead of taking forever to explore one island I can take forever to explore a few solar systems.  But then I can travel to any of the thousand other systems and explore them as well.  The different material types are as varied as Minecraft and then some.  You can grow food, build buildings, create better materials, hunt creatures, get into shootouts with the locals, etc.
in the latest version you can expand your ship.  You don't even have to develope planet-side buildings anymore if you don't want to.  You can literally live off your ship and expand it as you go.  There are now also more fuel types (fuel is needed to move between star systems), some more ceocentrated than others.
With the outpost you now have access to more quests, which means more adventures.  They can be as random as "Find me a stone USMC sign".  Do you remember what planet on what system you found that USMC prison colony?  You don't?  Time to go exploring and find another to get that sign!
There are "dungeons" on pretty much every planet.  You can dig down into the planet and find gnomish villages.  You can dig through several different layers of the planet and find everything from mushrooms to buried laboratories to underground lakes full of acid, all of which you can break down with your tool and use for yourself, either in a crafting recipe or as a decoration for your home(s).
If you like open-world construction games of a blocky nature, then this one is definitely worth trying out.  There are many to choose from these days and eveyone likes one more than the others.  If you're still searching for "the one" then play this one.  You search will be over.
The T.V. show can go die in a fire. This game is a must play.

Like many others, I grew up with Master of Orion 1 and 2 and (after the dissapointing MoO 3) waited for a very long time for a worthy sequel.
So far, Master of Orion looks that it might be that sequel, though given that its early access, it is too early to tell for sure.
Right from the start, the game feels very familiar to a veteran MoO 2 player. You can tell that this game was made by people who know and love the MoO franchise. Most changes made to gameplay (like starlanes) are minor in nature and, at least in my opinion, make sense. The ship designer in particular is still there and not too different from MoO 2  (You can still outfit you ships with tons of different weapons and specials, as well as modify the weapons themselves - missles, beam weapons, point defense, firing arcs, ecm jammers, fighter / bomber bays, you name it).
The only real big change is the - much discussed - replacement of the turn based space combat with a (pauseable) real time version. While I am not to stoked about this myself, I do not think this is the end world, and - if done right - might even a good thing. Unfortunately, given that the A.I. is very limted so far in Early Access (the A.I.  difficulty is set to average for now), I have not been able to experience any battle involving two large fleets so far, where you could truly test the depth of the real time combat system.
Just to be clear (because I have seen wrong information about this), the combat is not merely a interactive movie, like (unfortuantely) in games like Endless Space. You have full control over the ships, i.e. you can designate targets, maneuver the ships and manually activate specials on the ships.
Anyhow, whether you think that MoO is a worthy sequel or not, it at the very least looks to have the potential to be an excellent 4X game,

Well what to say about this one. Possibly the greatest MOBA ever made with the worst team of developers and worst community to ever be behind such a game to date.
This game really does get so many things right, its an original MOBA set in space with easy controls, great graphics and simple gameplay. The biggest shame is that the developers do not seem to be listening to their community *at all* despite this game having been in early access for over two years now, it actually seems like the playerbase is smaller in the game now than it was over a year ago, backwards progress like this seems to be the norm for these developers.
Monthly patches are not always monthly, and do not always contain much in the way of new features. Often they release new features that people do not care for, or feel the game needs, all while doing nothing to increase the game's playerbase.
This game's playerbase, and its matchmaker are the real reasons this game will never be great. Currently matchmaking wait times can be upwards of 75 minutes. Then you get paired with a bunch of trolling ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s for a game that lasts 10 minutes long before spending upto 75 minutes searching for another game, and as the game's playerbase is so incredibly small, chances are you will be getting paired with the same trolls you were just paired with the game before. And if by some miracle you are not paired with ragetard trolls, you will likely be on one side of an extremely one-sided win, as games are very seldom close matches as the matchmaker seems incapable of properly balancing teams.
That leads me to the next thing about this game: One of the worst communities I have ever seen in a video game. This game has a disproportionate number of hardcore trolls, particularly of late. The number of people who join games with the sole intent of finishing missions or just playing for personal scores are overwhelming, and will consistently ruin the game for the remainder of their teammates, every single game. And when you have to play with the same trolls game after game after game, it gets really old, really fast.
After two years of playing this one in Early Access, even as a free to play game, I say find something else to play. All that awaits you in Fractured Space is a severely immature community backed by developers that do not seem to give two craps about the game they have made. Now they are starting to ban people in the game as well, and when the roaming in-game premade groups of trolls are being paired with you almost every time you search for a match, its only a matter of time.
Skip this game, maybe in another year, or two, it will be worth your time but right now and nowhere in the immediate future would I call this one a worthy investment of anyone's time. I myself will be shelving this game for another long period, hopefully the next time I come back to this game it will be a worthwhile addition to my game library, but right now  its a complete dud. And note that I have close to 1000 hours into this one, I do not write this review lightly.

One of the main issues players have with the game is the matchmaker. In its current state, it can and will put high and low end players together, and can cause many one-sided matches. The currently low population does not help, however this should change as ECG are ramping up their marketing campaign. However, most other games have balancing issues, so don't knock the game or Devs too much for that.
By far, this is my most played game, surpassing hours in games I've played for years in 6 months. If that doesn't say something, I don't know what does. It's a truly F2P, and deserves a shot as much as any other game out there!

Many of the options feel very different from one another adding so much to the depth of the game. You'll definitely keep coming back to try new things for a long time.

I actually loved the Xen section, with its imaginitive environmental design and overall uncanny atmosphere.
In conclusion: I have nothing new to say about this game.

Often I found myself stuck in a circle of jumping when I just wanted to use a damn ladder. AC III and Black Flag I felt had a good control system but they added this intuitive control system that has you jumping on walls for no reason and unable to drop to the ground when you hit the drop button. If I want to take fall damage that's my freaking choice. It's maddening every single time and the game is full of it. The only bright side is I have yet to run across any serious race missions, though the 'modern day' (don't want to spoil it) may turn into that later on. I'm still relatively early in the game.
Combat does a similiar thing too. In ACI - IV I felt I could basically deal with any threat as long as I was fast with my block and my attacks. I lose all this in Unity. Every swing can hit, my target randomly changes, I have no awesome moves like in the other games and the combat feels like a drop down to ACI in keeping it simple - too simple.
Even after all these patches, that I waited for before I bought the game, the game still has floating NPCs and full of bugs. I had my psychic lady get caught between two NPCs walking the opposite way and dragged all the way across the district for example.
The game is also a step back. It feels more like it should have been released before ACIII (though the graphics are great and detail amazing). In ACIII and Black Flag you were building a commuity, manning warships, etc. You're stuck mainly in one city, granted the city is huge and there's probably 100+ hours of content but that's all there is. Yes, the game is still open world, but it feels closed when compared to the open seas of Black Flag and the vast wilderness and warfields of III.
And Dead Kings DLC pops up after Sequence 3 I believe but it takes place after Sequence 12, so here I am thinking I'll be playing it chronologially and enter with mainly default gear against 5 star baddies with no way to return. For some reason I'm rescuing a kid and a book, the storyline is never really flushed out. Eventually you can return after you beat memory 2 of it but it gives minor spoilers.
Oh, and almost forgot. They have this new feature that lets you solve crime. Fun stuff, but the box that you need to read things is CONSTANTLY being filled up with tips and information about where you're at. I literally waited ten minutes for these tips to disappear on the Marat murder before I gave up. The thing wouldn't let me read the clues.

The game that helped put Telltale on the map, Walking Dead features one of the finest stories ever told in a video game.
Set in the the same universe as Robert Kirkman's masterful comic series, this game is a tale of survival and relationships.  The voice acting is excellent and the writing is in a class of it's own.
The gameplay is a mix of point and click style controls, quick time events and branching dialog trees. The story of the game  is driven by decisions you make during these gameplay scenarios.
While some might criticise the lack of any major divergence in the way the story is ultimately told (all choices largely lead you down a similar narrative) but I feel the choices impact the emotional tone of the game. Whether you do the 'right thing', take the moral high road or simply act blasé will impact your conversations/relationships with other characters and the general atmosphere of the game.

I never mentioned this story, but Telltale's original point and click masterpiece "The Walking Dead" has a very special place in my heart. At the time I thought that Telltale created a whole new genre, which we all immediately fell in love with, but after their latest games (Borderlands, Game of Thrones and Batman) I can see now what actually made me love TWD.
Telltale's TWD was one of my first games on Steam. Back then I didn't know how to check the forums or even properly use Steam. So when this game came out, I bought it and when I finished episode 1, I thought that I had to pay the same amount for all the next episodes. That's way overpriced, I thought, and with no knowledge of checking the forums or with no Steam friends to ask, I just uninstalled and forgot about it.
After some months when all the 5 episodes came out, I realized that I actually don't have to pay for them separately and can play them all at once. I immediately installed the game and played from start to finish in one sitting (~6 hours).
I think that's the only proper way to play these Telltale games. Wait for all the episodes to come out, then play it. Unfortunately it will be extremely difficult to commit to this since spoilers and curiosity might ruin the wait.

This game represents a lot of things, all of them good.
1) The use of original characters in the same universe helps avoid comparisons to the critically acclaimed comic, feeling like growth of the work rather than a retread (like the inexplicable popular TV show).
2) This is the game license that alloud Telltale to break out, previously producing fun adventure games they are now producing the best ones to wide acclaim with more content set in comic and fantasy universe known to the general public.
3) This is one of the most accessable games out there.  Where the game play is less reliant on skill and more reliant on making decisions that impact the story.  There are still stakes, but since all of them are about the characters' feelings and relationships it ultimately has a deep impact.  Your input makes you feel responsible for ending and makes it hit harder.  And it is sad.
If I were to log a complain it is this: it is a modern adventure game based more around story than gameplay, it is one step removed from a “Chose Your Own Adventure” novel and thus you will not get a lot of traditional gameplay elements based on reflexes and accuracy (when those elements do show up the controls are not built for them so you may lose those sections frustratingly).
I will also say that the chapters are not uniformly good, with chapter 3 being the weakest, reason being that in an episodic game, it is an episodic chapter, there is no unifying story that tie all its parts together.  Chapter 3 is like they took all the standalone episodes in which “things happen” and put them in one place, whereas all of the other chapters have one big thing happen in several smaller parts.  It is fine, I like it, but compared to 2 and 5 (my picks for the best episodes) it stands out as weak, you could almost skip it entirely because so much of what happens in it could just be shrugged off as, “I guess that happened off screen” like all of the things a person assumes happens off screen in a TV series between seasons.  Again, it is still good, just not as good.

This is my inital review for the Early Access of Master of Orion.
Gametime: aprox 20 hours.
As a long time fan of Moo2 i am pleased to see that this game is way more Moo2 than Moo3.
It kind of reminds me of a crossover between Moo2 and Sins of a solar empire.
This game has a lot of potential to become great with some tweaks and polishing.
As it stand right now i think the game is unballanced in regards of research,
and the opponents are not much of a challenge. Frankly they are quite push-over.
Also combat is a little bit dull, its not engaging like the classic moo2 where you got to play your fleet.
Here it is real time combat and you have little control over whats happening. You can activate modules manually.
Also i miss being able to recruit ship officers and colony administrators for increased bonuses.
Would like to see this implemented, and perhaps with an xp system for the officers and administrators.
Some things that need adjusting and improving are Tool tips, Correct and updated stats on ship modules, Research,
Difficulty level, Sorting out misc bugs and strangely enough.. savegame size. My savegame folder now almost takes up 1gb of space.. with the largest save being 150mb.
There are also some bugs here and there, but nothing major, and a save and relog usualy resolves the issue.
If this is only on my client i do not know, my friend who purchased the game at the same time does not experience the same bugs as i do.
But i think the graphics looks great, races are pehaps a bit cartoony but i dont mind. Individual voice acting for each race, nice models and nice textures, nice cinematics. Engaging gameplay and it is easy to spend alot of time ingame.
To sum it up, the game as it stands right now has its flaws.. but it is an early access so what did you expect ?
Are the flaws game breaking ? no, not at all. The game is fully playable and quite enjoyable.
But i expect the game to become even greater with polishing and the correct tweaks.
Also i look forwards to more races and ingame content being implemented like higher difficulty and custom races.
• Should you buy it ? If you are a fan of the series i would say this is a must have. And buying into it right now you can give the developers feedback and help influence the game into becoming something great.
• Would i buy the game again ? Yes most deffinatly i would, even in early access.

Lugaru comes from Wolfire Games, the company that spawned the Humble Indie Bundle.  Their idea revolutionized the digital games market, and drove millions of copies of excellent games into the hands of users who otherwise would have never played them.  Lugaru was their first release as a developer, and it’s an interesting, although rough, experience.  It is a game about loss and revenge.  It is a game about morality and justice.  It has brutal hand-to-hand combat.  And rabbits.
You might think a game about anthropomorphic rabbits would be cute.  You would be wrong.  This game is dark.  The combat is visceral, tight, and bloody.  After Turner the rabbit sees his entire family♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and slaughtered by bandits, he sets out on an island-spanning quest for vengeance.  The vast majority of the game consists of different combat scenarios, with different numbers of enemies equipped with different weapons like staves, knives, or swords.  Kill them all to progress.  In between these fights are text cut scenes, and dialogue is harsh like an 80s action movie. “I swear, I will kill them all,” etc.  This is a little tough to get past when you see a rabbit with huge eyes and a cute chirpy noise for a voice say this.  Immersion is not the strong suit of this game.
Where this game really shines is the combat.  The developers were wise to not depend on lengthy combos or meters; your only commands are simple punch, jump, and crouch. Combining them results in different attacks.  There is no health meter, you can only tell Trevor’s condition by the blurriness of the screen and how he will pant and slump after hard hits.  There is no on-screen notification of your enemy’s actions, and even if there were, you wouldn’t be able to react to them fast enough.  You’ll have to watch your enemy carefully, and parry at just the right moment to disarm or incapacitate them long enough to get in a solid hit.  You can perform instant kills by stealthily approaching your opponent from behind (and in the case of wolves, from downwind) and snapping their necks.  Failure is not punished heavily, as you will restart at the beginning of the stage, most of which last only a few minutes.
The music matches the tone of the game well; a slow, unease will set over you on the main menu, letting you know this is not a game for the faint of heart.  When combat starts, your blood will get pumping as drums drive you to commit acts of rabbit violence.  The sound effects when you land hits are crucial, as they inform you of what’s happening in the hand-to-hand scrum faster than your eyes can probably process it.  Often, when delivering a killing blow, time will slow down and you will see that perfect kick to the head or knife throw in glorious slow motion.
The graphics are sparse, and the polygon count is low, even for the main character.  Structures are basic cubes and rectangles, and the ground is little more than a few rolling hills populated with the odd tree.  However sparse things are, though, it is impressive how much the team was able to build.  The graphics are lacking, though mildly impressive when you read Wolfire’s blog where they detail all the work that went into it, and the spiritual sequel that is still in Early Access, Overgrowth.  Everything in both games was built from scratch by the small development team.
Lugaru is a fast-paced game, and while the tutorial is thorough, the fight design leaves little room for error.  Oftentimes a well-placed hit by an enemy will send you flying, not only doing direct damage, but leaving you at the mercy of the ragdoll physics.  Land on your head, and you’ll potentially break your neck and have to start the fight over.  Aside from Trevor’s campaign for revenge, there is also a challenge mode that pits you against groups of enemies, and you can compete to achieve a high score against each group.  This is good practice for campaign mode, letting you quickly learn the systems and effective strategies against certain enemies and how to use different weapons.
While the graphics are unpolished, and the story feels “adult” for the sake of just being edgy, instead of in service of a grander point, the quick and weighty combat is entertaining.  For $9.99, it is a good few hours of entertainment.  I think of it more as a preview of what Overgrowth will offer.  Perhaps Overgrowth will deepen these systems while overcoming Lugaru’s faults, but I will wait until it is out of Early Access to find out.

This is the game that Master of Orion 3 should have been and beyond. As a veteran MoO2 player, I was at first hesitant about this reboot, but as time went on WG showed that they were extremely passionate about this project, and it has now been proven in the gameplay of this game.
Something to note if you're also a veteran MoO2 player, the new tech tree is going to seem simplistic to you, because instead of researching individual techs, you research things a group at a time. At first I thought it was going to be lame, but honestly, it's a good way of modernizing the game flow and it speeds up the gameplay without taking the strategy out of teching - it's all still there, just a little bit quicker.
The UI is clean and gorgeous - there are some things I'd still like added, like being able to buy production from the colony overview screen to save me from having to go to each individual planet, but that's really a quality of life thing that isn't necessary right now.
The voice acting is stellar, the visuals are clear and concise, and the galaxy layout is different now using a "warp node" system - and what this means is that now you can predict where enemies can attack you from and defend them. This is another thing that I thought would be a far departure, but again, it really just modernizes the same gameplay style we all love, and actually keeps you from getting merc'd by tech rushes and such.
This game is just going to keep getting better as more content is added, and I'm so happy that WG decided to pick this us and do something with it. Absolutely get this game. Now. Please and thanks.

While promising, Master of Orion is missing key elements to make it a true successor to it's namesake.
The game is going to have 10 races in the final release, six of which are playable now. These are the ten races of Master of Orion I, and include the Bird-like Alkari, the Bear-warrior Bulrathi, boring old Humanity, the Cat-like Mrrshan, the subterranean lizard Sakkra, and the scientific Psilon-- with the Ant-like Klackon, Rocky Silicoid, Mechanical Meklar and secretous Darloks planned for a later release.
are the Trilarians, Elerians, and Gnolam.
each of the races are drastically different from their originals, and overly diluted in characteristics. Rather than a race that is tuned in to it's heritage, each one must play more as a generalist instead of  focusing on a single strength or two.
The Alkari, for example, were originally highly effective in combat in space, and masters of propulsion-- a function of their evolutionary history with flight. Now, they have a 25% defensive bonus to certain combat scenarios, the end.
the Sakkra were the masters of overwhelming populations, able to reach twice as high populations thanks to their ability to live both on and below a planet's surface. Now? They grow a little bit faster.
An important mechanic of the MoO universe has always been research. New technologies, and important research decisions: Do you want to use the new Fusion technology to upgrade you ship bombs, engines, or beam weapons? This sort of decision made decisions critical, and brought diplomacy to a monumental forefront in the game. It wasn't just about which tech you chose, it was about which tech you let your opponents have. The Psilon used to have a special racial characteristic: While they sucked at most things due to their frail nature, their brilliant minds allowed them to capture all these options instead of just one-- and use these technologies to surpass their enemies. But the tech-tree has been redesigned such that technological decisions are few and far between, and the Psilon's unique advantage has been replaced with a flat bonus to research.
In the original MoO games, travel took time and fuel. If a star was close enough, you could reach it. If not, you did not go there. Later in the game, you could travel from any star directly to any other star, if fuel allowed. You expanded your reach by building colonies and outposts, or by researching new fuel technologies. This entire system has been scrapped in favor of a starlane system, with each star acting as a node-- and if you can navigate there, you can go anywhere in the galaxy from level one. The advantages of this system are, presumably, greater strategy-- creating choke points around the galaxy to protect your territory from opponents. Military bases can be built to "blockade" ends of starlanes, for example, from enemy travel. But it destroys the open feeling of space present in MoO2, and is completely not worth it.
The current version of the game includes pirate raiders who will occaisionally attack, forcing you to keep a few ships handy to quickly dispense them as an annoyance-- and a few stationary space monsters like a Giant Squid, Eel, or the Guardian of Orion-- usually guarding a particularly nice planet. There are a few scripted events and anomalies, but not nearly enough to keep the game interesting just yet.
This game shows promise of being true to the Master of Orion Spirit, but I am concerned that the scope will not go deep enough to make it worthy of the name. MoO fans from the original series will find the game fun for a few hours in it's current state, but the lack of complexity and depth really prevent this game from being the huge hit it may become if the developers revise the systems they've created to make it more like the original. The controls also are unintuitive for now, space combat is boring and unmeaningful, and ground combat is non-existent. Voice acting shows promise, but has way too much repetition. "I used to be an adventurer like you, but then I took an arrow to the knee" kind of repetition, only 1000 times worse. But if the developers do what they should, this game definitely belongs on any 4X fan's wishlist. But as is, it feels too much like Civilization and not enough like Masters of Orion.
Will continue to update throughout the game's development, and if the game ever reaches a fun state for non-MoO fans, I'll give it a thumbs up.
