The sorta kinda well-not-really sequel to the popular Machinarium. Except this time it isn't about scrap and robots but nature and what lives on a tree.
You play as Mr. Lantern and his 4 friends who are trying to save their home, a giant tree, from a parasitic spider-like creature that sucks out the life of said tree and its inhabitants. To do that, they need to bring a seed of the tree down to the ground, a journey that takes them to many interesting locations, situations and characters that are just plain charming and fun to watch. Such as when you encounter a genie and every character has to make a wish, one of them creating a Ferris wheel while the soundtrack by the Hungarian band DVA acoustically stimulates your endorphin production.
The puzzles are much simpler than in Machinarium which actually view as an improvement. I remember getting frustrated with some of the puzzles in that game and even more with the tip function that required you to get past a little shoot-em-up every time you wanted to take a look. On top of that it also had a tendency to just freeze up which is a natural occurrence when you make a game in Flash that is more ambitious and complex than the usual array of games made with it.
Luckily Botanicula doesn't suffer from any of those problems. There are just a few items here and there, other than that the puzzles can be usually solved on the same screen, just like Amanita Design's first two games, Samorost 1 and 2.
The many achievements might lead you to think that Botanicula is rather long, but that isn't the case. The 6 chapters can be played through in about half an hour each. The achievements are related to a little card collecting feature: each new character or creature you meet will give you its card and unlock the corresponding achievement. The majority are mandatory to meet in order to finish the game, but some are optional and require you to find them.

On the surface Brigador is a 2D isometric tank shooter.  Underneath there is a lot of customisation and a wide array of tactics you'll use to avoid an untimely demise.
The campaign mode has loads of missions, most with a choice of four loadouts.  These allow you to try to have a go at each scenario in very different ways.  Freelance mode allows you to set up your own vehilce and choose a set of missions.  There are three vehilce classes (tank, walker, agrav) which all handle in different ways and have significant pros and cons.  In each class there is a spectrum of sizes and the three factions each have their own strengths and weaknesses.
The difficulty in Freelance mode is entirely up to you, there are no easy/medium/hard settings.  Each pilot has a difficulty rating and many get harder as you progress through missions.  Certain vehicles and classes lend themselves to particular weaponry and each weapon has pros and cons.  Some maps are wide and open with lots of room to move but nowhere to hide, others are perfect for sneaking and setting up bottle-neck ambushes but with no room to turn and run.
Its easy to learn in a big heavy tank, able to take a beating and dish out huge damage but you cant run or hide.  In some more difficult missions run and hide is the only thing which can keep you alive.  Projectiles take your vehilces momentum, making fast agravs exceptionally good artillery platorms.
The central theme of Brigador experimentation.  It's easy to find a loadout you like and use it to learn the basics, then start swapping parts and branch out.  Soon you'll find something completely different which works just as well but in a totally different way.

Pros:
Tons of variety and choices in your loadouts. Whether you like being fast and nimble, a brawler, a sniper, the ol' bait-and-switch, or even stealth (yes, that's possible in a two story walking tank) there's a way to get what you want out of this game. Tons of chassis, tons of weapons, and 4 different special abilities that you can mix and match to make what you want.
Campaign does a good job of teaching the basics and how the different vehicle types work, and then starts to ramp up the difficulty over time until by the end you feel like you got gud. There are also some interesting wrenches in the works here and there (Joy Bus/Hell Ride anyone?). It's nice that you can select from 4 premade loadouts; doesn't break the balance of the missions while giving you choices to suit your playstyle and also introducing a new player to the concept of building a loadout. (NOTE: I haven't played the new E-series so I can't vouch for that.)
Very well done freelance mode lets you take things as slow and gentle as you want...or if you'd rather bend over and take it like a man, that's an option too. Build a loadout freely by picking a vehicle along with two weapons and a special ability and a pilot to go along with it. Then pick how many levels you want to run. The game determines how the difficulty scales based on which pilot you choose, as well as the payout, with the vehicle you choosing also providing bonus cash if you make it out. Precursor James Double Donkey runs are rumored to be the hot new thing but I haven't saved up the 100 million yet so don't ask me.
More subjective portion: I love this game's style and worldbuilding. Shots of all kind are distinct, the whole place has a sort of downtrodden industrial look to it and the color palette and art reflects that without compromising the gameplay (too much at least, see cons.) The backstory is great as well and the Lore section allowing you to read up on the game's world as told by its inhabitants is awesome.
When you actually get into the game, the environment doesn't feel limiting or like a playing field, more so a tool you can use if you're clever enough. Pretty much all 4 special abilities tie into it at least indirectly and all vehicle classes have one way or another of smashing through groves of trees or apartment blocks. No need to walk down the street into a tank platoon, bust out from behind them two blocks down and hit them where it hurts most. Kool-Aid Man Simulator 2016.
Cons:
Sometimes I find it hard to tell whether a particular piece of scenery is explosive or not. Dunno if that's just me or what.
Can be a little hard to see the red glow emitted by an enemy behind a wall sometimes.
Freelance mode is slow to start since you have to unlock the different equipment and pilots which can take a bit of doing. (Thankfully you can pick what to spend your blood money on rather than there being a linear unlock system.)
Some enemies have rather unexpected loadouts and can catch you way off guard, other enemies are quite hard to deal with based on what you brought to the fight. Some loadouts just don't have a good way of dealing with those red-headlight suicide bomber enemies.
The aiming system is a little weird at first, especially when fighting agravs.
Overall:
Not a perfect game but definitely a very competent example of a roguelite that will definitely scratch that big stompy robot itch. Solid gameplay mechanics but unless you find fun within said mechanics themselves it may get old fast.

So, I just realized I've yet to make any real review on this. I'm gonna be honest, though.
PROS
- Pretty good shooting mechanics
- SOME of the DLC is pretty great
- Settlement system can be pretty addicting at times
- Well designed open world to explore

- Excellent modding support, as Elder Scrolls and Fallout games have always had
CONS
- Story is pretty lackluster. Lacks most of the appeal that any of the previous Fallout games have had.
- Too much focus on the settlement building to the point where more than half of their DLC was focused solely on it.

- See Below for latest issues.
Now, if this review was posted a couple months ago, it probably would be positive. However, due to all the recent issues being brought on by Bethesda Game Studios, I have to give this a thumbs down. In particular, the Creation Club is total garbage. Sure, it can be avoided, or is supposed to be able to be. But even if that part of it worked, it still feels like a major slap to the face of the community. To start, I do understand the mindset behind them bringing back paid mods (yes, paid mods. Because that's exactly what they are, despite Bethesda being terribly NOT self aware). They want to be able to pay modders for their work. Okay. Fine.
However, there are also some major issues with this whole system. For starters, it's still downloading the CC content, even without paying for it, as part of the updates. The files take up hard drive space, but can't be used unless they're actually paid for. Likewise, each new bunch of content UPDATES the game, therefore breaking a lot of mods AND the script extender. This, I feel, directly contradicts their statements regarding not wanting to impact free modding at all. In their pursuit of doing this, they are inadvertently doing just that. I think that is probably the biggest part of Creation Club that pisses me off. I imagine it also pisses off the mod authors and the folks who work on the script extender as well.
Another negative point on the Creation Club itself is that it's literally Bethesda adding microtransactions to a AAA, single player game. Not to mention the quality of the items themselves. The only really good thing I saw out of the first batch was the backpack, and it was made by a pretty big modder. But even this second batch that just dropped, the armour looks goofy as hell and the BFG, in first person, takes up pretty much the entire lower half of your screen. Why is this necessary?
But anyways, in the end, it's a fun game, albeit not really a FALLOUT game. But due to all the tacked on crap that Bethesda has been doing, it's been severely impacting the quality of the game. This is me not just giving the negative review due to the developers, but because the game also has been impacted quite heavily.

Brigador is a game with a strong sense of identity. That identity is neon-soaked, synth-scored, vehicular mayhem. There's a ton of unlockables along with a good amount of lore if you care to read it, much of tinged with a dark sense of humor. But the real meat of the game is the all-single-player rampages you get sent on with your tank/mech/hovercraft across the cyberpunk planet of Solo Nobre.
Although there are some light stealth elements and discretion is important at times, overall this is a game that wants you to fully enjoy making damn near everything in sight asplode with the incredible firepower at your disposal. Even just fighting off enemies will often result in extensive collateral damage to the environment. Which is fine, because this game basically tracks "collateral damage" as "bonus points".
Beyond that, the "Freelance" mode offers quite a lot of customization, allowing you to combine whatever weapons with your chassis of choice before setting off for a string of missions. If you want a tiny, tracked motorcycle or battlesuit equipped with grenade launchers? No problem. A massive superheavy tank or hovercraft with a cloaking device? Done! It's all in there, waiting to be unlocked.
One last note: while some objections could still be made about the HUD, I think, (the icons are often rather small and hard to make out) the controls offer a satisfying amount of customization. If you're worried that you'll be stuck with a scheme you hate...don't sweat it too much. As long as twin-stick shooters in general are fun for you, you can likely find a setup that works for you in the options screen here.
If you're looking for something quiet, introspective, or with multiplayer then this isn't the game you want. But if your main objection to Mechwarrior and World of Tanks is that they don't let you demolish enough stuff with your war machines? This is one contract you'll want to accept, Brigador.

Starbound does for me what Minecraft couldn't.  Instead of taking forever to explore one island I can take forever to explore a few solar systems.  But then I can travel to any of the thousand other systems and explore them as well.  The different material types are as varied as Minecraft and then some.  You can grow food, build buildings, create better materials, hunt creatures, get into shootouts with the locals, etc.
in the latest version you can expand your ship.  You don't even have to develope planet-side buildings anymore if you don't want to.  You can literally live off your ship and expand it as you go.  There are now also more fuel types (fuel is needed to move between star systems), some more ceocentrated than others.
With the outpost you now have access to more quests, which means more adventures.  They can be as random as "Find me a stone USMC sign".  Do you remember what planet on what system you found that USMC prison colony?  You don't?  Time to go exploring and find another to get that sign!
There are "dungeons" on pretty much every planet.  You can dig down into the planet and find gnomish villages.  You can dig through several different layers of the planet and find everything from mushrooms to buried laboratories to underground lakes full of acid, all of which you can break down with your tool and use for yourself, either in a crafting recipe or as a decoration for your home(s).
If you like open-world construction games of a blocky nature, then this one is definitely worth trying out.  There are many to choose from these days and eveyone likes one more than the others.  If you're still searching for "the one" then play this one.  You search will be over.

I avoided the game at initial release because I had just migrated to PC gaming with a new rig. I read the reviews and saw the bugginess in the game that just truly ruined it for me. I don't mind little bugs, they make the game more humourous. But when crashing is involved or it just keeps recurring, it's hugely off-putting.
A few days ago I purchased it knowing it's been patched and fixed. It's the only numbered Assassins Creed game I hadn't played and I know that Unity and Syndicate both don't seem to matter too much on the modern-day storyline. Ubisoft even said they are a build up to something bigger (
).
The campaign is a huge yawn. I don't much care for who lives or dies, but certain elements that were missed in previous games were great to see. An Assassin's headquarters hidden underground. That's really cool! We've never really been treated to a proper, somewhat interactive HQ where all the Assassin's do their business since AC 1.
The combat is alright, except every 3 seconds you're getting shot in the bloody back. I would have to spend more time dodging than even landing a strike attempt in larger fights. This is good and bad though - it encourages you to be more stealthy in your approach, however it really annoys you when you just want to enjoy a bit of sword-fencing (or halbert-fencing if that's your thing!).
Customization is definitely the best. I'm fanatical about the Assassin AND Templar outfits in all the previous games. Must be in touch with my feminine side! ^_^ It finally feels satisfying choosing some nice mix-and-match clothing and colours, weapons and so forth. Syndicate did fail on this later on... Ubisoft, bring this kind of customization back.
Environment detail (that is, what the NPC's are doing and interacting with) are astonishing. You can spend a good couple of minutes idling, watching a pair of NPC's conversing over a cup of tea. In fact I did, and waited agonisingly for the looping animation to restart. I gave up. I was there for a good 2 minutes, which is a while for an animation loop, and no sign of the loop showing. OK not all the NPC animations are like that but even so, they contain great detail - people interacting with paper presses and such.
Graphics - well i'll keep it short. Stunning!
All in all, the game is very well done in terms of sorrounding and featured content. I'd give it around 85/100!
Tips for the next AC game after Syndicate:
- Syndicate combat for sure. Less shooting more melee.
- Make the campaign interesting, and much more lengthy than Unity.
- Let's hurry up with the modern-day storyline. We've had to deal with this yawn since AC 4.
- No more colour-coding the factions! It's understandable only with things like Redcoats and Bluecoats.
- I doubt this will happen judging by rumours but maybe another Templar POV? I loved Rogue. That inner Templar in me.

Lugaru is an extremely tight control arena-type fighter set in a bizarre world of humanoid animals who often find themselves beating the living crap out of each other due to reasons.
The combat system is fairly unique as well as surprisingly in-depth despite being very simple input wise (one attack button, a couple inventory buttons, the movement keys, duck and jump): There are aerial attacks, wall jumps, suplexes, finishers, jabs, a variety of kicks including an insanely powerful roundhouse, reversal moves, anti-reversal moves, weapon throws, you name it.
Movement feels incredibly fluid. Attacks are triggered through context sensitive timing (ducking while under attack will perform a reversal move) and combining keys (jumping, ducking and dropping a weapon in midair will cause you to air flip launch it into an enemy) which make for a very satisfying experience when you get the hang of it as the game does not let up and will constantly challenge you with scenarios that allow multiple ways of approaching whether it be through stealth for facing few enemies at a time or barging in and kicking everyone into space with your leg cannons while avoiding being counter-struck.
The campaign story is fairly simplistic and borderline cliche; You're Turner, a fairly chill herbivore, who then gets messed with, by not-so-chill herbivores that go out of their way to murder your family and friends, for an obscure purpose. With nothing to lose, you go out on a quest seeking  ＲＥＶＥＮＧＥ  as well as answers which are nonetheless secondary to the brutal rear kicking that ensues. There are optional challenge scenarios as well, which don't seem to have any story behind them but are still fun. In case you haven't noticed it yet, it's not a very plot-heavy game.
The graphics are fairly dated, but they get the job done. They're at best nostalgic, despite being a PC exclusive, and at worst disturbing, due to the admittedly bizarre art style. The soundtrack is rather atmospheric and give the game some much needed spirit depending on the situation you're facing, but it isn't anything to write home about.
:
It's a title focused on its fighting gameplay and challenges. Everything else in it is there to either accompany or support it, and not the other way around. If you're looking for a decent challenge, fluid Mouse+Keyboard gameplay or unconditional genocide of bunny rabbits, do consider checking it out.

Quick summary:
Master of Orion is a game that I really think will be fun with more development, but currently is not really complete or polished enough to enjoy for a long time.
Good points:
The faction leaders and assistants have great animation and voice acting. Related to this fact, the diplomacy backdrop screens are a blast.
The starmap is gorgeous and I was surprised at the amount of polish it got. In terms of interface, it feels like a hybrid between MOO1 and MOO2 in that it has systems and planets and moons and asteroids (like MOO2) but maintains a simple interface that allows me to easily see what's on the map without having to click through menus (like MOO1).
Spaceships are neat looking and space combat looks pretty cool.
Fun races, overall a classically zany feeling to everything.
I like the UI and think it was pretty well designed.
Bad points:
The technology tree is currently pretty messed up. You achieve a new technology like every 5 turns but most of them don't feel like they make a difference. Many just unlock a building type which has to be propagated over your empire for a million turns before you see the benefit, and in general I feel like the real bottleneck in getting to cool things is always production (making research pretty unattractive, since there's no point in unlocking another thing when you won't be able to capitalize it for 500 turns). There also doesn't really seem to be any reason to strategically cherrypick your way through the tech tree either; with a few exceptions the best approach is just to research everything in the current tier and then move on.
There are too many buildings, and the game encourages you to build all of them everywhere. What this results in is spending your midgame tediously making sure every one of your planets has a research lab and a biosphere and a hydroponics farm and a spaceport and a cloning facility and a marine barracks and a spaceport and a robotic miner and so on and you get the point so I'll stop listing all of the buildings in the game but believe me when I say that it keeps going on for quite some time. It all makes me wish that planets had a limited number of building slots so that I could just make a few smart choices per planet and move on.
It's not possible to make interesting diplomatic exchanges until you have convinced another empire to accept your embassy, which requires being friends with them. In an unfortunate catch-22, in order to become friends with an empire, you perform advanced diplomatic exchanges requiring an embassy. Some races even start with unfavorable relations with others and in these circumstances there's basically nothing to do except watch the AI refuse to let you establish an embassy until they ultimately declare war on you because you colonized a lot of planets. Obviously this is silly.
The real time tactical combat basically involves moving a big ball of ships at the enemy and hoping that you have more ships on your side.
There are a few other things but those are the big issues that come to mind right now, and I'm hopeful to see them ironed out before the release.

I've played through the game about 6 times now, 2 of those were multiplayer: I loved most things.  Since this is an early access review I won't be mentioning things like balance or tech-tree progression as things like that can be changed at a drop of a hat and I'm sure would be a utter waste of development time right now.
Things that are in place: Galaxy overview & planetary control, tactical battles, ship design and diplomacy.
These are all in a very basic form apart from the galaxy overview.
The
are pretty robust, you can move your ships around and most things already have useful tooltips.  You can see how long a planet's production has left to finish it's next item and stuff like that.  Even trading between planets in the same system can happen (including production points with the right setup!!!).
The
gets a bit micro management heavy later in the game but I'm still processing turns in less than 30 seconds now I know what I'm doing even then.  Things like build order lists would be good for different types of planets but you can queue 5 things at once and if you don't mind thinking about which 5 to build when you first colonise then it's good.  It's fun to balance between growth, research and production.  It's easy to see where the points are coming from and to balance that one point of research/production to finish the next item.  Although when you don't have enough food and your planet's population starts dying, it can be confusing as to why the food from your empire isn't getting there.  Income and expenses can also be confusing.
The
look great, but you can tell it's just not finished yet.  It plays ok and I'm able to sway battles in my favour if I use it and don't simulate (I reloaded a battle that lost on simulate, but won without loss on tactical).  This is the same with planetary defense... how strong are they?  We don't know but I'm sure it's just a work in progress and will improve later in the EA before release.
: I don't really care much for AI diplomacy on any 4x game and just declare war on everybody, so I'm not the man to ask about that stuff.
So if you don't mind playing a in-progress Early Access, then get it now and have fun!  If you want to wait until the complete experience is ready... well then wait.  I couldn't wait and I've already got my money's worth!

Despite being an "Early Access" title , this is one of the best examples of that much abused genre. There is plently to do already, and I played through a full campaign with no crashes at all. As a 4X game it is most excellent. Having ploughed many hours into GalCiv 3 I can happily state that MOO is more fun. In it current state it is not, perhaps, quite as deep as Stardocks behemoth, but it is immensley enjoyable with a deep tech tree and endless options for customising your ships (which is something i have not really delved into). The voice acting is superb, as might be expected from a cast which includes Mark Hamill, John de Lancie and Alan Tudyk.
Yes there are still missing features, and it could possibly do with better documentation and a tutorial but the game already feels like a finished product. In terms of extra features, the only thing I would add would be an experience system for your fleets, and possibly the option of adding Admirals who level up with them.
Overall, if you are looking to scratch the 4X itch, and GalCiv is a bit heavy (and graphically suspect) give this a whirl. I don't think you will be disappointed.

So here are the pros and cons about Master of Orion in its current state:
Positive:
Looks very pretty
High profile voice acting
Very stable build
Very few bugs
Comes with Master of Orion 1,2 and 3 (runs in Dos Box)
Of course I take a lot of things in the game for granted so I cannot list them as positive... they are supposed to be there.
Negative:
The introduction of Star Lanes might not be everyone's thing... I'd prefer the old system + fuel.
At this point the AI is fairly stupid, but this is subject to change according to the devs.
Technologies need to be more balanced (Missiles need ammo or a nerf), also future technologies do not make older tech cheaper and smaller.
Racial traits are very limited
Obviously the game is still in Early Access so a lot of things can change.
Also be aware that right now only 6 races are available and you cannot create a custom race yet.
There is no espionage in the game yet.

I should have picked this one up immediately when it came out; the design told me so. The reason I didn't - I guess - was (apart from me hoping it would be in an indie bundle) that I couldn't imagine how gameplay would fit into this when I saw the trailer. And to be honest, the game doesn't exactly score with its gameplay mechanics; they have something browser-gamerish, even almost dilettant about them. But really, I couldn't care less. Because no game since... actually I cannot even think of any right now that ensorcelled (does that word really exist? O_o) me in such a way as this one (of course some other games à la Final Fantasy VII captivated me in very different ways).
How does this game manage to do this? With its apparant randomness - you never know what weird creature will come up next, how you will make it react and how it will react. In the end, however, it's not just pure "let's make everything totally crazy and random cuz that's cool"-randomness which one easily sees through; no, here pretty much everything fits together in this whimsical little world and you get the feeling that there must be something in the Czech culture that inspired to something that feels so odd and magical to us non-Czechs...I dunno.
I guess one more aspect that makes this game so interesting is the simple fact that it's a world full of little animals and I for one was reminded of childhood days with adventurous atmosphere, catching little animals out of a pond and studying them and so on.
But all of this would not make it a good game if it wasn't for the wonderful graphics and sound design which also fit together perfectly. There is so much funny voice acting going on, so many eerie tunes (think Animal Collective + The Polyphonic Spree + chipmunks rubbing their butts over green grass) and the unique organic look of everything - it's just too much.
Sorry if I sound like a child♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on by a fairy but I just totally loved playing this ^^
Of course, there are some flaws, like the simple gameplay, the shortness ( I WANT MOOOAR!), but what the heck - if you want perfectly polished games, go play EA stuff...this is one for the heart :}
I'd even put it into my list of all-time-favorite games.
However, I'm sure many wouldn't like it at all. Guess you'll just have to figure it out yourself ;)

If you're a fan of the settings and feel of games from ACE Team or Blendo then you'll love this. Imagine being in a South or Central American country during one of the many periods of civil unrest in the 20th century. Now imagine being a freelance mercenary assisting one side or the other in that same period (albeit with a few minor, ever so slight technological upgrades, and you're on a whole 'nother planet, and you may or may not be a certified psychopath, but other than those minor differences, it's basically the same!).
That's basically where you start. There's a fascinating lore that goes with the machines, the worlds, the factions, the characters, the weapons, and everything else and it's obvious that care and consideration was given to each entry.
The combat is visceral and bombastic and frenetic and satisfying. Want to drive over something? Easy. Want to knock down the "Leave It To Beaver" facades in the Evora Estate Country Club? Just drive your mech into them.  The maps are bounded without feeling small, and those areas that do constrain you are done in a logical fashion. The explosions...well, let's just say don't be a cool guy, they are glorious. (Pro tip: shoot everything)
If you've already experienced hallucinogens or psychodelics *and* you've played Brigador, then I'm not telling you anything you don't already know. If you haven't, then legally I can only recommend that you try Brigador...but you absolutely should.

FEATURES
-----------
>Extreme amounts of customization

-Some actually do not like the power of customization and prefer a more straight-forward approach to playing.
>Ridiculously extensive grinding
-For most people this is a bad thing.

>Fun "action" MMO gameplay
+Think Warframe

Compared to New Vegas: It has better graphics, combat engine, cooler power armor, and crafting systems. Though for that you also get: poor storyline, bland characters, less interesting locations, less varied quests (also infinite grind quests can suck a chub), a severe downgrade in weapon variety though you get weapon mod crafting (still can't crafte guns without FREE mods), less intersting enemies , and by far the most pointless base building gimick that does nothing but downgrade the Commonwealth by crippling several locations simply for the fact that you can build stuff yours with a building system which is both clunky and hard to work with (and you have to be very very patient to actually manage to make something decent looking).
The game is heavily improved with mods but sadly you are shot in the knee for downloading them by locking achivements away from you, there are mods to unlock them again but the fact still stands. Modding community is nice, can recommend the Nexus for mods and it has its own mod manager. Bethesda on other hands want to muscle in on the modding market by literally making a market for it. You must PAY for mods which can very easily can be gotten for free on the nexus, can even get better mods on the nexus.
Dlcs are severly lacking. New Vegas had 4 expansion packs which added a new map and all the bells and whistles with that, as well as two extra equipment packs. All of that can be aquired for a reasonable price if you can get over the graphical downgrade and the clunkier combat, but it is still a more true rpg than 4. Fallout 4 has two dlcs adding newq areas, one adding a couple of dungeons, and three which add stuff to build (the setlement building stuff is not worth it unless you are very invested in that.) overall the dlcs quality is lacking quite a bit as well.
Can be worth it on a sale for simply the modding, but certainly not for the story, characters, area, dlc, graphics, or sound design. My recommendation is New Vegas if you want a truer rpg expreience and worth for your money. Do not get the season pass and all that doolaly with 4 unless you can snag an ultimate edition on sale.
All in all, Fallout 4 is a completely competant and good shooter with decent voice acting and a meh story struggling within the body of a malformed rpg with too many gimicks tacked onto its festering body. Additionally screw bethesdas Creation club, NEVER buy anything there, none of the mods there can outmatch that which you can find for FREE on the nexus (and those are mods that are fixed and fully functional and compatible with other mods) As a fan of Fallout 3 and New Vegas I am severly let down by this game which I wanted to be good quite a bit.
Tl;dr: Fallout 4 is alright, shouldn't have been called fallout. Feels lack luster compared to the others. Screw Paid mods and the creation club for trying to make people pay them for something you can already get for free. Dlcs are hardly worth the money. Buy only on a sale if ever. Recommended, with a but...
I played a vast amount of MoO2, and I've spent decades waiting for a worthy successor.  I've enjoyed many 4X space games, but all of them had something that made them not quite as engaging as the granddaddy of them all.  In that sense, it's nice to see the Psilons or the hapless Bulrathi back.
Unfortunately, in its current state, nostalgia is what the MoO reboot primarily offers.  The game plays essentially like MoO2 with some relatively minor gameplay changes.  The tech tree will be instantly recognizable to a MoO2 player, as will most elements of planet management, ship design, and overall strategy.  Real-time pauseable combat is new, but not terribly engaging, since most battles involve no more strategy than "fly straight at the enemy and open fire".
In theory, I'd like to say there's nothing wrong with a new MoO2 updated to modern graphics.  But the reality is, as much as prior 4X games might not have unseated MoO2 as the best of the breed, they've each done interesting things.  Endless Space had neat unique planets plugged into a complex backstory, GalCiv III had complex ship design and a more strategic feel, and I was even a fan of MoO3's planet habitability and client species spontaneously colonizing your worlds.  You'd hope that the MoO reboot would incorporate some of the positive developments of the last 20 years without losing what made the original game great.  Unfortunately, at least in its current version, there's not much more game than we had in the 90s.  So at the moment I find myself hopeful that there's a lot more coming in Early Access than what we've seen right now.
TL;DR: A gentle recommendation for nostalgia's sake; otherwise, wait to see how Early Access comes out.

I love this game to its core. Half-Life is one of my favourite games of all time. It's an excellent fps that does a fantastic job taking the player into it's world with a great selection of weapons, monsters and an overall outstanding atmosphere. It has aged quite ungracefully interms of graphics as the game was released way back in 1998 but the ai, music, atmosphere and gameplay still hold up very well. If you want to experience a fun, scary and action packed fps play this game! If I had any problems with it (not even things I find to be too much of a problem as I am a fanboy of this game) it would be that it may not always be clear to new players what exactly they should be doing in the story or overall goal. Alot of the more in depth stuff you will only find by searching up wikis about the story. It doesn't bother me but I can imagine it being confusing to newer players. It's told in a much more subtle fashion than some players might expect.
This game also has a huge libary of mods and addons. Games like conterstrike, day of defeat, team fortress and others wouldn't exist today if it wasn't for this game. Developers are still creating mods for this 18 year old game which I find amazing.
BTW if you're gonna play this game, play it in the dark alone. Half-Life is more of an experience than a game you play with your friends although it does have multiplayer in the form of deathmatch (and other mods such as sven coop) I find the best way of playing it and enjoying it a first time is to play alone.

It's really hard to say something about Half-Life that hasn't already been said before. The game has been showered with such praise and acclaim since it's inception, even in the modern day. While many people would be ready to just write it off as people looking at it through 'nostalgia goggles', it's really important to go back and look at what makes it such a masterpiece.
Half-Life begins in a way that no other shooter at the time had done. Instead of leading off with a mission briefing before throwing you into a room full of demons, or showing you a cutscene to serve as exposition, the game immediately puts you in the shoes of Dr. Gordon Freeman on his fated tram ride as he is late to work. Your control of Freeman is, well, free, and you're free to move about the tram and examine the surroundings of your tram. You, the player, help Freeman get into his HEV Suit, greet his colleagues, and push a specimen of crystal into a large machine which promptly wrecks the facility of Black Mesa. Gordon, with your aid, sets out on an epic quest to escape his workplace, fighting off freakish aliens and later on soldiers who are sent in to perform a cover-up operation. Only in one instance is direct control ever taken away from you and even then you see the event unfold through Freeman's eyes. Story isn't told to you via exposition, but rather by carefully placed scripted events and NPC's you can encounter who inform you of where to go next.
Half-Life's story, or rather the way it tells it's story still manages to be as immersive as it was when I first played it, way back in 2009. Gordon isn't some lunkheaded badass space marine who rips and tears the guts of his enemies but rather a normal person who just happens to be donning a powerful suit of experimental armor that prevents him from the same type of swift deaths that his co-workers are so subjected to. Black Mesa isn't a laid out level filled with awkward enemy traps that forces you to run around looking for arbitrary keycards to progress but rather a research facility that feels real and legitimate to go through, and it's still one of the most believable enviroments in a shooter today. The way the enemies interact with their environment makes them feel like actual living beings.
Of course, all of this wouldn't be anywhere near as good if the gameplay wasn't there as well. Thankfully, the combat in Half-Life is as visceral as other FPS games of it's time, featuring a wide array of weapons with meaty sound effects. Gordon's first weapon is his Iconic crowbar, which you wont be using so much as a weapon later on and more of as a 'hand' so to speak, it'll be the weapon you use to smash apart the environment to see what is and what isn't breakable, or to smash open a crate to gain supplies. Your ranged arsenal is very diverse, featuring basic weapons like a Submachine Gun, a Shotgun, and a Revolver to the Tau cannon, something akin to a wind up rail gun from quake, to a tranqulizer dart crossbow that you'll primarily be using to fight off underwater and aerial threats.
The weapons themselves are great but what makes them so fun to use is the fact that the enemies are just as diverse and require different strategies to take down. Something like a headcrab should be killed with the crowbar or the glock so as to not waste ammo, but faster, stronger moving targets like the HECU marines will be more easily dispatched with weapons like the MP5 or the Spas-12. You'll even come accross a giant hulking alien which is imperveous to all types of damage except for explosions. The sound designs on all the enemies is spot on, with the HECU sounding suitably intimidating over the radio comms, or the eerie roars of the Gargantua.
This already solid gameplay is also helped by various other factors, like level design. I already mentioned that Black Mesa feels like a real place, and so the Level Design is often in close quarters, with enemies often hiding around corners and enemies like the HECU marines will take advantage of the various routes they can take to flank you, just as you are able to do the same. The game also features in my opinion one of the best VGM soundtracks out there, with songs like "Diabolical Adrenaline Guitar", "Nuclear Mission Jam", and the Credits theme standing out as some of my favorites in particular. When the soundtrack wants you to feel like a badass, it will, and when it wants to be atmospheric, it will. Valve's sound team was absolutely on point here, as the game and it's various sound effects, quotes and music all feel spot on.
Half-Life isn't without a few flaws here and there though.  The game slows down towards the middle, with two chapters On a Rail and Residue Processing feeling a little tedious to play through, and with the final levels of Xen outside of the final boss being incredibly annoying and un-fun to play through. It seems like there was some pact between FPS devs of the time to make the final levels of their games to be as stupid as possible, but even then I really don't think these are enough to truly hurt the game. Half-Life is remembered so fondly not just because of itself as a game, but also the way it revolutionized the Genre. So many other FPS games tried to follow in it's wake, and it still remains one of the most influential FPS games of all time.
Half-Life is without a doubt one of my personal favorite games of all time, as well in my opinion being worthy of being called one of the best games of all time. Half-Life is a game that combines an unbroken narrative with kick♥♥♥♥♥gameplay, strong and realistic level design with a rockin' soundtrack to create one of the most celebrated games ever created. I didn't even touch upon the huge collection of high-quality free mods available for the game, but they absolutely exist. They Hunger, Afraid of Monsters and Poke646 stand out as some of my favorite mods for any game. Half-Life is absolutely worth your time and money, and you owe it to yourself to play it if you consider yourself a video game enthusiast.

Darkest Dungeon is not a game for everyone, that much is obvious. It's a RNG game and that in of itself is something most people aren't going to enjoy and that's okay! But it's not just pure RNG like a lot of negative reviewers seem to think, the entire purpose of the game is to influence the RNG to your favor as much as possible and that's the fun of it.
It's not just pure random luck and hoping everything goes well for you. It's all about strategy, planning, being smart, and most importantly realizing that even with all that sometimes things don't go your way and you have to figure out handle that. Sure it's frustrating but honestly my favorite experiences with this game involves pulling myself back up from a horrible encounter and not letting it ruin the run for me because it's satisfying!
I get that that kind of gameplay isn't for everyone, and that's fine. But don't condemn the game for being too hard when it's doing exactly what it's intended to do. It's a great game with amazing art, sound design, and fun mechanics that I've personally never encountered a glitch with. Red Hook Studios knows what they're doing.

While playing this, I couldn't help but to make constant comparisons to original Doom.  Whereas Doom is no doubt the classic staple of the First-Person Shooter genre (see my in-depth review), this is in may ways a vastly superior experience in terms of rich, engaging, and seemless storytelling.  Both games follow a similar plot: Our protagonist is an agent of a Goverment-funded research facility doing things they should not be doing; something goes awry; all Hell breaks loose; fighting to survive we get transported to a different dimension; beat the big baddie; and save the universe.. for now...
However, Doom is a collection of loosely interrelated levels ultimately culminating in a story arc showcasing our doomed (haha, get it?!) space marine's descent into the bowels of Hell, highlighted by expository text at the end of each episode, Half-Life is a fluid and constant narrative one experiences through the eyes of the protagonist - generally free of immersion-breaking cut scenes - no #@%&ing QTE's here! - sequences requiring the player to react play out in real time.  There's no level-end screens, but rather chapter titles appearing on screen as you progress through the different areas, letting the player know they are on the right track.  All part of the cohesive storytelling that keeps the player engaged right to the end.
The gameplay can be challenging, and at times, unforgiving.  The difficulty curve ramps up nicely as the player aqcuire better weapons, but ammunition can be sarce at times, which adds a good balance to the game. The visuals and voice acting are decent given the times, but the script is solid.
All in all: Great game. 2/3 ;)

I love this game. I must say I hesitated to buy it after the mix reviews. I was baffled after playing the game: disagree with most of the negatives:
First, timed missions are not a problem: You can DL mods to remove it in the steam workshop. I don't feel too rushed, but it adds another challenge layer for experienced players. The timer usually doesn't start before some trigger you're aware of, so you kind of know what to expect once the clock starts ticking. I enjoy it.
Second, the game looks and runs great. While I do see framerate drops during load screens, during regular play the game runs smooth.
Third, Haven't experienced any gamebreaking bugs, but hey, it's XCOM - there are some bugs - but they don't detract from the overall experience.
DLC - Digital Deluxe edition is worth picking up on sale, because it includes all DLC for a relatively low price than individual purchases; however, DLC for this game is kind of weak. The skin packages aren't very interesting (unless you like dressing your soldiers up like punks). Alien Hunters DLC adds new challenge to the game for experienced players, but new players best avoid it. A lot of people find the challenge to be game breaking. But worth checking out on a second playthrough - the bonus weapons are pretty sweet. Shen's Gift is the best of the DLC - adds an exciting new mission and a mech unit to play (however, a little expensive for what you actually get).
The game builds upon Enemy Unknown/Within. Not exactly the same game: New soldiers, enemies, and abilities make for a new experience, and another learning curve, even for experienced XCOM players. Some of it will feel familiar, and the rest won't - so give yourself some time to adapt.
If you loved the previous game in the series, definitely pick this one up.

Here's how I view NBA 2K16:
The MyCareer, while generating a lot of criticism from the playerbase, isn't all that bad in my opinion. Sure, the first year of that mode forces you to go through the story and play 8 games with minimal control outside of games, but a lot opens up after those 8 games. I beared through the average story and was rewarded with a cool game mode with lots of options. Don't hesitate to buy this game because people complain about the MyCareer mode.
That out of the way, NBA 2K16 isn't only MyCareer. There's MyLeague, MyGM, MyTeam (links with the mobile one), and of course exhibition games. The online community is pretty thin now that 2K17 is out, but I think the game offers plenty as is and can keep me occupied for hours at a time.
Graphically, the game doesn't disappoint; it rarely does, but the improvements from year to year are gradual. Gameplay is smooth and solid, diverse, and customizable.
Overall, NBA 2K16 is worth its price tag for the sheer amount of content it has. Although on the expensive side, the upside to the game is that it will most likely keep you entertained with its many game modes.

its very hard to decide if i want to recommend or not recommend this game because it is free to play, so i can't really say where the line is on that.  here's a few points that might be of interest to future players.
GRAPHICS:  the graphics aren't very good in this game, but run quite nicely.  it is very smooth, but not very detailed
PLAYERS:  the other players in the game don't have a huge effect on your experience.  they try to complete the objectives and don't say much.  its actually relaxing to not have a constant feed of BS going through mics or chat lines.
PAY TO WIN:  this game is very pay to win oriented.  without spending some hard-earned cash CONSTANTLY, you are pretty much sitting downhill from everyone else.  the reason i say its constant is because everything in game only lasts for a little while before it expires and you have to get new gear or deal with the original equipment.
GAMEPLAY:  the gameplay is that of an early 2000's game.  its bad, but not painfully so.  melee is really the kicker for me on that.  you have to press a key to switch to your melee weapon before you can use it, then switch back to your gun with another key.  plus, the melee weapons that are free, suck.  they take two hits and its rediculously hard to hit anyone with them.  the paid weapons are one hit kills.
MAPS:  the maps are extremely small and they are not detailed at all.  they work for the game, but with anything bigger than like a 6 on 6, would be just too many people on too small of an area.  they are similar to the size of nuketown 2025 on BlackOps II.
WEAPONS:  the weapons are decent.  they work, but unless you have a scope, you can't look down the sights, which was one of the most frustrating aspects of this game for me.  accuracy SUCKED.  weapons are also very pay to win oriented.
MENU:  the menu sucked but worked.  it was frustrating to have everything cost money.  the entire menu was just low quality, but it got the job done and wasn't lagging at all.

I could just say that Darkest Dungeon is the "Dark Souls" of rogue-like games and you'd probably get an idea of what this game is, but simply stating that does not give enough credit to this game.
Brutal and Unrelenting at its core, this game is a dark fantasy-themed turn-based dungeon crawler that takes sadism to a whole new level. You'd have to be a masochist to enjoy this game, and if you're not, you probably are, because you get to enjoy seeing your party die for maybe the first few hours of this game assuming you're going in blind. The gameplay mechanics are what makes this game a torturing experience. Here you have a game where your characters not only die physically, but mentally as well. Stress management is a huge part of this game and can completely derail an entire dungeon run. One party member dies in combat? Your other party members begin to lose hope and hinder progress. One party member goes insane? Have fun seeing him stress out the other members. Did you light the torch? did you bring food? Shovels? These are the questions that begin to surface as you get used to the game, and rightfully so. But even if you did all the right things, there is always something bound to go wrong at some point in the game. Don't let this get you down, RNG is a huge part of this game. Every move you make is a gamble.
There are a couple different dungeons in the game which feature a different variety of enemies. Given the nature of the game, planning is half the battle. Sometimes it might be beneficial to go to the rooms in a different order, change up the skills of your members, or even change up the roster of the party itself, which goes a long way depending on what type of quest you take on. For the first few expeditions of each dungeon, it is really just scouting the peculiarities of the dungeon to see what to expect. This is a rogue-like so try not to feel guilty and send in a dummy party of new recruits to scout out each dungeon and get a feel for them first, and then you can plan your way around it.
This game is really a management game disguised as a turn-based RPG. The closest comparison to this game would really be Fire Emblem, except this actually takes the management aspect up a notch. Lastly, I would like to add that the narration is an underappreciated aspect in this game and really adds in to the whole experience & atmosphere.
Pros
+depth/gameplay
+aesthetic
+narration
+atmosphere
+content updates
+- music blends into the game so well you might not notice it at first, not too many tracks stand out but is worth a listen
Cons
-story is ok

My first boss fight:
My crew, with weapons and armor held together with only hopes and dreams staggers into the last room of the dungeon. The torch is lit, but barely. The gray stone walls, lined with failing bookshelves, and tables with candles once lit eons ago. No sooner than they had entered, the master of death and afterlife himself had arrived, the Necromancer. Stress fills the minds of our heroes, some insane, and some teetering on the brink. With a swift strike, the Necromancer shrouds their minds in fear and paranoia; half of them writhe in selfish gestures, the other half filled with the hate of their comrades. The insanity finally takes hold, and the battle begins. The Houndmaster, refusing the aid of the Occultist, gets hit in the head with a club held by a bonehead skeleton, and dies instantly. The Crusader, unhappy with how the Arbalest handles her crossbow, kills her in the name of the Holy Land. He then suffers a heart attack, as he is unable to cope with the sudden appearance of more skeletons. The Occultist, ever fearful of death, rebuilds his body as many times as he can; withstanding an armada of boneheads weilding wood clubs. After a display of spooky shrieks and heavy swings, the Apprentice Necromancer leans in with one final word to the shriveled and beaten Occultist. "Boo." it whispered. Finally, a heart attack claims the last sign of true life in this, their Darkest Dungeon.

Review based on 32+ hours of gameplay. Will update review as patches are released.
Pros:
As a long time fan of the series, this is a VERY welcome reboot of the series.
I've played several short games to get a feel for the game, have an ongoing multiplayer game going with a friend around turn 250, and have completed a large 6 race game with the Psilons achieving every tech (was gaining 3000 tech a turn by the end), 24 colonies, 519 population, 646k credits, 1.3 million conquest, 1.14 million excellence, claimed Orion for my own, and after all the other races declared war on me I wiped them off the face of the galaxy by turn 448. Around turn 300 I was already insanely powerful (power through great technology) and could almost vote myself the supreme leader, but chose not to.
It feels a lot like MOO2 with a lot of nice new UI features like improved menus, empire management, game summary, etc. Below I'm going to say a lot of things to be aware of or cons to the game, but really the game has a lot going for it, namely it's a VERY good reboot of the game and while it's still missing a lot, it has placeholders to show it plans on implimenting everything we'd expect and then some.
I kinda miss the old MOO2 theme music (listening to it right now while writing the reivew), but I like the new soundtrack as well. Graphics are what you're epxect out of a game these days. The game feels a lot like the things I love about MOO. There are a lot of cool newer features like improvements to notifications, but I wish they could add a little bit of customization to them. Also really like the space factories element to the game. Just learned a new feature, if you goto the summary screen you can litterly got back to any turn in the past. You can click on the timeline graph and go back to a previous turn which means the save game remembers EVERYTHING that happened in every turn.
Things to be aware of with early access:
A lot of systems are not yet or BARELY implimented. Mainly the space combat (just hit simulate because tactical is poop atm), spying, dimplomacy in general needs to be improved, racial traits, AI difficulties, starting tech levels, ship customization (it's there but missing a lot of it's expected depth), half of the planned races, and everyon's favorite: custom race. A lot of the tooltips in the game are not very clear what those things do or even if they are fully implimented right now. The tech tree is flushed out but the UI needs some polish.
There are various minor weird UI bugs including hangs and the occasional crash. Thankfully the game autosaves every turn. There are some pretty annoying bugs for example the game insists that Neutron Blaster is stronger than the Mass Driver).
Multiplayer works, but can be a little weird when you are loading a previous multiplayer game. Also the invite friends feature doesn't work, your friends just need to join your game.
The voice acting is good, but sitll needs work, obviously that's finishing polish stuff for launch. A lot of times the text of what the voice acting is supposed to be saying doesn't match what is said likely only part of the script has been recorded / integrated or they want to limit the download for early access. Some of the characters you start to just hate how they talk to you (unless you're overwhelmingly powerful then they cower and lick your boots which actually is kinda awesome). Overall how the races react to you can largely be improved.
Cons:
No Elarians planned for launch. The Elarians smell like expansion fodder. No Gnolmans or Trilarians either, but no great loss there. Don't like that they are tying a "new" alternate human / pirate faction to the collectors edition but honestly, who cares since if you buy it now you're getting the "collectors edition" at like normal release price.
It's REALLY ♥♥♥♥ING ANNOYING when picking a race and trying to read the racial traits having to listen to the narrator.
Also I miss the old feature where if there was nothing notable happening (everything is queued up etc) then the turn auto passes to the next turn. I wish they would allow me to customize my auto build order.
There seems to be a lot less planets per solar system from what I remember from older MOO games. I wish there where more planets. Also I miss the inter-solar system colonization vs colonly ship. Maybe it's something that's less important since everyone is post warp. If they add in pre-warp age that becomes more important.
Summary:
I might be a fan boy of the series, but it seems pretty damn good for early access and I'm glad they did do early access so I can give my feedback. If you've apprehensive about the game, wait closer to launch. I know I will probably binge on the game for a while then dial back until patches come out and try out the new features.

In 2007 DLC was mostly restricted to map packs on consoles. Mr. Howard, our ever truthful dovahkin of a project leader decided in 2008 that Oblivion should have paid DLC that wasn't in the normative form of an expansion pack. To test the waters, the concept of the microtransaction was for something completely cosmetic: horse armor.
Now why would the audience be upset about something cosmetic costing $4 more than you've already spent on the game?
Well, why should any content be kept out of the game? Why should we have to pay extra for something that is useful? And if it isn't useful, then why bother?
If this paid scheme supplied us with games that we actually wanted to play: A new Obsidian spinoff, a Morrowind successor, or a "Fallout: Van Buren" remake then maybe the community could understand.
BUT, there's a huge problem here. We aren't getting the games that we want. We got ESO: Morrowind. We got an empty Fallout 4, and now insted of getting a new engine for the next generation, we are going to have a GoT game.
So what does this all add up to? In the last 10 years since Oblivion, nearly every single game on the market has DLC, is in early access, or has cosmetic microtransactions. TF2 literally broke underneath the weight of all their hats.
The takeaway in my opinion is that this incentivizes developers to release EVEN LESS content, knowing that they can outsource every missing feature to the community. Why bother programming a "vault" command, or a "climb" command when you can sell it as a "paid mod", and give the modder a small percentage of profit to appease them.
So i won't be buying any of your paid mods. And i probably won't be playing any new Bethesda games in the future, because i don't feel as though the player matters. We're just little cash cows that can be milked in as many different ways as possible, simultaneously.
All of this? It just doesn't work.

The game is currently in Alpha, the phase of development where the prototype is fuctional but major features are not compleate or even notationaly in the software yet. This means that, as it stands, the game can be played start to finish but major parts are missing (spying, several races, ect)
Other parts are implemented, but unfinished. Combat is currently playable, but has the hallmarks of a placeholder that will be barely recongizable at release. Many planet discriptions and technologies are likewise placeholders that are likely to be changed.
The basic turn-based empire management, planet mangment and map are the closest to done and are beaitful, with high production values in what is finished and a lot of fun.
If you are in this just for fun.. Play MOO2? Playing this game now is a lot of fun, but buying now is for people that just can't wait or enjoy being part of the development process.

I just went through some of the feedbacks here so I decided to make my own one since I read a lot of bs!
First, I'm relatively new to the game, playing it for about 3 Months now.
The game is so dam good looking! The ship models are insanely detailed and they look so fantastic! Something like "Dreadnought" can't compete with this!
It has quite a steep learning curve so make sure you learn about the mechanics like armour rotating or the gamma times. If you do so you will enjoy often hard and thrilling battles with a very close outcome. The victorys are so rewarding and you often feel good even if you loose a game because it is a close and hard fight.
The game is very skill based, so you need to know the ships and how to aim. There is almost no RNG involved, not like world of warships for example.
There is also a lot of help you get from the veterans of this game. Just hop on the discord, have a chat with them, ask for help or chat with the devs. The game gets developed very close to the community and you feel it balance and gameplay wise.
Every ship plays different with other abilities and strengths. You can try every ship with every configuration in solo play, try out a new bought ships in PvE and finally get into PvP and to the real challenge.
Yes it is free to play and definitely not pay to win! You can get almost everything via playing the game or through luck by completing the tasks and earn pots (yeah you get pots completely for free for just playing the game and you get quite a lot of them). You can even get rare ultimate skins out of the boxes that give you a 20% credit income boost for the battle.
Yes you can invest money into it to buy new ships, skins, or crew/implant pots to get a crew faster. But you don't need to. This is fine tuning for the late game. You will get a starter crew that do just fine and you earn new implants and crewmember by again just playing the game. Again no pay to win.
Also some say the grind is bad, the grind is not that bad! You get quite a lot of income and you can buy cheaper ships relatively fast so you get a little fleet on your hand. There are also 4 ships on rotation so you can try them out for free in PvE and PvP. Beside the income from battles you also get income from achieving medals by playing in PvP that grant platin or credits at certain stages.
And last but not least if you want to buy something, the prices are okay and not too expensive. For example you get a ship for 990 platinum that is around 4,40€. That is NOTING compared to a T8 in any WarGaming title that cost 10x as much! I already put some money into the game just because it is so great and I want to reward the devs for their great work and also get my ships some new colours.
I can't recommend it enough if you like the setting and the stile of game. But you need the will to learn the game because mistakes get punished. It is team based so communicate with the team and you will have some thrilling and rewarding games! Just try it out, it costs you nothing!
Only down side right now are the lack of players (this game isn't very known yet), only one game mode due to the lack of players (I'm sure more will come if more players play the game) and the lack of further tutorials (there is a short one that explains you the basics but for further information you have to deal with the game mechanics and ask other players if you don't understand something).
Apart from that this game is one of the best online games I have played so far!

It seems to be mostly based upon Colin McRae Rally 2.0, and seems to be ported version from mobile device.
General observations:
- Quite a simple graphics judged by today expectations (still found of sufficient level to my mind). Looks like CMR2.0 with modern processing effects applied.
- Quite an accurate car models of real vehicles
- Decent physical model with unique behaviour for each vehicle
- Each car seems to have it's own specific durability level of each system and tends to receive specific damage depending on your driving style
In comparions with CMR2.0 some content is removed:
- less cars avaliable
- no tuning
- simplified repairs
- less rallies (no Finland, Sweden, Kenya and England)
- no duel stages at the end of each rally
- no weather and night stages
- rallies are shorter (6 stages per rally max)
- less camera modes
- no arcade mode
- much less unlockable content
I used to be very found of CMR series and especially of 2.0, but still I can make some mistakes in my comparison cause it was long ago when I used to play it.
Summary:
Don't take it as one of CMR istallments, but consider it to be separate game of more arcade style.
Would siut casual players, those who llooks for CMR2.0 nostalgie sessions, people infamiliar with CMR series and looking for arcade with real vehicles with more or less realistic behavior.
Will fail to meet your expectations if you are looking for something in line with established CMR experience.
Anyway I'd still recommend this game as a good fun.

I love this game. I must say I hesitated to buy it after the mix reviews. I was baffled after playing the game: disagree with most of the negatives:
First, timed missions are not a problem: You can DL mods to remove it in the steam workshop. I don't feel too rushed, but it adds another challenge layer for experienced players. The timer usually doesn't start before some trigger you're aware of, so you kind of know what to expect once the clock starts ticking. I enjoy it.
Second, the game looks and runs great. While I do see framerate drops during load screens, during regular play the game runs smooth.
Third, Haven't experienced any gamebreaking bugs, but hey, it's XCOM - there are some bugs - but they don't detract from the overall experience.
DLC - Digital Deluxe edition is worth picking up on sale, because it includes all DLC for a relatively low price than individual purchases; however, DLC for this game is kind of weak. The skin packages aren't very interesting (unless you like dressing your soldiers up like punks). Alien Hunters DLC adds new challenge to the game for experienced players, but new players best avoid it. A lot of people find the challenge to be game breaking. But worth checking out on a second playthrough - the bonus weapons are pretty sweet. Shen's Gift is the best of the DLC - adds an exciting new mission and a mech unit to play (however, a little expensive for what you actually get).
The game builds upon Enemy Unknown/Within. Not exactly the same game: New soldiers, enemies, and abilities make for a new experience, and another learning curve, even for experienced XCOM players. Some of it will feel familiar, and the rest won't - so give yourself some time to adapt.
If you loved the previous game in the series, definitely pick this one up.

As it stands now, Master of Orion is an okay game. Not a great game, not an awful game, but a rather generic 4X. Much of what made it's predecessors sucessful, their quirky humor hidden in the descriptions of technology and buildings, the ability to truly customize ships to a greater degree, the ability to build numerous fleets without being limited by a "command cap", and the ability to build as many orbital bases as you wanted, is gone. The parts that made it great and unique are gone. Perhaps they're just waiting in development? Who knows.
Where once we had the "Mystery X" researches if you found them, they've been replaced by the standard "economic victory", "research victory", "diplomatic victory", and "conquest victory". While fun, it takes away some of the fun, y'know?
So I will recommend it, but not as Masters of Orion, but as another generic 4x space game, until they make it truly as good as it's predecessors.

Darkest Dungeon is one of my favorite games ever; however, i wouldn't recommend it to everyone. The reason for this is that the game is very difficult and this is mostly because of the RNG. Don't get me wrong, this is a fantatic game with amazing art. music, and especially narration. Wayne June was a perfect fit for the gothic and dark atmosphere of the game, and he did a terrific job. The gameplay is great, the animation is amazing considering it is one frame for the combat, and the crowquill art style looks so good. There are a lot of really interesting gameplay mechanics and different things to pay attention to. But, like I said this is a difficult largely in part because of the RNG. This will be very unappealing to many because it will seem unfair. However, I and many other people see this as a welcome challenge and I personally think it works well in this game. It makes it to where not everything is within your control so you have to work around the events that occur. Any player that pays attention to the characters, enemies, and areas will be able to put the odds greatly in their favor, and it is required. To play this game well and make it easier on yourself you need to know character combinations, enemy prioritization, the enemies in each area and how they affect your party, and how to play a characters strengths and mitigate their weaknesses. Overall I think Darkest Dungeon is a great game a definitely one of my top five of all time, it is like Dark Souls in the sense that it has a small yet passionate fanbase. I can't recommend it to everyone but if you know you like these kinds of games or think you might then definitely get Darkest Dungeon.

With that out of the way everything else about the game is great and can definitely feel like a virtual party.  You can just hang out in condos or play various games.  There are more basic games like typing derby and trivia.  There is the recently added bowling and the more full featured games like minigolf and Virus which is a quick fps game.  It's all tied together with a currency called units that rewards you for playing the game.   There is even a casino where you can gamble on units and hope to earn more.  All of the games are well designed, simple to play, and fun.
I also have to admire the developer for only charging for the game and not offering anything else for real world money.  You have to earn units in game and shows the developer has principles and doesn't just want to be greedy.  For me the current price of $15 is well worth it for what you can do now but others may want to wait until more games are added.   With a lot of more serious online games out with angry players this lighthearted and fun game stand out as something unique.

TIME RECOIL is an interesting game.  It combines the top-down perspective of  NEON CHROME with the slow-motion/bullet-time combat tactics of SUPERHOT.  Just like NEON CHROME, the graphics are slick and the music captures the tension of the story very well.
You play as Alexa, a woman endowed by a laboratory accident with the ability to survive time travel and dilate time in combat.  Chaining kills can prolong the time dilation for a tactical advantage.  Larger kill-chains unlock additional dash/blast abilities.
Each individual mission may not take long to complete, but the challenge lies in chaining kills in just the right ways to use the right abilities at the right moments to complete the mission.  It's important to note that one does not always have to kill every guard on a mission to succeed.
Fortunately, the game has adjustable difficulty levels and mappable controls.  The short mission lengths mean that failing won't set you back much timewise.  It look me 8 hours to finish the game the first time.  Learning the value of kill-chains enabled me to finish a second playthrough in 3 1/2 hours, and a third in 2 1/2.  I may play through again to see if I can reduce that time further ;)
There isn't much character exposition or development, but the story is told decently enough.  Being an action game, I can forgive the sparse story.
Generally, I recommend this game for gameplay that is challenging without being infuriating.

Colin Mcrae Rally for Steam is a wonderfully crappy experience that everybody ages 0 through 100 should experience. The overall horrible physics paired with irresponsive controls make for an absolutely blissful playtime when racing throughout Australia over and over on the same few tracks.
I felt right at home when my brake barely even responded, or when my speed sporadically went up or down a lot with the lightest change of the gas trigger. It felt like I was truly there.
The graphics were immersive enough to fool me into thinking I was actually looking at my PS1 over a CRT TV. I loved the completely flat bushes and trees, as well as the completely solid tree texture surrounding the tracks. I wish more games were like this.
The sounds were beautiful. I loved the monotonous whispers of the co-driver into my ear as I flew against every tree on the course. I loved the sound of a tin can engine pushing itself far too hard.
I would truly recommend this game to anyone if they want to have a delightful experience of what a racing game shouldn't be. 10/10 would give more money if DLC existed.

Being a game that exists for a long time, Lugaru is interesting and difficult. It is the first game developed by Wolfire Games, and has a good batch of levels throughout the story mode and challenge mode, focusing in action and having a good fighting mechanic, with simple graphics and animations.
You'll control a rabbit throughout the game, and will be able to perform high jumps, weapon throws and various attacks in a fight against one or more opponents, using your fists and throwing kicks or even weapons that can be found with the opponents or scattered around the map.
There's not much to say, the game is old and simple, it may not be incredible for "todays standards", but it certainly was during the time of its release and can be considered good for those who like fighting games or those who want to play something simple from time to time.
It may be fun but it's not worth the price for it's age. If you want to buy it, wait for a sale, or keep what you have to buy Overgrowth, considered the successor of Lugaru, with several other improvements, including the fighting mechanics.

Let me preface this by saying that I greatly enjoy Darkest Dungeon, for the most part. It is an incredibly well made game with a lot of positive aspects; the awesome art and badass narrator, one of the most enjoyable turn based combat systems that has ever been in a game for just a couple of instances of the good that this game has. But with so much good how in the hell can I not recommend this game? RNG.
There is very little actual skill in Darkest Dungeon. Or at least, it caps at a certain point. Ultimately though, the preperations you make before your expeditions, the training of your characters and all the strategising you do is simply to affect chances. Percentages that ultimately impact the outcomes of your journey. Send a bunch of low level recruits into a dungeonto bump up their resolve level? The game might throw hunger events constantly your way, running you out of food resources and potentially stressing and physically damaging your team. Got too many items? Fight the collector as a random boss in the middle of your quest; this can be especially bad depending on the type of quest your going on, could cause you to just leave the quest.
Everything is RNG in Darkest Dungeon, hell there are classes that are just very high risk for disproportionately high reward, such as the Occultist. As satisfying and engaging as the game can be, you can get completely screwed over by an enemy getting repeated crits, their status effects applying to much, a random boss encounter, ambush during the night when you camp. There is nothing you can say for definite with this game and building up your characters is just trying to affect a dice roll. As much as I love some of the design of this game, the simple over-reliance on randomness and luck means I can in no way realistically recommend it, despite other aspects of the game being presented incredibly well.

In 2007 DLC was mostly restricted to map packs on consoles. Mr. Howard, our ever truthful dovahkin of a project leader decided in 2008 that Oblivion should have paid DLC that wasn't in the normative form of an expansion pack. To test the waters, the concept of the microtransaction was for something completely cosmetic: horse armor.
Now why would the audience be upset about something cosmetic costing $4 more than you've already spent on the game?
Well, why should any content be kept out of the game? Why should we have to pay extra for something that is useful? And if it isn't useful, then why bother?
If this paid scheme supplied us with games that we actually wanted to play: A new Obsidian spinoff, a Morrowind successor, or a "Fallout: Van Buren" remake then maybe the community could understand.
BUT, there's a huge problem here. We aren't getting the games that we want. We got ESO: Morrowind. We got an empty Fallout 4, and now insted of getting a new engine for the next generation, we are going to have a GoT game.
So what does this all add up to? In the last 10 years since Oblivion, nearly every single game on the market has DLC, is in early access, or has cosmetic microtransactions. TF2 literally broke underneath the weight of all their hats.
The takeaway in my opinion is that this incentivizes developers to release EVEN LESS content, knowing that they can outsource every missing feature to the community. Why bother programming a "vault" command, or a "climb" command when you can sell it as a "paid mod", and give the modder a small percentage of profit to appease them.
So i won't be buying any of your paid mods. And i probably won't be playing any new Bethesda games in the future, because i don't feel as though the player matters. We're just little cash cows that can be milked in as many different ways as possible, simultaneously.
All of this? It just doesn't work.
