I suppose that any game that has kept me busy for more than 20 hours while I'm still far from finishing it and I haven't really gotten tired of it is a fine game in my book.
Darkest Dungeon is not a fancy game, but it is entertaining, deep enough and has a lot of personality. In a dark world of sickness, madness and necromancy, you lead an expandable group of adventurers. Many of them will die, and there's nothing you can do to avoid it, just play it slow and safe to minimise the casualties.
Pros:
- brave and different: it defies definitions
- dark and real: adventurers die or crumble under pressure, they are faulty individuals. You get attached even though you really shouldn't
- challenging, but not to the point of desperation (at least for now)
- not beautiful graphically, but it has a charismatic look
Cons:
- repetitive
- high risk of wasting hours upon hours of progress with one small mistake or just by chance. If you lose one of your strongest heroes or fail a mission at the wrong moment you could face a setback of days
- unclear progression: when does it end? How close are you at any given moment?
All in all it's a good game (especially if coming at a small price) that can keep you entertained for a while; do not expect miracles, but give it a try!

Review Reboot.  I like the general direction the game is taking.  The AI is not very challangeing yet but still fairly enjoyable early on.  I like the idea of NPC minor civs but they dont seem to do much yet other than to give me 40 to 70 credits upon killing nearby pirate ships and bases.  They are yet to offer any mission/quest other than to ask for a single tech early on.  Combat seems to be a little better other than the occasional freeze or CTD following the combat after action report during transition to main screen.  The ship build/refit changes took some getting use to.  They are not very smooth and the way systems are presented in the new drop down menu is muddy and a pain to work with.  The previouse version of ship fitting was more intuitive and smoother.  You should link the ship slot with the systems capable of inhabiting them so the process would go a little more smooth.  By the late game the dropdown menu is way too populated and there is no rhyme or reason to the order they are listed even after choosing a single class of system. There was little gained from the refit changes and in several respects it is less efficient.  First do no harm...then...  Non-gated travel, going off the beaten path, should be an option for later propultion techs.  I liked this ability in other MOO games. I agree with some others, Antarans should be brought back as slap-back "regulators" focusing on mega civs that progress too quickly.  Someone else mentioned the late game economy, and yes I have a game going where I can buy titans every oher turn, not realistic.  Maybe consider a cap on purchasable construction points on capitol ships.  I mean really, the parts still have to be fabricated and assembled.  Maybe cap capitol ship purchase to 75% of total.  I still dont see anything about fighters and bombers that make me want to include them in design.  They really seem to be useless at this point.  They add nothing to overall combat points in practice. I want to build a carrier variuent but dont see the point yet.  Anyway, keep up the good work.  So stoked that MOO is reborn.

They marked this game as Early Access so I'm assuming they will add many of the features I feel is lacking from this game in it's current state.
As for the main gripe I read about the 500 turn limit, I suspect this will go away since this release of the game (as of Feb 27th 2016) is the earliest release.
I recommend this game, not highly, but just plain recommend it.  I do see how they were trying to stay true to some aspects of Master of Orion 2 (MOO2) but other parts of it feel lacking.  Considering all they have to do is take MOO2, update the graphics and sounds, and CHANGE NOTHING ELSE to get an amazing game, I'm surprised nobody has done this...
After the crap that was given to us as MOO3 I had wrote off the Master of Orion series, thinking that MOO2 would just be a legendary game that other 4x titles would aspire to reach.
Pros:
- Graphics are impressive
- Voice Acting is very very impressive
- Races have personality
- UI is efficient and unobtrusive while still providing everything you need
- Mrrshan's never looked and sounded so... good!
Cons:
- Diplomacy is... dumb... No point in actually doing it now except to hear some of the excellent Voice Acting!
- No custom races... yet?
- Racial traits feel very underpowered, traits provide such a small bonus that it doesn't really matter who you pick
- Ship design is extremely limited (See suggestions below)
- Taxes are problematic in large empires pick +1BC per citizen and you don't make enough, but everyone is happy, pick +2 and make WAY to much, but some population goes on strike.  Needs more tweaking.
- Tech tree feels small compared to MOO2
- What happened to fleet and colony leaders?
- Space Monsters are borked... I took down the Space Eel with one Destroyer and one Frigate with about a fifth of it's Offensive rating.
Suggestions:
I am sure most of these have been suggested by others and I will be posting about these in other forums on the MOO website in hopes of being heard or at least considered.
Custom Races with meaningful racial traits
- This isn't a suggestion, this is a requirement.
Fleet and/or Planetary Leaders
- In M002, were they very powerful? Yes.  Too powerful?  Maybe.  Still, they added something more to the game
Ship design choices
- Why can't I put more than 2 specials or 2 weapons on a frigate?  Why can I put 4 Augmented engines on one ship?  How come I can't put on the Point Defense mod with autofire and continuous Fire?  Various other weird decisions were made regarding this, but I suspect this will change since it is still Early Access.
Miniaturization
- I miss this, it is what made using some of those old technologies over new ones actually preferable in many situations.  Maybe I want to fit 3000 Plasma cannons onto a Doom Star to blow out my old Sound Blaster 16 card like I used to.
Weapons are bland
- Some weapon choices are odd, but I don't like it that I can replace 10 Lasers with 10 Neutron Blasters for the exact same size cost.
Combat needs a huge overhaul
- MOO2 was turn based, we want turn-based at least as an option.  I kind of understand why many games don't do turn-based combat because it is very very easy to exploit AI weaknesses.  Also, why can't I retreat?
Space lanes?
- Seriously... wtf...  you used to be limited based on the range of your fuel cells, but now you can go EVERYWHERE from turn 1.  M002 didn't have space lanes, you could go from any system to any other system in range, seriously, this has to go...
Overall, I give this game many more negatives than positives, but I see where they are putting effort into it and seem to be trying to stay true to classic MOO elements so I'm excited to see where they will take this game in the future.

For some reason, people believes this is a port of the old CMR games from the ps1 days, and later on pc. Well, this is not.
I have all of them and, even though I never liked their handling model, this is even worse and the only things in common are the name and some assets.
It can't have the same gameplay anyway, since this one uses a different engine, Unity, which is also partly what makes this game so bad.
The performance of this game, compared to the graphics, are terrible. It runs just fine in my system, but DiRT2 and 3 at Ultra runs even better here, reaching solid 60fps at 1080p, while this one has worse graphics than CMR 2.0 and runs as badly as the last Batman game.
Then there's the "physics", if so can be called, that are so unrealistic that gives the game a much higher difficulty level than what's supposed to have. They could have opted for the arcade handling model of the CMR series, but instead tried to make something just too big for this terrible engine, and it ended up becoming one of the worst racing games of all times, on par with Team6 titles.
Controls? People, again, believes this supports gamepads and so "you can control it better than on the smartphone": nope.
Although it does support gamepads, the controls are not analog, meaning that the analog sticks will act as digital sticks, which adds problems to the already terrible handling.
That's at least what happens to me with the 2 different gamepads I own, and to many other people that can actually understand how analog handling feels like. If it only works for some specific gamepad model is beyond my knowledge, but since Unity has many problems with input devices, it might as well be.
There's a load of other little and big problems with this game, such as a terrible menu, terrible configuration screen, basically no graphics options, static tracks and backgrounds, no replays, bland and dated graphics, recycled music from CMR 3 (from what I remember)...
I can't really find a single positive thing to say about this game. I got it from the Codemasters bundle and I thank myself for not having spent even 1 euro on this title alone, because it doesn't matter how cheap you can buy it at, it's not worth the time it will make you waste.
If you think this could be a nice time waster or a little arcade racer to spend some time on between more serious games, well that's a mistake: the terrible handling and bad pad support makes racing artificially too hard to be enjoyable, and I'd like to see how many of the positive reviewers actually could, or wanted to, complete the game.

First impressions:
The Assassin's Creed franchise would do well to focus on developing high-quality, engaging content, rather than scattering monotonous tasks with overzealous liberty throughout the streets of Paris.
In that regard, the detective-work quests to compensate for the lazy police chief are a refreshing addition. They could have been great, had effort been spent on further development to their plots and character narratives.
I think most people aren't drawn to hundreds of meaningless chests and tokens that are rarely difficult to reach, but that more often left me with the feeling that my time had just been wasted. If you're like me, and you want to try everything in a game, I suggest you think carefully about buying this one.
If there were, say, 10 chests on the map, where I had to solve a complex puzzle to access them and the rewards were... actually rewarding, this would certainly appeal to me. This game could achieve great things were Ubisoft to abandon quantity as a metric for success over quality.
If I can be bothered, I'll update this when I've played more.

The voice acting is nice, the animation of the different races is nice.  I'm looking forward to more races getting added, and also how they design the espionage system.
The ships are neat, the buildings are neat.  The way you can block warp gates with military sations is really cool.
My only complaint is the thing that MOO2 does better than any other similar game out there (including this one):
In MOO2 you could go to the settings and turn off the end of turn wait.  This way you could essentially fast forward your long construction times and research times.  You can't do that in any modern game because your system has to process enemy turns.  In modern games, the enemy turns take a few seconds to process.  This really slows the pace down...  This game combats that by shortening build times and research times.  (Research now usually takes between 4-8 turns).
Also, I would much have preferred turn based ship combat...
All in all, though I won't put in the kind of hours on this game as I did MOO2, it's a solid buy (Though I would really put it's worth at $20 right now.  $49 is overpriced IMO).

Botanicula is a cute and (almost darkly) atmospheric point-and-click adventure game about little plant creatures following out a mythic quest. (Each of the cute little fellows has their own abilities to help overcome the challenges they encounter, though unfortunately they don't come into play more than a few times :/ Oh well, having a whole group of critters with you is still fun.)
Botanicula is not your usual point-and-click, where you pixel hunt to progress. Instead you'll be searching around for all the cool little creatures that inhabit the world, simply because you *want* to. Seeing them move around and interact (and all the sounds they make!) is really enjoyable, even more so because of how completely optional it is.
Neither will you have to worry about obtuse item combinations to proceed; quest items usually simply frame areas that you'll be exploring, without actually being difficult to collect. The primary difficulty/annoyance comes in the latter half of the game where there are multiple puzzles available at once and you're not sure in what order to do them. Your map is usually good (stylized line drawings on leaves!), although one area in the latter half of the game (the city) is just too jumbled (it's hard to tell where you've been and what's where).
Overall, Botanicula is a great little game (~4 hours, if you explore like I do) with excellent art design, sound design, music, and atmosphere. The first half of the game is particularly good, because of its focus on the environment (both on the natural home of the critters and what's happening to it...); the latter half sort of breaks down on that with one area too cluttered (and discordant with the prior environments) and another too spread out, both too unfocused.
I certainly enjoyed it, though, and I definitely recommend it (though for me the current $10 tag is a bit much; I got it on a Steam sale a while ago - but if you have money, throw it Amanita for me, ok? :P).
Botanicula's certainly a game focused on aesthetics rather than gameplay, and I do love those.

Serena is a first-person perspective mystery adventure game with one of the darker stories and most shocking endings I've seen in some time. You're a dude in a small cabin who seems to have lost his memory. The story takes about an hour to complete, and throughout you'll be told the story of two lovers and try to find out why the guy is now alone. You'll explore the humble abode and hear the main character's thoughts on things as he tries to remember, as well as hear the echoing voice of Serena, his love who has seemingly disappeared with no reason. No real puzzles to speak of, just you exploring and being told a story that gets progressively more unsettling.
After you've clicked on everything, the atmosphere will slowly change. Through subtle lighting and musical cues you'll know that things aren't quite right. Keep going back and looking at the same items, find new ones, and discover the dark truth and even darker future of their story.
Starts off nice and serene (ha) but then Serena happens and... yeah, it's not exactly such a happy and sun-kissed place to be anymore. This game uses its cozy, cabin atmosphere and the storybook love story against you to great effect. It's not exactly a scary horror game, but it definitely features some horrific and scary components. The music is haunting, the atmopshere is increasingly forboding, and the sense of place is fantastic. Voice acting is awesome as well, with some very effective performances that go from loving to surly to veangeful.
If you like adventure games in the style of the developer's other games (like Scratches), or just games with a dark and morbid story that catches you off-guard near the end, definitely check this out. And it's free, so I'd say just go for it.

Botanicula is a very simple point-and-click adventure game that uses minimalistic gestures, visuals, and sounds to guide the player on a tale filled with humor, playfulness, and, most of all, discovery.  Every new area holds a new creature or vegetable that manages to be both cute and mysterious.
There are very few games that can convey the simple and undiluted joy of discovering new things.  Botanicula is one of them, and does it all with zero dialogue.  Most of my first playthrough found me smiling gleefully as the five protagonists enthusiastically escaped the treacherous claws of the sinister shadow spider.
Botanicula is a short little game about a short little story that follows the example of Dr. Seuss and Shel Silverstein, and at only an hour or two of playtime, it never wears out its welcome.  It is an adorable journey that left me feeling like a child again.  There's a great, big, wonderful world out there full of adventures, and this game made me remember it.

SOLO NOBRE MUST FALL. WELCOME, BRIGADOR. Back in the days we had these shooters Jungle Strike and Desert Strike with (nearly) completely destructible terrain. Then came Syndicate and Syndicate 2, both upping the ante with even more full blown orgy of destruction and endorsing the player to do massive collateral damage on one's wake. Then, on the whole different perspective we had wonderful Mech games in the forms of Mech Warrior series (well, about half of 'em were wonderful, at least) and Mech Commander. From this background comes Brigador, cherry-picks the best parts from its role models and brings us the terrible, beautiful wanton of destruction.
Only after few hours under my belt I already love it. It is both a tactical shooter and nearly limitless sandbox of destruction - like playing with a huge Lego set without assembly instructions and a ton of explosives. Brigador's slightly pixelish, neon light drenched and shadow blotted landscapes get constantly pulverized  under heavy mortar strikes, rip-roaring chainguns, rampaging tanks, stomping mechs, even hover-like flying platforms - and they all are designed in a delightfully wonky way that is completely implausible and yet very delightful, like something out of any 2000AD comic strip pages.
The game has a quite lengthy campaign dealing with procedurally 'liberating' the colony planet as a group of mercenaries doing it all for money (handsomely paid by a shady megacorporation). You use the cash to buy more drivers, vehicles, weapons, missions and (also very delightful) intel and lore for the mission mode, which I think is the real beef of the game. (Although I have enjoyed the campaign so far, too.)
You set up your death machine by selecting a hull from towering huge mechs or 'tanks' (more like an apartment block with guns on treads) or flying behemoths to relatively tiny ACPA suits, IFVs or flying platforms, and bolting on them your favored methods of destruction, and off you go. This gives lots of variety into how you plan to pull your job through - level everything with massive firepower, screw dodging and try to just soak the incoming damage with you shields and armour, or be the nimble little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that nobody can hit into and surgically strike your targets and dance away from the blasts before the enemy gets their cumbersome big hiney on the spot. Your imagination is the limit.
Brigador hits my nerve perfectly with its payload of insane scale destruction, frantic shooty-action, tactical aspects and lovely old-skool visuals, not to mention the groovy retro-drenched Synthwave soundtrack pounding on the background. Cherry on the top, the lore is fun to read and gives names and faces on the odd looking things you're either driving yourself or blasting away with glee. Easy to get a grip on, simple enough to learn and time consuming to master with every aspect, Brigador reminds me of good old times - and that we have way too few good Mech games around. Luckily we have this one.

Brigador is easily one of the best games on Steam.
The frantic combat is tough-but-fair. High replayability with things kept interesting by a huge number of choices in vehicle type, each with pros / cons, and a large array of different kinds of weapons. Stealth mechanics are not particularly deep, but their simplicity lends itself well to the game's general sense of urgency. Fast-paced action and precision is balanced well with tactical maneuvering and thinking on your feet. Find your niche in personal style and thrive.
Like any proper retro-inspired action game, the story does not get in the way of the game. There are no cutscenes, or even screens that force you to read about what's going on. If you so choose, however, the game's grimdark setting shines through narrative in the form of technical and personal descriptions displayed as notes written by characters in game, complete with a touch of dark humor that never feels out of place.
I did not expect a game primarily about piloting mechs and blowing things up to have an incredibly rich, dark aesthetic. While not cyberpunk, it grips tightly to the same tone of a cold, cynical dystopia lit frequently by neon. The gritty style of the game's graphics is used to grand effect with cool-looking weapon effects and explosions. While it carries a certain oldschool feel, being set on an isometric plane, Brigador does not look or feel dated, partially due to its clever use of shaders.
The music, composed by Makeup and Vanity Set (MAVS), could singlehandedly give any best-of playlist put together by New Retrowave a run for its money. This reason alone should justify a purchase if you enjoy music like Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, Mega Drive, or Power Glove.

Well, well, well Chucklefish, been a while now, hasn't it. All the media ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t aside, I'm reviewing the core game itself. Singleplayer AND Multiplayer. So here's the skinny on the basis of the game: You're one of 6 races (Humans, Apex which are essentially Planet of the Apes, Glitch which are robots, Avians which are bipedal flightless birds, Floran which are plant people, and Hylotl which are amphibious fishmen. All of them play the same though. There's no racial ability thing. What is this, Skyrim?) on an intergalactic journey to essentially build and survive. But in light of a recent overhaul update that was in the work for a year or so, we now have even MORE to discover and at the same time LESS. I'll be dividing the new content into Pros and Cons.
PRO: More items. Always nice.
CON: More grinding for said items.
PRO: Outpost area. A quote, unquote hub area for trading, purchasing items, and questing.
CON: Quests are random difficulty, one minute you're looking for bugs, the next you're helping some dweeb climb a meteor.
PRO: Quests. More to do, more to gain. Makes it more worthwhile in singleplayer.
CON: Quests are a slow slope to climb. Yes, I know I shouldn't be killing some Worldending Hellbeast for my first quest but catching a bug is so easy it's pathetic in a sense.
PRO: Huge online community from what I've seen. A great way to integrate others into the swing of things.
CON AS ALL HELL: People are understandably concerned with grief and other shenanigans from people as they do in all games, but to have 4000 safety locks worth of passwords and stuff is a bit much.
PRO, GLORIOUS PRO: People have modded custom items into the game anyone can use that do a lot of unique things.
CON, SO MUCH CON: People are reluctant to give or duplicate by modding means their superior items. It's essentially the Hat System of Team Fortress 2 but in pixelated form.
PRO: Online and Offline handle the same.
CON: Hackers will try their best to systematically DDoS or spawnkill you if possible.
PRO BEYOND ALL PROS: Modding is very active and very supported. Chucklefish even has a forum for the mods.
CON: With the update, some mods don't work and/or the devs. of the mod have abandoned it.
So roll with the punches or blaze your own trail, the game plays either way. Just be ready to lose your money on the regular and do that grind loop. All of that aside though, it's a good game if you put the time or mods into it that it needs to get the ball rolling. Hopefully Chucklefish won't update for a while longer though so that I don't have to reinstall my friggen' weapons and race mods.

I've been playing this game since it was first released so this whole paid-mod deal is relatively minor in the grander scale of things. I don't care about or use paid mods so it doesn't affect me, other than seeing a couple of new things on the main menu.
Let's just talk about the game. If you're a fan of Fallout 3 and New Vegas and haven't played this one yet, you should do it.. you won't regret it! Why? Because everything that was so great about Fallout 3 has been made even better. The storyline, graphics, VATS, mechanics, everything.. plain awesome.
Yes, there are some bugs here and there.. but it's unsurprising considering the complexity of all the choice-driven quests and overlapping storylines going on. And maybe they should have spent more time fixing those bugs rather than introducing this "Creation Club" nonsense. Maybe I wish I could get back all that time spent in the Nuka World DLC (Far Harbor is great though).
But take away all the ridiculousness and you're left with one shining gem of a game, one that this Fallout fan has spent 160 hours on. There is simply so much to do. Maybe too much. Building settlements was fun for a while, even after building up 5 or 10 of them. But 20+? Yeah, no. And I'm so sick of those "Help defend...." sirens coming up when I'm in the middle of doing something.
Maybe I got sick of the endless and repeated quests from Preston and BOS. Fine, it turns out I've got a number of complaints about this game now that I think about it. But I've spent more time loving this game than hating it. It's been that way since release, and it feels that way even now.  The fact that I can spend multiple hours playing in one sitting despite all its flaws, that makes it worth it to me. As long as Bethesda stops introducing more flaws of course.
Highlights:
- So much to see and do, so much depth.. so many choices, so much crafting.. so much replayability.
- Well worth it if you're a fan of the Fallout franchise
Drawbacks:
- A little *too much* to see and do. Crafting and building settlements becomes tedious and boring after a while.
- I just completed what I thought was the game's primary mission, although I won't give out any spoilers. But the game is not over? You mean it never really ends?
Overall I'd give this game an 7/10, although that rating is subject to drop depending on what happens with the next patch.
I recommend this game.

I have played the game on the free weekend, for a couple of hours, but only now I finally took the courage to write a review. While Fallout 3 and New Vegas are my favorite games of the past 10 years, I cannot say I'm impressed by Fallout 4. Actually I was so underwhelmed by the whole experience during those 2 hours that, even though I had still some time to play it, I decided it wasn't worth my time.
+ The world is gorgeous and has more details and variety than the previous 2 Fallout games
+ The new VATS gives a little more excitement and adrenaline
- The speaking system is so atrocious, I didn't even want to speak to anyone (most of the time you can't really know for sure what your character is going to say, after you select something like "Yes", "No", "Sarcastic"...)
- Hand holding and scripted events for the first hour is not something that improves the experience, it detracts from it
- The way you acquire the power armor has puzzled me: why giving you the most powerful armor in the game, right at the start, for free, and then take it away from you because you cannot use it, since it requires batteries that you don't have any clue where to find at the start? That's not progression, it's a carrot on a stick, and thank you very much but I'm not a donkey
= I can't really talk about the rest of the game, I stopped playing with disgust and, frankly, a little bit of disappointment in myself for getting on the hype train at launch (Bethesda has done a great job at presenting it, kudos to them)
Now, after all that, here comes the Creation Club, the abomination everybody is talking about. After they presented it and people raised concern about the introduction of "paid mods", Bethesda reassured us they wouldn't be selling mods, but mini DLCs. Well,
.
My advice is: do not endorse that company behavior, please do not buy overpriced mods. Take a look at the Nexus, download some free mods, fix their game by yourself, do not rely on Bethesda to do it, and if you can spare any money donate to the mods creators. I think they will appreciate it more than Bethesda ever will.

Early Access review
I am a bit torn about the game in its current state.
It looks nice and has a streamlined interface and plays fluidly, also it has not crashed on me so far.
On the other hand currently it is just too easy, yes opposing powers declare war on you but that is all they do, they do not even attempt to attack, and if you do a counterstrike after just one fallen system they call for a truce.
Also as son as you developed the cruiser you will win every spacebattle as it seems no matter how long you play the AI never builds anything stronger then destroyers, and a shielded cruiser kills tons of destroyers without even breaking a sweat. So with 2-3 ships you wipe out the enemy spacefleet of 20-30 small ships in one battle and thats it for them.
I played MOO and MOO2 just recently and there if someone declares war, on the next turn they turn up with a spacefleet on your doorstep.
Also it does not really seam to make a difference if you specialize your planets as over time you can build everything you have on every planet. And the planet overview is terrible there need to be a list what you have built and not only a planet you have to scroll around and search to find your installations, even if you can build all some buildings make it easier to build others so it would be nice to see that, because after you own 10-20 planets you just loose the overview what you are building.
Same with the research tree, apart from the few times when you have to choose what to build after you complete a research there is no problem researching everything there is.
Diplomacy is hardly implemented right now, and really is not needed as you can pound the AI into the ground as soon as you get cruisers, and the AI wont attack you anyway. Same for the councilmeetings, most of the time all the parties withhold their votes, and even if there is an alliance you are so strong that you have more votes then the 2 together. Not sure if it is intended or a bug, but the AI seems to lie on a few times I had 2 or 3 parties who vowed to vote for me and when the meeting came they either withheld or voted for the other candidate.
The worst of all are the GNN news updates, the robot does not only look annoying he also sounds like a C64 doing some text to voice. That is too bad as some of the ticker news are quite funny (if not relevant to the game itself).
A bright spot is that the original MOO are included if you do not have them already.
If there were a neutral vote I would give it for now.
But considering the price and the dumbed down AI I will give it a thumbs down for now.

So, I just realized I've yet to make any real review on this. I'm gonna be honest, though.
PROS
- Pretty good shooting mechanics
- SOME of the DLC is pretty great
- Settlement system can be pretty addicting at times
- Well designed open world to explore
- A lot of customization to be had
- Excellent modding support, as Elder Scrolls and Fallout games have always had
CONS
- Story is pretty lackluster. Lacks most of the appeal that any of the previous Fallout games have had.
- Too much focus on the settlement building to the point where more than half of their DLC was focused solely on it.
- If you're not modding the game, it gets rather boring.
- See Below for latest issues.
Now, if this review was posted a couple months ago, it probably would be positive. However, due to all the recent issues being brought on by Bethesda Game Studios, I have to give this a thumbs down. In particular, the Creation Club is total garbage. Sure, it can be avoided, or is supposed to be able to be. But even if that part of it worked, it still feels like a major slap to the face of the community. To start, I do understand the mindset behind them bringing back paid mods (yes, paid mods. Because that's exactly what they are, despite Bethesda being terribly NOT self aware). They want to be able to pay modders for their work. Okay. Fine.
However, there are also some major issues with this whole system. For starters, it's still downloading the CC content, even without paying for it, as part of the updates. The files take up hard drive space, but can't be used unless they're actually paid for. Likewise, each new bunch of content UPDATES the game, therefore breaking a lot of mods AND the script extender. This, I feel, directly contradicts their statements regarding not wanting to impact free modding at all. In their pursuit of doing this, they are inadvertently doing just that. I think that is probably the biggest part of Creation Club that pisses me off. I imagine it also pisses off the mod authors and the folks who work on the script extender as well.
Another negative point on the Creation Club itself is that it's literally Bethesda adding microtransactions to a AAA, single player game. Not to mention the quality of the items themselves. The only really good thing I saw out of the first batch was the backpack, and it was made by a pretty big modder. But even this second batch that just dropped, the armour looks goofy as hell and the BFG, in first person, takes up pretty much the entire lower half of your screen. Why is this necessary?
But anyways, in the end, it's a fun game, albeit not really a FALLOUT game. But due to all the tacked on crap that Bethesda has been doing, it's been severely impacting the quality of the game. This is me not just giving the negative review due to the developers, but because the game also has been impacted quite heavily.

Problems that I found out pretty early which made the single player experience pretty bad for me:
-You always have to produce something at a planet. No options for passive choices like production boost, income boost or anything (you have the ability to rid your planet from pollution, but once your planet is clean again, forces you to build). The game doesnt let you end your turn as long as you have an idle planet. This is a pretty big deal because every building and ship has maintenance cost, so constantly building them can make it pretty hard to save up money. UPDATE: Later in the game you can actually get a passive income boost on planets but you have to complete 2 research options in order to do that which is just plain stupid.
-Diplomacy is not finished. (or if it is, its flawed to the core) When ever the computer proposes something to you, you either accept it, or not, you cant send a counter offer. Now this might not sound much, BUT every proposal you refuse hurts their little feelings and potentially makes them hostile towards you, and when they offer like a hundred something credits(when you have like 1000) for a pretty expensive tech you have over and over, well lets just say you better forget the whole inner peace in this galaxy.
-Unlike previous titles of the series, the battles are in real time, which is kinda bad, but thankfull you can pause and issue orders to your ships.
-Now, the ship customization is actually pretty good, its a bit buggy right now, since you cant remove core systems you dont want to have on a ship like shields once they are on. (when you select create new ship, the game automatically gives a sample ship fitted to the max, and yes usually including shields too) So its pretty hard to create glass cannon like ships at the moment.
-One major intented option I encounterd and basically where I dropped the game, is that when you delete a ship design, and you already have ships built with that design, those ships disappear(get scrapped) from the map....yup....I loved it when my attacking fleet just disappeared when it was one jump away from the enemy capital planet.
-One funny fact, is that there is an option to turn the whole GNN news cast thing off. Now this made me think why did they create it like that in the first place? But thank god for that option because those droids get really annoying really fast.
-I tried to play a multiplayer game, but when the room fileld with people,  just closed right after that, now I'm not sure it that was the host or not, but seemed pretty stupid to get a room full of people and just close the whole thing.
-Now I saw a lot of people compare it to endless space, well, I can see where they are coming from, but I personally prefer the style of this game over ESs. Its not as deep(not nearly as complicated) but still enough to have enough to keep you playing. Also ESs space combat is just a huge no to me.
Ok I'm done not gonna write a novel, but I still managed to list most of the major problems with the game that to me, just makes it unplayable for the time being. Now its still in early access. If they fix all the things I mentioned above, the game can be pretty fun. The voice actors are indeed top notch. Alan Tudyk is pretty funny, makes the psilons really fun to play. Human and the kitty advisors are less stellar, but still ok, but omg Dwight Schultz gets annoying pretty fast, which makes me pretty sad because I really like him, also the dinos assistant is I think probably even more annoying.

Pretty fun game that doesn't seem to get the exposure it deserves. Amazing synth soundtrack, beautiful isometric artstyle, and surprisingly deep and well written lore. However, I felt a bit mislead with the trailer. I expected a more visceral, lots of action and shooting all the time gameplay. Instead it's actually a very tactical and sometimes stealth driven which can actually be frustrating if you went in expecting otherwise. There's also a rather annoying gimmick level that raises a sudden roadblock while you're playing the campaign. Controls can feel a bit clunky too, tank controls just don't work well in a 2d isometric when you're trying to concentrate on so many little things on the screen. And they really don't give much ammo in some parts which ties into that tactical aspect they push. Often I found myself holding back and playing slow, which just became tedious rather than fun. Also you'll find the levels mostly boil down to the same thing, blow the things up and exit. Very 90s I guess, but repetitive. Repetition can be fun when it's mindless, but becomes a chore when having to be very careful about movement and ammo consumption, etc.
Overall it's an alright game, not given enough recognition, but also overrated by some fans. It's worth the money though, especially for the OST.

Pretty good for an early access release.  Some highlights:
* Graphics - awesome, looks great at a variety of resolutions and qualities, a lot of attention to detail in the models
* Sound - Excellent music and voice acting
* UI/Controls - minimalist and unobtrustive
* Gameplay - exactly what I'd expect from an MoO game
That said, here are some lowlights:
* Tactical combat is pointless and slow and not fun.  Just simulate it, you'll save yourself 10 minutes per fight
* The AI is sort of stupid, especially when it comes to diplomacy.  It got to the point where I could just ask other races to give me planets, and they would.  That seems like a thing that should almost never work.
* Research tree felt a little shallow.  Nothing in the way of domestic skills (different government types, for example), just lots of more or less sequential upgrades to ships/buildings
* The endgame can be super slow, especially if you're not fighting with anyone.  I went down the science path first before I realized that it was unfinished, so I switched over to the "Elect me king" path (after negoitating treaties with enough races to support me, something else that seems like it shouldn't work too easily), and man, there was a long time of me just hitting the end turn button over and over again.
Those are pretty minor gripes for what is shaping up to be a pretty fantastic game, and a worthy successor to the orignal MoO series.  Is it worth $50 for early access?  Meh, maybe not, but throw in the original games and you can overlook that in exchange for knowing that you're supporting the cause a little bit.

I'm a simple man.
I see a mech game, I investigate.
I was not disappointed.
Brigador is a fantastic little game that has a surprisingly large amount of world building for the universe that it has you playing around in. At its core, it’s a simple sandbox game that has you ploughing through sectors and wasting enemies while completing objectives. The main campaign serves to get you comfortable to the various vehicular control schemes (mechs, tanks, and hovercrafts) and weapon types while sprinkling some lore in short text briefings before each mission. Once you finish that though (roughly 20+ levels), the real fun begins. The meat and potatoes of this game are in its FREELANCE mode, where you can totally customize your player before you go play a series of “see how far you can go” type missions. Choose your pilot, vehicle, weapon loadout, and mission environment. Every run earns you cash to spend on other variations of the elements I just mentioned. Experimentation is greatly encouraged, as you can try different loadouts/vehicle combinations to suit your (any) playstyle.
The music is fantastic as well (80s synthpop/wave), thumping away as you blast away at baddies.
There is also an audiobook that’s included with the deluxe package (game+music+audiobook), as of this review I have not read it yet.
Overall: Fantastic game that gets even more entertaining once you finish the main campaign. Once you warm up to the control schemes (of which there are many options) and shooting mechanics, the game truly becomes a real fun experience.

Brigador is a game that I wish I had supported earlier in its development and even after dumping 50+ hours into it return every so often for a good hour or so of unbridled destructions and frantic top down mech/tank shooter action. In a nutshell the game takes place in a late 1980’s early 90s esc cyber punk dystopian future where humanity has spread colonies amongst the stars. The game takes place in the city of Solo Nobre, a former corporate mega city turned Cuban esc regime by the efforts of Great Leader and his army the NEP. You as the player take the role of a “Brigador” essentially a mercenary hired by the corporations to accomplish various goals and wreaking as much havoc as possible within Solo Nobre during the chaos brought by great leader’s assassination in exchange for cold hard cash.
In terms of gameplay brigador plays very much like the old SNES BattleTech top down mech shooter, albeit with a greater degree of polish. The player takes control of one of the various war machines in the game to accomplish their assigned goals and has a wide assortment of weaponry to do so. By completing missions and successfully extracting you earn cash which can be used to unlock various items in the game such as new pilots, vehicles, weapons, and lore documents. Brigador’s gameplay is divided into two major parts the first being the campaign/story mode, in this mode the player must accomplish a series of missions using premade vehicle loadouts. Campaign missions can have a wide assortment of objectives but most boil down to eliminate the target then get out of the district. The second mode is free lance where players can select a pilot (difficulty level and payout multipliers), vehicle and its weapons, as well as what operation (series of levels) they wish to play. Every level will pit you against one of three factions, the NEP, the Corvids, and the Spacers. Each faction has their own vehicle sets (many of which you the player can actually use your self) and have different strengths and weaknesses though these are hardly noticeable when you start deploying with weapons that destroy entire city blocks in a single shot.
In terms of sound design and eye candy brigador achieves what its going for. The sprawling neon lit city scapes are fully realized in an isometric style reminiscent of command and conquer tiberian sun and dripping with just as much atmosphere. The game’s soundtrack by Makeup and vanity set is simply fantastic and matches the visuals to the letter; I must point out however that the sound design for individual weapons and vehicles tends to rely on reusing sound assets though this is hardly noticeable in the grand scheme of things.
Brigador’s story and world building is perhaps the aspect I love the most about this game, every piece of equipment, vehicle, and pilot has back story detailed in various logs that take on different perspectives some of which going so far as to bring a bit of humor to what would otherwise be a bland lore document. The writing behind some of these logs is pretty clever and though not award winning materiel it certainly does add a bit of depth to what is otherwise just a top down shooter.
I do thoroughly enjoy this game and would highly recommend it, but I can’t help to see a few problems with it. The most glaring issue I see with the game is how repetitive it can get after a while, once you've completed every campaign mission you turn to freelance, but then it doesn't take long before you're running through the same city districts over and over again; the only real diversity coming from the vehicle and weapon set up your using as well as the possibility that you might be fighting a different faction this time around. A lack of any kind of multiplayer also kinda limits the game’s replayability and effectively makes this a game I play when I have no one else to play with. One last gripe I have is that though all three opposing factions are well fleshed out in terms of design, back story, and visible arsenals they tend to function all the same and lack any kind of behavioral differences.
If I could make suggestions for updates, or changes to be made in any prospective sequel it would be the following.
The inclusion of some kind of coop option for Freelance mode, or any kind of multiplayer really as this gives me incentive to actually recommend the game to friends and increases replayability.
Diversifying AI behavior between the various factions, everyone in sight rushing at you makes sense for the rag tag corvids or glory seeking spacers, but not so much for the supposedly disciplined NEP.
Perhaps more districts or variations of the various districts so players are not stomping down the same streets over and over in free lance.
The inclusion of further customisation options for the player vehicle, perhaps color tweaks of some kind or vehicles with more than just two weapons slots.

"LOOOL! THIS GUY DOESN'T LIKE A GAME THAT I LIKE EVEN THOUGH HIS REVIEW MAKES FAIR POINTS! I'M GONNA DOWNVOTE IT BECAUSE NOBODY IS ALLOWED TO DISSAGREE WITH ME!!! LOOL!"
Where do I begin? Why am I even making this review? I'm still gonna get 98 downvotes. Spoilers, too.
I'll start with this:
Half Life is very very mediocre compared to today's games. I understand how people could have liked it back then, but many modern games are doing right what Half Life didn't do.
THE STORY
I'm not sure what I should say, because the story in this game isn't interesting at all. You are a scientist working in a lab. The lab opens a portal that allows aliens to invade the world. While traveling all of Black Mesa, these aliens want to kill everybody. You are just simply trying to kill these aliens and escape. The military attacks Black Mesa because duh, aliens. Now the soldiers want to kill everybody. Seems like something that can build up, but it's just there for logical reasons. However, in one part of the game you get to travel to some alien planet to kill their mastermind, which sadly is the only good part of the story that makes you slightly more motivated to endure the tedious gameplay. Since I just mentioned the gameplay...
Also, don't get mad if I got the story wrong. It's confusing in every single way.
GAMEPLAY
I can't stand it. The only redeeming quality is the gunplay and weapon variety but that's it. The rest of the game is moving through claustrophobic spaces, and solving utterly stupid puzzles that drive me insane. Sometimes, you won't even know if you are MEANT to solve a puzzle and will walk in circles instead trying to realize what you are supposed to do. A majority of them are tedious as hell, not enjoyable and sometimes so confusing that you will need to ask people for help. The best example is the "Lambda Core" level, where you have to jump through a bunch of cores. What's worse, is that you must walk through a LOT of hallways that lead to random spaces and cause you to get lost and lose track of everything. It took me about 2 hours to solve the whole thing. Now, let's just skip the dumb puzzles and talk about actual levels.
LEVEL DESIGN
Claustrophobic, recycled and ugly. So many rooms and hallways look so alike, that you can't tell if you are heading the right direction or not. Many levels in this game have a variety of confusing rooms that make you wonder "wait, is this place optional or do i have to enter to press some switch or something?". Some of them have puzzles that turn out to be unnecessary, or just make you think if you did the right thing and don't know if you can proceed without any problems. Not much to say here.
MUSIC
75% of the game is silent, adding no atmosphere to the gameplay. However, the music was ahead of it's time and is too, impressive today. You would normally expect music in specific moments. When I reached the final boss, I expected to hear some sick track similiar to "Nuclear Mission Jam". But no. You can fight a giant fetus that can throw energy balls with moon gravity, but no music, making the final fight underwhelming.
I'm truly sorry for having a different opinion than everybody else in the review section. This game just wasn't fun for me.

Unfortunately there isn't much I can write about the game due to several issues stopping me from playing any further.
Controls are clunky and not easy to use at all. I tried switching cover to stay out of sight of a guard and I ended up standing in front of him while trying to switch. Really bad and a significant drop in quality from previous titles.
Assets don’t sit well together and NPC’s glitch and fall through walls and floors as well as walking through each other like ghosts.
Even with my GTX 1060, this game has to be played in 'High' just to get a playable framerate, (The graphics settings in this game go in this order: Low, Med, High, Very High, Ultra) and even then I’m only getting 30 - 40 FPS. Just as a comparison, I am playing through the Witcher 3 on Ultra @ 60 FPS with very few dips. Optimisation in this game is very poor.
The combat is absolutely awful. I have played AC1, 2, 3, and Black Flag and the combat in those games are fantastic and satisfying. This combat is clunky and slow. Some of your commands not even registering and Arno just stands there like a lemon and gets slashed across the chest by an enemy sword. Not only that, but it doesn’t feel adequate at all, there’s little feedback and it is really underwhelming.
From reading other reviews (note: I did not get this far) there is apparently chests you can’t open without having a 3rd party app on your phone as well as an in-game shop for micro transactions. This is something I cannot stand. A full price triple A game with a built in shop? What is this? CandyCrush? Free To Play games I can understand, but this is a business strategy I cannot support at all and shouldn’t exist.
Overall I think this is just a game to miss. After its horrendous launch, I thought I would give it a chance nearly 2 years on after it was ‘patched’, and the issues are still very prominent. If the issues are still here now, I can’t see Ubisoft doing anything to solve them. If you want an Assassins Creed game to play, try Syndicate instead, although that one still has an in-game shop. It’s a shame with what could’ve been a fantastic game set in one of my favourite time periods. I shall be refunding.

So in case you're wondering if this thing that suddenly jumped in to everyone's library is worth spending time on, here's my little review.
Do you have a little over an hour of your life to spare? If you do, I would recommend you putting aside that time for this short adventure. There is no save feature that I am aware of so you should probably make sure you have that hour when you won't be interrupted.
This game have focus on story telling and atmosphere, the graphics are what you'd expect from a free game and the voice acting can sound a little computerish at first but you'll get used to it. Everything is done by mouse, the only non mouse actions I've found are spacebar to find hot spots and escape to well...escape or exit game if you're looking for a better word.
The story is well written, intriguing and has plot twists. The twists are fairly obvious but they are still well written and goes hand in hand with the atmosphere. As you progress the story the lightning and sound effects does a good job of changing the mood, creating a creepy and gloomy atmosphere, and no - there are no jump scares.
It's a rather depressing themed game though, but if you're like me you love that stuff ;)
So if you have around an hour to spare, try it!

I'm not sure if there's really any one element of Darkest Dungeon that really sells it for me. It in truth is a mixture of all of it. The fantastic art, the fantastic music, the fantastic narration, the fantastic dungeon crawling, the fantastically difficult nature of it.
This game is really and truly fun for masochists who enjoy dungeon crawlers and Lovecraft. It sufficiently takes the best of both of these concepts and puts them together in a fun way. The strategy and coordination it takes in order to be able to balance heroes, how said heroes play off one another, and how they interact with each dungeon along with the weight of the cosmic horror that Lovecraft was all about. The crushing realization that this crew of adventurers are still mortal no matter how experienced and powerful they are and how deciding to faff about in a dungeon of dangerous beasts some people were not meant to see if never a good idea.
I know some would criticize the almost agonizingly brutal RNG of the game and how it makes no allowances for you. How it is fully possible to just get cheesed turn one and have one of your heroes die if you're extraordinarily unlucky (which has happened to me, rip Dismas #3). And while for some that might be a major turn-off I feel like for others it must be a challenge. Because while this game can and will kick your♥♥♥♥♥up and down the dungeon halls when it all clicks into place it feels fantastic. When that one hero gets the crit that slays the massive beast before it kills a party member. When you find that secret room full of treasure that'll let you upgrade your parties' equipment just that bit more. When one hero stands against a tide of blackness and Virtues as his allies crumble, one babbling to his sword in madness, another on the brink of death for the third time that night, and the last trying to find a way for the party to escape. That's what makes Darkest Dungeon.
It's not a game about light being there at the end of the tunnel. It's a game about rending that light out from the jaws of some beast and feeling great about doing it. Is this rending sometimes just luck? Perhaps. But sometimes a bit of luck stacked on top of skill and knowledge is all you need to crawl the depths of the Darkest Dungeon.

This is probably one of the purest and heartwarming games I've played on Steam so far. It's such a quaint and simple game on the surface, but it always feels like there's something deeper to be discovered. It has a touch of that lived-in world feel, with  history and possible conflicts, and a seemingly ancient air of mystery and magic to it. Although I wish it were deeper, and fuller, feel like this is one of the few games that has made a really positive impression on me. And it's all around solid for what is at it's price.
I feel like so much has been done right in this game and the developer deserves a few good pats on the back, imo. The limited amount of charcters feel well developed and rounded in their own depth. And despite the pixel-sprite design that has been done a thousand times over, the game comes off as very fresh and organic to me unlike Joja Cola. The main objective feels no important or dire than any side quests...If you can call them quests at all. It feels more like Harvest Moon and Animal Crossing, but with having to earn money rather than be in debt and pay mortgage.
The only thing that I can nitpick about is that the main goals and progression could be a little longer and more challenging. I'm not asking for a f***ing Dark Souls mode, but it could use some more grit and tests in the daily grind of the agrarian lifestyle. The dungeons and caves are well alright, but I'd rather chill on the surface and cook up some mad tasty cuisine, son. After you kinda break through the monetary struggles, upgrades, and the main town goals, the replay value kinda decays and feels less rewarding in the prospect of finding new things to keep it interesting...It has a beaten path issue imo, and leaves me hungry for more trails to blaze(xxx420xxx69)
with promises of a multiplayer mode on the horizon, I am hopeful for more replay entertainment. Despite the negative aspects I feel this game has, it's okay for the small price. Overall I am glad to have played it. I feel like it has added a glimmer of light to my cold dark void of a soul.

Overall, I would call this game an unworthy Terraria clone. I know even comparing the two may offend fanboys on both sides, but this game ultimately is a more expensive Terraria with less content to offer. Side by side, we see similar concepts across both games but Starbound ultimately falls short where you think it would shine best. In Terraria, you struggle to survive, create a defensive structure (or don't), and slowly (or rapidly) expand outward encountering what you want when you want with few restrictions. In Starbound, your hand is held and you are lead through a linear series of quests to progress at a predetermined pace with any noteworthy encounters at preset intervals. Starbound is never difficult due to the restrictions on progression and while the energy system shows promise, a lack of variety/usefulness in weaponry/tech until the very end leaves the player bored with combat through most of the game. While I intially enjoyed my time spent with starbound roughly a year ago, in that time I would say the development decisions have left the game in a fairly mediocre state and I would not recommend this game to anyone looking for a similar experience to Terraria. Yes, the game is still in early access, but another rehaul of game design is highly unlikely at this point so I think it is safe to assume the game will simply build on it's current foundation (which has potential). If the game was less linear/grindy but more dangerous/eventful it would be a solid recommendation, but its current state leaves you wanting a reason to explore new planets and waiting for random events as a reason to utilize it's building features (which never happens).

While this game is nothing to rave about, I definitely don't really agree with all of the negative reviews it has received. Though, I am a newcomer to the game/rally genre, so that could be why.
The first time I played the game, I was unaware that it was a rerelease of a mobile title; That being said, I'm still having a moderate amount of fun with it.
The textures are definitely lacking (though by no means horrible), the menu music is the same 5 second loop endlessly repeated, the game has a moderate handful of tracks (though admittedly, still only a handful) based on 3 regions, and only 4 cars to choose from, 3 of which are only usable after unlocking by placing first in certain championships, and none of which are even slightly customizable.
Though again, for a mobile title ported over to PC, most of this can be overlooked.
As a newcomer to rally, this game came with a little bit of a learning curve, but after a few races I got used to the handling of the cars (more accurately the lack of handling), and now I find it really fun drifting through hairpin turns at high speeds.
I do wish the game was a bit longer though, even from a mobile port. I've clocked about 5 hours of play time at the time of writing this, and I have three of the four cars unlocked, and only two more championships until I "finish" the game.
This game may not be able to hold it's ground against many of the modern, more in-depth console/PC racing titles out there, but for the few bucks this game costs, it's definitely not a horrible game.
If you're looking for a cheap, quick, simple, decently fun rally game, Colin McRae Rally is definitely worth a quick look.

Starbound: Great concept of exploration, building, crafting, and combat. All pushed into one beautiful 2d side-scroller. This game has had it's ups and downs but its finally starting to take it's shape. You choose from seven different races to play as, each with their own sets of gear & other recipes, spicing up your gameplay a little bit with every different character. The main selling point on this title is randomly generated, Meaning that there are TONS of combinations on guns, most melee weapons and nearly every monster in this game. With this being in the game it also shows that the planetary exploration system is near infinite, You found a something cool on a planet and want to share it with everyone? Post the coordinates and every else can go there and see it for themselves. While this game has alot of great points in it, It also has its downsides. It's not very well optimized at the moment, running very well for some low end pc's while not even budging on some high end pc's. This and many other bugs seem to throw people off in choosing to buy this game or not, But we have to remember that it is Early-Acess and isn't yet finished. So I highly reccomend this to anyone as long as they're willing to deal with the bugs & performance issue that may or may not happen.

MOO2, Star wars: Empire at War, and Civ 5, are 3 of my top 5 favourite games I've ever played.
This game is like a love child of all 3. It has the classic MOO2 feel, with the modern day mechanics that the other 2 have brought us.
This is the game that MOO3 should have been all those years ago (still to this day the only game I've ever returned).
The voice acting is top notch (and if you take a look at the cast, you'll see why!).
The graphics are crisp, the interface is intuitive.
The tactical battle introductions are amazing, however the battles themselves are pretty much pre-calculated (IE, it's pretty obvious who will win). One feature from SWEOW they carry over is the cinematic view of the space battles, love it!
For an early access game, it is incredibly bug free. There are some very minor bugs I've hit, but they're not game crashing by any means and easy to get around.
The only other complaint I have is that there aren't more leaders, and one of the key features (custom race) is not yet available. Once the game fills out more, this will be right up there with Civ 5 as one of the best games I've ever played.
I would highly recommend this game, I've already completed 1 game, and keen to start playing the other races.

Kid thinks about what to write. Narrating ain't so easy, after all. But Bastion does it best - the way it should be.
Rucks is the best, as far as narrators go. When he starts talking, you're compelled to hang on to every word he says. His voice breathes life into the journey, puts the 'story' into history. He tells tales the way tales were meant to be told - the way that keeps you coming back for more.
Bastion is a piece of art. The character / stage / enemy design, battle animations, the voiceacting, and the music. Oh my god the music. Easily the most captivating part of the game. Zia's theme, Zulf's theme, and their subsequent mash up Setting Sail, Coming Home are influential musical landmarks for me.
There are a variety of weapons in Bastion, each requiring their own distinct style of play. You get to pick two weapons at a time to run through the game with, and I believe the many combinations that exist are all potential game-winning ones. Playing with the increased difficulty NG+ and beyond (activating all Pantheon Gods for example) ramps up the challenge level significantly - that's when certain weapons begin to shine more than others.
A very solidly grounded hack-and-slash-esque indie title which expands the traditional definition of the concept of a game. Enjoyed every minute of it.
Besides, very few things have since surpassed the shocked elation I experienced when I heard Zia speak for the first time.

Bottom line: 4 hours went by just disappeared like it did when I turned on MoO1 for the first time. Mission accomplished, team. I've played MoO and MoO2 for the same 20 years that I imagine most fans have played it. When GoG made it available, it is one of those moments when the clouds parted and a ray of sunshine definitely showed through. I think the best thing we can all say about MoO3 is to not talk about it, except for the lessons about detail and colony management that were probably taken into account with this edition.
Die-hards already know alot of the changes: new in-depth and awesome backstories for each fo the races, updated visuals that are beyond words awesome, clean crisp interface that combines the simplicty of MoO with the needs of MoO2. But the new is also means starlanes, no turn by turn tactical combat (yet?), race characteristics tweakability not what we're used to and a few other limitations.
It's so clear that the team put so much love into this and that early access is where we the fans get to provide input now that if only we could have done with MoO3 could've changed our feelings from disdain to reverence. This MoO is beautiful, sounds like the original with updated music, and the visual RTS tactical combat made me swear up and down when I didn't do it in tactical when my major Psilon fleet went up again the Bulrathe (and lost of course).
It's not meant to be a clone of the originals. We can play those anytime we want now. But as a long-time fan, EA is worth it to see it, play it, and give suggestions on how to improve it.
New to the franchise, maybe you should wait for an even more polished copy at release.

This is early access, and it shows. It has its ups and downs. Despite my short play time, I have a list of positives and negatives. Edits will come as the game is rolled out further.
March 31st updates---
Positives:
+Better balancing of gameplay.
+Diplomacy now functions properly.
+Klackon, Meklar, and Terran added.
+Technological victory added.
Negatives:
-Meklar are massively overpowered in research.
-Terran have major environmental issues.
-Spies not implemented.
(Original Alpha release comments below)
Positives:
+Very good looking reboot of an excellent 4x game.
+Easy to play, and intuitive.
+Extremely stable, I have had no instances of lag whatsoever.
+It's as addictive as it should be.
+Excellent voice acting, audio, and music.
Negatives:
-Racial implementation is incomplete, several races not implemented yet.*
-Diplomacy needs work. Wars are next to impossible to get out of short of total genocide.
-No spies or espionage implemented yet. I suspect that the Darloks will be released with spies.*
-Combat needs balancing, it's like a less effective combat system from MoO 3. ~see additional comments.
-Ship design feels far more limited than previous Master of Orion games.
-Random events need to be balanced. Every one I have seen has been a planet's mineral classification increasing.
-Star systems need better balancing. Most systems are 2-3 objects orbiting the star, a (very) few have 5.
-Techs sometimes force you to choose between two things AFTER the research is complete. I experienced this several times before I finally noticed there is a bar between the icons in the research box. This needs to be clarified. I like the idea of having to branch research in some areas one way or another, but the choice should be when the research is beginning, not when it has concluded. ~see additional comments for furtherance.
Additional comments:
~Cannot rename stars and planets!!!!! --This drove me crazy with MoO 3 until it was patched.
~Cannot choose flag colour. --This also was an issue with MoO 3 before patching.
~Run spellcheck, there are several spelling errors throughout the game.
~Real time combat can  be nice, but MoO had very well balanced turn based combat before 3. Why not have a setting for turn based combat as well as real time?
~It might also be nice to branch the techs out further with the choosing specific research areas. With Fusion, if you choose fusion beam, you should get later research for enhanced targeting computers, if you go with fusion bombs, you should have later research options for hardened colony structures, or another defencive area for planets.
*Annoying, but it's early access, and these will be put in. I look forward to the full release!

Brigador is an isometric action game set in a 80's science fiction universe full of neon lights, hovertanks, and mechs.
The campaign lets you play through missions with set loadouts. It lasts about 9 hours and is pretty fun.
The "arcade" mode, Freelance, lets you choose one of several dozen vehicles including hardsuits, mechs of varying sizes, hovercraft, and tanks. You can then equip it with any two weapons that can fit in the vehicles mountings, as well as taking a unique power such as laucnhing smoke grenades or firing a massively powerful audio pulse.
Freelance will be the reason you come back to Brigador again and again. The different combinations you can create with each vehicle, pilot, weapon, and equipment make the game filled with potential. The small dev team also promises updates in the near future, but unfortunately, it's in Valve time.
I'd recommend this game for sure. I also recommend getting either the Deluxe Edition or just the Deluxe DLC Upgrade so you can get a really good soundtrack, and also a very well-written audiobook, too.

Overall this is a pretty good game. There are many pros, and unfortunately some cons.
Pros:
- Great graphics throughout the game except for some cutscenes in MyCareer where I feel like they could've done a better job.
- Entertaining storyline (controversial for many people)
- Great player control, I feel that whatever I want to do, I can, whether it be dribble moves, shots, defense, or any other thing.
- Accurate representation of NBA players and team play styles, the players as CPU play a similar style as they do in the NBA league.
- I like the fact that they included high school and college games in MyCareer, good way to get an accurate rating of your player for a team. In previous 2k games like 2k14 the team you were drafted to relied solely and strictly on 1 game, the Rising Stars I believe.
- Nice animations and options for signature styles.
- Practices give you boosts on your performance and some stats depending on the drills you run on that off-day.
-The ability to spend off-days with NBA stars for badges is a neat feature.
- The fan bonuses for in game performance on MyCareer. You can get them by hitting clutch shots, or nice shots and scoring a lot.
- Love the endorsements, they are a quick and easy way of making VC.
Talking about VC, that brings me here
Cons:
- Making VC is an EXTREMELY TEDIOUS process. I don't think I can emphasize it enough. I am aware that there are hacks and glitches, but those will get you banned eventually,  if you're just trying to make some honest VC to upgrade your MyPlayer, be prepared to spend tons of hours playing the game.
- I have had this game since March, put in a large amount of hours, especially during the summer, and I am still not satisfied with the stats on my player.
- Not a huge fan of the upgrade quantity availability. Tedious to have to go to practice often for the purpose of unlocking upgrade slots.
- Upgrades are quite expensive
- The A-F grade scale on MyCareer gets annoying when you were playing fine without fault, and the game blames you for an opposing player scoring whom you were not guarding.
Good game in general and I would recommend you buy it when it is on discount, because paying $59.99 for this game is still a hefty price. I got mine for about $25 when it was on sale early this year.

Usually, when I write some impressions I always speak about what the game is all about instead of what it could have been. However, in a rally game with Colin McRae in the title it’s a bit hard to not see the true potential that has gone to waste. The description of the origin of the game tell no lies, it’s a port of a mobile game so we are aware of what we can expect in terms of visuals and weather effects, sound, and so on. However, there is some information that not only I do not agree but I also find it to be a bit misleading.
The description of the game mentions different types of surfaces. While this may be true, aside of road and off-road I didn’t see any other variations. There is no mud, no heavy dust, no snow or wet tracks giving you a very limited window when it comes to variety. Speaking of variety, the number of cars you can drive is really small, only four are available. This is a very low number for a rally game and to make it worst you need to unlock them if you want to race with them in the championship. The four cars are the Ford Focus, Subaru Impreza, the classic Lancia Stratos and the Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VI. The sound is as important for me as the visuals and if you are a racing fan you will want to have those crazy sound engines screaming for the next shift but once again you can’t expect such thing in this game, which is fine for a mobile port but insufficient for a PC game.
In the end I played the game and got most of it, however there is not much to see and do which makes you search for better alternatives. The final line from the Store description ends with a bang but I’m afraid to be a really misleading sentence. It says “The Classic Rally Experience Races on PC and Mac” and I couldn’t agree less. This is not true at all no matter how big or small you are into racing games.

A hauntingly beautiful game, with artwork that fills me with childlike delight, and music and sound effects that make me giggle with glee, the tiny world of Botanicula is sure to leave the observant player in high spirits.
A puzzle game that rewards exploring and clicking on nearly anything that stands out in the environmnt, Botanicula is a spiritual successor to Amanita's previous Samorost games.  Though this game has a considerably greater degree of player control when it comes to exploring the surroundings, most of the puzzles are still solved by trial and error and investigating your surroundings as much as much as they are solved with critical thinking.
While this might sound tedious as first, the game often rewards interaction by the player with amusing actions from it's team of main characters and the other bizarre inhabitants of their dying home.
It's ease of play and charming audio and visuals makes it an absolute treat of a game for children and adults alike.

First off I recommend this game based on the potential it clearly has to be a classic turn based strategy / 4x space game. If the developers put some manhours into this thing it can be great, right now it's just good - and in alpha of course.
The gameplay right now is fine and I haven't noticed any bugs - This is a pleasant surprise. The galaxy map is set up to pen you in and make you wait for technologies or fight your way out, Read starlanes, dead ends, unstable / unusable starlanes and space bases that block passage unless you have open borders. Conversely you can use these features of the game to quickly pen an opponent in to a small area and keep them weak.
The tech tree and planetary screens are easy to understand and use, although there is a weird quirk in the tech tree: Some technologies you research have two different upgrades on them but by reasearching the tech you only get to pick one of the upgrades, the other is forever excluded from you. Perhaps they intend you to get them through espionage or maybe it's just supposed to make everybody's tech a little different. Either way it's weird but interesting and I'll have to see how I like it after a while.  Upgrading ships is easy, a single click upgrades the design with the latest goodies and a single click upgrades existing ships that are in orbit of a planet you own.
By far my biggest complaint is just the visual appeal of the game. It's absolutely awful. Everything is black and dark and two dimensional. Yes space is black but space is also amazingly colorful and beutiful. For god's sake wargaming, choose the colorful and beautiful, not the black; for example you can click on your planet to get an overall view of what it's doing, guess what, 4/5ths of your planet is covered in night (facepalm). And get rid of the two dimensional feel! For example, you can click on buildings on your planet, like a marine barracks and all that happens is a small tooltip comes up with a crappy two dimensional image of the barracks and a paragraph about what it does. How about bringing me to a 3 dimensional barracks with soldiers and tanks running around and letting me look inside multiple buildings and talk to advisors in those buildings? This game has too much potential to be so visually and auditorilly boring that people may not be able to sit through 100 turns.
I still recommend the game but beware of the boredom if you like your games to give you a feast for your eyes and ears.

Kid thinks about what to write. Narrating ain't so easy, after all. But Bastion does it best - the way it should be.
Rucks is the best, as far as narrators go. When he starts talking, you're compelled to hang on to every word he says. His voice breathes life into the journey, puts the 'story' into history. He tells tales the way tales were meant to be told - the way that keeps you coming back for more.
Bastion is a piece of art. The character / stage / enemy design, battle animations, the voiceacting, and the music. Oh my god the music. Easily the most captivating part of the game. Zia's theme, Zulf's theme, and their subsequent mash up Setting Sail, Coming Home are influential musical landmarks for me.
