When I caught wind of Brigador being similar to one of my favorite classic games, Urban Strike (part of a great series of Strike games), I was immediately determined to pick it up.  Those games and their gameplay were some of my favorite on my Sega Genesis as a kid.  While Brigador isn’t exactly like those games, it gave me just enough of a nostalgia trip to really get in to it and enjoy it's hearty gameplay.
Brigador: Up-Armored Edition is an updated version of the original game released in June of 2016 after eight months in Early Access.  The re-released update dropped in June of 2017 and added some missions to the campaign, updated the graphics, and did some rebalancing.  I had the pleasure of playing both since I got the game just before this update.  I can say that it is more appealing now than it was before, though even with the balance changes there can be some rough difficulty spikes that you will come across.  The core of the gameplay in the campaign is relatively simple.  You’ll grab one of the next missions in the group you’ve unlocked (usually three or four at a time), perhaps read the gist of what you’ll be doing and why, select one of the four pre-established vehicles, and head in to blow up nearly everything in sight.  The vehicles come in a large variety.  There are tanks and wheeled vehicles, hovertanks, and bipedal mechs, all of which range in size from tiny you lose them on screen to fairly larger and slow to maneuver.  These are each outfitted with a unique loadout of weapons and abilities that can be better or worse suited for the type of missions you encounter.  However, the campaign is designed to have you replay missions as many times as you want and receive marks for beating it in each provided vehicle.  Going through it the first time I gravitated toward the larger and more heavily armed and armored vehicles in most situations because that’s the playstyle I like, however I could see how the faster and more stealthy vehicles could work very well too if you practiced with them.
Once in the mission, you’ll have a list of your objectives in the top corner and little else guiding you through except some icons along the edges of you screen indicating the direction of the objectives.  You can move through at your own pace on your own path, or just carve it out of the destructible level.  Vehicles and buildings will crumble and explode at the whim of your mouse clicks.  Enemies vary just as much as your choice in vehicles from small and super-fast to much larger than anything you can pilot and equally slow.  Their firepower can be just as diverse.  Dispatching them may take a sweep of your machine gun or have you running around dodging their shots as you pick them apart.  Objectives are simple at best, usually requiring you to either blow up certain buildings or special vehicles, or just wiping out 70% of the enemies on the map (and sometimes both).  However, the unique design of each map makes it much less repetitive than such a limited set of objectives would indicate.  Plus, the real challenge comes to the surface when you have to manage both the health of your vehicle along with its  ammo that runs out several times a mission, requiring you to salvage ammo pickups from not-completely-destroyed enemies or finding the handful of ammo depots with limited supply.  The raw carnage and combination of action and tactical efforts from the player really define the beginning and end of what makes Brigador so fun.
Well, there’s a metric ton of story lore in the game.  There’s a tiny bit presented in the campaign, but the majority is unlocked via the money that you earn for each mission.  This money has no effect on the campaign itself as far as I can tell, but you earn a great deal going through the missions.  You can spend it on unlocking tons of in-game content including vehicle and enemy descriptions, story elements of all sorts including information about the factions involved, freelance mission items that include vehicles, vehicle pilots with varying mission modifiers, and equipment for those vehicles.  This leaves a pretty robust amount of gameplay even after you finish the campaign that, if you wanted to complete fully with all vehicles would take many hours beyond the four-plus I used to run through it once each.  The lore and descriptions you can unlock weave a giant web of story content that is entirely optional to the player, but it seems to be something the developers put a lot of effort in to.  There’s even an audio book included with the Deluxe edition, which I think I received just for having the game before it re-released.  Also included in that Deluxe edition is a great soundtrack of perfectly crafted synthwave music that meshes with the explosive gameplay surprisingly well.  It’s very prominent, so if it’s not a type of music you’re in to, you’re going to have to turn it off entirely.  However, for me it was great and I left its pumping beats and 80s aesthetic going strong the whole way through.
There were a few smaller issues and some larger ones that really had me drinking the rageahol.  The health system in Brigador has you maintaining both your standard health and a shield that can be recharged by enemy drops.  However, your normal health can’t be fixed by anything in a mission.  This isn’t a problem in most missions that are relatively short an simple, but some missions are a bit longer and any encounter with a lot of enemies can wear your non-reparable health down, making a small mistake force you to restart.  On top of that, shield drops disappear after a period.  This means that if you’re working with long range weapons or slow moving vehicles, a large firefight may have you missing out on the lifeblood you need to keep going.  Another small issue is that you have to learn about the environments in a bit of a trial by fire.  Some buildings will explode killing you instantly if you run into them or destroy them from too close.  It can be difficult to distinguish these and result in an unexpected and frustrating death.  They could easily be marked in an more obvious way, but they often blend in too well.  The most annoying thing I encountered was the difficulty spikes.  Some missions would be many times harder than missions before or after.  I played through one probably 15 or 20 times as it had you starting with no ammo and dodging insta-kill suicide enemies to get to the ammo depots.  In addition, the final optional campaign mission is significantly longer than previous ones and trying to maintain health during it is nearly impossible with what vehicles are supplied.  If this is the rebalanced version, I’d hate to have seen what some of these later missions were like before that.
This really is a good game and I would suggest getting it for $10 or less as it has been (and currently is on GOG) under that price.  While it may lack some of the things that I really enjoyed about those old Strike games, it does have some solid mechanics that the player can improve and master throughout the tons of replayability provided.  Fans of the whole ‘you against the world’ concept in games, where you’re mowing down enemies like a badass, will definitely find this appealing.

I've played very little of this game so far, less than 1 full hour, but 2 things already are disturbing as far as how I see this game ending up.
Yes this is a Beta, benefit of doubt and all but I'm wondering how many of the shortcomings I see being resolved in 3 or 4 months since the flaws appear to be part of the overall plan.
I hate turn limits in 4X games.
So here we go:
CONS:
1) A turn limit. Doesn't matter that it's a rather large 500, it's there and I hate turn limits, feels like board game I'd play with my 9 year old "ok, we'll play 10 turns then back to homework". WHY is there a turn limit??? Just kills the whole feeling of.. something, I dunno.
2) Small number of systems on "Large" which in itself is ok I guess, but unfortunately each system only hold 1 or 2 planets. The game feels teeny tiny already.
3) The Pathways to each system. I honestly don't get why game designers would opt for this route (no pun intended). It works in only 1 game series that I know of, "Sins of a Solar Empire" and that's because that game is so freaking stressful and fast that you need choke points from paths otherwise you'd go insane. But in a turn based open space game, it's a flaw to me.
And yes, people will argue that some of the earlier games we loved used paths to systems, still, today with current tech and the state of gaming and computer hardware an all that, it feels weak, like a crutch that the designers couldn't figure out how to overcome.
4) Lack of rotating view (view angle, rotating clockwise/counterclockwise). Make it feels smallish again and rather outdated. If they at least let us alter the view a touch to get a sense on the galaxy from any direction or height level. A bit nitpicky, but I guess it irrites me a bit.
Pros:
1) Runs smooth at max detail (there isn't much detail so this is to be expected)
2) UI and gameplay is clean and jumps from location to location easily upon orders being needed in certain places.
Summary: Feels like a highly scaled back Sins of Solar Empire remake but with turns and without the 3D view and all the cool 3D fleets and effects and much less planetary building options.

Brilliant game.
If the price of the game is under 15$, I'd personally say it's worth it.
This is an isometric, tiled game which only has the destruction part of Blast Corps(n64).
(You are a mech in the middle of a city, killing and crushing people and destroying their homes and power plants)
So it has an old style to it, which seems to be appreciated by most.
The campaign has a nice, not annoying tutorial, which not only teaches you the dirty way but you get to keep all your earnings and spend it in freelance mode. I believe if you play the entire campaign, you can get enough dough to buy some of the best available.
In freelance, you can buy a pilot, a vehicle, weapons and missions (and lore; intel but w/e)
Here's one of the brilliant part of the game.. The biggest, baddest vehicles are worth the least and the smallest, weakest vehicles are worth the most. Why? Because each vehicle has a payout modifier, wanna make it hard on yourself but earn three times more than anyone else? Use the tiniest vehicle. Wanna wreck havoc or get through a long and hard series of missions? Use a big bad vehicle and tear the place apart.
Pilots also get to have such modifiers but I first need to explain missions (Operations as they are called in-game).
Operations are basically a series of missions, smallest being a series of 2 but can get up to a whopping 39!
You have to be careful though, as your vehicle does not repair itself nor rearm itself between missions.
During each missions, you have a set of main objectives and a set of optional objectives (They're all about killing and destruction). You can end the current mission after completing at least one main objective, or you can stay and complete the level to gain more money. As you finish the entire operation, the money you've earned will be multiplied by some factors, such as the type of vehicle and pilot you've used.
And that brings us to the pilots.
Here's what the pilot named "Phil Bromlin" has for stats:
Let's say you're playing an operation that has 5 districts(missions).
The difficulty and the payout multiplier will grow by 0.50 per district.
Meaning by the fifth mission, you'll be at 3 difficulty level and 2.6 of payout (since it's the max).
So you really want to buy better pilots and better operations, so you can make more money and eventually try to beat the hardest missions the game can throw at you.
There's 38 pilots to hire, 63 vehicles and 44 weapons to purchase.
The vehicles are divided by 3 factions (Loyalist, Corvid, Spacer) and 3 vehicle types (Mech, Tank, Agrav(floating vehicles)).
Beyond that, you'll have to see for yourself.

Some games aren't games so much as they are experiences.  Botanicula reminds me of the feelings of innocent discovery I had as a child when I'd see something new outdoors for the first time. Gameplay wise, it's the graphical progression of those old text-based Adventure games from the days of games on 5 inch floppies, minus the death by minotaur because you didn't figure something out quickly enough.  In fact, there is no way to die or fail...you just haven't figured it out the solution yet.  Overall, it's a light-hearted affair of puzzle solving that's well worth the experience.

The gameplay is basically fantastic, with Harvest Moon-like controls and menu. However, they added new features to the gameplay and this control scheme to add new elements to the game (like fishing). One thing that struck me as interesting is that the weapon-wielding fighting system is very similar to the "Ys" series (after "Oath of Felghana") or "Legend of Zelda" on the SNES. This is a good thing, as both games had great fighting mechanics, and the blend well the Havest Moon style.
The story and characters are fantastic, and some of your decisions have major consequences or benefits to the game. Mainly, this will determine which areas in the town/forest will be open for you at what point in the game, depending on what you prioritize and unlock. However, one major choice will be extremely important and will change your overall gaming experience. What I will say is that while I like the villager-friendship system, I wish it had a bigger effect on the overall game. That being said, I enjoyed each character's story and there is something to be said for the simple nature of it that makes the game more peaceful.
There are a LOT of secret tips in this game that will help you. I strongly reccomend checking out youtube. And keep in mind that most items have SOME sort of use.
Personally, I feel that this game is superior to Harvest Moon and Rune Factory in its simulation and mechanics. Harvest Moon falls short because, while it is the true origin of this style of farming simulation gameplay, Harvest Moon games tend to judge your progress at the end of the game and....well....you know.....they actually end. Harvest Moon games (with the exception of a few) tend to have an ending, which is aggrivating as heck when you've spent hours building that farm.
Rune Factory had a different issue that Stardew Valley avoids entirely. While Rune Factory is a better looking game in terms of visual appeal and uses similar gameplay elements, it lacks Stardew Valley's humor and grace. Rune Factory struggles in that it bases and relies EVERYTHING on its villager friendship/romance system, preventing you from going to areas or doing certain things until you befriend/romance one of the people in town. Rune Factory is essentially more of a farming/dating sim hybrid, where the entire story centers around your romantic relationship with your chosen towns-person. This feels frustratingly limiting in a way, because it keeps you from accessing features of the game unless you focus on non-farming, non-adventuring tasks and character dialogue. Stardew Valley does not struggle with this issue, as EVERY CHOICE YOU MAKE IN THE GAME IS, AT ITS CORE, AN OPTION. There is a benefit to EVERY action and focus you take, and combining actions will give you greater rewards. There is no requirement for villager-friendship, but it is VERY beneficial. Want to focus on crops and cooking? Now you have access to enhanced healing items that help you work for longer time periods. Want to go dungeoneering? Now you have access to better equipment, new quests, and building materials. Want to combine these skills with construction? You can literally build items that gradually increase the value of your crops and products. And the list goes on and on and on. There is so much to do, and with some planning and strategy, you can literally do everything that the game has to offer and still be playing it for the fun of seeing how your farm can flourish.
With solid gameplay, limitless possibilities, and hours of fun and creativity, this is the best Fantasy Farm Simulation game that I have seen yet!
The art is gorgeous, the story is vibrant and whimsical and the music is beyond lovely. It's a beautiful game.
Yup, I'm hooked.  As the song goes, it's a fine line between pleasure and pain!

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
I have played four full games versus AI with various parameters and I believe I have enough game time under my belt to do an intelligent early access review.  I am a long-time fan of the Master of Orion IP and I must have played hundreds of MOO2 games.
MOO is well polished considering it’s an early access title.  The game did not crash once and performance was excellent. There were no hiccups or glitches as far as I could tell.  There were some minor UI errors that caused some data to not display correctly and the game does not scale for various resolutions perfectly.  It’s a solid base for a game with excellent voice acting.  (Mark Hamill, John de Lancie, and Michael Dorn!)
Early access is missing a great deal of content including 5 races (6 if you count the missing custom race), two victory conditions, and certain game mechanics like spies and leaders.  Also you can currently only play on ‘average’ difficulty with a maximum of 6 total players and limited galaxy selections.  Games are quite easy to win if you’re a veteran 4x, turn-based player.
As expected, there are no dedicated multiplayer servers, but multiplayer players of this genre tend to only play with close friends anyways so I don’t see this as a negative.
Ship to ship combat is in real time and works well, but actions and choices are limited to fleet formation and movement.  Otherwise combat is quite automated.  This is a negative for those players that enjoyed the turn-based combat of MOO2.  Ground combat is very basic (well, non-existent) in the current build.
Conclusion:  If you are a fan of the Master of Orion franchise and certain that you will buy the game no matter what, by all means purchase the collector’s edition. For those of you looking for a challenging, complete-game experience, you will want to wait until release.  Also there will be a version of the game offered for around $30 so if you’re really on the fence, wait for that.  In its current condition the early access game is appropriate for nostalgic, die-hard fans and players that have already decided to buy the game no matter what.

At launch, this game was a mess. There is no argument in that at all. But now? The game is extremely fun, and a blast to play.
The graphics are amazingly well done, all the way down to the small things in the streets to the fabric and clothes. Rarely I run into an instance of odd cloth physics or a out of place animation on character interactions. but other than that..from textures to the godrays..make the city beautiful.
The gameplay is amazing and not a button mash-fest like some in the series, meaning your attacks actually have 'weight' and an 'umph' when doing actions, this of course makes you take your time and sort of plan what to do depending on your enemy and the class that they are. Not saying its a bad thing to button mash, but I feel its more engaging this way and makes combat more enjoyable to me than "mash button until the enemy dies".
The sounds and effects of the city are actually really well done when you stop and pay attention to every little thing going on around you. The sound of footsteps changing depending on the terrain, the chattering of the locals, the fabric creating noises depending on if your wearing leather, cloth, or chainmail...its very impressive when you think about everything that is happening.
All in all the above makes this an awesome addition to the franchise. Even with its flaws such as..well, Coop is all but dead due to its really poor release state which turned a lot of people away from the title. First off:  Good game, for an Early Access.
But to be clear:  It's not MoO2, and if anything it seems to have a lot more in common with MoO3.  If you go into this expecting a MoO2 clone, you're going to be disappointed!
Major Complaints:
-- The races are cartoon-y.  All of them.  It's not TF2 endearing, it's not tasteful, it's not amusing. It's just embarrasing
-- Currently a 500 turn cap, or so I'm told.  I haven't hit the counter yet.... but I have no desire to have one, ever, in any strategy game I play.
Minor concerns:
- Diplomacy is barely implimented, extremely rough
- Tech tree is limited, with almost no branches
- Ship customization is there, but also extremely rough
- Your advisors are annoying as f*#!.  Not even kidding, I had other people in the room yelling at them to stop repeating the same lines over and over.
- Sadly, the Galaxy News is the same.
- Tactical battles functional, but bare.
..... but you DID notice that it's Day 1, right?  And still early access..... so NONE of the above should suprise you!  If you're looking for this already out of development, play GalCiv 2/3.
I, on the other hand, love where this game already is at Day 1, and as long as the developers keep in touch, I expect to see the Masters of Orion that never really was...
+ Crisp galactic maps (I look forward to bigger maps and variety!)
+ Natural barriers (advanced starlanes) to limit early game expansion.  No, you don't have to like it... but you're limited to your little corner until you grow up and can fly the big star lanes like all the other Big Kids.  No rushing for the enemy capitol and nuking them from orbit... not yet, at least.  Stop complaining.... if you remove it, the AI will nuke you ever time on turn 30 if given a chance.  It's there for a reason!
+ Ship designs have all the basics for a well thought-out design program.  It's fundamental, but the basics are there.
+ Building / Development trees for colonies are REMARKABLY well-fleshed.  If anything, they need to get a bit more restrictive of setting up colonies in horrible locations, like dumping all your giant cats on a giant aquatic infertile rock.
+ While combat is rough, it seems extremely fair and grounded in a good place.  They need to add features, but there doesn't seem to be the need for overhaul.
+ Graphics are smooth, with some intentional art-styling.  Hopefully they will move over to ALL art-styled or ALL crisp graphics, rather than a mix.
+ Mechanics are more or less intuitive, with the need for some minor UI tweaks.  If you've played Endless Space, MoO2/3, or GalCiv, you'll feel right at home.
Neutral Concerns:
There is a lot not fleshed out here, and we're going to optamistically cross fingers for further development.  If it was left in this state, it would NOT be a finished product... but I'm sure they know that.
I'll re-visit this as time progresses, and update as features are implimented.  If they listen to even a quarter of what I've seen posted on the Steam Forums, this game will be a gem polished to a stunning luster.
Right now it's a rough gem, with a little unpolished beauty poking out.  But I'm certainly smiling as I'm imagining what it's going to look like in 6 months.

So even if I'm the umpteenth one here, I have to say this: I was a HUGE fan of the original Master of Orion 2. First one was a bit before my time, and I picked the second one a few years after it was out, and was absolutely hooked. So much so that I gave Master of Orion 3 more than its share of tries, alas all ending in utter defeat at the hands of bugs and bad gameplay decisions.
And..I am absolutely thrilled its descendent through the years is shaping out to be follow in MoO 2's footsteps! I don't know how, but even with this as of yet incomplete version they got the mixture right to keep up you clicking through the night (erm).
Now, what many of the reviewers seem to lose sight of is that this is its earliest iteration of early access yet! Many things are obviously not implemented yet - Spying, for instance. Or all 10 races, and race customization. I don't know that Pollution works either. Some placeholders here and there - such as Ground Combat. Etc etc.
To my mind it's obvious that many of the things which are not really working right now - such as Diplomacy, or combat AI, or colony management AI - are still in their test phase and extremely likely to be improved upon.
Why such optimism? Well, for one, remarkably, the game is polished to look and feel as if it were a finished product. I've not crashed once in about 20 hours of play, and I only ran into a few bugs, fewer of which were important in any way (antimissile rockets module doesn't seem to work, for instance, or maybe it just seemed so to me).
And it's good! Everything that looks firmly in place is amazingly good. Such as:
Colony management is perfect MoO. Classic, and superb. Research - Food - Production, and Credits. Small to Huge planets, Radiated to Gaia, Low to High gravity, Ultra poor to Abundant, and random resources (gold, fungus, etc)
Space expansion, tried and true formula. Worm holes serve as bottlenecks, some of them are unmanageable until high end tech. It does allow you to treck further from the getgo than most 4X games, which I find to be a good thing. Space monsters. Pirate fleets (and bases). "Anomalies". RNG events (plagues, population booms etc). Orion and its Guardian! :)
The Tech Tree is..wow. As an example, Beam weapons upgrades never go "+1 dmg", "+2 dmg" etc - each successive variant is different in some way making it a choice - do I go with higher dmg ye olde Neutron Blaster, or do I pack in newfangled lesser dmg overloading Ion Cannon (the Mass Driver does seem too obvious a choice though). Some techs don't yet work (all the Spying tech, for instance) but that's just upcoming :)
Ship customization is sweet, and strikes a good balance between complexity and streamlining. Modules with all sorts of variants, various types of weapon mounts (6 types of Beams, 5 for Missiles).. it's good.
The one and only thing that does have me worried is Combat. Mostly because I feel like it should already be further along than it is. I don't really have an issue with it not being TBS - in MoO 2 the side who attacked and had 1st turn had a HUGE advantage over the defender - but it's kind of lackluster. The modules and weapon mounts are mostly passive, the battlemap doesn't offer much (there are some formations, and asteroids which can shield from weapon fire) but it's far too little yet. It needs more. Waiting for more.
It also tried for a few new ideas here and there, and I find no fault with any of them. Asteroid fields as a planet type, which can house Mine/Research Stations, and be made into planets. By a Worker unit a la the Civ Settler, which can do all sorts of things (mostly space lane turtling though :)) ). Choices between research results (from this researched tech do I take Fusion Beam or Fusion Bomb?) which also give Diplomacy more importance (since you can get the Tech you didn't choose via diplomatic swapping). Pollution which ruin your planet biome type. Etc.
One thing I left for the end because it really isn't that important for a Master of Orion game - IT'S BEAUTIFUL! It really is! Revised since EA:
TLDR, still no tactical combat option, the whole pollution mechanic is a major fun-killer, and the 'warp lanes' choice has really made it less than satisfying experience overall.  My EA recommendation is being changed now to a NO.  It's not a bad game.  It's just not MoO w/o at least a turn-based tactical combat option.  And, it's a simplistic 4x compared w/ so many others today.  The graphics and voices were great.  I'm not even upset about DLC races.  But, it's NOT MoO.  It's a MoO-basic.  I'll pass at this point.
EA Review:
So many good things about this game so far.  It is definitely early access--reduced races, weak AI (only average is available at this point), typical diplomacy issues for civ games (not clear there's the threat of war if you don't accept an offer, etc.), and similar minor issues.  But the game plays well so far and is true to the genre.  It's GalCiv w/ better graphics and smoother gameplay--but warp points and paths instead of freeform movement.  It's a different approach.  You can certainly better limit access to your homeworlds--but, you don't have the constant feel of threat either.
I haven't found a ship design feature--and that's good, b/c the game is more 4x, less tweaking your loadout on each vessel.  Again, it's a different approach, and this one I prefer b/c the races that exist and ship designs are very cool and just as I pictured from the MOO past.
The voice overs are fabulous.  The graphics are very nice.  Sound is nice.
My only real complaint at this point is an RTS approach to combat instead of Turnbased as in MOO2.  For me, this is a real disappointment.  It isn't a 'No' at this point--there is still hope they'll add it before release, or promise it as an expansion option or dlc.  But, it isn't MOO2.  It isn't even a good RTS--even w/ a pause feature.  I find myself auto-resolving all combats b/c of it (i.e., 'Simulate' instead of 'Tactical').  That really makes it a different take on GalCiv III instead of MOO.
Good game so far.  But, wait for 3 months until it releases if Turn-based combat is a big deal to you.

So I downloaded this in a fit of boredom the other night, having acquired this game in the first Humble Indie Bundle. I'd heard a bunch of negative responses to the game, with implications that it's some kind of "furry" sim. That's not the vibe I'm getting at all. Story-wise this game is a pure revenge tale that grows into story about betrayal and conspiracy. But forget about all the fluff for a moment and let's take a look at the meat of the game; The combat system. This is Batman Arkham Asylum with the difficulty cranked up to 11. And that's on Lugaru's Easy mode. The reversals and context sensitve hand -to-hand and melee combat  feel very much like a prototype for Rocksteady's Batman games. But you won't find enemies timing their attacks for you here. They will gleefully all attack at once, pounding your rabbit head into a sticky paste. Timing, stealth and smart response are absolutely necessary for success. If you want a great 3D brawler then this may be your game.

So, after countless hours and phase 2 fo EA here's what I've found;
CONS
- Map starlanes take away from the MOO2 experience and make it too easy to defend or hold territory for later stages of the game.
- Map sizes are too small
- Want to win?  Custom race > bonus to Production and income = outpace all races in production and cash flow and science.  Rinse and repeat.
- Custom race:  where did Creative/Uncreative go?  Where did gov't type like Unification go?
- Want to win Part 2?:  Mass colonize.  You get to a point where eventually the races will hate you for colonizing too quickly, but the bonus' you get from all the planets you own snowball into an unstopable machine.
Did I mention Starlanes?  Kind of puts a huge damper on the mechanics IMO
Fleet "battle points" make it too easy when sizing up oponents...remove please!
CONS OVERALL:
- Game is made too linear, especially with the starlanes forcing natural choke points.  Just send a few ships to guard starlanes in systems you want, and hold them until you are ready.
NOTE:  Still missing mechanics such as espionage, and boardring parties, etc
PROS:
- Upgrading system is good and allows for quick and easy upgrades to ships
- Planetary managment is good and heading in the right direction
- Got a good chunk of the MOO2 feel, with the races and GNN
OVERALL PROS:
It's getting there, slowly but surely.  I'm still optimistic that the Pro's outweigh the cons and seeing the progress from 1st stage release to 2nd gives me hopes they will reel in the line and keep it closer to the original instead of straying too far and making it a clone of some of the other more recent 4X games
- Improvements from EA phase 1 to phase 2 are fantastic, keep up the great work, but please don't lose sight of MOO2

Just finished first play-through!
Having played MoO and MoO 2 back when they first released, (ended up skipping 3) , its truly great to see this game updated.
Being an Early Access title, hopefully there will be more features added in. Its very playable as it is right now, and definately worth doing so!
One of the many  things I loved about MoO2 was the planet colonization sequence. Was a joy to see the colony craft landing on each new different type of planet, most of them so exotic and alien, at times made me wish i was was there. This newest edition takes the colonizing sequence to a new level. Beautifully rendered panoramic breathtaking cinimatic cut-scenes of your race's Colony ship descending from the atmosphere and camera pan flyby over mountains or into valleys, across lakes / oceans, through clouds, mist, or snow-storms to land in the perfect spot. Definately a "Whoa!" and pause to appreciate moment. I'm so glad they didn't skimp or cut-short this part of the game.
GNN is back and tongue-in-cheek with comedy. The GNN sequences still seem a bit rough, but this is early-access after all.
Galactic Council sequences has nicely been kept true to MoO 1 & 2, with a nice 3d facelift.
Love the "Next Planet" button, mind you it cycles through in the order of planets colonized.
The Planet Screen this time around is an Orbital Space View, with the planet slowly rotating with the daytime on the left, median, and night-time on the right. As for the buildings - are 3d iconic representations placed randomly on the planet's surface (poping through the atmosphere and right ino space), larger than life much like you'd expect from the units representation in the Civilization game series. Kinda takes the realism away but gives you an idea what you have. The downside is for bulding management, you have to click and hold to rotate the planet and click on the structure to remove it (takes several tries to find the correct bulding if you can't recognize it). A quick fix to this could be added later - would also list the buildings you can scroll through.
Love the new updated ship graphics. Ship edit screen gives you a selection of hull paint patterns (no colors though). Your able to view and rotate the 3d models.
The space combat is spectacular to watch. They added a new Cinematic Camera mode, lets you watch the combat much like it were a movie. Needs a little work, seems to randomly pick where to "point and shoot" including actual "Smart Missle Camera viewfinder" mode complete as you see in hollywood movies right up to the point of impact. Wish there were a few options to refine or pick / cycle / toggle the current camera selection.
Only thing missing is the true-tactical turn based fleet combat mode. Hope it gets implimented. To be fair, having seen the new 3d ships and graphics, it was fun to watch the automatic RTS mode, as the battle is over in a few minutes - fast, flashy, guns blazing and ships go "Boom!", litle star fighters zipping around in formation,  kinda watching a space battle sequence from Babylon 5. Still, would be nice to have the option to have the turn-based hands on combat again, control your fleet - movements and weapons.
Doomstars!!! These are a sight to behold in space battle - quite massive and dwarfing most ships but at the same time they're not "Moon sized" planets either. Gone is the "rounded borg cube" type design. Instead, the pyramid design is a nice nod to Stargate SG-1 - Goa'uld warships, and dwarfs all the other ships. These bad-boys do give you the option to actually blow up the planet. Interestingly, there hasn't been any GNN newsbreaks about it either when a planet does get blown up (turns into asteroid field you can later reform into a new barren planet). There isn't any "Planet-busting" visual sequence either for now just a second attack button icon, maybe will be added later.
The voice acting and rendering of the species is really good.
All in all, for an early-access title release, with only a handful of species available its definately worth playing. Been fairly stable, Lots of features still to be added, such as the Espoinage Training Center (even states that in the description - "to be added later")

Pros:
+ A challenging, dark adventure that forces you to learn or die
+ Constant influx of heroes means that permadeath is a setback but never an end
+ RNG makes sure you never know what's coming next
+ System is complex, but learning curve is doable
+ Wide variety of hero classes and extreme customizability means you play your way, on your terms...
+ ...But the game will definitely smack you down for goofing off and going in without this class or with too much of that class.
+ Unique exploration/battle system--not your grandpa's JRPG, nor a hack-and-slash, or RTS...
+ Long campaign with extreme replayability
+ Oozes that Lovecraftian style--not just in creature design, but at its very soul, with an all-is-lost tone and a look at the beauty and ugliness in the best and worst of humanity.
+ Creative, grim, and engaging story, which doesn't get in the way of enjoying hte game if that's not what you came here for
+ Awesome music, art that is both beautifully done and fiendishly grotesque, intuitive controls, play at your own pace
+ Price is more than reasonable--and if you get it on sale, you got a steal. I'd recommend getting the full DLC (I was a chump and didn't get it.)
Cons
- Game expects you to learn. If you don't pay attention, it will smack you down, which can be frustrating
- Interface can be confusing. (Also, if you play with a controller, even an Xbox controller, its button prompts are PlayStation buttons, which really threw me for a loop until I memorized which were which.)
- The game doesn't necessarily explain everything, which at times works and at times...doesn't
- Some missions can get a bit repetetive
- Some individual battles can get a bit repetetive (OH MY WORD THOSE ****ING RAPTUROUS CULTISTS)
- A d d i c t i v e.
If you like both Dark Souls-style difficulty (learn or die) and turn-based gameplay (for in-depth strategy), I'd recommend picking this one up. If you're a Lovecraft fan, doubly so. If none of the above is the case...well, watch a couple gameplay videos and see if it appeals.

Alright, I just have to say before you read this that I have MANY more hours than this says. I was logged out during almost all of my gameplay, so it didn't record it.
Starting out, there is a very slow progression and a rather high difficulty if you don't know what you're doing. Half of the beggining is based on the luck of having a decent starting planet, and I had one with barely any metals but tons of coal. This drastically slowed down how fast I could proceed, since I couldn't upgrade my tools or weapons until after I left it. Aside from that, it was very enjoyable. I spent two or three play sessions digging for core fragments before hitting a massive vein of them that got me off the planet in a jiffy, and suddenly I saw how truly magnificent the game was. Once you get off the first planet, everything becomes easier and more progressive. You can then go anywhere in the solar system and just have tons of fun. After you do some stuff(No spoilers) you finally get to leave and explore the entire universe. The game's tech progression makes allot of sense, and once you get off your planet progresses quite rapidly. I find it easier to collect weapons than to make them though, and often(almost always) these are far superior to what I can make at the time. If you like Minecraft, Terarria, or sandbox games in general, I recommend this game.
Pros:

-Infinite planets
-Multiplayer is awesome

-SO MANY TYPES OF WEAPONS!

-Basic ores are sometimes more rare than "uncommon" or "rare" ores. I find more titanium than iron, and tons of the red, green, and purple ores.
-Hotkey functionality isn't explained well and could use some tweaking.
Why should you get it?

Just to be clear, I recommend you get this game if it's on sale. So, first off, chances are this game has mixed reviews mainly because of launch day game breaking glitches and I don't blame people for being angry, but to give this game its dues, it's now playable and it IS fun. Again, just purchase it on sale because while it is fun, it isn't like Assassin's Creed 4 wherein I wouldn't regret dropping $60 to play at release.
This game is fun, but it suffers from a number of problems and I'll list the top 3 here:
1. Equipment: All of your stats are basically reliant on what equipment you wear, including ammo count, HP, ease of stealth, etc... Now while I understand why things like HP or Stealth are affected by your shirt and pants, but why is there no way to increase your ammo or lock pick amount outside of this? Expect to have to sacrifice some equipment for others, which isn't too bad, but it just isn't a needed restriction.
2. Multiplayer: The multiplayer is indeed fun, but the problem is that the multiplayer is mission specific only and you MUST play multiplayer to get a good amount of the points needed to get skills. Now this isn't something that should come as a surprise as since release it has been stated that the multiplayer would be mission specific, but, aside from the programming load, I don't understand why they didn't just make the whole game multiplayer, they don't even need to make multiple main characters, just let people play multiplayer without need to explain the extra players. This especially is displeasing when you find that the multiplayer missions take place in the normal map in single player mode so... it doesn't seem out of reach really.
3. Sessions Jumps: Not exactly sure what to call this, but basically it's their out of character gimmick. In AC4 it was when you went around gathering information for the assassins when out of the animus, before that it was when you played as Desmond, but (SPOILER) here you play as Arno, just going throught different time periods and trying to get into another animus session so that Abstergo doesn't find you... and it's not fun and not needed, it just randomly breaks fluidity of the story and it's just so clunky and not fun.

At least in early access, this game doesn't offer anything that other 4x games don't offer. All the familiar features are there; tech trees, colony ships, alien races, etc. However, what it does offer is streamlined play: everything that is implemented works smoothly, and a lot of the tedium of other 4X's seems swept away.  I actually liked it better than I liked GalCiv for the sheer scale of things it didn't make me manage. If you've got a friend you're trying to introduce gently to 4x's, this is the one: it's stable, brightly animated, and not as complex as most.
Things I'm hoping they'll fix before taking it out of early access are:
Diplomacy. Despite having spend full on effort in my second game trying to keep my diplomatic relationships positive (making treaties, giving in to demands, conducting myself in ways game lore might suggest would placate this species) my relationships with the AI's always ended up extremely negative. Also, once they went negative but I became mighty, there was no diplomatic option to bully them for specific planets or technologies as they had bullied me. Perhaps it's not implemented yet, but my one option to gain a concession from my enemies was to declare war and start stomping their worlds.
Pollution warnings. I kept getting these for the first world I colonized that got heavily polluted, even though that world wasn't polluted any longer. It was another world, but apparently because the pollution warning had locked on to the first polluted world, any pollution warnings anywhere got me a dialogue box that dragged me back to the first world. Annoying.
Coherent AI response to overwhelming force. I had such a technological edge by the end of the game that I could steamroll any of the other races. But nonetheless, two of them declared war on me, one when I outmatched her 5:1 and another when I outmatched him 8:1. They also never formed alliances against me, possibly because relationships default to bad so quickly they all hated each other.
Diverse voice messages. They hired good voice talent for the game, but unfortunately the diplomatic speeches don't vary much. They differ based on your relationship (usually very negative) but within a relationship level they repeat exactly over and over. If you're going to go the distance and hire voice, have them, you know, spice it up a bit.

Disclaimer! I have not played Trove in a few months some of my complaints about the game may have been fixed, some of the good aspects may have been changed.
I am hesitant to say "I recommend this game" not because it's bad but because I feel the overall direction of Trove does not  work. Trove at once tries to be an action RPG (similar to Diablo) and a Voxel based building game (similar to Minecraft).
I enjoy the overall open world feel of the game but I do enjoy the grind to upgrade shadow gear (and beyond) or level multiple characters by fighting the same monsters over and over again. What I feel is missing from the ARPG aspect of this game is the feeling of powerspikes, or a players feeling of being overpowered as they decimate weaker foes. I will not say the game is too hard, or too easy the difficulty level is fine. What I do not enjoy is the fact that I do not have the feeling of getting stronger as I gear especially because there is no real skill customization you get your skills fairly earlyo n and continue with them for the rest of the game. The dungeons are fun especially when you throw a few bombs into the mix and the jump system will let you get around easily even without a glider but do not expect deep combat mechanics.
The Shadow Arena/Tower is where I expected more varied mechanics but was again disappointed. This is especially the case because for example in shadow arena (end-game for some time) there was only one real "boss."
As an ARPG I will rate Trove 3/10, the combat is too simple and the grind gets old too quickly.
----
I enjoyed the building, block collection and "minecraft" aspects. I liked how a lot of the crafting worked leveling professions and trying to find those last few patterns I wanted to use in my house but just couldn't track down for the longest time. It was this aspect of the game that kept me going past the first 50 hours and if you are looking for a goofy, bright mono-color block building game then download Trove and check it out for sure. The various glowing and glass blocks have a great look to them, and being able to drop down your cornerstone is a really nice concept I would like to see in more similar games.
I have found some other games that have a better building games (especially those with more customizable blocks/rotations), so I will not call this groundbreaking but certainly solid.
As a Minecraft style sandbox/builder game I will rate it as 7/10.
----
Final Verdict: 6/10, fun game to play if you want to burn some time but don't get too heavily invested as there's better out there. The main reason I am not recommending it is the fact that (I feel) there are many other games out there such as Path of Exile (ARPG) or Creativerse (Voxel) which take the same gameplay elements found in Trove but do them much better.
I was going to recommend the game, however Trion's business model seems to be to push more (and more) grind, and sell "quick fixes" which means the game is unlikely to change for the better.

I nominated Tower Unite for the "Game Within a Game" Award.
Tower Unite is amazing. I played a little bit during the GMod Tower days, and I really wasn't fond of GMod for anything but playing on Tower. This game has so much potential to go way beyond the limits of GMod Tower.
This game is still Early Access, but as of now, when you buy you are able to experience:
*Four fully fleshed-out minigames; Minigolf (5 18-hole courses thus far), Ball Race (Basically multiplayer Super Monkey Ball, 5 courses), Virus (a zombie infection round-based game, 3 maps), and Planet Panic (I'll be homest, I'm the only one out of my friends who loves this). And there's 4+ games on the way!
*A free condo for every player that you can invite friends or other players over to and have fun, watch videos, decorate, play games, etc.
*A multiplayer lobby filled with: Shops for decking out your player's condo, minigames like Typing Derby and a Trivia game, boardwalk attractions, a Casino, a theater for playing videos, and more.
*The gigantic Casino has Multiplayer Texas Hold Em, Video Poker, tons of Roulette Machines, Spin the Wheel, and Double or Nothing.
And there's more on the way. If you're interested in seeing what's coming next (There's a new minigolf course on the horizon!) check out the game developers' Trello page, which has all of the features they are working on.
Lastly, I would like to say that these developers are definitely respectable, and that this is a game that will probably be in Early Access for a while, but the developers won't be abandoning this project, there's no way in hell. They care deeply about their community and Steam as a platform, having been in constant development since 2006 and publicly available since 2009, and the developers do pretty frequent livestreams showcasing new features and interacting with their players on stream, in game, and through their forums. Ask anyone who's been playing since GMod and they'll tell you the same, these are developers you can trust with the Early Access label. I would easily recommend this game to anyone in its current state, and it can only get even better from 2017 and beyond.
I hope you enjoy Tower Unite as much as I do! Make some new friends, play some minigolf, make your condo amazing, win at the casino, blow past people in Ball Race, make your friends rage when you destroy them at Planet Panic, do whatever you want! Have fun!

Alright, I just have to say before you read this that I have MANY more hours than this says. I was logged out during almost all of my gameplay, so it didn't record it.
Starting out, there is a very slow progression and a rather high difficulty if you don't know what you're doing. Half of the beggining is based on the luck of having a decent starting planet, and I had one with barely any metals but tons of coal. This drastically slowed down how fast I could proceed, since I couldn't upgrade my tools or weapons until after I left it. Aside from that, it was very enjoyable. I spent two or three play sessions digging for core fragments before hitting a massive vein of them that got me off the planet in a jiffy, and suddenly I saw how truly magnificent the game was. Once you get off the first planet, everything becomes easier and more progressive. You can then go anywhere in the solar system and just have tons of fun. After you do some stuff(No spoilers) you finally get to leave and explore the entire universe. The game's tech progression makes allot of sense, and once you get off your planet progresses quite rapidly. I find it easier to collect weapons than to make them though, and often(almost always) these are far superior to what I can make at the time. If you like Minecraft, Terarria, or sandbox games in general, I recommend this game.
Pros:
-So much variety in what you can do
-Tons of hidden collectibles
-Infinite planets
-Multiplayer is awesome
-Lots of crafting that progresses well.
-SO MANY TYPES OF WEAPONS!
Cons:
-Very slow start
-Sometimes quest objectives are vague or hard to understand. Reading the wiki helps though.
-Basic ores are sometimes more rare than "uncommon" or "rare" ores. I find more titanium than iron, and tons of the red, green, and purple ores.
-Hotkey functionality isn't explained well and could use some tweaking.
Why should you get it?
This game is a fun single player exploration game and is even more fun in multiplayer. It also is almost a full game right now and I would still buy it if it was finished as is. It also offers mod support if that's your thing.

There is a lot of controversy surrounding AC Unity due to how broken it was on release. While there are still issues in the game, I never encountered anything game breaking and the game itself is actually fun. Well, it is still Assassin's Creed, so if you don't like parkour and murdering Templars then this game won't be fun.
I got AC:2 vibes from Unity quite a bit, which I guess is a good thing as that one was a solid entry in the series. I can't really complain too much about it being more of the same when that seems to be the driving force in the series.
I didn't notice much difference in the combat in this compared to Black Flag or even AC:3 but the free-running system has gotten some additions which lower the instances of your assassin doing something completely different to what you wanted. The story is your typical AC stuff but with thankfully few interruptions by the "real world".
Overall Unity is a decent entry in the series but I could only really recommend it to fans of Assassin's Creed. It's not really a good starting point and the bugs are enough to put less determined players off.
Oh and I think the French soldiers are just reskins of the British ones from previous games, they even have a British accent most of the time.

While this game definitely has more than its fair share of issues, it is surprisingly fun. The biggest issue I had occured before I got my 8GB GTX 1070, and was using a 4GB R9 380X as my graphics card of choice. I was experiancing countless bugs when I had this card, even though it is a relativley decent card, with the biggest issue being when I finally reached Paris and climbed Notre Dame for the viewpoint, the game completely crashed. So I tried it again, and it crashed again. Thankfully, the game was still in the refund period on Steam, so I refunded it.
The biggest complaint to be had about the game is this though. WHY CAN I NOT DELETE MY SAVEGAME FROM WITHIN THE GAME MENUS?!? You would think that is the standard, but to delete the savegame, you must search through file system on your computer to do so.
After getting my new card, I decided to try it again. Thankfully, this card has the necessary power to actually play the game at a decent framerate with minimal issues. The biggest issue now with the game is the pop in is horrible. It does not really break the game, but it definitely is annoying. Also, sometimes missions glitch and you need to exit them and restart it. For the most part, the glitches are not game breaking, just annoying.
Graphically, the game looks pretty great. I play on High settings with framrates that usually stay around 55 fps.
I have not quite decided how I feel about the combat yet. It is very different from the other Assassin's Creed games. My only realy issue is that in the beginning of the game before I really was able to upgrade my armor, there were riflemen who could shoot me only once or twice and I would die. There is no visual low health indicator other than looking at the health bar, so you may not even realize you have low health. Thankfully, after getting much better armor, I hardly ever die now, regardless of the strength of the enemies I go up against.
I am not far in the story as of writing this review, simply because I have been doing all of the side missions to try to upgrade my armor and weapons. So far, the story is ok. It certainly is not very memorable and I would not consider it great. The best part so far is the very beginning where you play as a medieval Knights Templar.
Overall, if you have a powerful enough graphics card and want to play all of the Assassin's Creed games, then you should consider getting this. You may want to wait until a sale, but it really is not that bad of a game at all, it just has its issues. However, unless you have a really good graphics card, like a GTX 1070 or better, then I would probably hold off on getting this game until you have a more powerful system.
UPDATE: I have now completed the game and all of the singel player missions, and I have a few more little issues. The map is too clutterred, unless you tab over to narrow down what appears on the map. This makes it hard sometimes to see what you are looking for. The description of certain items as to how you can unlock them is pitiful and I would argue inaccurate. Example, Altair's outfit just say it unlocks by completing helix rift missions. In reality, it unlocks by either finding all of the artifacts in the helix rift missions (which I did not even know about until the last ones), or by collecting a specific one in the medieval france one. Also, the decription for Arno's Master Assassin outfit could be better. The description say you acquire it by completing all single player sequences. I took this to mean all of the single player side missions as well, so I did them. It should just say something about assassinating the final boss. I know they wanted to keep from spoiling who the final boss was, but they could have phrased it to just hide who the boss was. Overall, the story was OK. It is certainly forgettable, but it didn't suck like some people here say. Again, I will reiterate my main point, if you like the AC games and have a powerful enough system to handle it, then you should consider getting AC Unity

When I started the game for the first time, I got a black screen. The music started to play and I knew that the menu was actually loaded because of the sounds. So I decided to hit enter twice and guess what? That closes the game. I should have kept it closed, but I decided to give it another try and oh joy, it worked this time....in 4:3 screen format.
Now when I see a game do that, I immediately search for a settings button so I can rectify this and immediately tweak the rest of the graphical settings. But hey, why add such a button when you are in the first menu? Nah, I first needed to join a channel before I was even able to set a nickname and select a character. Still no settings button to be found.
So I selected a character, selected a gun type called ‘machine’, (because apparently that’s a gun type now) and created the character. But no no no, the game didn’t want me to use a ‘machine’ and decided to give me an assault rifle instead.
Thankfully there was a settings button now, so I figured I was past the worst part. I was not. Thank you developers, that’s very kind of you /s.
So after all this time, all I achieved was getting a nickname (for which you are required to manually click the namecheck button somehow), creating a character that was not even the same as what I got after I created it and changing my resolution and some other settings. Remember I said ten minutes? That was ten minutes.
Are you crying yet? No? Let me tell you a little story about gameplay then…

The game types are pretty similar and when you are dead, you need to wait until the next round. That much is okay about this game. What is not is the fact that it is unbalanced as hell! Sure, there is some kind of hack detection present in the game, but since some weapons are extremely OP, you can expect lots of kiddies whining about HAXXX nonetheless. Oh and when you áre able to respawn, you can expect the entire enemy team to be standing at your spawn point, ready to blow your head off after you lose invulnerability.
I don’t think I even need to go any further on that subject as this should basically be enough to stop you from playing it already.

As a piece of art, as an exhibition of neon-techno-giant-mech-destroying-buildings aesthetic, Brigador is pretty fabulous. There's no denying the sound, art, writing come together as a cohesive whole. But as a piece of design, as a game meant to be played, it leaves a lot to be desired.
I played long enough to beat the campaign and to give the more open-ended Freelance mode a couple whirls, and I kept waiting for the game to hook me. I tried playing with the biggest mechs with the best weapons and destroying everything in sight. I tried playing with the smaller vehicles, ones that required more strategy and were more difficult. I tried completing every side objective on a map. I tried speed-running through them instead. Didn't matter. The game never felt compelling. It never felt more than a superficial, mildly entertaining romp through rectangular districts that mostly look the same.
There's a lot of design approaches a game can take to hook the player and while Brigador dabbles in some of them, none of them were implemented well enough to draw me in:
-A game can hook by providing interesting characters with character arcs (like the Telltale Games). There are no characters in Brigador and certainly no character arcs.
-A game can hook by providing an interesting plot / environment with mysteries to uncover (like Bioshock). The plot here is paper-thin. You get summaries before each mission, but they're only providing an explanation of the objectives. Basically you're a mercenary who blows stuff up because some text told you to. There's no sense of progress, no meaningful advancement of story.
-A game can hook by providing a meaningful challenge (like Dark Souls). Difficulty in Brigador is problematic, as it primarily comes from willfully choosing poor tools for the job. For example, in a given campaign map, you can choose a massive mech with double lasers that can take a lot of punishment or you can choose a tiny sniper mech that is easily destroyed. Some people enjoy this - and I think these people may appreciate the options Brigador provides. I do not. I love difficulty - but I love difficulty that the game provides, not that I must generate by willfully making poor choices or placing arbitrary restrictions on myself.
-A game can hook by providing stat / gear / unlock progression (like Diablo 3). Brigador's open-ended Freelance method provides an extensive list of things to unlock, including new weapons, mechs, & pilots. While the pilots represent difficulty options and don't otherwise affect gameplay, the weapons all felt unique and interesting, an excellent feat given how many there are. Unfortunately, the campaign has NO progression. For each map, you're provided a couple pre-made loadouts and that's that.
-A game can hook by providing exploratory elements, such as new environments, hidden collectibles, bigger and scarier opponents, etc. There is some variety in the level design - rural vs. junk city vs. regular city - but none of it ever really *pops.* Same with unit design. You do eventually encounter some larger mechs but it's genuinely kind of hard to tell the difference because the game is so dark and zoomed out. It desperately needed paint jobs, decals, etc on the mechs, to distinguish them from each other. Even the three factions are remarkably similar. Furthermore, there are no hidden collectibles, no secret bosses, none of that. In fact, there are no bosses at all, which seems a wasted opportunity.
Ultimately, the game isn't compelling. This is unfortunate as it clearly has some excellent elements. I personally would love to play a Brigador 2 that bothered to create a compelling story with interesting characters; with levels that had unique & clear design (rather than the randomly generated feel they all have now); with an intelligent progression from small mechs and weak weapons to large mechs and powerful weapons. Maybe even some multiplayer elements, like horde defense co-op, CTF, etc. That game would be frikkin awesome. Unfortunately, Brigador is not that game.

Brigador is an isometric shooter, very much drawing on oldschool themes.
There's a fair bit of reading you can do if you're interested in the fluff, but that's entirely optional and the gameplay itself is very simply blowing someone/something up and then leaving the area.
The gameplay itself is excellent, the music and sound is great, and the artstyle is very well done.
The vehicles and weapons also have a significant amount of weight and oomph to them, which makes them feel very satisfying to use.
The only nitpicks I can really point out are the following:
Repetition can happen after playing a while, however, there are significant amounts of missions, vehicles and weapons to keep this in check. Again, it's an isometric shooter, so I'm not sure if I should even bother bringing this up or not, but now you're aware of it if you weren't before.
The music does not seem to have any sort of playlist or loop, so what this means is that if you're taking your time in a mission you will hear one track play to the end from the start of the game and then play the rest of the level in silence, which is actually a bummer since the game has very nice music that adds to the experience. This may simply be a bug I've been unlucky enough to encounter, however.
Overall, one of the best isometric shooters I've ever played, and it's a shame that the game did not sell enough copies to warrant major DLC. (As stated by the devs themselves)

Colin McRae Rally is an arcade-style offroad racing game, where you can drive different offroad racers in a variety of circuits and tournaments. Now, I compare all racing games to Gran Turismo 2, which is in my humble opinion, the best racing sim I have ever played. It reminds me of the arcade play of Gran Turismo 2, where you could drive cars like the Lancer Evo on dirt tracks, against a second player or versus computer drivers; However, with Colin McRae Rally, you are going up against computer players times, rather than the actual cars on the track. I think this takes away from the realism of the game, because you don't have other drivers as obstacles to conquer and overcome, it's all about time instead. Visually, the game is so-so, but the cars are pretty detailed. There doesn't appear to be a lot of customization. In all, I wasn't overly impressed with the game, though it isn't exactly a dumpster fire either. It skates by, but there are other racing games out there which would be better.

The combat is absolutely awesome and I keep finding little tricks and moves I had no idea about even after playing 25+ hours, like spinning and throwing a weapon at the same time. Because the gameplay is so excellent, I keep coming back again and again and again because it's so much fun. Tower Unite is a fantastic game which came from a mod for Garry's Mod and now is a stand alone title. For an Early Access game it has a lot of mechanics and features that are done great. The freedom of expression when customizing your condo is endless. Customizing your character also boasts a fair array of choices. The community is full of a huge mixture of people which can be both positive and negative. The minigames are a blast with a few friends, and have new maps and additions regularly. The Plaza in the game serves as a hub to do many things and is a nice way to hangout with others. The devs (Pixeltail) are fantastic with communicating to the player base. There are tons of options to be involved in the game's creation. For example they have made it easy to give input, make suggestions, see development progress, and influence the future of the game. The newest additions of The Casino and Bowling have also boosted the amount of things to sink your time into. Overall the game has kept my attention for many hours and will continue to do so in the future. I recommend this game for those who like roleplaying, freedom of expression, gambling, trying to get rich, and living milk cartons. So much in this game is done right.
[UPDATE Nov 24 2017]
The game is still changing and evolving, and it's all for the better. Everything I've said previous still holds up, and there are now more activities to participate in than ever. One person can just be a knight and possibly camp because they're so tanky which could prevent others from getting loot.
If you get into this game beware, you'll eventaully end up spending money on one of the various packs that are shoved in your face cause you figure "Why the hell not?" but I'd advise that you absolutely do not spend any money on this game.

I honestly used to think this game was fun, me and my 2 other friends always used to play it. Then one of my friends eventually got bored of it because his best character died. Me and my friend were still doing fine so we continued. I eventually got 2 great characters that both ended up dying due to the unfairness of this game. I tried to start up again with another character but after a week I couldn't bring myself to do it, which is how I eventually quit the game. My friend still plays and I honestly don't get how he does. This game is also heavily relied on luck through what items you get.
You may have noticed how I've been complaining about character deaths and there's one word to explain why: permadeath.
This game, has permadeath, once you die, no matter how good your character is, no matter how good his equipment is, no matter how many much you claim you pressed the nexus button, you will start all the way from the beginning with a level one character with basic default equipment, what makes the permadeath unfair is that even the items you pay ACTUAL MONEY FOR, you still lose when your character dies. Which is why I advise you to not spend any actual money on this game because you will eventually die and lose the items you paid for which essentially means you lost and wasted money.
Another thing that makes this game unbalanced and even more P2W is the pets.
Like others have stated there's a pet system in this game that can do various things (heal you, attack, etc)
But to make your pets good, you have to feed them
And you do that by using food, either high tier items (hard to get) or by paying money just to satisfy some pixels on a screen.
Here's some pros and cons to sum up those couple paragraphs;
Pro's:
Fun (by yourself or with friends)
Unique class system
Good guild system
Rewarding when you actually get loot
Cons:
EXTREMELY pay to play
Permadeath not executed that greatly
Unbalanced to a great degree
Pet system reliant on paying
Essentially a time waster

TL;DR: This game used to be reasonable and fun, now it's an example of how a Snowball can catch a lot of dirt on its way down the hills.
The invites: You can disable game invites entirely, or leave them only enabled for Friends and Clan.
The game: It's not a copy of Garena's Point Blank. This IS Point Blank. This version of Piercing Blow (oh, I witnessed the name change and I died) is actually Project
Blackout, formerly published by GameRage, who weren't getting enough profit from the game, and dropped it (after all, it IS a huge money-grab). The new managers decided to
include this same update that the Garena managers did, with all the class/outfit bullcrap, rather than the old inventory, perk and leveling system PB had, which was, in fact,
much better.
Now here's a few fun facts:
The maps: They (at least some) are "blatantly disguised" copies of Counter-Strike maps. For example: Look at Downtown and try to compare it to Dust2. Small houses making
tunnels into B, a CT base going under A(bombsites have been switched when comparing to Dust2, though), a straight passageway right into mid that can make sniper battles from
base to base. Pretty much a "city" themed Dust2.
Cash-shop: It used to be much worse, but better at the same time. You used to have items like Quick-Swap, Quick-Reload, Less Respawn Time, XP/Money boosters that boosted
different ammounts depending on how much you paid, characters that would boost XP, Credits or Mobility and HP, you could not get any of the ridiculously skinny female
characters without paying (though you could get the default female characters, which are much skinnier than the default fat guy), the masks (which give ridiculous stats like
an almost guaranteed second chance after being shot in the head, or more penetration to cancel that second chance).
The servers: They have been horrible for as long as I can remember. Not even back in GameRage do I recall having stable connections (Oh, but I can play on Russian, Arab and
Latino-American servers with barely any lag) and all my friends suffered from the same.
The game's always been Pay2Win, but after the transition to this "PB Extreme" game-revamp, which, in fact, was a complete throw-up, the gameplay itself went down a lot.
I used to have fun in this game with friends. We used to have fun to a point where one of my friends got a REALLY high-ranked account and got banned for "hacking". He decided
he didn't want to stop playing, so he started over, and he got banned AGAIN for "hacking". The game is too "community-managed", to the point where too much reports will get
you banned for allegedly hacking, even if you're active in the forums, constantly posting videos of cool plays you do. It's ALWAYS been this way.
I am not going to lie, I believe this game has potential as a fun Free-To-Play game, but, even though I've moved onto other games, if I ever play it again, I'll tell you
right now: I'll be playing on a server other than Piercing Blow. The old Point Blank/Project Blackout with the old level skills and old shop is much better, not to mention
that there are a few PB's where you actually can get GOOD permanent weapons without having to spend a single penny.
All in all, this all just means I'm extremely sad because of how this game went downhill in such a shameless way. After all, this game was one of the reasons I have some of
the best friends I could ask for.
*Phew* /rant over, sorry for the wall of text.

After 21 hours into the game, I can definitely say I recomment this game IF, they continue to improve it. If Civilization 5 and MOO2 had a baby, it would be this game. I'm a 35ish year old man-baby who loved Moo2, so the main reason I bought the game was that MOO2 was include with it as I lost my DOSBOX version. The Steam version is still just the DOSBOX version, but that's ok... at least i won't lose it.
Pro/con time.
PRO:
Draws heavily from MOO2/Civilization
Plays very smoothly and quickly, even on large maps you're not waiting too long between end turn clicks.
CON:
1) AI is very bad.
2) Only half the races are available.
3) Only two options for spaceship design per class.
4) Most of the game is clicking until you watch a cutscene.
5) Autobuild queue not customizable, it just starts building crap instantly.
6) Music repetitive.
7) Leader is not customizable at all.
8) No random heroes to pilot your ships.
9) Blueprint/upgrading your fleet is still a mystery to me after 21 hours and multiple playthroughts.
10) Too many cutscenes, which are nice, but if you've seen it once you've seen it enough and they play all the time.
11) Very limitted map design, every map feels roughly the same.
12) Lack of options to change things such as disabling tutorial, or turning off cutscenes,
13) Too easy.
14) Spend most of your time moving around the map, constantly zooming in and out as the game will force you to change zoom levels when events happen.
15) Tactical combat is severely limitted, best you can do is maybe avoid a missle by luckily moving behind an astroid or adjust which ships arrive to the enemy first.
16) Most games turn into a game of clicking next turn while you sit in a stalemate with your enemies until you get a DOOM/TITAN class ship to destroy them or win the Elections.
So the CON list is much bigger than the PRO list, but most of the CON list is stuff i hope to attribute it to be a non-complete game. And despite this list, this game still stole two of my days away almost completely and I don't regret an ounce of it, but i still had an enjoyable time playing the game in the current state and look forward to spending many more hours into it as it becomes complete.

This is a totally great game.
Three massive points about it:
1.) You can completely customise the difficulty. Want to destroy everything with a giant mech with overpowered weapons? You can do that. Or you can take a medium mech and have to be more tactical. Or you can take a tiny antigrav tank and zip around. Or you can fight in a paper armoured battle suit. It's incredibly customisable.
2.)  The combat is simple, but incredibly fun. You only have 2 weapons and a special ability, but the massive amount of different weapon types means that every single round can play differently.
3.) Incredible value for money. For a single player game, you can sink hours and hours into it. Reminds me of the game FTL in that way, where you can just keep playing for ages. The difference is that this isn't a randomly generated campaign, you actually have a whole scripted campaign and another mode called Freelance that you can work through. With all the options, you could get a hundred hours out of this game easy.
Overall, a true gem of a game, obviously made by people who cared about it. Great background music, great "lore" that you can unlock, and if you buy the special edition you also get all the music and an audiobook to listen to as well.
Really, really good game, and incredibly value for money.
