Brigador is one of those games where there's not a whole lot of things you can really say about it, because of how straight forward it is. But that's not a bad thing.
Brigador brings back a style of isometric action games that we've not really seen in some time. If you've ever played the "strike" series (Desert Strike, Nuclear Strike and so on), or the slightly more obscure "Mass Destruction", you know roughly what type of game it is. You're unleashed on the world in a heavily armed vehicle, and your goal is to destroy things. Brigador is not a clone of those mentioned games though, and in most ways, it's a better game. If nothing else, it's a lot faster, and has more going on at all time.


The graphics in Brigador is clean, sharp & detailed. While not as technically advanced as many other modern games, Brigador does still look darn good, owing to a strong consistent art style. The screenshots are representative, that is what the game looks like. And while they might look a bit cluttered, it's usually not too hard to figure out what's going on on screen at any given moment. And yes, those are coloured lights that would make a late 90's 3D action game, like Forsaken, green with envy. Unlike those late 90's games, the use of coloured light does not end up feeling tacky though, it works.
Brigador is no slouch in the audio department either. The soundtrack fits well in with the 80's/early 90's style cyberpunk feel that the game has, and helps set the mood. All weapons have suitable sound effects that make them feel like they have some weight behind them, without feeling overbearing and obnoxious. Audio feedback is very important in a game like Brigador, and it nails it.
You're playing as an armoured vehicle, be it a tank, mech or some other vehicle outfitted with heavy weapons. And your goal is to cause as much destruction as you possibly can. Each level has its own set of objectives, that usually boil down to "kill X, Destroy Y, then escape", with secondary objectives that are similar in nature. It's all very straight forward, and the game does not really stray from this formula. Depending on if you're playing the campaign, or just randomly generated maps, you either have a set of 3-4 different vehicles to chose from, or you get to design your own from parts that you've unlocked.
Exactly how you play will depend on your vehicle. Some are light and nippy, and need to always be on the move to avoid incoming projectiles, others are lumbering behemoths that can take a beating. And there's also a good variety in the weapons, with things like mortars, machine guns, heavy cannons, shotguns and so on making up the arsenal. So despite the games rather straight forward gameplay, the variety in playstyles between vehicles still make the game feel like it has a lot of variety.
The game encourages you to play aggressively in most cases. Collateral damage is not just not punished, but even encouraged, as you'll get greater rewards the more things you end up destroying along the way. And destroying things in Brigador feels far more satisfying than it has any right to do.
Brigador is a great game. It's easy to pick up and play, and it's just darn fun. It might not be the deepest game on the market, but few games I've played match the sheer amount of fun I've had with Brigador. It's going to be one of those games that will stay on my HDD for a long time, and whenever I just feel like blowing stuff up, I'll start Brigador. So for anyone who's looking for a straight forward action game, I can't recommend Brigador enough.

Today, in our top-speed modern world, there are some of us who just end up feeling down. As David Bowie and Queen so famously said, we, the people on streets, are constantly under pressure. Stardew Valley is, in my honest opinion, one of the best ways to relieve that pressure, being a game that's just... nice.
Stardew Valley isn't hard or fast-paced or awesome - if that's all you look for in videogames, go play Doom or Castlevania or Dark Souls. This game isn't so much a farming simulator as it is just a game where you live your life as a farmer in a small town. You can look after crops, care for animals, go fishing, explore huge cave systems, fight monsters (pretty cute monsters though), forage for berries, be a freelance deliveryman, befriend everybody, marry someone... it never ends, and that's a good thing. You don't have to specialise or focus on one particular craft like so many other RPGs try and force you into. The game allows you to be a jack-of-all-trades while also mastering everything. It's brilliant and it just flows so perfectly.
Games today are plagued by sh*tty dialogue, one-dimensional characters, and meaningless choices. Even games that advertise a "deep" story with multiple paths more often than not fall flat on their faces and then offer you a microtransaction. Stardew Valley doesn't go out of its way to be the greatest story-driven game ever; yet all the characters feel like real people. They all have surface-level qualities, just like we all do, and then once you get to know them a bit better they reveal the other facets of their personalities, and you just get drawn in to this friendly and vibrant community of people who are so happy to have you there. Sometimes I've genuinely smiled at this game's dialogue, because I actually feel good reading it - I feel like I'm talking to a real person, something no other game thus far has replicated for me. The fact that all these characters feel so lifelike and realistic might have to do with Eric Barone just writing what he feels like, just sharing his version of the human experience in such an honest and creatively-free way that brings the game to life like nothing else. Something like Mass Effect Andromeda probably feels so robotic and empty because it was developed by hundreds of people - not to discredit their hard work of course, but a big company can't possibly hope to communicate with us on the very basic and human level that Eric's pulled off.
For me, there are three defining characteristics that make a game "good"; fun, soundtrack, and graphics, in that order. I'm not saying that better graphics make a game better of course, but if something looks like monkey vomit then there isn't much that can be done gameplay-wise to save it. Luckily Stardew Valley nails all three of these categories. As I talked about earlier, the huge variety in stuff to do makes it overwhelmingly replayable and endlessly enjoyable. The soundtrack is so peaceful and soothing, and switching to a new season for the first time and hearing those new tracks feels like coming home on a Friday night to a warm family dinner. They're instant classics that sound familiar and welcoming even the first time you hear them - I never ever play this game without audio. Graphically, Stardew Valley is nothing new or impressive, but its visual aesthetic focusses so much on warmth and friendliness that 16-bit graphics help it rather than hinder it. Honestly, if the game was full-rendered 3D and done in a photorealistic style, I don't think I'd like it as much. It reminds me of old Super Nintendo games, especially EarthBound when you combine the style with the small-town vibe. Like the soundtrack, Stardew Valley's graphics are just divine, and significantly increase my enjoyment of the game.
I don't often get all sentimental and wordy in my game reviews on here, just because I try and make direct points and back them up with evidence to support my opinion on a game. But Stardew Valley for me is something real, something wholesome and genuine that causes a peacefulness in my soul like nothing else. I play games because I love them, because it's my hobby and I get enjoyment out of it - and Stardew Valley is perhaps one of the most enjoyable games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.

I knew I wanted to get it the moment I looked at it- the asethetic of the game is basically "Command and Conquer: Tiberian Sun" gets mooshed together with Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon's garish 80's gloss and plays like a isometric MechWarrior. These are all very positive things. From the get go it has an immediate personality in it's presentation that will suck you in, and the carnal combat within will get you hooked.
So let's break it down.
PROS:
-----------------------------------------------
- Great visuals, unique presentation
- A loving amount of detail has gone into desiging the weird and wild technological machines at your disposal, from the actual visual designs to the variety of weapons and their functions, stats and even flavortext herein. If you like customizing a mech not unlike armored core or such, you're gonna have fun with this.
- Gleeful amount of destructibility in all maps. The world is your sandbox to topple over and stomp.
- Great soundtrack. I'll admit I'm not as into the overt 80's synth stuff as some people, but if you like that kind of music, this is grade A material for you up with the likes of Hotline Miami.
-Surprisingly fleshed out world building in the descriptions of pilots, locations, weapons, mechs, etc. It's nothing groundbreaking in it's own right, but it provides quite a bit of grim flavoring to what is, at first glance, a seemingly simple game.
CONS:
-----------------------------------------
-Loadtimes are juuust long enough and the actual missions juuust short enough to give some noticable speedbumps to what is otherwise a fast and addictive game.
- The weapon trajectory beams and targeting reticule UI. They manage to do a lot with it that helps feed you immediate information on potential targets. However, the trajectory beams are so bright and colorful they wind up distracting you from the actual targeting reticule, making aiming a slapdash process in the middle of a raging firefight. It's something that I think ought to be tweaked, and a minor inconvience overall- nothing game breaking.
TL;DR :
-------------------------------------------
Can't reccomend it to everyone, but if you love mechs, mayhem, or just enjoy some of that garish neon 80s dystopia, this is a fun distraction that deserves a bit more recognition.

Works well on Linux even on somewhat dated hardware.  Gameplay is smooth and diverse.  Want to be an unstoppable killing machine? Go ahead, play a giant stack of cars with tracks under it that can be equiped with two anti-everything cannons.  Want to outsmart your opponents and be sneaky? Play a Tuktuk and go on a stealth operation where a single hit means the end of it all.  Want to joust large tanks with a short-ranged high damage weapon? I found the Tuktuk works for that too.  If you want to be more classy, go for the flying oldtimer instead.  Want to bulldoze through your enemies? Well... you can do that.  Want to stomp out enemies with a mech? You can do it.  My greatest issue would be that the description of the Treehouse promised me loud horns and the Keybind screen even offers a key to sound the horn but I can't hear it at all. I want to honk at them, damnit.
I also really like that the story is seperated from the actual gameplay, so it doesn't interject and slow down what I am doing.  Don't you hate it when you get all pumped up and then a 15 Minute cutscene starts before you are allowed to do anything?  Well, not in this game.  You want action, you can have action.  You want to read why you were fighting anyway?  You can read the story.
Also the graphics are very appealing if you like 2D isometric games.  So many nice details to look at.

Lets start with my complaints.
1. Uses what appears to be JPEG to compress desktop images, and makes them look horrible. It also takes about 20 seconds to load my configuration for some reason, until it does it just tiles my main desktop image over all monitors. Being the main feature I bought this product for makes me not reccomend it. There should at least be an option to allow me to not have compressed images.
2. changes how window management works, even with these settings disabled, trying to move a fullscreen window to a monitor above the one it is currently on causes it to snap into a window, then quickly go fullscreen on the monitor it was on before.
3. Multi-monitor taskbars are buggy. VERY buggy. the start button does nothing on my secondary monitors, there is no way to show my pinned applications on DF taskbar, the DF taskbars sometimes dissapear and will only reappear when I open the settings for them and hit apply (without changing anything.) I really want to use them because they allow me to see the time/date and sound/network settings unlike the normal windows 10 secondary taskbars, but they are basically unusable in this state.
But there's also things I like.
1. setting desktop wallpaper as different images on each monitor is easy.
2. ability to quickly change audio devices is quite handy when you use multiple soundcards on a single system
3. as stated above the DF taskbars would be much better than the standard windows 10 taskbar, if they worked right.
4. all of the customization options. Windows has become increasingly restrictive on how you can edit your workspace, this does its best to alleviate some of that.
Overall, its an ok program with a great vision, but seeing as I'm dissatisfied with the main reason I bought it, I cannot reccomend it in its current state.
I also had to let the program open and run for 5 minutes from steam to leave this review, because it did not count my time using it for some reason, not the program's fualt, but annoying.

"Gnawing uncertainty, the birthplace of dread."
Darkest Dungeon is extremely random.  This is its biggest flaw, but also its greatest strength.  It means you are never safe,  never secure, you can take nothing for granted.  The game will, inevitably and through sheer random chance, put you in an unwinnable situation, but this is the game's test: will you have the sense to swallow your pride and cut your losses or will you march your troops to their inevitable deaths?  Yes, the game absolutely will treat you unfairly, but your poor decisions in the face of this bad luck will do far more damage than it ever could.

new review December 2016:
Well then, currently this is Civilization in space. With starlanes. And a loss of immersion by all races being very much alike. 10 months ago I thought the game was on a good track to become a worthy successor, but so far it didn't manage to become that - well, hope dies last.

Still not sad to have bought it, as early access gave me copies of MoO 1 and 2 (and the lamentable third part which noone like to speak of), but as a game it does not hold the thrill of the originals nor their depth nor their complexity. Therefore I spend my time in Stellaris and MoO2, letting this game slowly rot in my library.
So, current oppinion: Nice 4x starter with obnoxious advisors, low complexity and nice artwork. Not a game recommended for anyone who liked the gameplay of the old series though.
old Review from February 2016:
Well, after a playthrough of one game of Master of Orion 2 and this new iteration of the series, I feel it is prudent to write a review ;)
First of all, it is NOT a real remake, but a reinterpretation. Secondly, this reinterpretation is done as faithful as can be (within reason). You'll  find lots of techs, buildings and modules that are basically the same in both games. At the time of this review, there are only 6 playable races, all of which have the flair of their counterparts of old. No, Psilons might not be creative any more, but their research boost is gargantuan if you tend to expand a lot like me.
All in all, this is the first game that might really be a successor to the heritage of Moo and Moo2. Keep up the good work!

I've never left a bad review for a game before.  I've always felt like if a bunch of developers spent a huge amount of time on a crappy game then it'd be messed up to leave a bad review.  Well in this case I figure it's ok.  Because they take a pretty good game and absolutely ruined it.  For insance.  This game has a shot based around a cage taht fills and a timed release.  Well you'd think they'd make sure that guage is always visible.  WELL THEY DON'T.  Occasionally the guage will go off screen, behind other players or behind annoying popups that tell you things like who the announcer is that's talking or how big the last run was.  It's so infuriating to go to take a shot and suddenly have the guage covered.  It's even more annoying because the guage fill time seems to vary based on which player is shooting and how far they are from the goal.  And sometimes it doesn't even fill up.  It just shoots.  And there's no real good tutorial in the game.  Like you're just suppose to already know how to play.  So then you get to the passing on offence.  You tell it to pass and maybe it'll pass somewhere good, maybe it won't.  WHO KNOWS.  Then on defence you switch players by pressing A.  So press A repeatedly until you get the player you want.  But it transfewrs you to the player closest to the ball.  Not the player who should be covering the shooter.  And there's no alternate button as far as I can tell to choose.  So when you're cycling players sometimes you periodically interupt another player running to position, disrupting him, then you get the player you want, but the person that other guy was suppose to be covering is wide open.  This kills the game.
So... given all of that, how do you make it worse?  Well, let's throw in a crap load of ads!  For instance, every time you try to shoot a free throw, on the second shot, the gatorade logo will always block you from seeing the guage.  This kills the game.
What else?  Well the game calls timeouts every friggen 2 minutes.  This is an unskippable 20 second loading screen essentially every 2 minutes.  There is no way to turn this off in options or alter the volume of timeouts that are called.  This more than anything... kills. the. game.
Now if this was a crappy game, I wouldn't care.  I wouldn't even want to play it.  But this game is actually fun when you can actually play it to spite the crappy passing and defense controls.  It just needs a good tutorial, a fixed position for the shooting guage that's always on top, and the ability to turn off timeouts.  If I could do that, I'd probably play the crap out of this game and LOVE it.  But... unfortunately I want to play this game all the time and it does nothing but infuriate me because it's so close to being good and just seems to be intentionally destroyed by ads, and timeouts.
Also as a side note... the story line is garbage.  It says it's a Spike Lee joint, but if I was Spike Lee I wouldn't want my name on some garbage like that.  It's horrible.  I haven't tried online play yet.  So maybe that'll be what saves the game.  But I know better than to play a game online before practicing offline for a long time.  I guess we'll see.

MoBAs are fun, space sims are fun, so why not both? *Que mariachi music*
Sadly though, striking a balance between the two appears to be a challenge that this game is yet to meet. The challenge is in finding a happy medium between the immersion that makes space sims fun, and the tactical and strategic thinking that makes MoBAs fun, and getting both to exist at the same time. Sadly, this game is too heavily weighted toward appealing to MoBA fans for the space sim element to exist happily.
A typical match begins with drafting, which occurs over three phases. In the first phase, you are only allowed to see one teammate's choice of ship, and some helpful hints, where it is intended for you to choose your class of ship and the role you will play in your team. In the second phase, you are allowed to see the choices of three other teammates, and two enemies, and here you get to choose how your ship is customised. It is here that the first real clash between a MoBA and space sim occurs.
What make space sims fun, for me anyway, is the sandbox aspect where you get to customise your ship; trying different combinations of chassis, engines, shields and weapons etc. to build a ship that is unique. Fractured Space is very limited in terms of customisation, and you only really get a choice between three modifications for your primary and secondary weapons, and zero degree of control over other aspects of your ship (except for some limited consmetic options). Considering that this is a MoBA, and allowing too much customisation would threaten to ruin the drafting process of a game, and fan the flaming of teammates that MoBAs are notorious for, limiting the customisation of ships is perhaps justified.
The developers have made a consession to space sim fans by allowing them to customise their ships in a more discrete way by giving the game the additional element of assigning and customising crew members. In this feature, you are allowed control of choice over your captain and 4 crew members, leaders of a particular division of your ship's workforce, be it communications, engineering, tactical etc. Each captain and crew member has influence over the ship's stats, such as attack, shields or sensor range. While this does give the effect of customisation space sim fans long for, it does not give players what they long for; changing their ship in such a way that their opponent gets a (nasty) surprise when that tiny frigate starts hammering their aft quarters with nuclear missiles, or that dreadnaught in the distance disappears and is suddenly on your broadside, blocking you from jumping to safety while members of his fleet quickly approach for an easy kill.
The objective is straightforward: Start from your base, capture points along each lane and finally capture the enemy base to win. Instead of destroying towers and outposts, each capture point is a mini-game of king of the hill. None of the towers or outposts fight back, but the enemy base does.
The developers have successfully balanced the MoBA and space sim elements here by making ship to ship combat the focus, where teams
fight eachother rather than rely on minions doing all the work. On that note, I should mention there are no minions who fight each other, only mining freighters which can be destroyed for resources, but are mostly ignored in favor of destroying the enemy team's ships.
The map you play on is unique to the MoBA format. Instead of top, mid and bottom lanes, with jungle between them, there are 'alpha' and 'beta' lanes where the objective is to capture mines, and Gamma. There is no jungle, ships jump between the sectors.
'Gamma' is a space station that opens every few minutes, where it is again a king of the hill game where the team with the most players within the space station will win control over the sector, and special bonuses for their ships, in addition to the bonuses won for capturing resources.
Gamma battles are a lot of fun, and the highlight of the match. For what it's worth, the space station in the Gamma sector  is properly designed for these kind of battles, where stronger ships are able to circle the station and fire at weaker opponents who find cover, but if the stronger ships enter the station they will be quickly overwhelmed. Bravo to Fractured Space for this aspect of the game.
In space sims, combat usually occurs over long, medium and then eventually close range, where long range battles are all about timing and accuracy, and close quarters test a player's skill in resource management. In MoBAs, players are typically given a main attack and three or four abilities including an 'ulitimate' finisher, where combat is all about timing abilities with your teammates in order to take down an opponent. Having the two completely different combat styles marry would be an epic challenge.
In Fractured Space, you are given three weapons: missiles and/or strike craft for long range engagements, a secondary weapon which deals an additional effect and a primary weapon which just deals damage. You are also given a utility, which could be a scanner sweep, cloaking or a healing ability etc. Missiles are usually given a maximum range of 25kms or so, while your primary and secondary weapons usually have a maxiumum effective range of around 17 kms. The developers have done well to marry the two combat styles in this respect.
However, because of the king of the hill objectives, most if not all combat occurs at close quarters and with primary weapons, and this is where the combat falls flat on its face. In a space sim, close combat is all about resource management. It is about choosing a side of your ship (top, bottom, port, starbord, bow or stern) to sacrifice, and then managing your shield strength and power to engines, shields and weapons in order to out-survive the opponent that you hopefully weakened during the long range phase of the engagement. Fractured Space has none of this.
Some ships are given specific weaknesses, such as an unarmored broadside or weapons that only fire forward from the bow. Although each ship has different shields protecting each quadrant, and each quadrant is seperately armored, the player has no control over power or shield management. While in a typical space sim, one player attempts to force an opponent to dedicate all their shield power to one quadrant while their fleetmates attempt to encircle the target and exploit quadrants that are left unprotected and vulnerable, because Fractured Space has no shield management battles inevitably turn into 2 or three teammates simply hammering a single quadrant into oblivion, with little to no thought about stratergy.
Turning your ship so the vulnerable side is no-longer exposed is a viable tactic, but a lack of shield management means you simply do-not have enough time to turn your ship, because your shields are already gone and there is simply no point. Most close-quarters combat involves brute force rather than tactics.
In this game, I say 'team' rather than 'fleet' for a reason; once you're in the game, it doesn't feel like a space sim because the immersion factor simply isn't there. Each ship is a capital ship, a few thousand meters long, but each structure and NPC in the game also appears to be a few thousand meters long, which destroys the illusion of scale. Because all combat is close quarters, it simply doesn't feel like you're commanding a giant ship.
This game could be improved with the addition of minions like small figates that battle it out, reviving the sense of scale. It could be improved again by ignoring the friction between ship modification and drafting, and unleashing the space sim.
For what it's worth, the game has serious potential, but will only be a great game if the developers stop trying to force a space sim and MoBA to marry, and simply allow all elements of each genre to exist at the same time.

I understand why people like this game, but I respectfully disagree and do not think it was worth my time playing it. Given the predictability of the story and the ridiculously easy point and click puzzles, I would say that this game is far too childish for me. The main selling point of this game seems to be that it will make you cry - it didn't make me cry. The game tries too hard to make you sad, and it comes off as far too contrived.
Pros:
- This 'game' is basically an interactive movie. This isn't a bad thing - it's something different to what we're used to and the focus is on the story and characters rather than gameplay. This is fine.
- Really good character development. You get very attached to each of the characters, and you genuinely start to care about the characters in the story.
Cons:
- The story is very linear. Despite the choices you make, you will always get the same ending.
- I found the story very predictable. I wasn't surpised at all by any of the 'plot twists'. You basically know how things will end at the beginning of the fifth chapter.
- The game tries too hard to give you a gut-wrenching story, and it actually made me lose interest - I didn't care. I often get emotional playing games/reading books/watching TV shows, but this game didn't make me feel sad at all. It just felt like it was trying too hard, and I didn't really care about the ending, since I knew it was coming anyway. I was very disappointed by this.
- Due to all of the above, I didn't enjoy the story. Since this is a story-based game, I didn't enjoy the game as a whole.
- Too many QTEs. I absolutely hate having to mash buttons - and this game makes you do it regularly.
- The dialogue is completely unskippable. Whilst I understand this is a dialogue-driven game, the player may still wish to skip dialogue if they're replaying a section. The fact that they've made dialogue-skipping impossible completely kills the replayability value of this game for me.
- The gameplay itself is essentially point and click. Whilst I love point and click, this is by far the easiest point and click I've ever played. The solutions are always painfully obvious, to the point that a 5 year old could figure it out.

Before I start my review, I am a huge Terraria fan. I moved to Linux and unfortunately that made Terraria unplayable. Starbound is currently the only alternative at this point. For those looking for a Terraria alternative or for those who wanted better content, Starbound is supposed to fill that void. I bought the game as soon as it was released as early access. At first there was barely enough content to make the game enjoyable. Frustrated I went back and forth whenever I felt like playing until two years later I came back to find a major update in which made the game a lot more enjoyable than before. However it still took a significant amount of time to get to this point. As a recommendation I would wait until the game is finished.
Comparing the current version with Terraria there are significant issues that does not make it as enjoyable as of yet.
Difficulty:
As much as some people complain about the game being hard, it is way too easy in terms of monsters. There are no raids, monsters are easy to kite and crafting armors are simple. Bosses may be hard for most people but health regen items are rediculously simple to craft. The quests can be quite long or nearly impossible in terms of the treasure hunting quests like finding a certain decoration in a dungeon. There was a removal of the hunger system which more or less an annoyance than a challenge but I would think it will return in the full game. There is an implimentation of a enviromental suit system, essentially gaining immunity to dangerous enviroments such as freezing to death, I enjoyed the concept in Terraria in which night time monsters were significantly stronger. I feel that as the player, I should always feel oppressed like I did in Terrarria, especially with the concept of the growth that would eventually take over.
Farming:
Currently farming and the time it takes to grow plants is very quick, which will probably be changed in the future. I would appreciate more of an empasis on hunger in the future.
Bosses:
The bosses I have fought are alright but not as impressive as Terraria. For most of them I have beaten after a few tries but again with the easy accessibility of healing items, makes boss fights easy.
Building/Items:
More or less the same as Terraria minus the concepts of future doors and switches. I would like to see elevators and more useable items.
NPCs:
This is what really made Terraria special was building your house to house necessary NPCs. Starbound is based on a centralized idea in which you can goto any gate and find the NPCs. I like the centralized idea however it does take away from the requirement of building a home.
Ship:
I love the idea of personalized ship however it does take away from the reason for having a house on a planet. Of course it will be the players choice to stay on their ship forever, the hunger system would prevent that.
Wire:
It is good that the wire system will be an important part of the game. Obviously having switches and traps would be a upgrade from Terrarria. Possibly having a stored pin code for keypads.
Tech:
Very interesting techologies that enhance players mobility and survivability.
What I want to see:
Difficulty, difficulty, difficulty. I am alluring to idle situations such as hiding inside your house and zombies breaking the doors to get in. Instatiable hunger and constantly being challenged, perhaps space pirates hunting you unless you pay them to stop. The only dangerous enviroment I have found was the meteor showers in which was impossible to inhabit due to metors destroying blocks.
Traps, I loved traps in Terraria. I would always hoard spear traps and set them on a 1 second timer.
Storage:
I am still waiting for a medical storage facility. Like the fridge for food and the mining chest for ores.
Shield generators:
I was surprised that unharvestable blocks was introduced due to the shield generator blocking its power. I would like to see more of this due to the amount of hoarding and collecting I do.
Multiplayer:
I just hope it will be extremely easy and simple to connect to friends

Hands down the best software for multi monitors. Nvidia Surround and AMD Eyefinity essentially tell Windows and other programs that the 3 monitors form a single screen; while this is a basis for displaying an image of a game on all 3 screens at the same time, this also means that if you want, like me, to display a different wallpaper on each monitor, you can't with Windows (or you can if you create the wallpaper in PS by pasting each wallpaper next to each other). DisplayFusion can "cut" the desktop area into any kind of shape; my 5760*1080 area has been cut into three separate 1920*1080 areas, each displaying a random wallpaper from a folder, rotating every 5 minutes. Simply magic. Add to this the task bar controls, the triggers, and you simply have a must have software.

I can see it was at least inspired by GTR2, as it shares a lot of design choices. But it just falls short when compared.
There are 4 different cars in the entire game, each with 2 different liveries. But they all feel the same.
there are also 6 different tracks in the entire game, each with it's own feel to them. Nothing bad to say here.
Options have been made well, there's a lot to change, controls, audio, display, and also difficulty of the game and rules of the races.
And then there's the driving physics. None of these cars have ever spun on me, even with every driving assist off. They just feel as if they were FWD, is that supposed to be that way? Other than that, clutch works, brakes do lock, and You do lose control in certain situations, but it's way too easy.
Same goes to the rival AI, once passed they do nothing to get their position back, and even before You pass them they seem like they were just moving obstacles on the road.
Graphics are... not that bad actually, the contrast etc is fairly well balanced, but everything else is just not there. True, there are working real-time shadows of the cars and the track but... that's it. No real-time car reflections, they're just reflecting the skybox (which isn't any good either, just about 20 small clouds on the sky), no motion blur, no depth of field, nothing! It's the middle of 2015, what were you thinking?
Sound is nice, You can hear everything happening around You, Cars do sound a little different but that's it, nothing spectacular again.
Long review short, it's an average game when compared to other racing "simulators" out there, but from what I've seen, it's a good way to get into "arcade-simulator racing" as I call it. There aren't many cars to master, and they all feel the same so it's not a huge hop to change a car, the tracks aren't too hard to master, the AI isn't too hard and unforgiving, etc etc.
So if You're new to the simulator genre, have an old computer which can't run modern games and a steering wheel do get it. It's for free so You can find out if You're going to like simulator racing or not. But if You do, please do get GTR2 and find some mods for it because that is the best way to get into "hardcore simulator racing". It's from 2005 so Your PC will run it, and it has a damn well written physics engine.

Its Early Access but apart from a single bug which just seemed like a graphical glitch this game feels complete even more so than a lot of other released games from certain publishing houses. Its got the full support from Wargaming so its not going to vanish and is certainly worth the money.
If you are looking for something that hits the sweet spot with being just the right mix of challenge and relaxation without ever feeling stressed or too challenged then this is it. I built the 'Titan' battleship and it got destroyed by six enemy cruisers so I built ten cruisers and carried on stomping the enemy into the ground without having to reload or pull hair out. Something goes bang.......just build another one.
There is a 'tactical' element to the game but at the minute it seems more just who has the biggest gun/guns wins. Its all relative to size and numbers as I mentioned earlier 5 cruisers can kill a Titan but it also depends on their tech level and you can use different abilities in battle but if you like you can just sit back and let the A.I do the work.
The game almost sits happily between the adult and child audience that it is no doubt targeted at but there are a notable few things that do seem more child friendly than adult and if you are looking for a hardcore space strategy simulation or even civiliazation in the stars then this will probably not quite be what you are hoping for but it is probably the closest thing to it and who knows where it might develop.
Would i recommend you buy this game right now; Yes. It feels complete even though you know when playing through it that there are certain element missing none of it detracts from the game experience.
Running everything on max in 1080p with all civilizations and the largest galaxy I would guess that everytime I hit the end turn key it was my go again in less than 5 seconds and that was still almost the same after 300+ turns
One word of caution though; it does at times to me feel sometimes overly simple and not as indepth as it could be but then again by the time of the final release it may feel deep and complex.

Realm of the Mad God is an awesome 8 bit game, It is a massive dungeon crawl/top down shooter. The character sprites really remind me of my favorite web comic 8bit theater. You run around as one of many classes pretty much killing mobs to get from one boss to another. Just killing things around another player gives you both experience. I played the game prior to playing it on steam it was cool then, it is cool now. Groups of players get together and run trains. Which is where a player follows one or more players The result is usually a line of characters. It is really addictively fun and I look forward to playing it again from a brand new account.
If you need a story, linear game, or require a realistic graphics experience you won't like this game. I
If you remember the hours of playing different nintendo games and miss the 8bit graphics, simplistic but challenging gameplay where the best way to win is to follow players around. You should check it out.
Oh and if you are one of the growing minority of gamers that absolutely hate all microtransactions, and the idea that a game developer and publisher has the right to make money off a game they spent time making. This game is made for co-op play and has no pvp. So even if you buy the items everyone that follows you and survives benefits from it if you beat the Mad God.  So everybody wins anyway.
10/10 Will challenge the Mad God again.

One of my favorite games of all time.
The story is like something that Philip K♥♥♥♥♥♥would write if he worked for Disney - it tells a kids story without being overly simplistic, and leaves enough to the imagination that it doesn't bog down into pages and pages of diaries and♥♥♥♥♥♥like in many full fledged RPGs.
The gameplay is a perfect Action RPG mix - it's also infinitely variable, from a mode where you can continue as much as you like, to tweaks that alter various aspects of the difficulty - emeny speed, damage etc. This proves to be the perfect antidote to the standard RPG issue of becoming overpowered by the end once you unlock all the weapons.
The soundtrack is something that deserves a listen to in its own right. The voice acting is a constant narration which fills in the story, while also commenting on your in game choices - a nice touch.
All of this complements the amazing artwork to create a fantasy world I would actually want to live in.
Although it may not have the deepest, most elaborate story, or the most replay value, Bastion is the perfect example of what indie games can be, of the magic that can happen when even a smallish budget is put into making so many brilliant parts that fit together to make a magnificent whole.
If you're any sort of action-RPG fan, you should definitely give this a try.

All elements needed to create an amazing experience are here.
The story follows a silent protaganist seeking to fix the "Bastion" the last refuge of his people. Overall, the game never lets up with it's lore and narration woven directly into the gameplay. Cinematics are cut down to very small scenes, but you always know what's going on. It's nearly perfect in it's delivery.
Gameplay is fantastic, nothing is wasted, and there isn't any filler between missions that break the flow of the game. A variety of 9 weapons are available, some ranged and others melee. They come in all different shapes, sizes, and uses, with mechanics to each being completely different. You can take up to 2 weapons with you on missions, as well as an additional "power" that you can further spice up the variety of your combat with. You will also always be able to dodge, and also block using your trusty shield.
The ambient, music, and combat sounds are perfect for the tone of the game, with the voice acting being very well done as well. The narrator may sound like something you'll hate, but it could arguably be the most important part of the game.
Overall the game is a must play, and I recommend buying it as soon as possible.

Half-life was the first game that I properly remember playing. It was given to me by a friend when I was in Grade 5 and I remember playing until the first part of 'Residue Processing'. By that time, holidays were over and my friend had entered the Xen world and I was full of awe when I saw him playing in a low-gravity world with alien weapons. I decided to return back to Half-life. But alas, I had to move houses and with the passage of time and age, I somehow forgot to continue playing Half-life.
Then surprise surprise I saw the half-life pack on a steam sale. No second questions were asked and I immediately bought the pack. I had to finish this game. With its outdated graphics and linear gameplay, I wouldn't be surprised if people thought Minecraft 'looked' better than Half-life. But let me tell you, there is no other game (aside from Half-life 2) that could even come close to the brilliance of its gameplay. The storyline and the gameplay itself is revolutionary and not many games today can even compare to the shooter known as Half-life.
I shall always remember today (15th August 2016) as the day that I finally finished the original Half-life after 14 years. Thank you Valve for making the game that introduced me to the world of gaming.
I can finally sleep in peace before I move onto another masterpiece known as Half-life 2.

Neon lights flashing, retro synthwave pumping, metal screaming. Pure intense mayhem. Brigador is an excellent isometric vehicular shooting game that brings the genre back, it is very similar to Bedlam and Bedlam 2: Absolute Bedlam from the '90s, and if those aren't familiar then let's say it's like the original Syndicate, but with mechs, tanks and hovercars.
A wide variety of freelance missions, that you can take on with a wide variety of destructive weaponry custom picked onto your vehicle of choice. Campaign missions are where you can try out a lot of pre-made vehicles with drivers that have their own styles of approaching the battlefield.
Gameplay is straight to the point, move through the destructible environments, the more you destroy the better, engage enemies either directly at the range of your weaponry, or use special abilities and equipment to flank them via stealth, there's a nice amount of playstyle variance. You and the enemies have more armor in the front, so flanking is good and so is keeping the enemy from flanking you. A bunch of different control schemes for you to find the most suitable, be it with keyboard+mouse or with a controller. You can also freely change the game speed to anywhere between 50% to 100%, so that acts as a difficulty slider, or simply putting the tempo of the action to what you find most comfortable. A neat feature.
There's a lot to love in this game, the only thing missing is a multiplayer mode, this would be an absolute blast with at least a 2-player co-op mode. Maybe if there's a sequel we'll get that.

I've seen a bunch of negative reviews for this game...
I do not know if you have VERY poorly running PCs, a version of Windows that runs this badly, or got a snagged file or three in your downloads, but this game looks pretty awesome for what it is, has zero popup, & zero drawin EVER... (something those retro games the negative reviews say this game is not like, but this is far superior to in all the ways that I care about)
Do yourself a favor, & set the launchers' graphics to low, but the highest rez possible, high has so much blurring that it not only eats framerate, it looks awful, & I got the feeling that I needed glasses all of the sudden on high, yeah it's THAT blurry, on low the textures look okay enough, & as I said there's no visual artifacts like stuff suddenly popping into the distant view, or texture drawins...
As for the handling? Well if you fancy yourself as a hip Rallycross player, turn sensitivity down (unless it's too low straight off, Mine defaulted max), & turn the deadzone ALL the way down... this even makes the cars pull to the side a tiny bit when they shift gears, JUST like cars do on real loose surfaces like gravel/sand.
If you fancy yourself as a casual rally player leave sensitivity maxed, & put deadzone 1, or 2 from the lowest setting, this negates the cars pulling to the side when they shift (except in the VERY odd circulstance when you're shifting, & jumping/cresting in 1st-3rd gears, & when that does happen don't hit a tree)
If you aren't quite sure exactly what the meaning of the word fancy is... go play NFS yah Yankee! No seriously then you can turn deadzone up really high, which makes the game play/run so smoooth, it almost looks like it's getting a better framerate (the camera is just jerking about less).
The tracks in the game all play/look JUST like real rally tracks should (yes up very close SOME of the many kinds of trees, & about 1/2 of the bushes seem to have fuzzy textures (on low, I don't play on high it gave Me motion sickness!), but you spend 99% of your time near the middle of the road, & in high rez that looks pretty darn good, & no popins (Marry?), the turns/hills/etc. are done VERY well (the 1st Championship is VERY easy, straight, & even bland looking tracks, keep playing m'kaaaaaay)
The physics in the game? I dunno if peoples Phys-X/Active-X is flarmed up, or they have other issues, but they're dead on except for the fact that the car pivots on an axis like a top, but devs do this because they may look odd from a 3rd person view, from inside the car [more on that...] it "feels" more like a car traversing a loosly surfaced plane. so if you use 2 of the 3 views you'll prob have zero objections to the physics, from the follow the car view it looks pretty artificial turning, drifting etc. {*note to devs* A tighter tail camera clears this up a bit}
The game has 3 views... the follow the car view, which is like any other game has, the hood view (bonnet) which lots of even modern games don't bother drawing the dang hood on, this does, & it damages in real time, & the inside car view (cockpit), which is like other games except this oddly has the body of the driver, & steering wheel gone, so it feels a little wierd at 1st, but works well, & once you start focusing on the road/navigator... Myself as with almost all racing games am very happy with this games hood view
I haven't beaten the game yet, so I cannot speak to bugs/glitches in later cars/tracks, but with like 28% unlocked (2 cars, & bunch'a tracks/variations) I haven't experienced any launch/play/control glitches Myself.
I also think those people surely must not have actually spent much time playing 1st gen Rally games, or even PS1 Colin McRae, because everything in this game is superior to that game for sure. No splitscreen, no multiplayer, boo hooooooo! Then you hotseat with your friends, taking turns, & noting the times... That's how We did it on LOTS of older games that lacked even splitscreen, so the store claiming this to be retro goodness is 100% correct! (No sorry no demo derby, tag, soccer, or any of the other goofy modes you guys are spoiled with now in other recent rally games)
If you have tons of cash, a monster PC, & want the worlds bestest rally experience, then Steam has about 5 better ones, BUT if you're stuck using a slow/cruddy PC like I am (for awhile *sigh*), & Like rally games, or racing in general... $7 bucks ain't to much to ask, & if it's on sale? (I just got Mine for like $1.60 I think) then it's well worth it!
Note I'm using Windows 8.1 which has trouble running some stuff, AND a very slow, cheap laptop... if My PC will run this game, yours should too! Using X360 for Win pad (works great)

One of the few near flawless games ever made, Half Life admitedly does have some frustrating and rather dated niggles, which I'll bring up before anything else. The platforming is actually quite bad. It never works that well in first person unless climbing mechanics are made entirely contextual. In Half Life, of course, nothing is contextual and you are in complete control of Freeman at all times. When the numerous platforming sections come around, though, the game feels extremely sensitive and you are expected to jump and land onto some really ridiculously narrow platforms to progress. It becomes a real exercise in frustration, and trial and error is often the only way of knowing whether or not Freeman will land on the platform or fall right to his doom. I guess the creation of such an impressive physics engine means that the developers will make it their civic duty to show it off as much of it as feasible in the game. It's just that Valve took a little too much liberty in showing it off in Half Life.
As I've said before, Half Life is a near flawless game, let down only by it's jumping sections. Ignoring those, and you should, this is one of the very best FPSs ever made, possibly THE greatest FPS game ever made. It's ridiculously good. The worldbuilding is astonishingly lifelike, the aliens quirky and instantly iconic thanks to their imaginative designs, the weapon selection is marvellous and transformed the straightforward crowbar into a symbol of gaming culture and the story is one of the strongest in gaming. Seriously, the feeling of being part of a grand conspiracy far greater than your own understanding, together with being the unwitting hero tasked to save the world from an alien invasion and travelling through the chaos happening all around you makes for a rip-roaring roller coaster of a game that never gets boring or repetitive, well, ever really.
Gunplay is appropriately meaty and cathartic, yet with an added sense of realism that you didn't find with other FPS classics like Quake and Doom. I rate this game better than Half Life 2, on the grounds that the gameplay is just as good but the story can be treated as one holistic story rather than the mere beginnings of a grander story planned to be told in something like, say, erm a TRILOGY. Yeah it basically boils down to Half Life 1 not ending on a cliffhanger which will likely never be resolved, as it's sequel did.
So yeah, buy Half Life if you haven't already, experience one of the few games that can truly be called a 'Citizen Kane of Gaming' and don't read THAT much into the greater plot going on. That way, you can feel wholly satisfied with everything this amazing game offers and not go mad waiting for the final chapter to be released sometime in the next 3000 years.

First of all before i start i just want to congratulate ConcernedApe for making a wonderfull game and also that he made it all by himself with no help at all. Not many people can do this these days. Alright let's start this review. i've only played this game for 29 hours (at the time i wrote this review) and i'm still pretty noob at it but i have done a lot of research to the game even months before i got it (thanks DangerouslyFunny, GameSharkHD and ThatDenverGuy for that) and i have 9 days till year 2 it so i feel comfortable making this review (will update it when i get more advanced and further into the game) ok let's start this review (this is only my second review on a game so don't hate on me if it's bad or not the best)
Introduction:
Stardew Valley is primarily a farming simulator but there's a lot more to it than just that and you never run out of things to do. You can mine up to level 120 in the mines and go endlessly in skull cavern, you can fish to your hearts content and you can make friendships with people and find that special soul mate and have a family. Not only do you farm but you farm in seasons and you can own animals (pigs are OP btw) you also do quests for people and earn money and friendship points from those quests. you also clear up your farm and get resources and upgrade your tools to make your farm better and earn more money. now probably the best thing from the game is the Community Centre and finishing the bundles to fix the rooms and eventually the centre it self which is a very satisfying to accomplish and i can't wait till i do it.
My own thoughts on the game:
I find this game very relaxing, peaceful and enjoyable to play (i've played it for 6 hours straight 2 times and didn't even realise it) it is also very addicting, you keep telling yourself "just one more tree, Just one more day, Just one more crop" and then you realise that you did a lot more than just "one more." Stardew Valley is also a very immersive game and the people in the game all give you different emotions. Pam gives you fear (and for most people i think so she gives fear to them to) Mayor Lewis gives you comfort. Abigail (for me and a lot of other people) gives you love and i'm also at 8 hearts with her atm so i'm hyped, Linus gives you sorrow and Abigail (for me and a lot of other people) gives you love and i'm also at 8 hearts with her atm so i'm hyped . Also i like the 16-Bit style of the game and i feel at home with the people of pelican town and i don't feel like an outsider. I have 210k ish gold in my wallet and i've made about 300k gold in total and it's satisfying to watch your money grow from nothing to something. There are also Festivals and Events that happen which are nice to attend and experience.
How you feel in the beggining of the game vs how you feel later: (at least for me)
In the beggining of the game when you only have 500 gold, 15 parsnips, no resources and a whole farm to clear up you feel like you just want to quit and refund the game. but after you played the game for a few days (ingame) you realise how satisfying it is to make progress and also how addicting the game actually is which is what makes you want to keep going and progress your farm and progress your character and progress the game. after your first sesson of spring you go into summer and the fun continues and you also realise how it feels to be part of a community (even though it's a virtual one)  and from there it goes to fall where you have made enough progress to go "Hey that's pretty good" (no meme intended) and in winter you rest... from farming. You continue to mine, chop wood and fish to make money and get resources for the next year which i am hyped to play.

I received this game as part of a bundle and this review is not a comment on the list price of the game.

This is the type of game I would have loved as a kid, and I found myself engaged and intrigued by it playing it now. I have always loved mech games, and this game manages to brilliantly avoid the "same-iness" of some mech games by creating three distinct classes of mechs, mech, tank, hovercraft. The game does a great job in creating a sense of weight to your mechs, allowing you to crush a hilarious number of cars and civilians in early stages before introducing you to the mech vs mech combat that is the core of the gameplay.

Unlike many indie games that have some novelty but no real depth in gameplay, or too much depth and no sense of novelty, this game brings you in softly and makes it feel like you are getting a better sense of the combat in the game without getting overwhelmed.

NOTE: I found the game MUCH more enjoyable after remapping a few keys. While the game does support controller, I could not find settings that would let the right analog aim in the right position quickly enough. It is much better with mouse+keyboard, but I personally remapped the special weapon from middle mouse to Q. This configuration REALLY helped me not get so frustrated. I still kinda dislike having primary and alternate as left+right click, since so often you want to be holding down both simultaneously and I don't find that very comfortable.

People are dismissing this as shallow, but it seems to be a misplaced judgement.  Even as an early access game, this 4X has far more depth than many recent games had at launch (cough GalCiv3).
For example:
-Multiple ways of invading/destroying planets.  Drown them in chemical weapons to kill off the population while leaving the infrastructure intact (but taking a big diplo hit).  Spend years nuking them from orbit until the planet is a polluted, irraddiated mess, then move in to clean up and terraform things back to habitabal.  Launch a good old fashioned infantry invasion, involving marines of different levels, tanks and mechs.  Or for the galactic conquerer on the go, simply erase the planet from existence with late-game planet-exploding tech.
-Customize your ships with more than just weapons and armour.  The biggest range of options comes not from the weapons, but from the utility/support modules that can be researched and fitted.  From active black-hole generators, SC2 Stalker-like blinks, missile retargetting and all kinds of countermeasures, your ship designs are just as much about your style of fighting as they are about how hard you hit.
-Think the starlanes are lame?  You don't even need to get half way through the tech tree to unlock warpgates, allowing you to make your own starlanes between colonies.  Combined with late-game engine tech, and the appearance of wormholes in the galaxy, mobilizing your fleets really isn't the painful process some people think after a brief early-game play.
- Someone complained that you can't transport food between planets?  Wrong.  Just need the tech unlocked (again, pre-mid game).  It'll also let you transport production, letting you focus late-game production at key planets (for when you want to start spamming those Titans or Death Stars).  Oh, and you can send population around from turn 1.  Did I mention population is tracked by race, and different races can be assimilated into your planets, complete with their racial perks?  What casual unfaithful nonsense!
On top of the depth that's already here, there's more promised to land before launch - and based on how much of this promised content is already heavily referred to across the game (such as in the tech tree), it seems pretty likely that these guys are on it.
Another thing I've seen people slate the game for: no ship bording.  Lemme quote an item off the tech tree called "Marine Pods" (under Advanced Tactics):
"Marine Pods house additional detachments of space marines, increasing the number of Marines on board a ship.  The additional marines both defend the ship and can board enemy ships."

As a new player, I'm very surprised by just how fun the core gameplay of Fractured Space is. For most games still in development the gameplay can feel thin, and not entirely fleshed out. For most free-to-play games the gameplay is typically frontloaded, quickly wearing thin while keeping what made the beginning hours of the game fun behind a paywall, Now, for Fractured Space to be both these things and still have gameplay that feels rich, complex, and engaging well beyond the 30 hour mark is a significant achievement, and has me very excited to see where this game will go. I will admit that there are a number of bugs. Crashes are common when joining a match, though matches are long enough for you to rejoin without losing much of an advantage. The tutorial could also be significantly more fleshed out. I felt important concepts like armor, point defense, damage vulnerability while jumping, gamma, and upgrades weren't explained enough. I know that over time the bugs will be patched and hopefully they expand the tutorial maybe into a kind of singleplayer intro campaign where it introduces new concepts to the player a few at a time and gives some rewards for completing levels. Despite some of the problems that make getting into the game kind of hard, I am very glad I stuck through with it because once you get what is going on the game feels at once action-packed and fast-paced yet slow, tactical, and complex. Definitely worth a look if you want a new free game to pick up. It definitely deserves more attention than it has gotten.
tl;dr: Game is fun, has some problems with explaining how stuff works and bugs, but sticking through with it is most definitely worth the early hassle. Excited to see where it will go in the future.

I ♥♥♥♥ing hate this game. Never before has a videogame made me so ♥♥♥♥ing miserable. It's an unfair piece of crap that takes away your agency by placing your survival on the hands of RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that's clearly rigged to favour the enemies. I have a tattoo of it and keep coming back for more.
Almost everything about this game is great. The setting is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. It's not just based on Lovecraft's work, it really gets it. The writers were able to perfectly translate the themes covered in his writing into the game, weaving it seamlessly with the mechanics. Due to the RNG based mechanics, no matter how good you get, no matter how prepared you are, no matter how well rounded your party is, things still can, and do, go wrong. You lose characters through no fault of your own. You are not in control. And while this may sound like a fault to some, isn't that what Lovecraft is all about? This is not to say, however, that you are at the complete mercy of the game. As you play, you will learn which party compositions are more effective, you will learn which characters are better suited for each situation, you will learn what's the best course of action for each battle. You can minimise the consequences of the RNG, its presence jusr guarantess that you are never perfectly safe.
The art is simply perfect. I even, as I said, got a tattoo of it (the Occultist, in case you're wondering). I remember the first time I entered the Warrens, and how I ♥♥♥♥ing hated these pigs the moment I laid eyes on them. They are disgusting, abominations that could only be brought to this world by a mind twisted with the desire of power. It's very visceral, and it couples brilliantly with the writing.
The sound, of course, doesn't lag behind. First thing I need to mention is Wayne June. Everything that comes out of the narrator's mouth is pure gold. He has a deep, raspy voice that creates a sense of gravitas. You will find yourself not just saying his lines with him, but remembering them during your day. A lot of the sound effects are great at conveying what the attacks do. And the music, despite not calling attention to itself, is very atmospheric.
The problems are mostly in the DLC. While the Crimson Court brought about amazing enemies and a very interesting interpretation of vampires, it gets very annoying to see all dungeons overrun with bloody mosquitoes. The Crimson Curse further takes away your agency, and the benefits it gives are not enough to make it worthwhile having a cursed hero. The Shiledbreaker, while a nice character, brought stealth as a mechanic, and I felt it didn't match well with the rest of the game. Her restrictions on camping also make her a character with limited use.
In summary, Darkest Dungeon is a great game. It's absolutely worth playing, easily one of my favorite games ever. It shows how strong the indie gaming scene is, and how a small team can bring about absolutely fantastic works.

Dayz is a great, open-world zombie survival mod. Its derived from Arma 2, which is also a very good game by itself. Dayz takes place in a large 225 km2 map, big enough to get lost and die of starvation. The game heavily relys on realistic survival elements, even being able to navigate with constellations and clouds. The game includes weapons to defend yourself, several methods of travelling - usually requiring fuel. Despite the name, zombies are only the real threat early on, and suriving them late in the game is easy by themselves. However, firefights with other players can quickly draw in mobs of them and they add a new layer to defending yourself. The vanilla DayZ mod itself has limitless replayability, and yet there is plenty of mods for the Dayz mod that add even more features, like base building and NPC's. I recommend this to anyone who enjoys apocalyptic genres, survival games, first/third person shooters, RPG's, and M.M.O. games. There is something here for everyone, and IMO this is the best game I have ever played.

Half-life was the first game that I properly remember playing. It was given to me by a friend when I was in Grade 5 and I remember playing until the first part of 'Residue Processing'. By that time, holidays were over and my friend had entered the Xen world and I was full of awe when I saw him playing in a low-gravity world with alien weapons. I decided to return back to Half-life. But alas, I had to move houses and with the passage of time and age, I somehow forgot to continue playing Half-life.
Then surprise surprise I saw the half-life pack on a steam sale. No second questions were asked and I immediately bought the pack. I had to finish this game. With its outdated graphics and linear gameplay, I wouldn't be surprised if people thought Minecraft 'looked' better than Half-life. But let me tell you, there is no other game (aside from Half-life 2) that could even come close to the brilliance of its gameplay. The storyline and the gameplay itself is revolutionary and not many games today can even compare to the shooter known as Half-life.
I shall always remember today (15th August 2016) as the day that I finally finished the original Half-life after 14 years. Thank you Valve for making the game that introduced me to the world of gaming.
I can finally sleep in peace before I move onto another masterpiece known as Half-life 2.

I got this game in the Humble Monthly Bundle and man was it a great little surprise when I actually took the time to try it out.
I'd like to call it a tactical isometric roguelike shoot'em up. While you control a single vehicle it kind of reminds me of Syndicate. Everything is destructible and this also plays into how you tackle opponents.
There are basically two modes; campaign and freelance. I haven't finished the whole campaign yet but missions so far have been varied and sometimes challenging. After the tutorial you can choose between three differents characters/vehicles which makes a large difference in many missions. The mission briefings also add background and builds up the dystopically satiric world of Solo Nombre through decent writing.
Freelance is the other mode which pretty much offers infinite replayability. There are a tons of unlockable weapons, missions, pilots and vehicles. These are unlocked by clearing either freelance or campaign missions for cash.
What makes the game actually great though is the actual gameplay and I find it hard to come up with anything to complain about. Controls are crisp, and vehicles actually handles very differently. Most weapons are immensely satisfying to use with great SFX and animations, and different loadouts excel at different tactics. Tying in to this is the destructible environments. Instead of rushing the enemy straight on you could for example make your own path, come in from behind and make a killshot to their vulnerable rear. You can also use smoke or cloaking to avoid enemies or combine it all with luring enemies with sound to set a trap.
When it comes to the art style I like it a lot. I would say it reminds me of old Amiga sci-fi/cyberpunk games. Pilot portraits are great with a zany quality and vehicle design is overall very good. The environments look like dystopian cyberpunk environments and serve their purpose of being levelled to the ground.
In closing I'd say that this game is a real little gem. It's perfect for picking up and playing for a short while if you feel that shooting itch most of us feel from time to time, but it also works for longer sessions, some of the freelance campaigns can take a couple of hours and you can't save in the middle of them which is a small negative. All in all, I'd say you have nothing to lose in Solo Nombre.

One of the few near flawless games ever made, Half Life admitedly does have some frustrating and rather dated niggles, which I'll bring up before anything else. The platforming is actually quite bad. It never works that well in first person unless climbing mechanics are made entirely contextual. In Half Life, of course, nothing is contextual and you are in complete control of Freeman at all times. When the numerous platforming sections come around, though, the game feels extremely sensitive and you are expected to jump and land onto some really ridiculously narrow platforms to progress. It becomes a real exercise in frustration, and trial and error is often the only way of knowing whether or not Freeman will land on the platform or fall right to his doom. I guess the creation of such an impressive physics engine means that the developers will make it their civic duty to show it off as much of it as feasible in the game. It's just that Valve took a little too much liberty in showing it off in Half Life.
As I've said before, Half Life is a near flawless game, let down only by it's jumping sections. Ignoring those, and you should, this is one of the very best FPSs ever made, possibly THE greatest FPS game ever made. It's ridiculously good. The worldbuilding is astonishingly lifelike, the aliens quirky and instantly iconic thanks to their imaginative designs, the weapon selection is marvellous and transformed the straightforward crowbar into a symbol of gaming culture and the story is one of the strongest in gaming. Seriously, the feeling of being part of a grand conspiracy far greater than your own understanding, together with being the unwitting hero tasked to save the world from an alien invasion and travelling through the chaos happening all around you makes for a rip-roaring roller coaster of a game that never gets boring or repetitive, well, ever really.
Gunplay is appropriately meaty and cathartic, yet with an added sense of realism that you didn't find with other FPS classics like Quake and Doom. I rate this game better than Half Life 2, on the grounds that the gameplay is just as good but the story can be treated as one holistic story rather than the mere beginnings of a grander story planned to be told in something like, say, erm a TRILOGY. Yeah it basically boils down to Half Life 1 not ending on a cliffhanger which will likely never be resolved, as it's sequel did.
So yeah, buy Half Life if you haven't already, experience one of the few games that can truly be called a 'Citizen Kane of Gaming' and don't read THAT much into the greater plot going on. That way, you can feel wholly satisfied with everything this amazing game offers and not go mad waiting for the final chapter to be released sometime in the next 3000 years.

All content free.

Good tracks

Cons:

Bring this into a next gen engine and Sim drivers will need to clean the white stains off their undershorts.
Thats about it for the cons really.
Titles such as this, for free, and others you can get pretty cheap these days, such as GTR2, the Race series, Rfactor 1 are still very enjoyable, great to drive and extrememly entertaining.
If you are new to simming and looking for titles to cut your teeth before investing more heavily, and you have a half decent FFB wheel, get this. Then go buy Stock Car Extreme.

A few hours in, the game is good and interesting, for now feels like a good alternative to replaying MOO2 all over again. Keep in mind it's still in Early Access, so it's not something I would recommend right away, unless you are a space 4X fan like myself. What I see is a solid product, especially for its price. Production value is of highest standard in space 4X, but I can't say it's of XCOM2 level (which has left all competitors behind).
What's good and new:
- overall feel is good, it's interesting to explore and exterminate and there's clearly 'just one more turn' effect
- controls and UI are overall good and easily understandable and the game seems to be well optimized
- systems have planets now and navigating inside a system takes extra turn, warp points become choke points and allow interesting space control strategies
- bases (something like in GalCiv) in choke points and asteroids, which is fresh and keeps you wanting to research them
- research has interesting choices
Not cool but bearable:
- lacks polish in some elements, for instance, icons and pictograms on research targets look like placeholders: it may look like unimportant detail, but in reality it adds a lot to anticipation of discovery
- customizing your race is not implemented yet: and that was very important part of MOO2
- some things are dumbed down and while some of these are good, like instant and mass upgrades of blueprints and ships in your planets, some are questionable: like fuel tanks / outreach concept is removed
- tactical battles are of the kind you'd rather always skip, designing your own ships is not very helpful as well
TL;DR Not likely to be as memorable as MOO2 or something of ratings higher than 8/10. But it's definitely not as bad as MOO3. When released, new MOO would make an excellent choice for all newcomers to the genre.

Just finished my 200th turn, and decided I've played enough to give some substantial feedback. They game of course is in early access, and several races are not playable at this point as well as some features that are sure to come at a later date. That being said, the game is absolutely playable, no bugs that I have encountered, and is entertaining as it is engrossing.
MOO and others like it are the sort of games that take up HOURS of your life in an eye blink. You are so enveloped in what your are doing that you are eagerly advancing turns to get that colony ship to that prime real estate planet before your neighbor, or rushing that ship to change the tide of war in a contested system.  That is what I want from a game, and so far I have not been disappointed.
The game's workings are fairly easy to understand, there is no tutorial match available (that I was able to access at least) but they game has an abundance of hints. Some things were a bit of a mystery, like worker strikes, but playing long enough provided the explanation needed. It's a straightforward game and unlike MOO3 (which was my favorite, don't judge) its streamlined things to a point where you aren't having to micromanage every aspect of gameplay. I am surprised with how well the game plays so far that it was put into Early Access. Stellaris may have a thing or two to do with that. We are still missing some races as I mentioned above, but other than expanding the map sizes, adding the races, beefing up the tech tree, I don't see much else that needs to be done.
Space combat is pretty much just like MOO3, over in 30 seconds. I don't think it has ever been MOO series strong point. The bombardment screen is really disappointing. I loved MOO3's planetary bombardment, It was visceral and made me feel like "This is genocide, the systematic extermination of all life on Arrakis!" Now it's "bloop" you dropped a bomb, there goes item A, B, or C. That's something I would like see fixed up before leaving Early Access.
Planet management is similar to other 4x titles, but like I said previously, you can fully automate planet management and no micro management required. I picked a large map and was a little miffed at first. It seemed so small, especially compared to MOO3. But as I played it became clear that just 4 or 5 planets is enough to keep you busy. Still, I want 200 plus star system maps like M003 in the future (Huge map size perhaps?)
The AI is fairly predictable, scooping up and taking every available world and stellar object available to them. I would have to play longer to say this isn't the case for all AI, but so far it seems to be. A little more variety would be nice to see, but with Early Access things are going to change. Some variation besides the rush, turtle, and other playstyles would be interesting. Maybe a randomized "arch enemy" that the AI will go after over all else, even if it's on the other side of the map.
I've played Star Ruler, Endless Space, Distant Worlds, Space Empires, Galactic Civ, etc. For me, MOO is the most fun to play and the one game that I believe will manage to keep my interest for longer than a few hours. However, I am eagerly awaiting Stellaris, and that could change things up quite a bit. Masters of Orion has more than just an homage to look and lore of the games previously in the series, it is very much a game of its time. Smooth gameplay, nice graphics, an easy but useful UI, I'd venture to say this game is about as good as a successor to the Master of Orion series as there could be.
TLDR: The game is a solid 8/10 even in Early Access. With the collector's Edition it's worth its 50 dollar price.
UPDATE: Finished a playthrough. Dissappointed by the 500 turn limit, wanted to see more of the tech tree than I did. I only ever lost one battle, and its because I didn't simulate it when I probably should have. AI needs to up its game. If I could tell the developers one thing it would be this: Expand on everything. More detail, more ship templates, more systems, more more more.
